b: HotStuff — PODC 2019 Maofan Yin, Dahlia Malkhi, Michael K. Reiter, Guy Golan Gueta, Ittai Abraham. HotStuff: BFT Consensus with Linearity and Responsiveness. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331591. Formalized version: arXiv 1803.05069 v6 (23 Jul 2019, the full version of the PODC paper, titled "HotStuff: BFT Consensus in the Lens of Blockchain"); numbering follows it. The replica code of Algorithm 3 is the same in v4 (Apr 2019), v5 (Jun 2019) and v6. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Safety survives: Basic HotStuff is safe as claimed, with a new proof of Theorem 2, and Chained HotStuff is safe for every n > 3f once Algorithm 3, which as printed lets a correct replica commit two conflicting nodes, gets the check b*.height = curView. Progress under a correct leader and synchronized views (Theorem 4) holds, proved for a partially synchronous implementation, but liveness of the whole protocol is lost: the doubling pacemaker of §4.4 does not give T_f overlap, and we proved no working pacemaker. The linear authenticator complexity, the paper's other main claim, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ §4.4 (pacemaker: "eventually at least T_f overlap") The claim that doubling the timeout intervals eventually gives all correct replicas T_f overlap is false: two replicas can share every view for exactly α < T_f time units forever (HotStuff.Pacemaker.overlap_constant). Impact. No liveness is established for the protocol as a whole: Theorem 4 is conditional and correct, but we proved no working pacemaker. This is the view-synchronization gap; Algorithm 5 later just assumes "synchronized leadership after GST". Details. Suppose a Byzantine leader sends decide only to replica A at time α. Then A enters view 2 with interval α, while B times out at the same moment with interval 2α. From then on the two replicas share every view for exactly α time units, forever. With α < T_f and n = 4 (one silent Byzantine), no later view decides. The Lean theorem covers the timer arithmetic only. 🔧 Theorem 5 (Chained HotStuff safety, Algorithm 3) Algorithm 3 as written is unsafe: with n = 4, f = 1, round-robin leaders and a synchronous execution, a correct replica commits two conflicting nodes (HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_false_roundRobin). Impact. The printed pseudocode is unsafe, but the intended protocol is safe: adding the check b*.height = curView restores Theorem 5 for every n > 3f. Basic HotStuff (Theorems 2 and 4) is not affected. Details. Round-robin leaders leader(v) = v mod 4; Byzantine replica 2 leads only views 2, 6 and 10. All correct replicas process every proposal. Correct leaders build their proposals with createLeaf, so height equals view. View 1: leader 1 proposes y on genesis. View 2: the Byzantine leader proposes w, which conflicts with y. In views 3–5 the correct leaders extend w to w ← w' ← w'' ← w*, and all correct replicas commit w. View 6: the Byzantine leader sends x, a direct child of y with justify QC(y). This is the only proposal whose height differs from its view. Every correct replica rejects it, but Lines 17–20 still run. Since y.parent = genesis = y.justify.node, they reset every lock to the genesis QC and every genericQC to QC(y). Views 7–10: the correct leader of view 7 extends its genericQC = QC(y), and the chain u ← u₁ ← u₂ ← u₃ commits u, which conflicts with w. Replica 0 commits both. The Lean theorem also checks that every correct leader's proposal has height equal to its view. Two simpler variants, with a Byzantine leader in every view, isolate the two causes. Both exploit that replicas never check b*.height = curView; a monotone lock stops the first but not the second. Lock downgrade. Line 20 sets lockedQC ← b''.justify unconditionally. Lines 17–22 run whether or not safeNode accepted b*. So a Byzantine leader can reset a correct replica's lock to an old QC with a proposal the replica does not even vote for. Counterexample: n = 4, f = 1, replica 3 Byzantine and leading every view. Replicas 0, 1 vote for y on genesis (view 1). Then they vote for the conflicting w and its chain w ← w' ← w'' ← w* (views 2–5), which commits w. In view 6 the leader sends x with parent y and justify QC(y). The replicas reject it, but y.parent = genesis = y.justify.node, so their lock becomes the genesis QC. Then they vote for u ← u' ← u'' extending y (views 7–9), which commits y. Replica 0 alone has committed both w and y. (HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_false) Views vs. heights. The proof needs "view numbers = node heights" ("createLeaf … so view-numbers are equated with node heights"). Only a correct leader ensures this; replicas never check it. Even with a monotone lock update, as in Algorithm 4, safety fails. A QC on a node c conflicting with w is formed in view 3, between the QC on w (view 1) and its children (views 5, 6). Replica 2 commits w in view 7. Replicas 0, 1, locked on (1, w), accept a child of c in view 8 by the liveness rule (3 > 1) and commit c in view 10. (HotStuff.Chained.monoLock_unsafe) In this execution every proposal passes safeNode. So reading Lines 17–22 as nested under if safeNode does not save Algorithm 3 either. Repair. Add the guard b*.height = curView (and check that b*.justify is valid and refers to a strict ancestor, which the paper says it "assumes"). With these checks Theorem 5 holds for every n > 3f (HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_fixed); the lock then becomes monotone by itself. 🔧 Theorem 5, proof in Appendix A ("by minimality of qc_s") Even with the height check, the step "by minimality of qc_s, m.node.justify.viewNumber ≤ v_{w''}" is unjustified: the justification can have a higher view and extend w. Impact. One step of the proof of the repaired theorem. The other wrong step, "the lock that r has on w is not changed", has the same root cause as the Algorithm 3 item above. Repair. The missing case extends w and gives the same contradiction. Our Lean proof is organized as an inductive invariant (HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_fixed). ✏️ Slips Lemma 3's proof cites the prepare votes (Line 10). What it needs are the pre-commit voters, who stored the prepareQC (Lines 16–18) (HotStuff.Basic.lemma_3). In Theorem 4's proof, the "highest lock among all replicas" must be among correct replicas (HotStuff.Basic.theorem_4). Typos Algorithm 2 Line 32 ("wait for message m from leader") duplicates Line 33. Theorem 5 leaves n > 3f, |F| ≤ f implicit. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 2 (Basic HotStuff safety) The proof's choice of v_s, the lowest view in (v₁, v₂] with a prepareQC conflicting with the committed w, does not establish that "the disjunct at Line 26/27 is false". Impact. The statement stands, but the proof had to be replaced (HotStuff.Basic.theorem_2). Details. View-minimality over conflicting QCs does not exclude two things: the lock of r moving, in a view in (v₁, v_s), to a QC on a strict ancestor of w, which a conflicting proposal may extend; m.justify being a QC on a common ancestor with a view in (v₁, v_s), or a QC with a view above v_s. Replicas never check m.justify.viewNumber < curView, and before GST views differ. Repair. A QC with view > v₁ whose node does not extend w is called bad. Take the first moment at which a bad QC becomes valid: before it, every correct replica that voted commit for w is locked on a node extending w and votes only for nodes extending w. So at most f correct replicas can still contribute to the commit QC on w once a bad QC exists. This is formalized as a state invariant. (HotStuff.Basic.theorem_2, commitQC_safety, invariant SInv) 🔧 Theorem 4 (Line 27 of Algorithm 1) The proof says Line 27 (liveness rule) makes every correct replica vote, but when highQC has the same view as the replica's lock, Line 27 fails (strict inequality). Impact. The statement stands (HotStuff.Basic.theorem_4). Repair. Line 26 applies instead, because two valid QCs of one view are on the same node (safeNode_of_correct_leader). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Abstract asynchronous system (Basic/Defs.lean, Chained/Model.lean), used for all safety proofs. Correct replicas take their protocol steps in any order and at any time. The pacemaker is arbitrary: a replica may jump to any higher view. Leaders may be Byzantine, so a replica may receive any proposal. Safety therefore holds for every leader schedule and pacemaker. Ideal (n − f)-threshold signatures: a QC is the signed tuple, and it is valid iff n − f replicas signed it. Byzantine replicas sign anything; correct ones sign exactly their votes (signers = Cslib.Byzantine.signers; quorum facts from Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/Certificate.lean and Cslib/Foundations/Data/Finset/Quorum.lean). Nodes are branches (lists of commands), with "extends" = suffix. In the chained model, nodes carry parent and justify. Results hold for every n > 3f with quorums n − f; the paper's case is n = 3f + 1. Partially synchronous implementation of Algorithm 2 (Basic/Impl.lean) in CSLib's PSync model (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync). Discrete time; correct replicas step every time unit, with drift-free clocks. At most f Byzantine replicas send arbitrary messages subject to unforgeability (Run.AuthValid). Messages between correct replicas sent at τ are delivered by max τ GST + δ. Replicas buffer all received messages and run the leader and replica handlers of Algorithm 2. Messages for a future view must be buffered, which the "wait for" pseudocode leaves implicit. A QC carries its signer set (the partial-signature tokens). The pacemaker (nextView interrupts) and the client commands are per-replica inputs; views increase by one. The implementation refines the abstract system (abs_reach). Safety thus holds in every run, for any GST, delays and pacemaker. Caveat (CSLib PSync): drift-free, always-awake replicas make this positive result weaker than in the textbook DLS model. Main results in Lean. Paper Lean File Lemma 1 (strengthened: same view ⇒ same node) HotStuff.Basic.lemma_1, Inv.node_eq Basic/Invariants.lean Theorem 2 (abstract system) HotStuff.Basic.theorem_2, commitQC_safety Basic/Safety.lean Theorem 2 (PSync implementation) HotStuff.Basic.impl_theorem_2 Basic/Main.lean Lemma 3 HotStuff.Basic.lemma_3 Basic/Main.lean Theorem 4, T_f = 8(δ+1) HotStuff.Basic.theorem_4 Basic/Liveness.lean Correct leader's proposal passes safeNode safeNode_of_correct_leader Basic/LiveCore.lean Theorem 5 for Algorithm 3: false (round-robin, synchronous) HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_false_roundRobin Chained/Counterexample.lean … with a Byzantine leader in every view HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_false Chained/Counterexample.lean … also with a monotone lock: false HotStuff.Chained.monoLock_unsafe Chained/Counterexample.lean Theorem 5 with the height check HotStuff.Chained.theorem5_fixed Chained/Safety.lean §4.4 pacemaker remark: constant overlap HotStuff.Pacemaker.overlap_constant Basic/Pacemaker.lean theorem_4 says the following. Let R be a valid, unforgeable run with 3f < n, and t₀ ≥ GST. Suppose all correct replicas are in view v at t₀, leader v is correct, and no correct replica is interrupted during [t₀, t₀ + 8(δ+1)). Then every correct replica has committed the leader's proposal cmd :: highQC.node by t₀ + 8(δ+1). Not formalized. Event-driven HotStuff (Algorithms 4–6, Appendix B, Theorem 8) and the two-phase variant with its livelessness scenario. Authenticator complexity (O(n) per view); Section 7. Chained liveness ("omitted for brevity" in the paper). An actual pacemaker: Theorem 4 is conditional, as in the paper. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity checks: HotStuff.Basic.nonvacuous applies Theorem 4 to a concrete run (n = 4, a silent Byzantine replica, δ = 1). The hypotheses are satisfiable, and every correct replica commits cmd 1. HotStuff.Chained.heightCheck_nonvacuous: the repaired chained protocol commits. The Chained counterexamples are checked by kernel decide on explicit executions; the abstract model is executed action by action. hotstuff_unforging shows the implementation satisfies CSLib's Algorithm.Unforging.

Atomic Cross-Chain Swaps — PODC 2018 Maurice Herlihy. Atomic Cross-Chain Swaps. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212736. Formalized version: arXiv 1801.09515 v4 (the latest); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. As printed, the protocol of §4.5 violates its safety theorem (Theorem 4.9: on the paper's own three-party example a 2-party coalition leaves a conforming leader Underwater) and its liveness theorem (Theorem 4.7: on the same example nothing is triggered even when everyone conforms). Both fixes are small, the standard HTLC deadline guard on secret release and one extra Δ in the timeouts, and the repaired protocol is proved safe, live (within 2·diam(D)·Δ) and atomic; the theory of §3 also holds: a uniform protocol is atomic iff D is strongly connected, or in general iff reachability is symmetric. The impossibility when L is not a feedback vertex set was checked only for this protocol, not for all hashed-timelock protocols. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 4.9 and Lemma 4.8 (safety: no conforming party ends Underwater) On the §1 three-party example, Bob and Carol rob a conforming leader Alice: she releases her secret after her own key has expired, and they extend the signed secret along a longer path whose key expires later (literal_unsafe_late). Impact. The protocol as specified is unsafe. Details. Lemma 4.8's proof says: "if v appears in p, then v has already received (and signed) a hashkey that triggers h on (u, v)." For a leader's own hashlock this fails. A leader releases its secret whenever its last entering contract appears, even if its own key has already expired. Its failed unlock call is public, since the pseudocode's unlock does not revert. Colluders then extend the signed secret along a longer path, whose key expires later. On the §1 example, Carol publishes C → A at the last moment, Alice's call fails, and Bob presents (B, C, A) on A → B. The counterexample uses timeouts already enlarged as in the next item, and no front-running. Ambiguity, not an error. A leader publishes its leaving contracts first and may see a foreign hashlock unlocked while still in Phase One. Suppose it then forwards that key once, to the entering contracts present at that moment. Then a single deviator can rob it on Figure 7's digraph (literal_unsafe_refwd). The proof of Theorem 4.9 says that a leader issues hashkeys only in Phase Two, after all its entering contracts exist; under that reading the attack disappears. Our repaired protocol implements this intended behaviour: it keeps forwarding to entering contracts that appear later. Repair. The standard HTLC guard: a leader releases only if its own hashkey still meets its deadline. Then no conforming party is ever Underwater, for any digraph, any leaders, any timeouts and any coalition (Setting.safety), and the protocol is atomic (Setting.game_atomic). 🔧 Theorem 4.7 and Lemma 4.6 (liveness: hashkey timeouts one Δ short) On the §1 three-party example with the timing of Figures 1–2, nothing is triggered even when everybody conforms, because a leader's own key (|p| = 0) expires before the leader may present it (literal_not_live). Impact. The protocol is not even uniform as specified. Details. A hashkey expires at (diam(D) + |p|)Δ. A leader's own key has |p| = 0, but the leader may present it only after Phase One, which itself may take diam(D)·Δ. This holds whether diam = 3, as the example's own timeouts imply, or diam = 2, the longest path between distinct vertices. Repair. Timeouts (diam + 1 + |p|)Δ, as in the single-leader formula of §4.6; then every arc is triggered by 2·diam(D)·Δ, as claimed (Setting.theorem_4_7). 🔧 Lemma 4.13 (needs simple paths) Under the paper's own path definition, which lets a path repeat its last vertex anywhere ("lassos"), the longest path from w to the leader may pass through v, and D(v, v̂) ≥ D(w, v̂) + 1 fails on five arcs on four vertices (Lasso.not_lemma_4_13_lax). Impact. It only concerns the timeout arithmetic of the single-leader protocol of §4.6. Details. Conversely, the contracts need the paper's lax paths. If isPath accepted only simple paths and cycles, a deviating leader could present a cycle key that conforming parties cannot extend. Our model checker found this; it is not in Lean. Repair. With simple paths the lemma holds (lemma_4_13, timeout_gap). ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.5 and the abstract need D connected: on two disjoint 2-cycles there is a uniform atomic protocol, although D is not strongly connected (theorem_3_5_needs_connected). §3 assumes connectivity "without loss of generality". The exact characterization, valid for all digraphs, is: atomic iff reachability is symmetric (SwapGame.atomic_iff). §2.1: the side condition of v + p ("does not include the arc (v, u₀)") should say that p does not include v. refund() should test "not unlocked and timed out". In the proof of Lemma 3.4 the coalition gets Discount, not FreeRide (it has no entering arcs). The proof of Lemma 3.4 silently assumes that coalitions can withhold their assets. We make this an explicit hypothesis and prove it for the protocol (Setting.game_canAbstain). The proof of Lemma 4.8 needs an unforgeability argument: a party's first observed key does not contain the party itself. True for the repaired protocol; proved (Setting.not_mem_first). The abstract (space O(|A|²)) and §1 (communication O(|A|·|L|)) disagree. Typos Lemma 4.14's proof cites itself; it should cite Lemma 4.13. §4.3 cites the require of claim() as Line 36, which belongs to refund(). diam is the longest-path length, so "time O(diam(D))" can mean Θ(|V|). §4.5 does not say when a leader still in Phase One forwards foreign keys; see the ambiguity under Theorem 4.9. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Swap digraph: a Mathlib Digraph on a finite type. Paths follow §2.1 (all vertices except possibly the last are distinct). diam = length of a longest path, cycles included (matches the §1 example). Reachability, strong connectivity, walks of bounded length and the follower subgraph are the shared notions of Cslib/Foundations/Combinatorics/Digraph/Walk.lean (Digraph.Reachable, Digraph.StronglyConnected, Relation.RelatesWithinSteps, Digraph.deleteVerts). Outcome: the set of eventually triggered arcs; the five payoff classes are taken literally. A protocol is abstracted as a SwapGame: for each deviating coalition, its possible outcomes. Strong Nash means no deviating coalition gets FreeRide or Discount. Execution model of §4, in Protocol.lean: Timing is synchronous: discrete time in units of Δ, conforming actions land exactly one Δ later (Figures 1–2), and deadlines are inclusive. One correct contract per arc, one hashlock per leader. A hashkey is the path p from the counterparty to the leader; it is valid until B + |p| (the paper: B = diam). The deviating coalition is arbitrary and shares knowledge. It knows its own leaders' secrets and every key ever submitted (even in failed calls), with all inner signatures. It can sign only as its own members. Two adversary settings: with and without front-running. Two protocol variants: the literal one (fixed = false) and the repaired one (fixed = true). Conforming parties follow §4.5 exactly. The scheduler resolves the only nondeterminism, which key to adopt first. Main results in Lean. Paper Lean File payoff classes, acceptable = ¬Underwater not_underwater_iff Atomicity.lean Lemma 3.3 SwapGame.atomic_of_uniform Atomicity.lean Lemma 3.4 SwapGame.not_strongNash Atomicity.lean Theorem 3.5 (connected D) / exact form SwapGame.atomic_iff_stronglyConnected / SwapGame.atomic_iff Atomicity.lean Theorem 3.5 without connectivity: false theorem_3_5_needs_connected Atomicity.lean Lemma 4.1 exists_fired_iff Pebble.lean Lemmas 4.2, 4.3 reachIn_diam, fired_diam Pebble.lean Lemma 4.5 Setting.con_of_fired Liveness.lean Lemma 4.6, Theorem 4.7 (repaired timeouts) Setting.liveness, Setting.theorem_4_7 Liveness.lean Theorem 4.7 with the paper's timeouts: false literal_not_live Counterexamples.lean Lemma 4.8 (repaired protocol) Setting.forward Safety.lean Theorem 4.9 (repaired protocol) Setting.safety Safety.lean Theorem 4.9 for the literal protocol: false / forward-once ambiguity literal_unsafe_late / literal_unsafe_refwd Counterexamples.lean main claim: the protocol is uniform / atomic (repaired) Setting.game_uniform, Setting.game_atomic Main.lean Theorem 4.12 (core; for this protocol) no_contract_on_follower_cycle, Setting.not_live_of_not_isFVS Pebble.lean, Main.lean Lemma 4.13 (simple paths) / with lax paths: false lemma_4_13, timeout_gap / Lasso.not_lemma_4_13_lax SingleLeader.lean Not formalized. The space bound (Theorem 4.10). The single-leader timelock protocol as an execution, including Lemma 4.14 (only its timeout arithmetic, Lemma 4.13). It seems to inherit the late-release problem of Theorem 4.9, but the repair is not proved for it. Lemma 4.11 and Theorem 4.12 for an undefined class of "hashed-timelock protocols". Only the core for this protocol is proved; whether the others can really collude to trigger (v, w), given that keys are signed along paths through v, was not investigated. The claim that assets are refunded by T + 2·diam·Δ when parties deviate. With the repaired timeouts the latest expiry is (2·diam + 1)Δ. Executions with variable latency below Δ, including the attack variant without public failed calls. The "simple paths and cycles" reading of the contracts' path check (model-checked only). Trust. Model limitations: Timing is lock-step: every conforming action takes exactly Δ. The adversary does not control latencies within Δ, so the safety proof covers only that setting. The model-checking claim below is informal. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The counterexamples are checked by kernel computation (decide +kernel) on the executable model, including admissibility of the adversary's schedule for all times. Non-vacuity: every coalition has an admissible schedule (Setting.idleSched_valid), and the three-party example satisfies all hypotheses of Setting.game_atomic (example in Main.lean). The infrastructure is self-contained (Mathlib only). A bounded Python model checker of the same model (modelcheck/, run under a memory cap) was used to find the counterexamples. On the repaired protocol it searched 323 instances: strongly connected digraphs with 3 vertices, all leader sets and coalitions, B ∈ {3, 4}, with front-running. It completed 316 of them and found no attack; the other 7 hit its state cap. It is not part of the development.

All You Need is DAG (DAG-Rider) — PODC 2021 Idit Keidar, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Oded Naor, Alexander Spiegelman. All You Need is DAG. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467905. Formalized version: arXiv 2102.08325 v2. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Integrity, total order, agreement, validity and the expected number of waves until a commit all hold (agreement and validity given infinitely many good waves, which occur with probability 1), but the probability argument of Claim 6 needs a new object, a robust core fixed before the coin is revealed. Lemma 1 is false for indirectly committed leaders, chain quality holds only for round-major delivery orders, and the proofs of Claim 2 and Validity have gaps; all of these are closed by local changes. The complexity claims and the link from executions to the coin game were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 1 and the proof of Proposition 2 (total order) Lemma 1 is false for indirectly committed leaders: with n = 4, f = 1, a process commits v₁ and then v₃, while the later wave-2 leader v₂ sits in its DAG with no strong path to v₁ (Lemma1Counterexample.lemma1_false). Impact. The proof of Proposition 2 (total order) applies Lemma 1 to every committed leader, so it has a gap. Total order still holds: Lemma 1 for direct commits is enough (lemma1_direct, total_order). Details. Section 6.1 says a process commits a leader when it pops it from the stack. Leaders reached in lines 39–43 count too. Lemma 1 says every later leader in anyone's DAG has a strong path to every committed leader. The proof assumes the commit rule of line 36 was met, which is true only for direct commits. Section 5 introduces Lemma 1 right after the commit rule, so it can be read as speaking of direct commits only. Under that reading Lemma 1 is true (lemma1_direct), and the gap moves to Proposition 2. The counterexample is observed by correct process 3, whose DAG at wave_ready(w) holds all vertices of rounds 1..4w except its own (4w, 3) (a realizable view): Waves 1 and 2 fail the commit rule (only one round-4/round-8 vertex reaches the leader). The wave-2 leader v₂ = (5,0) points only to round-4 vertices that avoid v₁ = (1,0). Wave 3 commits v₃ = (9,0) directly. v₃ reaches v₁ (via (5,1) → (4,0)) but not v₂. Repair. The output of a process is always the delivery of the full greedy chain of its last directly committed leader, and that chain depends only on the global DAG. (lemma1_direct, orun_inv, delivered_prefix, total_order) 🔧 Section 3 (chain quality) Chain quality, stated without proof, fails if the unspecified "deterministic order" of order_vertices lists vertices by source first: with n = 4 the prefix of size 2f + 1 = 3 has only one correct block (ChainQualityCounterexample.chain_quality_false). Impact. An under-specified definition: for any round-major delivery order the claim is true (chain_quality). Details. The counterexample is a lock-step run with n = 4 and a Byzantine process 0 that behaves correctly: wave 1 delivers the leader (1,1); wave 2 then delivers (1,0), (2,0), …. For a round-major order (rounds non-decreasing, any order within a round, even Byzantine first), every prefix of the output has ≥ 2f + 1 vertices in each round below its top round, and at most f Byzantine vertices per round. ✏️ Slips Claim 6's "≤ 3/2 + ε" is slightly off for ε > 0: 1/(2/3 − ε) > 3/2 + ε. Line 7 requires predecessors in ⋃_{k≥1} DAG[k], which excludes the genesis round, so literally no round-1 vertex is ever added. Line 25 does not check that strong edges point to round r − 1. The prose requires it, and without it a Byzantine leader could skip a committed leader and break total order (described in words only). Typos Algorithm 2 calls wave_ready(0) with round(0,1) = −3 (harmless). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 2 → Claim 6 (probability of a commit) The probability argument needs a stronger Lemma 2: Lemma 2 gives each process a set V from its own DAG when it completes the wave, but the coin is revealed as soon as f + 1 processes have called it, so the adversary may know the leader before slower correct processes complete the wave. Impact. Statement true; we prove the needed robust version, and with a perfect coin the expected number of waves until a commit is ≤ (3f+1)/(2f+1) ≤ 3/2 (lemma2, Coin.dagRider_expected_waves). Repair. Take any 2f + 1 round-3 vertices that exist; this already holds when the first correct process completes the wave, i.e. before the reveal. Let the core be the round-1 sources reached by ≥ f + 1 of them. Then: the core has ≥ 2f + 1 members (double counting; this replaces the informal appeal to the common-core protocol); every round-4 vertex ever created, Byzantine or not, strongly reaches the whole core; the core is determined by the past of those vertices. (core_card, sPath_of_mem_core, core_congr, lemma2, goodWave_of_core, Coin.dagRider_expected_waves) 🔧 Claim 2 and the proof of Claim 7 Claim 2's "induction on rounds" is unsound as written: line 25 checks only the strong edges, so a Byzantine vertex may have weak edges to vertices of the same or a higher round. Impact. Statement true; repaired (claim2). Details. The proof also assumes every correct process eventually reaches the vertex's round. That progress claim is never proved and itself needs Claim 2. Claim 7's proof likewise ignores the buffer conditions. Repair. We prove progress and Claim 2 jointly: induction on rounds, with an inner induction on the time at which the vertex was added. (round_liveness, claim2, claim7) 🔧 Proposition 4 (Validity) The proof skips a step: weak edges only guarantee that vertices created later by correct processes reach v, but the committed leader may be Byzantine. Impact. Statement true; repaired (run_validity). Details. Missing step: a vertex of a late enough round has 2f + 1 strong edges, so at least one of them goes to a correct vertex, which reaches v. The proof also needs RBC authenticity: a correct sender's message is delivered only if it was sent. The paper's list of RBC properties omits it, but Section 2 says it in prose, and we model it as Run.Valid.auth. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n = 3f + 1 processes, at most f Byzantine (a static set chosen by the adversary). Asynchronous network. Reliable broadcast is abstract. A run gives each correct process an arbitrary sequence of batches of delivered vertex ids. RBC Validity, Agreement and Authenticity are hypotheses (Run.Valid). Non-equivocation is built in: vertices are identified by (round, source) and have one global content. Correct processes run Algorithm 2 step by step (one main-loop iteration per step). When a process advances from round 4w, the ordering layer runs on its current DAG. Algorithm 3 is implemented literally (waveReady, orun); "some deterministic order" is an arbitrary function sortV. The global perfect coin is a function coin : ℕ → P (agreement). Safety theorems hold for arbitrary closed, valid local DAGs, with no assumption on schedules (only n ≤ 4f + 1 is used: two sets of 2f + 1 sources intersect. The bound on Byzantine processes enters only through the RBC abstraction, i.e. non-equivocation). Agreement and Validity assume infinitely many good waves: every correct process's round-4 vertices reach the leader. Such a wave occurs whenever the coin hits the robust core. In an abstract adaptive-adversary coin game (perfect coin, ε = 0), k consecutive misses have probability ≤ (f/(3f+1))^k, and the expected waiting time is ≤ 3/2. The identification of the execution's probability space with this game is informal (see differencies.md). Main results in Lean. On the Power of the Congested Clique Model — PODC 2014 Andrew Drucker, Fabian Kuhn, Rotem Oshman. On the Power of the Congested Clique Model. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611493. Formalized version: the 10-page author copy (no arXiv version; the "full version" cited for several proofs is not online). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The circuit simulation (Theorem 2, after repairing a counting error in its proof), the reduction from set disjointness (Lemma 13) and the lower bounds for cliques (Theorem 15) and cycles (Theorem 19) hold. One of the three lower-bound families is lost: the K_{ℓ,m} gadget of Lemma 21 is wrong for every ℓ ≠ m, and the case ℓ = m was not checked. The degeneracy upper bound (Claim 6, Theorem 7) is proved only for connected H, and the consequences for triangle detection (Sections 2.1 and 3.6) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 21 and Theorem 22 for ℓ ≠ m (the K_{ℓ,m} lower-bound gadget) The construction in the proof of Lemma 21 contains unintended copies of K_{ℓ,m} for every ℓ ≠ m, so Lemma 21 and Theorem 22 are unestablished there (lemma_21_counterexample). Impact. A broken proof, not a refuted statement: Lemma 21 only claims that some lower-bound graph exists, and in the smallest case other gadgets exist. Nothing we proved replaces the step, so the K_{ℓ,m} lower bound stands without a proof for ℓ ≠ m. The lower bounds for cliques and cycles do not use it. Details. The proof claims that each side of a copy of K_{ℓ,m} contains at least two nodes of V_A ∪ V_B, "as |W^L| = ℓ − 2 and |W^R| = m − 2 (and no mixing between W^L, W^R is possible)". But in a non-induced copy, nodes of W^R can sit on the ℓ-side. Smallest case ℓ = 2, m = 3, so W^L = ∅ and W^R = {w}. Take F = the path i – k – i' with i, i' ∈ L and k ∈ R (bipartite, C₄-free, 2 edges, at least ex(3, C₄)/2). Then {w, u_k} × {u_i, u_{i'}, v_k} is a K_{2,3}: w is adjacent to φA(L) ∪ φB(R), u_k to its F_A-neighbours and to v_k. Its four nodes in V_A ∪ V_B are not of the form φA(e) ∪ φB(e), so condition II of Definition 10 fails. The copy uses only Alice's edges and fixed edges, so with Bob's input empty the reduction graph contains K_{2,3}: Observation 11, and with it the reduction, breaks. The same happens for every m = ℓ ± 1 as soon as F has a vertex of degree 2 on the relevant side, which every F with ≥ ex(N, C₄)/2 = Θ(N^{3/2}) edges does for large N (counting argument, not formalized). For |ℓ − m| ≥ 2 there is even a copy of K_{ℓ,m} avoiding all of F_A and F_B, so every input looks "intersecting". We do not know whether a lower-bound graph exists for ℓ ≠ m in general. For the 2-edge F above, a brute-force search finds valid (K_{2,3}, F)-lower bound graphs on 2N + ℓ + m − 4 = 7 vertices, so that instance of the lemma is true. (lemma_21_counterexample, lemma21_fails_succ, lemma21_fails_succ', lemma21_fails_free) ⚠️ Claim 6 and Theorem 7 for disconnected H The proof of Claim 6 needs H connected, but the paper states Claim 6 and Theorem 7 for every graph and also applies Theorem 7 to forests. Impact. Proved only for connected H with at least one edge, which covers cycles, cliques, complete bipartite graphs and trees (claim_6, claim_6_isDegenerate, theorem_7). Disconnected forests are not covered. Details. The proof uses that ex(n, H) is non-decreasing in n and that ex(2n, H) ≥ 2 ex(n, H) (two disjoint copies of an extremal graph). Both fail for disconnected H, e.g. H = K₂ ∪ K₁ has ex(2, H) = 1 > ex(3, H) = 0 (extremalNumber_edge_plus_point). For forests the doubling step fails too: ex(3, 2K₂) = 3 (a triangle) but ex(6, 2K₂) = 5 (a star). 🔧 Lemma 18 for ℓ = 5, N = 4 (lower-bound graphs for cycles) Lemma 18 claims an extremal C_ℓ-free F with a (C_ℓ, F)-lower bound graph for every even N; for ℓ = 5, N = 4 none exists (lemma_18_false, no_lowerBoundGraph_C5_K4). Impact. One condition changes and the construction stays. For N < ℓ every graph on N vertices is C_ℓ-free, and Theorem 19 (asymptotic in n, ℓ fixed) never uses this range. Theorem 19 is proved from a corrected Lemma 18. Details. For odd ℓ the proof takes F = K_{N/2,N/2} "since ex(N, C_ℓ) = N²/4". That holds only for large N. For ℓ = 5, N = 4 the unique extremal C₅-free graph is K₄, and no (C₅, K₄)-lower bound graph exists on any number of vertices. The witness cycle for an edge {u, v} has a single vertex outside V_A ∪ V_B, so it contains a direct edge A_x B_y with x, y ∈ {u, v}. Two such edges for the disjoint edges {0,1} and {2,3} of K₄ close a 5-cycle through three vertices of V_A, which violates condition II. (not_lemma18Statement) Repair. With "extremal" replaced by "C_ℓ-free, with all edges between the two halves when ℓ is odd" the construction is correct for all N; we prove this (including condition II for every cycle, which the paper does not argue) and derive Theorem 19 from it. (lemma_18) 🔧 Lemma 18 (proof), the bound for even ℓ The proof claims "ex(N, C_ℓ) = Ω(N^{3/2})" for every even ℓ; for ℓ ≥ 6 this contradicts Bondy–Simonovits (ex(N, C_{2k}) = O(N^{1+1/k})). Impact. The claim is never used: deleting it saves everything, and the even case is proved without it (lemma_18_even). ✏️ Slips Theorem 22 is stated "for any ℓ, m ≥ 1", but for ℓ = 1 (and, symmetrically, m = 1) one round with one-bit messages suffices, not Ω(√n/b) (theorem_22_false_of_l_eq_one, starAlg): K_{1,m} is a star, and G contains it iff some node has degree ≥ m. Lemma 21 assumes ℓ, m ≥ 2, so this is evidently a typo. Theorem 4 says "depth c·R" with c > 1; the simulation gives depth R / c (theorem_4). After Theorem 7 the paper says that for a fixed tree or forest ex(n, H) = O(1). It is O(n), which is what the stated running time O(log(n)/b) needs. Lemma 14's construction connects u_1, …, u_{ℓ−1} to everything; it should be u_{ℓ−4}. Lemma 18's index ranges for the path nodes u_{i,j} give ⌊ℓ/2⌋ (resp. ⌈ℓ/2⌉) internal nodes; it should be ⌊ℓ/2⌋ − 2 (resp. ⌈ℓ/2⌉ − 2), consistent with the stated path lengths and the (ℓ−4)N/2 extra nodes. Typos Lemma 21's proof says "assume n = 4N + ℓ + m − 4"; it should be 2N. Section 3.6 prints the bound as Ω(n/(e^{O(√n)} b)), while the introduction has e^{O(√log n)}. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2 (circuit simulation) The proof's count of heavy gates is off by a factor 2: the total weight is 2N, not ≤ n² s. Impact. Only the thresholds change, and the rest of the proof stands (theorem_2). Details. The proof calls G heavy if w(G) = |in G| + |out G| ≥ ns (N = n² s wires) and claims that "the number of heavy gates cannot exceed n". It also claims that the greedy assignment of light gates never gets stuck with load 2ns. Both rest on "total weight ≤ n² s", but the total weight is 2N. With n = 2, s = 1, a path of 5 gates has 4 = n² s wires and 3 heavy gates (heavy_count_counterexample). Repair. Heavy iff w ≥ n(2s + 1) (counting input gates with weight +1) and light load ≤ 2n(2s + 1). With these thresholds the simulation runs with bandwidth b + 4s + 3 in 2D + 4 rounds. We use oblivious routing (König splitting) instead of Lenzen's algorithm; all communication patterns are fixed in advance. (theorem_2) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CLIQUE-UCAST (Section 2): deterministic synchronous rounds on n players with known identities, no failures, free local computation. A program is a sequence of communication steps (Prog, staged in Podc/). A step whose longest per-pair message has w bits costs ⌈w/B⌉ rounds at bandwidth B (Prog.roundsAt). Each player starts with its own input bits; the protocol may depend on the circuit and the input partition. CLIQUE-BCAST (Section 3): synchronous rounds; every node broadcasts b bits per round (Bcast.Algorithm, staged). The input of a node is its incident edges. Randomized algorithms get private coins, uniform over a finite set. CONGEST-UCAST: CSLib's deterministic CONGEST (Cslib.Congest.Algorithm) on the input graph. Detection convention: all nodes accept iff the input graph is H-free. Copies of H are Mathlib Copys, i.e. not necessarily induced subgraphs, as in the paper. Randomized lower bounds take the randomized communication complexity of set disjointness as a hypothesis (RandDisjLB). Deterministic bounds are unconditional (CSLib's CC(DISJ_K) ≥ K). VABA: Asymptotically Optimal Validated Asynchronous Byzantine Agreement — PODC 2019 Ittai Abraham, Dahlia Malkhi, Alexander Spiegelman. Asymptotically Optimal Validated Asynchronous Byzantine Agreement. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331612. Formalized version: arXiv 1811.01332 v1, the only arXiv version. Numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Agreement, validity and expected constant views are proved for all n > 3f, once the hard-coded 2f + 1 thresholds become n − f and two pseudocode bugs get local fixes. But the protocol never halts, so the total message bound behind the O(n²) claim fails as printed and no halting rule is proved, and Quality has no proof in the paper at all. The O(n²) word count itself was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Definition 4 (Quality) Definition 4 requires Quality, that a value proposed by an honest party is chosen with probability at least 1/2, but the paper never proves it. Impact. The word occurs only in Section 2.2, and Appendix A proves only agreement, validity, termination and efficiency. Nothing we proved says anything about Quality, which is not formalized; we neither prove nor refute it. ⚠️ Lemma 20 and Definition 4 (termination proved vacuously; Efficiency fails as stated) Algorithm 6 loops forever, because deciding does not stop a party, so termination holds only vacuously and honest parties send infinitely many messages, which violates Efficiency (Definition 4). Impact. A halting rule is missing, and no halting rule or total message bound is proved. What survives is the content up to the decisions: every view completes (Lemma 19) and each view decides with probability ≥ 2/3, so an honest party is undecided after k views with probability at most (f/n)^k and the expected number of views is < 3/2 (view_progress, card_undecided_le, vaba_undecided_prob, vaba_expected_views). Details. The proof of Lemma 20 says that honest parties never stop sending messages, "therefore, termination trivially follows". That uses the vacuity of "all messages have been delivered". Lemma 24 only bounds the messages sent before everybody decides. A party cannot just halt after deciding: others may only be locked and still need its messages. 🔧 Lemmas 3 and 13 (PB-provability, Agreement): 2f + 1 thresholds for f < n/3 The protocol hard-codes 2f + 1 thresholds although the paper allows any f < n/3, and with n = 5, f = 1 a corrupted leader makes honest parties decide true and false (Counterexample.agreement_fails). Impact. Lemmas 3 and 13 are false for the algorithms as written whenever n > 3f + 1; the protocol is correct for n = 3f + 1. Theorem 1 itself, an existence claim, survives: with threshold n − f, all our results hold for every n > 3f. Details. Signatures, skip shares and view-change waits all use 2f + 1. The paper never restricts to n = 3f + 1 (§2, §3 and Theorem 1 say f < n/3). Lemma 3 (PB-provability) concludes that two sets of 2f + 1 signers share an honest party. That needs n = 3f + 1. Lemma 8 says "2f + 1 = n − f". Take n = 5, f = 1. The corrupted party 4 is elected leader of view 1 and equivocates in every stage of its broadcast: 0 and 1 deliver true, 2 and 3 deliver false, and 4 signs both. The broadcasts of 0 and 1 complete normally, so the skip certificate forms, and honest parties 0 and 2 decide true and false. This is a 58-step run of our model (Counterexample.agreement_fails). Repair. Threshold n − f; everything (agreement, validity, view completion, expected views < 3/2) is proved for all n > 3f. 🔧 Algorithm 6, line 4 (key check: j ≠ 1 must be j ≠ 0) Read literally, every honest proposal of view 1 fails validation, so view 1 never completes, and keys of view 1 would be accepted unchecked. Impact. One condition changes; with the fix, honest proposals pass validation (proposal_valid). Details. Here j is the key's view, and the initial key is ⟨0, ⊥⟩. The proof of Lemma 15 reads j as the current view ("no key required in view 1"). That reading fails in view 2 whenever nobody got a key in view 1. Repair. We use: the key view is 0, or it carries a stage-1 certificate of that view's leader, and in both cases it is ≥ LOCK. 🔧 Algorithm 7 (view-change messages that arrive early) Algorithm 7 validates a view-change message against L[j], which is ⊥ until the receiver's own elect returns, so read literally, early messages lose their content but still count among the 2f + 1. Impact. Lemmas 8, 9 and 14 assume that the content is processed, so Lemma 8 needs these messages buffered. Repair. One guard: a view-change message is processed only once L[j] is known (recvVC in Model.lean), which buffers it. Agreement is proved for this algorithm (vaba_agreement). ✏️ Slips Lemma 6 is stated for stages 2–4 but used for stage 1 in Lemma 12; the proof works for all stages (Inv.qc_agree). Typos Algorithm 3 has return σ for σ_in. Algorithm 7 has lock and key.round for LOCK and KEY.view, and forwards unvalidated skip messages. Lemma 21 has "2f = 1". The proof of Lemma 3 has σ'_1 for σ'_j. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 14 (stated too narrowly for its use) Lemma 14 is stated only for a lock set in view j, but locks can be set later and Lemma 15 needs the general form. Impact. The general form is true: the same quorum argument proves it (Inv.key_of_lockQC). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Model.lean): Protocol and parties. Algorithms 1–7 form an interleaving transition system on n = |P| parties. The 4-stage provable broadcasts are inlined: an honest party delivers stage s of proposer k iff the message passes ex-sbc/ex-bc-validation and the sender could have sent it. An honest proposer sends only its proposal. Asynchrony. The adversary schedules every enabled action in any order. Adversary. It corrupts up to f parties adaptively. A corrupted party's local state is frozen, and it signs anything. Threshold signatures are ideal: a certificate exists iff Q shares exist (QC is the shared Cslib.Byzantine.Certified, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/Certificate.lean). The paper's threshold is 2f + 1; theorems take n + f < 2Q for safety and Q + f ≤ n for liveness, i.e. Q = n − f for any n > 3f. Common coin. It is ideal: a sequence of leaders, view j's revealed at the first honest elect(j). View-change messages. They are buffered until the receiver knows the leader. A corrupted sender can include any existing certificates. Probabilistic statements. The adversary is a deterministic strategy on the full history of global states, which contain only revealed coins. That the adversary's "good set" of view j depends only on the coins of earlier views is proved (good_congr). Probabilities are counts over uniform leader sequences, in the shared coin game Cslib/Probability/CoinGame.lean (also used for DAG-Rider). All cryptographic "except with negligible probability" qualifiers disappear with ideal functionalities. Main results in Lean. Iterative Approximate Byzantine Consensus in Directed Graphs — PODC 2012 Nitin H. Vaidya, Lewis Tseng, Guanfeng Liang. Iterative Approximate Byzantine Consensus in Arbitrary Directed Graphs. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332505. Formalized version: arXiv 1201.4183 v2 (technical report with all appendices). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The tight characterization (Theorems 1–3: an iterative algorithm exists iff the graph satisfies the partition condition, and Algorithm 1 then works) and all of Section 6 hold as stated, under the paper's standing assumption n ≥ 2. The necessity proof has one unjustified step, which a short local-validity lemma repairs; the rest are slips. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proof of Corollary 3: it takes R = V − F − {i} without checking R ≠ ∅, which Corollary 1 requires. It follows from Corollary 2 (|R| ≥ 2f ≥ 1) (Condition.inDegree). At the end of the proof of Claim 4 (Appendix A), v_i[s + τ] should be v_i[s + τ + 1]. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 1 (necessity of the condition) The proof uses validity (1) to force v_i[1] = m for a node i ∈ L that receives only m from fault-free nodes, but (1) only gives v_i[1] ≤ M. Impact. Statement true; repaired by a separate "local validity" argument (condition_of_correct). Details. (1) bounds v_i[1] by μ[0] and U[0], the extremes over all fault-free nodes, including nodes of C ∪ R that i cannot hear and that start at M. This already fails in the simplest case F = N'(i) = ∅ with R ≠ ∅. The argument needs a different execution in which the nodes outside i's in-neighbourhood start in [m, m]; since Z_i sees only in-neighbours, i cannot tell the two apart. The induction to t > 1 uses the same step, plus the fact that Z_i does not depend on t. Repair. We prove this "local validity" property separately (IterAlg.localValid) and derive Theorem 1 from it. The paper's auxiliary values m⁻ < m, M⁺ > M turn out to be unnecessary. (condition_of_correct) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finite node set V with a directed graph (Mathlib Digraph, self-loops ignored); synchronous lock-step iterations; every node sends its state on all outgoing links. Static Byzantine set F, |F| ≤ f; faulty nodes may send arbitrary, different reals to different out-neighbours in every iteration. Authenticated links. Correctness quantifies over every F, all real inputs and all Byzantine messages. Iterative algorithms (IterAlg): one fixed function Z i (received vector) (own state) per node, seeing only in-neighbours, with no clock and no other memory; the state is the output. This is the paper's Z_i(r_i[t], v_i[t−1]), and the impossibility depends on exactly this restriction. Validity both as "outputs in the hull of fault-free inputs" and as the per-iteration form (1); we prove them equivalent for iterative algorithms (IterAlg.correct_iff_correctStep). Convergence is U[t] − μ[t] → 0. Algorithm 1's "ties broken arbitrarily" is quantified universally: Theorems 2–3 hold for every run of the step relation alg1Step, where the trimming may be chosen anew (even adversarially) each iteration; every deterministic tie-breaking rule gives an IterAlg (TieBreak.alg). Optimal Deterministic Routing and Sorting on the Congested Clique — PODC 2013 Christoph Lenzen. Optimal Deterministic Routing and Sorting on the Congested Clique. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2501983. Formalized version: arXiv 1207.1852 v4 (10 May 2013, the PODC version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Both main results hold for every n: routing (Theorem 3.7, 16 rounds) and sorting (Theorem 4.5, 37 rounds); we prove them with packets of a constant number of O(log n)-bit items, in 15 and 32 rounds. The square case n = s² follows the paper's algorithms after local repairs to the relay nodes of Corollary 3.3, the global information of the sorting algorithm's final step, and the "bundling" and "exactly f|W| messages" steps. The non-square case of Theorem 3.7 does not work as written and needed a different reduction through virtual nodes. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Problem 4.1 asks for the keys with indices i(n−1)+1, …, in; it should be (i−1)n+1, …, in, as in the introduction. Proof of Corollary 3.3: node i receives exactly one message (not f) for each destination j. The nearby claim "each node will receive exactly one message of each color" is also wrong (node c receives only messages of colour c). Corollaries 3.3/3.4 are stated for exactly f|W| messages per node but used with fewer or with upper bounds only (Corollary 3.4, Lemma 4.4, Theorem 3.7). The paper's "at most" remark and dummy messages cover this (we prove the "at most" version, mem_tagged_c33). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 3.7, non-square n (the reduction to three sub-instances) With s = ⌊√n⌋ the proof splits the messages into sub-instances on V₁ = {1..s²}, V₂ = {n-s²+1..n} and V₃, but the cover claim fails for n = 3 and Corollary 3.4 is applied outside its hypotheses (coverClaim_false_three, cor34_size_fails_eight, cor34_load_fails_seven). Impact. The 16-round bound for every n survives, by a different reduction: we simulate the square algorithm on ⌈√n⌉² ≤ 2n virtual nodes, at most two per real node (theorem_3_7). Details. Four things go wrong: The cover claim fails only for n = 3: there the message from node 2 to itself belongs to none of the sub-instances (coverClaim_false_three). For n ≠ 3 the claim holds, because 2⌊√n⌋² ≥ n (kernel-checked for n ≤ 40 in coverClaim_small, elementary for larger n). Corollary 3.4 is applied to W = V₁ ∩ V₃, but it requires |W| ≤ √n. This fails, e.g., for n = 8, where |W| = 4 (the arithmetic is recorded in cor34_size_fails_eight). Corollary 3.4 also requires every node to hold exactly ⌊n/|W|⌋·|W| messages. This fails, e.g., for n = 7, where up to 21 messages must be spread over 3 nodes holding at most 6 each (the set identities and arithmetic are recorded in cor34_load_fails_seven; this is not a full execution). The square algorithm run on V₁ (s² nodes) is built for s² messages per node, but nodes can have up to n > s² messages inside V₁. The paper's "factor 2" accounts for running the V₁ and V₂ instances in parallel. Its remark after Problem 3.1 (overloaded instances "can be split up into smaller ones") partly covers this, but how to split them without coordination is not worked out. 🔧 Corollary 3.3 (relay nodes lack routing information) In round 1 the messages go to nodes 1..m, which need not be in W, but only nodes of W know the routing pattern. Impact. The two-round routing survives, at a constant factor in message size (c33a/c33b). Details. This causes no problem when a message's current target is its final destination, which the message header contains. It does in Step 5 of Algorithm 2 and Step 3 of Algorithm 1 (Corollary 3.5), where the targets are intermediate. Repair. Attach the target (and the target group in Algorithm 2) to the message (c33a/c33b). 🔧 Theorem 4.5, Algorithm 4 Step 8 (global information never distributed) To send a key to the node responsible for its global rank, a node must know the sizes of all buckets of the other groups, but no step announces these counts. Impact. The round count survives: one extra round (P29) still fits easily into 37 rounds. Details. Corollary 3.3 (with W = V) also requires everyone to know all sources and destinations. Repair. We add one round in which every node broadcasts how many keys it holds (P29). 🔧 Theorem 4.5, Step 6 (bundling arguments) "Bundling up to two keys in each message, nodes need to … receive at most n messages" does not follow. Impact. The 37-round claim is kept, at the cost of constant factors (load_tgt, box_deliver). Details. Step 6 of Algorithm 4: "receive at most 2n keys" is true. It follows from ⌈|K_{i,j}|/√n⌉ ≤ d_i + 1, not from the stated bound Σ|K_{i,j}| < 2n^{3/2}. With per-sender bundling a node can need about 1.5 n messages. Repair. We use packets with a few more slots and route Step 6 through the routing algorithm on a virtual clique of 4n nodes, which allows receiver loads up to 4n (load_tgt, box_deliver; box_spec in the docstring of RoutingBox.lean). 🔧 Lemma 3.6, Algorithm 2 Steps 2–3 (quotas not known in advance) Nodes cannot know how many messages they "need to move to each set" before knowing the others' counts, so the group-level colouring must be distributed over the group members (a transportation problem). Impact. The round count survives (HB_of_inp, Setup.q). Details. The paper hands this to a footnote ("deferred completion"), which only half states it. Repair. Step 3 announces counts per destination group, and the quota is settled afterwards by a transportation step among the group members. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Network. Synchronous congested clique (Model.lean) on nodes Fin n with known identifiers. Algorithms are deterministic and in full-information form: in round t node v computes its packet to each node from its identifier, its input and all packets received so far. The algorithm may depend on n. No failures, no randomness. Packets. In every round every node sends every node (itself included) one packet of B slots. A slot carries one message/key or one number. The theorems fix B as an absolute constant (12 for routing, 384 for sorting) and bound numbers by 8n² resp. 32n². So packets have O(log n) bits, as in the paper. Opaque messages and keys. They can only be forwarded: a node may send only items it holds, i.e. its own inputs or items it received (Holds, SortHolds). Keys can be compared. Routing (Problem 3.1). Every node sends at most n messages and receives at most n (Solves). theorem_3_7_exact is the paper's "exactly n" version. Sorting (Problem 4.1). Node i gets n distinct keys; the key of global rank r must reach node ⌊r/n⌋ (SortSolves). Distinctness is the paper's w.l.o.g. assumption. Proof technique. Algorithms are built as intended runs (global formulas for all packets). We then prove that every packet is determined by its sender's view (IsLocal, Knowledge.lean), which yields a genuine distributed algorithm (synth_sent). Main results in Lean. Optimal Distributed APSP — PODC 2012 Stephan Holzer, Roger Wattenhofer. Optimal Distributed All Pairs Shortest Paths and Applications. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332504. Formalized version: the authors' "preliminary full version" of 22.05.2012 (38 pp., with proofs; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Algorithm 1 computes APSP in O(n) CONGEST rounds (Lemma 1, Theorem 1, Lemmas 2–6), and the diameter lower bounds (Theorems 4, 8, 9 with Lemmas 8, 9, 15 and the exact parts of Lemmas 10, 11, 16, Theorem 11) are proved. But Theorem 5 is false: Algorithm 2, the S-SP algorithm, computes wrong distances already on a triangle, and still does so with any tie-breaking rule and any neighbour numbering. The (×, 1+ε) approximations built on it are therefore not established by the paper. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 5 (Algorithm 2 computes S-SP in time O(|S| + D)) Algorithm 2 outputs wrong distances: on the graph with edges 1-3, 1-4, 3-4, 2-4 and S = {2, 3, 4}, node 3 ends with δ[4] = 2 although 3 and 4 are adjacent (Alg2.exB_wrong, Alg2.theorem5_false). Impact. Theorem 5, as a claim about Algorithm 2, is false, and running the algorithm longer does not help (Alg2.not_eventuallyCorrect). Theorem 6, Corollary 4 and Theorem 7 (the (×, 1+ε) approximations of eccentricities, diameter, radius, center, peripheral vertices and girth) use Algorithm 2 and are therefore not established by the paper. Their bounds are still plausible, because a correct O(|S| + D) algorithm for S-SP is known from later work, for example Lenzen–Peleg's source detection (PODC 2013). The APSP result does not use Algorithm 2. Details. In round 1 nodes 3 and 4 send their own IDs to each other. The smaller ID wins the edge, so ID 4 does not cross. Node 4 then sends the smaller ID 2 to node 3 first. Meanwhile ID 4 crossed the edge 4 → 1, and node 1 forwards it to 3 in round 2 with δ = 2. When the direct copy finally arrives, 3 already knows ID 4 and ignores it. The run has no ties, and Alg2.exB_wrong checks all 24 neighbour numberings, both for the paper's rule (the lowest neighbour index wins) and for "take the smallest δ received in the round". The proof of Theorem 5 assumes that the same smaller IDs delay ID u on every path. That is false: whether a message is delayed on an edge depends on what the other endpoint sends at that moment. Its claim that each smaller ID delays u at most once is false too. The minimal counterexample is the triangle {1, 2, 3} with S = {1, 3}. ID 3 reaches node 1 in round 2 simultaneously from 2 (with δ = 2) and from 3 (with δ = 1). If node 1 numbers its neighbours by increasing ID, the lower index (node 2) wins, so δ[3] = 2 (Alg2.triangle_wrong). The round budget |S| + D' with D' = 2·ecc(1) is also too small. On K₄ with a pendant node 5 attached to 1 and S = {1, 2, 3, 4}, node 5 has no δ for ID 4 after the 6 rounds (Alg2.exC_late). Repair. None formalized. A correct algorithm forwards tokens in order of (distance, ID), not by ID alone. ✏️ Slips §5.2: the bit index k(n)·(μ − k(n) + 1) + ν of the edge (l_ν, l_μ) is out of range [k(n)² − 1]. The pairing of Lemma 8's proof is the intended one. Any bijection works; Lean indexes the inputs by Fin k × Fin k. §7.1: in Theorem 9's proof "i ∈ [n − 1]" should be i ∈ [k(n)² − 1]. §7.1: in E_b "i ∈ [n − 4k(n) + 1]" should be the index range of V_b's fill-up nodes, and with [k] = {0, …, k}, V_b's "[n − 4k(n) − 2]" is one too many. Theorem 11's proof says "n − 1" nodes in the "k-neighbourhood" (meant: n nodes in the 2-neighbourhood, since v ∈ N₂(v)). Claim 2 says p + 3 = d/2 + 2 is "less than d". It equals d for d = 4; "at most" is what is used. Typos The prose on p. 28 writes the lower clique as "{k(n), …, k(n) − 1}" (the formal E_a has {k(n), …, 2k(n) − 1}). Lemma 16's proof says "diameter 2 from graphs of diameter 2" (meant: 3). Figure 1 uses a third indexing of the bits, and Figure 2's caption uses a different bit indexing than E_a. Any bijection works. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 9 (disjoint ⇔ diameter d) and Theorem 4 For disjoint inputs the proof only shows diam ≤ d; that the diameter is not smaller (so exactly d) is never argued. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma9). It needs k(n) ≥ 1, which follows from n ≥ d + 6. Repair. For disjoint inputs the two path ends l'_ν (upper) and r'_μ (lower) are at distance exactly 2p + 2 = d. The lower bound is proved with a potential that changes by at most one along edges. 🔧 Lemma 8 (non-disjoint ⇒ diameter d + 2) The upper-bound part says that any two nodes of G_a are within p + 3 "via c₀", which is false for p ≥ 2 (two path ends l'_ν, l'_ν' are at distance 2p + 2). Impact. Statement true. The bound actually needed, ≤ d + 2 = 2p + 4, holds (lemma8, claim2). 🔧 Theorem 4 (construction for odd n) Each side receives n/2 nodes, which is impossible for odd n, although the theorem claims every n ≥ d + 6. Impact. Statement true; the Lean construction splits the fill-up nodes ⌊r/2⌋ / ⌈r/2⌉ (theorem4). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous CONGEST, deterministic, no failures, CSLib's Cslib.Congest.Algorithm V I σ B. Vertex names are the IDs. Each round, every node sends a B-bit message to each neighbour and updates its state. Upper bounds are written with typed messages (Cslib.Congest.TAlgorithm, staged in Podc/Computability/Distributed/Congest/Typed.lean). They are compiled to ⌈log₂ |M|⌉-bit messages with the same executions (run_toAlgorithm). Algorithm 1 uses the paper's assumptions: n is known (V is a Fintype), there is a known root r (the node "with ID 1"), and IDs are ordered (LinearOrder V, used for the smallest child). The input is ignored, since nodes learn their neighbours from messages. Algorithm 1 runs in three stages switched by a round counter: rounds 1…n: BFS from r builds T₁; from round n + 1: depth-first pebble plus BFS waves, all distances known after 5n rounds; from round 5n: max/min flooding of eccentricities, so after 6n rounds every node knows the diameter and the radius. Since nodes know n, T₁ is built in n rounds rather than O(D). This only changes constants. Messages carry at most one tree message, one pebble bit, one BFS token (ID, distance) and two numbers < n + 1. That is ≤ 5⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ + 2 bits (msgBits_le). The pebble (Pebble.lean) is analysed as a global transition system and then shown to be followed by the distributed run (pebble_corr). Remark 3's O(n) traversal is firstVisit_le: at most 3n − 1 slots including the waiting slots. It is proved with a potential that grows by one per slot. Lower bounds use CSLib's two-party simulation (LBFamily, node input = adjacency row) and the proved deterministic bound CC(DISJ_K) ≥ K. Algorithms only need to be correct on connected graphs inside the paper's promise: diameter in {d, d+2}, resp. {2, 3}. The paper states ε-error, public-coin randomized lower bounds. Lean proves the deterministic versions outright. The randomized versions (theorem4_randomized, theorem8_randomized) use private coins and are conditional on a hypothesis RandDisjLB (randomized CC of disjointness ≥ κK, Kalyanasundaram–Schnitger/Razborov), which is not proved. Output conventions: "each node knows X" means the value is a field of the node's state after T rounds; lower bounds use per-node read-outs. A node accepts iff its local value passes a threshold, and CSLib's "all nodes accept" replaces the paper's O(D) aggregation. Algorithm 2 (Algorithm2.lean) is modelled literally on Fin n, with the pseudocode's neighbour index order. A received ID that is already known is ignored and not removed from L_i. Signature-Free Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus — PODC 2014 Achour Mostéfaoui, Hamouma Moumen, Michel Raynal. Signature-Free Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with t < n/3 and O(n²) Messages. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611468. Formalized version: the full version, IRISA technical report PI-2016 (February 2014), HAL hal-00944019 (file RR-2016-Consensus-optimal-V5.pdf, 13 pages; same algorithm, lemmas and numbering as the proceedings version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The algorithm of Figure 2 does not terminate: in the paper's own model, an adversary that controls the schedule and the Byzantine process prevents every decision, for every coin sequence. So Theorem 2, Lemma 5 and the four expected rounds of Theorem 3 and the abstract fail, and we proved no repaired algorithm. BV-broadcast (Theorem 1), Lemmas 1–4, validity and agreement hold, and so do the two deterministic steps of the termination proof. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 2 (BC-Termination), Lemma 5 and Theorem 3 (termination, four expected rounds) The algorithm of Figure 2 does not terminate: for n = 4, t = 1 and inputs 0, 0, 1, an adversary that controls the schedule and the Byzantine process, and sees each coin only after two correct processes have called random(), prevents every decision forever, for every coin sequence (Attack.counterexample, Attack.prob_termination_eq_zero). Impact. The probability of termination is 0, not 1, and the expected number of rounds is infinite, not 4. Theorem 2 claims Figure 2 solves randomized consensus, and the abstract claims it decides in 4 expected rounds; the paper's own algorithm is wrong, and we proved no repair. Safety (Theorem 1, Lemmas 1–4, validity, agreement) is unaffected. Details. The proof of Lemma 5 has a "Claim": with probability 1 all correct processes eventually have the same estimate. Its third case (some correct processes adopt the value v of a singleton values at line 09, others adopt the coin s at line 10) says that "s is equal to v with probability 1/2", because the coin is independent of the scheduler. But v is not fixed before the coin is drawn. The adversary can wait until the coin of the round is known and then decide which value the remaining processes see. The paper's model gives it this power: Byzantine processes control the message schedule, and the coin is only required not to be computable in advance (Section 4.1 and footnote 2). Our counterexample: n = 4, t = 1, processes p0, p1, p2 correct with estimates a, a, ¬a (initially 0, 0, 1), p3 Byzantine. In every round: p3 sends B_VAL(¬a) to everybody. So ¬a gets t + 1 copies, everybody echoes it, and both values enter every bin_values. The adversary picks the order: p0 sees a first and broadcasts AUX(a), p1 sees ¬a first and broadcasts AUX(¬a). p0 and p1 receive AUX(a), AUX(¬a), AUX(a) (the last from p3). So values = {0,1}, both call random() and adopt the coin s. Now the adversary knows s. It makes p2 see ¬s first in bin_values, so p2 broadcasts AUX(¬s). Then p2 receives AUX(¬s) from itself, from p3 and from whichever of p0, p1 sent ¬s. Its values = {¬s} differs from the coin, so p2 does not decide and adopts ¬s. The next round starts again with two processes at one value and one at the other. Nobody ever decides, for every coin sequence. The execution is weakly fair: every message between correct processes is delivered and every enabled step is taken. It is also an execution of the deterministic code: processes react to each message at once, and every bin_values and values they use is the only possible one. (Attack.coin_used_late, Local.eager, Local.forced) Scope. The adversary needs the coin of a round only after p0 and p1 (and p3) have called random(). So the attack also works against a threshold coin that is revealed by n − t shares. It even works against an ideal coin that tells b_r only to the caller: the adversary reads s off p0's next broadcast B_VAL[r+1](s), which the Byzantine p3 receives (this is exactly what Attack.strat looks at). The argument of the Claim would go through only if the adversary could not see the coin before all correct processes have fixed their values, e.g. with a scheduler that does not see message contents (the "oblivious scheduler" of the paper's footnote 2). The paper's model explicitly gives the Byzantine processes control of the schedule, and no common-coin implementation in an asynchronous Byzantine system can wait for all correct processes. The same liveness problem was reported by P. Tholoniat and V. Gramoli, Formal Verification of Blockchain Byzantine Fault Tolerance (arXiv:1909.07453, 2019), with another n = 4, t = 1 scenario; according to them the authors confirmed it, and the journal version (J. ACM 2015) remarks that a fair scheduler and a perfect common coin are needed for this algorithm and gives a new algorithm. We did not check the journal version. Typos In the proof of Lemma 2, "p_x sent AUX[r](v) to p_i and AUX[r](w) to p_i" should end with "to p_j". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The interleaving model Cslib.Byzantine.AsyncBroadcast (staged in Podc/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/). Asynchronous reliable authenticated point-to-point channels; each delivery is a separate event chosen by the adversary. At most t Byzantine processes; they can make anybody receive anything from them. Corruption is adaptive (at any time), which is stronger than the paper's static model. The algorithm (Model.lean, mmr t coin): messages bval r v tag = B_VAL[r](v) and aux r v = AUX[r](v). The local tag on a process's own B_VAL (ignored by receivers) records its estimate and whether its values was a singleton. Guards are liberal: a wait may be passed later than possible and with any admissible set of n − t messages, and echoes and decisions are separate steps. This is a superset of the paper's behaviours, so the safety results cover the code. Common coin: a fixed sequence coin : ℕ → Bool, the same for all processes. Safety holds for every coin sequence. Liveness is proved in every weakly fair execution. Counterexample: the adversary is a function strat of the time and the current global state (full information about the past, including coins already used by processes, and nothing about other coins). The execution is generated from strat for each coin sequence. The schedule of a round is a finite, decidable script, checked by decide. coin_used_late shows that the script of round r depends on the coin of round r only after p0 and p1 have called random(). eager, forced and quiet_final show that the schedule uses none of the liberal freedoms within the round. In the other rounds no step is enabled during the round (they are closed, or nothing of them has been delivered yet); we argue this in prose, not in Lean. Main results in Lean. Distributed k-Core Decomposition — PODC 2011 Alberto Montresor, Francesco De Pellegrini, Daniele Miorandi. Distributed k-core decomposition. PODC 2011 (brief announcement). DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993836. Formalized version: arXiv 1103.5320 v2 (full version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The algorithm is correct: estimates never increase, never drop below the coreness and converge to it, in the one-node-per-host version (synchronous and asynchronous) and in the many-nodes-per-host version, and the bounds of Theorem 4 (1 + Σ(d − k)), Theorem 5 (N) and Corollary 1 (N − K + 1) hold. The liveness proof of Theorem 3 fails in its induction step and needed a new fixpoint argument. The bound N − K + 1 is not met exactly as claimed: the "worst-case" family of Fig. 3 needs N − 2 rounds, within 2 of the bound for this family, and no other result depends on this. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Introduction and §6 (the upper bound "is met exactly") The Introduction says §4 "describes a worst-case graph that requires exactly" N − K + 1 rounds, and §6 calls the upper bounds "strict for specific worst-case examples", but for the Fig. 3 family K = 1, so the bound is N, while the family needs N − 2 (worstGraph_execTime); even the paper's own count N − 1 misses it. Impact. Exact tightness is not saved. What is proved is tightness up to an additive 2 for this family, which still shows that time grows linearly in N; the theorems are unaffected. Details. An exhaustive search over all graphs with N ≤ 8 nodes (computational, not formalized) finds a maximum execution time of N − 2 for 4 ≤ N ≤ 8. So the family is optimal there, and the bound N is never reached. 🔧 §4.2, Fig. 3 (the "worst-case" family) The paper claims the family of Fig. 3 needs exactly N − 1 rounds for every N ≥ 5, but in the paper's own synchronous model it needs N − 2 (worstGraph_execTime). Impact. Off by one, not a typo; changing the constant keeps "close to the bound" and linear time, and the theorems are unaffected. Details. The family: hub N joined to all nodes but N − 3, a path 1 – 2 – … – N − 1, and the chord (N − 3, N − 1). We use the paper's own definition of execution time; that accounting gives the 3 rounds of the Fig. 2 example. Round 1 broadcasts the degrees; already in that round node 2 drops to 2 and the hub to 3. Nodes 3, …, N − 4 then drop one per round, and two more rounds settle N − 3, N and then N − 2, N − 1. The paper counts the initial round twice. (worstGraph_execTime) 🔧 Corollary 2 (message complexity) The bound Σ_v d(v)² − 2M counts only update messages and ignores the initial broadcast of the degrees, so for a single edge it gives 0 while 2 messages are sent (corollary_2_false). Impact. The bound holds for update messages, which is what the proof counts, and O(∆ · M) stands. Details. Algorithm 1 sends every degree to every neighbour at initialization, which is 2M messages. Repair. We prove the bound for update messages, and Σ_v d(v)² for all messages. (corollary_2_updates, total_messages_le) ✏️ Slips In Theorem 1's proof (⇐), "d_{G(U)}(v) ≥ k + 1" should be ≥ k. Algorithm 2 returns 1, not 0, when no neighbour has estimate ≥ 1; this is harmless, because it never happens in a run. Algorithm 5 (§3.2.1) builds S from all boundary estimates every round without testing changed[u], so as printed it never becomes silent; the test is in Algorithm 3. The Fig. 3 family has diameter 2 (not 3) for N = 5, 6. Typos In Theorem 2's proof, "|V₁| = k(u)" should be k(u₁), and "⟨u₂, core(u₃)⟩" should be ⟨u₃, core(u₃)⟩. In Theorem 4's proof, "at most one message is broadcast per round" is loose wording for "at least one estimate decreases in every round but the first". Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 3 (liveness, induction step) The proof builds a cycle of stuck nodes of coreness k and assumes each of them has k neighbours of coreness > k, which nothing guarantees. Impact. Statement true; proved by a fixpoint argument (le_coreness_of_le_hIndex, theorem_3). Details. The proof says "the remaining f − 1 ≥ k neighbors of u₁ have coreness k + 1 or more". Such a node may have many neighbours of coreness exactly k. Repair. A stable estimate vector c with c(u) ≤ h-index of the neighbours' c lies below the coreness, since {v : c(v) ≥ c(u)} induces minimum degree ≥ c(u). (le_coreness_of_le_hIndex, theorem_3) 🔧 Theorem 5 (execution time ≤ N) The proof says "the execution time equals T + 1", which is off by one in the model of §4.2, and its compensating argument for T ≤ N − 1 skips the case where the last two wrong nodes become correct in consecutive rounds. Impact. Statement true; proved via the progress claim (progress, corollary_1, theorem_5). Details. T is the first round in which all estimates are correct. In the model of §4.2 the execution time equals T: in Fig. 2, T = 3 and the time is 3. (With the indexing of the Fig. 2 narrative, T + 1 is right, and the lost round is instead that the nodes of minimal degree are correct already before round 1.) To compensate, the proof adds an argument for T ≤ N − 1 about the last two wrong nodes, which is incomplete. Repair. The real content is the progress claim: in each round some wrong node of minimal coreness becomes correct. With the correct accounting this gives execTime ≤ N − K + 1 ≤ N at once. The paper argues the progress claim only informally; we prove it. (progress, corollary_1, theorem_5) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A finite simple graph G : SimpleGraph V. Definitions 1–2 are formalized literally: IsKCore is the maximum induced subgraph of minimum degree ≥ k, kCore is its unique witness, and coreness is the largest k with u ∈ kCore k. Estimates live in ℕ∞, with ⊤ = +∞. Synchronous rounds (§4.2), Algorithm 1 at message level (Run.lean). Round 1 broadcasts the degrees. In each later round a node processes the previous round's messages with Algorithm 1's handler, which calls Algorithm 2's computeIndex after every lowering of est. The messages are processed in an arbitrary order, and the node broadcasts iff changed. All results hold for every order. Execution time is the number of rounds in which some node broadcasts, as in the paper. Asynchronous Algorithm 1 (Async.lean), used for Theorems 2–3 in the paper's general setting. Reliable channels with arbitrary delays and reordering, no crashes, and arbitrary scheduling of the periodic repeat every δ block. Liveness assumes fairness: every node ticks infinitely often and every message is eventually delivered. One host, many nodes (MultiHost.lean): Algorithms 3–4 in synchronous rounds with an arbitrary node-to-host assignment. Each host runs improveEstimate to a local fixpoint. The result is the greatest quiescent vector below the input, so it does not depend on the pass order, and processing messages one at a time gives the same state as processing them together. Hosts then broadcast the changed estimates of their own nodes. Messages are delivered to all other hosts, following the text of §3.2. Besides safety and liveness, we prove that after round s + 1 the estimates are at most those of the one-to-one algorithm. So the one-to-many version needs at most as many rounds. Main results in Lean.
