Good-case Latency of Byzantine Broadcast — PODC 2021 Ittai Abraham, Kartik Nayak, Ling Ren, Zhuolun Xiang. Good-case Latency of Byzantine Broadcast: a Complete Categorization. PODC 2021, pp. 331–341. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467899. Formalized version: arXiv:2102.07240v3 (numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All the lower bounds of Table 1 hold after local repairs, and we formalized every one of them: 2 rounds (asynchrony and partial synchrony), 3 rounds for n ≤ 5f − 2, 2δ, Δ + δ, Δ + 1.5δ with unsynchronized start, and Θ(n/(n−f))Δ; for f = n − 1, n ≥ 4 only ⌊n/2⌋Δ is proved instead of (n − 1)Δ, which keeps the Θ. The Δ + 1.5δ executions are invalid with signatures until slightly modified, and several theorems need very small n excluded, mostly outside the paper's intended ranges. Of the upper bounds, on which tightness rests, we checked only the 2-round BRB protocol and the timing core of Lemma 1. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 19 for f = n − 1 (dishonest majority) For f = n − 1 the proof of Theorem 19 does not work, so for n ≥ 4 the claimed (n − 1)Δ is unestablished: the groups of size n − f − 1 are empty and every execution has a single honest party, so agreement gives nothing. Impact. The bound holds for n − f ≥ 2 (even one Δ stronger, dishonestMajority_lower_bound, theorem_19) and for n = 3 (theorem_19_three). For f = n − 1, n ≥ 4 we only get ⌊n/2⌋Δ (allButOne_lower_bound), which still matches the O(n/(n−f))Δ upper bound up to a constant. Details. The hypothesis n − f ≥ 2 of our stronger bound is necessary. For n = 3, f = 2, the 3-party protocol above (at δ = Δ) commits by 2Δ < 3Δ = ⌊n/(n−f)⌋Δ; we argue this transfer informally. The paper's claim (n − 1)Δ for f = n − 1 does hold for n = 3, since it is Theorem 9 with δ = Δ (theorem_19_three). For n ≥ 4 and f = n − 1 the bound ⌊n/2⌋Δ follows by monotonicity in f; this is proved, but not shown tight (allButOne_lower_bound). ✏️ Slips Theorem 10 is false for n = 3 if read literally: a simple 3-party BRB protocol has good-case latency Δ + δ for every f (ThreeParties.theorem_10_false_three). For n = 3 no integer f satisfies the paper's intended range n/3 < f < n/2 (Table 1, §5.4), and the counterexample has f ≥ n/2, so it refutes only the literal hypothesis f > n/3. Theorem 10 holds for all n ≥ 4 (Thm10.theorem_10). Theorems 4, 8 and 9 are false for n = 2: with a single non-broadcaster, "commit the first value received from the broadcaster" is BRB and commits after one message delay (theorem_4_false_two, theorem_8_false_two). The proofs need two non-empty groups besides the broadcaster, and our theorems assume n ≥ 3 (theorem_4, theorem_8, theorem_9). Theorems 6 and 7 fail for n = 1 (theorem_7_false_one). That case forces f ≥ n, outside the paper's implicit f < n. Typos In Theorem 19 the broadcaster's split assigns both values to the middle group (overlapping index ranges). Execution 1 of Theorem 10 is described differently in Section 5.4 ("C pretends to start late") and in Appendix C.4 (modified delays). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 10 (signatures in the lower-bound executions) The paper assumes ideal signatures but never checks unforgeability, and with it Executions 2 and 3 of Theorem 10 are not valid executions as written. Impact. The statement stands and the indistinguishability chain is kept, with some links delayed in Executions 1 and 4 (Thm10.theorem_10, X_authValid). Details. In Execution 1 the Byzantine C and h behave honestly with value 0 and reach the honest B within δ. In Execution 2 the Byzantine B must replay its Execution-1 messages to g until about Δ + 0.5δ. Those messages can relay C's signatures on 0-messages, which the honest C of Execution 2 (holding 1) never produces. The replays in Theorems 7 and 9 need truncation in time, which is harmless. Repair. Delaying C → B and h → B in Execution 1 (and the mirror links in Execution 4) fixes it (X_authValid). 🔧 Lemma 1, parts (1) and (2) (the Δ + 1.5δ protocol) The proof argues that a conflicting proposal reaching h by its commit time t "stops h from committing", but Step 4a only checks for equivocation until t_prop + Δ + 0.5d, which can be earlier than t. Impact. The lemma stands (Lemma1.part1, Lemma1.part2). Repair. Compare with t_prop + 0.5d instead; we check this timing core abstractly (Lemma1.part1, Lemma1.part2). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Base model. We use the shared Byzantine message-passing model of CSLib (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync): discrete time and deterministic state machines; at most f static Byzantine parties; the adversary chooses every delivery time; ideal unforgeable signatures as abstract tokens. Every lower bound is proved for authenticated protocols and therefore also covers unauthenticated ones. Synchrony. The protocol knows Δ and must be correct in all runs with delays ≤ Δ. Good-case latency for an actual bound δ quantifies over runs with delays ≤ δ. Time is counted with effective delays: a message received at time t is in the state at time t, and a reply can leave at t. So "commits before T" means "decided in the state at T − 1". Delays are ≥ 1, which only weakens the adversary. (This SyncValid f d is the shared library class Run.SyncValid f (d − 1) of Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/PartialSync/RunClasses.lean up to the GST, bridge syncValid_iff.) Partial synchrony. We use CSLib's convention: rounds of length D, and "within r rounds" means the state at rD + 1. The lower bounds use lock-step executions. Asynchrony. Asynchronous executions are all runs of the model, i.e. runs with an unknown GST and an unknown post-GST delay bound (asyncRuns f = library Run.AsyncValidBounded f, bounded asynchrony; not the unbounded class Run.AsyncValid). Asynchronous rounds (Appendix A) are not formalized: Theorem 4 is stated for lock-step executions, and Theorem 5's latency as "two message delays". Unsynchronized start. The wrapper lateStart gives each party its own start time; nothing reaches a correct party before it starts. This constraint also covers time-0 batches, so every correct party starts before time d (the run's delay bound). Theorem 10 assumes skew δ/2, δ = 2e even and δ < Δ. Byzantine parties "behaving honestly with other delays" are correct parties of an auxiliary run, made Byzantine with Run.enlarge. Main results in Lean (namespace GoodCaseLatencyBB). Coordinated Consensus in Dynamic Networks — PODC 2011 Fabian Kuhn, Yoram Moses, Rotem Oshman. Coordinated Consensus in Dynamic Networks. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993808. Formalized version: the 10-page proceedings version (no full version exists); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All the bounds survive, and most hold as printed or after a local change: Lemma 3.1 (the knowledge test for "I have heard from everybody"), Theorem 5.1 (nothing non-trivial is common knowledge before time n − 1 with known n, or n with unknown n, so simultaneous consensus needs exactly n − 1, resp. n, rounds), Theorem 6.1, Lemmas 6.2–6.4 and Theorem 6.7 (the static-line lower bound n − O(Δ^{0.28} n^{0.72})). The lower bound Ω(nD/Δ) of Theorem 6.8, one of the results the abstract closes on, is only a sketch that never specifies its graph H; we had to supply a new construction of H and the walk. Theorem 4.1, the running-time claim of the dynamic-diameter protocol (its final bound nD/(D+Δ) + Δ holds) and Lemma 6.5 are false as printed, each with a local fix. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 4.1 (quantifier order) Theorem 4.1 claims one bit i such that, in every execution with all inputs i and the upper bound 2n, no node decides before hearing from everybody, but the bound 2n reveals n, so a correct algorithm may favour 0 for some sizes and 1 for others (theorem_4_1_literal_false). Impact. No single bit works for all network sizes. Details. Counterexample: decide b = [⌊N/2⌋ odd] as soon as an input b is heard, else decide ¬b at time N − 1. This is a correct comparison-based consensus algorithm for every valid bound N ≥ n. It decides at time 0 in the all-0 execution with n = 2 and in the all-1 execution with n = 3. The stitching proof tacitly assumes that both bad executions have the same size. Repair. The per-n version ("for every n there is an i") and its proof are correct (theorem_4_1). 🔧 Running time of the dynamic-diameter protocol (§6) The paper says nodes can stop at n − kmax·Δ − 1 once kmax ≥ ⌊n/(D+Δ)⌋, but level k fires only when k(D+Δ) ≤ n − 1; a counterexample is the static graph on 6 nodes with D = 2, Δ = 1 (diamProtocol_counterexample_strict). Impact. Only the intermediate claim fails; the final bound t < nD/(D+Δ) + Δ is still true (diamProtocol_decides, diamProtocol_time). Details. The paper's side condition (k−1)D < n − kΔ − 1 is necessary but not sufficient. To know that the diameter was ≤ D up to time (k−1)D, a node must hear every node's state at that time, which takes until kD. The paper is inconsistent about the side condition: the rule says (k−1)D ≤ n − kΔ − 1, and the later remark says <. With ≤, the 4-clique with D = Δ = 1, kmax = 2 is a counterexample: nobody decides at time 1, because a node cannot exclude that round 1 was a star centred at itself (diamProtocol_counterexample). With the strict < and D = 1, the paper's condition coincides with the correct one, so a counterexample needs D ≥ 2. One exists: n = 6, D = 2, Δ = 1, kmax = 2, and the static graph with edges 01, 02, 03, 14, 24, 35, 45 (diameter 2). Node 3 cannot decide at time 3: it cannot exclude an execution in which node 2 has not heard from node 5 by time 3 (diamProtocol_counterexample_strict). Repair. Use the condition k(D+Δ) ≤ n − 1 and kmax ≥ ⌊(n−1)/(D+Δ)⌋. 🔧 Lemma 6.5 (wrong node) The node that cannot distinguish the cycle-prefix from the path-prefix execution is u_{k+s+1} (the start of P_{k+s}), not u_{k+s−1} (lemma_6_5_paper_node_false). Impact. The wrong index is repeated in the statement, the proof and Figure 2, but later uses need only some node. Details. In the instance n = 6, k = 0, s = 2, a = 1, b = 2, t = 3, u_1 does distinguish. Repair. Corrected index: lemma_6_5. ✏️ Slips Lemma 6.5, case s < 0: the hypothesis must be a + b < n − |s| (lemma_6_5_neg_false). This case is never used: only s ≥ 0 is used later. Fast and Exact Majority (AVC) — PODC 2015 Dan Alistarh, Rati Gelashvili, Milan Vojnović. Fast and Exact Majority in Population Protocols. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767429. Formalized version: the full version, Microsoft Research technical report MSR-TR-2015-13 (February 2015, with appendices). Numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. With a one-symbol typo in Figure 1 fixed, AVC solves exact majority with probability 1 from every configuration with non-zero sum (Lemma A.1, Theorem 4.1 first part), for all n, m, d. The four-state lower bound announced in the abstract (Theorem B.1) is proved only for unordered interactions, the convention of the paper's proof, while the paper states it for all protocols in its ordered model. The convergence-time bounds, the paper's main claim, and the Ω(log n) lower bound were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem B.1 for ordered interactions (unestablished) Theorem B.1 is stated for "any majority algorithm using four states" with ordered (initiator, responder) interactions, but its proof treats [S0, X] and [X, S0] as one interaction with a single outcome, so it does not cover protocols whose two orientations differ. Impact. Not refuted, and very likely true: we prove Theorem B.1 for unordered interactions, the convention of the paper's proof (theorem_B_1, hypothesis Symmetric P); for ordered protocols the gap is closed only by a script, not in Lean. For unordered interactions, every correct four-state protocol preserves #S0 − #S1, so the probability of converging within t steps is at most 2t(ϵn+1)/(n(n−1)). Details. Section 2 defines δ : Q × Q → Q × Q with ordered (initiator, responder) pairs, and AVC itself assigns different states to initiator and responder. Claims B.2–B.5 do not need symmetry (we prove them for both orientations), and an exhaustive search over ordered protocols with populations of at most 5 agents refutes every protocol that does not preserve #S0 − #S1. Since refuting certificates on small populations are valid for every n, this search would close the gap, but it is a script, not Lean. Symmetric P means that both orientations of a pair give the same multiset of states, though possibly to different agents. See differencies.md (item 7). ✏️ Slips Figure 1, line 12 (value for weight). Line 12 reads "weight(x)·weight(y) = 0 and value(x) + value(y) > 0", so a weak node meeting a node of negative value skips lines 12–14 and falls through to line 19, which changes nothing: +0 never becomes −0, and AVC can fail when B is the majority (literal_fails, not_tendsto_literal). Counterexample with m = d = 1, the four-state protocol, and inputs A, B, B (states 1₁, −1₁, −1₁). The first two agents interact by line 17 into −0, +0. The configuration −0, +0, −1₁ is silent, and agent 2 outputs A forever. This happens after one step with positive probability, so the probability of converging to B does not tend to 1. A model checker finds the same failure for m = 3 (inputs A, B, B give +3, −3, −3) and every other small parameter set we tried, from many initial configurations. The prose under Figure 1 describes the intended condition weight(x) + weight(y) > 0 ("zero meets non-zero"). With it, the protocol is sign-symmetric (update_neg) and solves exact majority with probability 1 (lemma_A_1, theorem_4_1_correct). The proof of Lemma A.1 assumes "without loss of generality S > 0", and for S > 0 the literal rule happens to work; it is the sign symmetry behind this WLOG that the typo destroys. "three nodes starting in C0" (Case 2.3) should be S0. In Case 2.4.1 the configuration "two X, three S1" needs two applications of [X, Y] → [S1, X], not one. At the end of Case 2.4.1 ("[X, Y] into [S0, Y]") the contradiction is with the second property, not the third. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Population protocols on the complete graph, CSLib's model: n labelled agents, a deterministic transition function δ on ordered (initiator, responder) pairs, no failures. AVC is avc d; its states are ±0, ±1_j and strong values v (odd, 3 ≤ |v| ≤ m). Figure 1 is transcribed line by line (update): lit = true is the printed version, lit = false the corrected one. Randomness: the uniformly random scheduler of Section 2, i.e. an ordered pair of distinct agents drawn uniformly at each step (CSLib's uniformKernel, a Markov kernel on the finite set of configurations over valid states). "With probability 1" means that the probability of not being converged after t steps tends to 0; the converged set is proved closed. Algorithm 1 is undefined in every phase j = 0, which uses D_{i,0} = √(2^i/0^{1+ε}) and t_{i,0} = 2^{i+2}/0^{1+ε}, and for k = 1 the proof uses exactly this phase. Also, "O(log^{1+ε} k)-competitive" literally means a bound 0 for k = 1. We use (j+1)^{1+ε} and prove Thm 3.3 as C (1 + log₂ k)^{1+ε} (D + D²/k) (theorem_3_3); the 1 + handles k = 1. Algorithm 2 (Thm 5.1, distribution at the source). p(u) = c/d(u)^{2+δ} is infinite at the source s. We set p(s) = 0 (harmonicPMF). Thm 5.1 (wording). "With probability at least 1 − ε, the expected running time is O(…)" is meaningless as written. The proof shows the intended claim, that with probability ≥ 1 − ε the running time is O(D + D^{2+δ}/k), and this is what we prove (theorem_5_1). Footnote 2. The bound Ω(D + D²/k) is stated for the distance D, but the footnote's argument finds a treasure at distance at most D, which is what we prove (footnote_2); see below. Thm 4.2 (empty range). The proof bounds φ(k̃) by the number of admissible i in [⌈(1−ε)/2 · log k̃⌉, ⌊½ log k̃⌋]. This range may be empty when ε(k̃) log k̃ < 2. Then Ω(ε log k) needs the trivial bound φ = Ω(1) (footnote 2). We add it (one_div_le_of_competitive). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Thm 4.1 (the shells need not be nested) The proof's claim |Sᵢ|/kᵢ = Ω(T/φ(kᵢ)) "since φ(kᵢ) = O(i)" needs Dᵢ > Dᵢ₋₁, i.e. φ(2ⁱ) < 2φ(2ⁱ⁻¹), which does not follow from φ(k) = O(log k). Impact. The theorem stands, and the paper's intermediate claim is proved for every φ (theorem_4_1, sum_inv_le_of_isCompetitive). Details. The proof takes kᵢ = 2ⁱ, Dᵢ = √(T kᵢ/φ(kᵢ)) and the shells Sᵢ = B(Dᵢ) \ B(Dᵢ₋₁). Even Dᵢ > Dᵢ₋₁ is not enough; it needs a quantitative version of it. An O(log k) function may jump by a factor 4 at some i, and then Sᵢ = ∅. (For O(log k) alone, the paper's proof can also be saved by running it with φ replaced by its bound c·log k, for which the radii do increase.) Repair. Replace the radii by their running maxima R'ᵢ = max_{j≤i} Rⱼ. A node within distance Rⱼ, j ≤ i, is still visited with probability ≥ 1/(2·2ⁱ). The shells are then combined by Abel summation. This proves the paper's intermediate claim for every φ: if a uniform algorithm is φ-competitive, then ∑ᵢ 1/φ(2ⁱ) ≤ 320 (sum_inv_le_of_isCompetitive, summable_inv_of_isCompetitive). Thm 4.1 follows (theorem_4_1). The bound also excludes, e.g., φ = O(log k · log log k), since ∑ 1/(i log i) diverges (this remark is not formalized). 🔧 Thm 5.1 (constants in the proof) With α = 12β/c and λ = 4βD^{1+δ}/(ck), the hypothesis k > αD^δ gives only λ < D/3, not the claimed λ < D/4, so "√(λD) < D/2, hence 3D/4 < d(u) < 5D/4" does not follow. Impact. The theorem stands; both errors only change constants (theorem_5_1). Details. Also, "there are at least λD/2 nodes in B_λ" is false for small radii. For example, radius √(λD)/2 = 1.9 gives λD/2 ≈ 7.2, but the ball has 5 nodes. Repair. We prove the theorem with α = 16σγ, γ = 2·(5/4)^{2+δ}·ln(1/ε)/c (theorem_5_1). The restriction δ ≤ 0.8 is not needed. 🔧 Thm 3.3 ("half of the ball") The proof says "at least half of the ball of radius √t_{i,j} around the treasure is contained in B(D_{i,j})", but the fraction can be less than 1/2. Impact. The theorem stands: a constant fraction suffices (card_near_ge). Details. The proof also uses radius √t where its own spiral convention gives √t/2. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Grid ℤ², source s = (0,0), d = hop (ℓ₁) distance. The search is synchronous: one node per time unit, and all agents start together. The treasure τ is chosen adversarially; we quantify over all τ. Agents are probabilistic and identical, and they do not communicate. Lower bounds (§4, footnote 2). An agent is a probability law on trajectories ℕ → ℤ². The k agents are independent (Measure.pi). The running time is the first time some agent is at τ; T(D,k) is its expectation (expectedTime). A trajectory up to the find time cannot depend on τ, so a τ-independent law is no restriction. Uniform means one law for every k. With advice, agent a uses the law A k̃ₐ of its own estimate. φ-competitive means T ≤ φ(k)(D + D²/k) for all k ≥ 1 and all τ ≠ s. The lower bounds do not assume grid walks: an agent may move arbitrarily (one node per time unit), which makes them stronger. Footnote 2's Ω(D) part assumes walks from the source (IsWalk). Upper bounds (§3, §5). We use the paper's atomic navigation procedures (§2, footnote 1). Walking to u takes d(u) steps, returning from the end of a spiral of length t takes ≤ d(u) + t steps, and a spiral of length t from u visits every v with σ·d(u,v)² ≤ t. The paper's convention is σ = 4; we keep any σ ≥ 1 as a parameter. A phase "uniform u ∈ B(R), spiral t, return" thus lasts ≤ 2R + 2t. An agent whose u satisfies the spiral condition has found τ by the end of the phase. All random choices of all agents in all phases are independent (Measure.infinitePi). The running time bound is ∑_b dur(b) · 1[not found before block b], where block b is a stage or big stage and dur(b) bounds every agent's block duration (phasedTime). Its expectation is computed exactly (lintegral_timeBound). For the harmonic algorithm, the time of an agent that picked u is d(u) + σ d(u,τ)² when the spiral reaches τ (harmonicBound). The navigation procedures themselves are not constructed in Lean, matching the paper's abstraction. Main results in Lean. Formalized version: arXiv 1302.2543 v1 (full version with appendices); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The main contribution stands: Theorems 1–5 and Lemma 1 hold, so exact BVC in synchrony is solvable iff n ≥ max(3f+1, (d+1)f+1), and approximate asynchronous BVC needs n ≥ (d+2)f+1 and is achieved by the paper's algorithm, given the AAD exchange primitive. The tight bounds for restricted algorithms announced in the abstract are lost: the synchronous necessity in Theorem 6 (Section 4, stated without proof) is false for the class as defined, though likely true for the intended hull-preserving iterative class. The asynchronous necessity has no argument and is unchecked, and only the sufficiency halves survive, the asynchronous one after a one-constant change to Step 2. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 6, synchronous necessity (restricted algorithms need n ≥ (d+2)f+1) The necessity claim is false as stated: for n = 4, d = 2, f = 1 (where (d+2)f+1 = 5) a restricted algorithm whose vector state encodes the received inputs solves even exact BVC in two rounds (theorem_6_sync_necessity_false, round-independent: theorem_6_sync_necessity_false'). Impact. The definition is under-specified, so the tightness claimed for restricted synchronous algorithms fails for the class as defined. The claim is likely true for the intended hull-preserving iterative class, but we formalized nothing under such a reading. Section 4 states it without proof, and Theorems 1–5 and Lemma 1 do not depend on it. Details. Section 4 defines the restricted synchronous structure only as "send your vector state to everybody, then compute the new state as a function of the old one and the received vectors". But the update function is unrestricted, and one vector of reals can encode any finite amount of real data. So the state can carry a full-information history. The algorithm: in round 1, store the encoded vector of received inputs. In round 2, for each k, take the majority of the values for k relayed by the three other processes (OM(1)), then output the chosen point of Γ. It is a restricted algorithm. The claim presumably needs an extra restriction that the paper does not state, e.g. that the new state lies in the hull of the received states. Our restricted class lets the update depend on the round number t. This is harmless: in synchrony processes know t, and the paper's own algorithm stops after a fixed round. A second counterexample does not use t at all: inputs lie in the box [0,1]², encodings lie outside it, so the own state tells the rounds apart. (theorem_6_sync_necessity_false, round-independent: theorem_6_sync_necessity_false') ✏️ Slips Theorems 4 and 5 ("necessary and sufficient"): Theorem 4 fails for inputs of width ≤ ε. Theorem 5 assumes known bounds [ν, U]^d, and with U − ν ≤ ε approximate BVC is trivial for every n (ownInput_solves_of_narrow). So the pair is tight only when U − ν > ε; theorem_4 needs inputs of width > ε, as in the paper's own 4ε inputs. The round count 1 + ⌈log_{1/(1−γ)}((U−ν)/ε)⌉ is meaningless for U = ν and negative for U − ν < ε. Read it as 1 + ⌈·⌉₊, which works (rounds_spec). Typos Section 4: "the proof of correctness … is similar to the proof of Theorem 4" should say Theorem 5. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 6, asynchronous sufficiency (Step 2 under-specified) The paper's Step 2 "analogous to Section 3.2" averages over subsets of B_i of size n − f, but here |B_i| = n − f, so Z_i is a single point and two correct processes need not share a point of Z. Impact. Sufficiency holds for n ≥ (d+4)f+1 with a repaired Step 2 (theorem_6_async). Details. The paper's argument (a common point z_ij) breaks. Section 4 says the proof relies on |B_i ∩ B_j| ≥ (d+1)f+1; it needs a common C ⊆ B_i ∩ B_j of the subset size used in Step 2. Repair. With subsets of size n − 3f, or any s with (d+1)f < s ≤ n − 3f, the argument goes through and gives sufficiency for n ≥ (d+4)f+1 (theorem_6_async). 🔧 Theorem 4 (scenario with a slow correct process) In the scenario "p_j faulty, p_{d+2} correct but slow", validity gives the hull of X_i^j ∪ {x_{d+2}}, not H(X_i^j), and with the paper's fixed choice x_{d+2} = 0 and j = d+1 the argument gives no contradiction. Impact. Statement true (theorem_4); only the choice of x_{d+2} changes. Details. The paper's own remark that "p_i has no information about x_{d+2}" already implies the fix: choose x_{d+2} per scenario inside H(X_i^j). Only the later sentence fixing x_{d+2} = 0 for all scenarios is inconsistent with that remark. Repair. We pick the slow group's input per scenario (theorem_4). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Exact BVC and the lower bounds use CSLib's Byzantine message-passing model Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync. It has a complete network of n = |P| deterministic state machines and at most t Byzantine processes. The adversary chooses the faulty set, the inputs, the Byzantine messages (which may differ per receiver) and the delivery times. Synchronous runs are runs with gst = 0; the bounded delay δ is arbitrary. "Asynchronous" lower bounds are proved in the partially synchronous model (any finite gst). It has fewer runs than the asynchronous model, and its processes have synchronized clocks, so the impossibility is stronger than the paper's. Specifications. Exact BVC uses CSLib's SolvesConsensusSync with bvcValidity (decision in the convex hull of the correct inputs). Approximate BVC is SolvesApproxBVC/SolvesApproxBVCSync: termination, ε-agreement in every coordinate, and validity, for correct inputs in a domain K. Theorem 5's algorithm is modelled on the level of round exchanges (RoundExec), exactly as the paper's proof uses them. In each round, every correct process obtains a set B_i of senders and tuple values. Byzantine values may differ per receiver. Correct senders carry their current state (Property 3), and at most one tuple per sender is built in (Property 2). Properties 1 and |B_i| ≥ n − f are hypotheses (RoundExec.Valid). AAD's Component #1 itself (reliable broadcast + witnesses, from [AAD04]) is not implemented: Theorem 5 is proved for every execution in which Component #1 delivers sets with Properties 1–3, as in the paper. The Section 4 synchronous structure is modelled directly (RestrictedAlg, SyncExec): the state is a vector, the update is arbitrary and may depend on the round number, and Byzantine processes send arbitrary vectors to each receiver. Communication Complexity of Byzantine Agreement, Revisited — PODC 2019 Ittai Abraham, T-H. Hubert Chan, Danny Dolev, Kartik Nayak, Rafael Pass, Ling Ren, Elaine Shi. Communication Complexity of Byzantine Agreement, Revisited. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331629. Formalized version: arXiv 1805.03391 v4 (15 Feb 2020); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Both lower bounds hold with new arguments for their central steps: Theorem 4 / Theorem 1 (strongly adaptive adversary ⇒ Ω(f²) expected messages), with a better constant εf²/2 instead of (εf)², and Theorem 13 (no setup ⇒ no sublinear-multicast Byzantine broadcast), which needs n ≥ C + 2. The proof of Theorem 7, the expected constant rounds and O(λ) multicasts of the synchronous subquadratic protocol, has a wrong step whose apparent fix is not proved in Lean. The upper-bound sections (4–6, 9) were otherwise not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 7 and Lemma 2 (Section 5.3, wrong threshold; not formalized) Theorem 7's proof claims that (1/2+ε/2)n so-far-honest nodes have not terminated, which needs fewer than εn/2 terminated honest nodes, not fewer than n/2. Impact. Not formalized and not Lean-checked, so nothing we proved saves the step. With the case split at εn/2, Lemma 3 still holds with probability 1 − (1−λ/n)^{εn/2} ≥ 1 − e^{−ελ/2}; this is argued informally only. Details. Lemma 2's statement is true, but its proof's n_h > n/2 is wrong: fewer than n/2 terminated forever-honest nodes only gives n_h > εn, because there are only about (1/2+ε)n honest nodes. This still gives a Θ(1) probability, so Lemma 2 survives. The real error is in Theorem 7. 🔧 Theorem 13 (Byzantine broadcast without setup) for n = 2 Theorem 13 is false for n = 2: with nodes {sender, S} and C = 1, the sender sends its bit once and S outputs it, which solves Byzantine broadcast with probability 1 with at most one speaker (theorem_13_false_n2). Impact. The impossibility survives with one added condition: the theorem holds for n ≥ C + 2 (theorem_13). Details. The protocol solves broadcast against one adaptive corruption. The proof needs a forever-honest node other than S in world W_{h,b}, so it needs n ≥ C + 2. The counterexample is Lean-checked against our restricted (injecting) adversary. It is also valid against the full Byzantine adversary: an honest S can only be fooled by a corrupt sender, and then validity is vacuous. That part is argued informally only. Repair. We prove the theorem under 1 ≤ C, C + 2 ≤ n (theorem_13). ✏️ Slips Lemma 1 (Section 5.3, not formalized) says that, except with probability exp(−Ω(λ)), fewer than λ/2 eventually-corrupt nodes are eligible for any given message; this is false as stated. In iteration 1 all honest nodes vote for their common input b, and about (1/2+ε)λ eligible honest nodes send (Vote, 1, b). The adaptive adversary then corrupts them all, after the fact; its budget f ≈ n/2 ≫ λ allows this. So more than λ/2 eventually-corrupt nodes are eligible with probability close to 1. The proof ("each so-far-honest node independently has a λ/n probability") ignores that corruption can depend on revealed eligibility. The intended term counts nodes that were already corrupt when they mined the message, the distinction the paper itself makes in Section 4.3. With it the consistency proof (Theorems 5 and 6) goes through, as argued informally: the node i* only needs to be honest when it sends Commit, not forever-honest. The same imprecision ("forever-honest" / "eventually-corrupt") appears in Theorems 5, 6 and 9. Theorem 8 says "O(λ) messages" and Theorem 12 says "O(λ² log Δ) messages". Both mean multicasts; Theorems 7 and 11 say O(nλ) / O(nλ² log Δ) messages. Proof of Theorem 4: V must avoid the designated sender, so one needs f/2 ≤ ⌈n/2⌉ − 1 rather than f/2 < ⌈n/2⌉. With f < n and |V| = ⌈f/2⌉ it is fine. Typos "Section 8 presents the model" / "for the reasons mentioned in Section 8" should refer to Section 2. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4 (the key conditional-probability step) The proof's claim Pr[Y₁ | X₁ ∩ X₂] ≥ 1/2, "by the definition of V", is unjustified: V only bounds the unconditional probability that p, receiving nothing, outputs 0. Impact. The bound survives through a new argument, with a better constant εf²/2 instead of (εf)² (theorem_4, theorem_4_paper, Protocol.core_bound). Details. The proof conditions on X₁ ∩ X₂: under adversary A, the randomly chosen p ∈ V receives at most f/2 messages. Both p's silent output and X₁ ∩ X₂ depend on p's own coins. Under A, p behaves honestly towards U, so it can reveal its coin, and U can then contact p exactly when p's silent output would be 1. With a plain union bound the paper's constants only give Pr[Y₁ ∩ Y₂] > 1/4 - 3ε, which is no contradiction. Repair. Two steps. For every p ∈ V, the event "p does not output 0 when silent" is covered by three events: failure under A, failure under A'_p, and "U sends p more than f/2 messages". Markov's inequality is applied to each p separately, instead of the paper's Markov-plus-averaging step. This gives E[#messages] ≥ 2ε·⌈f/2⌉·(⌊f/2⌋+1) ≥ εf²/2. Since ε ≤ 1/4, this is at least the paper's (εf)². (theorem_4, theorem_4_paper, Protocol.core_bound) 🛠️ Theorem 13 ("Pr[A_s] ≥ p" and the speaker count of A_r) The proof's bound "Pr[A_s] ≥ p" is unjustified, and A_r is measured wrongly: the protocol's complexity guarantee counts only messages of honest nodes, and the simulated execution A_s is not an execution against any adversary. Impact. For n ≥ C + 2 the threshold 5/6 survives: the bound Pr[A_r ∩ A_s] ≥ 2p − 1 is re-proved by a first-crossing argument (theorem_13_general, Protocol.not_E, Protocol.output_S_symm). Details. In W_{h,b} the adversary has corrupted the simulated speakers, so the guarantee does not bound the number of speakers of the whole real copy, which is what the symmetry argument needs. No guarantee applies to A_s directly. Repair. The first-crossing argument uses only the worlds W_{c,b} and W_{c,1−b} (there only S is corrupted): whichever copy exceeds C speakers first does so identically in the corresponding W_c world. The paper's "without loss of generality Pr[X | A_r ∩ A_s] ≥ 1/2" is also replaced by an explicit symmetry. A measure-preserving exchange of the two copies' tapes maps W_{h,0} to W_{h,1}. Measurability is never needed. (theorem_13_general, Protocol.not_E, Protocol.output_S_symm) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model for Theorems 4 and 1 (Model.lean). n nodes, lock-step synchronous rounds, infinite executions. Each node's output is its first decision. Randomness is one probability space (Ω, μ), and nodes may use ω arbitrarily. This covers private coins, shared coins and any setup (PKI, CRS, random oracle), as the paper claims. The protocol is history-based: send p x ω h q : Option M and decide p x ω h : Option Bool. Regularity: messages are countable, and send/decide are measurable in ω for each fixed history (Protocol.IsMeasurable). This is needed only for Markov's inequality and for the classification of silent outputs. The adversary is a deterministic strongly adaptive omission adversary with budget f. It sees the communication pattern, including the current round. It then corrupts nodes and removes any current-round message whose sender or receiver is now corrupted (after-the-fact removal). Corrupted nodes otherwise follow the protocol. This is the weakest adversary class the proof needs (the paper notes the bound holds even for omission adversaries). Against a weaker class, "the protocol is secure" is a weaker hypothesis, so the lower bound is stronger. Failure events are measured by the outer measure. The expected number of messages sent by forever-honest nodes is ∫⁻ honestMsgs. Model for Theorem 13 (NoSetupModel.lean). No setup: independent private tapes ω p ~ ν p. Plain authenticated channels with multisets of messages per channel and round. The adversary has independent fresh tapes ρ. It sees all past messages, corrupts adaptively (at most C nodes), and injects extra messages on channels with a corrupted endpoint. Corrupted nodes keep running the protocol. This is a restriction of the paper's Byzantine adversary, which makes the impossibility stronger. Complexity is "at most C forever-honest nodes ever speak". Multicast complexity ≤ C implies it. We assume the BB guarantee and the complexity guarantee hold separately, each with probability p. This is weaker than assuming them jointly. Main results in Lean. On the (Limited) Power of Non-Equivocation — PODC 2012 Allen Clement, Flavio Junqueira, Aniket Kate, Rodrigo Rodrigues. On the (Limited) Power of Non-Equivocation. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332490. Formalized version: the 8-page author copy (A. Kate's Purdue page; no arXiv version), which includes the appendices. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The two lower bounds hold for n ≥ 3: Claim 3.1 says non-equivocation without transferable authentication does not beat n > 3f, and Claim 3.2 says signatures without non-equivocation do not beat it either. The positive direction holds for r-broadcast: with both primitives it works for every n and f. But the paper's generic crash-to-Byzantine translation (Section 4, Figure 2, Appendix B) is unsound: a crash-safe 3-process protocol becomes unsafe after translation with one Byzantine process, because a Byzantine process can replay messages that were addressed to other processes, and no repaired compiler is proved. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Section 4, Figure 2, Appendix B (crash-to-Byzantine translation) The translation does not preserve the guarantees of crash-tolerant protocols: a 3-process protocol in which server 0 records only client 1 in every crash execution, once translated, lets a single Byzantine client 2 replay the grant addressed to 1 and get itself recorded by the correct server (Translation.translation_unsafe). Impact. Refutes the paper's witness for the claim "it is possible to … transform" any crash-tolerant protocol (abstract, intro, §4), which stays unestablished; a repaired compiler appears to exist. The lower bounds of Section 3 are unaffected. Details. Section 4 claims that Figure 2 turns any protocol tolerating f crashes into one tolerating f Byzantine faults with the same number of processes ("provides the same guarantees", abstract and introduction). A translated B-message ((k, m, R, S), σ) carries the sender's received messages R and sent messages S. The receiver replays the sender's state machine on R. Neither the signed tuple nor the checks mention recipients. So a Byzantine process can feed its replayed state machine an authentic message that a correct process sent to someone else, and everything it then sends passes the checks. It learns such messages, signature included, from the R field of any later message of their recipient. The paper's Integrity requirement (§4.1) has the same blind spot: a valid message is "the output of applying a sequence of valid messages to the state machine", with no condition on who those messages were sent to. So Appendix B's argument cannot exclude this attack. Counterexample (n = 3, f = 1). Server 0 grants a token to client 1 only. A client granted by 0 multicasts use to the two other processes, and the server records who sent use. In every crash execution the server records only 1 (any crashes, losses, or orders). In the translated system: client 1 T-receives the grant g and multicasts u₁ = ((1, use, [g], []), σ₁); the Byzantine client 2 takes g out of u₁ and sends u₂ = ((1, use, [g], []), σ₂) to the server; u₂ passes all checks, so the correct server records 2. The adversary signs only as 2, relays 0's signature that it has seen, and uses key 1 once, so it respects unforgeability and non-equivocation. u₂ is exactly what the translated code of a correct 2 would send after receiving g. Its signed contents equal those of the honest u₁; only the signer differs. So every reading of the sloppy check kp = |Rp| = |Sp| that accepts u₁ from 1 also accepts u₂ from 2. A verifier could reject u₂ by recomputing, during the recursive replay, each input's recipient set (grant goes to {1}). But Figure 2 compares only payloads with Sp, and neither §4.1 Integrity nor Appendix B asks for a recipient check. Adding one changes the protocol; it is not a reading of it. So the failure is real, not just a gap. Every statement of the claim (abstract, intro, §4) is existential ("it is possible to … transform", "there exists a translation"), not "Figure 2 is correct". The counterexample refutes only the paper's witness, and a repaired compiler appears to exist. (Translation.translation_unsafe, Translation.check_u₂, Translation.attack_eq_honest) Repair. One repair is to sign recipient sets, check that every replayed input was addressed to the sender, and reject duplicate inputs. Ben-David, Chan and Shi (PODC 2022) give a corrected compiler in a multicast model. We did not formalize a repaired translation. 🔧 Claims 3.1 and 3.2 for n ≤ 2 Both claims are stated for every n < 3f + 1, but for n ≤ 2 r-broadcast is solvable for every f, without signatures and against equivocation (claim_3_1_false_small, claim_3_2_false_small). Impact. The added condition 3 ≤ n saves the bound: both claims hold for 3 ≤ n ≤ 3f (Claim31.claim_3_1, Claim32.claim_3_2). The proof of Claim 3.2 is otherwise correct. Details. Both proofs assume "w.l.o.g. n = 3f" with three nonempty groups. For n ≤ 2, the sender delivers its message and keeps sending it, and the other process delivers the first message it gets from the sender. Two distinct correct processes then include the sender. ✏️ Slips Figure 2, check kp = |Rp| = |Sp|: read literally, it rejects every honest message (for example u₁ has k = 1, |R| = 1, |S| = 0). The key is the sender's sequence number, and Appendix B does not depend on the exact form; we read the check as k = |S| + 1. Figure 2, receive handler: the received message is added to R only after the T-receive handler runs, so outputs caused by it are not justified by R and honest messages fail the replay check. We add it before, the order Appendix B describes. Typos In Claim 3.1's proof, Run 2 says "by the Agreement property", but the step also needs Completeness (L2). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Claim 3.1 (Run 3) In Run 3, messages between A and B are "delivered in a timely fashion" throughout, but the processes of A do not crash at time t, so after t the processes of B may act differently from Run 2, and then C need not deliver m', as the proof claims. Impact. Statement true for n ≥ 3; repaired (Claim31.claim_3_1, Claim31.claim_3_1_imitating). Repair. Also delay the A → B messages sent after t, like the other slow links. With this change all four runs go through. They work even against an adversary that only imitates correct processes of another run, and even in partially synchronous runs. (Claim31.claim_3_1, Claim31.claim_3_1_imitating) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Section 3). CSLib's Byzantine message-passing model (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync). Deterministic processes on authenticated point-to-point links. Runs are given by the adversary's data: faulty set, inputs, Byzantine messages, and delivery times. The lower bounds are proved for the runs Run.Valid f δ (partial synchrony, any δ). That is a smaller class than the paper's asynchronous one, so the results are stronger. The asynchronous corollaries use Run.AsyncValid f, where every message between correct processes is delivered at some finite time. Definition 1 (IsRBroadcast): the sender r-broadcasts its input, and "delivers v" means "its decision is v at some time". Non-equivocation: messages have keys (key : M → κ). NonEquivocating key R: a faulty process never sends two different messages with the same key. RespectsNE A key: the protocol uses the primitive as intended, so correct processes never equivocate. No transferable authentication: there are no tokens, so a relayed claim cannot be checked. Claim 3.1 is proved against the even weaker imitating adversary (Imitating A R). Every faulty process sends, on each link, nothing or exactly what it sends in some run in which it is correct. Transferable authentication: CSLib's ideal signatures (Algorithm.Unforging, Run.AuthValid). For the positive result, messages are transferable attestations valid_p(k, v) (Att), and AttNonEquivocating forbids two attestations of a faulty signer with one key. Model (Section 4). A separate event-based model. Crash-model protocols (Protocol): deterministic automata with recipient lists. Crash executions (CReach): any delivery order, losses, crashes. The translation of Figure 2: TMsg, check, tsend, trecv. Executions of the translated system (TReach) with a static Byzantine set. The adversary may inject any message whose correct-signed parts it has seen (Unforged) and which never reuses one of its keys (NonEquiv). Main results in Lean. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331589. Formalized version: arXiv 1906.05574 v1 (extended version, the only arXiv version; the journal version, Distributed Computing 2022, was not checked); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 2 (consensus number exactly k, k ≥ 1), Corollary 1 and Lemma 2 hold, but the wait-freedom proof of Lemma 2 is false as stated and we replaced it with a new potential argument. Theorem 1 needs a local change to Figure 1, the linearizability proof of Lemma 2 needs local repairs, and Figure 4 needs a one-term fix, which we prove only on the counterexample. The safety of the message-passing algorithm (Theorem 3) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 1 (Figure 1 is not linearizable as written) Figure 1 keeps successful transfers in a set ops_p, so repeating an identical transfer is never debited: an owner with balance 2 calls transfer(a, b, 1) three times solo and all three return true (Fig1.Bug.literal_not_linearizable). Impact. That is double-spending, the very thing the paper sets out to prevent, but the intent is evident: Figure 3 tags transfers with unique sequence numbers. Details. Each process adds (a, b, x) to the set ops_p. Repeating an identical transfer therefore does not change ops_p, so the second withdrawal is never debited. Repair. Keeping ops_p as a sequence is a two-line change, after which the paper's proof goes through with its linearization points (Fig1.fig1_linearizable, Fig1.fig1_waitFree). 🔧 Lemma 2, proof ("the linearization of a prefix of E is a prefix of L") The side claim that prefixes linearize to prefixes is false, because failed transfers are linearized retroactively at the proposer's snapshot. Impact. The claim is not needed for linearizability, and the paper's linearization points stay. Repair. We drop the claim and insert such operations retroactively (Fig3.fig3_linearizable). ✏️ Slips Lemma 3 and Theorem 3, liveness (Figure 4, line 25). Figure 4 as written blocks a correct process that spends money it has just received: process 0 (balance 5) pays 5 to process 1 (balance 0), and process 1's transfer of the 5 back never returns, even with two correct processes and a perfect broadcast (Fig4.lemma_3_false). A process may spend balance(a, hist[p] ∪ deps), i.e. including freshly received incoming transfers deps, and it ships them as the dependencies h. Validation (line 25), however, checks balance(c, hist[q]) without h, and incoming transfers enter hist[q] only after a later transfer of q has been validated. So process 1's message is invalid at every process forever. As written this falsifies Theorem 3, since Definition 1 requires every operation of a correct process to return; only the safety part of Theorem 3 is unaffected. The intended check is balance(c, hist[q] ∪ h) ≥ y: line 2 spends that amount, and Lemma 3's proof assumes the receiver's check passes because the sender checked its balance. With it the transfer completes (Fig4.fixed_completes). Lean shows this on the counterexample only, not Theorem 3 for the fixed algorithm. Theorem 2 for k = 0. With "k-shared" defined as max_a |μ(a)| = k, an object whose accounts have no owner is 0-shared, but its consensus number is 1, not 0, since one process always solves consensus (atSolvable_one). For k ≥ 1 Theorem 2 holds (theorem_2). The transition relation Δ is not total, contrary to the paper's assumption: a self-transfer transfer(a, a, x) with x > 0 has no successor state. We use "debit, then credit". Figure 4's balance omits initial balances, so taken literally no transfer of a positive amount ever succeeds. The prose of Section 3 includes them. Definition 1 (2) cannot hold for finite executions, and it also covers reads and failed transfers of other processes. The comment after the definition gives the intended reading. Typos Figure 3's proposal((a, b, q, x), ·) has the wrong arity. The successful-transfer case of Lemma 2's proof writes L_k where L_s is meant. Proof gaps (statements true) Figure 3 implements asset transfer from a snapshot, registers and k-consensus objects. The algorithm is correct, and we proved it linearizable and wait-free (Fig3.fig3_linearizable, Fig3.fig3_waitFree). 🛠️ Lemma 2, wait-freedom The argument "some instance will be only accessed with o" is false as stated: processes with stale collected sets keep proposing other transfers. Impact. The paper's argument does not survive; the statement does. Repair. We replace the wait-freedom argument with a potential argument. (Fig3.fig3_waitFree) 🔧 Lemma 2, incomplete transfers The linearizability proof completes incomplete transfers "with response true" even when they were decided as failures. Impact. One-line change: complete them with the decided response, or linearize at the proposer's snapshot. (Fig3.fig3_linearizable) 🔧 Lemma 2, non-owner transfers (lines 1–2) The proof gives no linearization point to non-owner transfers. Impact. One extra case: we linearize them at their invocation. (Fig3.fig3_linearizable) 🔧 Lemma 2, successful-transfer case The proof leaves the key "no outgoing transfer in between" step unjustified. Impact. Verifying Linearizability with Hindsight — PODC 2010 Peter W. O'Hearn, Noam Rinetzky, Martin T. Vechev, Eran Yahav, Greta Yorsh. Verifying Linearizability with Hindsight. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835722. Formalized version: the 10-page author copy (no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The main results hold: the optimistic set algorithm of Fig. 1 satisfies all the integrity invariants and is memory safe (Thm 4.1), contains is wait-free (Thm 6.4), the algorithm is linearizable (Thm 7.5), and the Hindsight Lemma (Lemma 5.2) and the Local Window Lemma (Lemma 5.7) are proved as intended. The Backbone Lemma (Lemma 5.4) is false as printed: the claimed j₀ < j₁ < … < j_k = i_k must be weakened to j₀ ≤ j₁ ≤ … ≤ j_k ≤ i_k, which is what its proof gives and what Thm 7.5 uses. The only other correction is reading "its atomic section" in Thm 7.5 as the successful one, as the paper's proof does. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 5.4 (Backbone Lemma). The lemma's indices i₀ = j₀ < j₁ < … < j_k = i_k do not exist in general: both j_k = i_k and the strict inequalities fail on a real execution of the algorithm, add(5) followed by remove(5) (lemma_5_4_false, lemma_5_4_as_stated_false). The weak form i₀ = j₀ ≤ j₁ ≤ … ≤ j_k ≤ i_k is what the lemma's proof gives and what Thm 7.5 uses; nothing downstream is affected, and we prove it (backbone_lemma). The lemma claims that for a temporal backbone ζ through τ(i₀), …, τ(i_k) there are indices i₀ = j₀ < j₁ < … < j_k = i_k such that ζ(m) is a backbone link in τ(j_m). Counterexample: thread 0 runs add(5), giving H → a → T, then thread 1 runs remove(5). Let i₀ be the state just before the atomic section of remove and i₁ = i₀ + 1 the state right after it. Then ⟨H, a⟩, ⟨a, T⟩ is a temporal backbone through τ(i₀), τ(i₁), since the removed node a keeps its successor. But ⟨a, T⟩ is a backbone link only at i₀. So j₁ = i₁ is impossible, and so is j₀ < j₁ ≤ i₁. The trace is shape-legal by Thm 4.1, so every hypothesis of the lemma holds. The last link of a temporal backbone need not be a backbone link when it is crossed; that is the whole point of hindsight. The paper itself shows that the weak form is intended: the lemma's clause i₀ ≤ j_m ≤ i_m, its one-line proof via Lemma 5.2, and the choice of ι for contains in Thm 7.5 ("the last state at or before the last crossing state in which the last crossed link is a backbone link") all fit only the weak form. In Thm 7.5, "the transition in which t executes its atomic section" must mean the successful one. An add/remove may run its atomic section several times, restarting after failed validations. Typos Lemma 5.7's conclusion is printed as K_σ ∩ {u.k_σ, v.k_σ} = {u.k_σ, v.k_σ}. That only says both keys are backbone keys, which is trivially true (local_window_as_printed). The proof of Thm 7.5 uses the interval form K_σ ∩ {u.k_σ, …, v.k_σ} = {u.k_σ, v.k_σ}, which we prove (local_window). The interval form needs only φ_s and the backbone being a single heap path. Def. 7.2 is sloppy: it mixes indices of H and of π, and "linearizable with respect to a sequential history". We use CSLib's standard (amended Herlihy–Wing) definition. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, sequentially consistent, in CSLib's Impl model with arbitrarily many threads (P any type with decidable equality). The scheduler is adversarial. There are no crashes and no randomness. The whole heap with the shared variables H and T is one base object. Its operations are the shared-memory accesses of Fig. 1: read H; c = p.n (atomic, as in footnote 1); read c.k; and the atomic sections of add and remove. Nodes are natural numbers, and node u is allocated iff u < cnt. alloc(E) returns the fresh node cnt, and memory is never reclaimed, as the paper assumes. The initialized state comes from init(): tail 0 with key ∞, head 1 with key -∞. Keys live in WithBot (WithTop ℤ). A null dereference sends the thread to an error state err. Memory safety means err is never reached. Threads may run many operations one after another; the paper assumes at most one per thread, so this is more general. Linearizability is CSLib's Impl.Linearizable against the set specification of Fig. 2, with abstract states Set ℤ. Wait-freedom is over infinite executions: a thread whose contains stays pending forever takes finitely many steps. Sections 4–5 (heap states, Fig. 4 properties, shape-legal traces, Lemmas 5.2/5.4/5.7) are stated for arbitrary heap traces (HeapState N K), independently of the algorithm, as in the paper. The trace of every execution of the algorithm is shown to be (data-)shape-legal. The Hindsight Lemma silently uses that nodes are never reclaimed and that pointers point to allocated nodes. Our shape properties include both. Its proof also does not need δ_e; ours avoids it. Main results in Lean. Locally-Iterative (Δ+1)-Coloring — PODC 2018 Leonid Barenboim, Michael Elkin, Uri Goldenberg. Locally-Iterative Distributed (Δ+1)-Coloring below Szegedy–Vishwanathan Barrier, and Applications to Self-Stabilization and to Restricted-Bandwidth Models. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212769. Formalized version: arXiv 1712.00285 v2 (Aug 2021). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The core of the paper, Section 3 (the additive-group algorithm AG, one-bit halving, Refine-AG, and Corollary 3.6: a locally-iterative (Δ+1)-colouring in O(Δ) + log* n rounds), holds end to end after local changes; the introduction's 2p + 1-round bound for p = Δ + 1 fails, and Section 3's q > 2Δ replaces it. Algorithm 3AG of Section 7 never terminates on K₂, which refutes Corollaries 7.2 and 7.3, and no uniform replacement is proved, but nothing else in the paper uses it. The applications to self-stabilization, edge colouring and arbdefective colouring were not checked beyond the AG bounds they use. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Section 7, Algorithm 3AG (Corollaries 7.2 and 7.3) Algorithm 3AG never terminates on K₂ with the proper colouring ⟨1,0,0⟩, ⟨1,0,1⟩, for every p ≥ 2, so Corollaries 7.2 and 7.3 are false (threeAG_never_finalizes). Impact. Refutes the 3-D variant of Section 7, including p ≥ 3Δ + 1 and p ≥ 2Δ + 2, and we proved no uniform replacement. The phase-based alternative at the start of Section 7, which 3AG was meant to avoid, is not affected, and neither is the core of the paper (Section 3); nothing else in the paper uses 3AG. Details. The two vertices always have the same b. So in every round both conflict, both move to ⟨1, b+1, ·⟩, and c never becomes 0. The termination argument says "each neighbour may have a conflicting b_u at most three times". It assumes that two neighbours in the same phase with the same c have different b. That is forced by properness in 2-D AG, but in 3-D, ⟨c, b⟩ can coincide while only a differs. 🔧 Section 1.2 (2p + 1 rounds of AG for p = Δ + 1) The introduction's claim that 2p + 1 rounds of AG over GF(p), with p = Δ + 1 prime, turn a proper (Δ+1)²-colouring into a proper (Δ+1)-colouring is false on a 16-vertex tree with Δ = 4, p = 5 (intro_claim_false). Impact. A claim of the introduction, not used later: Section 3 itself correctly assumes q > 2Δ and still gets O(Δ) rounds (ag_final_of_two_mul_lt, corollary_3_6). A correct bound with q = Δ + 1 is (Δ + 1)·q rounds (ag_final_of_lt). Details. After 11 rounds vertex 0 still has colour ⟨1,1⟩, 6 colours are in use, and vertex 0 finalizes only after 13 rounds. (On paths, Δ = 2, the claim does hold.) The argument breaks because with q = Δ + 1, a neighbour that finalizes inside a window of q rounds can conflict twice in that window, so a window may have no free round. Repair. Rewrite the paragraph with Section 3's prime q > 2Δ. For any prime q > Δ, everything is final after (Δ + 1)·q rounds (ag_final_of_lt). ✏️ Slips Section 3.1 picks a prime √k ≤ q ≤ 2√k but then uses q > 2Δ; we use the least prime above max(2Δ, ⌊√k⌋). Refine-AG's conflict definition has b_u for b_v, and index ranges j ≤ k for j < k. The final-state case of Lemma 3.12 swaps u and v. Typos Algorithms 1 and 2 loop one round longer than needed. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Section 5 (edge colouring: the condition on q) Section 5 only requires q ≥ 2Δ − 1, i.e. q > Δ_L for the line graph, but the cited O(Δ) argument of Corollary 3.5 needs q > 2Δ_L, so the bound is unestablished (not refuted). Impact. Under the stated condition our bound is O(Δ²). We did not look for a counterexample. Details. Edge colouring runs AG on the line graph, whose degree is Δ_L ≤ 2Δ − 2. Repair. A prime q > 4Δ − 4 is still O(Δ) and satisfies the printed lower bound; the bound is then our general theorem applied to G.lineGraph (ag_final_of_two_mul_lt). Section 5 itself is not formalized, so this covers its AG part, the only part affected. 🔧 Lemma 3.2 (properness of AG) The proof overlooks the case where the conflicting vertex already has a = 0. Impact. The statement stands: then the second coordinates differ (ag_isProper). 🔧 Corollary 3.13 (Refine-AG running time) The proof needs "each neighbour blocks at most one index per round", but never says so. Impact. The statement stands (corollary_3_13, corollary_3_13_paper). Details. It follows from Lemma 3.11 for working neighbours and from j = c_u for final ones. We count blocked (round, index) pairs instead. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A simple graph, possibly infinite but locally finite. Δ is any upper bound on degrees. Synchronous, deterministic, fault-free rounds in locally-iterative form: each vertex's new colour is step t (own colour) (set of neighbours' colours). This is CSLib's LocallyIterative model. Only the set of neighbour colours is used, so the results also hold in SET-LOCAL. The round number is global knowledge, used only to switch phases in the composite algorithm. Scheduling Loop-free Network Updates — PODC 2015 Arne Ludwig, Jan Marcinkowski, Stefan Schmid. Scheduling Loop-free Network Updates: It's Good to Relax! PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767412. Formalized version: the 10-page proceedings version (no arXiv version exists); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The NP-hardness reduction for 3-round schedules is wrong: Theorem 2 is false, the paper's network has no strongly loop-free 3-round schedule even for satisfiable formulas such as x ∨ y ∨ z, and so Theorem 1 (NP-completeness for k = 3) is unestablished; we neither prove nor refute it. The other results hold: the 2-round characterization, the Ω(n) lower bound of Fig. 2 (exactly n − 1 rounds), and the O(log n) bound for Peacock with relaxed loop-freedom (Theorem 3, Lemmas 2–3). So the case for relaxing survives, resting on Ω(n) against O(log n). Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 2 (§3.2 reduction for 3-round schedules), hence the NP-hardness of Theorem 1 Theorem 2 is false: for a variable x set true by a satisfying assignment, round 2 of the claimed schedule contains a forwarding ring through the exclusive gadget, and every other choice of round-1 copies closes one of the paper's own gadget cycles, so the reduction maps satisfiable formulas such as x ∨ y ∨ z to no-instances (gadget_cycle, theorem_2_false). Impact. NP-hardness of the 3-round problem (Theorem 1) has no valid proof in the paper; we neither prove nor refute it. The ring seems inherent to the gadget design, since an implication gadget must lead from the consequent back to the antecedent. Details. Theorem 2 claims that if the copies set to true by a satisfying assignment of C′ are updated in round 1 (and all BB nodes in round 2), the second round is cycle-free. Take any variable x, say with one positive and no negative occurrence (every variable of x ∨ y ∨ z), and set x true. Then the second round contains the ring x₀ ⇢ x₁^IN → x₁ ⇢ x_l^IN → x_l ⇢ v₃ → v₄ ⇢ x̄_l^H → x̄_l^IN → x̄_l → x̄_l^BB ⇢ x̄₀^H → x̄₀ → v₁ᴬ ⇢ v₂ᴬ → x₀^H → x₀. (⇢ = new rule, → = old rule.) The true copies jump forward along their implication edges. x_l's dashed edge enters the exclusive gadget, and v₄'s BB edge leads to the false copy x̄_l. The implication BB edges then lead backwards through all false copies to x̄₀. Finally the assignment clause's path and its BB edge lead back to x₀. Every edge is one the paper draws, with the colours it prescribes. The proof's claim that from x_l "there is no way back" overlooks the exclusive gadget. Every other choice of round-1 copies violates a clause of C′ and closes one of the paper's own gadget cycles. So no choice of round-1 nodes makes the second round cycle-free (formalized for a variable with pₓ = 1, nₓ = 0; the same argument works for any pₓ, nₓ, so the network of every formula is a no-instance). Lifted to instances: every network containing these gadgets with the required node types has no 3-round schedule (not_hasSLF_three_of_realizes, non-vacuous by realizes_example). This covers every completion of the under-specified connection step §3.2.4 that keeps the gadget edges and node types, as the paper says its completion does (it only adds nodes above the vertical paths and in R). ✏️ Slips Lemma 1 says "the same holds true for nodes of type FF"; read literally, all FF nodes of a 3-round schedule can be moved to round 1, which is false for the 7-node instance with new route 0, 5, 4, 1, 3, 2, 6 (lemma_1_FF_literal_false). There a 3-round schedule exists, but with both FF nodes 0, 1 in round 1 the BB node 4 closes the loop 1 ⇢ 3 → 4 ⇢ 1 in round 2. The literal reading would also make the 3-round problem trivial, and the paper's own Fig. 4 shows why it fails. The proof moves nodes only from round 2 to round 1, and that intended version holds, also in the backward direction (lemma_1, lemma_1_backward). Lemma 2 ("reduces the number of nodes on the path by n_t/3") is true only when the updated start nodes are merged into their new successors, as §4 does, but not if they are counted as path nodes (old route 0,1,2,3, new route 0,2,1,3). Algorithm 1, line 7, ranges over all of X instead of the forward edges sorted in line 6. Typos §3.2.3 places x_l^H "just below x_l on the first path" while also saying v₂ points "back to the second solid path"; Fig. 6 and the paper's listing of its cycle settle it. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Centralized scheduling of a single route update; no failures, no randomness. An instance is the paper's reduced line representation (§2): two duplicate-free lists old (r₁) and new (r₂) over the same nodes, both from s to d (Instance, Model.lean). A state is the set of updated nodes; each node forwards along its new rule if updated and its old rule otherwise (fwd). Asynchrony within a round is modelled as in the paper: in round t every state U_{<t} ∪ X, X ⊆ U_t, must be loop-free. Strong loop-freedom (LoopFree) = no directed cycle; relaxed (RelaxedLoopFree) = no cycle reachable from s, equivalently the walk from s reaches d (relaxedLoopFree_iff). Schedules are lists of pairwise disjoint rounds covering the nodes with out₁ ≠ out₂ (IsSLF, IsRLF). Node types FF, FB, BF, BB as in §3.1. Main results in Lean. Limitations of Highly-Available Eventually-Consistent Data Stores — PODC 2015 Hagit Attiya, Faith Ellen, Adam Morrison. Limitations of Highly-Available Eventually-Consistent Data Stores. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767419. Formalized version: the authors' copy of the PODC paper (10 pages). Lemmas 5 and 7 and parts of Theorem 12 are proved there only "in the full version" (IEEE TPDS 2017, not open access); we give our own proofs. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The paper proves two limitations, and one of them stands: the message-size bound of Theorem 12 holds (with ⌊n' lg k⌋ bits) by a new decoding argument. The OCC result, Theorem 6, is left unestablished by two broken proof steps that we could not repair, although it is not refuted. Lemmas 3, 5 and 7 and Corollary 4 hold (Lemma 5 needs two replicas), and Definition 14, which no store satisfies when read literally, is used with its evident intent. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 6, Section 5.2.1 ("without loss of generality" revealing) The proof assumes without loss of generality that the OCC abstract execution is revealing, but the extension by reads r_w need not be OCC (Gap.revealing_extension_not_OCC). Impact. Theorem 6 (no eventually consistent store with invisible reads and op-driven messages satisfies a consistency model strictly stronger than OCC), and with it Lemma 11, is unestablished, not refuted: we have no store and OCC execution for which the construction of Section 5.2.2 actually fails. We state it (Theorem6Statement, for finite OCC abstract executions with distinct written values) without proof. Details. Section 5.2.1 assumes the OCC abstract execution A to be realized is revealing: before each write w there is a read r_w of the same object with the same visibility as w. It justifies this by "adding the appropriate r_w operations and vis edges to A". But the inductive argument (Lemma 11) is then applied to every read of the extended execution, including the added r_w, and needs OCC for them. The extension need not be OCC. Take writes a at R₀ and b at R₁ to one MVR, concurrent, both visible to a write c at R₂, and no reads. This is OCC (vacuously). The added read r_c returns {a, b}, and there is no write to another object that could serve as an OCC witness. So the revealing extension is not OCC. (Gap.revealing_extension_not_OCC) This particular A is trivially realizable (no reads), and a cleverer extension (ordering a before b) is OCC. We do not know whether a suitable revealing OCC extension always exists. ❌ Theorem 6, proof of Lemma 11 (use of Lemma 7) The proof of Lemma 11 uses Lemma 7 for w'_i →vis w_0, where w'_i is an OCC witness, a write to another object, which Lemma 7 does not cover. Impact. This is the core step showing that the store cannot add "fake" visibility edges, so Lemma 11 and Theorem 6 stay unestablished, independently of the previous item. No repair is proved. Details. Lemma 7 transfers visibility between writes of the operation context of a read, i.e. writes to the same object. "w'_i ∈ ctxt(A, e) since w'_i →vis w_0 →vis e" is wrong: contexts contain only writes to obj(e). For writes to different objects the conclusion of Lemma 7 fails in general: visibility between them is constrained by nothing that the reads r_w reveal, and eventual consistency only concerns writes to the same object. See differencies.md (item 15) for an example. Repair. None proved. A repair would need revealing reads of every object before each write, which makes the previous gap worse. ✏️ Slips Lemma 5, one replica. Lemma 5 is false with one replica: a single-replica store that never sends satisfies all assumptions, and after a write no message is pending (lemma5_false_one_replica). This degenerate case is the only numbered statement we refute; with two or more replicas the lemma holds (lemma5). Definition 14, read literally. It is satisfied by no store with two replicas, so Theorems 6 and 12 would hold vacuously (Store.literalEC_false). It requires that every abstract execution that an infinite execution complies with be eventually consistent. Compliance (Definition 9) fixes only the per-replica operation sequences, so the abstract execution whose visibility is just the per-replica order always complies. In an infinite execution where two replicas read the same MVR forever and nothing is written, this abstract execution is correct and causally consistent but not eventually consistent. The proofs use "some correct abstract execution that the execution complies with is eventually consistent", which we adopt. Theorem 12, bound. It claims n' lg k bits. The counting argument gives ⌊n' lg k⌋ (e.g. three distinct messages may have lengths 0, 1, 1). Its hypothesis "k ≥ min{n−2, s−1}" plays no role; we prove the bound for all k ≥ 1, and need n ≥ 3 and s ≥ 2 (otherwise n' ≤ 0). Typos Definition 18, condition 1 writes w'_i →vis w_{i-1}; the prose and the proof use w_{1-i}. Definition 18 also implicitly needs w_0 ≠ w_1. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 12 (message size), the decoding argument The sketch claims R_n "cannot return w_y" before it has received R_i's g(i)-th message "since R_n does not know this value", but m_g itself may carry R_i's writes. Impact. Statement true (with ⌊n' lg k⌋ bits); saved by a different decoding argument (theorem12, Cx.key, Cx.decode, Cx.mg_injective). Details. A store may piggyback everything it knows on m_g. The paper also never shows that R_n exposes w_y once it has the g(i)-th message, and defers both facts to the full version. Repair. R_n receives only the first g(p) messages of every writer, and m_g. Its state is then final: it has heard everything sent in the sub-execution where every writer stops after g(p) rounds. So, by eventual consistency, its reads return exactly {1} from y and ⟨g(i), i⟩ from x_i. If m_g = m_{g'} with g(i) < g'(i), the same state of R_n arises in the g' execution. There R_{n-1} read ⟨g'(i), i⟩ before writing y, so causal consistency makes ⟨g'(i), i⟩, which overwrites ⟨g(i), i⟩, visible to R_n's read of x_i. (theorem12, Cx.key, Cx.decode) 🔧 Lemma 5 (hypothesis) The hypothesis "e →hb w ⇒ e →rcv w for any do event e" cannot hold for earlier events of R itself, since a replica does not receive its own messages, so the lemma says nothing at its uses. Impact. With a changed hypothesis the lemma holds (lemma5). We read it as: nobody has a message pending before w, and R has received every message sent by another replica. Repair. The lemma is proved only in the full version; we give a proof. Insert an invisible read r before w and complete the execution quiescently. If R sent nothing after w, late reads at another replica would never see w, but by Lemma 3 they return what r returned. A late read at R sees w, so w is overwritten by some w₂ returned by r, while w₂ is visible to r and hence to w (Definition 4(2)). This is a visibility cycle. (lemma5) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n replicas (finite type ι), each a partial, possibly nondeterministic state machine (Store, Section 2); objects are multi-value registers; written values are arbitrary. Events: do(o, op, v), send(m) (broadcast), recv(m). Asynchronous message passing, no failures. Messages may be lost, delayed, reordered and duplicated; an execution only requires that every receipt follows a send by another replica (IsExec, Definition 1). Infinite executions are considered only when sufficiently connected (SuffConnected, Definition 3). Assumptions on stores, as in the paper: a send leaves nothing pending (SendClears), op-driven messages (OpDriven, Def. 15), invisible reads (InvisibleReads, Def. 16); and, made explicit, high availability (Available) and input-enabled receipts (RecvEnabled). The paper says both in prose and uses them, but never states them as properties of the transition function. Abstract executions (AE, Def. 4) carry the total order H and visibility; MVR specification, correctness, causal and eventual consistency are Defs. 7, 8, 12, 13. Compliance (Def. 9) is "an abstract execution on the execution's own do-events with the same per-replica order" (AE.On), which is the same up to renaming events. Store-level consistency: CausallyConsistent (every finite execution complies with a causally consistent abstract execution) and EventuallyConsistent P (every infinite sufficiently connected execution complies with a correct, eventually consistent abstract execution, in the model P) — the latter is Definition 14 with "some" for "every" (see above). No randomness; all universal statements quantify over every store satisfying the hypotheses and every execution (adversarial scheduling and message delivery). Main results in Lean. The Greedy Spanner is Existentially Optimal — PODC 2016 Arnold Filtser, Shay Solomon. The Greedy Spanner is Existentially Optimal. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933114. Formalized version: arXiv 1605.06852 v2 (full version, January 2020); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Lemma 3, Observation 2, Theorem 5 (greedy is existentially optimal for size and lightness in any family closed under edge removal), Lemmas 5 and 6, Observation 7 and Theorem 6 (near-optimality in doubling metrics) are all proved, with only a radius typo, an off-by-one count, a maximum that should be a supremum and loose connectivity conventions to correct. Corollaries 1–3 are proved relative to the cited external bounds, which are taken as hypotheses. The approximate-greedy construction of Section 5 was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips In the proof of Observation 7, the covering balls in M should have radius r/4, not 4r (the next step's "t · 4r ≤ 2r" is false; with r/4 the proof goes through, observation7). OPT_t(𝒢) is defined as a maximum over 𝒢. For lightness over an infinite family of weighted graphs the maximum need not be attained; we use the supremum. Section 2 assumes all graphs connected, but a family closed under edge removal contains disconnected graphs. We define the MST weight as the weight of a minimum spanning forest. For connected graphs it is the minimum weight of a spanning tree (mstWeight_eq_iInf_isTree). In the proof of Observation 4, "contains at least n + 1 edges" should be n: replacing one edge of a spanning tree by a path of at least two edges gives at least n edges, which already force the cycle the proof needs. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The setting is sequential and centralized: Section 3 is pure graph theory, with no distributed model. A weighted graph is a CSLib SimpleGraph V on a finite vertex type (n = |V|) with weights w : Sym2 V → ℝ≥0. Distances are CSLib's wdist, in ℝ≥0∞, equal to ⊤ when disconnected. The stretch t is a real number t ≥ 1. IsWSpanner G H w t: H ≤ G and δ_H(u,v) ≤ t·δ_G(u,v) for all u, v. Algorithm 1 is modelled literally (greedySpanner w t L, see greedySpanner_eq_foldl). It scans an edge list L and adds e = {u,v} iff δ_H(u,v) > t·w(e) for the current H. "The greedy t-spanner" (IsGreedySpanner) is the output of any execution: L lists every edge exactly once, in non-decreasing order of weight, with ties broken arbitrarily. Every result holds for every execution. Lightness is Ψ(H) = w(H)/w(MST(G)) in ℝ≥0∞. w(MST(G)) (mstWeight) is the minimum weight of a subgraph with the same connected components as G, i.e. a minimum spanning forest. A graph family is a set 𝒢 of weighted graphs on V. "Closed under edge removal" means (G,w) ∈ 𝒢, H ≤ G ⇒ (H,w) ∈ 𝒢. A metric is a weight function on the complete graph ⊤: zero on the diagonal, positive off it, triangle inequality. M_H is the complete graph with weights δ_H. IsDoubling w D means every closed ball of radius r is covered by ≤ 2^D balls of radius r/2. M(n, D) is metricFamily V D. Main results in Lean.
