How to Meet Asynchronously at Polynomial Cost — PODC 2013 Yoann Dieudonné, Andrzej Pelc, Vincent Villain. How to meet asynchronously at polynomial cost. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484245. Formalized version: arXiv 1301.7119 v2 (full version, 2015); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Lemma 2.1, Lemma 3.1, the synchronization Lemmas 3.2–3.6 and the main Theorem 3.1 are all true as stated, for the paper's fully adversarial continuous asynchronous model and any exploration procedure with a non-decreasing polynomial step count, with Reingold's theorem (UXS) as a hypothesis. Two proof steps need local repair: the case analysis of Lemma 3.3 misses a case, and the length estimates that define the polynomial Π are wrong for slowly growing P. Neither changes a statement, and the applications of Section 4 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Definition 3.8: the pseudocode loop body should be "Follow trajectory X(k, v)", not Ω(k, v). §2: |x| = ⌈log x⌉ should be ⌊log x⌋ + 1, the length of the binary representation, which is what is used. Lemma 3.6, Case 2, µ = 1: the contradiction comes from Lemma 3.3 (a has not completed the first atom N of piece j+1 when b ends its fence), not from Lemma 3.4. Proof of Lemma 3.3: Ω_b(2(n+l)) contains (4(n+l)−1)|K(2(n+l))| copies of X(2(n+l)), not 2(2(n+l)−1)|K(2(n+l))|, and the printed "at most" bound for (2k−1)|K(k)| fails at k = 2(n+l). This is harmless, since the printed count is smaller. The proof of Theorem 3.1 says "since the polynomial P(k) is non-decreasing". Monotonicity of P (and P ≥ 1) is used already in the correctness proof (Lemmas 3.2–3.6 compare |A(·)|, |B(·)| at different parameters), but it is stated only there. It is harmless: the step count can always be padded. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.3 (missing case) The proof says "if during this time interval agent a has not started any fence, it would have to follow a trajectory included in a piece T_a(k)", overlooking that a may spend the whole fence Ω_b(2(n+l)) of b inside one of its own fences, started before b's. Impact. Statement true; proved with a different argument (lemma_3_3). Details. That case satisfies the lemma's conclusion anyway, but the proof then derives that a must start a fence during the interval, which is not shown. Repair. Let j be the last piece of a completed by the end of the interval. Then the last atom of piece j cannot have been followed entirely during the interval (catching, Lemma 3.1). Neither can the first atom of piece j + 1. Nor can a stay inside the single piece j + 1 (counting); here j + 1 ≤ 2(n+l) because b finished first. (lemma_3_3) 🔧 Theorem 3.1 (length estimates defining Π) The proof's bounds |Y(k, v)| ≤ Y*_k = 2P(k)·Q*_k and |A(k, v)| ≤ A*_k = 2P(k)·Z*_k are false, e.g. for P ≡ 1, |Y(1)| = 10 > 6 = Y*_1 and |A(1)| = 42 > 12 = A*_1 (paper_Ystar_wrong, paper_Astar_wrong), so the paper's Π(n, m) is not justified. Impact. Theorem 3.1 only claims that some polynomial Π exists, and that is true: we define Π from the exact lengths (piBound) and prove that it is polynomially bounded (theorem_3_1). Details. Y'(k, v₁) inserts Q(k, ·) at each of the P(k) + 1 nodes of R(k, v₁) and adds P(k) edges, so |Y(k)| = 2(P(k)+1)|Q(k)| + 2P(k). Similarly for A. The same values arise for P(k) = k. At k = 1 the bound fails for every P: |Y(1)| = 4P(1)² + 6P(1) > 4P(1)² + 2P(1) = Y*_1. A numerical check (P ≡ 1, n = 2, labels 1 and 3) shows that the paper's Π is even smaller than the length of the first 2(n+l)+1 pieces of the agent with the longer label (2.92·10¹¹ vs 2.77·10¹¹). (paper_Ystar_wrong, paper_Astar_wrong, theorem_3_1) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graph: finite, simple, connected, nodes anonymous. For Lemma 2.1 and theorem_3_1_ports, a CSLib port-labelled graph (PNGraph, IsSimple). For the rendezvous analysis, any SimpleGraph with an exploration family. Exploration procedure (UXS "axiom"): Explorer G P is a family of trajectories R(k, v). Each is a walk from v of exactly P(k) ≥ 1 edges. It traverses every edge whenever G has at most k nodes (the paper's "integral"). P is non-decreasing, and polynomially bounded for the polynomial claim. The family may depend on G arbitrarily, so this is more general than Reingold's port-local procedure. Explorer.ofProc instantiates it with deterministic port-local procedures (Proc: history of (degree, entry port) ↦ exit port). Agents: deterministic, distinct positive labels, modified labels M(x). Before the meeting, the route of an agent is a fixed node sequence E.route (modLabel L) v (the infinite concatenation of the iterations of the repeat loop). Asynchrony and adversary: exactly the paper's walks. A walk is an increasing time sequence τ 0 = 0 < τ 1 < … (accumulation allowed) and a progress function p. On each [τ i, τ (i+1)], p is continuous with values in [i, i+1] and p (τ i) = i. The adversary may stop agents and move them back and forth inside edges. Positions live in the embedding v ↦ e_v ∈ ℝ^V (edges = segments, pairwise disjoint except at endpoints). A meeting is equality of positions, at a node or inside an edge. No randomness. Cost: "meeting by the time one of them performs Π traversals" is t ≤ τ_a(Π) ∧ t ≤ τ_b(Π). Main results in Lean. Seeing is Believing — PODC 2017 Natacha Crooks, Youer Pu, Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement. Seeing is Believing: A Client-Centric Specification of Database Isolation. PODC 2017. DOI 10.1145/3087801.3087802. Formalized version: the 10-page author copy (identical in content to the 11-page UT copy; the appendices and the technical report TR-17-06 with the deferred proofs were not available). Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The state-based characterizations are equivalent to Adya's: serializability ⇔ PL-3 (Theorem 1), snapshot isolation ⇔ PL-SI (Theorem 2), read committed ⇔ PL-2 (Theorem 3), read uncommitted ⇔ PL-1 (Theorem 4) and PSI ⇔ PL-2+ (the dependency-graph half of Theorem 10), once Adya's side is read, as the paper's proofs do, as "for some version order (and some start/commit timestamps)". The proof sketches of Theorems 1 and 2 go through, the missing steps are routine, and the only labeled mistake is loose wording of the model. The comparisons of Theorems 5–9 and the PSI half of Theorem 10 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 3 says states hold values "produced by writes from aborted or committed transactions", but executions apply only the transactions of 𝒯, which must be the committed ones (otherwise Theorem 1 ⇒ fails on aborted reads). Typos Phenomenon G1b (intermediate reads) is vacuous under the paper's assumption that a transaction writes a key at most once. Theorems 1–4 and 10 do not say which history the phenomena refer to; see "What ≡ ¬G1 ∧ ¬G2 quantifies over" below. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Purely combinatorial; no processes, failures, timing or randomness.) Keys K and transaction identifiers ι are arbitrary types; values are uniquely identifiable: the value written by T to k is some T, the initial value ⊥ is none (Model.lean). A TxnSet lists, for every transaction, its reads (with the values returned) and writes in program order, and the finite set of committed transactions 𝒯; other transactions are aborted. An execution is a permutation of 𝒯; states s_0, …, s_n are indexed by position (Execution.state), so a read-only transaction yields two equal but distinct states, as in the paper's sequence 𝒮_e. Read states (Definition 2, including the conventions for writes and for reads after an own write), PREREAD, COMPLETE, NO-CONF, D-PREC (▶), sf_o, sl_o and the commit tests of Table 1 (SER, SI, RC, RU, PSI) are transcribed literally; TxnSet.Satisfies CT := ∃ e, ∀ T ∈ 𝒯, CT e T is Definition 5. Adya's side (Adya.lean): a version order is a strict total order per key on the committed writers; ww/rw edges use the next version (the first committed version after x_init for reads of ⊥), wr edges reads of committed versions, all between distinct transactions; timestamps are distinct with start < commit, T →sd T' iff commit T < start T'. G0, G1 = G1a ∨ G1c, G2, G-single, G-SIa, G-SIb as in Adya's thesis (item reads/writes only). Theorems assume TxnSet.WellFormed: a value of another transaction that is read was written by it, and a transaction reads its own value only after writing it (Adya's well-formedness; without the latter the equivalences fail trivially). What "≡ ¬G1 ∧ ¬G2" quantifies over. The left-hand sides of Theorems 1–4 and 10 only see the transactions and the values they read; Adya's phenomena are properties of a history, which also fixes a version order (and, for SI, start/commit timestamps). The theorems are true when the history's version order and timestamps are existentially quantified — exactly what the ⇒ halves of the proof sketches construct from e — and false if they refer to a given history: two transactions that blindly write x and y are serializable, but with the version order x₀ ≪ x₁, y₁ ≪ y₀ the history exhibits G0 (so also G1); for that history Theorem 4 would even claim ¬G0 (fixed_versionOrder_counterexample). The paper's remark that its definitions "do not rely on timestamps" and Theorem 4 (both sides then trivially true) confirm the existential reading, which we formalize. Proof remarks. Theorem 1 (⇐) argues only with anti-dependency edges that a version read by T is not overwritten before T; a writer whose version precedes the one read must be excluded via write-dependency edges, and aborted reads via ¬G1a. Theorem 2 (⇒) needs NO-CONF (not just completeness) to give write-dependency edges a start-dependency; its start points coincide for transactions sharing a snapshot (the paper's time oracle assigns distinct timestamps — we perturb them); and for a transaction without operations every state is "complete", including states after its parent state, so the chosen snapshot must be capped at the parent state. Automatic speedup (round elimination) — PODC 2019 Sebastian Brandt. An Automatic Speedup Theorem for Distributed Problems. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331611. Formalized version: arXiv 1902.09958 v1 (the only version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The forward direction of Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Lemmas 1–4 and the lower bounds (§4.4, Theorem 4) stand, though Lemma 4 and Theorem 4 were checked only in the port-numbering model with input orientations, not in their LOCAL form. The converse of Theorem 1 ("Π_1 in t − 1 rounds ⇒ Π in t rounds"), and with it Corollary 1 and the "reversible" / "exact complexities T − 1, T − 2, …" claims, is false: it fails for the natural class of input-free Δ-regular high-girth graphs with arbitrary port numbers. It holds once the endpoints of each edge can be told apart (edge symmetry breaking). Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 1, (2) ⇒ (1), and Corollary 1 (the converse of the speedup) Without edge symmetry breaking, Π_1 in t − 1 rounds does not give Π in t rounds: for edge orientation Π_1 is solvable in 0 rounds on every graph, but Π is unsolvable on the t-independent class {K_2} (theorem_1_backward_false). Impact. Corollary 1 and the "reversible" / "exactly one round faster" / "exact complexities T − 1, T − 2, …" claims of the abstract and §1.1 fall with it, already for the natural class of input-free Δ-regular high-girth graphs with arbitrary port numbers. The forward direction and all applications (Theorem 2, §4.4, §4.5, Lemmas 3–4, Theorem 4) have edge symmetry breaking and stand. Details. The proof turns a (t−1)-round algorithm for Π_1 into an algorithm for Π_{1/2}. Both endpoints of an edge e look only at N^t(e) and must pick a pair (o, o') with {o, o'} ∈ g_{1/2}; v takes o and u takes o'. If N^t(e) looks the same from both sides, they make the same choice, so a pair with o ≠ o' cannot be split. Counterexample. Optimal Dynamic Distributed MIS — PODC 2016 Keren Censor-Hillel, Elad Haramaty, Zohar Karnin. Optimal Dynamic Distributed MIS. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933083. Formalized version: arXiv 1507.04330 v2. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 1 (E_π|S| ≤ 1 for every single topology change) and Theorem 7 (Algorithm 2: expected O(1) rounds and broadcasts, O(min(log n, deg)) for abrupt deletion) hold in the synchronous model. The repairs are all local: the recursion defining the layers S_i is ill-formed as written, rule 4 of Algorithm 2 needs one condition, Lemma 3 as stated ("= 1/|P|") is false for edge changes but its own proof concludes the ≤ that Theorem 1 needs, and several proofs have small gaps. The asynchronous model, the deterministic lower bound and history independence of Algorithm 2 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Recursion (1) (the layers S_i) The rule for M̄-nodes is cumulative ("every v ∈ I(u) ∩ M is in S_0 ∪ … ∪ S_{i−1}"), so taken literally a node that enters some S_i by this rule is in every later S_j, i_u = max{i | u ∈ S_i} is undefined, and Algorithm 1's loop "until S_i = ∅" never terminates when S contains such a node (mem_layer_of_inMbar). Impact. Notational: Theorem 1 concerns only |S| = |⋃ S_i|. Details. In the paper's own example, u2 lies in every S_i with i ≥ 1, not just S_1 and S_4. Repair. We use S as the least set closed under the two rules (Influenced). 🔧 Algorithm 2, rule 4 (graceful node deletion) Algorithm 2 never says that a gracefully deleted node, which keeps participating, must not enter M. Impact. The pseudocode needs one condition; Theorem 7 is proved for it (Alg2.theorem7_graceful). Repair. We add this to rule 4: only active nodes enter M. ✏️ Slips Lemma 3 ("= 1/|P|" for edge changes). Lemma 3's equality is false for edge changes: on the path v* – z – v**, inserting or deleting the edge {v*, v**} with any order z < v** < v* gives S′ = P = {v*, z, v**} and conditional probability 0, not 1/3, that v* is first in P (lemma3_eq_counterexample). The paper's proof handles this case ("clearly 0") and concludes only ≤ 1/|P|, which is all Theorem 1 needs. In the counterexample π(v**) ≤ π(v*), so the probability that v* is first in P, given this event, is 0. For node changes (v** = v*) equality does hold. As a by-product we get E|S| = 1 exactly for effective node insertions and deletions, which is stronger than Theorem 1's ≤ 1 (theorem1_node_eq). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 12, second part (entries into C) The claim that each entry of v into C "can be associated with a different v_i*" is argued incompletely: the paper itself concedes that the new path may pass through v_i*. Impact. Statement true; repaired (abrupt_card_entries_le). Repair. The missing fact: the root of the entry at t₂ stays in C throughout [0, 2t₂+1], whereas the root of the entry at t₁ is already final by time t₂ − 1 − t₁, so the two roots differ. 🔧 Lemma 2, proof The proof mixes states computed for π and for π′. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma2). Details. We prove S = S′ whenever S ≠ ∅ (the paper states S ⊆ S′). 🔧 Claims 4–5, as used in Lemma 3 Claims 4–5 are stated for π|P = σ|P, which fixes v*'s position, but Lemma 3 applies them to orders that agree only on P \ {v*}. Impact. Statement true; the repair is one condition, because S′ does not depend on π(v*). Details. The end of Lemma 3 rests on an independence claim. It is true, and we replace it by a counting argument: swapping v* with its successor in P is an injection. 🔧 Lemma 11, final claim (abrupt deletion) Correctness of the final MIS after an abrupt deletion is asserted without argument ("straightforward to verify"), although the modified start makes several nodes enter C at once. Impact. Statement true; proved by two invariants (abrupt_stableFrom). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A configuration is a simple graph on a finite vertex type plus a set of present nodes. All four changes (edge/node insertion/deletion) are covered, with no validity hypotheses; vacuous changes give S = ∅. π is a uniformly random bijection V ≃ Fin |V|, and expectations are finite averages. The adversary is oblivious: the change is fixed before π. The MIS is the greedy MIS for π. Corollary 6 and Section 4 are synchronous only. The direct implementation is a SET-LOCAL algorithm in CSLib's LOCAL model (run_directAlg, via Algorithm.run_semiconj of Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Local/Identifiers.lean; t-locality: directAlg_isLocal). Algorithm 2 runs in synchronous broadcast rounds, with its four rules encoded literally. Ranks replace the real IDs ℓ_v, and message sizes are not modelled. "Rounds" = stabilisation time; "broadcasts" = (node, round) pairs where the visible state changes. Main results in Lean. Formalized version: arXiv 1003.1608 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The proof of Corollary 4.4 has a wrong case split on a; the corollary is proved with a corrected three-way split. Theorem 4.5 and Corollaries 4.6 and 4.7, the polylogarithmic colourings that answer Linial's question, were not formalized. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 5.3 says "O(a/t)-coloring" for O(a·t) (Section 5 is not formalized). In the proof of Theorem 3.2, "for each parent w of u, len(u) ≤ i−1" should be len(w). Typos Theorem 4.3 states p = ⌈a^{μ/2}⌉, while the text and the proof use ⌊a^{μ/2}⌋. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Corollary 4.4 (case split on a) The proof claims that p = ⌊a^{μ'}/log n⌋ > a^{μ'/2} for every superlogarithmic a, but this needs a > (log n)^{2/μ'} and fails for a = (log₂ n)² (corollary_4_4_proof_gap). Impact. The statement stands, with a corrected threshold and a three-way case split (corollary_4_4). Details. For "superlogarithmic" a the paper runs Legal-Coloring with p = ⌊a^{μ'}/log n⌋, μ' = μ/2. The claim p > a^{μ'/2} "since a is superlogarithmic" would bound the number of iterations by a constant. This needs a^{μ'/2} > log n, i.e. a > (log n)^{2/μ'}. Counterexample: take a = (log₂ n)² (superlogarithmic) and any μ' ≤ 1/2. Then p ≤ 1 < a^{μ'/2} for every n ≥ 4 (p = 0 if μ' < 1/2). With p = 1, line 15 gives α ↦ ⌊(3+ε)α⌋ ≥ α, so the while-loop never ends (line15_one). So the second case is only valid for a > (log n)^{2/μ'}, not for all superlogarithmic a. The a below this threshold are polylogarithmic, and the paper's remark before the corollary (Theorem 4.3 for polylogarithmic a) can handle them, but only if the threshold is made explicit and Theorem 4.3 is used with a smaller exponent (μ'' = μ²/4). DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538430. Formalized version: the PODC paper (Protocol ICC0, Figures 1–2, and the three lemmas of Section 4). The PODC version has no proofs; they are deferred to the full version (IACR ePrint 2021/632), which we did not use. All proofs here are our own. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Safety (Property P2) and Deadlock freeness (P1) of ICC0 hold as stated for t < n/3, and so does the consistency of the honest outputs. Liveness under partial synchrony (P3) holds in the intended sense, that the honest leader's block is committed by every honest party, but read literally its conclusion ("B_Q is in every honest pool as a finalized block") can fail because of Figure 2's kmax skipping, and rewording it keeps the intent. Protocols ICC1 and ICC2, the ones meant for large blocks, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Liveness lemma (conclusion "as a finalized block") The lemma promises that every honest party has Q's block B_Q "in its pool as a finalized block", but if the adversary delivers the round-(k+1) finalization shares before the round-k ones, every honest party skips B_Q via Figure 2's kmax and never forms a finalization of it (counterexample in words only). Impact. The literal conclusion can fail, but what P3 and its discussion are after still holds: every honest party outputs B_Q. Details. By Section 3.4, "finalized" means that a combined finalization is in the pool. But Figure 2 combines round-k finalization shares only if k > kmax. After the two synchronous instants of hypothesis (iv) the network is asynchronous. The adversary can deliver the round-(k+1) finalization shares before the round-k ones to every honest party. Then every honest party finalizes the round-(k+1) block first, jumps to kmax = k + 1, and outputs B_Q without ever forming a finalization of it. Nobody honest broadcasts one, so the literal conclusion fails. This counterexample is argued in words, not in Lean. Repair. State the conclusion as commitment: every honest party holds n − t finalization shares of B_Q, has kmax ≥ k, and has committed B_Q: the chain ending at B_Q is a prefix of its output (liveness). Typos Section 3.5 describes clause (c) with "at least Δntry(t) time units"; it should be Δntry(r), as in Figure 1. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous interleaving transition system for ICC0 (Model.lean). Parties run Figure 1 and Figure 2 concurrently, one clause per step, with arbitrary choice among enabled clauses. Byzantine faults: a static corrupt set F with #F ≤ t and 3t < n. Corrupt parties are represented by everything the adversary can inject into honest pools. Cryptography is idealized: collision resistance: a block contains its parent; authenticators and shares cannot be forged; a notarization or finalization exists iff n − t parties signed, corrupt parties signing anything (the ideal (t, n−t, n) threshold signature, CSLib Byzantine.Certified); the unique random beacon gives a fixed rank function rank k, assumed injective for each round. Network: insecure broadcast. The adversary delivers any available message to any honest party at any time; self-delivery is immediate. No randomness is involved: the leader's honesty is a hypothesis. Time is discrete, with one global clock read by all parties. Safety is proved for all interleavings and clock behaviours. For liveness, runs follow the paper's "wait for" semantics: time advances only when no honest party has an enabled clause (UStep), and δ-synchrony at a time T₀ is a property of the run (SyncAt). Stronger or weaker than the paper: ranks only injective (more general); k ≥ 1 instead of k > 1; δ ≥ 1; arbitrary payloads. The deadlock lemma's "will have finished" is read as "in a state where no honest party in a round ≤ k has an enabled Tree Building clause". Main results in Lean. The checked results hold after local changes: O(1)-round 4-cycle detection (Theorem 4, with Lemmas 12 and 13), O(n^{1/3})-round semiring matrix multiplication (Theorem 1), and Lemma 14 and the case split of Theorem 15. They need one short repair in the proof of Lemma 12 and two slips corrected. The paper's main point, fast ring matrix multiplication and its applications, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 2.1, Step 1 (3D matrix multiplication: recipients of the T-blocks). Step 1 sends the T-blocks to the wrong nodes, so for n^{1/3} ≥ 2 some node never receives a row of T it needs (step1_as_written_wrong). The paper says node v sends T[v, w₃∗∗] to every w ∈ ∗v₂∗, and that v receives T[w, v₃∗∗] from every w ∈ ∗v₂∗. But node v multiplies S[v₁∗∗, v₂∗∗] T[v₂∗∗, v₃∗∗], so it needs the rows w ∈ v₂∗∗ of T; the paper itself says "each node v receives … T[v₂∗∗, v₃∗∗]". Corrected, v sends to w ∈ ∗v₁∗ and receives from w ∈ v₂∗∗. We implement this pattern; the algorithm is then correct and Theorem 1 (semiring part) holds (step1_corrected, theorem_1_semiring). Lemma 12 (missing hypothesis ∑ deg(y)² < 2n²). As stated, Lemma 12 claims disjoint tiles A(y) × B(y) ⊆ V × V with |A(y)| ≥ deg(y)/8 for every graph, which fails for the complete graph K_n once n ≥ 67: the tiles would need total area at least n(n−1)²/64 > n². The lemma is meant under the bound ∑_y deg(y)² < 2n² derived just before it ("Using this bound, we obtain the following lemma"), and it is only used there. We state it with that hypothesis, and then it holds (lemma_12). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 12, proof (f(y) for degrees 1–3) f(y) is "deg(y)/4 rounded down to the nearest power of 2", which is undefined for 1 ≤ deg(y) ≤ 3, and the natural fix f(y) = 1 breaks the first step of the paper's chain. Yet |A(y)| = f(y) ≥ deg(y)/8 > 0 must hold. With f(y) = 1, the first step of the chain ∑ f(y)² ≤ ∑ deg(y)²/16 < n²/8 < k² fails. Repair. The conclusion ∑ f(y)² ≤ k² still holds: 16 f² ≤ deg² + 15 gives 16 ∑ f² < 2n² + 15n ≤ 16k² for n ≥ 3, and n ≤ 2 is direct. Network (Podc/Computability/Distributed/CongestedClique/Phases.lean, shared). Synchronous congested clique on a finite node set with known identifiers. The algorithms are deterministic, with no failures and unbounded local computation. An algorithm is a Prog: a sequence of communication steps. In a step, every node computes from its own state a list of words for every node; every node then computes its new state from its old state and the received lists. So locality holds by construction. Direct steps. A direct step is sent over the links, one word per ordered pair per round. It costs the length of its longest list. This is the plain congested clique. Routed steps. A routed step has the same semantics. It requires every node to send and receive at most n words and costs 16 rounds. This is the black box of Lenzen's routing (PODC'13, Theorem 3.7), formalized separately in Papers/PODC2013/CongestedCliqueRouting for opaque messages but not composed with this model. Only the final step of the 4-cycle algorithm uses routed steps. The 3D algorithm uses direct steps only. Words. For 4-cycle detection a word is a triple of numbers ≤ 64n (O(log n) bits). For matrix multiplication a word is one semiring element, as in the paper ("entries of O(log n) bits"). Inputs and outputs. For 4-cycle detection, node v starts with N(v) of a simple undirected graph on Fin n, and every node must output whether a 4-cycle exists. For matrix multiplication, n = q³ (the paper's assumption that n^{1/3} is an integer); node v starts with rows S[v,∗] and T[v,∗] and must output row (ST)[v,∗], over any (even non-associative, non-unital) semiring. Specification and Space Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing — PODC 2016 Hagit Attiya, Sebastian Burckhardt, Alexey Gotsman, Adam Morrison, Hongseok Yang, Marek Zawirski. Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933090. Formalized version: the journal version Specification and space complexity of collaborative text editing, TCS 855 (2021) 141–160, which has complete proofs. Lean docstrings use the TCS numbering. The verdict judges the PODC 2016 paper (and its extended version with appendices); we checked that its RGA pseudocode, Definitions 1–13 and the lower-bound construction are the same as in the TCS version. Numbering map (PODC → TCS): Theorem 1 → 1 (PODC claims only the strong list specification; TCS adds eventual visibility), Lemma 3 → Lemma 6, appendix Lemmas 13–16 → Lemmas 3, 4, 5, 7, Theorems 4–5 → Theorems 8–9, Claims 6–9 → Claims 10–13. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 1 (RGA implements the strong list specification) fails for the protocol as literally written, because its insert procedure counts tombstones when it locates the insertion position, but a local index change that the paper's own definition of ins(a, k) dictates makes it hold. The main lower bound holds: any push-based protocol with at least three replicas that satisfies the weak list specification has metadata overhead Ω(D) (PODC Theorems 4 and 5), and we formalized the encoding/decoding proof completely, with two local repairs. The O(D lg k) upper bound for RGA was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 1 (RGA of Section 4.2 implements the strong list specification) RGA as written violates condition (1c), because its insert locates the parent in s(N), which still contains tombstones: at one replica, ins(x,0); ins(y,1); del(x); ins(b,1) returns b y, while (1c) requires b at position 1 (RGA.literal_not_weak, RGA.literal_not_satisfies). Impact. A local index fix that the paper's own definition of ins(a, k) dictates; with it Theorem 1 holds (RGA.theorem1_strong). State, messages and tree rule stay the same. Details. The RGA do transition builds the new node "as described in the Insert procedure of Section 4.1". That procedure takes the parent p = a_{k−1} of s(N) = a₀ … a_{n−1}, a list that still contains the deleted (tombstoned) elements. However, ins(a, k) and condition (1c) count positions in the user-visible list s(N) \ T. In the example, before the last insert, s(N) = x y and the visible list is y. The parent of b is a₀ = x, so s(N) = x b y and the response is b y. But (1c) requires b at position min(1, 1) = 1. No abstract execution of this execution is in A_weak, let alone A_strong. The proof says only that "(1c) follows directly from the properties of the TI data structure". The same counterexample works with any number of replicas. The intent is recoverable from the paper: Section 3 defines positions on the returned list, and Insert's prose says "the element to the left of the insertion position". The proof never reasons with the tombstone-counting index. Repair. Take the parent in the visible list, p = w_{min(k,|w|)−1} with w = s(N) \ T. This is what the original RGA does, and it is what the meaning of ins(a, k) in Section 3 requires. With this fix we proved Theorem 1 (RGA.theorem1_strong). ✏️ Slips Definition 10 (eventual visibility, TCS version only) lacks the network-connectivity assumption, so the TCS claim that RGA guarantees eventual visibility fails when replica 0 runs ins(a,0) and never sends its message while replica 1 reads forever (RGA.def10_needs_connectivity). Every read returns [], so by (1a) the insertion is visible to none of them, and no abstract execution in A_weak satisfies eventual visibility. Definition 10 asks that every execution with causal broadcast comply with such an abstract execution, but no protocol can do better. The assumption is evidently intended: the remark after Definition 10 says so, the proof of Theorem 1 relies on it, and under Definition 1 the claim holds (RGA.theorem1_eventualVisibility). PODC 2016 does not claim eventual visibility. Typos Section 4.1 is inconsistent about how a node names its parent. PODC 2016 declares p ∈ C ∪ {◦} (the parent's timestamp, with n′.p = n.t, as in the node (b, t_b, t_a) in the proof of appendix Lemma 15). Fig. 2 and the Insert procedure (p = a_{k−1}) instead name the parent by its element. The TCS version switches the declaration to p ∈ U ∪ {◦} but keeps n′.p = n.t and (b, t_b, t_a). We name parents by their element. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 9, Claim 12 (PODC Theorem 5, Claim 8): adjacency of the brackets Claim 12 (PODC Claim 8) says that R₂'s read returns …[ᵢ₋₁ ]ᵢ₋₁… with the two brackets adjacent, because R₂ must be able to insert x "between" them, but the weak specification alone gives only the set of elements. Impact. A few lines fix it, with no new idea (recover_correct). Details. Adjacency follows because lo orders the read's response and also R₁'s response at ins ]ᵢ₋₁, which has the same elements, and lo is transitive on the read's response. We prove the read returns exactly R₁'s list (recover_correct, step hv). 🔧 Theorem 9 (PODC Theorem 5): the choice of σ_w The paper takes σ_w to be R₁'s state after the final read, but in the general model a read may change the state, including the send buffer, so distinct pairs (q, m) need not have distinct internal states q. Impact. Moving σ_w one step earlier repairs the counting (theorem9). Repair. We take σ_w before the read, right after send(m_{d+3}), so its buffer is empty and its user-visible content is [∗]. The read only witnesses this content. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing, with no failures and no randomness (Section 2). A replica is a deterministic state machine. Its state is (q, buf) with a one-slot send buffer. A do(op, v) event is always enabled; its response is a function of the whole state (q, buf), and it may change the whole state. A send moves to (q′, ⊥) where q′ = sendStep r (q, buf) is arbitrary. This is exactly the protocol class of PODC 2016 (the TCS version is narrower: responses depend on q only and sends keep q), so Theorems 8–9 cover every protocol of either version. A send broadcasts the buffered message to every replica, the sender included, and empties the buffer. A receive is always enabled. All replicas use one common type Q. An execution is a list of actions (an infinite sequence ℕ → Act for eventual visibility). A receive names the position of the send whose message it delivers; this makes messages unique, as the paper assumes. HB is Lamport's happens-before on positions. We formalize causal broadcast (Def. 2) and causal atomic broadcast (Def. 3), and sufficient connectivity (Def. 1) for infinite executions. An abstract execution is a visibility relation vis on the positions of the do events. It must contain the replica order and be transitive and irreflexive (Def. 4). The execution and its abstract execution share event ids, so compliance (Def. 5) is built in. We drop the linearization H: on the hypothesis side this only weakens the hypothesis, and for RGA we show vis ⊆ <. The user assumptions of Section 3 (UserOK): inserted elements are unique, and del(a) only deletes an element returned by the replica's previous operation. Lower bound. PushBased P S Adm is Def. 13, relative to a class Adm of executions. Theorem 9 assumes push-based only on executions with causal atomic broadcast that respect the user assumptions. This hypothesis is weaker than the paper's, so the theorem is stronger; theorem9_causal is the paper's form. The list universe is infinite. The size of an internal state is the length of its code under an arbitrary injective encoding Q → List Bool. RGA. Theorem 2 (linear convergence of gradient descent with the CGC filter under 2f-redundancy) is fully proved; its part (i) ρ ≥ 0 fails only when W* = ℝ^d. Theorem 1 ("2f-redundancy is necessary") is under-specified: read literally it is vacuous, and read as what its proof shows (indistinguishability) it is true and tight, provided exactly f agents are faulty, n > 2f and the honest costs share a minimum point; we prove this repaired form in both directions. So the necessity half of the paper holds only in this weaker, per-execution form. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 1 ("2f-redundancy is necessary"; under-specified) Definition 2 does not say on which inputs the algorithm must be correct, so Theorem 1 is vacuous when read literally and true only when read as what its proof shows, indistinguishability (theorem1, theorem1_indistinguishable). Impact. Necessity survives only per execution: the indistinguishability reading is true and tight, provided exactly f agents are faulty (see the next item), n > 2f and the honest costs share a minimum point; we prove this repaired form in both directions. Details. There are three readings. (a) Literal: vacuous. The proof turns the faulty agents' functions into honest functions of a second execution, so it asks for correctness on all executions. In that model no deterministic algorithm is f-resilient once f ≥ 1, so "f-resilient ⇒ 2f-redundant" holds trivially. Even a 2f-redundant execution is confused there. Example: n = 3, f = 1, received x², x², (x−2)²; honest agents {0, 1} (minimum 0) vs. {1, 2} (minimum 1). The partner x², (x−2)² has no common minimum point. (theorem1, no_resilient_allExecs, redundant_execution_confusable) (b) Sharp: false, but not claimed by the paper. "An algorithm that is f-resilient on all 2f-redundant inputs cannot also be f-resilient on a non-redundant input." Counterexample in the paper's sensing setting: n = 3, f = 1, honest costs x² and y² on ℝ². More generally, any execution whose honest costs share a minimum point can be added to the 2f-redundant class. The paper never states this reading, so it is not an error of the paper. It does show that 2f-redundancy is not a maximal solvable class. (sharp_necessity_false, exists_resilient_redundant_insert) (c) Indistinguishability: true and proved. This is what Part II actually shows. Let f ≥ 1, 2f < n, exactly f agents faulty, and suppose the honest costs share a minimum point. Then the execution is not 2f-redundant iff the faulty agents can send convex differentiable functions such that another execution yields the same received vector, has honest costs with a common minimum point, and has a solution set disjoint from the true one. Then no deterministic algorithm is correct on both. The (⇒) direction is the paper's construction with C_B = ‖x − ŵ‖². For (⇐), the two honest sets share ≥ n − 2f agents, and the partner's common minimum point solves that subset, hence by 2f-redundancy the true execution. (theorem1_indistinguishable) ⚠️ Theorem 1, Part II of the proof (exactly f faulty agents) Part II assumes exactly f faulty agents ("Then |H| = n − f"), and with fewer faults reading (c) is false: n = 3, f = 1, no faulty agent, costs x², y², x² + y² on ℝ² (theorem1_indistinguishable_false_fewer_faults). Impact. Under reading (c) "up to f" is not saved; the repair is "exactly f faulty agents", the case the proof treats. Details. In the counterexample the execution is not 2f-redundant, yet every execution producing the same received vector has the origin as a solution. ✏️ Slips Theorem 1 needs n > 2f, which the proof uses but the statement omits, and it is false for n = f = 1 (theorem1_false_n_eq_one). Definition 1 then includes the empty subset, so a single honest agent with cost x² violates 2f-redundancy, while "output a minimum point of the received function" is f-resilient. "2f-redundancy implies n > 2f" (Appendix B) does not follow from Definition 1. Theorem 2 (i), ρ ∈ [0, 1), fails when W* = ℝ^d (e.g. all honest costs constant): with n = 3, f = 1, μ = 1, λ = 30, η = 29/3 < η̄ = 58/3 we get ρ = −840 (theorem2_rho_nonneg_false). Appendix B derives λ ≤ μ from a point outside W*; without one, λ is unconstrained. Part (ii) is trivially true there, and (i) holds under W* ≠ ℝ^d (theorem2_rho_nonneg). Existence of minimum points is assumed tacitly. Definition 2 and the projection in Assumption 4 need W* ≠ ∅. Theorem 2, step (29) ⇒ (30) ("every honest gradient vanishes on W*") needs f ≥ 1 and fails for f = 0. Theorem 2 still holds for f = 0 via the Lipschitz bound on the aggregate gradient (Assumptions.key_estimates). Honest agents send their own convex differentiable cost; faulty agents send arbitrary convex differentiable functions. f-resilience is relative to an explicit class K of executions (honest set + honest costs). Approximate Byzantine Fault-Tolerance in Distributed Optimization — PODC 2021 Shuo Liu, Nirupam Gupta, Nitin H. Vaidya. Approximate Byzantine Fault-Tolerance in Distributed Optimization. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467902. Formalized version: arXiv 2101.09337 v5 (full version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Formalized: Section 3 (Lemma 1, Theorems 1 and 2). Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 2 ("(2f, ε)-redundancy ⇒ (f, 2ε)-resilience") holds as stated, and a local change repairs the case its algorithm misses. Theorem 1 ("(f, ε)-resilience ⇒ (2f, ε)-redundancy") does not say on which inputs the algorithm must work: read for the given cost functions it is false, read for all inputs it is vacuous, and read for the class of (2f, ε')-redundant inputs it is true, which we prove for all n > 2f ≥ 2 by a new argument because the paper's proof does not cover that reading. The gradient-descent results (Sections 4–5) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Theorem 1 ((f, ε)-resilience ⇒ (2f, ε)-redundancy) Theorem 1 does not say on which inputs the algorithm must work: read for the given cost functions it is false (n = 3, f = 1, d = 1, theorem_1_false_per_profile), read for all inputs it is vacuous (theorem_1_uniform), and read for (2f, ε')-redundant inputs it is true but not covered by the paper's proof (theorem_1_corrected). Impact. Under the meaningful class reading the statement holds for all n > 2f ≥ 2 and every ℝ^d, d ≥ 1. With Theorem 2, the best resilience on that class lies in [ε', 2ε'] (resilience_window). Details. Definition 2 is a property of an algorithm in the executions with given cost functions. The theorem talks about "the agents' cost functions". We formalize three readings. (a) Per profile (literal): false. Take n = 3, f = 1, d = 1 and costs (x − a)², (x + a)², 2a|x| with a > 0. They are convex and every aggregate has a unique minimum point, as in the proof's own scenario. Every pair of agents has arg min = {0}, so the algorithm "always output 0" is (1, 0)-resilient, i.e. exactly fault-tolerant. But arg min Q₀ = {a} is at distance a from arg min (Q₀ + Q₁) = {0}, so the costs are not (2, ε)-redundant for any ε < a. Since a is arbitrary, no constant factor helps either. For a fixed profile, an (f, ε)-resilient algorithm exists iff some point is within ε of every (n − f)-arg min. Redundancy plays no role there. (theorem_1_false_per_profile, exists_isResilient_iff) (b) All inputs: vacuous. The proof turns the faulty agents' fabricated functions into the true costs of a second execution. So it needs the algorithm to be correct on all profiles. On that class no deterministic algorithm is (f, ε)-resilient once 1 ≤ f < n, whatever the redundancy, even with quadratic costs ‖x − cᵢ‖². The theorem then holds only because its hypothesis is never met. (theorem_1_uniform, no_uniform_resilience) (c) Redundant inputs: true, proof repaired. The meaningful version is: if ε < ε', no deterministic algorithm is (f, ε)-resilient on all profiles satisfying Assumption 1 and (2f, ε')-redundancy. Equivalently, resilience ε on that class forces ε' ≤ ε. The paper's proof does not establish this: its second profile (the reflected faulty functions) is not shown to be (2f, ε')-redundant. Repair. We prove (c) for all n > 2f ≥ 2 and every ℝ^d, d ≥ 1, with one profile supported on the three points −v, 0, v, ‖v‖ = ε'. The f agents of group 2 pull towards v, the f agents of group 3 towards −v, and the rest prefer 0. A set has v (resp. −v) as a minimum point only if it contains group 2 and not group 3 (resp. the converse). So nested sets always have their arg mins together in {0, v} or in {0, −v}, and the redundancy is ε'. The n − f agents outside group 3 have arg min {v}, those outside group 2 have {−v}, at distance 2ε' > 2ε. These costs are discontinuous, which Section 3 allows. (theorem_1_corrected, theorem_1_class, resilience_window) ✏️ Slips Lemma 1 fails for f ≥ n: for f = n the only set of n − f non-faulty agents is ∅, whose arg min is all of ℝ^d, so every algorithm is (n, 0)-resilient (lemma_1_false_of_le). For f > n the condition is empty. For n/2 ≤ f < n the lemma holds in the reading of its proof (no algorithm works for all profiles) (lemma_1); in the uniform reading, f ≥ 1 already suffices (no_uniform_resilience). Read per profile, Lemma 1 is false (e.g. all costs equal), just like Theorem 1. Typos Theorem 1's proof writes n − 2f ≤ |Ŝ| < n − f, while Definition 3 has |Ŝ| = n − 2f. Appendix A, last sentence: "extends easily for the case when n > 2, and f > n/2" should say f ≥ n/2, as the lemma does; the omitted case f = n/2 is equally easy. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2 (the algorithm misses a case) Step 2 of the algorithm picks x_T ∈ arg min ∑_{i∈T} Qᵢ for every set T of n − f received functions, but if T contains faulty agents this arg min may be empty, and then Step 2 is undefined. Impact. The theorem holds as stated, with the repaired algorithm (algorithm, theorem_2). Details. Step 2 also takes distances to arg min ∑_{i∈T̂} Qᵢ. For example, a faulty agent can send minus the other agents' aggregate plus a non-zero linear function, so that the aggregate is linear and has no minimum. Repair. Pick an arbitrary point, and let the distance to ∅ be +∞. The proof then goes through unchanged, since it uses x_T ∈ arg min only for a fully non-faulty T. (algorithm, theorem_2) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. This is the paper's "best case for the server" (Section 3). There are n agents, each with a cost Qᵢ : E → ℝ. The server receives one function per agent and applies a deterministic map alg : (Fin n → E → ℝ) → E. Non-faulty agents send their true cost. A set B of at most f Byzantine agents may send arbitrary functions. There is no synchrony or randomness issue in this one-shot model. IsResilient f ε alg Q (Definition 2) quantifies over all faulty sets |B| ≤ f, all behaviours of B, and all sets S of n − f non-faulty agents. Take two asymmetric 6-vertex graphs F₁ and F₂ = F₁ + {01}, and let ι(F) be whether 01 is an edge, a bit that v_A sees locally. Each node draws one random bit, and the bridge nodes both receive (ι(F_A) ⊕ r_{x_A}, ι(F_B) ⊕ r_{x_B}). v_A and v_B check their halves, and x_A, x_B check that the two halves unmask to the same bit. 𝓜_A(F, r) depends only on the A-side challenges and the two bridge challenges r_{x_A}, r_{x_B}, and symmetrically for 𝓜_B. So the two sets are independent once the bridge challenges are fixed. Proofs are bit strings ℕ → List Bool, and the proof size is the maximum length. A verifier with horizon r is any function whose output at v depends only on the induced radius-r view: the ball V[v,r], the induced edges and marked edges, labels and proof labels (IsLocal). Proof remarks. A few proof steps are only sketched and a few details are imprecise; all are repaired or confirmed in Lean, and none affects a statement. Theorem 5.1, graph problems with edge labels. The glued instance inherits only node data L(v) and P(v). For spanning trees and matchings the solution lives on edges, and the paper does not say what label the new edges {b_{i-1}[1], a_i[1]} get. We store the label of the edge to a node's successor at that node, so a new edge inherits the label of the removed edge {a_i[1], b_i[1]}, and we put these labels into the colour c(a,b). The argument then works as the paper says, and the lower bound holds for weak schemes too. (glue_accept, theorem_5_1_spanningTree, theorem_5_1_maxMatching) Theorem 6.1. The paper says that "by the construction of G" every non-trivial automorphism of G₁ ⊛ G₂ swaps G₁ and G₂, and gives no argument. This is true in general, with a short argument (checked on paper, not in Lean). The connecting path lies in a run of degree-2 nodes with at least k nodes. Every other such run lies inside one copy and has fewer than k nodes. So ϕ fixes or reverses this run. If it reverses the run, the two sides have equal size, and ϕ maps the G₁ copy onto the G₂ copy. If it fixes the run, it restricts to automorphisms of G₁ and G₂, which are trivial. We sidestep the step with a smaller family of G₁: asymmetric graphs in which any two vertices have three common neighbours. In G₁ ⊛ G₂ the degree-2 nodes are then exactly the path nodes. We prove that this family still has at least 2^{C(k,2)}/2 labelled members, replacing the citation of Erdős–Rényi. (symmetric_lcp_lower_bound, exists_many_good) Theorem 7.1. Nesting-Safe Recoverable Linearizability — PODC 2018 Hagit Attiya, Ohad Ben-Baruch, Danny Hendler. Nesting-Safe Recoverable Linearizability: Modular Constructions for Non-Volatile Memory. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212753. Formalized version: the authors' copy of the conference paper (10 pages, proofs included; no arXiv version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Lemma 1 holds, the recoverable read/write object (Lemma 2) and the recoverable compare&swap object (Lemma 3) satisfy NRL, and Theorem 4 (no wait-free recoverable test&set from read/write and test&set) is true, though its proof needed a repair. But the paper's only example of nesting, Algorithm 4, the "nesting-safe recoverable counter", does not satisfy NRL: its READ loses its partial sum when a nested recoverable READ crashes. No repair is proved, so the promised modular construction has no working instance. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Algorithm 4, READ (the "nesting-safe recoverable counter") Algorithm 4's READ is not NRL: when a nested recoverable R[i].READ crashes, the caller resumes after R[i].READ.RECOVER with its volatile partial sum val and loop index i lost, so a READ after a completed INC can return 0 (Alg4.read_not_nrl). Impact. The counter is an example built on top of the other results, which do not depend on it, but it is the only nesting the paper shows. Repairing it requires a design change, e.g. keeping val and i in non-volatile memory; we proved no repair. Details. READ sums R[1..N] with nested recoverable R[i].READ calls, keeping val and i in volatile variables. Under the paper's own model, a crash inside R[i].READ is recovered by R[i].READ.RECOVER, the innermost pending recoverable operation, and not by the counter's READ.RECOVER. The caller then continues line 14 with val and i lost. Counterexample with two processes and the most benign reset (volatile variables become 0): process 0 completes INC. Process 1 starts READ, reads R[1] = 1, and crashes inside R[2].READ. After R[2].READ.RECOVER it adds 0 to the reset val = 0 and returns 0. ✏️ Slips Algorithm 4, INC.RECOVER. The test LI_p < 4 should be LI_p ≤ 4, so a crash just before line 4 makes INC return ack without incrementing (Alg4.inc_recover_not_nrl). The prose ("before line 4 – INC is re-executed") gives the intended test. Suppose process 0 crashes in INC when it is about to execute line 4, before invoking R[p].WRITE. Then LI_p = 4, and INC.RECOVER returns ack without incrementing. A later READ returns 0. Lemma 2 (Algorithm 1). Written values must also differ from the initial value: the lemma is false if a process may write v₀, and the paper assumes only that "all values written to the object are distinct" (alg1_not_nrl_of_initial_rewritten). This is an implied assumption, satisfied by the paper's counter; lemma2 is proved with it. p writes 1 and crashes after its write to R. Then q writes v₀. p's recovery sees R equal to its saved old value, so it writes 1 a second time, and a reader sees 1, v₀, 1. Algorithm 3, lines 26 and 28. They read await(R[p] = …) where they should read R[i], so as printed line 26 never terminates. Not formalized. Lemma 3 (Algorithm 2). new must not be null, because the helping registers start at null. This is the paper's sentinel convention. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4 (no wait-free recoverable test&set from read/write and test&set) At each critical configuration the proof assumes "w.l.o.g. C₁∘p is p-valent" and crashes p, so the renaming can change the crashing process from round to round, and a process that crashes infinitely often does not contradict wait-freedom. Impact. Statement true; repaired by always crashing the same process (theorem4, round). Details. The concluding step needs "a crash-free execution of q" with infinitely many steps, which the infinite construction does not provide once the roles of p and q can swap. Repair. Always crash the same process p. Whichever of D·p, D·q is p-valent, one of D·p·q·crash_p and D·q·p·crash_p is bivalent. The two configurations share a valency, because p's solo recovery cannot tell them apart. Each also inherits the valency of D·p or D·q, because q cannot see p's crash. We proved the theorem for all base objects that are read/write-like or test&set-like. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/NRL/Model.lean, a staged CSLib candidate). Asynchronous shared memory with atomic base objects in non-volatile memory, for one implemented object O. Deterministic processes; the adversary chooses the schedule and the crashes. There is no randomness. Individual crash-recovery. A crash erases the volatile variables, and the system restarts the process in Op.Recover with the same arguments and LI_p, the location it was about to execute. The crash and the recovery step form one event. After a primitive, the next location does not depend on the primitive's response; this is how we read LI_p, and Theorem 4 depends on it. After a crash the algorithm fixes the values of the volatile variables; the paper says "arbitrary values". This gives algorithms more power, so the impossibility is stronger, and the positive algorithms do not read their volatile variables before writing them. NRL is Definitions 3–4: recoverable well-formedness, and linearizability of N(H) (the history without crash and recovery steps) in CSLib's sense. It is required for every finite history that satisfies the paper's assumptions on invocations (Env). Wait-freedom is stated on infinite schedules: a process that never crashes again and takes infinitely many steps completes. This covers both the operation and its recovery function. Nesting (Algorithm 4) is modelled by a separate concrete interpreter with two-level frames. A crash inside a nested operation runs the nested RECOVER, and the caller keeps only its return address. Proof remarks. The paper's proofs of Lemmas 2 and 3 leave implicit that "linearize the recovered WRITE / failed CAS right before / after another process's step" is a speculative point. Our proofs linearize speculatively and retract the entry if the guess turns out wrong. Main results in Lean. Crash-Tolerant Consensus in Directed Graphs — PODC 2015 Lewis Tseng, Nitin H. Vaidya. Fault-Tolerant Consensus in Directed Graphs. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767399. Formalized version: arXiv 1412.8532 v2 (Crash-Tolerant Consensus in Directed Graphs, same authors); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The tight conditions hold. Synchronous crash consensus with at most f crashes is solvable on a digraph iff every reduced graph G_F (|F| ≤ f) has a node reaching all of it (Theorems 1–4, binary and multi-valued), and in the asynchronous case the necessity (Theorem 6) holds, while the sufficiency (Theorem 7, only sketched) fails for Algorithm WA if phase-p messages are handled as soon as they arrive, but holds for the evident fix, which we verify. The side result Theorem 5 (no fixed iterative algorithm) survives only with "eventual" outputs: with outputs at a fixed iteration, as Min-Max does, the paper's counterexample graph admits a fixed iterative algorithm. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 5 (no fixed iterative algorithm), under fixed-iteration outputs If an iterative algorithm outputs its value after a fixed iteration, as Algorithm Min-Max does, the paper's own counterexample graph admits a fixed iterative algorithm for f = 1: Z(R) = ¬max R with output after iteration 4 (notMax_solvesAt). Impact. Section 3 never says when an iterative algorithm outputs. With "eventual" outputs the paper's argument is sound and we prove Theorem 5 for every f (theorem5). Under the fixed-iteration reading the theorem is unestablished: whether it holds for some other graph is open. Details. The proof claims that a fixed transition function Z must map all-0 (all-1) collections to 0 (1) and that the source's value never changes. With fixed-iteration outputs this is false. For f = 1, Z(R) = ¬max R with output after iteration 4 solves binary crash consensus on the paper's graph (source, clique of f + 1 = 2 nodes, leaf), against every crash pattern with one crash, including mid-round crashes with partial delivery. The values alternate between "true" and "negated", so ¬max simulates alternating Max and Min rounds. Python search also confirms this for f = 2; for f = 3 the same Z fails at T = 4. Repair. With "eventual" outputs (from some iteration on, the fault-free values agree and are inputs) we prove Theorem 5 for every f (theorem5). 🔧 Algorithm WA and Theorem 7 (early messages, deadlock) If a phase-p message is handled on arrival, as the pseudocode's wording suggests, a node can lose it before entering phase p and then wait forever, already in a failure-free run on 5 nodes with f = 1 (found by simulation, not in Lean). Impact. The pseudocode does not say what happens to early messages, and the evident fix (keep early messages, re-check WAIT on entering a phase) works: we prove Theorem 7 for the fixed algorithm (theorem7). The asynchronous characterization stands. Details. "On entering phase p" resets Rᵢ[p] and heardᵢ[p], but phase-p messages can arrive and be marked as seen while i is still in phase p − 1. They are then lost: later copies are not "received for the first time". In a failure-free run on 5 nodes with f = 1 (edges 0→1,2,3; 1→0,2,4; 2→0,1,3,4; 3→4, which satisfies the condition of Theorem 6), node 4 gets the phase-2 messages of nodes 1 and 2 before finishing phase 1. In phase 2 it then waits forever: Condition WAIT would need reach₄(F) ⊆ {0, 3, 4} with |F| ≤ 1, but reach₄({1}) ∋ 2 and reach₄({2}) ∋ 1. The run was found by simulating the pseudocode. If early messages are instead buffered until i enters phase p (and nodes keep relaying), simulation finds no deadlock. Repair. Keep early messages and re-check WAIT when entering a phase. The proof of Theorem 7 is only a sketch ("the rest of the proof is standard"). We prove the fixed algorithm correct, including the liveness and the 1 − 1/n contraction per phase that the sketch omits (theorem7). ✏️ Slips Algorithm MVC and Theorem 4: "inputs in the range [0, K]" must mean integers. With all inputs equal to 1/2 and K = 1, everybody outputs 1, which is nobody's input. The OUTER-LOOP tests tᵢ = l for integers l, so integer inputs are evidently meant. We prove Theorem 4 for inputs in {0, …, K} (theorem4). Claim 3's "iff" holds only in the "only if" direction, which is the one used (inv_iteration). The induction step of Lemma 3 says "l ≥ r" for "l ≤ r". The executions of Theorem 5 crash a clique node, which is impossible for f = 0; our proof also covers that case (theorem5). Typos Step 4 of MVC: |min{b | …}| > 0 should be "{b | …} is non-empty". Claim 8 speaks of "sets of 2f + 1 values" of size f + 1; Claim 8 is not needed for the case analysis. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 1 (first step) The proof uses without proof that "no single root" means "some pair i, j without a common ancestor". Impact. The statement stands (theorem1). Repair. A short finite argument fills the step: a node with a maximal set of descendants reaches everything (ctConn_iff_oneReach). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous (SyncModel.lean). Static digraph G on a finite node set. Deterministic algorithms know G and the node identities. In lock-step rounds a node sends an optional message to each out-neighbour and updates its state from the messages received. Crash faults: a node crashing in round c behaves correctly before, reaches an adversarial subset of its out-neighbours in round c, and is silent afterwards. At most f crashes, chosen adversarially (they may depend on the inputs). Consensus = termination, agreement and validity (output = some node's input) for fault-free nodes. Theorem 1 holds against every algorithm in this model and uses only crashes before the start. Iterative algorithms (Iterative.lean). Binary values. A fixed transition function Z : Multiset Bool → Bool is applied to the own value plus the received values, in the same crash model. Two output conventions: eventual (SolvesEventually) and fixed iteration T (SolvesAt). Asynchronous (Async.lean). The event-driven model on digraphs of the PODC 2020 formalization (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/ApproxConsensus/Async/Model.lean, shared with the PODC 2020 paper): reliable FIFO links with adversarial finite delays and fairness on links between correct nodes. For Theorem 6 the faulty nodes are initially dead, which makes the impossibility stronger. For Theorem 7 (AsyncCrash.lean) nodes crash at arbitrary times: a crashed node takes no more steps, and its messages still in transit may or may not be delivered, which models a crash in the middle of a broadcast. Initially dead nodes are a special case (crashSolvesOn_of_gen). Validity: output between two inputs of any nodes. The input range [lo, hi] is known, so that p_end can be chosen. Main results in Lean. Optimal Resilience of Fast Byzantine Consensus — PODC 2021 Petr Kuznetsov, Andrei Tonkikh, Yan X Zhang. Revisiting Optimal Resilience of Fast Byzantine Consensus. PODC 2021, pp. 343–353. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467924. Formalized version: extended version arXiv:2102.12825v3 (numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The tight bound holds: for 1 ≤ t ≤ f, an f-resilient t-two-step consensus protocol exists iff n ≥ 3f + 2t − 1 (5f − 1 for t = f). We proved both directions in one formal model: the lower bound (Theorem 4.5), and the safety, liveness and two-step property of a concrete implementation of the protocol. The paper's safety proof has one gap, which we repaired with a harmless extra check. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 4.5 fails at f = 1, t = 0: then 3f + 2t − 2 = 1, and with one process "decide your own input" is an f-resilient t-two-step protocol (theorem_4_5_fails_f1_t0). §4.1 assumes n ≥ 3f + 1, and the lower bound holds for every 2 ≤ n ≤ 3f + 2t − 2 (no_fastConsensus_of_le). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Protocol safety (Sections 3.2–3.3, Appendix A: votes from "future" views) The safety proof's induction on views breaks because nothing requires a valid vote sent to the leader of view v to carry a proposal (or commit certificate) from a view u < v, so the highest view w among the valid votes can be ≥ v. Impact. A gap in the proof, not a known protocol bug; repaired with a harmless extra check (Protocol.ValidBallot, Protocol.ValidCC, Protocol.consistency). Details. A vote (x, u, σ, τ) sent to the leader of view v is valid if its certificates check out. During asynchrony, other processes may already be in higher views, so a Byzantine voter can attach a correctly certified proposal from some view u ≥ v. The proof's induction on views ("every certified value of an earlier view is safe") cannot then be applied to w. The commit certificate carried in a vote has the same problem. Safety of the unmodified protocol is plausibly provable by a different induction, for example on certificate creation time. Repair. We add the check that a vote for view v may only carry a proposal and a commit certificate from views < v. Correct processes only send such votes, so liveness is unaffected. (Protocol.ValidBallot, Protocol.ValidCC, Protocol.consistency) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. We use a shared partially synchronous model with Byzantine faults (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync). n deterministic processes, at most f of them statically Byzantine. Point-to-point links with ideal unforgeable signatures; the unauthenticated case is a special case (theorem_4_5_noAuth). Discrete time with an unknown GST and a known δ > 0. Correct processes step at every tick from time 0 (synchronized, drift-free clocks), as in the paper's §4.1. Consensus means weak validity, agreement and termination in every valid run. t-two-step (TwoStep): in the T-faulty two-step execution tsRun with |T| = t, every correct process decides by time 2δ. Differences from the paper. Simultaneous deliveries are processed atomically, so the two-step execution is unique rather than "some ordering of simultaneous events". The lower bound therefore covers a slightly smaller class of protocols. A reply leaves one tick after its trigger, so the two-step notion matches the paper's only for δ ≥ 2. The headline theorem assumes δ ≥ 2. Positive side. It is proved twice. First, for an asynchronous interleaving transition system over all emitted signed tokens, with arbitrary leaders and view changes. This over-approximates any implementation, so safety transfers. Second, for a concrete algorithm in the model above: gossip of signed tokens, clock-driven views of length 6δ + 12, a rotating leader. Synchronized clocks make a view synchronizer unnecessary, which is friendlier than the paper's setting. Main results in Lean (namespace FastByzantineConsensus). Proof remarks. Commit certificates in case (3) of the Appendix A.3 safety induction (used for Theorem A.4): an imprecision. The proof argues that a slow-path decision for x in view w would leave a commit certificate for x in view w in votes′. This needs two things. First, a correct process commits only for its current view; this follows from the paper's rule behind Lemma 3.1. Second, "the latest commit certificate" must mean the one with the highest view rather than the most recent in time. The two coincide once the first point holds. We make both explicit. Theorem 4.5 in the degenerate case f = 1, t = 0. Then 3f + 2t − 2 = 1, and with a single process "decide your own input at once" is an f-resilient t-two-step protocol (theorem_4_5_fails_f1_t0). This is outside the paper's intended scope, since §4.1 assumes n ≥ 3f + 1 and the protocol assumes t ≥ 1. We prove the lower bound for every 2 ≤ n ≤ 3f + 2t − 2, not just n = 3f + 2t − 2 (no_fastConsensus_of_le). Unstated hypotheses (not errors). Lemma 4.4 uses n ≥ 2t + 2, which follows from n ≥ 3f + 1, and at least two input values. Shared infrastructure. The two-step execution tsRun and the executions ρ₃, ρ₄ with their indistinguishability and admissibility lemmas are Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/PartialSync/TwoStepLowerBound.lean (shared with GoodCaseLatencyBB); Run.DecidesBy is Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/PartialSync/QuietRuns.lean; weak validity is CSLib's weakValidity P V. The progress and commit certificates Protocol.Certified, Protocol.HasCC are threshold certificates Cslib.Byzantine.Certified (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/Certificate.lean), the quorum arithmetic is Cslib/Foundations/Data/Finset/Quorum.lean, and the concrete protocol is an instance of Algorithm.Gossips (Impl.algo_gossips, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/PartialSync/Gossip.lean), which gives gossip, unforgeability and token origin. Not formalized. Section 4.3 (suspect sets), Section 4.4 (disjoint proposers and acceptors, 3f + 2t + 1), extended validity, and bounded certificate size. The reduction of the vanilla protocol (Theorem 3.6) to the generalized one with t = f is argued on paper, not formalized. Liveness with a view synchronizer under loosely synchronized clocks is open: liveness is proved only with perfectly synchronized clocks. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. leaderEcho_fastConsensus (NonVacuity.lean) shows that FastConsensus is satisfiable, and Impl.algo_fastConsensus exhibits a nontrivial instance. The model comes from CSLib, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/PartialSync/.

The Impact of RDMA on Agreement — PODC 2019 Marcos K. Aguilera, Naama Ben-David, Rachid Guerraoui, Virendra Marathe, Igor Zablotchi. The Impact of RDMA on Agreement. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331601. Formalized version: arXiv 1905.12143 v2 (extended version, Feb 2021); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Algorithm 7 (Protected Memory Paxos) violates agreement as printed, with a Lean run in which two processes decide different values, but a one-line fix and one condition on the first ballot make it safe (proved). Theorem 6.1 (no 2-deciding consensus with static permissions, for the read-first notion of "common-case execution") and Lemma 4.1 (reliable broadcast from SWMR regular registers, n ≥ 2f+1) hold after local proof repairs. The Byzantine algorithm beyond Lemma 4.1, and the termination and two-delay claims, the core of the paper's main point, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem D.2 (agreement of Protected Memory Paxos, Algorithm 7 line 21) Algorithm 7 violates agreement: line 21 writes (propNr, ⊥, ⊥) into the leader's own slot, erasing its accepted value, so a decided p2 that starts a new attempt lets p1 decide a different value (theorem_D2_false). Impact. A local fix whose intent is recoverable from the paper makes the algorithm safe (theorem_D1, theorem_D2), so the safety part of Theorem 5.1 survives. Details. The bug. Line 21 writes (propNr, ⊥, ⊥) into the leader's own slot, which erases the value it accepted there earlier. The loop is repeat forever, so a process that has decided starts new attempts. The run. One memory, two processes, no crashes, unique ballots: p2 runs both phases and decides true. p2 starts a new attempt; its line-21 write erases (2, 2, true). Before p2's phase-2 write, p1 takes the permission and reads: no slot holds a value, and no minProp is larger than its ballot. p1 writes its own input false and decides it. p2's next write fails. The run works under every reading of the ambiguous lines 24–26. Where the proof fails. The proof of D.2 assumes that a decided leader's slot still holds its value when a later leader reads it ("q must have seen p's value"). This is exactly what line 21 destroys. Caveat. The run needs the decided process p2 to start another attempt. The pseudocode allows this: decide sits inside repeat forever. But elsewhere the paper treats deciding as the end of the instance ("irrevocable decision", "p1 terminates, deciding", "the leader terminates one instance"). If decide ends the loop, this run is impossible, so a missing return after line 39 is an equally local fix (not formalized). Either way the D.2 proof reasons with the intended behaviour (a decided value stays in the decider's slot), not with the erasing one. Repair. Keep the own accepted pair in the line-21 write, as in Disk Paxos. The prose ("write a new proposal number in its slot") and Algorithm 10's {propNr, -, -} suggest this. With this fix (and the reading of lines 24–26 fixed by Algorithm 12), we prove D.1 and D.2 for any number of processes and memories, including zombie operations of aborted attempts. (theorem_D2_false; repaired: theorem_D1, theorem_D2) 🔧 Theorem D.2 (Algorithm 7 line 13, p1's first ballot) Protected Memory Paxos also needs p1's first ballot to be the smallest: the paper only says propNr = a higher value than any proposal number seen before, and a first ballot of 100 lets two values be decided even with the line-21 fix (first_ballot_not_minimal_false). Impact. One added condition restores agreement: only the lowest ballot may skip phase 1, the standard convention, which we assume (theorem_D2). Details. p1's first attempt skips phase 1 and has seen nothing, so it may pick, say, 100. The run (even with the line-21 fix; two processes, three memories): q decides c at ballot 5 on memories 2 and 3. p1's first attempt then writes (100, 100, a) on memory 1, where it still holds the initial permission, and aborts. q's next ballot 200 reads memories 1 and 2, adopts a, and decides it. Where the proof fails. Case 2 of the D.2 proof assumes that the minimal "bad" ballot performed phase 1, which this attempt did not. Halting reading. The Lean run again lets the decided q start a new attempt. If deciding ends the loop, a third process r can run ballot 200 instead of q, so the problem remains for n ≥ 3 (argued, not formalized). Ballot uniqueness is also only implicit. (first_ballot_not_minimal_false) 🔧 Lemma 4.1, Observation 1 (no slot written twice) Observation 1 says no slot of a correct process is written twice, but Value[p,k,p] is written at line 12 and again at line 40 (p echoes its own message), and L2Proof[p,k,q] at line 64 and again at line 18. Impact. The overwrites are harmless: weaker invariants suffice and are proved; Lemma 4.1 holds (lemma_4_1). Details. As a consequence line 38 must also accept the sender's own doubly signed echo. Repair. All writes to a correct slot endorse one signed pair, a non-⊥ slot stays non-⊥, and every L2Proof write is valid. (lemma_4_1) ✏️ Slips Algorithm 7, lines 24–26. "Non-null value" and "highest propNr" do not say which slot field is meant. Read literally, a slot with a larger minProp and no value causes no abort, though the proof of D.2 needs one, and one reading adopts the leader's own fresh slot and decides ⊥. Algorithm 12 prints the intended version, which we use (theorem_D2). Theorem 6.1, one process or one value. With one process, or a single possible value, a process decides at time 0, so we need n ≥ 2 and two values (theorem_6_1). Algorithm 2, line 27. try_deliver starts at key last[q] = 0 although keys start at 1, so taken literally nothing is ever delivered. With the evident fix Lemma 4.1 holds (lemma_4_1). Algorithm 2, lines 38 and 47. They check the reader's own signature (sValid(p, ·)) instead of the sender's, so a correct reader rejects valid values (lemma_4_1). Typos Algorithm 2: state must be per sender, line 30 uses an out-of-scope proof, and proof validity must require distinct signers, which is left unspecified. The proof of Observation 2 says try_deliver has no loops, but it has the finite for i ∈ Π loops. Lemma D.3 ("the values a leader accesses cannot change between when it reads them and when it writes them") holds only for a write that succeeds, which is what its proof shows. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 6.1, proof (the arbitrary execution E) The proof takes an arbitrary run E in which p decides in two delays and claims p cannot distinguish it from a run where everybody else starts later, which is false if p's reads in E returned values written concurrently by others. Impact. Statement true for the read-first notion of "common-case execution"; repaired (theorem_6_1, not_twoDeciding). The paper never fixes how simultaneous operations are ordered, and on the other reading the theorem fails: if "2-deciding" only requires some common-case run, and simultaneous operations may take effect write-first, Theorem 6.1 fails for n = 2 (sketch in differencies.md, not formalized). Details. In that sketch p2 writes its input while p1 reads it; p1 decides what it read, and both then run any consensus algorithm with that value. Repair. We take E to be the synchronous run in which simultaneous operations take effect reads first. There, p's reads return the initial memory, and write responses are fixed by the static permissions. (theorem_6_1) 🔧 Theorem 6.1, proof ("p′ must eventually decide value v′") The proof needs "p′ running alone must decide", which the model does not give when n ≥ 3 and only one crash is tolerated, and it does not explain why p′ decides a value other than p's. Impact. Statement true; repaired (theorem_6_1). Repair. We let all processes except p run; to them p looks crashed. We give the others input v′ and use validity. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Theorem 6.1 (LowerBound/Model.lean). Memory and processes: asynchronous shared memory, atomic registers with arbitrary static read/write permissions, a memory that never fails, crash-prone deterministic processes. Operations: each is invoked, takes effect later, and its response is delivered later still. A process may have any number of pending operations. Safety: agreement and validity are required in all executions. Termination: required only in synchronous runs in which at most one process is crashed from the start. This is weaker than the paper's partial synchrony, so the impossibility is stronger. Time: in the synchronous run an operation invoked at time t takes effect at t+1 and is answered at t+2 (two delays). Simultaneous operations take effect reads first. Result: no process has decided by time 2, for any inputs (needs n ≥ 2 and two values). Protected Memory Paxos (PMP/Model.lean). Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemmas 2 and 3 (a leader that withholds its secret) Lemma 2 is false for v = Lᵢ withholding its own secret: on A ⇄ B with leader A, Alice's net redemption-premium profit is −p, not ≥ p (TwoCycle.lemma_2_false). Lemma 3's split claim (escrow profit ≥ 0 and redemption profit ≥ p per escrowed asset) fails in the same execution (TwoCycle.lemma_3_split_false). Impact. The hedging result (Lemma 6) is unaffected. Lemma 2 holds for every v ≠ Lᵢ (lemma_2) and for a leader that released its secret (lemma_2_leader_released). In Lemma 3 the redemption part is −p but the escrow part there is +2p, so the total, +p, is what matters, and it is what we prove (lemma_3). Details. The claim: if hashkey kᵢ never appears on v's leaving arcs, then v's net redemption-premium profit is at least p per escrowed asset. Take v = Lᵢ withholding its own secret. It pays its whole redemption premium R(Lᵢ) and receives only p per leaving arc, because Lᵢ ∥ q is a cycle. The proof's cycle case ("v is awarded at least p") forgets the leader's own deposits. Counterexample: the two-party digraph A ⇄ B with leader A. Bob deposits all his premiums but does not escrow his asset. Alice escrowed hers, so she withholds her secret. She pays R(A) = 2p and receives p, a net of −p. (TwoCycle.lemma_2_false) The proof of Lemma 3 charges the leader's own redemption premiums to the escrow premium E(u, v) = R(v) ("the premium E(u,v) is enough to cover…") and only then cites Lemma 2. (1) recurses on R(v ∥ q, u), which never ends when v already occurs inside q (this happens with two or more leaders). Impact. One case condition changes: the value p in that case is what the protocol needs, since a conforming v does not extend such a q (R_eq). Details. When v occurs inside q, v ∥ q is not a path. The argument "each path is finite, being acyclic" covers only paths. (R_eq) 🔧 §5.2 (Alice's redemption rule) §5.2 is hedged for Alice only if she redeems Bob's principal whenever he escrows it, even if she escrowed nothing, and the paper does not have this rule. Under the other reading, Bob can escrow without paying his premium, and Alice loses pa + pb (TwoParty.alt_reading_alice_loses). Impact. With this one rule Alice never loses premiums (TwoParty.aliceNet_nonneg, TwoParty.hedged_alice). Details. The parties run the swap only "if this premium distribution phase is successful". If Bob skips his premium, Alice does not escrow, and Bob escrows anyway, her unredeemed Bob principal awards her premium to Bob. This does not violate Definition 1, since Alice escrowed nothing, but it contradicts the claim that a party's risk is limited to locking up premiums. ✏️ Slips Lemma 7 needs at least one conforming bidder, and it fails without one (Auction.lemma7_needs_compliant_bidder).
