Generalized Lattice Agreement — PODC 2012 Jose M. Faleiro, Sriram Rajamani, Kaushik Rajan, G. Ramalingam, Kapil Vaswani. Generalized Lattice Agreement. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332458. Formalized version: the 10-page extended abstract as distributed by Microsoft Research; numbering follows it. There is no arXiv version. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The algorithm of the title does not solve its problem: Theorem 5.15 is false, so with three processes, one of which crashes, a value received by a correct process is never learnt, even with reliable channels, and the abstract's claim that "every value received by a correct process is learnt in O(N) message delays" falls with no repair proved. The safety part of Algorithm 2 holds (Theorems 5.1, 5.3 and 5.6 and Lemmas 5.4 and 5.5), and so do the round lemmas behind the O(N) bound (5.7, 5.10, 5.11, and the Propose half of 5.9). Algorithm 1 as written also violates Consistency; a one-conjunct fix of Decide repairs that. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 5.15 (liveness of Algorithm 2) Algorithm 2 does not solve generalized lattice agreement: with three processes, one of which crashes, there are fair executions in which a value received by a correct process is never learnt, even with reliable channels (Cex515.theorem_5_15_false, Cex515b.theorem_5_15_false_reliable, Cex515c.theorem_5_15_false_singleton). Impact. Sinks the abstract's claim that "every value received by a correct process is learnt in O(N) message delays", the progress claims of Section 6, and the O(N)/O(k) bounds; a repair needs a protocol design change. The safety results (Theorems 5.1, 5.3, 5.6) stand. Details. Each process is a proposer, an acceptor and a learner (the setting of Section 6). Process 2 crashes; 0 and 1 are correct, which is a majority. In all three executions, the learners stay at learntValue = {2} (respectively {1}, ⊥) forever, and every correct process ends passive with nothing to do. Singleton inputs, a crash in the middle of a step. Process 2 proposes {3}, and acceptor 1 accepts it. Proposer 1 gets {2} chosen and learnt. Proposer 0 proposes {1,2}. Acceptor 0 and acceptor 2 acknowledge it, and proposer 0 decides. But acceptor 2 crashes in the middle of this Accept: its ACK reaches proposer 0, not the learners. Acceptor 1 holds {3} and rejects {1,2}. So the learners count only one ACK for {1,2}. Late NACKs with {1,2,3} reach the passive proposers 0 and 1. ProcessNACK is enabled for passive proposers too, so both proposers join {1,2,3} into proposedValue. Their buffered values are now below proposedValue, so Propose is never enabled again. The value {1}, received by the correct process 0, is never learnt. Every other message is delivered. (Cex515.theorem_5_15_false) Reliable channels, a clean crash, a non-singleton input. Process 2 proposes {2}, which only its own acceptor accepts, and then crashes between two steps. Proposers 0 and 1 each get {1} chosen and decide. Then each receives a late NACK {1,2} from acceptor 2 and absorbs it. Afterwards process 0 receives the input {1,2}. It is already below its proposedValue, so it is never proposed, and the learners stay at {1}. Every message sent to a correct process, including those of the crashed process, is processed. Theorem 5.15 also fails under the paper's literal definition of "learnt" (see below). (Cex515b.theorem_5_15_false_reliable) Singleton inputs, no help from late NACKs. Executions 1 and 2 use that a passive proposer still processes late NACKs; one might read a guard status = active into ProcessNACK. This one does not depend on it. Process 2 proposes {3}, which acceptor 1 accepts. Proposers 0 and 1 both propose {1}; acceptors 0 and 2 acknowledge both proposals, so both decide. Acceptor 1 rejects both. The faulty acceptor 2's ACKs to the learners are lost (assumption (d) covers only messages between correct processes). Each proposal reaches the learners with one ACK only, and the learners stay at ⊥. Every message between correct processes is processed. Without the late NACKs the proposers stay at proposedValue = {1}, which is just as stuck. (Cex515c.theorem_5_15_false_singleton, Cex515c.run_trNoNack) The proof of Theorem 5.15 says: "once a value is chosen, a correct learner will eventually receive the acknowledgments sent for the chosen value". This is false when the quorum contains a faulty acceptor. Both this and the Lemma 5.14 step below are protocol problems, not just proof gaps. The paper explicitly allows crashes in the middle of a step and message loss, and asks only that messages between correct processes be delivered. So no implicit assumption rescues the theorem. Execution 3 shows that the learner problem alone breaks the theorem. So a repair needs a design change (for example, deciders forwarding their decisions to the learners), not a local fix of the pseudocode. The same executions break the progress claims of Section 6. In Algorithm 4, ExecuteUpdate waits forever for cmd ∈ LearntValue(), so it is not wait-free. They also break the O(N)/O(k) message-delay bounds of the abstract and Section 5.3. We did not formalize a repaired algorithm. ❌ Lemma 5.14 (a passive proposer initiates every received value) In execution 2 above no proposal and no ACK ever covers the received value {1,2} (Cex515b.theorem_5_15_false_reliable). Impact. A second, separate cause of the failure of liveness; no corrected lemma is proved. Details. The proof says: "if any correct proposer … is passive when it receives u, it will initiate u". This ignores that proposedValue grows while the proposer is passive. 🔧 Algorithm 1 and Lemma 5.9 (the guard of Decide) ProcessNACK enlarges proposedValue while ACKs are still counted and Decide has no conjunct nackCount = 0, so the output may be a value that was never chosen. Impact. Algorithm 1 violates Consistency even failure-free, "at most one Decide per round" fails, and the proof step "v₂ must be a chosen value" is false. Lemma 5.11 needs only the Propose half of Lemma 5.9. Details. Algorithm 1 (Consistency, failure-free). With initial values {1}, {2}, {3} and three acceptors, two proposers decide the incomparable {1,2} and {1,3} (Cex1.alg1_consistency_false). ProcessNACK joins a rejection value into proposedValue while ACKs for the same proposal are still being counted. Decide (guard ackCount ≥ ⌈(N_a+1)/2⌉) then outputs this enlarged value, which was never proposed. Proposer 0 processes a NACK {1,2} (caused by proposer 1's {2}) and then two ACKs for {1}, and it decides {1,2}. Proposer 2 is rejected, refines to {1,3} and decides it. The prose of Section 3 has the intended rule: "if all these responses are acceptances, the proposer is done". Lemma 5.9 ("at most one Decide per round"). It fails for the same reason, even failure-free: proposer 0 decides the unchosen {1,2} (its {1} was chosen) and then the chosen {1,2,3}, which lie below exactly the same chosen values (Cex59.lemma_5_9_decide_false). Lemma 5.9, Propose half. "At most one Propose per round" is true, but the proof's "v₂ must be a chosen value" is false. Repair. Adding the guard nackCount = 0 to Decide makes every output a chosen value, and Consistency holds (consistency_of_clean). We prove the Decide half of Lemma 5.9 for decisions with nackCount = 0 (lemma_5_9_decide_clean). For the Propose half, which we prove for the printed algorithm (lemma_5_9_propose), the right argument uses the last proposal before the Decide, which a quorum acknowledged. ✏️ Slips Lemma 5.13 (missing "initiated by a correct proposer"). A proposer may initiate {3}, crash, and lose its messages; then {3} is never part of a chosen value (Cex513.lemma_5_13_false). The lemma is only used for correct proposers. Section 5 (definition of "learnt"). "A value v is learnt by p if p executes Learn(w) for some w ⊒ v" makes Theorem 5.6 false if taken literally: every ACK makes all values below it "learnt", so one ACK of {1,2} "learns" the incomparable {1} and {2}. We read Theorem 5.6 as being about learntValue, and Theorem 5.15 with the problem definition "v ⊑ a learnt value". Execution 2 above refutes Theorem 5.15 under both readings. Typos "Proposed" literally means "proposed exactly"; Lemma 5.14 needs "included in a proposal". The first author's name is misspelled "Falerio" on the paper. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 5.11 (length of the covered chain) The proof shows covered₂ ⊇ Prev and then asserts "the strictly increasing sequence … can have length at most N_p + 1", which also needs covered₁ ∩ Curr ≠ ∅. Impact. The lemma stands; a few lines close the step (lemma_5_11). Details. covered₁ ∩ Curr ≠ ∅ means that w₁ is not a join of values of earlier rounds. That holds because the chosen values form a chain. With it, covered₂, …, covered_k lie between Prev ∪ {u₀} and Prev ∪ Curr, and |Curr| ≤ N_p. Formalized version: the extended version with the appendix proofs (§A, §B; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. The JACM 2018 version was consulted. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main results hold as stated: the dependency-graph characterisation of SI (Theorems 9 and 10, with Lemmas 12, 13, 15), the dynamic chopping criterion (Theorem 16, with Lemmas 17, 24, 26, 27) and its static version (Corollary 18), and the robustness criteria (Theorems 19, 22). The proof of Lemma 26 misses a case, closed by proving its two parts in the other order. A typo in Definition 20 (ExecSI instead of ExecPSI) makes Theorem 21 false as written; it holds for the intended definition. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Definition 20 defines HistPSI = {H | ∃VIS, CO. (H, VIS, CO) ∈ ExecSI} with ExecSI instead of the ExecPSI defined on the line above, which makes Theorem 21 false as written: the long-fork history of Figure 2(c) has a graph in GraphPSI but is not in HistSI (Examples.theorem21_literal_false). Read literally, HistPSI = HistSI, and Theorem 21 would then say that SI histories are exactly the histories of graphs in GraphPSI. With ExecPSI, Theorem 21 holds (theorem21), and no other result is affected. The JACM version has the same typo. We prove Theorem 21 for the intended definition although the paper cites it. Some derived anti-dependencies S' —RW→ V' in the proofs of Lemmas 26 and 27 need S' ≠ V'; the excluded case is a short cycle forbidden by G ∈ GraphSI. Typos §6.1 refers to "the long fork anomaly in Figure 4"; it is Figure 2(c). The proof of Theorem 10(i) says "Figure 3" for Figure 4. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 26 (transitivity of WW_splice(G)) The first part of the proof rules out S'' —WW→ T' with a cycle of DCG(G) (Figure 10(f)) that is in DCG(G) only if S'' ≉ T', and the case T ≈ S is not covered at that point. Impact. Statement true; the proof only needs reordering (Chopped.Hyp.splice_ww_trans). Details. The proof first shows T' —WW→ S'' and only then T ≉ S. Repair. Prove the second part first (it does not depend on the first); then the cycle is in DCG(G). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Purely combinatorial and declarative: no processes, failures, timing or randomness. Everything is finite-relational, and finiteness is never needed. Transactions are lists of read(x,n)/write(x,n) operations in program order, with values in an arbitrary type. T ⊢ read(x,n), T ⊢ write(x,n) and INT are as in §2. A history (𝒯, SO) has an arbitrary SO in §§2–4 and §6; all results there hold for every SO, which is more general than the paper's union of total orders. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 2.2.1: the textual construction defines no arcs out of r_c, so taken literally r_0 and end both have out-degree 0 and no input has a Hamiltonian path (paperArc_not_hamPath). On the Resilience of Routing Tables — PODC 2012 Joan Feigenbaum, Brighten Godfrey, Aurojit Panda, Michael Schapira, Scott Shenker, Ankit Singla. Brief announcement: On the resilience of routing tables. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332478. Formalized version: arXiv 1207.3732 v2 (full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Both theorems hold: Theorem 3.1 says every (connected) network has a 1-resilient forwarding pattern, and Theorem 4.3 says some network has no perfectly resilient one; the Figure 3 network is indeed such a network. But both lemmas behind Theorem 4.3 are false as stated, its proof applies Lemma 4.1 where it does not hold, and the algorithm of §3.2 is too under-specified to verify. We prove Theorem 3.1 with a different construction and repair the proof of Theorem 4.3, so extending arbitrary loop-free routing tables and the polynomial running time stay unproved. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Lemma 4.2 (nodes route along a cyclic ordering) Lemma 4.2 is false: on the path d – 1 – 2 – 3 with no failures, the perfectly resilient pattern "forward to the neighbour closer to d" makes node 2 send packets from 1 and from 3 both to 1, so it routes along no cyclic ordering (lemma_4_2_false). Impact. Only the instance used by Theorem 4.3 is needed, and it is true: node 1 of Figure 3 with all four of its links up permutes {2,3,4,5} in one 4-cycle (Fig3.exists_cycle). Details. The lemma claims that every node in d's component routes along a cyclic ordering of its live links. The proof assumes that every neighbour of the node has its own route to d; dead ends and links to d break this. ⚠️ Lemma 4.1 (do not send packets back) Lemma 4.1 is false as stated: on d – 1 plus the triangle 1, 2, 3, where every node forwards to 1 and node 1 forwards to d (a perfectly resilient pattern), node 2 has the path 2, 3, 1, d avoiding edge 21, yet sends packets from 1 back to 1 (lemma_4_1_false). Impact. The corrected lemma (hypothesis: a path avoiding the node u) holds (lemma_4_1), but it does not apply where the proof of Theorem 4.3 uses the lemma; Theorem 4.3 itself is true (see Proof gaps). Details. The lemma: if v has a working path to d that avoids the edge vu, then v must not send packets travelling u → v back to u. The proof fails all other links of u, so it needs a path that avoids the node u. Repair. We prove the corrected Lemma 4.1: v reaches d after the other links of u fail (lemma_4_1, pass_through). ⚠️ §3.2.1 (the algorithm behind Theorem 3.1) The algorithm of §3.2.1 is not well defined and the proof of Theorem 3.1 is only a sketch, so the algorithm's correctness is unestablished (we did not formalize it). Impact. The existence part of Theorem 3.1 is true; we prove it with a simple construction from a rooted spanning tree (see below) (theorem_3_1). That construction does not extend arbitrary loop-free routing tables, as the introduction claims, and polynomial time is not proved in Lean, so these parts of the claim stay unproved. Details. Some steps are ambiguous or wrong: Step 1 makes the forwarding functions partial (∅), but the model requires total functions. In Step 3, T is the set of failed links (it says "the highest element of E^i_D not in T"), while the model's second argument is the set of live links. The condition "T ∩ E^i_D ≠ ∅" should say that some outgoing DAG link is up. Steps 4e–4f drop the failure-set argument, so it is unclear for which failure sets the new rules apply. The loop of Step 4e starts at c = k−1, so it never installs a rule at i = v_k itself. The proof of Claim 3.2 takes a route "not in D", but every edge is in D. Case II of the correctness proof is argued on a picture (Figure 2). Nodes connected to d only through bridges are never handled. Neither is condition (2) (no forwarding loops) in components cut off from d. ✏️ Slips §2 (forwarding paths: the destination must be a sink): taken literally, the definition lets a path go on after reaching d, and then no pattern is even 0-resilient on any network where d has a link (literal_K2). The definition constrains only nodes i ∈ [n], so on the network d – 1 with no failures, d, 1, d, 1 is a forwarding loop. We let paths stop at d. Theorem 3.1 (disconnected networks): "For every network" fails if a component without d has a link: with no failures, packets there bounce forever (theorem_3_1_disconnected). We assume the network is connected. Typos Lemma 4.1's proof says "sends it back to i" (should be v). Lemma 4.2 cites "figure ??", and Theorem 4.3 cites "figure (c)" (both mean Figure 3). The Case II proof says "iteration q₁ of Step 2" (should be Step 4) and uses "i_1 <_D γ" without defining γ's role. Claim 3.2 and Step 4b write "i ⋬_D x" without saying it means x is not above i. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4.3 (Figure 3 has no perfectly resilient pattern) The proof applies Lemma 4.1 to node 2 in the Figure 3 scenario, where every path from 2 to d passes through node 1, so only the false literal statement applies and the corrected lemma says nothing. Impact. Statement true; repaired with three extra scenarios per cycle (Fig3.theorem_4_3). Details. The paper's other ingredients do not suffice: one pattern is good in the four scenarios that force node 1 to route cyclically (those of Fig3.closed_false) and in the Figure 3 scenario of each of the six possible cycles. A SAT check (satcheck/, not part of the Lean development) finds it. So the written proof is incomplete, though Theorem 4.3 is true. Repair. We add three scenarios with the same local views. They force node 2 to pass packets from 1 on to 10, node 10 to pass packets from 2 on to 4, and node 4 to pass packets from 10 on to 1 (pass_through). For the other five 4-cycles of node 1 we use the matching scenarios. Then the packet of node 5 loops 5 → 1 → 2 → 10 → 4 → 1 → 5 → …, as the paper says. Only condition (1) is used, so even "every connected node has some forwarding path to d" is impossible on this network. (Fig3.theorem_4_3) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Model.lean). A static simple graph G and a destination d. A forwarding pattern gives each node i a total function next i A u. Here A is the set of neighbours of i over live links (the paper's E_i \ F), u is the neighbour the packet came from, and the result is a neighbour of i (adj_next; the paper's f_i : E_i × 2^{E_i} → E_i). If the result is a failed link, the packet is lost. Forwarding is deterministic and uses no packet-header bits. A failure scenario is any set F of edges. A forwarding path is a walk in G \ F that follows next at every interior vertex, and interior vertices are not d. The first hop is free, as in the paper. Good G d f F holds when (1) every node i ≠ d connected to d in G \ F has a forwarding path to d, and (2) no forwarding path repeats a directed link (the paper's loop notion, §4). A pattern is t-resilient (IsResilient) if it is good for all F ⊆ E with |F| ≤ t, and perfectly resilient if it is good for all F ⊆ E. Proof tools: a forwarding path is a prefix of the deterministic trajectory of its first link. So condition (2) follows from termination of all trajectories (good_of). A set of directed links that avoids d and is closed under forwarding refutes condition (1) (not_good_of_trap). Theorem 3.1, our construction (Theorem31.lean). We take any spanning tree rooted at d; the theorem uses a BFS tree from CSLib. An exit of a subtree is a non-tree link leaving one of its nodes. Its value is the depth of the lowest common ancestor of its endpoints, and it leaves the subtree of u iff its value is < depth u. Each node fixes a minimum-value exit of its subtree and an escape hop towards it. A packet from the parent goes to the escape hop if that link is up, otherwise back to the parent. Any other packet goes to the parent if that link is up. Otherwise it goes to the escape hop if the parent link is not a bridge, and is dropped if it is. When the parent link of u fails, a packet reaching u follows escape hops down the subtree of u. All minimal exits on the way have the same value, so it leaves the subtree and then climbs to d on a path that avoids the failure. Our result is stronger than the paper's 1-resilience: with at most one failure, every packet in d's component is delivered, whatever its first hop. Main results in Lean. Binding Crusader Agreement — PODC 2022 Ittai Abraham, Naama Ben-David, Sravya Yandamuri. Efficient and Adaptively Secure Asynchronous Binary Agreement via Binding Crusader Agreement. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538426. Formalized version: the 11-page proceedings version (no arXiv version; the proofs it defers to the "full version" are supplied here). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All four (G)BCA protocols are correct as intended: Algorithm 3 (crash BCA, n ≥ 2t + 1), Algorithm 4 (Byzantine BCA, n ≥ 3t + 1, Lemmas 4.4–4.9), Algorithm 5 (crash GBCA) and Algorithm 6 (Byzantine GBCA) satisfy agreement, validity, binding and termination against an adaptive adversary, with at most 2/4/3/6 broadcasts per party. Two proof steps of Section 4 need local repairs, and the pseudocode of Algorithm 5 needs one more word. The deterministic core of the framework (Theorems 3.1, 3.3–3.5: agreement, validity, the binding step of termination) holds; the efficiency comparisons and the probabilistic parts of the round bounds were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Algorithm 5, line 9 (output "⊥ grade 2"). Read literally, "if all of the messages contain the same value v then decide v, 2" also fires when all n − t echo2's are ⊥, e.g. for n = 3, t = 1, inputs 0, 1, 0, no crash, so Algorithm 5 can output "⊥ grade 2", which is not a GBCA output. Line 10 counts ⊥ as "a value other than v", so "value" includes ⊥. In the example, every party first receives one ⟨val, 0⟩ and one ⟨val, 1⟩. Then everybody sends ⟨echo, ⊥⟩ and then ⟨echo2, ⊥⟩, and line 9 outputs ⊥ with grade 2. That is not one of the five buckets of Definition 3.2, so Theorem 5.1 fails for the literal code. Line 11 becomes dead code, and Algorithm 2, line 7 ("if grade = 2 then commit val") would commit ⊥. The prose above the algorithm says that a party with all ⊥ decides ⊥. We prove Theorem 5.1 for this intended version (all ⊥ gives ⊥ grade 0) (Alg5.decideG, Alg5.theorem_5_1). No other checked theorem or lemma is false. Typos Algorithm 6, line 11 reads "if 1 then"; it means "if (1) then", as in Algorithm 4, line 11. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 4.5 (validity of Algorithm 4) The proof says that to decide 1 − v a non-faulty party "must have 1 − v in its approvedVals set (line 15)", but line 15 only asks for n − t messages ⟨echo3, 1 − v⟩. Impact. Statement true; repaired by one more link of the chain (Alg4.validity). Repair. An uncorrupted sender of ⟨echo3, 1 − v⟩ saw n − t messages ⟨echo2, 1 − v⟩. One of their senders is uncorrupted and has 1 − v approved, which needs an uncorrupted party with input 1 − v. 🔧 Lemma 4.9 (binding of Algorithm 4, adaptive adversary) The proof argues with "the t + 1 echo3 messages from non-faulty parties", but under adaptive corruption who is non-faulty depends on the extension, while b must be fixed at the first decision. Impact. Statement true; repaired by fixing b from the prefix (Alg4.binding, Alg6.graded_binding). Repair. If some party has broadcast ⟨echo3, u⟩ with u ≠ ⊥, then b = u, by Lemma 4.8 applied inside the extension. Otherwise the decider's quorum contains at least n − t − |bad(τ)| genuine ⊥'s. A later ⟨echo3, w⟩ quorum would then need n − t parties among at most 2t candidates. The same repair works for Algorithm 6 through its first ⟨echo4, ⊥⟩. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing among n parties, with authenticated reliable channels and arbitrary finite delays. It is an interleaving system: a broadcast is one event, and each delivery is a separate event chosen by the adversary. The adversary is adaptive. It corrupts up to t parties at any time. A corrupted party stops following the protocol. In the Byzantine mode it can make anybody receive anything from it (equivocation); in the crash mode it just stops, and its earlier broadcasts may be delivered to only some parties. Liveness is proved for every weakly fair infinite execution. Messages between never-corrupted parties are delivered, and their enabled guards are eventually taken. Nothing is required of corrupted parties or injected messages. A round-robin execution shows that fair executions exist (exists_fair). Protocol guards are liberal: "n − t messages, all with v" is "v from n − t parties", and either branch of a "wait until" may fire when both hold. This is a superset of the paper's behaviours, so safety transfers. Parties keep running after deciding. Deterministic protocols; randomness appears only in the framework, as coin values per round. A strong coin is one value per round, a weak coin one value per party. The expected-round bound for Algorithm 1 is a counting statement over coin prefixes, for a deterministic adversary whose binding values depend on earlier coins only. Safety statements are stronger than the paper's. Agreement, validity and binding cover all recorded decisions, also of parties corrupted after deciding, in every reachable state and every extension. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The equivalence of f-tolerance and (n−2f)-disjointness (Theorem 2), the reduction behind co-NP-hardness (Theorem 1) and the tight bounds Tₙ(h) = Θ(n³/h²) (Theorems 3, 5, 7) all hold. Impact. The extremal structure and every asymptotic consequence are unchanged, and we prove the corrected formula for all h ≤ n/3 (theorem_13). Details. The proof minimises abc over integers a, b, c ≥ h with a + b + c ≥ (n+3h)/2. It only treats n ≡ h (mod 2) and says the other case "is proved similarly". When n − h is odd, c must be at least ⌈(n−h)/2⌉. For odd h the paper's formula is not even an integer. In the example, any three of the four triples on 4 vertices form a 1-disjoint hypergraph, two do not. 🔧 Proposition 15 (inside the proof of Theorem 13) Its second bullet calls (n+h)²h/16 the minimum of g(a,b) = ab((n+3h)/2 − a − b) along each face of the triangle, but that value is the face maximum: n = 4, h = 1, (a,b) = (1,1) gives g = 3/2 < 25/16 (prop_15_face_false). Along a face, g is a concave quadratic, so the face minimum is at the endpoints. Repair. We replace the calculus by abc ≥ h²(a+b+c−2h) for a, b, c ≥ h, a two-line integer argument (mul_mul_ge). ✏️ Slips Theorem 2 fails for n = 0, where f-tolerance holds vacuously but no hypergraph is (−2f)-disjoint (theorem_2_card_zero); we prove it for n ≥ 1 (theorem_2). Message Adversaries vs Failure Detectors — PODC 2013 Michel Raynal, Julien Stainer. Synchrony Weakened by Message Adversaries vs Asynchrony Restricted by Failure Detectors. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484249. Formalized version: the full version, IRISA research report PI 2002 (Round-based Synchrony Weakened by Message Adversaries vs Asynchrony Enriched with Failure Detectors, hal-00787978v2, Feb. 2013); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. With the paper's own definition of solving a task in the synchronous model (every process outputs), the QUORUM characterization of Σ is false: a three-process task is solvable in AMP[fd: Σ] but not in SMP[adv: QUORUM] (Theorem 4, Lemma 6, Theorem 5), and the SOURCE + TOUR characterization of Ω (Theorem 2, Lemma 2, Corollary 1) fails in the same way, as does the hierarchy of Figure 1. The simulations of the asynchronous models in the synchronous ones leave weakly correct processes without output, and the converse simulations need exactly those outputs, so no reading of "solve" saves all lemmas and Theorem 3 stays unestablished. Theorem 1, Theorem 6 and the facts about strongly correct processes hold. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemmas 2, 4, 6 against Section 2.4 (Theorems 2, 3, 4, 5, Corollary 1, Figure 1, Conclusion) The asynchronous-to-synchronous simulations treat weakly correct simulators as crashed and give them no output, although SMP processes are reliable and Section 2.4 lets only crashed processes lack an output. Impact. Three things fail, and no corrected characterization is proved under any reading of "solve". The QUORUM characterization of Σ is false, and so is Theorem 5 (SOURCE, QUORUM ≃ Σ, Ω, theorem5_false). Lemma 5 (the other inclusion, not formalized) is not affected. The SOURCE + TOUR characterization of ARW[Ω] is false, and so is Corollary 1 (which adds the TP and PAIRS variants via Theorem 6; corollary1_false). The other inclusion (Lemma 1, not formalized) is not affected. Theorem 3 (SOURCE characterizes Ω in AMP) is unestablished. We found no counterexample (the counterexamples below do not apply, since Tseen and Tcons are not solvable in AMP[Ω]); the statement is neither proved nor refuted. Details. Theorem 4 and Lemma 6 (QUORUM characterizes Σ). The task Tseen ("of p₁, p₂ each outputs alone or both inputs, and at least one outputs both") is solvable in AMP_{3,2}[fd: Σ] but not in SMP_3[adv: QUORUM] (lemma6_false, theorem4_false). In SMP_3, let only p₃'s messages be delivered, every round, to everybody. Every two in-neighbourhoods contain p₃ and p₃ is strongly correct, so QUORUM holds (SOURCE too). The processes are reliable, so p₁ and p₂ must output (Section 2.4: "if no value is computed by p_j, it is because p_j has crashed"; Section 2.3: SMP_n is "made up of reliable processes"); neither ever learns the other's input, so both must answer alone (tseen_not_solvable). In AMP_{3,2}[fd: Σ], p₁ and p₂ write their input to a Σ-quorum and then read from a Σ-quorum (ABD); quorum intersection makes one of them see the other (tseen_solvable_amp_sigma, a complete proof in the CHT model). The proof of Lemma 6 fails at its last step: the simulation of Figure 7 stops the weakly correct simulators, which are reliable synchronous processes that must output. Here p₁ and p₂ are weakly correct and the simulation never gives them an output. Theorem 2 and Lemma 2 (SOURCE + TOUR characterizes Ω in ARW). Consensus between p₁ and p₂, with p₃ as a helper whose output is free (Tcons), is solvable in ARW_{3,2}[fd: Ω] but not in SMP_3[adv: SOURCE, TOUR] (lemma2_false, theorem2_false). Take the patterns in which p₃ sends to everybody and hears nobody, while between p₁ and p₂ the adversary delivers one or both messages each round. They satisfy SOURCE (p₃), TOUR and even QUORUM. p₃ never learns anything, so p₁ and p₂ are in a two-process TOUR system. A Santoro–Widmayer bivalence argument then shows they cannot agree (tcons_not_solvable). In ARW[Ω] all three processes run an Ω-based consensus with commit-adopt rounds; p₃ proposes an input it has read (tcons_solvable_arw_omega). As for Lemma 6, the proof of Lemma 2 says weakly correct simulators "simulate a faulty process", which is not allowed for reliable synchronous processes. Figure 1 and Conclusion (hierarchy of adversaries). The arrows SMP[adv: QUORUM] → SMP[adv: TOUR] and SMP[adv: SOURCE, QUORUM] → SMP[adv: SOURCE, TOUR] ("the first model is stronger"), the first of which the Conclusion repeats, are false. The same inconsistency affects all six lemmas. Lemmas 2, 4 and 6 (asynchronous → synchronous) treat weakly correct processes as crashed. That is valid only if they need not output. Lemmas 1, 3 and 5 (synchronous → asynchronous) need correct asynchronous processes to output, and their simulated processes may be weakly correct (Figures 2, 4, 6: for instance with Σ constantly {ℓ} in Figure 6). The paper never defines task solvability in SMP other than in Section 2.4, where only crashed processes may lack an output. Liveness of Transactional Memory — PODC 2012 Victor Bushkov, Rachid Guerraoui, Michał Kapałka. On the liveness of transactional memory. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332435. Formalized version: the PODC preprint (EPFL Infoscience record 170486, dated 2011/12/5, 10 pages); numbering follows it. We also used the later write-up of the same results, V. Bushkov and R. Guerraoui, Liveness in Transactional Memory (Euro-TM book chapter, 20 pages), called "the chapter" below. Its Theorem 1, Lemma 1 and Theorem 2 are the PODC ones. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 1, Lemma 1 and Theorem 2 hold in the model the paper intends, in all three fault-prone systems, and even with plain serializability, as the introduction claims. Read literally, the PODC formal framework makes them false, because a TM that never answers satisfies its definitions of opacity and local progress vacuously, so the framework had to be redesigned, and the proof of the crash-free case had a gap that a new schedule repairs. Theorem 3 (the automaton F_gp) and finite value sets were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ §2.2–2.3 and Definition 3 (the formal framework; Theorem 1, Lemma 1, Theorem 2 read literally) Read literally, the PODC framework does not force a TM to answer, so the silent TM, which accepts one invocation per process and never responds, ensures local progress and opacity in every fault-prone system, contradicting Theorem 1 (PodcModel.silent_ensures). Impact. In the model the paper intends (the chapter's step model) Theorem 1, Lemma 1 and Theorem 2 hold (theorem_1, lemma_1, theorem_2). The missing condition cannot be added as an assumption to the printed model, and always answering would exclude the blocking TMs the paper discusses (the global lock), so the framework has to change. Details. In §2.2 a TM is an I/O automaton over invocation and response events. It has no internal steps and no fairness. §2.3 says a process crashes in an infinite history iff its projection is finite and non-empty, and liveness (Definition 3) only constrains the automaton's infinite histories. So a process whose invocation is never answered just counts as crashed. With finitely many processes the silent TM has no infinite history, so it ensures every TM-liveness property. All its transactions are live, so it is opaque. Hence it "ensures local progress and opacity in any fault-prone system". The proofs silently assume that every operation eventually returns ("p₁ invokes a read operation … and receives as a response v or A"). The intent is clear from §2.1 (classical asynchronous shared memory) and from the introduction (local progress as the analogue of wait-freedom). Repair. The chapter fixes the model: executions consist of steps, a process crashes iff it takes finitely many steps, and a process that keeps taking steps in an operation that never returns is correct. We prove the results in that model (theorem_1, lemma_1, theorem_2). 🔧 §2.2 (well-formedness H|p_k ∈ Σ_k^∞) §2.2 requires H|p_k ∈ Σ_k^∞ for every history of a TM, but histories are prefix-closed, so this forbids accepting any invocation. Impact. One clause in one definition fixes it; in the step model well-formedness holds by construction. Repair. The chapter allows a final pending invocation (Σ_k^* · Inv_k). ✏️ Slips Theorem 1 says "for every fault-prone system" with no restriction, but it fails with one process, with no t-variable, or with a single value. In each case a TM that answers every operation immediately from a single store and never aborts is opaque and ensures local progress. We assume two processes, a t-variable x and infinitely many values. §2.3 defines a crash as a finite non-empty projection. Then a process that never takes a step is correct and starving, and local progress fails trivially in every history where some process does not participate. The chapter drops "non-empty". Typos The proof of Lemma 1 writes pₙ for p₂ twice. Theorem 2 says "serializable safety property". The definition in §5.1 is "strictly serializable", while the introduction claims "at least as strong as serializability". Both readings are true (theorem_2, theorem_2_serializable). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 1, crash-free case (Algorithm 2) Algorithm 2 runs one process at a time until its operation returns, but a crash-free system may block p₂'s operation until p₁ takes another step, so this schedule need not be admissible and the obstruction-freedom argument yields nothing. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a round-robin schedule and a sturdier strategy (lemma1_crashFree, stratRun_ne_commit₁). Details. The gap appears once the framework is fixed as in the first item; the PODC proof simply assumes that every invocation is answered, and under that stronger assumption Algorithm 2 works with two processes. Algorithm 2 is part of the proof, not of a stated claim. Algorithm 2 (Strategy 2 in the chapter) runs one process at a time until its operation returns, and only p₁ and p₂ ever take steps. A crash-free system admits only executions in which every process takes infinitely many steps. If p₂ runs alone, p₁ "crashes", the execution is not admissible, and the obstruction-freedom argument ("if the operation does not return, pₖ takes infinitely many steps and is correct") yields nothing. With three or more processes the idle processes crash as well. (The PODC definition of a crash as a non-empty finite projection hides this; see Slips.) Repair. Our repair uses a round-robin schedule. It needs a sturdier environment strategy, since p₁ must now keep taking steps while p₂ works. Idle processes invoke filler reads of x. p₂ writes bump a, where a is the first read of p₁'s current transaction, and invokes tryC only while p₁ is not "ready". p₁ writes a value that no committed transaction of p₂ read first, and only once p₂'s last commit wrote a value ≠ a and p₂ has no pending commit request. This handles the "stale" commits that interleaving creates: a tryC of p₂ that is pending when p₁ is aborted can commit after p₁'s next transaction has begun. With this strategy p₁ can never commit, under any schedule. In a crash-free system the analysis is then short: if p₁ is parasitic, p₂ is correct but makes no progress, so it does not run alone; otherwise p₁ is correct and never commits. (lemma1_crashFree, stratRun_ne_commit₁) 🔧 Algorithms 1 and 2 (the conflict argument, Figures 8 and 11) Each process writes v + 1 for its own read, and the argument that H_s is illegal assumes that p₁ and p₂ read the same v, which the text never justifies. Impact. Statement true; a few lines close the step (conflict_seq). Repair. For a committing transaction of p₁, safety of prefixes forces both reads to return the current committed value. The chapter uses cross values instead, which needs no such argument, and so do we. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory with finitely many processes and read/write t-variables. Each step belongs to one process: an invocation by an idle process (the environment chooses it), or a step of the TM implementation for a process with a pending invocation. In such a step the implementation either returns a response or takes an internal step (tau). This is the chapter's step-based model. The TM is an arbitrary nondeterministic agent. It sees the whole execution so far and chooses each step's outcome; its responses must fit the invocation. Every implementation from base objects induces such an agent, so the impossibility covers all implementations. The adversary is the environment, which picks the invocations and the schedule. There is no randomness. Failures (PODC §2.3 with the chapter's crash notion). A process crashes iff it takes finitely many steps. It is parasitic iff it invokes infinitely often but is aborted and invokes tryC only finitely often. It is correct iff neither. It makes progress iff it commits infinitely often. The fault-prone systems are those of PODC: crashes and parasitic processes allowed, parasitic-free, or crash-free; a system constrains which executions the liveness property must hold for. Liveness properties are predicates on executions. This is more general than the paper's sets of fair histories, which induce such predicates. "Runs alone" follows PODC: the process is the only correct one. Safety (strict serializability, serializability, opacity) is checked on the history of every finite execution, using sequences of transactions and the usual read/write semantics. Hardness of Minimal Symmetry Breaking — PODC 2019 Alkida Balliu, Juho Hirvonen, Dennis Olivetti, Jukka Suomela. Hardness of minimal symmetry breaking in distributed computing. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331605. Formalized version: arXiv 1811.01643v3 (full version with Sections 5–8). Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Every checked statement holds: Lemma 2, the speedup Lemmas 7/8/14/15, Claim 16, the Ω(log* n) lower bound for weak 2-colouring (Theorems 6/13), and Θ(log n) for the pointer problem P* (Theorem 4, with Lemmas 3, 17, 18). The lower bound needed only local repairs to its proofs, but the algorithm in the proof of Lemma 3, which the classification of Theorem 5 relies on, is wrong, and we replaced it with a different, correct one. The classification itself (Theorem 5) and the minimality argument of Section 8.3 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips In Claim 11 the recurrence for p̂ is written with ĉ_t; it should be ĉ_{t−1}. Section 3.2 defines the distance to a cycle C using ℓ(C) ≈ |C|/2. Section 8.1 uses "the length of the cycle" instead. Typos In the proof of Lemma 2, "u must be the closest node of different colour to w" is imprecise under ties. Only the distance matters. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 3 (Section 8.1, the P* algorithm) The algorithm in the proof of Lemma 3 does not produce a valid P* labelling: on a 4-cycle of degree-4 nodes with a leaf hanging on one of them, either tie-break breaks the labelling (condition (3) fails at a, or d(d) ≠ d(a)). Impact. Lemma 3, the upper bound behind Theorem 4 and the homogeneous LCLs, is nevertheless true; we prove it (and Lemma 17) with a repaired algorithm (lemma3_repaired, lemma17, theorem4). Details. The paper's case analysis for a node v on a cycle C with irr(v) = C only checks that pointers do not backtrack. It never checks d(v) = d(p(v)) when p(v) chose a low-degree irregularity. Counterexample (Δ = 4, r = 2): a 4-cycle a, b, c, d of degree-4 nodes with IDs a < b < c < d, a leaf x hanging on b, and deep degree-4 trees elsewhere. Node a sees C and x at the same distance 2. b's closest irregularity is x, at distance 1, so d(b) = deg x = 1. If a's tie-break picks C, then a outputs d(a) = 0 and points to b (the orientation goes from the smallest ID a toward its smaller neighbour b). Condition (3) fails at a. If the tie-break picks x, then node d points to a with d(d) = 0 ≠ d(a) = 1. The alternative reading "cycles take precedence whenever one is within r" fails as well. A degree-Δ node whose shortest path to the cycle starts at a degree-< Δ neighbour w points to w with d = 0, while w must output (⊥, deg w). The claim "each node v on C will have a cycle as their closest irregularity" is false. Repair. The repaired algorithm: A node is in low mode if its distance to a degree-< Δ node is at most its distance to the set Z of nodes on short degree-Δ cycles. Low-mode nodes point towards the nearest low-degree node and copy its degree. Otherwise the node is in cycle mode: d = 0, pointers lead towards Z, and inside Z each node follows the least (in a fixed global order) short cycle through it. Both modes are closed under following pointers. Non-backtracking inside Z follows because both endpoints of an edge compare the same candidate cycles. (lemma3_repaired, lemma17, theorem4; analysis scripts in the work notes.) 🔧 Claim 10 (proof of Lemma 9, independence) The proof treats failure events of nodes at pairwise distance ≥ 2t+1 as independent, but a node's failure depends on its (t+1)-ball, and two such balls intersect when the distance is 2t+1 or 2t+2. Impact. Lemma 9 and Claim 10 are not refuted, and Theorem 13 is unaffected; the exact bound n^{1/(3(2t+1))} of Claim 10/Lemma 9 is not re-derived (succProb_le, theorem_6). Repair. We use disjoint (t+1)-balls (distance ≥ 2t+3), which changes the counting. (succProb_le, theorem_6.) 🔧 Claim 10 (proof, step Pr[X | Y] ≤ Pr[X' | Y']) The step Pr[X | Y] ≤ Pr[X' | Y'] mixes conditionings on different events, and X' (all nodes of B_k(v) succeed) is not determined by the identifiers in B_k(v), since nodes near the boundary see outside the ball. Impact. The local-to-global bound survives once this step is replaced (succProb_le). Repair. We bypass the conditioning step: we choose identifiers that are injective on the central ball by averaging, and extend them to a bijection. (succProb_le, theorem_6.) 🔧 Lemmas 7/8/14/15 (circular choice of the threshold) The proofs set f = p'/(5c), where p' is the failure probability of the algorithm built with threshold f. Impact. The lemmas hold as stated, and the inequality the paper derives is unchanged (lemma_14, lemma_15). Repair. We set f from the target bound instead and argue by contradiction. This needs p > 0, which holds on the infinite tree because of the 0-round bound (lemma_14, lemma_15, NodeAlg.failProb_pos). The lower-bound form used by Claim 11 needs no fixed point (nodeLB_succ_of_edgeLB, edgeLB_of_nodeLB). 🔧 Lemma 3 (tie-break between cycles) The tie-break "cycle with the smallest maximum identifier" is ambiguous, because two cycles may share their maximum-ID node. Impact. Nodes need not agree on the chosen cycle; the repaired algorithm of Lemma 3 does not use this rule. Repair. Any fixed total order on candidate cycles works (lemma3_repaired). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Lower bound (Sections 5–7). The network is the consistently oriented Δ = 2k-regular tree, i.e. the Cayley graph of the free group on k generators, Tree k. Each node has an independent random value from a finite probability space (Ω, μ) with arbitrary weights. The paper uses infinite random bit strings; ours covers every algorithm that reads finitely many random bits. A t-round anonymous algorithm is a function of the random values in the radius-t ball around the origin. Node v applies it to the shifted field, so it knows n and Δ implicitly and has no identifiers. Local failure is evaluated at the origin; all nodes look alike. Finite instances (Claim 10, Theorem 6). An instance is an n-node set V ⊆ Tree k containing the ball of radius K = ⌊log_{2k+1} n⌋/3. Such subtrees exist for every n (theorem_6_instances). The network is the subgraph induced by V. Identifiers are an injection V → Fin n, i.e. exactly {1..n}. Each node also gets an independent random value. A t-round algorithm (IdAlg) sees, within tree distance t, which nodes exist, with their identifiers, random values and the orientation. For connected V this is the LOCAL view, and seeing more only strengthens the lower bound. Success means every node of V has a neighbour in V with the other colour. Lemma 2 and P* (Theorem 4). Deterministic LOCAL in CSLib's extensional form: Cslib.Local.IsLocal R f, where f maps graph × labels to outputs. Node names serve as identifiers, and n = |V| is known. P* pointers are neighbour names, which is equivalent to port numbers. The randomized lower bound of Lemma 18 holds for arbitrary random input labels (lemma18_randomized). Main results in Lean. Randomized Test-And-Set: the space lower bound — PODC 2012 George Giakkoupis, Philipp Woelfel. On the Time and Space Complexity of Randomized Test-And-Set. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332436. Formalized version: the authors' copy of the PODC paper (HAL hal-00722947, 11 pages; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The space lower bound (Theorem 5.1: any leader election algorithm with nondeterministic solo-termination needs Ω(log n) registers, concretely ⌊log₂ n⌋ - 1) is proved in Lean, together with Claims 5.2, 5.3, 5.5 and Lemma 5.4, and its proofs needed only local changes. The one issue in the definitions is that GroupElect omits "if no process crashes", so read literally Figure 1 does not satisfy it (Lemma 2.2). The paper's probabilistic upper bounds, its expected step complexities, are not formalized, so they were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 2.1, definition of GroupElect (used by Lemma 2.2): "If some processes call elect(), then at least one process must get elected" lacks the "if no process crashes" qualifier of LeaderElect, so in the paper's crash model Figure 1 violates it (p writes flag and crashes, q reads flag = 1 and returns False; GroupElect.not_groupElectLiteral). The intended crash-free reading is clear from the LeaderElect definition just before it and from its only use ("if no process crashes then some process wins … at least one of the processes that call GE_i.elect() gets elected"). Under that reading Figure 1 is a GroupElect object (GroupElect.isGroupElection). Claim 5.3 is false for R = R' = ∅, Q = ∅: then β must be empty. It is only applied with R ≠ ∅, which we assume. Lemma 5.4(e) relates m_k to m_{k-1} of a different witness. It only makes sense for the sequence the inductive construction builds, and that is what we formalize: m_k ≥ f(k). Proof of Lemma 2.2, last line: "since ℓ = ⌈log n⌉ ≤ log k" should be ≥. The estimate holds (GroupElect.lemma_2_2_final_bound; in fact 2 log k + 4, GroupElect.final_bound). Proof of Lemma 2.2, computation of E[Y_j]: for i = ℓ − 1 the factor should be (1 − 2^{-(ℓ-1)})^{j-1}, because Pr(x = ℓ) = 2^{-(ℓ-1)}. So "=" is really "≤", and the bound is unaffected. Proof of Lemma 5.4: "every register in R is covered by exactly two processes" should read "at least two" (it is n − k ≥ 2). This does not affect the argument. Proof of Lemma 5.4: "No process in Q covers a register in R'" should say "no chosen representative": other members of Q may cover R'. This does not affect the argument. Section 5.2: "Further, let for k ≥ 1 δ(k+1) = …" should be k ≥ 0, because Claim 5.5 uses δ(1). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 5.1 (reduction to deterministic algorithms) The proof's claim that the random choices can be fixed so that "the algorithm becomes deterministic and obstruction free" (every process finishing solo "within a bounded number of steps") is not justified. Impact. The step is not needed: Section 5.2 works verbatim with nondeterministic executions, and we formalize it that way (theorem_5_1). Details. Nondeterministic solo-termination only says that from every reachable configuration some choice sequence lets the process finish solo. Choices that work from every configuration at once need not exist if they depend only on the local state. Example gadget: choose a bit b, announce it in r₃, read r₂, finish if r₂ = b, otherwise forget and retry. Another process writes 1 − r₃ into r₂. Put this gadget in front of any correct algorithm. Then every local-state-based fixing of b loops forever solo from a reachable configuration. The gadget does not refute the usual reading "fix each process's coin tape" (the i-th coin of p): a tape that is not eventually constant finishes it within two tries. The paper does not show that a tape with finite solo runs from every configuration reachable under it exists, and solo runs need not be bounded. So this is a missing justification of an unnecessary step, not a refuted one. 🔧 Lemma 5.4(e), case R = ∅ When no register is covered by n − k representatives, the proof keeps the configuration and says the claim for k + 1 "follows immediately", but (e) then needs m_k ≥ n − k, which is not shown. Impact. A few lines of arithmetic close the case. Repair. f(k) ≥ n − k holds by induction (sub_le_f), so f(k+1) ≤ f(k) (f_succ_le) and m_{k+1} = m_k ≥ f(k) ≥ f(k+1). 🔧 Claim 5.2 (indistinguishability) "C(E) and C(D) are indistinguishable to all processes in Q" is too strong under the paper's definition of indistinguishability, which includes all register values. Impact. The erasure argument goes through with a weaker invariant (Alg.claim_5_2_paper). Repair. Only the states of Q agree, together with the registers last written by Q (erase). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Model.lean, self-contained; CSLib's shared-memory Impl model is deterministic only.) Asynchronous shared memory with n processes (any finite type P) and atomic multi-reader multi-writer registers (any type Reg) with arbitrary values V and initial values v₀. Processes are nondeterministic automata. A randomized algorithm is modelled by allowing every coin outcome. The next action (read r, write v to r, return win/lose) depends on the local state; the successor state is any element of a set. Initial states are nondeterministic too. Crashes: finite executions in which some processes stop. No adversary is needed, since the lower bound is purely combinatorial. Registers carry a ghost "last writer" field. This is the paper's w.l.o.g. "values are pairs (x, ID)" made invisible to processes, so the theorem holds for arbitrary algorithms. Leader election follows Section 1.1. For every set S of callers and every finite execution in which only S steps: at most one process of S has won, and if all of S returned, one has won. Nondeterministic solo-termination: from every reachable configuration every process has a finite solo execution after which it has returned. For n not a power of two we run the construction on 2^⌊log₂ n⌋ active processes (the paper's w.l.o.g.). Main results in Lean. Error-Free Multi-Valued Consensus — PODC 2011 Guanfeng Liang, Nitin Vaidya. Error-Free Multi-Valued Consensus with Byzantine Failures. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993809. Formalized version: arXiv 1101.3520 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Algorithm 1 achieves consensus on L-bit values for 3t < n (Lemmas 1–3 and 5 and the correctness part of Theorem 1 hold). The claim that the diagnosis stage runs at most t(t+1) times (Lemma 4, and thus the complexity bound) is false for the pseudo-code as printed: an already isolated faulty processor can trigger the diagnosis stage in every generation. It holds once announcements of isolated processors are ignored, as the paper's prose intends. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 4 and Theorem 1's t(t+1) bound (Algorithm 1 as printed) An already isolated faulty processor can announce Detected = true in every generation, so the diagnosis stage runs forever without removing an edge: with n = 4, t = 1 there are already 3 > t(t+1) diagnosis stages in 3 generations (Counterexample.literal_not_theorem_1, Counterexample.literal_lemma_4_false). Impact. Only the complexity bound is affected, and only for the printed pseudo-code: ignoring the Detected bits of isolated processors, as the prose intends, restores Lemma 4 and the t(t+1) bound (Run.theorem_1_numDiag). Correctness holds for both versions. Details. In Algorithm 1, every P_j ∉ P_match broadcasts Detected_j, and the diagnosis stage starts as soon as one of these bits is true. A faulty processor whose vertex is already isolated is never in P_match: the fault-free members do not trust it. Take n = 4, t = 1, P₃ faulty, all inputs equal. P₃ behaves correctly except that it broadcasts M₃ = false…false and Detected₃ = true. In generation 1, step 3(f) isolates vertex 3. From then on the diagnosis stage runs in every generation and removes nothing, since vertex 3 has no edge left. Case 2 of the proof of Lemma 4 assumes that step 3(f) removes some edge at j, and misses the case where none is left. So Lemma 4 is false ("at least one edge … will be removed") and so is the t(t+1) bound; with 3 generations there are already 3 > 2 diagnosis stages. This is a false statement about the printed algorithm. The intended algorithm is clear from the prose: §3.3 says of an isolated processor that "the fault-free processors will not communicate with it anymore", and the proof of Theorem 1 argues that once all faulty processors are identified "the diagnosis stage will not be performed any more". Repair. Ignore the Detected bits of isolated processors. For this repaired algorithm we prove Lemma 4 and the t(t+1) bound. (Run.theorem_1_numDiag) ✏️ Slips ⊥ in the checking stage (steps 2(a), 2(c)): read literally, a received vector with a ⊥ entry is never in C₂ₜ, so a fault-free processor that distrusts a faulty member of P_match always reports a detection, and step 3(f) can then isolate this fault-free processor. Untrusted senders give R_i[j] = ⊥, and "R_j/P_match ∈ C₂ₜ" is defined by equality with a codeword. The prose of §3.2 ("checks whether the symbols received from the trusted processors in P_match are consistent") and the proof of Lemma 4 (case 2(a)) state the intended reading, which we formalize: ⊥ entries are ignored, and the check and decoding use the trusted members of P_match. The literal reading's failure, a 2-generation scenario with n = 4, is described in differencies.md but not proved in Lean. Lemma 3 should assume that no processor announces a detection, not that none detects one. "v_i(g), represented by n − t symbols" in §3.1 should be n − 2t. Typos "Detected_i" in §3.2 should be Detected_j. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous, fully connected network of n processors with a static set F of |F| ≤ t Byzantine processors and 3t < n. The paper's adaptive corruption is equivalent to this: the algorithm is deterministic and the adversary omniscient. Each generation is computed at the level of Algorithm 1's steps. Broadcast_Single_Bit is a black box with its specification: all fault-free processors get the same value, which is the source's value if the source is fault-free. So the broadcast values of faulty sources (M_j, Detected_j, R#[j], Trust_j) are adversary choices. The point-to-point symbols of step 1(a) are explicit, and a faulty sender may send a different symbol to each receiver. The adversary also picks P_match and P_decide among the valid sets. This covers every deterministic selection rule. The code C₂ₜ is an abstract code with the MDS property: any n − 2t symbols determine the data. A D-bit part is a data word, and an L-bit value is a vector of N = L/D data words. A Reed–Solomon instance shows that the hypotheses are satisfiable. The diagnosis graph is a SimpleGraph (Fin n), complete at the start and common to all fault-free processors. Two variants: Variant.literal (pseudo-code as printed) and Variant.repaired (Detected bits of processors without edges are ignored). Main results in Lean (namespace Podc.ErrorFreeMultivaluedBC). Truly Tight-in-Δ Bounds for Bipartite Maximal Matching — PODC 2020 Sebastian Brandt, Dennis Olivetti. Truly Tight-in-Δ Bounds for Bipartite Maximal Matching and Variants. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405745. Formalized version: arXiv 2002.08216 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result holds: in the deterministic port-numbering model on 2-coloured Δ-regular trees, bipartite x-maximal y-matching (the encoded version Φ^W_Δ(x, y)) has white round complexity exactly T_Δ(x, y) for 0 ≤ x ≤ Δ, 1 ≤ y ≤ Δ − 1, in particular 2Δ − 1 for maximal matching, and we prove both bounds and the round elimination step they use. Several proofs needed small repairs (empty sets in R_B, an ill-defined problem in Lemma 4.3, two errors in the output rule of the algorithm), and the tightness claim of Theorem 1.2 and §6 is false in the degenerate case y = Δ. The randomized and LOCAL lower bounds (Theorems 1.3 and 1.4) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 4.3 (undefined problem Ψ^W_Δ(y, x, 0) for x > Δ − y) Lemma 4.3 produces Ψ^W_Δ(y, x, 0), which is undefined for x > Δ − y, since the family requires a + b ≤ Δ. Impact. We prove the lemma with Ψ^W_Δ(y, min{x, Δ − y}, 0) (lemma_4_3). Theorem 4.5 is unaffected, since it only uses the lemma when x < Δ − y. ✏️ Slips Theorem 1.2 and end of §6: the tightness claim fails for y = Δ and x < Δ: the formula gives T_Δ(x, Δ) = 1, but matching every edge is a valid 0-round solution (theorem_1_2_false_y_eq_Δ). The paper itself notes the trivial algorithm after Theorem 4.5. The paper claims tightness "for any combination of integers x ≥ 0, y ≥ 1, Δ ≥ 2"; we prove Theorem 1.2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ Δ, 1 ≤ y ≤ Δ − 1 (theorem_1_2). Lemmas 4.1–4.3, proofs: the empty set is ignored. R_B(Π) uses labels from 2^Σ, and a configuration such as (∅, MZPOX, …, MZPOX) is vacuously universal and maximal, but for a ≤ Δ − 2 it extends to none of the three configurations listed in the proof of Lemma 4.1 (emptyConf_counterexample). ∅ never appears in a correct solution, and we use nonempty sets throughout. Theorem 2.1 says "complexity min{0, T − 1}"; it should be max. The proof of Lemma 4.1 says the universal quantifier is applied to the white constraint; it should be the black one. Typos "Δ-regular balanced trees" is imprecise: finite trees have leaves, while the problems are defined for Δ-regular graphs (§2 uses regular graphs of girth ≥ 4Δ + 2). We use the infinite 2-coloured Δ-regular tree. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 §5 (output rule, last round) White nodes do not accept proposals received in the last round, so an unmatched black node that proposed in the last round may see more than x labels X. Impact. The text hints at the fix, and with it the bound holds on all Δ-regular properly 2-coloured port-numbered graphs (upper_bound). Details. Example: Δ = 2, x = y = 1 (2 rounds) on an 8-cycle, where a black node gets X from both neighbours. Repair. White nodes must accept proposals received in the last round. 🔧 §5 (output rule of the 2⌈(Δ−x)/y⌉ − 1-round variant) Whites are active only k − 1 times in this variant, so outputting P only where they proposed can give too few labels P. Impact. The text hints at the fix, and with it the exact bound holds, also on all Δ-regular properly 2-coloured port-numbered graphs (upper_bound). Details. Example: BMM with Δ = 2 (3 rounds) on a 6-cycle, where an unmatched white node outputs P X, which violates x = 0. Repair. Unmatched whites must output P on all ports, not only where they proposed. 🔧 Theorem 4.5 (case ⌈(Δ−x)/y⌉ = 1) Theorem 4.5's parameter formulas break down when ⌈(Δ−x)/y⌉ = 1; this case needs Φ^W and Φ' to be not 0-round solvable, which is asserted without proof. Impact. We prove this case (phi_not_zero, phi'_not_zero). Details. The proof also ignores the caps min{c + a, Δ − a} of Lemma 4.1. They are inactive (seqBC_le). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic port-numbering model, no identifiers, no randomness. Graphs are Δ-regular and properly 2-coloured, and the colour is a node's only input. White algorithms: white nodes label their ports, and the black constraint is checked on the labels written by the white neighbours, as in §2.2. View model (Views.lean). A t-round algorithm is a function of the radius-t view, an inductive type of port-numbered rooted trees. Solves A Act Pas means correctness on every port numbering of the infinite 2-coloured Δ-regular tree. CSLib model (Bridge.lean). For CSLib message-passing algorithms (Cslib.PortNumbering.Algorithm): in every Δ-regular 2-coloured port-numbered graph, the state of a node after t rounds is a function of its view (state_eq); every view is realized at the root of an explicit port-numbered infinite tree treeGraph d arr. So the lower bound applies to genuine algorithms on these trees (theorem_4_5_PN). Not covered: the paper's finite graphs of girth ≥ 4Δ + 2, where algorithms may know n. The transfer from trees to such graphs is standard but not formalized. Δ = d + 1 in Lean. Problems are transcribed literally as unions of condensed configurations (Cond.Gens). The round elimination theorem (forward direction, bipartite form) is proved from scratch. It needs no edge symmetry breaking, unlike the converse (cf. Papers/PODC2019/AutomaticSpeedup). Tight Bounds for Asymptotic and Approximate Consensus — PODC 2018 Matthias Függer, Thomas Nowak, Manfred Schwarz. Tight Bounds for Asymptotic and Approximate Consensus. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212762. Formalized version: arXiv 1705.02898 v2 (the JACM 2021 version was not consulted). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The contraction-rate lower bounds (Theorems 1, 2, 3, 5, 6) and the approximate-consensus bounds (Theorems 8–11) are correct, and Theorems 1 and 2 are tight (Algorithm 1 and the midpoint algorithm). Theorem 4 (⇐) is false: "valencies singleton or disconnected ⇒ exact consensus solvable", the converse of the paper's topological characterization of exact consensus, fails for two agents in {H₀, H₁, H₂}. It becomes true once the asymptotic algorithm is required to have a continuous consensus function. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 4 (⇐: valencies singleton or disconnected ⇒ exact consensus solvable) For two agents in N = {H₀, H₁, H₂} the "first deviation" algorithm solves asymptotic consensus with every valency finite (a singleton or disconnected), yet exact consensus is unsolvable in N (theorem4_false, fd_not_vanishing). Impact. Only the converse direction fails: (⇒) holds as stated. Adding continuity of the consensus function (valency diameters vanish along every execution of every submodel) makes (⇐) true (theorem4_mpr_repaired). Details. H₀ lets both agents hear each other, and in H₁/H₂ one of them is deaf. The "first deviation" algorithm: before any non-H₀ round the output is x₀. At the first non-H₀ round t, the deaf agent decides its own value if t is odd and the other's value if t is even. The other agent copies that decision, or applies the same parity rule if it is itself deaf in round t+1. This solves asymptotic consensus, and every limit is an initial value, so every valency Y*_{N'}(C) is finite. Yet by Theorem 1 an exact algorithm would have contraction rate 0. The proof fails at "δ_{N'}(C_t) → 0 in any execution, by Convergence and Agreement". That holds only if the consensus function (pattern ↦ limit) is continuous, and the paper itself notes in §2.1 that it need not be. Here, along the all-H₀ execution, both x₀ and x₁ stay reachable forever. The refutation also covers binary inputs. Theorem 4 quantifies over network models N' ⊆ N, which the paper defines to be nonempty (§2); this matters, since for N' = ∅ the valency would be empty. Repair. With continuity, the full equivalence follows, conditional on the cited characterization of Coulouma et al. [12] (theorem4_repaired). ✏️ Slips Definition 15 (α-relation) writes In_S(G) as a union of node sets, but [12, Def. 4.7] and every later use need the per-agent version In_i(G) = In_i(H) for all i ∈ R(K); under the literal reading Lemma 20 and Theorem 5 fail (lemma20_literal_false, theorem5_literal_false). The α-diameter of {H₀,H₁,H₂} would be 1. Lemma 20 would fail for Algorithm 1 from (0, 1), since the valencies after H₁ and H₂ lie in [0, 1/3] and [2/3, 1]. Theorem 5 would claim rate ≥ 1/2 for Algorithm 1, whose rate is 1/3. The remark D = 2 for {H₀,H₁,H₂} and the proofs of Lemmas 20 and 24 use the per-agent version, under which Lemma 20 and Theorem 5 hold. The proof of Theorem 11 writes log₃ for log_{D+1}. The proof of Theorem 11 writes δ_N(C₀) ≤ Δ/n for ≥ Δ/n. Lemma 24 swaps the endpoints of its chain relative to its own definition of H_r. Typos The cited Theorem 1 of [8] and the continuity theorem of Section 2.2 share their numbers with the main Theorems 1 and 2. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 11 (restarting A) The proof builds Ã by restarting A with the decision values, but with a fixed ε this need not converge, so Ã is not an asymptotic consensus algorithm. Impact. The reduction to Theorem 5 fails; we prove Theorems 8–11 directly on finite-horizon decision sets (theorem11). 🔧 Theorem 3 (claim (8)) Claim (8) asserts the bound "for every initial snapshot", but Lemma 13 gives only one. Impact. One snapshot suffices for the theorem (theorem3). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finitely many agents; synchronous, communication-closed rounds (Heard-Of style). A pattern is any sequence of communication graphs from the model N (oblivious adversary). Self-loops are implicit. No failures beyond what the graphs encode. Algorithms are deterministic and full-information-capable: arbitrary state, agent-dependent initial state, outputs need not lie in the hull of received values. This is a larger class than the paper's, so the lower bounds are stronger. Asymptotic consensus: in every execution all outputs converge to a common limit in the hull of the inputs. Values lie in any nontrivial real normed space (covers ℝ^d); the midpoint algorithm is on ℝ. Valency = set of limits reachable from a configuration (equal to the paper's Y* on reachable configurations). Diameters and rates live in ℝ≥0∞. Snapshots and properties (§6.1) are replaced by block patterns. Approximate consensus: ε, Δ are fixed parameters, and only time-T decisions are constrained (weaker than the paper's spec, so stronger lower bounds). Section 8: only the network model N_A ("wait for n − f messages") is formalized, not the reduction from asynchronous crash executions. Main results in Lean. Lemma 20 needs R(K) ≠ ∅, which follows from the cited rootedness result [8]; we prove it. Not formalized. Theorem 7 (MinRelay, asynchronous crashes); the characterization of exact consensus from [12] (Theorem 19, β-classes), which appears only as the hypothesis CouloumaHyp of the repaired Theorem 4; the amortized midpoint algorithm of [9] (Theorem 3's tightness remains cited). Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: Algorithm 1 and the midpoint algorithm are proved to solve asymptotic consensus with the matching rates. The Heard-Of round model and chain/diameter lemmas are in CSLib (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/DynamicNetworks/{HeardOf,Chain}.lean). Anonymous Networks: Randomization = 2-Hop Coloring — PODC 2014 Yuval Emek, Christoph Pfister, Jochen Seidel, Roger Wattenhofer. Anonymous Networks: Randomization = 2-Hop Coloring. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611478. Formalized version: the authors' 10-page copy from the ETH DISCO publication page (with proofs); there is no arXiv version. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both main theorems hold: Theorem 1 (Π ∈ GRAN ⇒ Πᶜ is solvable by a deterministic anonymous algorithm) and Theorem 2 (the same in the infinity model), and so do the graph-theoretic results (Lemmas 2–4, Norris' Theorem 3 and Corollaries 1–2). The proof of Lemma 9, the correctness of the paper's algorithm A*, has an off-by-one in the view depth that port numbers make essential, so Lemma 9 is unestablished for A* as written. With one more level of view (at the same round cost) A* is correct, and that is how we prove Theorem 1. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 9 (correctness of algorithm A*, §3.2) The proof says that "the first k rounds … are fully determined by L_k(v, I)" and the random bits, but they need L_{k+1}(v) even without ports and L_{k+2}(v) with port numbers (locality_gap), while A* matches views L_p and simulates up to p − 1 rounds. Impact. Theorem 1 is not affected. Lemma 9, and with it the claim that the paper's A* (as written) solves Πᶜ, is neither proved nor refuted. If Update-Graph uses the view L_{p+1}(v, I^p) instead of L_p(v, I^p), all lemmas of §3.2 go through and Theorem 1 follows (theorem_1). Computing L_{p+1} takes p rounds, which is the round count the paper states for this step. The repair changes the algorithm (one view level), not only the argument; it is a local fix that the paper's own round count points to. Details. L_1(v) is the root alone, so L_k(v) has tree depth k − 1. Even without ports, k rounds depend on tree depth k, i.e. L_{k+1}. That alone does no harm here: the simulation of phase p lasts l ≤ p − 1 rounds and L_p has tree depth p − 1. Port numbers add one more level. The simulated algorithm A_R may send different messages on different ports. The port number at the far end of an edge depends on the far node's other neighbours. The paper never fixes the port numbering used in the simulations of A*; any numbering that is a local function of the colours (for instance sorting neighbours by colour) has this problem. locality_gap is a concrete instance. Take the 2-hop coloured paths 1–2–3 and 1–2–0 (labels: degree and colour). Their endpoints have equal views L_2. Under colour-sorted ports, a one-round deterministic algorithm (every node sends its port number) puts the two endpoints in different states. Lemma 9 needs exactly this case: l = p − 1, all candidate nodes carry p − 1 bits, and the selected candidate agrees with the real graph only up to L_p. Then the output of v* in the simulation may differ from the output of v in the lifted execution η, which is what Lemma 9 asserts they share. We did not construct a full counterexample to A*: that needs a problem in GRAN, an adversarial A_R, and an analysis of A*'s candidate selection over all small graphs. Repair. AStar.Lv is trunc p (relabel (bL p) W), the view of tree depth p, i.e. L_{p+1}(v, I^p). With it, Lemma 9 is AStar.outPhase_eq, proved with the locality lemma decided_local. ✏️ Slips Corollary 3 is said to follow "from Corollary 1 as |V̂*| ≤ p". It follows from Fact 1 and Lemma 2 (the finite view graph is a factor of the candidate). Typos §3.1: "node v computes L_p(v, I^p) (requires p rounds)". p − 1 rounds suffice for L_p; p rounds give L_{p+1}, the view the repaired algorithm uses. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3 (G∞ is the unique prime factor) The proof shows that every prime factor of G is isomorphic to G∞ but not that G∞ itself is prime, which Lemma 7 later uses for I*^p. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_3). Repair. In G∞ distinct nodes have distinct views (Fact 1). So every factorizing map out of G∞ is injective, hence bijective. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Labelled graphs are finite, connected and simple (LGraph). Problems are arbitrary sets of instances with arbitrary sets of valid output labellings (Problem). Inputs need not contain the degree; nodes know their degree from the port numbering. Algorithms run synchronously in the anonymous port-numbering model of CSLib (PNGraph, ports 0, …, deg − 1). Messages may depend on the port, and the receiver learns the port number at the sender's end. There are no failures and states and messages are unbounded. Local computation is unrestricted (computability is not modelled). Randomness: one random bit per node and round (RAlg.recv receives it). Outputs are irrevocable: a node's output is its first output (RAlg.decided). Deterministic means the transition ignores the bit. Solvability (Las Vegas) must hold for every simple port numbering of every instance. The paper's probabilistic definition, with independent fair coins (product measure bitMeasure), is SolvesAS. The proofs use the combinatorial Solves: every finite bit prefix extends to a terminating run, and every terminated run is valid. SolvesAS.solves shows the paper's definition implies ours, so theorem_1_AS and theorem_2_AS hold for the paper's GRAN (GRAN_AS). Local views: TEq … k is equality of view trees of depth k, i.e. of L_{k+1}; ViewEq … d is the paper's L_d. L_∞(u) = L_∞(v) (ViewEqInf) means equality at all depths. In 2-hop coloured graphs siblings have distinct marks, so the infinite view is represented canonically by the set of label words of walks (⟪X⟫ v, forall_teq_iff_lang). The infinite view graph G∞ (viewLGraph) has these languages as nodes. Infinity model: an algorithm is a function A∞ of ⟪X⟫ v. This language is determined by the view tree L_∞(v) (lang_eq_of_forall_teq), so A∞ is a function of L_∞(v). Simulations of A_R (in A∞ and A*) use the colour-sorted port numbering (colorPN). Colours are taken from a linear order (the paper's colours are bit strings). The canonical choices of the paper (the total orders on V∞, on bit assignments and on finite view graphs) are replaced by choice functions of the canonical data. The analysis only needs that every node computes the same function of the same data. A* (AStar.lean) is written as functions of views: bL p W is b^p(v) for a node with infinite view W. The simulation runs on the infinite view graph of a canonically chosen graph realizing the selected view set; it is isomorphic to the paper's finite view graph (Corollary 2). The message-passing algorithm astar floods truncated walk languages and in round r evaluates phase ⌊√r⌋ (Flood.lean). This changes only the timing of outputs, not their values. Main results in Lean.
