Topological Characterization of Consensus under General Message Adversaries — PODC 2019 Thomas Nowak, Ulrich Schmid, Kyrill Winkler. Topological Characterization of Consensus under General Message Adversaries. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331624. Formalized version: the PODC'19 paper is arXiv 1905.09590 v1 (23 May 2019); numbering below follows v1. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf; note that this copy is arXiv v3 (2024), Topological Characterization of Consensus in Distributed Systems. v3 extends the paper to models with benign faults, and we formalized it as well (see the last section and the v1 ↔ v3 table). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The core characterization (Theorem 5.5) is correct: under any message adversary, consensus is solvable iff the admissible executions split into decision sets that are open (hence clopen) in the minimum topology and contain the valent executions; its limit form (Corollary 5.18) holds too. But the paper's succinct characterizations built on it are false: Corollary 5.6 ("no connected component contains two valences"), Theorem 5.11 ("every component is broadcastable") and Theorem 6.7 (the non-compact case). For compact adversaries, Corollaries 6.1 and 6.5 are false as well and the characterization by ε-approximations (Theorem 6.6) is unestablished. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Corollary 5.6, Theorem 5.11 and Theorem 6.7 ("if" direction) On three processes, the message adversary {π_k | k ≥ 1} ∪ {σ_∞} has only broadcastable components and no component with valent executions of two values, yet consensus is impossible (V1Cex.v1_theorem_5_11_false). Impact. The paper's succinct characterizations built on Theorem 5.5 are false; Theorem 5.5 itself and the "only if" directions stand. v3 repairs Theorem 5.11 by adding "the strong broadcaster decision sets are clopen" (Theorem 7.9). Details. Model. Three processes; message adversary {π_k | k ≥ 1} ∪ {σ_∞}. σ_∞ has 1→0 and 1→2 in every round. π_k has no edges in rounds 1..k-1, 2→0 in round k, and then 0→1, 0→2 forever. The conditions hold. The executions with pattern π_k fall into clopen sets, one per (x₀, x₂, k). Inside each, nobody ever hears of process 1, and process 0 broadcasts. The component of (x, σ_∞) is {(y, σ_∞) | y₁ = x₁}, and process 1 broadcasts there. So every component is broadcastable, and no component contains valent executions of two different values. Consensus is impossible. ((1,0,1), π_k) must decide like ((1,1,1), π_k), because process 0 never hears of process 1. So it decides 1. For large k, process 1 cannot distinguish ((1,0,1), π_k) from ((0,0,0), σ_∞) before it has to decide in the latter. Why the proofs fail. Theorem 5.11 "⇐" and the meta-procedure behind Corollary 5.6 assume that the union of the components of the v-valent executions is open. That holds only with finitely many components. Here the components {(x, σ_∞)} are not open. The adversary is not limit-closed, which is why it also refutes Theorem 6.7 (the non-compact case). ❌ Corollaries 6.1 and 6.5 (finitely many connected components, ε-approximations of components) The limit-closed adversary {σ_n} ∪ {σ_∞} on two processes, with σ_∞ = (1→0)^ω and σ_n equal to σ_∞ with 0↔1 in round n+1, makes consensus solvable but has infinitely many components (CanonicalCex.v1_corollary_6_1_false), and for every ε > 0 the ε-approximation of (y, σ_∞) contains executions (x, σ_n) from other components (CanonicalCex.v1_corollary_6_5_false). Impact. Both statements are false, and nothing we proved recovers finiteness or a matching ε. This also invalidates the proofs of Lemma 6.4 and Theorem 6.6 (next item). Details. Every (x, σ_n) is its own component. The proof's "open covering" by components is not open. ❌ Lemma 6.4 and Theorem 6.6 (unestablished) Theorem 6.6 is derived from Theorem 5.11 and Corollary 6.5, both false, and the proof of Lemma 6.4 rests on Corollary 6.1 and on the step "setting ε < d/2", which gives no bound on the iteratively grown PS^ε, so the proofs are invalid. Making Objects Writable — PODC 2014 Zahra Aghazadeh, Wojciech Golab, Philipp Woelfel. Making Objects Writable. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611483. Formalized version: Chapter 4 of Z. Aghazadeh's PhD thesis Efficient Shared Memory Algorithms for Bounding Space (U. Calgary, 2018), which contains the paper with full proofs; numbering follows the thesis (the PODC version is not openly available). Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All checked statements hold: the template lemma (Lemma 4.5), the correctness of the wait-free algorithm (Lemma 4.8, hence the linearizability part of Theorem 4.1 and of Corollary 4.4) and the sequentially resettable (k,b)-array (Lemma 4.2). The proof of Lemma 4.5 has a genuine gap: it never uses the template's "not in use" requirement, without which the lemma is false, and it took a new construction of the linearization to save it; the proof of Lemma 4.8 has smaller gaps. The wait-freedom and complexity claims of Theorem 4.1 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Claims 4.15(b) and 4.16 (inside the proof of Lemma 4.8) are literally false at the level of single points, because within one recycle() line 26 can add i* to free_p at the same point at which lines 27–28 read i* from Annc and enqueue it (the mechanism is checked on the local queue state by an example in Lemma48.lean; no full execution was built). Their uses (Claims 4.17, 4.21–4.22) keep one recycle() call of margin. Typos Lemma 4.2, proof of Part (b1): "[t_W@rsp, t_R@inv] = [t_W@64, t_R@60]" and "q reads (x_W, v_W) from A[i*] in line 60" should say line 59; "when p reads this variable in line 60 of R" should say q. Lemma 4.8, proof of (4.32): "q completes" should be "p completes". Lemma 4.2 needs k ≥ 1 (the version counter is taken mod k); implicit. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 4.5 (template lemma, proof of Claim 4.7) The proof obtains a linearization of the sub-history Λ_ℓ of the timestamp-ℓ calls from sequential writability, an inference that fails without the template's "not in use" requirement, which the proof never uses (notInUse_necessary, lambda1_not_linearizable). Impact. Statement true; repaired with a different construction of the linearization (lemma_4_5). Details. The step reads: "no A[i_ℓ].SWrite() overlaps any other operation call on A[i_ℓ]. Therefore, there is a linearization S_ℓ of Λ_ℓ". But a sub-history of a linearizable history need not be linearizable, and without "not in use" Lemma 4.5 itself is false. Counterexample to the step (all other hypotheses of Lemma 4.5 hold): a register over ℕ, three processes. p₀ writes 1 with index 0; then p₀ starts Write(2) reusing index 0 while Ptr = 0 and completes A[0].SWrite(2); p₂'s Exec(read) sees Ptr = 0, reads 2; p₁ writes 3 with index 1 and returns; p₀ sets Ptr := 0 and returns; p₂ reads 2 again. Condition (C), ownership and sequential writability hold, but the high-level history is not linearizable: the first read forces Write(2) before it, real time puts Write(3) between the two reads, so the second read must return 3. Here Λ_1 = {A[0].SWrite(1), read → 2} has no overlapping SWrite and is not linearizable, while the whole history of A[0] is. Repair. Take one linearization L_i of the whole history of each A[i]. Using "not in use", show that on each A[i] an operation of a call with a smaller timestamp returns before any operation of a call with a larger timestamp is invoked (IsCtrl.ret_before_of_keyPos_lt), so the timestamps are sorted along L_i; each timestamp-ℓ block is then a contiguous segment of L_{i_ℓ} starting with its SWrite, and its legality follows from that of L_{i_ℓ}. The high-level linearization lists these blocks by increasing timestamp (linWT, IsCtrl.isLinearization_linWT). 🔧 Theorem 4.1 (the algorithm follows the template) Lemma 4.5 requires that the write-index of a Write is not in use when chosen, but this is never proved for the algorithm of Figure 4.5; the proof of Theorem 4.1 only establishes condition (C) (Lemma 4.8). Impact. Statement true; it follows quickly from Claim 4.22(a) (a Write contains only one recycle()), and is proved as part of our invariant (WF.lemma_4_8, which gives Template ∧ CondC). 🔧 Lemma 4.8 (the algorithm satisfies (C)), proof of (4.32) The count "p invokes more than n Write() calls during [t_E@36, t_E@39], and so q completes at least n Write() calls during this interval" may include a Write invoked before t_E@35, to which Claim 4.20 (stated for Writes completing during (t_E@35, t_E@40]) does not apply as stated. Impact. Statement true; only line 14 of that Write (its read of S_q) needs to come after t_E@35, which holds (WF.lemma_4_8). Details. Claim 4.19's "both writes happen in the same Write" is asserted without argument; it is true. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, any set of processes, deterministic algorithms, no failures other than processes stopping (pending operations), linearizability in CSLib's sense (IsLinearization, the amended Herlihy–Wing definition). Lemma 4.5 is stated on transcripts (Ev): the high-level invocations/responses of Write/Exec, the invocations/responses of operations on the base objects A[i], and the writes to Ptr. The base objects are not atomic; the hypothesis "A[i] is sequentially writable" is the hypothesis that the history lowH i α of each A[i] is linearizable whenever no write overlaps another operation on it (SeqWritable). Template (Template): a per-process control automaton (PStep) for Figure 4.4, ownership of indices, and "not in use" at the invocation of SWrite (implied by the paper's "at the invocation of Write", notInUse_of_atWriteInv). Condition (C): CondC. The algorithm of Figure 4.5 (WF.Step, Algorithm.lean) is a nondeterministic transition system for n ≥ 1 processes: one atomic register access per step (local lines attached as on p. 58–59 of the thesis), indices Fin n × Fin (8n+9) owned by their first component, free_p.remove() arbitrary, the objects A[i] black boxes whose invocation and response are separate steps with arbitrary responses (their correctness is the SeqWritable hypothesis), environment-chosen invocations, ghost variables that no guard reads. Executions (WF.IsExecution) start with the solo Write(v₀) of process 0, as in the paper; the high-level history includes that Write. Lemma 4.2 and Figure 4.2 use CSLib's Impl model with atomic registers as base objects. Main results in Lean. Efficient Fault-Tolerant Spanners — PODC 2020 Michael Dinitz, Caleb Robelle. Efficient and Simple Algorithms for Fault-Tolerant Spanners. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405735. Formalized version: arXiv 2002.10889 v2. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The sequential part (Sections 2–4) holds as stated: the modified greedy algorithm, which uses the length-bounded-cut approximation (Algorithm 2), outputs an f-VFT (2k−1)-spanner with O(k f^{1−1/k} n^{1+1/k}) edges, weighted and unweighted, and we prove it with the explicit constant 32. Lemma 7's hypothesis f = o(n) is too weak for its proof's estimate, which needs kf = o(n); the statement stays true (when kf ≥ n the claimed subgraph exists trivially), so only the proof needs repair, and the proof of Lemma 3 has a wrong step (p = 1). Running times and the distributed results were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 3 (weighted, "if" direction, case p = 1): the paper writes d_{H\F}(u, v) = w(u, v) = d_{G\F}(u, v), but H need not contain the edge uv. What holds, and suffices, is d_{H\F}(u, v) ≤ t·w(u, v) by hypothesis. We prove the full iff by a different argument: a non-tight edge has a strictly lighter walk made of strictly lighter edges, so strong induction on the number of lighter edges applies; no shortest paths are needed (isWeightedVFTSpanner_iff). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 7 (hypothesis f = o(n)) The lemma assumes f = o(n), but the estimate s(s−1)/(n(n−1)) ≥ (1−o(1))/(4((2k−1)f)²) needs kf = o(n), since k may grow with n. Impact. Theorem 8 is not affected, because it is trivial when kf = Ω(n), but its split on f = Ω(n) has to move there; Lemma 7 is replaced by an exact form (SimpleGraph.IsBlockingSet.exists_dense_subgraph). Repair. We replace the asymptotic lemma by exact counting over all s-subsets: if |B| ≤ D·m and 2Ds ≤ n, some s-set carries a subgraph of girth > 2k with m·s(s−1) ≤ 2n(n−1)·|E(H′)|. A case split at n < 8(2k−1)f replaces "if f = Ω(n) the theorem is trivial". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Sequential, deterministic algorithms on a finite simple graph. Distances are unweighted in ℕ∞, or weighted with weights ≥ 0 in ℝ≥0∞; ⊤ means unreachable. G \ F keeps the vertex type and deletes all edges at F. For u, v ∉ F this gives the same distances as G[V \ F]. The edge order is any list of the edges, in either orientation, with duplicates allowed. For Algorithm 4 it is sorted by weight. "Run BFS to find a path of length ≤ t in G \ F" is an arbitrary oracle that returns some short walk if one exists. All theorems hold for every such oracle, i.e. for every choice of path. Running times are not modelled. Structurally, Algorithm 2 makes at most α + 1 oracle calls. Main results in Lean. Vertex Fault Tolerant Spanners — PODC 2019 Greg Bodwin, Shyamal Patel. A Trivial Yet Optimal Solution to Vertex Fault Tolerant Spanners. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331588. Formalized version: arXiv 1812.05778 v2. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Theorem 1 (the FT greedy spanner has O(f² · b(n/f, k+1)) edges) and Corollary 2 (O(f^{1−1/k} n^{1+1/k}) edges for stretch 2k−1) hold, with explicit constants, for both vertex and edge faults. There are only imprecisions: the literal fault test of Algorithm 1 lets the fault set contain the edge's own endpoints, and Theorem 1's bound degenerates to 0 when f > n/2. The optimality claims rest on the lower bound of [BDPW18], which we did not check. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Algorithm 1 (the fault test does not exclude the edge's endpoints): the test asks for a set F of ≤ f vertices with dist_{H\F}(u, v) > k·w(u, v), but does not require u, v ∉ F. Read literally, it lets the fault set be F = {u}, which makes the distance ∞, so for f ≥ 1 every edge is added and on K_n with f = 1 and stretch 3 the output has n(n−1)/2 edges, contradicting Corollary 2's O(n^{3/2}) (literal_violates_corollary2). This assumes that the distance to a deleted vertex is ∞; if it is read as undefined, the literal test is merely ill-posed. The proof of Lemma 3 clearly uses F ⊆ V \ {u, v}, so the intended algorithm is unambiguous, and we formalize that. Theorem 1 for large f: once n/f < 2, b(n/f, k+1) = 0, so the stated bound is 0 even though H has edges. With floor rounding this happens for f > n/2, with ceiling rounding for f ≥ n. The proof dismisses the regime f = Ω(n) as "trivially O(n²)". We prove |E(H)| ≤ 32 f² · max(b(⌊n/2f⌋, k+1), 1) for all n and all f, k ≥ 1 (ftGreedy_card_edges_le). Typos The proof of Theorem 1 swaps n and m ("n edges and m nodes"). f ≥ 1 is used but left implicit. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A finite simple graph with non-negative real edge weights; weighted distances in ℝ≥0∞. This is a sequential, centralized algorithm, and its running time is not modelled. The edge order is any weight-sorted list of edges. Ties are arbitrary and duplicates harmless. Algorithm 1 (ftGreedy) adds (u, v) iff some set of ≤ f vertices avoiding u, v stretches the current u–v distance beyond k·w(u, v). The edge-fault variant is ftGreedyEdge. b(N, g) is the maximum number of edges of a graph on N vertices with no cycle of length ≤ g (CSLib SimpleGraph.girthExtremal). The Moore bound b(N, 2k) ≤ N^{1+1/k} + N is proved. Main results in Lean. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933108. Formalized version: arXiv 1612.01514 v1 (the only version; a revised version of the conference paper). Numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Linearizability and wait-freedom (Theorem 3.4 and the early-termination variants of Section 6) are proved for all three versions of Find and every fixed order of the ids, after easy repairs of the proofs in Section 3. The paper's efficiency results (Sections 4–5) were not checked in Lean. The one step of them we examined, the Chernoff bound in the proof of Lemma 4.2, on which the O(log n) high-probability bound and part of Theorem 5.1 rest, is wrong, and its repair exists only on paper. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 4.2 (exponent h², checked in the arXiv text) The proof claims the bound exp(−(c/2−1)²h²/c) "by a Chernoff bound", but Chernoff gives only exp(−(c/2−1)²h/c), linear in h, and the quadratic bound already fails for fair coins with c = 4, h = 6 (chernoff_step_fails). Impact. We do not know whether the stated lemma is false; only its proof is broken. Corollaries 4.2.1 and 4.2.2, Theorem 4.3 and the case d < 1 of Theorem 5.1 inherit the gap. Corollary 4.2.1 and Theorem 4.3 survive with a larger constant c, and Theorem 5.1 can be repaired on paper with another threshold; not checked in Lean. Details. The proof bounds the probability that fewer than h of c·h independent links are "good", each good with probability ≥ 1/2. Fair coins are allowed by Lemma 4.1: with c = 4, h = 6, fewer than 6 heads among 24 coins has probability 55455/2²⁴ ≈ 3.3·10⁻³ > e⁻⁹. The case d < 1 of the proof of Theorem 5.1 uses the quadratic form to show that there are very few "middle" nodes. With the paper's threshold 4h and the linear exponent, its charge is not O(m). Repair. A threshold 7h repairs the proof of Theorem 5.1 (on paper; not formalized). ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 4.1: "rank … never less than the rank of its parent" should be "never more". Proof of Lemma 4.2: "fewer than h bad links" should be "good links". Proof of Lemma 5.3: "depth 1 before the Find" should be "depth 2". Typos Algorithm 4, line 7: u.p should be u.parent. Proof of Theorem 5.1: the two exponents h²/16 and h²/4 are inconsistent. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.1 ("u, v and w are distinct"; same point in the proof of Lemma 3.3) The proof's claim that u, v and w are distinct is false: a splitting Find can read v ← u.parent = u while u is a root, and if u is linked before the next read, it executes Cas(u.parent, u, w) with u = v (cas_same_node, a concrete 2-process execution). Impact. Lemma true: this Cas always fails. The same execution gives a Find iteration in which u does not advance, contrary to a sentence in the proof of Lemma 3.3; this happens at most once per Find. Both lemmas are proved with this case added (lemma_3_1_union, waitFree). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model: any set of processes, deterministic programs, no crashes, an arbitrary (adversarial) scheduler. Each process runs one operation at a time, and every invocation is allowed. Each atomic step is one read or one Cas on one parent pointer (casObject E a, initially a). Local computation is folded into the preceding access. No randomness. The node ids are an arbitrary injective key : E → ℕ, so the random order of the paper is a special case. E is finite. The object is DSU over E. Its state is the same-set relation, initially equality. sameSet answers membership; unite merges the two classes and returns a dummy true. Find comes in three versions: Algorithm 1, two reads per iteration as written; and splitting with k + 1 tries (k = 0: Algorithm 4, k = 1: Algorithm 5). Linearizability is CSLib's IsLinearization, and wait-freedom is CSLib's Impl.WaitFree. Main results in Lean. Linearizability. An invariant over (history, configuration, linearization) says that the abstract state of the linearization is the partition into trees of the current memory. Responses of SameSet = false are inserted retroactively, at a cut of the linearization recorded when Find(v) found its root; this uses IsLinearization.insert from Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/LinPoints.lean. The proof of Lemma 3.2 leaves two facts implicit; both are easy (linearizable): When SameSet returns false, the answer is decided at the later test u = u.parent, but the operation is linearized earlier, at the last read of Find(v). One needs that u was a root already at that read: it was a root when Find(u) returned and is one at the test, and non-roots never become roots again. Linearizing at the test instead would be wrong, because v may have been linked into u's tree in between. The link case needs that the larger node is not in the smaller root's tree. This holds because ids increase along parent pointers. Wait-freedom. The potential is bound · Σₐ #{ids above a.parent} + Φ. The first term decreases at every successful Cas. Φ is a lexicographic local potential: positions of u, v (taken at their roots while a Find runs), then the phase, then the Find's progress. It decreases at every own step that leaves memory unchanged (Impl.waitFree_of_cfgPotential, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Potential.lean). Not formalized. It proves only a weaker bound (Theorem 5.2, m/(np²) in place of m/(np)) and calls the original claim "an open problem" (Section 7). We could not consult the proceedings text and do not formalize Sections 4–5, so we neither confirm nor refute the claim. Trust. No sorry. Uniform Local Algorithms via Pruning — PODC 2011 Amos Korman, Jean-Sébastien Sereni, Laurent Viennot. Toward More Localized Local Algorithms: Removing Assumptions Concerning Global Knowledge. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993814. Formalized version: arXiv 1512.03306 v1 (journal version, Distributed Computing); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The main transformers hold after local repairs: Theorem 1, Theorem 2 (randomized: weak Monte-Carlo to Las Vegas), Theorem 3 (deterministic case) and Theorem 4, and uniform maximal matching survives with matchings encoded by partner identities. The randomized half of Theorem 3 and the arboricity applications are not saved: Corollary 3 has only a sketched repair, and Corollary 4 is proved only under an extra hypothesis. The coloring results of Section 5 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Corollaries 3 and 4 (families not closed under inclusion; hence Corollary 1(i)) The corollaries apply Theorems 1 and 3 to the families F_large, F_med and "arboricity o(√log n)", which are not closed under inclusion (deleting isolated nodes lowers n, deleting edges lowers a), as Section 2 requires. Impact. The non-uniform algorithm has no guarantee on residual instances. The bounds can be recovered by working on all graphs; we sketch this for Corollary 3 in differencies.md but did not formalize it. corollary_4 is proved under one extra hypothesis (next items). Details. Section 2 requires every family to be closed under inclusion, and a pruning algorithm must map the family into itself. ⚠️ Theorem 3 (inverse functions in the proof) The proof sets g_j⁻¹(x) = min g_j⁻¹({x}) and uses g_j(g_j⁻¹(x)) = x, but an ascending g_j need not take the value x. Impact. Statement true; repaired for the deterministic case (theorem_3). The randomized case has the same broken step and no Lean proof; the reduction below acts on the non-uniform algorithm, so it would transfer verbatim, but this is not formalized. Details. The argument also mixes reals with integer coordinates. Repair. Take g_j⁻¹(x) = max {y : g_j(y) ≤ x}. We prove Theorem 3 by a direct reduction to Theorem 1: guesses for the correctness parameters Γ are computed from guesses for the time parameters Λ. This needs only Λ-monotone pruning, not Λ ∪ Γ (theorem_3). ⚠️ Corollary 4 (time bound of the cited algorithm for every good guess) Corollary 4 also needs the cited algorithm's time bound f(ñ) to hold for every good arboricity guess, including ã = ñ, and the paper does not argue this. Impact. Our corollary_4 assumes it, and it is stated on all finite graphs. 🔧 Observation 3.3 (P_MM is a pruning algorithm for maximal matching) P_MM does not satisfy gluing for the paper's own encoding of matchings: on the path v₀ — u₀ — u — v with tentative output (5, 5, 1, 2) it prunes {v₀, u₀}, the residual edge u — v is solved by (5, 5), and the combined output (5, 5, 5, 5) matches nobody (observation_3_3_false). Impact. With matchings encoded by partner identities the same rule is a pruning algorithm, so Corollary 1(vi) survives (observation_3_3_repaired, corollary_1_vi). Details. In the paper, u and v are matched if they are adjacent, output the same value, and no other neighbour of u or v outputs that value. In the example, v₀ and u₀ are matched, while u and v are neither matched nor surrounded by matched nodes, so P_MM prunes W = {v₀, u₀}. A solution of the residual graph may reuse the values of pruned nodes, and the paper's "matched" notion looks at neighbours' values. This fails for any new inputs the pruning algorithm might assign. Repair. Output the partner's identity. The same pruning rule is then a pruning algorithm, and it needs 2 rounds instead of 3 (observation_3_3_repaired). Corollary 1(vi) holds for this encoding (corollary_1_vi). ✏️ Slips Theorems 1–4: the claimed bounds O(f*·s_f(f*)) and O(f_min) fail when f* < 1, since the transformed algorithm always spends at least one iteration. Degenerate case; we prove C·(f*·s_f(⌊f*⌋) + 1) and C·(f_j + 1) (theorem_1, theorem_2, theorem_3, theorem_4). Observation 3.2 needs β ≥ 1. Degenerate: the (2,0) case. Observation 3.3: the pruning algorithm is monotone only with respect to non-decreasing parameters, not "any parameter". Formalized for any non-decreasing parameter (observation_3_3_repaired). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2 (expected-time bound) The proof claims α_{i+1} ≤ K·α_i "since s_f is moderately slow", where α_i is the number of rounds of the first i iterations of τ, but this does not follow. Impact. Statement true; repaired (theorem_2). Details. Only |S_f(2^j)| ≤ s_f(2^j) is known, and the actual sizes can be far smaller for some j and then jump. Repair. Use the upper bound α_{s+i} ≤ C·s_f(2^s)·2^s·(2a)^i (a is the moderate-slowness constant). With the failure bound (1−ρ)^{i(i+1)/2} the series still converges, so the claimed bound holds (theorem_2). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. LOCAL model with unique identifiers, synchronous and fault-free, with simultaneous wake-up. The identifiers are the elements of a type V. An instance is (G, x : V → Option α). Its nodes are those with x v ≠ none, and its graph is the induced subgraph res G x. Pruned nodes get none, so residual instances live on the same type. An algorithm (Alg) gives every node's output after t rounds (none = not yet terminated). That output is a function of the radius-t view (CSLib Cslib.Local.IsLocal), and outputs are final. "Running time ≤ T" means all nodes of the instance have output a solution by round T. A non-uniform algorithm is a family A g of such algorithms, one per guess vector g. It is required to work only for good guesses (DependsWithTime). Pruning algorithms (Pruning) run in constant time and satisfy solution detection and gluing (Section 3.2). The alternating algorithm (Pruning.alg) runs fixed-length stages known to every node, so all nodes stay synchronized and no synchronizer (Observation 2.1) is needed. A node outputs at the end of the iteration in which it is pruned. Randomness (Theorem 2): every node has a private random tape, i.i.d. with law ν. A randomized algorithm is an Alg on inputs (x v, ω v). Outputs must be measurable in the tapes, inputs and outputs come from countable sets, and instances are finite. Every sub-iteration of τ reads a fresh coordinate of the tape ℕ → R (joint law: nested Measure.infinitePi). Las Vegas means correct for every tape whenever all nodes have output; the expected running time is a lintegral of the first round at which all nodes have output. The cited non-uniform algorithms ([4], [6], [19], [22], [34]) are hypotheses of the corollaries. Main results in Lean. Byzantine Agreement with Homonyms — PODC 2011 Carole Delporte-Gallet, Hugues Fauconnier, Rachid Guerraoui, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Eric Ruppert, Hung Tran-The. Byzantine Agreement with Homonyms. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993810. Formalized version: HAL hal-00580133v1 (PODC paper plus appendix with the detailed proofs); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The whole characterization of Table 1 holds as stated, both directions in all six cells: necessity (Props. 1, 4, 16, Thms. 19, 20) and sufficiency (Props. 2, 5, 18), including both partially synchronous algorithms. The necessity proof of Theorem 19 rests on a non-WLOG assumption and needed a different argument, while the other proof errors have local repairs. Lemma 34 is not established under the reading of the pseudocode that Lemma 36 needs, but no result needs it. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 34 (Appendix A.3, "at most one lock pair at the end of each phase") Lemma 34 is unestablished, not refuted: its proof assumes that the lock-removal test (lines 24–26 of Figure 7) still sees the n−t witnesses of line 16, which fails under the per-superround witnesses that Lemma 36's proof needs. Impact. No other result depends on it. Prop. 39 cites it, but only needs that some lock (v₁, ∗) is held, because line 6 then excludes every other value (Restricted.decAt_agree). Details. The paper defines witnesses per superround, and line 25 does not say which superround's accepts it uses. Lemma 36 needs the accepts of superround 4 of the current phase, which is the reading we formalize. Before T, all echoes sent to p in that superround can be lost. A process locked on (v′, ph′) that locks (v, ph) in a later phase then keeps both pairs: a hand-built run with n = ℓ = 4, t = 1 works (not in Lean). The pseudocode is ambiguous: under a cumulative reading of witnesses (all accepts so far), the paper's proof of Lemma 34 goes through. ✏️ Slips Proposition 26 (correctness of the broadcast with multiplicity, Appendix A.3.1): for α = 0 the statement asks every correct process to perform an Accept(i, α′, m, r) although nobody broadcast m, which Figure 6 never does. Degenerate case: Prop. 26 is only used with α ≥ 1, and the paper's own Lemma 24 separates the case α > 0. We prove the witness form (Restricted.cc_le_witnesses: the number of correct broadcasters is at most the number of witnesses after GST), which is trivially true for α = 0. Appendix A.4 (Thm. 19): "Assume that for ℓ < 3t" should be ℓ ≤ 3t; "a number of processes less than 3t" should be "at most 3t". Appendix A.4 (Thm. 19): "If ℓ ≥ t, the result is clear" should be ℓ ≤ t. Proof of Prop. 5 (termination): "(since n ≤ 2ℓ−3t)" needs the strict inequality, which the hypothesis gives. Proof of Prop. 5 (termination): acks are sent in "round 1 of superround 3", which should be superround 4. The overview of Section 4.2 has the same slip. Typos Proof of Lemma 33 cites "Lemma 22"; it means Lemma 32. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 19 (necessity, Appendix A.4) The reduction to the classical n ≤ 3t bound assumes "w.l.o.g." that q₀ (whose homonym group has n−ℓ+1 clones) is correct in the classical run, which is not without loss of generality. Impact. Statement true; proved directly (thm19_lower). Details. If q₀ is Byzantine in the classical run, the paper's simulation would need all n−ℓ+1 processes with identifier 0 to be Byzantine. So the derived algorithm A′ is only shown correct in runs where q₀ is correct. That weaker classical problem is solvable for any ℓ (everyone adopts q₀'s broadcast value), so no contradiction with [9, 13] follows. A possible repair, not proved: per run, choose the identifier of the clone group among the correct qᵢ. A must work for every identifier assignment, so this is allowed. Repair. We reuse the covering system of Proposition 1 instead. The stacks of the hexagon are clones, so with innumerate receivers a Byzantine process only needs to send one copy per identifier, and the scenarios become restricted runs (not_solves_three_t_innumerate, restricted_scenario_dedup). 🔧 Lemma 12 (Prop. 5, Case 2) and Lemma 37 (Prop. 18, Case 2) The case split "if there are t+1 correct processes with the same input value, that value will be in the proper set of all correct processes" fails with homonyms (and should be on the current proper sets, not on inputs). Impact. Statements true; repaired (Psync.common_value, Restricted.common_proper). Details. In Prop. 5 the rule adds v when it is received from t+1 different identifiers. The t+1 correct processes sharing an input may all have the same identifier. The right split is on the current proper sets: either some value is in the proper sets of correct processes of t+1 distinct identifiers (in Prop. 18: of t+1 correct messages), so it spreads to everyone after GST; or the ≥ 2t+1 Byzantine-free identifiers (correct messages) witness the "add all values" rule at every correct process. This second branch reads the rule "received proper sets from 2t+1 different identifiers and no value appears in t+1 of them" existentially: some 2t+1 received sets with no value in t+1 of them. That is the literal reading ("them" are the 2t+1 sets), and the paper's validity remark ("t+1 of the proper sets are from correct processes") argues about such a subset, so we count it as the paper's rule, not as a change. Under the universal reading (all received sets) a Byzantine process that sends each process its own input blocks both rules forever. Example (Prop. 18 setting): n = 4, t = 1, correct inputs a, b, c; no common proper value ever appears and no lock is ever requested. The existential reading keeps validity. 🔧 Lemma 36 and Prop. 40 (use of relay, Prop. 27) Prop. 27 gives the relayed accepts only in superround max(r′, T)+1, but with per-superround witnesses Lemma 36 and Prop. 40 need them in later superrounds as well. Impact. Statements true: the proof of Prop. 27 gives relay in every later superround (Restricted.thr_relay). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Model.lean) n processes (any finite type with n elements) share ℓ authenticated identifiers; the assignment is surjective and arbitrary (Solves quantifies over all of them). Algorithms are deterministic and identical within an identifier. A process sends one message per round to all processes with a given identifier (including itself) and receives the multiset of (identifier, message) pairs. Numerate algorithms see the multiset; innumerate algorithms (Algorithm.Innumerate) depend only on the set. Static Byzantine set, at most t processes, full information. Byzantine processes deliver arbitrary pairs tagged with their own identifiers. Restricted Byzantine processes deliver at most one pair per recipient and round (at most #{Byzantine with identifier j} pairs tagged j). Synchronous: lock-step rounds without loss (gst = 0). Partially synchronous: the basic model of Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer, in which messages between correct processes may be lost only before an unknown round gst. All processes start in round 0 and step every round. BA: termination, agreement (also for p = q, so decisions are stable) and validity (unanimous correct input). Lower bounds use two distinct values; algorithms work for any value type. The paper's standing assumptions n > 3t, t > 0, ℓ ≥ 1 are explicit hypotheses where needed. Main results in Lean. Paxos vs. Raft, and porting optimizations — PODC 2019 Zhaoguo Wang, Changgeng Zhao, Shuai Mu, Haibo Chen, Jinyang Li. On the Parallels between Paxos and Raft, and how to Port Optimizations. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331595. Formalized version: the extended version with Appendices A–C (TLA+ specifications and the refinement proof). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The first half of the paper holds for a repaired Raft*: a Raft variant whose leader adopts the voters' extra entries refines repaired MultiPaxos under the Appendix C mapping, so it is safe, though this takes a new inductive invariant. The porting guarantee, the other half, is proved only for single-step refinements (the general theorem of Section 4), which excludes the multi-step Raft* refinement, and the ported protocols Raft*-PQL and Raft*-Mencius were not checked. The printed protocols are unsafe, and short local changes repair them. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Section 4.3 applied to Raft* (porting Paxos optimizations to Raft* "with guaranteed correctness") The correctness argument for ported optimizations assumes single-step refinement (b_j ⇒ a_i), but the Raft* → Paxos refinement is multi-step (one AppendEntries is several Phase2a/Phase2b steps). Impact. The abstract's claim that optimizations port from Paxos to Raft "with guaranteed correctness" is unestablished for Raft*, whose refinement of Paxos the paper itself proves only multi-step (Appendix C 2.4/2.5); Raft*-PQL and Raft*-Mencius are neither proved nor refuted (not formalized). The general theorem of Section 4.3 is true (port_correct). For multi-step refinements, evaluating the added clauses at the end points is unsound in general (naive_multistep_port_unsound). 🔧 TLA+ module MultiPaxos, theorem Invariance (Appendix B.1) With 3 acceptors and majority quorums the spec reaches a state where one ballot has two proposals and both TRUE and FALSE are chosen at index 0, violating OneValuePerBallot, Inv and agreement (tla_invariance_false). Impact. The paper's formal MultiPaxos is unsafe, and its stated invariance theorem is false. The pseudocode MultiPaxos (Figure 1) has the same flaw. A repaired MultiPaxos is safe (safety). Details. Propose(a, i, v) records nothing in logs[a]. So a leader may propose TRUE and then FALSE for the same index in the same ballot. Then {a0, a2} accepts one value and {a1, a2} the other. The grey comment "⇒ v is safe at i, b" does not help: both values are safe at ballot 1. Figure 1's Phase2a also records nothing. Repair. In Paxos.lean, a proposal per instance and ballot is recorded. Safety is proved in chosenAt_agree and safety. 🔧 Appendix B.1, Phase1b and BecomeLeader (two leaders of one ballot) 1b messages are not addressed to the proposer, so two acceptors can become leaders of the same ballot from the same 1b messages (tla_two_leaders_same_ballot). Impact. This breaks the spec independently of the previous item; the repaired MultiPaxos is safe (safety). Repair. Phase1Succeed needs the proposer's own report. 🔧 Figures 1 and 2 (leadership guards) The pseudocode lacks leadership guards: Figure 1's Phase1a does not reset phase1Succeeded, and Phase1Succeed and BecomeLeader can re-run, which in Figure 2 can shrink lastIndex. Impact. The repaired protocols are safe (safety, raftStar_commitSafe_raftVote). Repair. In Paxos.lean, Phase1a resets leadership and Phase1Succeed needs ¬leader; BecomeLeader in RaftStar.lean is guarded in the same way. 🔧 Figure 2, ReceiveVote (lines 9–11, the vote rule) Because a voter compares its entry at the candidate's last index (not its last entry) with the candidate's last term, it can vote for a candidate behind it, and a committed entry is overwritten (fig2_not_commitSafe; key step fig2_voter_reports_higher_term). Impact. Raft* as printed is unsafe and refines no safe Paxos. Step 4.2 of Appendix C is false for it. The fix is local: Section 3 says Raft* is "identical to Raft" except for two differences unrelated to voting, and the TLA+ spec B.2 and Raft compare the voter's last entry, and with that rule the refinement holds (raftStar_commitSafe_fig2Fixed). Details. The run uses five servers; every AppendEntries carries a value: A writes x@1 only to itself. C writes y@2 only to itself. A is re-elected in term 3, appends z@3, replicates [x@1, z@3] to B, D, E and commits x at index 0. C (log [y@2]) runs in term 4. B, D, E vote for it: their entry at index 0 has term 1 < 2, although their last term is 3. C keeps y at index 0 and commits it. 🔧 Figure 2, AppendEntries with no new value (heartbeats) Figure 2 does not exclude vals = [], and with empty appends Raft*'s commit rule loses committed entries in Raft's "Figure 8" scenario, even with Raft's own vote rule (heartbeat_not_commitSafe). Impact. Section 3 says re-stamping ballots makes Raft's §5.4.2 rule unnecessary. That holds only if every append carries an entry of the leader's term. The TLA+ spec B.2 always appends one value, and under that assumption the refinement holds (refinement_repaired). ✏️ Slips Figure 3 maps instance.bal to the per-entry bal field, which gives no refinement even for repaired Raft* (scenario in differencies.md, in prose only). The intended mapping is in Section 3 and Appendix C, and the refinement is proved for it (refinement). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Appendix C, steps 2.3 and 4.2 (BecomeLeader ⇒ Phase1Succeed) Step 4.2 ("the leader's entries are already the safe entries") has no argument. Impact. For the repaired Raft* the step holds (sim_becomeLeader). Details. Step 4.2 needs a real inductive invariant of Raft* (Raft.Inv, 18 clauses): log matching; one candidate with a quorum of votes per term; a candidate's log is its own vote; voters' last terms are at most the candidate's; every entry is a proposal of its term and of its log's last term. 🛠️ Appendix C, step 2.5 (ReceiveAppend ⇒ Phase2b) Step 2.5 maps only the new entries, although under the mapping a follower re-accepts its whole log in the leader's term, and it ignores the follower's commitIndex update. Impact. For the repaired Raft* the step holds (sim_receiveAppend). Details. The commit update maps to Paxos Learn steps. Showing that committed entries are never overwritten needs MultiPaxos safety itself, so the refinement and the invariant are proved together (inv_and_reachable). Raft* never truncates: a replaced entry is a Paxos acceptance in a higher ballot. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing. Every message ever sent stays in a set, so messages may be lost, duplicated and reordered. Crash-stop servers: a crashed server takes no further steps. No timing assumptions, deterministic protocols. Any intersecting quorum system; majorities are QuorumSystem.majority. Interleaving transition systems for MultiPaxos (Paxos.lean, Figure 1 repaired) and Raft* (RaftStar.lean, Figure 2 parametrised by the vote rule and by whether heartbeats are allowed). Ghost history variables record the implied Paxos accept/acceptOK messages. The mapping is Appendix C's: ballot = term, phase1Succeeded = isLeader, the accepted ballot of every entry is the term of the last entry, chosenSet = committed prefix. Figure 3's per-entry bal mapping does not give a refinement even for repaired Raft* (scenario in differencies.md, not formalized). The repaired Raft* needs no bal field. The refinement theorem covers every vote rule that never lets a server vote for a candidate with a smaller last term. This includes Raft's rule, the index-fixed Figure 2 rule and the permissive "last term ≤". Main results in Lean. Paper Lean File MultiPaxos is safe (assumed in §4.1; TLA+ B.1 Invariance, repaired) Paxos.safety, Paxos.proposal_eq_of_chosenAt PaxosSafety.lean App. C: every Raft* step implies Paxos steps refinement_step Refinement.lean App. C: Raft* is a refinement of Paxos refinement, refinement_repaired Refinement.lean §3: Raft* is correct (state machine safety) raftStar_commitSafe, raftStar_commitSafe_raftVote, raftStar_commitSafe_fig2Fixed Refinement.lean Invariants behind step 4.2 Raft.Inv, Raft.Inv.step RaftInv.lean Fig. 2 as printed is unsafe Raft.fig2_not_commitSafe, Raft.fig2_voter_reports_higher_term Counterexamples.lean Fig. 2 with heartbeats is unsafe Raft.heartbeat_not_commitSafe Counterexamples.lean TLA+ B.1 Invariance is false TLA.tla_invariance_false, TLA.tla_two_leaders_same_ballot TLAMultiPaxos.lean §4.2: A∆ refines A Porting.Opt.refines Porting.lean §4.3: B∆ refines A∆ and B Porting.port_refines_opt, Porting.port_refines_base, Porting.port_correct Porting.lean §4.3 recipe fails for multi-step refinements Porting.naive_multistep_port_unsound Porting.lean Not formalized. The TLA+ module Raft* (B.2), PQL, Mencius and their Raft* ports (B.3–B.6, Appendix A), the classification of Paxos variants (Fig. 6), and the evaluation. The ProposeEntries of B.2 also records nothing in the leader's log, so its Invariance very likely fails the same way as B.1's; not checked. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: repaired Raft* commits entries (Raft.repaired_commits); MultiPaxos chooses values (Paxos.exists_reachable_chosen). Self-contained models; only Mathlib is used.

Low-Congestion Shortcuts for Graphs Excluding Dense Minors — PODC 2021 Mohsen Ghaffari, Bernhard Haeupler. Low-Congestion Shortcuts for Graphs Excluding Dense Minors. PODC 2021, pp. 213–221. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467935. Formalized version: full version arXiv:2008.03091v1 (numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The main upper bound is proved: Theorem 3.1, and hence the existential Theorem 1.2, with 8δ + 1 blocks and after local repairs of Observations 2.6 and 2.7 and of case (II). The matching lower bound behind the paper's tightness claim is not saved: the construction in the proof of Lemma 3.2 does not have the claimed diameter, and no repair is proved. The distributed algorithms were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 3.2 (lower bound: diameter of the construction) The graph constructed in the proof of Lemma 3.2 violates the diameter bound: for δ' = 5, D' = 12 (so δ = 3, k = 2, D = 6, 174 vertices), the vertices v_{3,3} and v_{10,11} are at distance exactly 15 (LowerBound.paperGraph_dist_eq, LowerBound.paperGraph_not_diam_le). Impact. The proof fails, so Lemma 3.2, and hence Lemma 1.3, is unestablished; the statement is plausibly true with different constants. The upper bounds are unaffected. Details. The proof shows that every vertex is within 1.5D + 1 of the middle of the top path. That bounds the radius, but the proof concludes "diameter ≤ 1.5D + 1 ≤ D'"; the diameter can be nearly twice as large. Numerical experiments (not formal) suggest that k = ⌊(D' − 2)/(3δ)⌋ repairs the construction. 🔧 Theorem 3.1 (block count 8δ) The proof of Theorem 3.1 only bounds the block count by 8δ + 1, and the literal 8δ is false on the one-vertex graph, where δ(G) = 0 but the part {v} always has one block (theorem_3_1_literal_false_singleton). Impact. An off-by-one: we prove the theorem with 8δ + 1 blocks (theorem_3_1), so Theorem 1.2 gets dilation (8δ + 1)(2D + 1) instead of 8δ(2D + 1). Details. In case (I), the blocks of P_i are counted by their topmost vertices. The proof counts only overcongested edges (e, P_i) ∈ B, but the topmost vertex of a block can also be the root, which has no parent edge and is never overcongested. On the one-vertex graph this makes 8δ = 0 blocks impossible. 🔧 Observation 2.6 (blocks far from the part) Observation 2.6 is false as stated: on the path 0 – 1 – 2 rooted at 0, with part {2} and H = {01}, there are two blocks, but 2 is disconnected from 0, so the dilation is infinite (observation_2_6_counterexample). Impact. It fails only for shortcuts with useless tree edges far from the part, and it is fixed by the evident condition that every block meets its part, which the shortcuts built in Theorem 3.1 satisfy (observation_2_6, blocksMeetPart_shortcut). Details. Definition 2.3 lets a tree-restricted H_i contain tree edges far from P_i. A block of such an H_i need not meet P_i, so G[P_i] + H_i can be disconnected. Repair. Require every block to contain a vertex of its part. We add this to Definitions 2.4/2.5. The shortcuts built in Theorem 3.1 ("all ancestor edges of P_i") satisfy it. (observation_2_6, blocksMeetPart_shortcut) 🔧 Observation 2.7 (number of halving rounds) The proof's log₂ k halving rounds are not enough to cover k parts, which need ⌊log₂ k⌋ + 1 rounds (for k = 1 part one round is needed but log₂ 1 = 0), so the stated congestion c log₂ n is not established. Impact. Harmless asymptotically: we prove congestion c(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1) (observation_2_7). ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.1, case (II): "at least half of the parts have degree at least 8δ" yields only ≥ where the proof needs <. Take the exact negation of case (I): more than half of the parts have degree strictly greater than 8δ (caseII_false). Theorem 3.1, case (II): the claim that each edge-node is included with probability 1 − 1/(4D) is wrong, since an edge-node whose v_e lies in no part is always present. This is harmless for the arithmetic, which only uses the bound |O| ≤ k/c on the number of edge-nodes, but it means the strict inequality must come from the part-nodes. Typos Figure 3.2 uses δ' = 3, outside the lemma's range δ' ≥ 5. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3.1, case (II) (edges of B never present in B_{P'}) When the lower endpoint v_e of an overcongested edge lies in a part P_i, the pair (e, P_i) is never present in B_{P'}, so the bound E|E_{P'}| ≥ 3k/(16D) is unjustified. Impact. Repaired with a sharper presence probability (exists_blocker, caseII_false, final_arith). Details. The representative is then v_e, so the path "from v_e to r excluding r" is empty. Moreover, the edge-node e exists only if P_i ∉ P', so the pair (e, P_i) is never present. Repair. Each edge-node loses at most one such pair, since parts are disjoint. We compensate with a sharper presence probability (1 − p)^{D−1} ≥ (3D+1)/(4D) instead of 3/4, together with δ ≥ 1/2 for any graph with an edge. The arithmetic then closes. (exists_blocker, caseII_false, final_arith) 🔧 Theorem 3.1, case (II) (representatives must be topmost) "Some representative r ∈ P_i reachable from v_e via T \ O" does not give the claimed independence from the event P_i ∈ P', which needs the path from v_e to r to avoid P_i. Impact. Repaired by choosing r as the first vertex of P_i on the way down (exists_rep). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Purely graph-theoretic. No distributed model is formalized, because the CONGEST algorithms are cited from other work. G is a finite simple graph. "Diameter D" means connected with all distances ≤ D. Rooted spanning trees are given by parent pointers with depths. Parts are pairwise disjoint vertex sets, each inducing a connected subgraph. A shortcut is a family of edge sets of G. Congestion bounds per-edge multiplicity. Dilation bounds the diameter of G[P_i] + H_i. Blocks are the components of (P_i ∪ V(H_i), H_i). Minors are branch-set models. MinorDensityLE δ means every minor has |E| ≤ δ|V|. minorDensity is the (attained) supremum. Theorem 3.1 holds for every δ ≥ δ(G). Overcongested edges: instead of running the greedy, we take a set O with the greedy's fixed-point property (exists_stable). The connectivity and disjointness of the branch sets of B_{P'} are only asserted in the paper; we prove them. The probabilistic method (independent Bernoulli(1/(4D)) parts) is an explicit weighted sum over subsets, without measure theory: bernWeight and its lemmas come from the shared finite probability library Cslib/Probability/Finite/Bernoulli.lean. Main results in Lean (namespace LowCongestionShortcuts). Paper Lean File Observation 2.6 (with the block hypothesis); counterexample observation_2_6, observation_2_6_counterexample Observations.lean Observation 2.7 observation_2_7 Observations.lean Theorem 3.1 (8δ + 1 blocks, congestion 8δD) theorem_3_1, theorem_3_1_minorDensity Theorems.lean Theorem 3.1 with 8δ blocks is false theorem_3_1_literal_false_singleton Literal.lean Theorem 1.2 (congestion 8δD(⌊log₂ n⌋+1), dilation (8δ+1)(2D+1)) theorem_1_2, theorem_1_2_of_minorDensityLE Theorems.lean Lemma 3.2: construction has diameter > D' LowerBound.paperGraph_not_diam_le LowerBoundGraph.lean Not formalized. Lemma 3.2 itself (it needs planarity and Euler's formula); Lemmas 1.1, 1.3, 2.8, 3.3, Theorem 1.5, Corollaries 1.4, 1.6, 1.7, 3.4 (cited results, distributed algorithms, genus/treewidth bounds). Whether 8δ blocks hold for non-degenerate graphs is left open. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The graph notions (rooted trees, BFS trees, minors and minor density, shortcuts) come from CSLib, Cslib/Foundations/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/.

Byzantine Consensus under Local Broadcast — PODC 2019 Muhammad Samir Khan, Syed Shalan Naqvi, Nitin H. Vaidya. Exact Byzantine Consensus on Undirected Graphs under Local Broadcast Model. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331619. Formalized version: arXiv 1903.11677 v2 (full version with appendices). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The tight characterization holds for every graph with at least two nodes: under local broadcast, consensus tolerating f Byzantine faults is solvable iff the minimum degree is ≥ 2f and the graph is (⌊3f/2⌋+1)-connected. The sufficiency proof needs local changes only: step (b) of Algorithm 1 needs simple paths, Observation B.1 is used in an unstated direction, and Lemma 5.5 is applied outside its hypothesis. The hybrid model and the O(n)-round algorithm were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 4.1 and Lemma A.2 (single-node graph): Theorem 4.1 (necessity) is false for n = 1, f = 0, which the standing assumption f < n allows: the node decides its own input, so consensus is trivial, but under West's definition (k-connected requires n > k) the graph is not 1-connected (not_theorem_4_1_single_node). We prove the statement under n ≥ 2 (theorem_4_1). The proof of Lemma A.2 starts "not (⌊3f/2⌋+1)-connected ⇒ there is a vertex cut of size ≤ ⌊3f/2⌋". This misses complete graphs with n ≤ ⌊3f/2⌋ + 1, which have no cut. For f ≥ 1, Lemma A.1 (degree ≥ 2f) excludes them; for f = 0 only the single-node graph remains. The same case breaks the §4 remark that the complete graph on 2f + 1 nodes satisfies the conditions "for any f". The hypothesis f < n is also needed: for n = 1, f = 1 consensus is solvable but the minimum degree is 0 < 2 (not_degree_single_node). Typos Proof of Lemma A.1, item 4: the sentence describing Figure 2 orients the F²–W edges the other way round from the formula in the same item and from the figure. The executions need the formula's version. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Algorithm 1, step (b), in the proof of Lemma 5.3 (simple paths) The paper lets P_uv be an arbitrary uv-path avoiding F, and its paths are walks, so along a path P_wv that repeats a node v may receive nothing and wrongly put w into N_v. Impact. With simple paths, which Lemma 5.4 provides, the proof goes through (exists_selSpec). Details. If P_wv repeats a node x, then x discards the value forwarded back to it by rule (iii). So v receives nothing along P_wv and wrongly puts w into N_v, even when w flooded 0. The step "v receives 0 along P_wv and correctly puts w in Z_v" in Lemma 5.3 then fails. 🔧 Observation B.1 (used in an unstated direction) Observation B.1 states soundness (a value received along a fault-free path is the origin's value), but Lemma 5.3 also needs completeness: along every fault-free simple path the value does arrive within the phase's n rounds. Impact. Statement true; we prove both directions (floodInv). Details. Completeness depends on the default message (1, ⊥) and on the round in which each path prefix is accepted. For a faulty originator, "the value it floods" must be defined, as what its first-round transmission says about ⊥. 🔧 Lemma 5.3 (Lemma 5.5 applied to faulty nodes) Lemma 5.3 applies Lemma 5.5 to faulty w, but Lemma 5.5 is stated only for non-faulty nodes. Impact. Statement true: the proof of Lemma 5.5 works for any w, and we prove it that way (pathsExist). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finite node set with a simple undirected graph known to all nodes. Synchronous lock-step rounds (CSLib LockStep). Protocols are deterministic and history-based, and may use any message type. Local broadcast is a restriction on both sides. Honest protocols send the same message to all neighbours. The Byzantine adversary (static set, |B| ≤ f: the shared threshold structure atMost f of Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/LockStep/Parallel.lean) also broadcasts, but is otherwise arbitrary (covers adaptive, rushing adversaries). Consensus (§3): termination, agreement (the shared Problem.Termination, Problem.Agreement), and validity (output = input of some non-faulty node); binary values. Impossibility quantifies over all broadcast protocols. Possibility uses Algorithm 1, with phases for every F with |F| ≤ f in an arbitrary fixed order, n flooding rounds each, and rules (i)–(iv). Ambiguities (ordering within a transmission, ties in step (c)) are resolved deterministically, and the proof works for every choice of simple paths in step (b). Byzantine nodes may send arbitrary, even contradictory, sets of pairs. Proof remarks. Lemma A.2's cover edges are only "deduced from Figure 3"; we give them explicitly. Both covers tacitly need each Byzantine node to be simulated by a single cover node, so that it can still broadcast. Lemma 5.4 cites Menger, but it follows from the definition of connectivity. Main results in Lean. Theorem 5.6 / Appendix C (the O(n)-round algorithm for 2f-connected graphs) and Section 6 / Appendix D (the hybrid model with equivocating faults). Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The necessity proofs are FLM-style covers with two copies per node, done once in three_scenarios. Menger's theorem (vertex version) and the fan lemma were formalized for this paper, since Mathlib has none: SimpleGraph.menger, SimpleGraph.fan in CSLib Cslib/Foundations/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Menger.lean, with connectivity in VertexConnectivity.lean next to it; removing vertices without changing the vertex type is CSLib's SimpleGraph.deleteVerts (Spanner.lean). The round model is CSLib's LockStep (delivery lemmas deliver_honest/deliver_byz from Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/LockStep/Parallel.lean).

The Universe of Symmetry Breaking Tasks — PODC 2011 Damien Imbs, Sergio Rajsbaum, Michel Raynal. The universe of symmetry breaking tasks. PODC 2011 (brief announcement). DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993857. Formalized version: the full version, IRISA technical report PI 1965 (January 2011; HAL inria-00560453v1, the PDF in this repository). There is no arXiv version. Numbering follows the technical report. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The combinatorics of GSB tasks (feasibility, kernel sets, anchoring, the hardest task and the canonical form) and the reductions (perfect renaming is universal, Theorem 10's parity reduction, the slot-to-renaming algorithm) hold after local changes. Theorem 9 is correct for index-independent algorithms but false for the comparison-based algorithms that Section 2.3 requires of all algorithms, and Lemma 1 misses the hypothesis ℓ_v ≤ u_v. Theorems 1, 2 and 11 were not checked, and the cited impossibility of WSB is a hypothesis. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 9 (no-communication solvability) vs. Section 2.3 Theorem 9 is false for the comparison-based algorithms that Section 2.3 requires of all algorithms: then ⟨2,3,0,1⟩ meets the criterion (ℓ = 0, ⌈3/3⌉ ≤ 1) but is not solvable without communication (theorem_9_comparisonBased_false). Impact. Theorem 9 is correct for index-independent algorithms that may use the identity's value; we formalize it that way (theorem_9). The same goes for the "decide your own identity" solution of (2n−1)-renaming and for Corollary 2. Details. Section 2.3 says that only index-independent and comparison-based algorithms are considered, and Theorem 2 claims this is without loss of generality. That claim only holds with communication: its transformation runs a renaming algorithm first. Without communication, a comparison-based decision function is constant. Then a GSB task with m ≥ 2 is solvable iff ℓ = 0 ∧ u ≥ n, and Theorem 9's "if" direction fails (noComm_comparisonBased_iff). Index independence is essential: with index-dependent decisions, perfect renaming needs no communication (perfectRenaming_indexDependent). 🔧 Lemma 1 (missing hypothesis ℓ_v ≤ u_v) "Feasible iff Σℓ_v ≤ n ≤ Σu_v" is false for asymmetric bounds with some ℓ_v > u_v: n = 3, ℓ⃗ = [2,0], u⃗ = [1,5] satisfies 2 ≤ 3 ≤ 6, but value 1 would have to be decided at least twice and at most once (lemma_1_false). Impact. The correct statement adds ℓ_v ≤ u_v for all v (lemma_1). Lemma 2, the symmetric case, is correct as stated. ✏️ Slips Theorem 4 (anchoring criterion, ℓ = 0): "u-anchored iff ℓ ≤ n − u(m−1)" fails in integer arithmetic whenever ℓ = 0 and u(m−1) > n, e.g. for ⟨6,3,0,6⟩ and every (2n−1)-renaming task ⟨n,2n−1,0,1⟩ with n ≥ 3 (theorem_4_int_false, theorem_4_int_false_renaming). Every ⟨n,m,0,u⟩ task is trivially u-anchored, as the paper itself says, but the right-hand side is negative; ⟨6,3,0,6⟩ is the task that Figure 1 labels "trivially u-anchored". Corollary 1 uses max(0, n−u(m−1)), so the authors knew the expression can be negative. With n − u(m−1) truncated at 0 the theorem holds (for m ≥ 1), and we prove that version (theorem_4). Section 4.2, the canonical representative: "an (ℓ,u)-anchored task is its own representative" picks two different representatives when u > n: ⟨4,2,0,5⟩ and ⟨4,2,0,4⟩ are synonyms and both (ℓ,u)-anchored (canonical_not_unique). This happens only in degenerate cases (also for m = 1), and Theorem 7's map f fixes it (theorem_7, theorem_7_iff): f reaches its fixed point after one step, and two feasible tasks are synonyms iff they have the same f-image. The f-image is the pair (least, largest) number of times a value is decided in a legal output. Theorem 8 needs a feasible task (theorem_8). Corollary 2 needs x ≥ 1 (corollary_2). Theorem 11 needs n ≥ 2: for n = 1 election is trivial. Table 1 claims to list all feasible ⟨6,3,ℓ,u⟩ tasks with u ≤ 6, but ⟨6,3,2,6⟩ is missing. Every printed entry is correct (table_1, table_1_missing_row). The kernel set of ⟨6,3,1,4⟩ is printed as {[4,1,1],[4,1,1],[2,2,2]}; it should be {[4,1,1],[3,2,1],[2,2,2]}. Section 4.2 says ⟨6,3,2,2⟩ is the representative for four tasks, but §4.1 and Table 1 list six synonyms. Lower bounds for MIS and bounded-outdegree dominating sets in trees — PODC 2021 Alkida Balliu, Sebastian Brandt, Fabian Kuhn, Dennis Olivetti. Improved Distributed Lower Bounds for MIS and Bounded (Out-)Degree Dominating Sets in Trees. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467901. Formalized version: arXiv 2106.02440 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The whole deterministic port-numbering part (§3) is correct: the round-elimination step Π_Δ(a, x) → Π_Δ(⌊(a−2x−1)/2⌋, x+1) (Lemmas 6, 8, 9, Corollary 10), Lemmas 5, 11, 12 and the sequence of Lemma 13 (with an explicit condition in place of "Δ large enough") are all formalized and, with a Lean proof of the forward direction of round elimination (Theorem 3), give the Ω(log Δ) port-numbering lower bound for k-outdegree dominating sets, k ≤ Δ^ε, with ε = 1/6. Only Lemma 15 for Δ = 1 and one symbol in the definition of R̄ are wrong. The lifting to LOCAL (imported Theorem 14, hence Theorem 1 and Corollary 2) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 15 for Δ = 1 (randomized 0-round failure probability): the lemma claims that for all x ≤ Δ − 1 and a ≥ 1, every randomized 0-round algorithm for Π_Δ(a, x) fails with probability at least 1/Δ⁸. This bound is 1 for Δ = 1, but on K₂ the algorithm that outputs M or A with probability 1/2 each fails only with probability 1/2 (lemma_15_false_delta_one): both M and A are node configurations of Π_1(1, 0), and the algorithm fails only on MM or AA. The proof gives a failure probability of at least 1/(3Δ)² and then uses 1/(3Δ)² ≥ 1/Δ⁸, which needs Δ ≥ 2. The paper only uses large Δ, so nothing downstream is affected. We prove the lemma for Δ ≥ 2 with the bound 1/(36Δ²), which also covers algorithms whose outputs are not always valid configurations (lemma_15). §2.3, definition of R̄: Σ_{Π''} is "the sets that appear in the configurations of E_{Π''}", but E_{Π''} is defined from Σ_{Π''}. It should say N_{Π''} (Problem.alphRbar). Typos §2.3, definition of R̄: "Σ_{Π''} =⊆ …". Lemma 8 says Π⁺_Δ(a, x) "has time complexity max{T − 1, 0}", but its proof gives only "at most", as Corollary 10 says; we prove this "at most max{T−1, 0}" form (lemma_8). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic port-numbering model on the infinite Δ-regular tree. The tree is the Cayley graph of CSLib's free Coxeter group FreeCox Δ, so its edges come with a proper Δ-edge colouring. Port numbers equal colours at both endpoints, as in the graph family of Lemmas 12 and 15. The colours are known, so arbitrary port numbers would carry no extra information. Input: an edge orientation, i.e. the paper's edge port numbering {1, 2}. Correctness is required for every orientation. Algorithms are functions of the radius-t view (IsLocal). The view contains the orientation of every edge whose two endpoints are within distance t. So a 0-round algorithm sees no orientation, which is the paper's convention in Lemma 12 ("they do not even see the port numbering of the edges"). Problems and operators. Node-edge-checkable problems (Problem): node configurations as colour-indexed tuples, plus a symmetric edge relation. R and R̄ are defined exactly as in §2.3, including maximality and the derived alphabets. 0-round reductions ("Π' is solvable in 0 rounds given a solution of Π, given the colouring", ZeroRoundReduction) are maps between colour-indexed configurations. k-outdegree dominating set (SolvesODS): each node outputs membership in S and one direction bit per edge. S must be dominating, every edge inside S must be claimed by exactly one endpoint, and every node of S has outdegree ≤ k inside S. Theorem 3, forward direction. The paper imports Brandt's round elimination theorem ([13], Thm 4.3). We only need "T rounds for Π ⇒ T−1 rounds for R̄(R(Π))", and we prove it in this model (RoundElim.lean). Being on the full infinite tree with free inputs, the proof needs no independence hypothesis. The orientation is used exactly once: both endpoints of an edge must extend their label pair to the same maximal edge configuration. Randomized model (Lemma 15). A randomized 0-round algorithm is one output distribution, sampled independently at every node. Strength of the result. This setting (tree, colouring, orientation) is the strongest one in which the paper proves its port-numbering bound. The paper also allows arbitrary port numbers; as argued above, this changes nothing. Proof remarks. Lemmas 5 and 11 need k ≤ Δ and x ≤ Δ, since without them the configuration M^{Δ−x}X^x does not exist. This is the paper's convention 0 ≤ a, x ≤ Δ for the family. In the proof of Lemma 8, the step "each Yᵢ contains B" does not need the earlier fact Yᵢ ⊆ OUABPQ: a right-closed set without B already lies in PQ. Main results in Lean. Coordination Without Prior Agreement — PODC 2017 Gadi Taubenfeld. Coordination Without Prior Agreement. PODC 2017. DOI 10.1145/3087801.3087807. Formalized version: the author's copy (10 pages, proofs included; no arXiv version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All checked results hold: the impossibility results of Section 6 (Theorems 6.2, 6.3, 6.5), and correctness of the three algorithms (Figure 1 mutex, Theorems 3.2–3.3; Figure 2 consensus, Theorems 4.1–4.2; Figure 3 renaming, Theorems 5.1–5.3) for every adversarial numbering of the registers. But the correctness proofs of all three algorithms are sketches with false intermediate claims, and those of deadlock-freedom (Theorem 3.3) and of unique names (Theorem 5.2) needed new arguments. Figure 2 also breaks on an input equal to the initial value 0, which a local change fixes. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Figure 2, line 4 (an input equal to the initial value 0) Figure 2 ignores the value 0 at line 4 but does not exclude 0 as an input, and with an input 0 agreement fails for n = 2. Impact. Multi-valued consensus needs inputs kept apart from the empty value: Section 6.3 uses inputs in {0, 1} and refers back to this algorithm. We type inputs apart from the empty value, and consensus then holds (Consensus.consensus_solves). Details. Process 1 with input 0 fills the registers and decides 0; then process 2 with input 1 ignores the 0 entries and decides 1. ✏️ Slips Figure 2, line 6 and Figure 3, line 15 (the "arbitrary index"): the lines write to "an arbitrary index k such that myview[k] ≠ own record; clearly, such an entry exists", but in the deciding iteration no such index exists, because the until-test comes after the write. The prose of Section 4.1 has the intended order, deciding before the write. We let the write go anywhere, and the theorems hold for every admissible choice. Typos Theorem 6.5's proof says "in y" for "in x". Theorem 5.1's item (3) says "increments mypref" for myround, and the prose of Section 5.1 cites line 19 for the round update, which is line 20. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 5.2 (Figure 3, uniqueness) The proof argues as if collects were atomic and ignores later rounds, so its claim that after the first decider all other processes find v in at least n entries of round r is false. Impact. Statement true; the proof needs a new argument (Renaming.renaming_solves). Details. A process whose collect started earlier sees a partly stale view, may keep another value and write it once more. Also, processes that already left round r keep writing records of later rounds, so the number of (v, r) records does drop below n, and the catch-up of lines 8–12 is ignored. Repair. The counting invariant of Theorem 4.1 (below) is kept per round: records of later rounds force catch-up and carry (v, r) in their history. With well-formed histories this gives agreement per round. A ghost invariant on collects shows the invariant holds when the deciding collect starts. (Renaming.renaming_solves) 🛠️ Theorem 3.3 (Figure 1, deadlock-freedom) The proof claims "exactly one of the two processes must find that less than ⌈m/2⌉ registers are set to its identifier, will give up, …, enabling the other … to enter its critical section", but with m = 3 both processes can give up with no CS entry in between. Impact. Statement true for every odd m; the printed argument cannot be patched, and we replaced it (Mutex.theorem_3_3). Details. The first loser is not blocked. The schedule: q scans while p is exiting and writes nothing; it then collects three 0s and gives up. Meanwhile p calls lock again, q leaves its wait loop on the empty memory, q writes two registers, p writes one, and p gives up too. (schedule in modelcheck/mutex_scenario.py) Repair. At most two give-ups occur while no operation completes. Without give-ups the memory stabilizes, and oddness of m forces a decision. (Mutex.theorem_3_3) 🔧 Theorem 4.1 (proof treats collects as atomic) The proof for Figure 2 argues as if collects were atomic: after the first decider i has seen all registers equal to (i, v), every other process is claimed to find v in at least n entries at line 4. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a counting invariant (Consensus.consensus_solves). Details. A process whose collect started earlier sees a partly stale view, may keep another value and write it once more. Repair. The invariant is "registers not carrying v plus processes that may still write one stale value ≤ n − 1". A ghost invariant on collects shows the invariant holds when the deciding collect starts. (Consensus.consensus_solves) 🔧 Theorem 5.1 (Figure 3, termination) Item (4) of the proof claims that a process continuing alone into the next round wins it, but earlier records of that round may hold another value at least n times, so the solo process adopts it and loses that round too. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Renaming.renaming_obstructionFree). Details. Also, the proof never shows that myround stays below n. Repair. Termination is proved by induction on n − myround, using the invariant myround + 1 ≤ |P|. (Renaming.renaming_obstructionFree) 🔧 Theorem 5.3 (Figure 3, adaptivity) The proof's "the algorithm will terminate after k rounds" does not bound the names. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Renaming.renaming_solves). Repair. A process acquiring name a sees a history naming a − 1 other distinct participants. Two processes cannot both get the name n by a counting argument. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory (CSLib Impl), atomic read/write registers, deterministic processes with arbitrary identifiers (any type P); process code may depend on the process, so the impossibility results also cover non-symmetric algorithms. No randomness. Unnamed registers: each register is a separate base object; every process p uses its own adversarial numbering π p : Equiv.Perm ι of the registers, and all registers start with the same value (Impl.unnamed, Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Unnamed.lean). An algorithm is correct iff it is correct for every π. Collects are not atomic: every read and every write is one step. "Arbitrary index" choices in the pseudocode are parameters, and the theorems hold for all admissible choices. Failures: crash-stop is implicit (a process may stop taking steps); progress conditions are obstruction-freedom (consensus, renaming) and deadlock-freedom (mutex, CSLib's definition with fair client-well-formed infinite executions; participation not required). Tasks are CSLib one-shot tasks (consensus P V; adaptiveRenaming P = distinct names in {1..k} for k participants). "Number of processes not a priori known" = an infinite set P of potential participants. Safety and obstruction-freedom only involve finite executions; for Theorem 6.2, deadlock-freedom is required only of infinite executions with finitely many participants (DeadlockFreeFin); with CSLib's DeadlockFree (also executions with infinitely many participants) it is the paper's "unbounded" case. "n processes" = Fintype.card P = n (or ≤ n for the algorithms). Main results in Lean. Distributed Spanner Approximation — PODC 2018 Keren Censor-Hillel, Michal Dory. Distributed Spanner Approximation. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212758. Formalized version: arXiv 1802.03160 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main hardness results hold: the Ω(n/(√α·log n)) deterministic and (given the randomized communication complexity of set disjointness) Ω(√n/(√α·log n)) randomized CONGEST lower bounds for α-approximate minimum directed k-spanner, k ≥ 5 (Thms 2.8, 1.1), with their supporting lemmas, including the cited gap-disjointness bound (Lemma 2.5), which we prove. The vertex-cover reduction (Claim 3.1) is correct, and Lemma 3.2's gap, that a node cannot compute its cover membership "without any communication", is closed by one extra round, which does not touch the asymptotic uses. The algorithms of §§4–6, the weighted k-spanner bounds and Thms 3.3, 3.4 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Typos Proof of Lemma 2.4: "V_B = Y1, V_A = V \ V_A" should read V_A = V \ V_B. Claim 3.1 / Lemma 3.2: the conversion H → H' gives w(H') ≤ w(H). It has "the same cost" only because H is a minimum spanner in Claim 3.1. Lemma 3.2 applies the conversion to an α-approximate H, so there only |C_H| ≤ w(H) holds, and that is all the proof needs. Proof of Thm 2.8: the constants c₁, c₂ are handled loosely (β is defined from α(n'), the bound is used with α(n)). The argument is routine; our version has explicit constants and no monotonicity assumption. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.2 (from a 2-spanner algorithm to vertex cover) The proof claims that after simulating the 2-spanner algorithm on G_S every node converts the spanner H into C_H "without any communication", but node v cannot know whether u₂ output the cross edge {v₁, u₂}, which decides whether v ∈ C_H (localRule_counterexample). Impact. Repaired with one extra round: T + 1 rounds of 3B-bit messages, or 3(T + 1) rounds of B-bit messages, instead of 3T (lemma_3_2, lemma_3_2_congest). The +O(1) does not affect Thms 3.3/3.4. Details. By §1.5, a node outputs some of its incident edges and the spanner is the union of the outputs. The natural local rule (apply C_H only to the edges that v's own copies output) fails. Take the triangle and the optimal 2-spanner of G_S made of all weight-0 edges plus the cross edge {0₁, 2₂}. Either 0₁ or 2₂ may be the node that outputs that cross edge. The rule then gives {0} or {2}, and neither is a vertex cover. The exact count 3T(3n) is neither proved nor refuted: we refuted only this rule, not every algorithm. Repair. In one extra round each node tells each neighbour whether it output their shared cross edge. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous CONGEST from CSLib (Cslib.Congest.Algorithm): deterministic nodes, IDs = vertex names, B-bit messages per edge, direction and round, no failures. Randomized algorithms (Thm 1.1) get private uniform random strings r v : ρ; they may fail with probability ≤ δ on each instance. Directed k-spanner: a digraph is a loopless arc set E : Finset (V × V); the network is its underlying undirected graph (communication is bidirectional) and must be connected; node v knows the directions of its incident arcs. Each node selects some incident arcs; the output is the union. H is a k-spanner if H ⊆ E and every arc of E is joined by a directed walk of length ≤ k in H; α-approximate means |H| ≤ α·|H'| for every k-spanner H'. Algorithms run on a fixed vertex set V, n = |V|, and must be correct on every such digraph on V. The lower-bound graph G(ℓ, β) is padded with pendant vertices to exactly n vertices (the paper uses monotonicity of α(n) instead). Bounds are stated concretely in n, α, B, T; B = O(log n) gives the paper's Ω-bounds. Two-party communication: CSLib protocol trees. Lemma 2.5 (gap disjointness, deterministic) is proved; the randomized lower bound for set disjointness (Lemma 2.1) is the hypothesis RandDisjLB δ κ. §3: undirected graphs G on V with a linear order (IDs). G_S lives on V × Fin 3, with weights in ℕ; the cross edge for v < u is {v₁, u₂}. A 2-spanner is H ≤ G_S covering every edge by a path of length ≤ 2, and its cost is the sum of the weights of its edges. The spanner algorithm's node input is its incident edges with weights; the MVC algorithm's node input is its neighbourhood; the MVC output is the out bit. Algorithms may be required to be correct only on a class P of graphs. Main results in Lean.
