DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933084. Formalized version: arXiv 1602.02991 v2 (the latest arXiv version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The local constant factor on bounded genus graphs stands: on graphs whose depth-1 minors have edge density ≤ c and which exclude K_{t,3} as a depth-1 minor, the modified Lenzen–Pignolet–Wattenhofer algorithm is a (6c²t + (2t+5)c + 4)-approximation (Lemma 12), which we prove with the paper's constant, for every choice of dominators, and it runs in 6 LOCAL rounds. The counting lemmas behind it are false as stated (Lemma 7, Corollary 8 and Lemma 11 with Lean counterexamples, Lemma 9 with an informal one), but local changes repair them. With the genus facts as hypotheses, the O(g) factor of Theorem 13 is only proved as O(g²), and Section 4's 24g + O(1) factor was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 13 (O(g) approximation factor) The O(g) factor is not established: the proof treats the density bound c as a constant, but Lemmas 5 and 10 need it for small depth-1 minors, where genus-g graphs have density Θ(√g), so the argument only gives O(g²) (density_unbounded). Impact. The O(g) factor is unestablished, not refuted. A local constant factor for every fixed genus stands: we prove an O(g²) approximation (≤ 1100(g+1)², theorem_13, factor_le). Details. Lemma 12's factor 6c²t + … is O(g) only if c = O(1). The paper takes c ≈ 3 ("c ≤ 3.01 in sufficiently large graphs", §4). However, Lemmas 5 and 10 apply the density bound to small depth-1 minors as well, and small graphs of genus g have density up to Θ(√g); for example, K_k has genus ⌈(k-3)(k-4)/12⌉. So c = Θ(√g) is necessary, and with t = 4g + 3 the argument gives O(g²). We show that the hypotheses alone force c to grow with g (density_unbounded). The claimed O(g) rounds are an overstatement in the other direction: the algorithm needs 6 rounds (output_isLocal). Repair. We prove the theorem with the genus facts as hypotheses: c(g) = 3 + ⌊√(3g)⌋ + 1 suffices, and the factor is ≤ 1100(g+1)² (theorem_13, factor_le). 🔧 Lemma 7, items 2 and 3, and Corollary 8 (neighbours between stars) Lemma 7 fails on the planar graph m_i – c' – u_k – m_j (k = 1..K), where all K leaves of m_j see the star of m_i, beyond the bound 2ct = 12 (item 2, K = 13) or 4ct = 24 (item 3, K = 25), and in the same graph Corollary 8's |Y| ≤ 6c²t|M| fails for K = 145, since Y contains all u_k, so |Y| ≥ K, while |M| = 2 (lemma_7_2_false, lemma_7_3_false, corollary_8_false). Corrected versions (bounds 2c(t-1) and 4c(t-1), a smaller Y) suffice to prove Lemma 12 with the paper's constant (lemma_12). Details. The K_{t,3} argument picks c ∈ C_{m_j} and contracts the star of m_i minus c. If c is itself a leaf of m_i (c ∈ N_i), the vertices u ∈ N_j whose only neighbour in N_i is c are not bounded at all. In the counterexample, the graph is K_{2,K} on {c', m_j} × {u_k} plus the pendant edge m_i c'. Assumption 6 holds with c = 2, t = 3. M = {m_i, m_j} is a minimum dominating set and D = ∅. The stars are N_i = {c'} and N_j = {u_1, …, u_K}. Item 2 uses the order m_i, m_j; item 3 the order m_j, m_i. Item 1 has the same gap but is not refuted formally. Repair. Count only leaves outside C = ⋃ C_m that have a neighbour outside C. Then the bounds are 2c(t-1) and 4c(t-1) (Setup.lemma_7_12, Setup.lemma_7_3). Our Y excludes C. With the corrected Lemma 7 we get |Y| + |Y_D| ≤ 6c²(t-1)|M|, where Y_D is the part seeing stars of M ∩ D (Setup.corollary_8). Lemma 12 then counts dominator images instead: M ∪ C, Z (Lemma 10), and the corrected Y; images of sources in M ∪ C or in Y_D; images inside stars (corrected Lemma 11). The total is (c+1) + 3(2c+1) + 6c²(t-1) + (2(t-1)+4)c ≤ 6c²t + (2t+5)c + 4 (per |M|). 🔧 Lemma 11 (dominators inside a star) Lemma 11 fails on the book K_{1,1,K} (spine m x, pages u_k) with the legal dominator choice dom ≡ x: all K + 1 leaves of m have their dominator inside the star outside Y ∪ Z, beyond the bound (2(t-1)+4)c|M| = 16 for K = 17 (lemma_11_false). Impact. Repaired by also excluding C from the dominator's range; then the paper's bound holds and Lemma 12 goes through. Details. The proof applies Lemma 9 to dom(u), which may lie in C_m. In the counterexample, Assumption 6 holds with c = 2, t = 3; M = {m}, D = ∅, C_m = {x} (every admissible C_m contains x), and Y = Z = ∅. Since m and x tie for the maximal residual degree, dom ≡ x is a legal choice ("choose any"). Repair. Exclude C from the dominator's range as well. Then the paper's bound (2(t-1)+4)c|M| holds (Setup.lemma_11). 🔧 Lemma 9 (for some admissible C_m) Lemma 9 fails when m and v are both adjacent to 18 vertices forming 6 paths a_i – c_i – b_i and C_m = {c_1, …, c_6}: v has 18 neighbours in the star, more than 2c(t-1) = 12 (informal counterexample, not formalized). In the example the graph is planar, so c = 3, t = 3, and D = ∅; C_m covers N(m) and v ∉ C_m. Repair. We prove ≤, which is all the paper uses (Setup.lemma_10). Lemma 12 assumes "edge density at most c", but it needs Assumption 6 (density of all depth-1 minors). The final line of the proof of Lemma 12 drops the factor |M|. Typos Algorithm 1 has a stray end if. Use the residual degree: d_{V-D}(m) ≤ d_{V-D}(dom(u)). 🔧 Lemma 7 (m_i ∉ C_{m_2}) In the proof of Lemma 7, "m_i ∉ C_{m_2}" should be C_{m_j}, and the corrected claim is still unjustified, since C_{m_j} is arbitrary and may contain m_i. Impact. Harmless, because m_i covers no vertex of N_j (Setup.lemma_7_12). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finite simple graphs G : SimpleGraph V. LOCAL model: synchronous and deterministic, with no failures and unique identifiers. The algorithm is the paper's modified Algorithm 1 with integer parameter c (line 5: |A| ≤ 2c). Synchronous Approximate Agreement with Asynchronous Fallback — PODC 2022 Diana Ghinea, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Roger Wattenhofer. Optimal Synchronous Approximate Agreement with Asynchronous Fallback. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538442. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (no arXiv version exists). Numbering follows it. The full version (IACR ePrint 2022/354, single version of 2022-03-18) has the same protocols and statements; it contains the proof of Theorem 4.1 (Section 6.1). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The protocol the paper is about fails: the Reliable Broadcast Π_rBC is not consistent in a synchronous network when tₛ ≥ n/3, the very range it was built for, so Π_AA is not a tₛ-secure AA protocol there (for n = 3, tₛ = 1, tₐ = 0, one Byzantine party keeps the two honest parties at 0 and 1 forever), and no repaired broadcast is proved. The impossibility result (Theorem 5.1: no AA protocol when 2tₛ + tₐ ≥ n) is correct for n ≥ 2, even with signatures. The iteration analysis (Lemmas 3.2–3.7) is correct if the Overlap All-to-All Broadcast has the guarantees of Definition 2.2, so the tight characterization is only half established by the paper. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 4.1 (Π_rBC synchronized consistency) and Theorem 3.1 (1) (Π_AA agreement in a synchronous network) Π_rBC is not consistent in a synchronous network when tₛ ≥ n/3: for n = 3, tₛ = 1, a Byzantine sender whose conflicting proposals arrive late at 2Δ makes the two honest parties output 0 and 1 at 3Δ (RBC.rbc_not_syncConsistent, RBC.rbc_attack), and a Byzantine party that runs this attack keeps the two honest parties of Π_AA at outputs 0 and 1 (AA.theorem_3_1_sync_false). Impact. The protocol half of the tight characterization is not established: the range of honest values is not halved at all, and the attack can be repeated in every iteration. Validity and termination are not violated; agreement is. Theorem 4.1 is false for every tₛ in the paper's range n/3 ≤ tₛ < n/2 (only n = 3 is formalized), and it is the root cause of the failure of Theorem 3.1 (1). The characterization claimed in the abstract may still hold with a correct hybrid broadcast primitive, but the paper does not establish it and we prove no such primitive; the impossibility half (Theorem 5.1) stands. Details. Lines 2–4 detect a Byzantine sender's equivocation only for proposals that arrive by time Δ. Their forwards then reach everybody by 2Δ, as the paragraph before the pseudocode argues. The failing step is in the proof of Lemma 6.2 of the full version: "as P sent a vote for v at time τ, P has received and forwarded a valid propose message for v at time τ − Δ". By line 4, P forwards and votes at the same time when the proposal arrives at 2Δ. But a Byzantine sender may deliver its proposals late. Take n = 3, tₛ = 1, tₐ = 0, honest P₀, P₁, and a Byzantine sender C. C sends propose 0 to P₀ and propose 1 to P₁, both arriving at time 2Δ. Each honest party has seen no conflicting proposal, so it forwards its proposal and votes for it at 2Δ. The conflicting forwards arrive only at 3Δ. C votes for both values. At 3Δ, P₀ holds the n − tₛ = 2 votes {P₀, C} for 0 and outputs 0, while P₁ holds {P₁, C} for 1 and outputs 1. Both parties output at 3Δ, so (tₛ,1)-Synchronized Consistency fails. The run is synchronous (every honest message arrives after exactly Δ), has one corruption and forges no signature. The same idea works whenever n ≤ 3tₛ: split the honest parties into two groups of size ≥ n − 2tₛ each. The proofs of Lemma 4.3 ("Π_rBC guarantees that P′ has received each value reported by P") and of Lemma 4.4 (tₛ-Consistency of Π_oBC) rely on Theorem 4.1. So does Lemma 3.3 (|V ∪ V′| ≤ n). We ran the whole protocol in the setting above (n = 3, tₛ = 1, tₐ = 0, ε = 1/2, δmax = 1, hence S = 1 iteration). Honest inputs are 0 and 1. C performs the attack above in its own Π_rBC instance. It then reports to each honest party exactly that party's set O, so C becomes a witness of both. Both honest parties terminate Π_oBC just after 4Δ, with O₀ = {0, 1, 0} and O₁ = {0, 1, 1}. Discarding one value at each end gives the outputs 0 and 1. If C instead withholds its reports, neither honest party ever terminates Π_oBC. This contradicts Lemma 4.3 too; we checked it by running the encoding, not by a proof. ✏️ Slips Theorem 5.1 is false for n = 1 (e.g. tₛ = 0, tₐ = 1, so 2tₛ + tₐ ≥ n): "output your input" is a secure AA protocol (theorem_5_1_false_n_eq_one). It holds for n ≥ 2. Definition 2.1 does not require termination, while the impossibility proof uses it ("the honest parties output +ε"). We include termination in the definition. In the proofs of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5, "length(T ∪ T)" should be length(T ∪ T′). In lines 9 and 15 of Π_oBC, "(v′, P′)" should be (v, P′). Typos In Lemma 3.6, "0 ≤ tₐ, c ≤ tₛ" should read 0 ≤ tₐ ≤ tₛ (c is not defined there). In the proof of Lemma 3.6, "i_v + m_V(u) − 1" should be i_u + …. In the proof of Lemma 3.5, "Let P and P" should be P and P′. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 5.1 (reduction to n = 2tₛ + tₐ, and tₛ = 0) The proof's "let n = 2tₛ + tₐ" is not always possible, and for tₛ = 0 the groups S±ε are empty and the argument gives nothing. Impact. Statement true for n ≥ 2; repaired (exists_split, not_secure_sync_and_psync). Details. For example, n = 3, tₛ = 2, tₐ = 0 has no thresholds t′ₛ ≤ tₛ, t′ₐ ≤ tₐ with 2t′ₛ + t′ₐ = 3. Repair. Use groups of size at most tₛ/tₐ; for tₛ = 0, use groups of size ≤ max(tₛ, tₐ), with scenarios 1 and 2 read as asynchronous executions when needed (a synchronous execution is also an asynchronous one). 🔧 Definition 2.2 (asynchronous guarantees of the Overlap All-to-All Broadcast) Lemma 3.4 uses that "at most tₐ values are sent by corrupted parties", which needs the value attributed to an honest sender to be its actual input, and Definition 2.2 does not require this in the asynchronous case. Impact. Under-specified definition: a gap in the interface, not in the result. It holds for the concrete Π_oBC; we add it as the hypothesis AsyncOBC.authentic, and Lemmas 3.4–3.5 go through (theorem_3_1_async). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's Byzantine message-passing model Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync. Time is discrete; parties are deterministic state machines; the adversary chooses a static Byzantine set, their messages, the GST and all delivery times. Signatures are CSLib's abstract unforgeable tokens: the adversary may emit only its own tokens or tokens already sent by honest parties (Run.AuthValid). Synchronous network: gst = 0, delays ≤ δ, and at most tₛ faults (syncRuns). Asynchronous network: at most tₐ faults and arbitrary finite delays, with no bound at all (asyncRuns = library Run.AsyncValid, unbounded asynchrony; explicit form asyncRuns_iff). All parties step every tick, so their clocks are synchronized. Impossibility: the theorem is stronger than the paper's. It needs security only on synchronous runs and on partially synchronous runs (psyncRuns), and inputs only from a domain containing two points at distance > ε. It covers every signature scheme (Auth) and arbitrary message and state types. The adversary is static, while the paper's is adaptive. Protocols are deterministic, as in the paper. Counterexamples: Π_rBC, Π_oBC and Π_AA with S = 1 are encoded line by line (RBC.lean, OBC.lean, AA.lean). A message produced at time kΔ is processed at (k+1)Δ (Δ = one tick, delay 0). Messages that arrive at the same time are processed before the time-triggered actions. FIFO channels use sequence numbers, as the paper suggests. The attack runs are synchronous executions of the paper's model in which every honest message takes exactly Δ. The runs are computed by decide with Boolean values and transferred to real values by an equivariance lemma (the broadcast layers only compare values for equality). Iteration analysis: abstract. The i-th call of Π_oBC is a partial map "sender ↦ value" per party, satisfying the synchronous (SyncOBC) or asynchronous (AsyncOBC) guarantees of Definition 2.2. Main results in Lean. All listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Asymmetric Progress Conditions — PODC 2010 Damien Imbs, Michel Raynal, Gadi Taubenfeld. On Asymmetric Progress Conditions. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835709. Formalized version: the extended IRISA research report PI-1952 (May 2010, HAL inria-00486977), whose numbering matches the PODC paper and adds the proofs of Appendix A. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All results hold for n ≥ 2 processes: the impossibility of (n,1)-liveness from (n−1)-port objects (Theorem 1), the (n,x)-liveness hierarchy (Theorems 2, 3, Corollary 1), the fault-freedom variant (Theorem 4), the arbiter (Theorem 5) and the group-based consensus algorithm (Theorem 6). The proof of Theorem 2, on which the hierarchy rests, had to be redone in a new model of base objects that may withhold responses, with a new adversarial object. Theorems 1 and 4 and Lemmas 3–9 are false only in the degenerate one-process case, and the proofs of Lemma 6 and Theorem 6 need only local repairs. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorems 1 and 4, Lemmas 3–9: with n = 1 these statements are false, because one process that decides its own input is a wait-free consensus algorithm without any shared object, and it has no bivalent run (theorem1_false_one_process, lemma3_false_one_process). The paper never states n ≥ 2, but every proof needs two processes (Lemma 3 picks two processes with different inputs). With n ≥ 2 all of them are proved. The text of Section 6.1 describing Figure 4 says "the owners win the arbitration and p_i updates consequently WINNER to guest (line 03)"; it should say owner, as line 03 does. Typos Lemma 10 says "y ∈ [1..n]"; it should be [1..m] (groups). Its end marker reads "Lemma 11". Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 2 (blocking base objects) The proof applies Lemma 6 (developed only for atomic events) to implementations from non-wait-free (n,x)-live base objects and lets processes "access o simultaneously" forever, without saying what a step on such an object is. Impact. Statement true (for every 0 ≤ x < n − 1); repaired (theorem2). The upper bound of Theorem 3 and Corollary 1 rest on it. Repair. Base objects are deterministic, caller-aware objects that may withhold a response (BObj). Lemmas 1–6 are proved in this model. The adversary lets every (n,x)-live base object behave as advCons: wait-free ports are answered at once, any other process only at a step that directly follows its own previous step on the object. This is a legal (n,x)-live consensus object (advCons_isLive). At the configuration of Lemma 6 take a process w wait-free for the implementation but not for o (it exists since x + 1 > x) and another process r ∉ X_o (it exists since x + 1 < n). Alternating w and r keeps both blocked forever, so w violates wait-freedom. 🔧 Lemma 6 (induction step) The proof applies Lemma 1 to x and z (and xq, zq, y), claiming that all objects p can access have the same state there, although the steps of s in z − x may write registers that p can access. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma6, CritK.extend). Lemma 9 has the same proof and the same repair. Details. Lemma 1 needs equal states of every object p may touch in its solo run, not only of the object of its next step. So the hypothesis of Lemma 1 fails as soon as s writes a register before reaching o. Repair. The step of p on o commutes with the steps of s, which avoid o. So z p = x p (z − x) is an extension of x p, and z q p = x q p (z − x) one of x q p. Compatibility follows without Lemma 1 (run_comm_of_avoids, Avoids.step_of_poised). 🔧 Theorem 6 (use of the arbiter's validity) The proofs of Lemma 10 (Case 2) and Lemma 11 (Case 2) need "a guest (owner) invoked arbitrate() before the return", but the arbiter specification of Section 6.1 only says "if no guest (owner) invokes arbitrate(), the value guest (owner) cannot be returned". Impact. Statement true; repaired. The Figure 4 implementation satisfies the real-time version (arbiter_validity_owner, arbiter_validity_guest), and Theorem 6 is proved for the inlined algorithm (group_agreement, group_termination). Details. The non-⊥ argument for ARB_VAL[y+1] (and VAL[y]) needs an invocation that happened before the read. An invocation later in the run would have written the register too late. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, n deterministic processes, crash-stop. Infinite executions are schedules ℕ → Fin n; a process is correct iff it is scheduled infinitely often. No randomness; the adversary chooses the schedule and, for non-wait-free base objects, a legal behaviour. Theorems 1–4: every process proposes a binary input at time 0. This only restricts the executions, so the impossibility results transfer to the paper's setting. Valency is on configurations, since the system is deterministic and outputs persist. Base objects (BObj): deterministic, possibly caller-dependent, possibly withholding the response. Atomic objects always respond. "Atomic register" is generalized to read/write-like objects (every operation is read-only or a blind overwrite). Ports are a property of the algorithm (RespectsPorts). (n,X)-live consensus (Live A X): agreement and validity in all finite executions, obstruction-freedom of every process (solo runs from reachable configurations decide), wait-freedom of the processes in X. Fault-freedom (FFree): a process decides in every execution where all processes are correct. Section 6 (Arbiter.lean, GroupConsensus.lean): a separate concrete model with proposals of an arbitrary type V. A process participates iff it takes a step. Registers are atomic, and GXCONS[g] and the arbiters' XCONS (wait-free (x,x)-live objects accessed only by group g) are atomic consensus objects. Figure 4 is inlined for every ARBITER[g]. The two tasks of a process alternate (T1, T2, T1, …). Deciding does not stop T1, which only adds executions. Main results in Lean. TM Consistency via Observational Refinement — PODC 2013 Hagit Attiya, Alexey Gotsman, Sandeep Hans, Noam Rinetzky. A Programming Language Perspective on Transactional Memory Consistency. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484267. Formalized version: the PODC author copy (10 pp.; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. The journal version (JACM 2017) was only used to confirm intended definitions. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Sufficiency holds after fixing two slips in the definitions: the opacity relation implies observational refinement with respect to traces and to states (Theorem 21, Corollary 19). Necessity is proved for trace-observational refinement, which makes the opacity relation an exact characterization there. Necessity for state refinement (Theorem 24) is not saved: it is false as printed, only because of the Figure 2 mistake that also breaks Proposition 13, and for the abort semantics the prose states it is neither proved nor refuted, since the proof sketch's program cannot tell an aborted call from a returned one and a marker assignment after each call is a plausible fix that is not proved here. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 24 (third implication of Theorem 16, necessity) Unestablished: the proof sketch's P_H cannot tell an aborted last call from a call that returned the initial value, and the marker fix is plausible but unproved; as printed (literal Figure 2, deterministic commands) the theorem is even false (theorem_24_false), but that counterexample fails for the abort semantics the prose states (theorem_24_cex_fails_intended). Impact. Half of the necessity claim is lost: for states the proof is broken and the statement is neither proved nor refuted for the intended semantics. Figure 2 as printed lets an atomic block run on after one of its calls was aborted, against the prose "Once this happens, the execution of C terminates"; our refutation needs exactly this mistake, so it does not refute the intended theorem. For trace-observational refinement necessity holds outright (trace_necessity). Details. Let H_C be the prefixes of H = (t,txbegin)(t,OK)(t,call o.f(1))(t,aborted), and H_A the prefixes of S_v = (t,txbegin)(t,OK)(t,call o.f(1))(t,ret(v) o.f)(t,txcommit)(t,aborted) for all v ∈ ℤ. Both are transactional systems. No complete history of H_A has the per-thread projection of H, so H_C|complete ⋢ H_A|complete. With Figure 2 as printed, H_C ⊑_state H_A. Take a program trace whose history is H. Replace the aborted response by ret(v), where v is the current value of the call's target variable x; x := v changes nothing. If the call ended its atomic block, also let the transaction abort at txcommit. The new trace has a history in H_A and, with deterministic commands, the same final states. This uses Figure 2 as printed: if the body has more commands after the call, say z := 1, an aborted call there never lets the block finish with r := aborted. The trace with history H can only run on into z := 1, and the successful call reproduces that. With the intended semantics, r := atomic { y := o.f(1); z := 1 } has a trace with history H that ends with r = aborted and z unchanged. Every trace with a history in H_A that sets r runs z := 1 first, so H_C ⋢_state H_A (theorem_24_cex_fails_intended, minimal language, one thread). The proof sketch's P_H really is insufficient, even for the intended semantics. It records each return value in a dedicated variable that starts at a "distinguished initial value". When the aborted call is the last command of its block, "aborted" and "returned the initial value, then aborted at commit" leave the same final state. So the claim "from the final state … we can reconstruct the interaction of each thread" is false as stated. A marker assignment after each call (the device TraceNecessity.lean uses for traces) separates the two cases. We did not formalize this repair for states. Repair. Necessity from refinement with respect to traces holds for all histories, not only complete ones (trace_necessity, trace_necessity_complete). Combined with Theorem 21 this gives H_C ⊑ H_A ⟺ H_C ⊑_trace H_A (theorem_16_repaired). 🔧 Figure 2 and Proposition 13 (A(P) contains only well-formed traces) Proposition 13 is false: Figure 2 lets the body of an atomic block continue after a method call in it was aborted, so txbegin OK call aborted call is the history of a trace in A(P) (prop_13_false). Impact. The prose says "once this happens, the execution of C terminates", so the intent is clear and the fix is local (stop the body at the aborted call, as JACM Figure 4 does). What the paper uses it for holds: a program trace with a well-formed history is a well-formed trace (wfTrace_of_inA). The same clause of Figure 2 is what makes Theorem 21 fail with the printed Definition 2, and Theorem 24 fail as printed (above). ✏️ Slips Definition 2 (txcommit outside transactions): the third condition lists only call/ret, so a "stray" txcommit outside any transaction is well-formed, and then Lemma 17 and Theorem 21 are false (lemma_17_false_literal, theorem_21_false_literal). The intent is evident: txcommit is "issued when a transaction tries to commit upon exiting an atomic block", and the journal version adds it to the condition. With the fix, Lemma 17 and Theorem 21 hold (rearrangement, theorem_21). A stray txcommit is a non-transactional action, so ∼ fixes its position among the non-transactional actions of other threads, while ⊑ can move it. Lemma 17 fails for H = (t₁,txcommit)(t₂,txcommit) ⊑ S = (t₂,txcommit)(t₁,txcommit). Programs really produce stray txcommits, because of the Proposition 13 issue above. Two threads run x := atomic { x := o.f(1); x := 1 }. Both calls abort, both threads go on with x := 1 and then issue txcommit. This is a trace with a history in H_C whose stray txcommits H_A reorders, and no trace of H_A is observationally equivalent to it. Definition 12 (global accesses inside transactions): the third condition looks for committed/aborted of any thread after t's txbegin (the projection τ₁|t is missing), and then Lemma 18 is false (lemma_18_false_literal). The intent is evident (the journal version uses τ₁|t). With the fix, Lemma 18 holds (lemma_18, even without the hypothesis eval(s, τH) ≠ ∅). Program traces satisfy the repaired condition, so Corollary 19 is unaffected. Counterexample: thread t₁ opens a transaction, thread t₂ runs a whole transaction, then t₁ writes g := x inside its transaction and t₂ writes g := x outside. Swapping the two writes preserves ∼, because t₁'s write is transactional, but changes the final value of g. Typos Lemma 18's statement binds s twice ("eval(s, τH) ≠ ∅ ⟹ ∀s. …"). The proof shows equality of the evaluations for every s. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 22 (rearrangement step), footnote 3 The footnote classifies the actions of τ₃ on their own ("all non-transactional" without txbegin), and read literally this gives τ^{i+1} = τ^i, breaking the invariant H^{i+1}_{i+1} = S_{i+1}. Impact. Statement true; the classification must be taken relative to the whole trace (nontransFrom with the status after the prefix). Repaired in rearrange_step. Theorem 21's proof also needs τH to be well-formed, which the paper takes from the false Proposition 13; repaired by wfTrace_of_inA. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Histories and traces are lists of actions of a fixed finite set of threads; there is no scheduler or failure model beyond the paper's: finite traces, prefix-closed trace sets (incomplete computations, preempted threads), no liveness. The transactional system is a set of histories. IsTS uses repaired Definition 2, IsTSLit the printed one. The language is a class Lang. Primitive commands are an arbitrary type with classes LPcomm_t/GPcomm_t and a nondeterministic semantics that only reads and writes the variables its class allows. It provides assume(b), assume(e = n) and the assignments x := n, g := x, x := g; expressions are abstract. Programs (Cmd, Cmd.Allowed) obey the syntactic restrictions of Section 2. Figure 2 as printed is the inductive Tr, and A(P) is the prefix closure of interleavings (InA). All positive results use Tr. TrI (Theorem24Intended.lean) is Figure 2 with the intended abort semantics: the body of an atomic block stops at its first aborted call. Observational refinement: StateRef (Definition 14) and TraceRef (Definition 15). There is no randomness. The results are proved for every instance of Lang; the Theorem 24 counterexample needs deterministic commands and Figure 2 as printed. Main results in Lean. For trace observation the opacity relation is an exact characterization: with τ'|t = τ|t for every thread, even pending actions are reproduced. This closes, for traces, the gap Section 8 attributes to incomplete histories. The proof (TraceNecessity.lean) builds the program P_H and adds unique non-transactional marker assignments before and after each atomic block, so that nontrans carries the real-time order. It needs one local variable (Inhabited LV) and no global variables. Not formalized. Proposition 10 (equivalence with the original definition of opacity; proved only in the technical report). A Complexity-Based Hierarchy for Multiprocessor Synchronization — PODC 2016 Faith Ellen, Rati Gelashvili, Nir Shavit, Leqi Zhu. A Complexity-Based Hierarchy for Multiprocessor Synchronization. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933113. Formalized version: arXiv 1607.06139 v2 (2018). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All formalized theorems hold: the space lower bounds (⌈(n−1)/ℓ⌉ ℓ-buffers, ⌈(n−1)/2ℓ⌉ locations with multiple assignment, one max-register / one read-write-FAI location insufficient, unboundedly many test-and-set locations) and the matching algorithms. Several proofs needed only local repairs: Lemma 9.1 has a real gap, Lemma 7.1's proof is wrong (statement true), and Lemma 8.2 is false as stated, though never used in the false case. What is lost is minor: Theorem 8.8's n − 1 swap/read protocol is proved only with process identifiers, not as anonymous. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 8.8 ("anonymous", Section 8) The protocol is called anonymous, but every swap argument carries a process identifier, and without unique tags the double collect is not a linearizable scan. Impact. The n − 1 location bound is proved, but only with identifiers (theorem_8_8), so the word "anonymous" is not saved. The space hierarchy depends only on the bound. ✏️ Slips Lemma 8.2 (swap/read algorithm): for a scan S with ℓ_v(S) = 1, it asks for an earlier scan T in which all laps are 0, but no such T exists, since every scanner has lap ≥ 1 on its own input from line 1. This is an unused edge case: the lemma is applied only with ℓ_v(S) ≥ 2 (Lemma 8.4), where it holds, and Theorem 8.8 is unaffected (invariant SwapRead.AInv). The Section 7 introduction says ⌈n/2ℓ⌉ locations are necessary; Theorem 7.5 and the proof give ⌈(n−1)/2ℓ⌉. Lemma 7.3: "Cζβ1β2" should be "Cξβ1β2". Theorem 4.2: "(r,x) ≺ (r′,x)" should be "(r,x) ≺ (r′,x′)". Typos Lemma 7.4: "at mostwot two". Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 9.1 (test-and-set) The proof runs z's preliminary steps of β after p_1's steps ψ, ψ', which may set locations to 1, so z need not perform β at all, and the claims that "β sets r to 1" and that the two configurations are indistinguishable to p_0 are unjustified. Impact. Statement true; Lemma 9.1 and Theorem 9.2 hold as stated (lemma_9_1). Details. The proof takes β, the shortest prefix of z's solo execution from Cα_kξ that ends with a test-and-set on a location r ∉ L_k. It then reasons about Cα_kξψβ and Cα_kξψψ'β, where ψ, ψ' are steps of p_1. But in those executions z's preliminary steps of β (reads, test-and-sets on L_k) run after ψ. They may then return different values. Repair. Run z's preliminary steps first (they change no memory), so that z is poised on r; its single remaining step commutes with any single step of p_0/p_1. This also removes the case analysis on ψ'. 🔧 Lemma 7.1 (re-packing along an Eulerian trail) The proof re-packs along any maximal Eulerian trail r_1, …, r_t from each r_j to r_t, which does nothing if the trail visits r_t earlier (lemma71_trail_counterexample). Impact. Statement true; taking a shortest such sequence fixes the proof. Details. Example: locations A, B, C, processes p1, p2, p3, 2-packings g = (A, B, C) and h = (B, C, B). The unique maximal trail from A is A→B→C→B, and re-packing from j = 2 leaves B unchanged. Repair. We prove Lemma 7.2, the only use of Lemma 7.1, directly, by an augmenting-path argument (fullyPacked_of_cov). 🔧 Lemmas 6.5 and 7.3 for R = ∅ (used by Theorems 6.8 and 7.5) The proofs of Lemmas 6.5 / 7.3 start from a process p ∈ R, but Theorems 6.8 / 7.5 use them for n = 2, where R = ∅. Impact. Theorems true; the needed conclusion (at least one location) follows from a separate easy argument: with no locations, two processes cannot communicate (no_locations). 🔧 Lemma 3.2 (validity) Validity is not argued, and it needs every scan to see a nonzero component: otherwise the argmax of an all-zero vector could be an unproposed value, since decrements lower counts. Impact. Statement true (lemma_3_2). Repair. One invariant (pending decrements + 1 ≤ total count) closes the step, with no change to the algorithm. 🔧 Lemma 8.6 (validity) Section 8 announces validity, defined as "equal to the input of one of the processes", but Lemma 8.6 proves only weak validity: if all inputs are x, then only x is decided. Impact. Statement true; standard validity also holds (theorem_8_8, SwapRead.AInv.valid). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (CSLib asynchronous shared memory, Cslib.SharedMemory). Deterministic processes, arbitrary interleavings, no randomization; a process may stop taking steps. Every location supports the same atomic instruction set. Initial memory is arbitrary, and the lower bounds hold for every initialization. Multiple assignment (Section 7): the whole memory is one base object with an atomic multi-location ℓ-buffer write. Section 6's per-location model embeds into it, so both lower bounds are instances of one theorem (lowerBound_core). Consensus as a one-shot task: a process participates by invoking it with its input. Lower bounds assume only weak validity ("all inputs v ⇒ decide v") and only one-shot obstruction-freedom (solo termination). Upper bounds prove agreement, standard validity and full obstruction-freedom. Both directions are thus at least as strong as the paper's. Lower bounds are proved for binary consensus and transferred to n-valued consensus (*_multivalued). Main results in Lean. Help! — PODC 2015 Keren Censor-Hillel, Erez Petrank, Shahar Timnat. Help! PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767415. Formalized version: the full version, Chapter 4 of S. Timnat's PhD thesis (Technion, 2015) — no arXiv version exists; numbering (Definitions 4.4.x, 4.5.1, Claims 4.5.x, Theorems 4.3, 4.7, 4.8, 4.11) follows the thesis. All findings below were checked against the PODC extended abstract too (author copy, 10 pp.); its numbering: Definitions 3.2/3.3 = 4.4.2/4.4.3, Observation 3.4 = 4.4.4, Claim 3.5 = 4.4.5, Definition 4.1 = 4.5.1, Claims 4.2/4.3 = 4.5.2/4.5.3 (Remark 4.4 = the thesis remark on (3)), Claim 4.11 = 4.5.10, Theorem 4.18 = Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.1 = Theorem 4.8 (Section 5 only sketches the single-scanner snapshot case and defers the definition of global view types and the proof to the full paper), Claim 6.1 = 4.8.1, Figures 3/4 = 4.4/4.5. Theorem 4.11 appears in the PODC version only as a claimed result (Section 1.1 and Section 6.2), with the proof deferred to the full paper. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The definition of help, the impossibility for exact order types such as the queue (Theorem 4.3, after a repair of Claim 4.5.10) and for snapshots (Theorem 4.7), Claim 4.8.1 and the help-free wait-free set and max register all stand. But the stack is not an exact order type, Theorem 4.8 is proved only when a view tells which competing operations precede it, which leaves out the claimed fetch&increment and increment, and the proof of Theorem 4.11 (read/write max registers) has a gap we could not repair. Universality of fetch-and-cons was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Examples after Definition 4.5.1 (the stack is an exact order type) The stack is not an exact order type: a stack can hide the swap of op and W_{n+1}, so no operation of R(m) tells the two executions apart (stack_exists_equal, stack_not_exactOrder, stack_not_exactOrderStrong). Impact. Theorem 4.3 therefore says nothing about stacks; the conclusion "no wait-free help-free stack" remains true by the direct proof of V. Aksenov, P. Kuznetsov and A. Shalyto (On Helping and Stacks, NETYS 2018), who observed the error. The mistake concerns an example: the queue is an exact order type and Theorem 4.3 holds. Details. The claim appears after Definition 4.5.1, in Sections 4.1 and 4.5.1, and in the PODC version ("Natural examples of exact order types are FIFO queues and LIFO stacks" in Section 1.1 and "Examples of such types are a queue, a stack, and the fetch-and-cons" after Definition 4.1). Exact order types must tell apart every execution of W(n+1) ∘ (R(m) + op?) from every execution of W(n) ∘ op ∘ (R(m) + W_{n+1}?) by the results of R(m). Since W_{n+1} may be moved into R(m), a stack can hide the swap. For example, with op = push(a) and W_{n+1} = push(b), compare W(n)∘push(b)∘push(a)∘R(m) with W(n)∘push(a)∘R(m) where push(b) is re-inserted right after the pop that removes a: all operations of R(m) return the same values. The other three op/W_{n+1} cases are similar. This holds for every choice of op, W, R, n, m, so the stack is not exact order in the paper's literal form nor in the weaker form. ❌ Theorem 4.11 (read/write max registers): unestablished The proof (Claim 4.7.1, second case for lines 4/7) infers "R₁ cannot possibly return a value ≥ 3, hence R₁ is decided before W₃" for a pending ReadMax R₁, which is invalid (claim_4_7_1_inference_fails). Impact. We found no repair; whether Theorem 4.11 holds is open here. It is not formalized. Details. A linearization function may leave a pending read out of the linearization until it returns, so R₁ is not decided before W₃ although its result is fixed. Once R₁ returns, it is decided before W₃, but that decision is taken by R₁'s owner, which help-freedom allows, so the intended contradiction disappears. (claim_4_7_1_inference_fails) ⚠️ Theorem 4.8 for global view types as defined (fetch&increment, increment) The proof of Theorem 4.8 (Claim 4.6.8) needs a view to tell which competing operation precedes it, but Definition 4.6.18 only tells how many, so the paper's claimed instances fetch&increment and increment are not covered (fetchInc_not_strongGlobalView). But Claim 4.6.8 infers from "op₁ is decided before op₃ in h∘p₁∘p₃ but not in h∘p₃∘p₁" that a solo run of p₃ returns different results in the two histories. When p_k's step at line 25 would decide op_k before the next view, the next steps of p₁, p₂ are competing successful cas, and lines 17–20 are applied instead. (Ctx.cas_move) ✏️ Slips Claim 4.8.1 needs that the linearization grows only by appending, that the implementation is obstruction-free and that processes can invoke operations (all true in the paper's uses). A Thin Self-Stabilizing Asynchronous Unison Algorithm — PODC 2021 Yuval Emek, Eyal Keren. A Thin Self-Stabilizing Asynchronous Unison Algorithm with Applications to Fault Tolerant Biological Networks. PODC 2021, pp. 93–102. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467922. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv:2102.12787v2 (18 May 2021). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Theorem 1.1 is correct and fully proved, with explicit constants: AlgAU with k = 3D + 2 (12D + 6 states) is a self-stabilizing asynchronous unison on graphs of diameter ≤ D, and it stabilizes within 70(D+1)³ rounds. Corollary 1.2 (the synchronizer) is false for arbitrary tasks, as stated; it holds for static tasks such as LE and MIS, which are the paper's applications, and we prove that for deterministic Π. The randomized LE and MIS results (Theorems 1.3, 1.4) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Corollary 1.2 (the synchronizer Π*, arbitrary tasks) Corollary 1.2 is false for tasks constrained at every time instant: with D = 1, the task "all nodes output the same bit at all times, and the outputs change infinitely often" is solvable synchronously but by no asynchronous stone-age algorithm, Π* included (toggle_sync, no_async_alg_roundRobin). Impact. Theorem 1.1 is unaffected. The construction is correct for static tasks (eventually fixed legal outputs), which covers the paper's applications LE and MIS; we prove that version, for deterministic Π, with the bound f + N(D) + D rounds (corollary_1_2). Details. The synchronizer Π* does not make the nodes simulate one global synchronous execution. Each node shows the synchronous execution at its own simulated round, and neighbouring rounds may differ by 1. Tasks constrained at every time instant therefore cannot be transferred. Synchronously the task is solved on every complete graph within one round by δ(b, S) = ¬(true ∈ S). On K₂ under the fair round-robin schedule, no deterministic stone-age algorithm (Π* included) solves it. A node that is not activated keeps its output, so the first output change after agreement breaks agreement. 🔧 Lemma 2.19 (the constant k(k−1)) The proof of the bound k(k−1) charges one application of Lemma 2.13 per level, which does not cover all moves, so the constant is unestablished (lemma_2_19 proves 4(k−1)²). Impact. Still O(k²); the final O(D³) of Theorem 1.1 is unaffected. We did not decide whether k(k−1) itself holds. Details. The argument ignores three things: both endpoints of an edge may move; a node may have several non-protected edges that resolve one after another; edges {k, −k} may become non-protected in the meantime. Repair. We prove 4(k−1)² in two phases. The node first moves inwards until it is protected or at ±1; then every neighbour reaches ∓1 or becomes protected. (lemma_2_19) 🔧 Lemma 2.13 for |ℓ| = 1 The proof needs the endpoint at level ℓ to make an AF move, but levels ±1 have no faulty turn, so for |ℓ| = 1 the lemma is unestablished (lemma_2_13_edge is proved for |ℓ| ≥ 2). Impact. The lemma is used only with |ℓ| ≥ 2, so we prove it under that hypothesis. Whether the |ℓ| = 1 case is false is open. Details. A non-protected node at level ±1 is stuck. ✏️ Slips Lemma 2.13's time bound has t' for t. Obs 2.9 requires |λ_v^s| < k − d also for s = t', and with that the application in Lemma 2.20 at d = D fails, because v is at level exactly k − D at t'. Obs 2.9 needs the bound only for s < t', and the paper's proof only uses s < t'. (AURun.obs29, lemma_2_20) Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 2.22 (the potential argument) The potential argument re-chooses x_t at every time, so "the distance decreases or v becomes grounded" does not follow literally. Impact. Repaired (lemma_2_22_aux, lemma_2_22). Details. When the node to which Lemma 2.19 was applied becomes protected, x_t may already be a different node at the same distance. Repair. Fix the walk at the start of each phase and recurse on its length. 🔧 Obs 2.8 (window of D + 1 levels) The proof omits a short extremal-point step: pairwise distances ≤ D imply a window of D + 1 levels only because 2k > 3D. Impact. Statement true; replaced in Lean by an integer lifting along walks (AURun.exists_offsets). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finite simple graph with G.ediam ≤ D (Mathlib), which implies connectivity. Stone-age model: anonymous deterministic finite-state nodes that sense the set of states in their closed neighbourhood. The paper's model allows randomized transitions, but AlgAU is deterministic. Schedule: an adversarial asynchronous daemon A : ℕ → Set V, which may also activate the empty set. It is fair, i.e. every node is activated infinitely often. Rounds are measured by the paper's operator ϱ. Faults: arbitrary initial configuration, no other faults. AU specification: clocks in ZMod (2k); neighbours differ by at most 1; clocks change only by +1; at least i ticks in [t, ϱ^{d+i}(t)). The AlgAU transition rules (Table 1) are formalized as written. An explicit-state model checker (tools/algau.py, on K₂, K₃, P₃, C₄) was used to sanity-check this reading. Main results in Lean (namespace ThinUnison). Consensus with an Abstract MAC Layer — PODC 2014 Calvin Newport. Consensus with an abstract MAC layer. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611479. Formalized version: arXiv 1405.1382 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All lower bounds hold: Theorems 3.2 (with n ≥ 2), 3.3, 3.9 and 3.10 are proved, and Theorem 4.1 holds for the two-phase algorithm described in the prose, with the 2 F_ack time bound, although line 23 of Algorithm 1 has a one-symbol slip. Claim 3.4 fails for D = 4, a non-degenerate case that Theorem 3.3 covers, so the networks of Figure 1 do not prove Theorem 3.3 there; we prove the theorem for every even D ≥ 4 with a different gadget, found by computer search. The multihop algorithm wPAXOS was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Claim 3.4 for D = 4 (the networks of Figure 1) For D = 4 (d = (D−2)/2 = 1) the paper's Network A has diameter 6, not 4, because node a₂⁺ of the gadget is at distance 2 from c (claim_3_4_false_D4). Impact. D = 4 is the smallest case of Theorem 3.3, not a degenerate one, so Figure 1 does not prove Theorem 3.3 there. The theorem is still true: we prove it for all even D ≥ 4 with another gadget (theorem_3_3, exists_nets). Details. In Lean the counterexample is the 15-node network for k = 0, i.e. 4 ≤ n ≤ 15. The padding nodes a*_j are attached to a_{d−1} = a₀, which does not exist. Repair. Our gadget, found by computer search: a core c, t, s, r, u, p, padding twins of p, and a path of length d − 1 below t. B is a 3-fold voltage cover of it. (theorem_3_3, exists_nets) 🔧 Lemma 3.8 (lines of every length d) Lemma 3.8 claims one t for lines of every length d, but its hypothesis only concerns networks of diameter D, so only d = D follows. Impact. Only d = D is used, and we prove that case (lemma_3_8). Nothing is known for d ≠ D. ✏️ Slips Algorithm 1, line 23: read literally, the algorithm violates agreement on two nodes, because the line looks for ⟨phase 2, *, decided(0)⟩ in R₂ only, while a phase-2 message received during the receiver's phase 1 goes into R₁ (twoPhaseLit_not_solvesConsensus; counterexample below, under Proof remarks). With the check over R₁ ∪ R₂, Theorem 4.1 holds, including the bound "decide by 2 F_ack" (theorem_4_1, theorem_4_1_time). Theorem 3.2 needs n ≥ 2: with one node, deciding one's own input solves consensus with any number of crashes (theorem_3_2_card_one); theorem_3_2 assumes 2 ≤ n. Lemma 3.8: "all nodes begin with initial value 0" should be b. Lemma 3.6: the synchronous scheduler does not fix the order in which a node receives the messages of one round, and corresponding nodes must use the same order; we sort messages by a fixed order. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.1 (valency and crashes) The proof's valency notion is ill-posed and Case 1 applies the valency of β₁ to an execution in which w crashes, which is not an extension by valid steps. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_3_1, exists_decision_off, stepV_comm). Details. Valency is defined over extensions by valid steps. Then a fragment with no deciding extension is vacuously both 0- and 1-valent, and it is unclear whether extensions may contain crashes. Case 1 applies the valency of β₁ to an execution in which w crashes. Such an execution is not an extension by valid steps of the paper's kind. Repair. valency counts crash-free valid extensions; every reachable configuration has a possible decision; the decision obtained by crashing w is transferred to the crash-free extension in which w is merely silent; both runs perform the same events and agree off w; both cases of the proof become one: the two orders of the steps agree except at one node. (lemma_3_1, exists_decision_off, stepV_comm) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/AbstractMAC/, staged for CSLib as Cslib.AbstractMAC). A graph G and deterministic algorithms: an initial state from an identity (Unit = anonymous, ℕ = unique ids) and a binary input, transitions on receive and on ack, an optional broadcast, an irrevocable decision. Events recv u v, ack u, crash u; disabled events are no-ops. An ack is enabled only after every neighbour received the current message. Executions are sequences of blocks of events. Crashes. A crashed node stops and its message is no longer delivered. Deliveries to a crashed node are bookkeeping events and acks wait for them: a sub-model of the paper's, so impossibility results transfer. SolvesConsensus A G id f: agreement, validity and termination in every timely execution (bound F_ack on ack delay, for any F_ack) with diverging time and at most f crashes. Every fair execution is timely (Fair.exists_timely). Synchronous rounds, possibly holding some nodes' broadcasts for some rounds (the paper's semi-synchronous scheduler), with a simulation lemma for covering/embedding maps (syncLoc_comp) and a locality lemma (syncLoc_congr_of_walk). Theorem 3.2: clique, tolerance f = 1. All other results: no crashes (f = 0). Knowledge of n or D is modelled by quantifying only over networks with that size or diameter. Main results in Lean. Low-Congestion Shortcuts without Embedding — PODC 2016 Bernhard Haeupler, Taisuke Izumi, Goran Zuzic. Low-Congestion Shortcuts without Embedding. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933112. Formalized version: the journal (Distributed Computing) version, arXiv:1607.07553v3; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The deterministic core of the paper is proved: Lemma 1 (for distances between vertices of the part, or after discarding the irrelevant edges that make it false as literally stated), Lemma 2 (pipelined convergecast/broadcast on subtrees in D − 1 + c rounds), Theorem 2 (leader election and part-wise aggregation in O(b) supersteps of O(D + c) rounds), Lemma 3/Corollary 6, Lemma 5 (CoreSlow), the combinatorial part of Lemma 4 (CoreFast), and the deterministic version of Theorem 1. The proofs of Lemma 3 and of the broadcast half of Lemma 2 needed local repairs. The randomized construction and the end-to-end CONGEST round bounds, which carry the paper's main speed claim, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 1 is false as literally stated because Definitions 4 and 5 allow shortcut edges in components that miss the part: on the path 0 – 1 – 2 rooted at 0, the part P = {2} with H = {01} has block parameter 1, but E_G[P] ∪ H is disconnected, so the dilation is infinite (lemma_1_literal_false). The bound holds for distances between nodes of the part, which is what the proof shows and all Theorem 2 needs, and in full once the useless components are dropped (lemma_1, lemma_1_dilation). Details under Proof remarks. In the proof of Lemma 4, "Pr[X₁+…+X_t ≤ 2E[S]] ≤ exp(−δE[S])" should read ≥, as the next sentence uses. Typos In CoreFast, an edge is unusable if |L̃_v| ≥ 4c·p (Algorithm 2, "at least 4c·p" in the outline), while the detailed description assigns the edge if |L_v| ≤ 4c·p and otherwise tests > 4·p. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3 (verification) The proof has each leader r build a BFS tree of "all the nodes that believe r is the leader", but these nodes need not be connected to r within that set, so some node belongs to no BFS tree. Impact. Statement true; repaired with 4b₀ + 1 supersteps (verification_correct, corollary_6). Details. The proof floods the minimum ID for b₀ supersteps; then neighbouring nodes of different trees report failure. Example (not formalized): supergraph r – u – w plus a path s – x – u, b₀ = 2, IDs s < r < u, w, x. w believes in r (s is at distance 3 from w), but its only neighbour u believes in s. So w belongs to no BFS tree and cannot learn the outcome from one. Repair. BFS only along edges whose endpoints share a leader, let unreached nodes reject, and add "unreached neighbour" to the failure flags. We prove that a node then accepts iff the supergraph has at most b₀ nodes, using 4b₀ + 1 supersteps. (verification_correct, corollary_6) 🔧 Lemma 2 (broadcast half claimed by "symmetry") The induction on height(v) + p for the convergecast does not transfer to the broadcast, because the rank of a subtree is not monotone along its root-to-leaf paths. Impact. We prove the O(D + c) bound by time reversal (IsConvergecastSchedule.reverse, exists_schedules). Details. The induction uses that a higher-priority subtree containing a child edge of v also contains v's parent edge. This holds upwards (convergecast) but not downwards. Example (not formalized): c − 1 higher-priority subtrees share i's first edge, then branch off. Then i's message reaches depth 2 only at round c + 1, while the per-edge invariant would give 3. Repair. The reversed greedy convergecast schedule is a valid broadcast schedule of the same length, D − 1 + c rounds. (IsConvergecastSchedule.reverse, exists_schedules) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graph-theoretic part as in CSLib. G is a finite simple graph and T a rooted spanning tree (parent pointers, depth ≤ D). Parts are disjoint and connected. A shortcut is ι → Finset (Sym2 V), T-restricted (Definition 4). Block parameter = Definition 5 (blockParam: components of (V, H_i) containing a node of P_i). Round complexity in synchronous CONGEST is modelled at the level of message schedules: each tree edge carries one O(log n)-bit message per round, causality between messages, no message contents. Lemma 2's greedy algorithm is an explicit round-by-round process. A convergecast (broadcast) schedule is a send round for every (subtree, edge) pair with the causal order and the one-message-per-edge-per-round constraint. Local Approximability of MDS on Planar Graphs — PODC 2014 Miikka Hilke, Christoph Lenzen, Jukka Suomela. Brief Announcement: Local Approximability of Minimum Dominating Set on Planar Graphs. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611504. Formalized version: arXiv 1402.2549 v1 (3 pages, complete proof); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The main theorem holds as stated: no deterministic T-round LOCAL algorithm finds a (7 − ε)-approximation of a minimum dominating set on planar graphs, and the Ramsey argument of Lemma 1 and the construction of Figure 1 work as described. The only flaw is that the last step of the proof of Lemma 1 needs internal areas of at least 3 × 3, while the lemma says "for any m". The paper fixes m ≫ T just before, and the theorem takes m large anyway. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 1, last step: "the common output cannot be 0" needs an internal node whose whole closed neighbourhood is internal, i.e. m − 2T ≥ 3, while the lemma says "for any m". The paper has already fixed m ≫ T, and we prove Lemma 1 under 2T + 3 ≤ m (lemma_1); see Proof remarks. Typos The graph G and the set D* are given only by Figure 1. The paper says D* contains 1/7 of the internal nodes, but it must also dominate the border of the whole grid; the bound |D*| ≤ (1/7 + ε′)n is right once these O(rm) extra nodes are added. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic LOCAL model with unique identifiers, extensional form (CSLib Cslib.Local.IsLocal T). The nodes of a network are its identifiers Fin n = {0, …, n − 1}. An algorithm is A : SimpleGraph (Fin n) → Fin n → Bool, and its output at v may depend only on the edges at nodes within distance < T of v and on the identifiers within distance ≤ T. An algorithm that reads the whole induced radius-T ball is (T + 1)-local, so it is covered too, because the theorem holds for every T. There is no randomness and no failures. The algorithm may depend on n (A n in no_local_approx_planar); in main_theorem n is fixed and A is arbitrary for that n. The identifier space is exactly {0, …, n − 1}, the most restrictive choice. A lower bound for this choice implies the bound for any larger identifier space. Instances: G = grid (r·m) m is the rm × m triangulated grid: the triangular lattice (x, y) ~ (x ± 1, y), (x, y ± 1), (x + 1, y + 1), (x − 1, y − 1). It has r blocks of m × m nodes side by side, as in Figure 1a. An instance is an identifier assignment σ : GV W H ≃ Fin n, and the network is lab σ (the grid relabelled by σ). Planarity: Mathlib has no planarity, so we use straight-line planar drawings (IsStraightLinePlanar: injective points in ℝ², edges as segments meeting only at common endpoints, no vertex on a non-incident edge). By Fáry's theorem this is equivalent to planarity for finite graphs. We prove that every piece of the triangular lattice has such a drawing. The theorem is stronger than the paper's in two ways. In main_theorem, A only needs to be correct on the relabelled copies of one grid. The grid sizes W, H (and hence n) depend only on T and ε, not on A. Main results in Lean. Embedding a Deterministic BFT Protocol in a Block DAG — PODC 2021 Maria A. Schett, George Danezis. Embedding a Deterministic BFT Protocol in a Block DAG. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467930. Formalized version: arXiv 2102.09594 v2 (full version with appendix); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The paper's main theorem, that the embedding keeps all properties of any deterministic BFT protocol, fails as printed: an equivocating Byzantine server makes a correct server receive the same message twice, so the interpreted block DAG does not give an authenticated perfect link. We prove a repaired Theorem 5.1 for every property that P keeps over authenticated links that may duplicate messages of Byzantine senders; the transfer of arbitrary liveness properties was not checked. Everything else we checked holds: the block DAG lemmas of Sections 2–3, gossip safety and liveness, the order-independence of the interpretation (Lemma 4.2), reliable delivery and authenticity. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Lemma 4.3 (2) and Theorem 5.1 (no duplication and property transfer) Lemma 4.3 (2) is false: with n = 4, f = 1, a Byzantine server that equivocates with two genesis blocks makes the correct server 1 receive the same message (3 → 1, ECHO) twice (Counterexample.lemma_4_3_2_false), so Theorem 5.1 fails for a deterministic protocol that relies on the promised no duplication (Counterexample.theorem_5_1_false). Impact. The interpreted block DAG does not give an authenticated perfect link, and Theorem 5.1 does not hold as stated. What holds is a repaired Theorem 5.1 for every property that P keeps over authenticated links that may duplicate messages of Byzantine senders (theorem_5_1_repaired). No duplication does hold for correct senders when messages are unique (lemma_4_3_2_correct, trace_noDupCorrect). The paper's demonstration protocol (Algorithm 4, Bracha's broadcast) counts senders, so it is not affected. Details. The proof of Lemma 4.3 (2) says a correct s₂ can receive the same message m twice only by referencing the same block twice, which Lemma A.6 forbids. But two different blocks can trigger the same m. Take n = 4, f = 1, with server 3 Byzantine. Server 3 builds two genesis blocks Bb₁ and Bb₂ that differ only in their payload. Both are valid, and this is exactly the equivocation of Example 3.5 / Fig. 3. Each triggers the protocol message ECHO from 3 to 1. The correct server 1 follows Algorithm 1: it references Bb₁ in its first block D₁ and, after receiving Bb₂, references Bb₂ in its second block D₂. In the interpretation, 1 receives the message (3 → 1, ECHO) at D₁ and again at D₂. The 12-event run is a checked run of Algorithms 1 and 3. Theorem 5.1 transfers properties that P has "using the reliable point-to-point link abstraction", and Lemma 4.3 says this abstraction is Cachin et al.'s authenticated perfect link, no duplication included. A protocol written for that abstraction may rely on no duplication. Our example is the deterministic protocol "echo once when requested; deliver after 2f+1 = 3 received messages". Its messages are unique and carry their sender. Over authenticated perfect links it satisfies "if a correct server delivers, then two different correct servers were requested". In the run above, only server 0 is requested. Yet shim(P) at server 1 delivers, since it counts 0's echo once and 3's echo twice. The variant that echoes on every request, as the paper's convention "messages triggered by requests do not depend on the state" requires, fails the same way (Counterexample.theorem_5_1_false_stateless). Section 4 says in passing that a BFT protocol "can deal with duplicate messages". If "BFT protocol" is read as assuming that, the theorem survives in the form we prove (theorem_5_1_repaired). But Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 5.1 explicitly promise a link with no duplication. Repair. Restrict Theorem 5.1 to properties that survive Byzantine duplicates (theorem_5_1_repaired). Dedup per receiver chain in Algorithm 2 is an alternative, which we did not prove. ✏️ Slips Definition 3.3 (iii) is under-specified: "s considers all B' ∈ B.preds valid" must mean "has already inserted them"; under the recursive reading ("would consider valid") line 6 of Algorithm 1 may insert a block before its predecessor, and Lemma A.5 (G is a block DAG) fails. We use the reading under which Lemma A.5 holds (lemma_A_5). Line 6 of Algorithm 2 assigns B.Ms[out, ℓⱼ] ≔ B.PIs[ℓⱼ].rⱼ inside the loop over B.rs: with two requests for one label, the messages of the first request are lost. We accumulate them. In Lemma A.7, "any G ⩾ G_s ∪ G_{s'}" should be the union itself (or a block DAG containing it). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Blocks are content-addressed: Block is a nested inductive type whose blocks contain their predecessors. This idealizes collision and preimage resistance of ref, and makes Lemma 3.2 and acyclicity structural. Signatures are idealized in the execution model: a Byzantine server may send any block in which every block built by a correct server was really created by it (Authentic). System (Gossip.lean). Asynchronous message passing, with servers S, an arbitrary set Byz of Byzantine servers and no bound on |Byz|. The network is a set of sent messages that may be received any number of times, in any order. Correct servers run Algorithm 1 handler by handler, each handler atomic, plus the request buffer of Algorithm 3. disseminate seals all buffered requests. valid(s, B) means "locally valid, and all predecessors already in G_s". Liveness (GossipLive.lean). Fair runs: a message between correct servers is received at least once (Assumption 1, slightly weaker than the paper's version). Lines 6–9 and 10–11 are weakly fair, with the timeout Δ abstracted away, and every correct server disseminates infinitely often (Algorithm 3, lines 10–11). Protocol P (Interpret.lean). A deterministic black box, given by init ℓ s and step : state → (request | message) → state × messages × indications. Messages have a sender and a receiver. For sender-related lemmas we assume P.Owned (messages carry their process's identity). For no duplication with correct senders we assume SendUnique (Cachin's convention that messages are unique). Link abstraction (Link.lean). Finite executions over authenticated links, for one instance ℓ: events at correct servers, authenticity (LinkSafe) and no duplication (NoDup). A property is a predicate on the interface trace (requests and indications with their server). Interpretation (Interpret.lean). Algorithm 2 is given both as a canonical function interp P ℓ B and as the nondeterministic traversal (TStep), which computes exactly interp. Main results in Lean. Recoverable Mutex with Sub-logarithmic RMR on CC and DSM — PODC 2019 Prasad Jayanti, Siddhartha Jayanti, Anup Joshi. A Recoverable Mutex Algorithm with Sub-logarithmic RMR on Both CC and DSM. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331634. Formalized version: arXiv 1904.02124 v2 (full version, proofs in Appendices C–E); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Lemma 9, the 39-condition invariant on which all the correctness proofs rest, is false as stated: several of its conditions fail in crash-free runs with two processes. We replace it with our own invariant and a new liveness argument, and prove that the k-ported algorithm of Figures 3–4 is correct: mutual exclusion, starvation freedom (finitely many crashes), wait-free exit, wait-free critical-section re-entry and critical-section re-entry (Lemmas 4–8), and Theorem 1 on the Signal object. The paper's main point, the sub-logarithmic RMR bounds of Theorems 2 and 3, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Lemma 9, Condition 5 (and hence the proofs of Lemmas 4 and 5) Lemma 9 claims that all 39 conditions hold in every configuration, but Condition 5 fails as soon as one process has executed line 14 in a crash-free run (PaperInv.cond5_csSignal_false, PaperInv.cond5_nonNil_false). Impact. The proofs of Lemmas 4 and 5 (mutual exclusion and starvation freedom) cite conditions of this invariant, so they are not established by the paper: the proof of Lemma 4 is one line from Condition 19, and the proof of Lemma 5 uses Conditions 15 and 19. The algorithm itself is correct: we prove Lemmas 4–8 from a new invariant (inv_reach). Details. Condition 5 says qnode.CS_Signal = 0 ⇒ qnode.Pred ∈ {NIL, &Crash, &InCS}. Every waiting node (lines 15 and 25) has CS_Signal = 0 and Pred pointing to its predecessor. So does an exiting node at line 28, with Pred = &Exit. Condition 5 also says qnode.NonNil_Signal = 0 ⇒ qnode.Pred = NIL. Between lines 14 and 15 (and between lines 18 and 23 after a crash) Pred is already set while NonNil_Signal is still 0. The fixes are not evident from the paper: one would have to add node values and &Exit to the right-hand side, which makes the conjunct nearly empty. Reversing the implications gives true statements, but they merely restate Condition 5's = 1 conjuncts. The proof of Lemma 9 (Appendix E) claims that the conjunction of all conditions is preserved by every step, but never re-checks Condition 5 at line 14. Repair. Our invariant (Inv, InvDefs.lean) is preserved by every step and crash (inv_reach); Lemmas 4–8 follow from it. Lemma 4 (mutual_exclusion). The new invariant's core: every node has at most one successor, nobody is behind Tail, and at most one node "holds the right to the CS" (InH). A node holds it if it is in the CS, is behind a released node, or is exiting with a successor. The hard part is the repair code (lines 30–49). We characterise what the non-atomic scan of Node[] still says when the decision at line 46 is taken. It uses a ghost set of nodes that had already done their FAS when Tail was read (line 31): every later node hangs behind that Tail value. Then the FAS branch never creates a cycle. In the attach branch, the chosen predecessor has no successor and is not Tail. If headpath = NIL, nobody holds the right to the CS (ScanInv.fas_facts, ScanInv.attach_facts, ScanInv.none_noH). Lemma 5 (starvation_freedom), true under finitely many crashes and the paper's fairness conditions. After the last crash, every recovering process gets through RLock. The repair terminates: the waits at line 35 end, and the loop over maximal paths is finite. Eventually nobody is in the recovery code or in RLock (eventually_no_rec). From then on, the unique holder of the right to the CS is an ancestor of every waiting node. A rank (10 × number of unreleased ancestors + stage of the holder) never increases and drops at every step of the holder (token_step, phase2_cs). 🛠️ Lemma 9, Condition 4 (third conjunct) Condition 4 asks that Pred be iterated at most k times from a node to reach {NIL, &Crash, &InCS, &Exit}, which fails once two processes are queued (PaperInv.cond4_false). Impact. The paper uses this bound to exclude cycles in the proof of Condition 23. The correctness lemmas it served are proved from our invariant (inv_reach). Details. With k = 2 and both processes queued behind SpecialNode, the second node needs 3 hops (node → first node → SpecialNode → &Exit). The proof's Condition 4 case counts b1 + b2 ≤ k and forgets the fragment's head (SpecialNode or an exited node). Repair. The bound should be k + 1. We did not prove the invariant with this bound; the proved repair is our invariant (Inv, inv_reach). ✏️ Slips Condition 18 quantifies over the real program counter PC_π' where \hat{PC}_π' is meant (as in Condition 19(g)). Read literally it fails in the initial configuration, where every PC_π = 10. Theorem 2 claims O(1) RMRs "for a process that does not crash during its passage". A passage that starts after a crash runs RLock and the repair scan of all k entries of Node[], even if no crash happens during it. The intended statement is about crash-free super-passages, and O(fk) should read O(1 + fk). Not formalized. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory with NVRAM and individual crash–recovery failures. A crash resets the program counter to line 10 and erases all local variables. Shared memory is unaffected. Deterministic algorithm; executions are arbitrary interleavings of steps and crashes (an adversarial scheduler). One process per port (Fin k). Round-Efficient BA via Proxcensus — PODC 2021 Matthias Fitzi, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Julian Loss. A New Way to Achieve Round-Efficient Byzantine Agreement. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467907. Formalized version: the 8-page proceedings version (no arXiv version; the IACR ePrint full version 2021/814 was not accessible to us); numbering follows the proceedings. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Of the paper's two equal results, the (κ+1)-round BA for t < n/3 is wrong as printed for every n ≥ 3t + 2 with t ≥ 1, but is saved by one constant: with the threshold t + 1 instead of n - 2t (the same thing when n = 3t + 1) everything is proved, including error ≤ 2^{-κ}. The 3κ/2-round BA for t < n/2 runs the coin in parallel to the last Proxcensus round, and this fails against the paper's adaptive strongly rushing adversary: one iteration errs with probability at least 1/2, not 1/4. Tossing the coin after round 3 costs 2κ rounds, no gain over prior work, so the improvement claimed for t < n/2 is lost; the Proxcensus protocol itself (Lemmas 3.4–3.6) and Theorem 3.7 are correct. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Cor. 3.8 for t < n/2 (coin tossed in parallel to round 3) The claim "the slot pair is fixed after round 2" is false against the paper's adaptive strongly rushing adversary, which corrupts a party in round 3 depending on the coin, so one iteration errs with probability ≥ 1/2, not 1/4 (coin_parallel_adaptive_attack). Impact. For κ = 2 this contradicts Cor. 3.8's 2^{-κ}, so the 3κ/2-round claim does not stand against the adversary the paper names. The Proxcensus protocol (Lemmas 3.4–3.6) and Theorem 3.7 are correct, and the claimed 1/4 holds against coin-independent corruptions, for one iteration (coin_parallel_static). Details. To get 3 rounds per iteration, the coin is tossed in parallel to round 3 of Prox_5. The coin is revealed during that round (§2.2), so a strongly rushing adaptive adversary can corrupt a party in round 3 depending on the coin, and drop its round-3 forwarding. Example: n = 5, t = 2, inputs 1,1,0,0, party 4 Byzantine. Party 4 makes everybody hold Σ on 1, and lets only party 0 form Ω on 1. Coin 4: nothing more happens. Party 0 outputs (1,2) and the others (1,1), split by coin 4. Coin 3: the adversary corrupts party 0 in round 3 and forwards Ω only to party 1. Party 1 outputs (1,1) and parties 2, 3 output (⊥,0), split by coin 3. Repair. We prove the claim for coin-independent corruption (e.g. a static adversary), even when the adversary picks its round-3 messages after seeing the coin (coin_parallel_static). Tossing the coin after round 3 also works, but costs 4 rounds per iteration, i.e. 2κ rounds and no gain over prior work. 🔧 Lemma 3.2, Cor. 3.3 and Cor. 3.8 for t < n/3 (Proxcensus expansion, n ≥ 3t + 2) For every n ≥ 3t + 2 with t ≥ 1 the expansion's threshold n - 2t lets one Byzantine echo move a receiver by several grades; with n = 5, t = 1 the (κ+1)-round BA errs with probability 3/8 for κ = 3 (lemma32_counterexample, paper_cor33_counterexample, paper_cor38_counterexample). Impact. The printed protocol is wrong outside n = 3t + 1, but with threshold t + 1 (the same as n - 2t when n = 3t + 1) Lemmas 3.1–3.2, Cor. 3.3 and Cor. 3.8 (t < n/3) hold for all n > 3t (expand_isProx, proxProtocol_spec, ba_third). Details. A party outputs the slot "between" or "on" two adjacent old slots. The choice depends on which slot has ≥ n - 2t echoes. If n ≥ 3t + 2, the ≥ n - t honest echoes may split so that neither slot reaches n - 2t without Byzantine help. Then one Byzantine echo moves a receiver by several grades. Example: n = 5, t = 1, honest Prox_5 outputs (0,1),(0,1),(0,2),(0,2). A receiver getting the extra echo (0,2) outputs grade 3. A receiver getting nothing from the Byzantine party outputs grade 0. The protocol then breaks down from honest inputs 0,0,0,1. After 3 rounds the honest Prox_9 outputs are (0,2),(0,2),(0,3),(0,0), and the BA of Cor. 3.8 (κ = 3) fails for 3 of the 8 coin values (error 3/8, not 1/8). Using the largest admissible t does not help: n = 5, t = 1 already is that case. Repair. With threshold t + 1 we prove Lemmas 3.1–3.2, Cor. 3.3 and Cor. 3.8 (t < n/3) for all n > 3t, including error ≤ 2^{-κ}. For n = 3t + 1 that is the paper's protocol verbatim. (expand_isProx, proxProtocol_spec, ba_third) Typos The pseudocode of Prox_{2r-1} (§3.3.2) writes s for the number of rounds r. In the proof of Theorem 3.7, 2G + 1 - j should be 2G + 1 - r, and this r = s mod 2 clashes with r = rounds. In the first bullet of the proof of Lemma 3.2, "any honest P_j has g_j = g_i" needs maximality of g_i plus some slot having n - 2t honest echoes, which the proof does not say. Harmless for n = 3t + 1. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.2 for n = 3t + 1 (case b = 0, gᵢ = gⱼ = 1) The proof claims n - 2t honest parties in S_{yᵢ,0}, where only n - 3t are guaranteed. Impact. Statement true; our proof is organized differently (expand_isProx). Details. The proof then adds counts from two receivers' views, which differ in their Byzantine echoes. The correct argument compares honest counts. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Proxcensus (Def. 2.2) is a property IsProx s x H out of the honest outputs: grades in [0, ⌊(s-1)/2⌋], validity, consistency for every ordered pair. Theorem 3.7. The binary slots and the extraction function f are the paper's. The coin is ideal and uniform on [1, s-1] (PMF.uniformOfFintype). It is independent of the Proxcensus outputs, and the adversary may corrupt more parties after seeing it. t < n/3. CSLib's synchronous lock-step model on the complete network: deterministic protocol, static Byzantine adversary sending arbitrary messages per round, sender and receiver (this covers rushing). Adaptive corruption reduces to static corruption of the finally corrupted parties, since the phase is deterministic. Values come from any finite linearly ordered domain. t < n/2. Our own model with ideal unique (n-t)-out-of-n threshold signatures: Certificates are represented by certified values. The adversary can send exactly the certificates it can form, from shares of parties honest in that round plus the keys of the corrupted parties. Corruption is adaptive, at round granularity: a party corrupted in round k has its round-k messages replaced.
