Rational Consensus — PODC 2016 Joseph Y. Halpern, Xavier Vilaça. Rational Consensus. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933088. Formalized version: arXiv 2005.10141 v1 (full version with proofs and Algorithm 1); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 1 (no fair consensus protocol is an f-Nash equilibrium, f ≥ 1) is correct for n ≥ 2 and fully verified. Theorem 2 (σ_cons solves fair consensus whenever f + 1 < n) is verified for Algorithm 1 as written, but its agreement proof is wrong (the first crash-free round need not seem clean) and took a new counting argument. Theorems 3 and 4 (π-Nash and sequential equilibrium), the positive half of the paper's main point, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips The forwarding step of round f + 1 (Algorithm 1, line 20) is under-specified: line 20 includes the agent's own share, while the prose forwards the shares received. Under the prose reading Theorem 2 is false for n = f + 2 and for f = 0, because a nonfaulty agent holds only one point of a degree-1 polynomial and decides ⊥ (Cons.theorem_2_receivedOnly_false). Line 20 as written (own share included) satisfies Theorem 2 for every f + 1 < n (Cons.theorem_2), and the intended protocol is correct. Line 20 of Algorithm 1 has agent i send j the tuple (y_li)_{l ≠ j}. The index set includes l = i, so i also sends its own share y_ii = q_i(i). Elsewhere the pseudocode writes l ≠ j, i when it wants to exclude i (lines 6, 28). But line 14 defines y_ij only for j ≠ i, and the prose says i forwards "the secret shares y_li it received in round 1 from each agent l", which excludes the own share (though the next sentence, "this enables j to compute the polynomials q_i^t", again needs it). The proof needs the own share: "since there are at least n − f ≥ 2 nonfaulty agents, i and j will be able to interpolate q_l" counts l itself as a forwarder when l is nonfaulty. So does the hypothesis f + 1 < n. Under the received-only reading, take n = f + 2, let agents 0 and 1 be nonfaulty, and let the other f agents crash at the start of round 1 without sending anything. Agent 0 then holds a single point of agent 1's degree-1 polynomial, cannot interpolate x_1[t] and decides ⊥. The same holds for f = 0 and any n ≥ 2: round f + 1 = 1 comes before any share is received. (Cons.sigmaCons_receivedOnly_not_fair_3_1) We formalize line 20 as written, with y_ii = q_i(i), and prove Theorem 2 for every f + 1 < n (Cons.theorem_2). Under the received-only reading Theorem 2 holds only for f ≥ 1, n ≥ f + 3 (Cons.theorem_2_receivedOnly). Theorem 1 needs n ≥ 2: with a single agent, "decide your own preference" is fair consensus and an f-Nash equilibrium for every f (theorem_1_false_of_card_eq_one). Theorem 1 holds for every n ≥ 2 (theorem_1). The secret sharing is under-specified: no field is given, and shares are evaluated at agent identifiers 0, …, n−1, so agent 0 receives q_i^t(0) = x_i[t], the secret itself. We use 𝔽_p with a prime p > n and evaluation points j + 1. The pseudocode's status-report update (lines 29–30) compares against the record from the start of the round, so the result depends on the order in which messages are processed: a later, larger report can overwrite a smaller one. We take the minimum, which is what the proof assumes. Check 8 says "more than f crashes", then "(i.e., f or more agents …)". Typos In Theorem 1's proof, the step "there is a failure pattern F² where i fails after the decision" silently uses countable additivity: decisions happen at unbounded times, but with positive probability by a fixed time T. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 2 (the first crash-free round need not "seem clean") The proof claims that the first round m* in which no agent crashes seems clean to every nonfaulty agent (NC_{m*} = NC_{m*−1}), which is false for n = 4, f = 2 (not_clean_example). Impact. Statement true; agreement is repaired by a different counting argument (crash_chain_of_disagree, ghost_agree). Details. Agent 1 crashes in round 1 sending nothing, and agent 0 crashes in round 1 sending only to agents 2 and 3. Round 2 is crash-free, but agent 0's crash is detected only in round 2, so NC_2 ≠ NC_1. The first seemingly clean round can therefore come after m*, where the paper's agreement argument does not apply. Repair. Suppose two nonfaulty agents disagree about agent l at threshold m. Then l crashed in round m, and there is a chain of agents crashing in rounds m+1, …, f+1 that carried the information to one of them only. Add the m − 1 agents that make rounds 1, …, m−1 look unclean, and there are f + 1 crashes. (crash_chain_of_disagree, ghost_agree) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous rounds, complete network, reliable channels, crash failures. This is CSLib's SyncCrash/LockStep model. A context is the preferences plus a failure pattern: crash round, and the agents reached in the crashing round. At most f agents crash. Strategies: a profile is a history-based protocol whose input is (preference, private seed). The seed vector ω : P → Ω is drawn from an arbitrary probability measure μ; Theorem 1 holds for every Ω and μ. This covers behavioural strategies: the paper's per-information-set randomization is drawn from the seed. A deviation deviate σ τ i replaces only agent i's protocol and uses i's own seed. Decisions are Option Bool (none = ⊥). An agent's decision is its first one, so Integrity holds by construction. Outcome: consensus on b iff every nonfaulty agent decides b. Utilities ("care only about consensus"): β₀ i > β₁ i > β₂ i. Expected utility is taken over the seeds, for each fixed context (ex post). An ε–f-Nash equilibrium requires a measurable outcome, and only deviations with a measurable outcome are compared. This only makes "not an equilibrium" harder to prove. Fair consensus: agreement, termination and validity hold almost surely in every context with ≤ f crashes. Fairness: P(consensus on b) ≥ #{nonfaulty agents preferring b} / n. σ_cons (Theorem 2), with seeds drawn uniformly: per t ≤ f, a secret x[t] ∈ {0..n−t−1} and the slope of a line over 𝔽_p. It sends status reports (earliest known crash round of every agent), round-1 values and shares, and forwards shares in round f+1 (flag selfShare: true = line 20 as written, own share included; false = the received-only reading). The decision is the paper's: first seemingly clean round, NC, t, S = Σ x_l[t] mod (n−t), then the (S+1)-st highest identifier. We do not model the random "signatures" z, reporter identities, and consistency checks 1–3, 5–7: they never fire when nobody deviates, and Theorem 2 is only about such runs. Main results in Lean. They need conditional expectations over information sets, the full consistency-check machinery of σ_cons, and a case analysis over all deviations. Randomized Proof-Labeling Schemes — PODC 2015 Mor Baruch, Pierre Fraigniaud, Boaz Patt-Shamir. Randomized Proof-Labeling Schemes. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767421. Formalized version: the 10-page author copy (no arXiv version; the proof of Theorem 3.6 is omitted there). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main message holds: Theorem 3.1 (a PLS with κ-bit labels becomes a one-sided RPLS with 2 log₂ κ + 6-bit certificates) and Corollary 3.5 (O(log n + log k) certificates for every predicate). Proposition 4.3 and Theorems 4.4 and 4.7, stated for any G with P(G) ≠ P(σ(G)), are false when G is illegal and all its crossings are legal, but they hold for a legal G (as do Propositions 4.6 and 4.8), which is all that the acyclicity bounds of Theorem 5.1 and the other applications use. The MST parts of Theorem 5.1 and the upper bounds of Theorems 5.2 and 5.3 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Proposition 4.3, Theorems 4.4 and 4.7 (the crossing tool for an illegal G) The crossing lower bounds are stated for any G with P(G) ≠ P(σ(G)), but they are false when G is illegal and all its crossings are legal: on a windmill graph a PLS with 3 + log₂ log₂ r bits exists, while Theorem 4.4 promises Ω(log r) bits (thm_4_4_false, thm_4_7_false, prop_4_3_false). Impact. The tools are over-general as stated; all applications in Section 5 use a legal G, and in that case we prove the tools (prop_4_3, thm_4_4, thm_4_7_correct, prop_4_8). The paper's main message (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.5) is unaffected. Details. Theorems 4.4 and 4.7 only ask that every crossing flips the predicate: P(G_s) ≠ P(σ^{ij}₁(G)_s). The proof of Proposition 4.3 covers the case "G_s is rejected" with a single labelling of G (the pigeonholed prover labels). Rejection of the crossing, though, is about every labelling, and a legal crossing comes with its own prover labels. Counterexample. Take the windmill: a hub joined to L_k and R_k (k < r), plus the edges L_k R_k. These r edges are independent port-preserving copies of one edge (s = 1). States are identities, F is G together with its crossings, and P says "some (k,·) has a neighbour (k',·) with k' ≠ k". So P(G) is false and every crossing is legal, and all configurations are connected. A PLS with 3 + log₂ log₂ r bits exists: a crossed L_k raises a flag, and the hub checks that some flag is up; each R_m publishes a bit position t and the bit m_t, and checks them; a flagged L_k checks that its port-0 neighbour's bit differs from k_t. In G, the flagged L_k faces R_k, so G is rejected under every labelling. Theorem 4.4 promises Ω(log r / s) = Ω(log r) bits (thm_4_4_false). Compiling this PLS with Theorem 3.1 gives an edge-independent two-sided RPLS with O(log log log r) bits. Theorem 4.7 promises Ω(log log r) bits (thm_4_7_false). For r = 2^32 and 8-bit labels, Proposition 4.3 fails for every pair: G is rejected and the crossing is accepted (prop_4_3_false). Repair. Add the condition P(G) = TRUE, which Propositions 4.6 and 4.8 already carry (prop_4_3, thm_4_4, thm_4_7_correct). ✏️ Slips Propositions 4.3, 4.6 and 4.8 count as if every label or certificate had exactly κ bits. With "at most κ bits" there are 2^(κ+1) − 1 strings, so our thresholds read r ≤ (2^(κ+1)−1)^(2s) (Prop. 4.3) and r ≤ 2^((2^(κ+1)−1)·2s) (Prop. 4.8). The asymptotics are the same. In the proof of Theorem 5.4 the first copy is printed as H_1 = G_e{v₀, v₁}. v₀ is adjacent to every other node, so this copy is not independent of the others (printed_H1_not_independent); {v₁, v₂} as in Theorem 5.2 is clearly meant. Theorem 5.6's graph ("n/c cycles, except one of at most c nodes") is vague when the leftover has 1–2 nodes; we take n = m·c. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Proposition 4.6 (rounding the certificate distributions) The proof rounds the joint distribution of the certificates of a copy, but Eq. (6) uses that one arc's marginal is ε-close, while equal joint roundings only give closeness ε·2^((2s−1)κ). Impact. Statement true; repaired (prop_4_6, thm_4_7_loglog). The chosen ε happens to absorb this factor (the total error is exactly 1/3), so Eqs. (6)–(8) need fixing, but the conclusion survives. Repair. We round each arc separately and get log₂ log₂ r ≤ 2κ + 5 + 2 log₂ s. 🔧 Theorem 5.1 (Theorem 4.7 applied outside its hypotheses) The crossed path is not in F; the proof uses its cycle component instead. Impact. Statement true. This is sound because verification is local. We state the tools for crossings whose union of components is an illegal member of F (Refuted). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Configurations. A configuration is port-numbered: a finite node type, neighbour lists by port, and states, which carry identities when the paper assumes them (Config, Basic.lean). Networks are connected wherever the paper needs it. The Section 5 lower bounds hold for every family that contains the connected configurations with distinct identities (hFF). Verification. One synchronous round, no failures. PLS: the verifier sees its state, its label and its neighbours' labels by port. Labels are bit strings. RPLS: every node draws private uniform coins. The coin space may depend on the node's state, label and degree, and so may the certificate it sends on each port. The decision is a function of the state, the label and the certificates received. One-sided means acceptance with probability 1 and rejection with probability ≥ 1/2; two-sided means 2/3 on both sides. Edge independence means one coin per port (EIScheme). Complexity. Verification complexity is a bound on label (resp. certificate) length on legal configurations. It may depend on the configuration, e.g. on n. Crossings. Eventually Linearizable Shared Objects — PODC 2010 Marco Serafini, Dan Dobre, Matthias Majuntke, Péter Bokor, Neeraj Suri. Eventually Linearizable Shared Objects. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835723. Formalized version: the authors' copy with the appendix (full proofs of Theorems 1–3); no arXiv version. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. Eventual Consensus is not shown to suffice for Eventual Linearizability: Algorithm 1 is not even weakly consistent over an Eventual Consensus layer, and with Eventual Stability read per run (as the rest of the layer specification) no implementation over such a layer is eventually linearizable. The nonblocking part of Theorem 1 and Lemma 5 are false as well, while locality (Theorem 1, Lemmas 1–2) and Theorem 2 hold. The tradeoff (Theorem 4) and Aurora were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 3, sufficiency (Lemma 6, Algorithm 1) Algorithm 1 over a layer satisfying Eventual Consensus can return 0 to a read of p0 after an earlier read of p0 returned 1 written by swap(1), so its history is not weakly consistent (algorithm1_not_weaklyConsistent). Impact. The proof of "Eventual Consensus is sufficient" fails at its first step, under every reading of Eventual Stability. Theorem 2 and the definition of Eventual Consensus as a target are unaffected. Details. In the counterexample (tr₁), p1 submits x = swap(1), p0 submits o' = read and gets [x, o'], so o' returns 1. Then p0 submits o = read and gets [o, x, o'], which set stability allows (it only requires the old operations to be present). Algorithm 1 executes the sequence up to o and returns 0. Weak consistency is violated: τ(p0, o') must contain x (the only swap(1)), condition (iii) puts x into τ(p0, o) before o, so o must return 1. The layer is stable from time 7 on and converges to [o, x, o']; all processes are correct. The paper's claim "weak consistency directly derives from the set stability and nontriviality properties" overlooks that set stability allows observed operations to move after the new one. Repair. None formalized. With a uniform stability time, completing o after the operations observed earlier (rather than at its position in the delivered sequence) restores weak consistency; whether the rest of Lemma 6 then goes through is not checked. ❌ Theorem 3 and Eventual Stability (the stability time, Lemmas 6–7) The definitions do not say whether the stability time of Eventual Stability may depend on the run, and no reading gives both halves of Theorem 3: read per run, no implementation over such a layer is eventually linearizable, even for a single-writer single-reader binary register (not_eventuallyLinearizable_eCons). Impact. With Eventual Stability read per run, sufficiency is false for every implementation. This uses one t_l for all runs, which the paper requires and its proof of Theorem 2 uses. Read uniformly over runs, sufficiency may hold with a repaired algorithm, but then the necessity proof (Lemma 7) yields only a per-run stability time. If both t_l and the stability time are read per run, sufficiency is not refuted; only Algorithm 1 and the proof of Lemma 6 fail. Details. Every other layer property is a property of a run, and Lemma 7 constructs a run-dependent time (t_s > max(t_l, t_d), where t_d depends on the run). With that reading the proof of Theorem 2 applies verbatim to Eventual Consensus: its layer behaviour becomes stable at the final delivery. So no implementation over such a layer has one t_l for all runs, which Eventual Linearizability requires (not_eventuallyLinearizable_eCons). The proof of Lemma 6 is also built on the false Lemma 5, and its t_l = max(t_s, t_p, t_c) depends on the run through t_p and the crash time t_c. ❌ Theorem 1, nonblocking part "Eventual Linearizability is nonblocking" is false: in a weakly consistent, 3-linearizable history with a pending swap(2), every response breaks one of the two properties (theorem1_nonblocking_false). Impact. Only locality survives from Theorem 1. Weak consistency alone and t-linearizability alone are nonblocking (Lemmas 3 and 4 hold), but not their conjunction, which is what Eventual Linearizability requires. Details. One swap register (initially 0), time = event position, t = 3: p1 invokes i1 = swap(1) (pending forever); p0 runs o' = read → 1; p0 invokes o = swap(2) (pending); p2 runs r2 = read → 2, then r3 = read → 1. This history is weakly consistent and 3-linearizable (o', o, r2, i1, r3). t-linearizability forces o to return 0: r2 (late) needs o as the last swap before it, and r3 needs i1 after r2, so no swap precedes o. Weak consistency forces 1: τ(p0, o') contains i1, hence so does τ(p0, o), and i1 is the only other swap. The proof "directly follows from Lemmas 1, 2, 3 and 4" combines the response chosen by Lemma 3 with the one chosen by Lemma 4. Reading Eventual Linearizability of one history as "for some t" would make the claim true but empty, since every finite history is t-linearizable for a late t, as the paper notes. ❌ Lemma 5 (t-stability implies t-consistency) False: two correct processes can hold [c, a] and [c, b] forever in a run satisfying Eventual Consensus, stable from time 0 (lemma5_false). Impact. Lemma 6 uses it. It holds if all processes are correct. Details. The proof applies (C3) to the operations at the first position where the two sequences differ, but (C3) covers only operations submitted by correct processes. In the counterexample a faulty process submits a and b; the common prefix [c] contains the only operation of a correct process. ✏️ Slips Definition of Eventual Linearizability and Theorem 2: the definition has no liveness requirement, so literally an implementation that never responds is eventually linearizable and Theorem 2 fails. The proofs use termination ("Let t_w be the time when the write operation completes"); with it Theorem 2 is proved (theorem2). Lemma 4's proof says "L only contains completed operations", contradicting (P1); under (P1) the pending operation is always in L, and totality is not needed. Section 3.2: "every well-formed history has a t-permutation for each t" needs total operations. Theorem 4's proof puts all messages sent after σ_{k-1} into M_k, "not received in σ_k", but messages inside Π_m before t_k must be received, or p_i could tell σ_k from σ_E1 up to t_k. Theorem 4's proof says "Runs σ_E21 and σ_E22 are indistinguishable"; it should read σ_E22 and σ_E23. Typos Lemma 3's proof writes p_j for p_i. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 2, "if" direction (t-linearizability is local) The minimal-cycle argument asserts o_k <_{H,tmax} o_i <_{H,tmax} o_j, which does not follow. Impact. Statement true; repaired (tLinearizable_of_restrictX). Repair. Merge the L_x by a key: the latest invocation time of a late operation at or before the operation in its L_x. Keys are monotone along each L_x and strictly increase along <_{H,t}. 🔧 Lemma 1, "if" direction (weak consistency is local) Reusing τ_x(i, o) from H|x for H violates condition (iii) across objects: τ(i, o') of an earlier operation on another object is not contained in τ_x(i, o). Impact. Statement true; repaired (weaklyConsistent_of_restrictX). Repair. For each object y, glue τ_y of the last operation of p_i on y before o, and put τ_x(i, o) last. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Histories (Section 3): CSLib Herlihy–Wing histories (inv p x o / res p x r, operations identified by (p, x, k)). Weak consistency (WeaklyConsistent), t-permutations (IsTPerm) and t-linearizations (IsTLin) are transcribed literally; the operations "invoked after t" are an arbitrary set A (after invTime t for a global clock), so locality is proved for any A ⊆ A_x. Nonblocking is the Herlihy–Wing notion used by Lemmas 3–4, for a fixed t. Consistency layers (Section 4): runs S(i, t) with submissions and correct processes; Eventual Consistency, Eventual Stability (per run), Eventual Consensus, t-consistency. Implementations (Theorems 2–3): asynchronous, crash failures, no failure detector, deterministic processes that communicate only through the layer. An adversary chooses one action per time unit: an invocation, a delivery, a local tick, or nothing. Admissible runs: crashed processes stop, correct processes tick infinitely often, single-writer/single-reader environment, and the layer run meets its specification. We require termination for correct processes (implied by the paper). Our Eventual Linearizability uses one t_l for all runs; prefixes must be weakly consistent and, in crash-free runs, t_l-linearizable. This is weaker than the paper's uniform and non-uniform notions, so the impossibility results are stronger. Algorithm 1: deterministic object, runs given as lists of invocations and deliveries. On the Validity of Consensus — PODC 2023 Pierre Civit, Seth Gilbert, Rachid Guerraoui, Jovan Komatovic, Manuel Vidigueira. On the Validity of Consensus. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594567. Formalized version: extended version arXiv:2301.04920v3 (numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The classification of solvable validity properties (trivial ones for n ≤ 3t, those satisfying the similarity condition C_S for n > 3t) and the Ω(t²) message lower bound are proved, after one local repair of Lemma 3 for n < 2t. The sufficiency direction is unconditional, because we also verified a vector-consensus protocol for every n > 3t, which replaces the paper's black box, in a model without clock drift or sleeping processes. The O(n²) message complexity of Universal was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 3 claims a Turing-computable Λ, but the model allows arbitrary deterministic state machines, so solvability only yields some function Λ, not a computable one (similarityCondition_of_solvable). Computable algorithms are implied throughout. We prove both versions: any Λ for arbitrary algorithms, and a computable Λ (in Mathlib's sense) when the algorithm's transition functions are computable (similarityCondition_computable). Theorem 1 fails when the proposal set is empty and V_O = ∅: then there are no executions and every algorithm vacuously solves consensus. The proposal set must be nonempty, which we assume. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3 (proof of Theorem 1), case n < 2t The proof builds a configuration in I_{n−t} from all t processes outside π(base) plus n − 2t processes of π(base), which is impossible for n < 2t (smallest instance n = 3, t = 2, allowed by 0 < t < n ≤ 3t). Impact. Statement true; repaired (trivial_of_solvesConsensus_auth). Details. For n < 2t, t processes do not fit into a configuration of size n − t, and n − 2t < 0. Repair. Take min(t, n − t) processes outside π(base) and fill up from π(base). This configuration is compatible with base in the whole range. (trivial_of_solvesConsensus_auth) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A shared partially synchronous Byzantine model (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync). n processes; at most t are statically Byzantine with arbitrary behaviour. Algorithms are deterministic, links are authenticated point-to-point, and there is no randomness. Discrete time with an unknown GST and a known δ. Correct processes step at every tick from time 0, so they have drift-free clocks and are always awake. "Waking up late" is simulated by delaying a process's messages. Optional ideal signatures (unforgeable tokens, eavesdropping rushing adversary). All impossibility results are proved with signatures and specialized to the plain model. Message complexity counts messages from correct processes to other processes after GST. Effect on the results. The adversary is weaker than the paper's: it has no clock drift and no sleeping processes before GST. This makes the impossibilities (Theorems 1, 3, 4) stronger. The possibility side (vector consensus, Theorem 5, the full classification) is correspondingly weaker. Lifting it to the paper's model would need a view synchronizer, which is not formalized. Solvability quantifies over algorithms whose state and message types are in Type. Remarks. Theorem 2 is formally trivial. "A finite procedure returning an always-admissible value" exists as soon as one always-admissible value exists, which Theorem 1 gives: return that constant. (alwaysAdmissible_computable) "A correct process decides at most once" is stated in the paper (§3.2); our Agreement also covers p = q to encode it. Main results in Lean (namespace ValidityConsensus). Memory-Anonymous Symmetric Mutual Exclusion — PODC 2019 Zahra Aghazadeh, Damien Imbs, Michel Raynal, Gadi Taubenfeld, Philipp Woelfel. Optimal Memory-Anonymous Symmetric Deadlock-Free Mutual Exclusion. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331594. Formalized version: arXiv 1810.03723 v1 (the only version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Theorem 2 is false: the read/write algorithm (Algorithm 1) livelocks for n = 4 processes and m = 5 ∈ M(4) registers. So the tight characterization m ∈ M(n) \ {1} for read/write anonymous memory is only half established: necessity holds, sufficiency does not follow from the paper. Theorems 1, 3, 4 and 5 hold, and the characterization for read-modify-write (compare&swap) registers is proved, with a new proof of Theorem 4. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 2 (Algorithm 1, deadlock-freedom) Algorithm 1 livelocks: with n = 4 processes and m = 5 ∈ M(4) registers there is a fair execution in which all four processes stay in lock() forever and nobody enters the CS (theorem_2_false). Impact. The tight characterization m ∈ M(n) \ {1} for read/write anonymous memory is only half established: necessity holds (theorem_5), sufficiency does not follow from the paper. Theorems 1, 3, 4 and 5 and the read-modify-write characterization stand. Details. The fair infinite execution has a 28-step period. All four processes snapshot the empty memory. p0 and p1 fill it, with p0 owning 2 registers and p1 owning 3. p0 (2 < 5/2) starts shrinking. Then the stale writes of p2 and p3, decided on the old empty snapshot, overwrite two of p1's registers. Now p1, p2, p3 own one register each, below the averages 5/3 and 5/4. So everybody shrinks and the memory is empty again. The proof breaks in two places. Claim 4 shows only that at every time some competing process does not withdraw. The proof of Theorem 2 then concludes that some process never calls shrink(), but the non-withdrawing process may change over time. Also, writes based on outdated snapshots, which can destroy the registers of the process owning the most, are never considered. Claim 5's "w.l.o.g. all competing processes have the same view" has the same issue. Scope. Line 6 says "write into some x with view[x] = ⊥" without fixing x, so Theorem 2 must hold for every resolution. The Lean counterexample uses "first ⊥ in the process's local order". Since the permutations are adversarial, this covers every "first ⊥ w.r.t. a fixed order of local names" rule. Our model checker also finds the livelock when line 6 may pick any ⊥. ✏️ Slips §1.3 says compare&swap(x, old, new) succeeds "iff new = v"; it should be old = v. The algorithm uses it correctly. Typos The proof of Theorem 5 describes the schedule awkwardly via "order(pᵢ, k)" and reuses ℓ for the divisor of m; the real argument, a lock-step execution preserving a rotational symmetry, is sound. We use g = gcd(ℓ, m) processes and rotation permutations; in each round they access different physical registers (theorem_5). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4 (Algorithm 2, deadlock-freedom) The proof is only a sketch: "Repeating this argument, eventually one of the processes will find…" ignores non-atomic views and re-entries. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a new proof (theorem_4). Details. First, Algorithm 2's views are read non-atomically, so a process may count registers another process held at different times. Second, a waiting process may re-enter after a non-atomic all-⊥ scan while others still hold registers. Repair. Our new proof has three steps. (1) A no-inflation lemma: a view never shows q owning more registers than q owned simultaneously at some point of the scan. (2) Let c* be the eventual maximum number of owned registers; a process owning c* registers late never withdraws. (3) Once the memory is constant and full, all competitors own equally many registers, which contradicts m ∈ M(n). (theorem_4) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory (CSLib), deterministic processes, no crashes. Processes may stay in the remainder (or in the CS) forever. The memory is m registers, initially ⊥, with atomic read-modify-write accesses and atomic snapshots. Reads, writes and compare&swap are special cases. Memory anonymity: each process has its own adversarial permutation of register names, fixed for the execution. Symmetry: one program for all processes, which differ only in their identifier. "Compare identifiers only for equality" is formalized semantically: the algorithm commutes with every renaming of identifiers, and ⊥ is not an identifier. Deadlock-freedom follows §2.3: in every fair, client-well-formed infinite execution, if an operation is pending and nobody is in the CS, some operation later completes. Fair = every process with a pending operation eventually steps. Granularity: each loop iteration is one atomic access; local bookkeeping is folded into the preceding access. Algorithm 1 uses an atomic snapshot, as the paper assumes. Main results in Lean. Distributed Maximal Matching: Greedy is Optimal — PODC 2012 Juho Hirvonen, Jukka Suomela. Distributed Maximal Matching: Greedy is Optimal. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332464. Formalized version: arXiv 1110.0367 v1 (the only version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. On anonymous k-edge-coloured graphs, maximal matching needs exactly k - 1 deterministic rounds, so the greedy algorithm is optimal (Lemma 1, Theorem 2), and for k ≥ 3 the lower bound holds already on (k-1)-regular graphs (Theorem 6), which gives Ω(Δ) (Corollary 3). All of this is proved, and the template / extension / critical-pair argument of §3 goes through as written. One step is missing: the paper's formal model uses infinite trees, and passing to finite simple graphs needs an extra construction, which we supply. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Typos The proof of Lemma 8 says "w ∈ ȳY"; it should be "w ∈ ȳX". Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2, Theorem 6 and Corollary 3 (from infinite trees to finite graphs) The lower bounds are proved in the formal model of §2.3, whose instances are edge-coloured trees, all infinite in the proof, while Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 talk about k-edge-coloured graphs; the paper does not give the passage to finite graphs. Impact. Statements true; we add the missing step, so all lower bounds hold for finite simple graphs (completion, findsMaximalMatching_of_finite, theorem2_lower_messagePassing, theorem6_messagePassing). Details. The trees built in the proof (realisations, and the final U, V) are infinite. For finite graphs one more step is needed: every finite ball of a d-regular colour system must appear as the view of a node in a finite, simple, d-regular, k-edge-coloured graph. Repair. A 2^k-copies construction (completion): 2^k copies of the ball; a boundary node lacking its colour-c edge is joined to its twin in the copy with coordinate c flipped. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. View model (§2.3, used in the proofs). G_k is the free product of k copies of ℤ/2, implemented as reduced words (FreeCox k). A colour system is a prefix-closed V ⊆ G_k, i.e. a k-edge-coloured tree, possibly infinite. An algorithm is any function A : Set G_k → G_k → Option (Fin k); none means unmatched, some c means matched along colour c. It has running time r if (ūU)[r+1] = (v̄V)[r+1] implies A U u = A V v. Correctness is (M1)–(M3). The model is deterministic and anonymous; local computation and message size are unbounded. Message-passing model (§1.2). A k-edge-coloured network is a ColouredGraph k α: each colour class is a partial involution, and IsSimple means a simple graph with a proper edge colouring. Nodes may be finite or infinite in number, and cycles are allowed. A node starts knowing its incident colours. In each synchronous round it sends one message per colour, then receives and updates. It outputs after r rounds. Equivalence. We prove that the two models are equivalent (state_eq_of_view, hasRunningTime_toAlgorithm, out_ofView, isMaximalMatching_view). The lower bound needs correctness only on finite simple (regular) networks. The upper bound holds on all networks (on non-simple networks the maximal-matching spec lets a node be matched along a half-loop, so its usual meaning is for simple graphs). Main results in Lean. The delay schedule behind the grey zone lower bound (Theorem 3.17) breaks for the c ≥ 2 messages per local broadcast that the model allows, and no repair is proved. The lower bounds for c = 1 (§3.3) and the enhanced-model algorithm (§4) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 3.20 and Theorem 3.17 for c ≥ 2 messages per broadcast (not formalized) The delay schedule of Lemma 3.20 assumes one MMB message per local broadcast, but §2 allows a constant number c, and for c ≥ 2 the schedule breaks, so Theorem 3.17 is unestablished for c ≥ 2. Impact. The lower bound is not established for the model of §2. This comes from reading the proof and is not checked in Lean (the lower bounds are not formalized). We did not determine whether Theorem 3.17 holds for c ≥ 2. Details. §2 says "only a constant number of these messages can fit into a single local broadcast message". In the delay schedule, b_{i+1} receives a_i's m₀-broadcast over a G' edge. With c ≥ 2, b_{i+1}'s later broadcast "containing m₁" may also carry m₀. The schedule delivers that broadcast to a_{i+2} over a G' edge, so m₀ jumps ahead and the frontier no longer advances one hop per F_ack. Against "always send everything you know" the schedule only costs O(F_ack + D F_prog). ✏️ Slips Lemma 3.12, part 5 (ℓ F_ack ≤ t_{0,ℓ} for ℓ > 1) is off by one F_ack: it is false whenever F_ack > 2 F_prog, the regime the paper cares about. With r = 1, ℓ = 2, F_prog = 1, F_ack = 3 we get ℓ F_ack = 6 > 5 = t_{0,2} (lemma_3_12_5_false). This holds for our t_{d,ℓ}, for the formula read off Theorem 3.16, and for every definition satisfying part 4 and t_{D,k} ≤ t₁ (needed to get Theorem 3.16 "directly from Lemma 3.15"), since part 4 gives t_{0,2} = t_{D,2} − D F_prog ≤ 5 (lemma_3_12_5_false_any). Connectivity is implied by the use of the diameter D. We prove the per-component statement and the paper's statement for connected G (theorem_3_16, theorem_3_16_connected), and use the component version (SolvesMMB). The composition "BMMB + standard abstract MAC layer" is one event-driven transition system (Model.lean). A node's state is its log, the messages it got in order: rcvd, and the order of bcastq. It also holds the number acks of acknowledged broadcasts. The queue is log.drop acks, and its head is the message currently being broadcast (zero-delay bcast). An instance is a pair (sender, message), since BMMB broadcasts each message once. ack u happens only after all G-neighbours received: acknowledgment correctness. Disabled events are no-ops. Topology. Early-Deciding Consensus is Expensive — PODC 2013 Danny Dolev, Christoph Lenzen. Early-Deciding Consensus is Expensive. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484269. Formalized version: the authors' camera-ready copy (10 pages, proofs included; the paper says no full version exists). Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Every checked result holds: the t²f/44 Byzantine bound for (f+2)-deciding consensus (Theorem 3.2), the f + 2 decision bound (Theorem 3.6), the Ω(n²f) crash bound (Theorem 4.3), the orderly-crash algorithm (Theorem 4.5), and Lemmas 3.4–3.8 and 4.2. The lower bounds need only local repairs of their proofs. But the correctness proof of the orderly-crash algorithm, one of the paper's three results, never uses orderliness, and the algorithm is wrong without it, so it took a new induction. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 3 fixes "an (f+1)-deciding algorithm". So do the proofs of Lemmas 3.5 and 3.7 and of Theorem 3.2. All of them need, and Theorem 3.2 states, (f+2)-deciding. Taken literally the section would be vacuous, since Theorem 3.6 shows that no algorithm is (f+1)-deciding. Proof of Lemma 3.8, "In summary": (i) and (ii) are swapped. In E₀ the non-faulty nodes of W₀ decide 0; in E₁ the non-faulty node v decides 1. Proof of Theorem 4.3: the closed form of ∑_{i=1}^f (n-i-1)² is off by (n-f-2)². The subtracted term should be (n-f-2)(n-f-1)(2(n-f)-3)/6; for n = 5, f = 1 the sum is 9, not 13 (sum_identity_false). The next line carries a spurious +6n². The final bound nf(n-f) + f³/3 - O(nf) is right (sum_sq_bound). Typos Definition 4.1: "a subset W \ V" should read W ⊆ V. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4.5 (correctness of the orderly-crash algorithm) The correctness proof claims "a unique node i₀ deciding in round i₀ on its input", which is false, and never uses that crashes are orderly, although without orderly crashes the algorithm violates agreement (not_crash_correct). Impact. The statement is true, but the printed proof lacks the idea; we prove the theorem with a new argument (Orderly.correct, Orderly.decidedBy, Orderly.stopping, Orderly.totalCount_le). Details. If node 1 crashes before sending, node 2 also decides its own input, so i₀ is not unique. The real issue is the claim that every node > i₀ adopts the value of i₀. It needs messages from nodes < i₀ never to reach nodes beyond i₀ when i₀ itself received nothing, and only orderliness gives that. With ordinary crashes, take n = 3, t = 1. Node 1 (input 0) crashes in round 1, reaching only node 3. Node 2 has received nothing, so it decides its input 1, while node 3 decides 0. Both stay correct. Repair. Let i₀ be the last node that decides its own input. Every node before i₀ crashed. By induction on rounds, every message delivered to a node after i₀ carries i₀'s input. A sender before i₀ would also have reached i₀ (prefix property) in a round ≤ i₀. 🔧 Theorem 3.6 (decision before round f + 2 is impossible) The theorem is stated "for any consensus protocol", but its proof iterates Lemma 3.5, which needs the algorithm to decide within f' + 2 rounds whenever there are f' < f faults. Impact. Statement true for every algorithm; a small change of the paper's construction proves it (theorem_3_6_general, not_deciding_succ). The deadline-based version is theorem_3_6. Details. In the paper's E(W) the faulty critical node v_r falls silent after round r + 1. So E(V \ F_r) looks like E₀ to the honest nodes only before round r + 2. Its output equals that of E₀ only if E₀ (with r - 1 faults) has decided by round r + 1. Repair. Let v_r equivocate forever: in every round k ≥ r it sends to W what it sends in E₀ and to the rest what it sends in E₁. Then E(V \ F_r) and E(∅) look like E₀ and E₁ forever, and their outputs follow without any deadline. The pairs obtained satisfy Definition 3.3 except that faulty nodes may keep talking. They send the same messages in both executions to everybody but the critical node (IsCriticalG, lemma_3_5_general). This is all the final step of the proof of Theorem 3.6 needs. 🔧 Lemma 3.8 (uses more than Lemma 3.7 states) Lemma 3.7 bounds the round-(r+1) messages of all non-faulty nodes, including the critical node v_r, but Lemma 3.8 averages this bound over V \ F_r, which excludes v_r. Impact. Statements true (lemma_3_7, lemma_3_8). Details. For t < 22 the nt/22 messages of Lemma 3.7 could all come from v_r (it can send n - 1 of them). Then inequality (1) of Lemma 3.8 does not follow. Repair. The proof of Lemma 3.7 only counts messages from senders in V \ F_r, so it gives the bound we need. lemma_3_7 states it that way: n t ≤ 11 (c₀ + c₁), counting the senders of V \ F_r in both executions. 🔧 Theorem 4.3 (case f ≥ n - 2) The proof's reduction to t ≤ n - 2 only covers f ≤ n - 3, while the theorem claims every f < t, including f ≥ n - 2 when t ≥ n - 1. Impact. Statement true for every f < t (theorem_4_3_all', theorem_4_3_omega_all). Repair. Take the execution for n - 3 faults. Let f - (n - 3) more nodes crash silently after round f + 1. This changes no counted message, and ∑_{i=1}^{n-3} (n-i-1)² still meets the bound nf(n-f) + f³/3 - 3nf for f ≤ n. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchrony. Synchronous rounds 1, 2, … on a complete network of n nodes (V, any finite type). Links are authenticated: the receiver knows the sender. Messages and local computation are unbounded. Algorithms are deterministic CSLib lock-step protocols with binary inputs and outputs (Cslib.Byzantine.LockStep.Protocol); a node's messages and decision depend on its input and history. Decisions are first decisions, so they are final. Executions. An execution fixes the inputs, the faulty set F and, per faulty node, the round from which it is faulty (the paper's F₁ ⊆ F₂ ⊆ …). It also fixes the messages faulty nodes send. Before its fault round a node follows the algorithm. f = |F|. Our histories are exactly CSLib's lock-step histories of the corresponding static-Byzantine scenario (hist_toScenario). Fault classes. Byzantine (byzAdm t): at most t faulty nodes, arbitrary messages, n > 3t as in Section 3. Crash (crashAdm, Definition 4.1): in its fault round a node sends a subset of its algorithm messages, then nothing. Orderly crash (orderlyAdm, Definition 4.4): that subset is a prefix of an order fixed by the algorithm. No randomness. The adversary picks inputs, faulty nodes, fault rounds and faulty messages with full knowledge. Specification. Termination, agreement and validity (the decided value is some node's input) for the nodes that never fail. d-deciding (Definition 3.1) requires the never-faulty nodes to decide within d(f) rounds. The paper also constrains nodes that fail after round d(f), so as a hypothesis our version is weaker and the lower bounds are slightly stronger. For the algorithm of Theorem 4.5 we prove the paper's strong form. Message counts. Counts include messages sent in rounds 1..R by nodes that are not faulty in the round of sending, which is the paper's convention. Theorem 4.5 counts all messages, faulty senders included. Time-Optimal Self-Stabilizing Leader Election in Population Protocols — PODC 2021 Janna Burman, Ho-Lin Chen, Hsueh-Ping Chen, David Doty, Thomas Nowak, Eric Severson, Chuan Xu. Time-Optimal Self-Stabilizing Leader Election in Population Protocols. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467898. Formalized version: arXiv 1907.06068 v5 (29 Nov 2021); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The paper's time bounds, its main point, and Section 5 (Sublinear-Time-SSR) were not checked. What was checked holds apart from one typo and a by-product: SSLE needs ≥ n states and exact knowledge of n (Theorem 2.1, proved here), Silent-n-state-SSR solves ranking (Lemmas 2.2, 2.3, Theorem 2.4), Observation 2.5 holds, and Optimal-Silent-SSR, which as printed never stabilizes, is correct with the evidently intended guard ≤ n (from every valid configuration a silent, correctly ranked configuration is reachable, for Rmax, Dmax ≥ 2, which the paper's choices satisfy). Only the explicit tail bound of Observation 2.6 is lost, and nothing depends on it. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Observation 2.6 for n = 2 and n = 3 (explicit tail bound) The claim "for any α > 0, probability ≥ ½ n^{-3α} to require ≥ α n ln n convergence time" fails for n = 2, where Silent-n-state-SSR is correctly ranked after the first interaction (obs26_n2_counterexample), and for n = 3 with large α. Impact. The paper uses only the Ω(n) expected time of the observation, which is fine. The claim holds for n ≥ 4 with the exact success probability 2/(n(n−1)), but this was checked by hand, not in Lean. In Lean we have the two-leader core and the geometric tail, for deterministic protocols. Details. With two agents, Silent-n-state-SSR is correctly ranked after the first interaction from every configuration, under every schedule, so its convergence time is at most 1/2 < 2 ln 2. The proof has a wrong estimate: (1 − 3/n²)^{α n² ln n} ≥ ½ e^{−3α ln n} is false for large α (e.g. n = 10, α = 7), and 1/C(n,2) < 3/n² needs n ≥ 4. Also, "expected time ≥ n/3" fails for n = 2. For n = 3 the claim fails e.g. for α = 10 (checked numerically, not in Lean). The deterministic core and the geometric tail are obs26_null_of_ne, obs26_two_leaders, obs26_stay_prob. ✏️ Slips Protocol 3 (Optimal-Silent-SSR), line 9, and Theorem 4.3: the guard 2 · i.rank + i.children < n should be ≤ n. As printed, the protocol never stabilizes. New ranks are created only by Reset (rank 1) and by recruitment (rank 2·rank + children), so no agent can ever obtain rank n unless it already had it. Hence from the all-Unsettled configuration, or from any configuration after a complete reset, no correctly ranked configuration is ever reached, for every n ≥ 2 and all Rmax, Dmax, Emax; the protocol stabilizes with probability 0 (OptimalSilent.asWritten_never_ranked, asWritten_not_selfStabilizes). Figure 1 (rank 12 assigned for n = 12) shows that ≤ n is meant, and with it we prove Theorem 4.3's correctness for Rmax, Dmax ≥ 2 (OptimalSilent.fixed_selfStabilizes). Proof of Lemma 2.2: ∑_{j=1}^{n−1} m_j = n should start at j = 0, and S_k − S_{k−r+1} should be S_{k−r−1}, S_{−1} = 0. Proof of Theorem 2.4: the slow initial configuration is "m_1(C_0) = 2" but should be m_0(C_0) = 2. Typos Under-specified pseudocode of Protocols 2–4. Two-Bit Messages Suffice for Atomic Registers — PODC 2016 Achour Mostéfaoui, Michel Raynal. Two-Bit Messages are Sufficient to Implement Atomic Read/Write Registers in Crash-prone Systems. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933095. Formalized version: arXiv 1602.02695 v1 (the only version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The algorithm of Figure 1 implements a linearizable SWMR register in CAMP_{n,t}[t < n/2], every operation of a correct process terminates, and messages carry a two-bit type, plus a value for two of the four types. FIFO channels are not needed, as the paper itself states (§2.1 assumes non-FIFO channels): the parity bit and the wait at line 11 form an alternating-bit protocol. The algorithm stands unchanged under the standard convention that code between two waits runs atomically; the proofs of Lemmas 5 and 10 need only an extra case, an extra invariant conjunct and two corrected steps. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Figure 1 / Section 3: the paper never says that code between two waits runs atomically with respect to the message handlers. This is the implied, standard convention, and the algorithm is wrong without it (see "Implicit convention" below). Claim 3: "computed by p_i" should be p_j. Typos Claim 2: i and j are mixed in the quorum Q_w. Lemma 8: w_sync_i[i] ≥ w_sync_w[i] = wsn is awkward, but every part of it is true (Lemmas 2 and 6). What line 3 needs is w_sync_w[i] ≥ wsn. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 5 (alternating-bit invariant) The case analysis for a pair (i, j) omits p_i receiving a WRITE from a third process p_k, and the induction lacks the hypothesis "at most two unprocessed WRITEs per channel, with different parities". Impact. Statement true; we prove an exact invariant covering both points (lemma5, lemma5_sent). Details. The paper considers p_i invoking write and p_i receiving a WRITE from p_j. A reception from p_k may raise w_sync_i[i] (line 14) and send a WRITE to p_j (line 15), changing the premises of the paper's counts R1/R2 of the WRITEs sent to p_j. The missing hypothesis is what makes the parity test of line 11 pick the right message. 🔧 Lemma 10, Claim 2 Claim 2 says w_sync_k[k] = x when the read starts, but only ≥ x is true, because a later write may already have started. Impact. Only ≥ x is used (lemma10). 🔧 Lemma 10, Claim 3 Claim 3 asserts a correct process in the intersection of two (n − t)-quorums, which does not follow. Impact. Correctness of that process is never used (lemma10). Details. With n = 3, t = 1, quorums {1,2} and {2,3}, p_2 may be faulty. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finitely many asynchronous deterministic processes; the writer w and readers p ≠ w. The writer does not read; the paper only remarks that its reads are local. A complete network of reliable, unordered channels (a multiset of in-transit messages). Crash failures. Messages of crashed senders may be dropped (a crash mid-broadcast), but dropping is never forced. Safety is proved for any number of crashes. Liveness assumes at most t crashes, 2t < n, and weak fairness for steps of correct processes (this includes reliable delivery). Each block of code between waits is one atomic transition. A WRITE that fails the parity test of line 11 stays in the channel. Atomicity is CSLib's linearizability (amended Herlihy–Wing) for a register. Pending operations may or may not be linearized. No randomness, no timing. Implicit convention: code between two waits is atomic. The paper never says how an operation's code interleaves with the message handlers. We use the standard convention for this pseudo-code (last Model bullet); it is a convention, not an error, but it is necessary: without it the algorithm is wrong. Suppose a WRITE handler runs between lines 1 and 2 of write(). Then the writer can send the same WRITE(b, v_x) twice to one process: once at line 16, while it handles a late echo of v_{x−1}, and again at line 2. The stale copy later passes the parity test as message x + 2, and the receiver appends a wrong value to its history. Our model checker found a 14-step execution with n = 3, t = 1, no crashes, no reads and three writes, in which p2 accepts the stale WRITE(0, v2) as its 4th value. Lemma 9. Channels are not FIFO and READ()/PROCEED() carry no sequence number, so "r_sync_i[j] = rsn means p_j answered the current request" needs a counting argument, which the paper only asserts. It is routine: each READ() is at all times in exactly one place (in transit, a pending handler, a PROCEED() in transit, or already counted) (read_terminates). Theorem 2's message complexity (O(n) per read, O(n²) per write) holds when messages are attributed to the operation (value) they belong to, as the paper's proof does, i.e. amortized; it does not bound the messages sent during an operation. Catch-up messages for old values (line 16) may be sent long after the write returned. We prove the amortized bounds. Main results in Lean. Disjoint-Access Parallelism and Real-Time Order in TM — PODC 2015 Sebastiano Peluso, Roberto Palmieri, Paolo Romano, Binoy Ravindran, Francesco Quaglia. Disjoint-Access Parallelism: Impossibility, Possibility, and Cost of Transactional Memory Implementations. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767438. Formalized version: the Virginia Tech technical report of May 2015 (14 pp., with the proofs of Section 3); no arXiv version. Numbering is the same in both versions. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The two impossibility theorems (Theorems 1 and 2: no weakly disjoint-access-parallel TM with wait-free read-only transactions and obstruction-free, resp. weakly progressive write transactions with invisible reads, ensures real-time order) are true, and the claims about the histories of Figure 1 hold. But Lemma 1, on which their proofs rest, is false as soon as a third process takes steps, so we re-prove both theorems by a new commutation argument. The other two parts of the paper's point, the algorithm of Section 4 and the lower bounds (Theorems 3 and 4), were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 1 (disjoint-access transactions never contend) "In a WDAP TM two concurrent disjoint-access transactions cannot contend on a common base object" is false: there is a WDAP TM with three processes in which a transaction Tⱼ reads a base object written by a concurrent, disjoint-access transaction Tᵢ (Lemma1.lemma_1_false). Impact. Lemma 1 is the basis of Lemmas 2 and 3, so the paper's proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 (and the uses of Lemma 1 in the proof of Theorem 3) are not valid as written. Theorems 1 and 2 themselves are true (see the proof gap below). We have no general replacement for the lemma, only the commutation of two sides split by accessed objects. Details. The proof only considers executions in which Tᵢ and Tⱼ are the only transactions taking steps: it delays the first contending event of Tⱼ until it is concurrent with that of Tᵢ. With a third process, information can flow from Tᵢ to Tⱼ through two different transactions of that process. The counterexample TM Lemma1.chainTM has base objects o(y,q) (written once, by the first write of process q to y) and a board f(x) per transactional object x. A write to x writes o(x, self) the first time, then publishes on f(x) all pairs (y,q) it knows to be written. A read of x reads f(x), then the published o(y,q) and all o(x,q). The execution Lemma1.exec: Tᵢ (process 0) writes x₀ and stays live; T_k1 (process 1) reads x₀, sees o(x₀, 0) written, commits; T_k2 (process 1) writes x₁, publishing (x₀, 0) on f(x₁), commits; Tⱼ (process 2) reads x₁, finds (x₀, 0) on the board and reads o(x₀, 0). Tᵢ and Tⱼ are live, hence concurrent. Their only conflict edges are Tᵢ — T_k1 (object x₀) and T_k2 — Tⱼ (object x₁), so they are disjoint-access. Yet Tⱼ reads the base object Tᵢ wrote. They never contend concurrently: Tⱼ reads o(x₀,0) only after learning that it is written for good. In every reachable configuration, two processes poised to contend on a base object run transactions with intersecting data sets (Lemma1.chainTM_strongWDAP). So chainTM is WDAP for the data-set/conflict-graph definition of Attiya, Hillel and Milani [4], which the paper says it uses. It is not WDAP if "disjoint-access" is read literally as "no path in the DSG" of the current history: then two transactions with pending operations on the same object are "disjoint" until one of them commits, which rules out even a reader and a writer of the same object touching a common base object concurrently. ✏️ Slips Section 2 progress definitions, Theorems 1 and 2: as defined, obstruction-freedom and weak progressiveness only forbid aborts, so a TM whose write transactions never return satisfies them and trivially preserves RTO. The intended (standard) definitions include termination of operations that run solo, as in the cited [15, 17]; with it both theorems hold. The proofs need T₃ and T₂ to commit ("they cannot be aborted"). We assume that a write transaction running solo completes its operations (ObstructionFreeWrites), resp. that a write transaction running with no concurrent transaction completes and commits (IsolatedWritesCommit). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorems 1 and 2 (the indistinguishability argument) The proofs apply Lemma 3 (via the false Lemma 1) to T₄ and T₂ in H_WRTO, and the proof of Lemma 3 only reorders the steps of these two transactions, ignoring T₃. Impact. Statements true; re-proved without Lemmas 1–3 (theorem_1, theorem_2). Details. To move T₂ before T₄'s first read one must also move it before T₃. In H_WRTO, T₂ and T₃ are connected through T₄, so WDAP does not directly say that they do not contend. Repair. We use WDAP only at the moments where it applies. At every configuration reached by interleaving the steps of T₂ with those of T₃ after R₄(y) (or with those of R₄(y)), T₂ has accessed only x and the others only y: transactions are not known a priori, so T₄ has not yet read x. Hence the two sides never contend, and their steps commute (commute, noContendFrom_of_wdap, commute_scenario). So E = R₄(y) · T₃ · T₂ · R₄(x) c₄ and E' = T₂ · R₄(y) · T₃ · R₄(x) c₄ are executions in which R₄(x) returns the same value. If it is T₂'s value, E's history is H_WRTO and violates RTO (T₃ ≺RTO T₂ →wr T₄ →rw T₃). If it is the initial value, E' violates WRTO (T₂ ≺WRTO T₄ →rw T₂). In particular, under WRTO the TM produces H_WRTO (theorem_1_wrto, theorem_2_wrto; this contains the instance of Lemma 3 used by the paper). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory from CSLib (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl): deterministic processes, arbitrary atomic base objects, arbitrary scheduler, environment choosing the invocations; crashes are processes that stop taking steps (only finite executions are used). A TM is an implementation of the interface read x, write x v, tryC; a transaction begins with its first invocation (no separate begin step) and ends with an abort or a successful tryC. Histories, versions (initial version and committed writers in commit order), the DSG edges wr, ww, rw, real-time order and the paper's "H preserves RTO / WRTO" (no cycle through Tq, Tk after adding an edge for every Tq ≺ Tk) are defined on arbitrary histories (Model.lean). Read-from is determined by values, so "the TM ensures RTO / WRTO" quantifies over histories with unique written values (UniqueWrites: every write to x writes a value different from x's initial value and from the other writes to x), the usual convention that makes the paper's Rᵢ(xⱼ) well defined; accordingly, Theorems 1 and 2 assume that the value domain has a value other than the initial values of x and y. WDAP: whenever two processes are poised to contend on a base object (at least one non-trivial primitive), their transactions are joined by a path in the conflict graph of the history so far (vertices: begun transactions; edges: intersecting data sets). This is weaker than the definition of [4] and than the paper's DSG-based wording, so the theorems cover more TMs. Progress, as hypotheses only for the operations the proofs use (each implied by the paper's notions plus termination): a write transaction without step contention completes its operations solo without abort; a write transaction running with no concurrent transaction commits; an operation of a transaction that has not written completes solo without abort (WFRO); the steps of its reads are trivial (IRO); a read returns the initial value or a value some invoked write writes (implicit in the paper's histories). Main results in Lean. Fair and Resilient Incentive Tree Mechanisms — PODC 2013 Yuezhou Lv, Thomas Moscibroda. Fair and Resilient Incentive Tree Mechanisms. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484252. Formalized version: the journal version (Distributed Computing 29(1), 2016, DOI 10.1007/s00446-015-0250-y, author copy, full proofs in the appendix); all theorem, lemma, section and algorithm numbers below are the journal's. The PODC 2013 version (10 pp, proof sketches only) numbers the same results differently: Theorems 1–4 = PODC Theorems 4.1–4.4, appendix Lemmas 1–5 = PODC Lemmas 4.5–4.9, Theorem 5 = PODC Theorem 4.10; journal Sections 4.4, 5, 6 = PODC Sections 4.2, 4.3, 4.4. The two versions state the definitions of Section 3 identically (in particular PO with R(u) ≥ C(u)). Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All four checked theorems hold once slips are fixed: the impossibility result (Theorem 3), the geometric mechanism (Theorem 1), TDRM (Theorem 4: everything except UGSA, in particular Sybil-proofness USA) and the CDRM family (Theorem 5: everything except URO and PO, in particular UGSA). The slips are a ≥ that should be > in the formal definition of PO (with it, Theorem 3 is false for budget Φ = 1), Theorem 5 also losing PO, and zero contributions / zero parameters. But the long appendix proof of TDRM's USA (Lemmas 1–5), the heart of the analysis of the paper's main mechanism, does not work, and we replace it by a new short induction. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 3.1, definition of PO (makes Theorem 3 false as stated). With PO formally defined as "R(u) ≥ C(u)" (zero profit suffices) and the allowed budget Φ = 1, the mechanism R(u) = C(u) satisfies SL, PO, UGSA and the budget constraint, contradicting Theorem 3 (theorem_3_false_for_weak_PO). The prose of the same paragraph says PO means positive profit, and the proof of Theorem 3 uses P(v*) > 0. With R(u) > C(u) Theorem 3 holds and the paper's proof is correct (theorem_3). R(u) = C(u) is subtree-local and has total reward C(T) = Φ·C(T). Every node makes profit 0 whatever the shape of its subtree, so PO (weak) holds, and any Sybil split has total profit 0 = the single node's profit, so UGSA (hence USA) holds. It also satisfies CCI and φ-RPC for every φ ≤ 1, but not CSI or URO. Whether the weak-PO version of Theorem 3 holds for Φ < 1 is open: the paper's argument needs a strictly profitable node, and we neither proved nor refuted that case. Theorem 5 (CDRM mechanisms: "all properties, except URO"). A successfully contribution-deterministic mechanism also violates PO, since R(x, y) < Φx ≤ x (theorem_5). Section 4.4 announces that the Section 6 mechanism "achieves all the properties except PO/URO" and notes URO ⇒ PO. Everything else in Theorem 5 is proved, including UGSA. Zero contributions and zero parameters (Theorems 1, 4, 5). Several claims fail only when a contribution or parameter is 0: CSI fails when the newcomer contributes 0 (all mechanisms) or C(u) = 0 (TDRM, CDRM), TDRM's chain for C(u) = 0 has N_u = ⌈0/μ⌉ = 0 nodes, Theorem 5 never constrains R(0, y), and Theorems 1 and 4 allow b = 0 (if φ = 0) and a, λ ≤ 0, where CCI/CSI/URO fail. We add the evident positivity assumptions (0 < b in Theorem 1; 0 < a, 0 < b, 0 < λ, 0 ≤ φ in Theorem 4; right-continuity of R(·, y) at 0 in Theorem 5, which forces R(0, y) = 0), use a one-node chain for C(u) = 0, and require positive contributions in CSI. Appendix, Lemmas 1–5 (structure of an optimal Sybil partition for TDRM). The uniqueness parts ("must be an ε-chain", "at most one node below μ", "forms a tree") fail in degenerate cases: Lemma 5 fails whenever u has no solicitees (then R^e ≡ 0 and every partition maximizes it), and Lemmas 1–3 fail when a Sybil identity contributes 0. The proof of Theorem 4 only needs that some optimal partition is an ε-chain (which is what its proof idea says), and Theorem 4's USA is proved without these lemmas (tdrm_USA). Algorithm 4. It creates the RCT edge (m^u_{N_u}, m^v_1) for an edge (u, v), but in Section 2 (u, v) means "u is a child of v"; Figure 3 shows the intended direction (tail of the parent → head of the child). The UGSA counterexample after Theorem 4. P(u) should be ½((ak + ½)λμb + φμ − μ), not (ak + 1); the conclusion P'(u) > P(u) is unaffected (theorem_4, last conjunct). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4 (TDRM satisfies USA; appendix Lemmas 1–5) The proof argues about a reward-maximizing Sybil partition without showing that one exists, and its exchange steps only weakly increase the reward (Lemma 2 case (b) even leaves a 0-contribution node below μ), so "contradiction with maximality" does not follow. Impact. Statement true; we give a new proof (tdrm_USA). Details. The number of Sybil identities is unbounded and contributions are real, so the existence of an optimum is itself what has to be shown; with weak improvements the contradiction scheme of Lemmas 1–5 would have to be replaced by "some optimum has the structure", which presupposes the optimum. Also, Lemma 2's auxiliary fact S1 > S2 only covers transfers away from the balanced split; when C(x) < C(y) the transfer towards x first passes through it, and what is needed is convexity of the quadratic in the transfer. Repair. We compute the closed form R(u) = (λb/μ)(Q(C(u)) + a·G(C(u))·X) + φC(u) (tdrm_node). Here Q, G are explicit functions of the ε-chain and X is the depth-weighted contribution of the children's RCTs. We then prove by induction on the Sybil forest (sybil_bound) that a Sybil tree of mass m earns at most Q(m) + a·E·G(m), the single-node value. Every optimisation fact of Lemmas 1–5 reduces to five inequalities about Q, G, H (Qc_add, Qc_superadd, Hc_add_le, Gc_add_le, Gc_subadd): concatenating chains never loses, and branching loses at least what the extra ancestor weight gains. 🔧 Theorem 5 (CDRM satisfies USA) The minimal-counterexample merging argument is incomplete: merging can lower the reward of other Sybils, and "at least the same reward" does not contradict minimality of k. Impact. Statement true; a direct induction on the Sybil forest with the same key inequality proves it: a Sybil tree of mass m with real contribution E earns at most R(m, E) (theorem_5; uses (iv) and monotonicity in y). Details. In case (a) the merged ancestor–descendant pair need not be adjacent, which lowers the reward of the Sybils in between; case (b) ignores Sybil ancestors of p₂, which lose x₂ + y₂ from their subtrees. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Not a distributed-computing model: a mechanism maps a weighted referral tree (contributions C(u) ≥ 0) to rewards. No time, adversary or randomness. Sybil attacks are compared on final configurations, which under SL is the same as "for every i" along join sequences. Only subtree-local mechanisms are modelled: a mechanism is f : Tree → ℝ, the reward of the root of the given subtree. All mechanisms of Theorems 1, 4, 5 are of this form, and Theorem 3 assumes SL. Trees are rose trees with ordered children lists. Theorem 3 is thereby proved for a larger class (order-dependent mechanisms included); all our mechanisms are order-invariant. A Sybil attack of u is a forest of Sybil trees (Sybil.node c sybilChildren realChildren). Every real child subtree of u is attached to exactly one Sybil (up to permutation). With SL, where the Sybil trees are placed in the rest of the referral tree is irrelevant. Single-identity "attacks" (k = 1) are included, as in the paper's UGSA counterexample for TDRM. The budget is required over all nodes of every tree, including a root of contribution 0 (at least as strong as the paper's R(T) ≤ ΦC(T)). PO is "positive profit" (PO); the printed weak version is POWeak. Main results in Lean. Easy Impossibility Proofs for k-Set Agreement — PODC 2011 Martin Biely, Peter Robinson, Ulrich Schmid. Easy Impossibility Proofs for k-Set Agreement in Message Passing Systems. PODC 2011 (brief announcement). DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993846. Formalized version: arXiv 1103.3671 v2 (full version, latest arXiv version, March 2011); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Theorem 1, the paper's main tool, is saved by local repairs and its asynchronous consequences hold: k-set agreement is impossible with f crashes when k ≤ (n−1)/(n−f) (Theorem 2 with asynchronous processes, Corollary 5, by the paper's reduction to FLP), and with up to f < n initially dead processes it is solvable iff kn > (k+1)f (Theorem 8). But the claim that Theorem 2 tightly captures the impossibility is lost: its bound is not matched, and the exact border is proved only for initial crashes, by a separate partitioning argument. The failure-detector part (Section VII) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Section VI opening and contribution list ("Theorem 2 tightly captures the impossibility") The bound (n−1)/(n−f) of Theorem 2 is not matched by the solvability bound f/(n−f) for initial crashes, because the two results are about different failure models. Impact. A tight border is proved only in the initial-crash model, by a separate partitioning argument (theorem8). Tightness of Theorem 2's own bound is not saved. Details. Theorem 2 assumes a different and harsher failure model (f − 1 initial crashes plus one crash during the run). Example: n = 5, f = 3, k = 2 is impossible under Theorem 2's failures but solvable with initial crashes only (theorem2_vs_theorem8). 🔧 Theorem 1 (unstated property of the model) Theorem 1's proof tacitly assumes that the processes of D̄ cannot decide a value proposed only in D, and without this the theorem fails in a model where process 0's input is fixed (Abstract.Counterexample.theorem1_statement_false). Impact. The theorem fails only in the literal "arbitrary system model" generality the paper claims; the statement is under-specified. In the paper's own models the missing hypothesis holds, and the applications are not affected. Repaired by one added condition (E): Abstract.theorem1_corrected. Details. Fact 1 ("in every run of R(D̄) all of D̄ decide on a common value") is derived from (B) and k-agreement alone. Then A|D̄ is said to solve consensus in M'. Both steps need the unstated property. Otherwise D̄ may split between v₁ and a new value w, which together with v₁, …, v_{k−1} are still only k values, and A|D̄ need not be valid in M'. Counterexample: n = 3, k = 2, D₁ = {0}, D̄ = {1, 2}, no communication, and process 0 always proposes 0 in M. "Everybody decides 0" solves consensus in M, yet (A)–(D) hold, with M' = two silent processes with inputs in {1,2,3}. The counterexample needs a model in which D̄'s view is correlated with D's inputs (here: process 0's input is fixed). The paper's models ([DDS87]-style, all inputs x_q ∈ V possible, admissibility independent of input values) exclude this. There the missing hypothesis follows by changing the inputs of D. 🔧 Theorem 1, condition (B) (fixed values v_i) Condition (B) cannot hold as written in the applications: the values v_i are fixed in advance, so a run of R(D̄) in which a process of D̄ proposes v₁ has no D̄-indistinguishable partner in R(D, D̄) (Abstract.condB_fails). Impact. The statement is under-specified: the values must be allowed to depend on the run, and the proof works verbatim then (Abstract.theorem1_corrected). Details. R(D, D̄) requires v_i to be proposed in D. With arbitrary distinct inputs (Theorems 2 and 10) such runs exist. 🔧 Theorem 1, proof ("Therefore, we have that, in fact, ρ ∈ R(D̄)") "Clearly ρ ∈ R(D̄)" does not follow from indistinguishability until decision. Impact. Requiring the runs given by (D) to lie in R(D̄) repairs it, and this holds by construction in the applications (Abstract.theorem1_corrected). Details. A process of D̄ that decided early may hear from D in ρ before the other processes of D̄ decide. 🔧 Theorem 1, proof (termination of A|D̄) Termination of A|D̄ in M' is never argued: a process correct in ρ' might be faulty in the compatible run ρ. Impact. One clause added to (D), preserving correctness, closes the gap, and it holds in the applications (Abstract.theorem1_corrected). Condition (A) is never used. 🔧 Section VI ("complete and consistent knowledge of G after the second stage") The claim that processes have "complete and consistent knowledge of G" after stage 2 is too strong: a process only learns its ancestors. Impact. The algorithm is correct as intended (InitDeadAlg.kSafe). Details. Ancestor knowledge suffices, but one must also argue that a chosen root's ancestor set is frozen once all its ancestors have chosen their in-lists. ✏️ Slips Theorem 8 (in the form kn > (k+1)f) fails for f = n ≤ k, where "decide your own input" works (theorem8_false_of_f_eq_n, theorem2_false_of_f_eq_n). The paper implicitly assumes f < n (its sets D_i of size n − f must be nonempty). Theorem 2's bound (n−1)/(n−f) is undefined at f = n; in the multiplied-out form k(n−f) ≤ n−1 it would fail for f = n = k. Lemma 6 needs a nonempty graph: the empty graph has no source component (SourceComp.exists_sourceComponent). For k = 1, what Section VI chooses is a source component, not a "clique" (a fully connected subgraph). Typos In the proof of Theorem 10, "applying Theorem 2" should be Theorem 1. The proof of Lemma 7 cites "the previous theorem", meaning Lemma 6. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 8, "only if" (proved only for kn = (k+1)f) The paper proves impossibility only for the border case kn = (k+1)f and for kn < (k+1)f relies on "Theorem 2 tightly captures the impossibility", which does not transfer. Impact. The paper's partitioning argument works unchanged for all kn ≤ (k+1)f, with k+1 groups of size n−f (initDead_impossible). Details. Theorem 2's failure model is harsher than initial crashes, so its impossibility does not transfer, and its bound (n−1)/(n−f) is not f/(n−f). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing on top of CSLib's FLP model (Cslib.FLP.Algorithm), with n processes, deterministic state machines and reliable, unordered channels. A step receives one message and atomically updates the state, sends messages and possibly decides. A crash means the process stops receiving; crashes are clean (no partial last broadcast). This adversary is weaker than the paper's, so our impossibilities imply the paper's. KAlgorithm lets a process have an input in an arbitrary V. Messages arriving before a process' first step are buffered (only restricts schedules). k-set agreement: k-agreement and validity in every reachable state, for faulty processes too; termination of every non-faulty process in every admissible infinite run. Failure models: InitDead f (up to f processes never take a step, all others correct), OneCrash f (Theorem 2's pattern: f − 1 initially dead plus one more crash) and Crash f (CSLib's runs with ≤ f faulty processes). Theorem 2 is proved for asynchronous processes (Corollary 5's setting) with Theorem 2's failure pattern. The paper's version with synchronous processes and atomic broadcast relies on [DDS87, Table I] and is not formalized. Theorem 1 is formalized twice. Abstract.lean has the generic version (a model is a set of runs with views, Definition 2 is equality of views); there the literal statement is refuted and a corrected one proved. theorem1_async is the concrete asynchronous instance: (C) is CSLib's FLP theorem, and the other conditions follow from solo runs, merging and lifting.
