(Δ + o(Δ))-Edge-Coloring and Clique Decompositions — PODC 2017 Leonid Barenboim, Michael Elkin, Tzalik Maimon. Deterministic Distributed (Δ + o(Δ))-Edge-Coloring, and Vertex-Coloring of Graphs with Bounded Diversity. PODC 2017. DOI 10.1145/3087801.3087812. Formalized version: arXiv 1610.06759 v1 (full version with appendix); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The combinatorial correctness of the clique-decomposition colouring (Lemmas 2.1–2.3, Theorems 2.4–2.6), its colour count D^{x+1} S (Theorem 3.2), Lemma 5.1, Theorem 5.2 (Δ + O(a) colours) and Theorem 5.3 (Δ + o(Δ) colours when a = o(Δ)) all hold. But the last step of Theorem 5.4, which carries the abstract's polylogarithmic-time claim through Corollary 5.5, does not give the stated colour count, and it is not repaired. No running time was checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 5.4, last stage of the proof The last stage colours subgraphs of in-degree ≤ Δ^{1/x} and out-degree ≤ â^{1/x} "with Δ^{1/x} + â^{1/x} + 3 colours by Theorem 5.2", but Theorem 5.2 does not give that many colours. Impact. The bound (Δ^{1/x} + â^{1/x} + 3)^x feeds Corollary 5.5's Δ(1 + O(1/log Δ)) colours, and through it the polylogarithmic-time claim. Nothing about Theorem 5.4 is proved in Lean, so the step stands unrepaired. Details. Theorem 5.2 only gives Δ' + O(a') colours (Δ' + (2+ε)a' − 1 with the paper's own procedure), and those subgraphs can have total degree up to Δ^{1/x} + â^{1/x}. So the exact constant +3 in (Δ^{1/x} + â^{1/x} + 3)^x is not justified as written. ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.2 for D = 1: the proof assumes D ≥ 2, which the statement does not; 𝒜_1 produces up to ⌊√S⌋⌈S/⌊√S⌋⌉ colours, e.g. 6 > 5 for S = 5. The graph is a disjoint union of cliques, and the S colours of the statement are reached by the colour reduction the paper allows. Our theorem_3_2 assumes D ≥ 2. The (p,q)-clique-decomposition is defined with clique size "is q"; "at most q" is meant. Typos The proof of Lemma 2.3 (i) speaks of "a clique Q of G'" where a clique of G_i is meant. The heading of Appendix B reads "Proof of Lemma 3.2"; there is no Lemma 3.2, and the proof is that of Theorem 3.2. "See Theorem 5.1" before Theorem 5.4: there is no Theorem 5.1, and Lemma 5.1 is meant. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3.2, colour bound (appendix proof, inductive step for 𝒜_2) The inductive step's inequality (D(t−1)+1)·D^{i+1}⌈S/t⌉ ≤ D^{i+2} S is justified only for i ≥ 2, and for 𝒜_2 (i = 1, t = ⌊√S⌋) it fails for arbitrarily large S (paper_inductive_step_fails). Impact. The proof as written does not establish 𝒜_2, but the parameter the same proof states for the running time closes the step. We prove the bound with a stronger invariant, for every S ≥ 1 and without colour reduction (theorem_3_2, theorem_3_2_algA). Details. The proof builds 𝒜_{i+1} from 𝒜_i with t = ⌊S^{1/(i+1)}⌋. It uses only the induction hypothesis "𝒜_i uses D^{i+1} S' colours". Then it claims (D(t−1)+1)·D^{i+1}⌈S/t⌉ ≤ D^{i+2} S "for S larger than some constant, since (D−1)(S/t) > Dt because t = ⌊S^{1/(i+1)}⌋ and i ≥ 2". But 𝒜_2 is the case i = 1. There t = ⌊√S⌋, and the inequality fails for arbitrarily large S. For example, D = 2, S = 31, t = 5 gives 9·4·7 = 252 > 248 = 8·31 (paper_inductive_step_fails). In the running-time part the proof uses a different parameter, t = ⌊S^{1/(i+2)}⌋. With that choice the step works for S above a constant (constant S is covered by §3's direct D(S−1)+1-colouring), so the gap is repairable from the paper itself. Repair. The bound is true for the actual algorithm. For D ≥ 2, the invariant pal_j · (D·S_j − 1) ≤ D^j (D S − 1) holds whenever every level uses some t with t² ≤ S_cur. Here pal_j is the number of subgraphs after j levels and S_j the current clique bound. So 𝒜_x uses fewer than D^{x+1}S colours, for all S ≥ 1, with either choice of t and with no colour-reduction rounds (theorem_3_2, theorem_3_2_algA). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic synchronous message passing (LOCAL) with unique IDs (LinearOrder V), finite simple graphs. We verify the combinatorial correctness of the algorithms: properness, decomposition properties, colour counts, the round schedule, and the consistency of parallel choices. Running-time claims of the Õ(·) form are not formalized. The subroutines are black boxes given by their output specifications: the (Δ+1)-vertex colouring of [17] is IsDeltaColorer. Non-vacuity: identifiers followed by CSLib's standard colour reduction, isDeltaColorer_reductionColorer; the H-partition of [4] is IsHPartition. It is instantiated with the peeling algorithm formalized in Papers/PODC2010/ArbdefectiveColoring/HPartition.lean: degree 3a (ε = 1) and L = 2(⌊log₂ n⌋+1) sets (exists_hPartition); the edge colourings of the H-sets (via [17] or §4) are given as any proper colouring with k₀ colours. Greedy 2d − 1 colours: exists_hSet_coloring. Clique identification: IsCliqueCover G 𝒬 D S. It is a family of cliques covering every edge, with every vertex in at most D members and every member of size at most S. This covers both the paper's "consistent identification" (e.g. stars of a line graph) and all maximal cliques (maximalCliques, diversity). The bound "every clique of G[U_i] has size ≤ q" is proved when 𝒬 contains every clique (CoversCliques, true for maximal cliques). Algorithm 1 is unrolled level by level (stages). The parallel recursive calls on the colour classes G_i form one call on their disjoint union sameColor G φ. The output pair ⟨φ, ψ⟩ is encoded as φ·B + ψ. "Uses N colours" means all colours are < N. The round-by-round procedures of Lemma 5.1 and Theorem 5.2 are formalized as a schedule (EdgeSchedule). Edges inside A/B, resp. inside the H-sets, are pre-coloured. The crossing edge ab (h a < h b) is coloured in round (ℓ−1−h a)·d + lab a b by b. A run is any colouring obeying the local rule (EdgeSchedule.Follows), so we quantify over all of the paper's "any assignment of distinct available colours". Every run is proper, runs exist, and two adjacent edges coloured in the same round are chosen by their common endpoint. Theorem 5.3's Lean conclusion is existential ("some proper edge colouring with N colours", which alone would also follow from Vizing). The algorithm is captured by the colouring the proof builds (⟨φ, ψ⟩ from runs of Theorem 5.2) and by theorem_5_3_combine, which holds for every such φ, ψ. Orientation connector (§5): the acyclic orientation is a rank r. Incoming/outgoing edges are grouped by ID into groups of sIn/sOut, with virtual vertices V × Fin (m+1). The paper's k = ⌈√Δ⌉ groups of size ⌈Δ/k⌉ become groups of size ⌊√Δ⌋+1, and similarly for √d. Asymptotically this is the same. Remarks on the paper (not mistakes). Theorem 3.2, base case 𝒜_1: the chain of inequalities is valid (the +(D−1)² term is absorbed by the −1 in 2⌊√S⌋ − 1, since t + k ≥ 2⌊√S⌋ and D(D−1) ≥ (D−1)²). It is not tight: the 2 colour-reduction rounds are unnecessary, the count is already ≤ D(DS − 1) < D²S (the case x = 1 of theorem_3_2). Theorem 2.4's S/t^x + 2 can be sharpened to ⌈S/t^x⌉ ≤ S/t^x + 1. Algorithm 1 passes ⌈S/t⌉ as the next S, and the nested ceilings equal ⌈S/t^x⌉. §4: (2t−1)(2k−1) ≤ 4Δ already holds for t = ⌊√Δ⌋, so the extra reduction round is unnecessary (theorem_4_1_count_one). Disjoint-Access Parallelism and Wait-Freedom in Universal Constructions — PODC 2012 Faith Ellen, Panagiota Fatourou, Eleftherios Kosmas, Alessia Milani, Corentin Travers. Universal Constructions that Ensure Disjoint-Access Parallelism and Wait-Freedom. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332457. Formalized version: the full version, HAL research report hal-00697198v2 (May 2012, 34 pp.); no arXiv version. Numbering follows the full version. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The impossibility result (Theorem 5: no feebly disjoint-access parallel universal construction is wait-free) holds, and its proof (Lemma 4 and the construction of the infinite execution α') goes through as written, apart from assumptions the statement leaves implied and an ambiguous wording of Assumption 3. The positive half of the paper's main point, the construction DAP-UC and its correctness (Theorem 6), was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 5 omits "linearizable", "satisfying Assumption 3" and "with at least two processes", all of which the proof uses. The surrounding text and the abstract state the first two, and one process is degenerate. The Lean theorems take them as hypotheses (theorem_5_list, theorem_5). Assumption 3 speaks of "the sets of base objects read from and written to during any solo execution of a sequence of consecutive instances"; the proof needs these sets per instance (it uses B(ℓ), the objects written by the ℓ-th instance alone). The per-instance reading is the one we formalize. Typos Section 4 calls the pointer to the first node L.first (Section 3: first/last), while the code of Figure 6 calls it L.start/L.end. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, CSLib's Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl: deterministic processes, every step applies one primitive to one base object, base objects are arbitrary sequential objects (registers, CAS, LL/SC, …), the scheduler is arbitrary. Crashes need no extra structure: wait-freedom (Impl.WaitFree) quantifies over all infinite executions, so a process that stops taking steps is a crashed one. Every process may invoke every operation. Randomized implementations are not covered (the paper reduces them to deterministic ones by fixing the coin tosses). A primitive is trivial if it never changes the state of its base object (ObjSpec.ReadOnly); two executions contend on b if both apply a primitive to b and one of them is non-trivial (Contend). Base objects cannot see the caller, so LL/SC is encoded with a version number kept by the caller (versionedLLSC: LL reads the value and version and is trivial, SC is a compare-and-increment on the version); this gives the paper's classification. (CSLib's llscObj keeps the link set in the object's state, making LL non-trivial; with that encoding feeble DAP would be a stronger hypothesis.) A sequential data structure (SeqDS) is its sequential specification together with the data items each operation accesses from each state (its data set, determined by the code). A universal construction maps every data structure to an implementation (UniversalConstruction). The list of Figures 5/6 is listDS: states are lists of keys, data items are L.start, L.end and the nodes; the data sets are read off the code of Figure 6. Definition 1 (FeeblyDAP): for every quiescent configuration C reached by an execution α all of whose linearizations end in the same state s, solo executions (complete or partial) from C of two operations by two different processes whose data sets from s are disjoint do not contend. Assumption 3 (ImplValueOblivious): from every reachable quiescent configuration, the base objects accessed and the base objects written by each instance of a solo sequence of instances of a value-oblivious operation do not depend on the parameters (UniversalConstruction.ValueObliviousAssumption: for every value-oblivious operation of every data structure). Linearizability is CSLib's Impl.Linearizable. Proof remarks. Self-Stabilizing Leader Election in Regular Graphs — PODC 2020 Hsueh-Ping Chen, Ho-Lin Chen. Self-Stabilizing Leader Election in Regular Graphs. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405733. Formalized version: the proceedings version (no arXiv version exists); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. SS-EulerCycle (Theorem 3.3), which answers the open question, fails as printed because no configuration is output-stable, but a natural one-line repair saves it: we prove Theorem 3.3 on every connected 2k-regular graph, assuming (as the paper does) that the Ring-Protocol of [11] solves SSLE on directed rings. SS-Tree (Theorem 4.3), the O(k¹²) protocol, is false: there is a configuration in which every node is a root, hence a leader, forever, no detector ever fires, and no repair is proved. The odd-degree and general-graph extensions (Section 3.5) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 4.3 and Lemma 4.2 (SS-Tree, MultipleRootDetector) SS-Tree does not detect multiple roots: in a configuration where every node is a root with a "ghost" parent colour and all coins are +1, every node stays a leader forever (ssTree_all_roots_forever, ssTree_not_solvesSSLE). Impact. The detector needs a redesign, not a typo fix, and no repaired SS-Tree is proved, so the O(k¹²) protocol is not saved. The failure occurs for every k ≥ 2, every graph of maximum degree ≤ k (e.g. K_{k+1}, ssTree_fails_on_complete), every neighbourhood-injective k²-colouring and every ring protocol; it also fails with probability 1 (ssTree_prob_zero). Details. MultipleRootDetector only moves coins between a parent and its child. A root tosses only when its coin is 0, and a root's coin never returns to 0 (only a child is reset), so the re-tossing that the proof relies on ("there must be a time when two roots toss different coin values") never happens. Counterexample: let every node be a root whose parentColor is the colour of none of its neighbours, with all coins +1, counters 0, ring states and copies non-leaders, and SS-TwoHop memory consistent. Then there is no parent–child pair. No coin ever moves. The ghost parents are never checked, because roots do not count. CycleDetector never runs the ring protocol and only copies non-leader states. Every node stays a leader forever. ❌ Lemma 4.2, proof (case analysis) Lemma 4.2's case analysis is incomplete: it forgets the invalid configurations that already have one leader but are not output-stable (a cycle elsewhere in the pedigree graph, ghost parents, a bad colouring). Impact. The lemma is not repaired, because SS-Tree itself is not; no remedy can exist without a working detector. ❌ Lemma 4.1, proof (chain argument; existence of a stable SS-Tree configuration) Lemma 4.1's proof does not cover CycleDetector's dynamics, so the lemma is unestablished (not formalized, not refuted). Impact. The step stands unrepaired, and SS-Tree already fails by Theorem 4.3. Whether a leader can appear depends on the internals of [11]. Details. The proof cuts a chain out of a stable ring of [11]: such a chain never creates a leader. But nodes unmark at random and leave stale loopChild/loopParent flags. A re-marked parent then copies a fresh ringState and runs the ring protocol with a child whose copy has already evolved. These mixed configurations are not reachable on the static chain. 🔧 Theorem 3.3 and Lemma 3.1 (SS-EulerCycle, Protocol 1 as printed) No configuration of Protocol 1 as printed is output-stable on any 2k-regular graph (k ≥ 1), because the coherence check raises an error whenever the scheduler lets the head of a virtual edge initiate (literal_not_solvesSSLE, literal_fails_on_complete). Impact. The printed protocol fails whatever the ring protocol, but a one-line change fixes it: use the virtual edge in either role. With this repair we prove Theorem 3.3 (repaired_solvesSSLE). Details. The coherence check accepts an interaction only if there is a virtual edge from the initiator to the responder; otherwise u.errFlag ← True. An Euler cycle traverses each edge in one direction, but both nodes of an edge get to initiate. We show that from every configuration an error is reachable. Either some ordered pair of neighbours has no forward virtual edge (one interaction suffices). Or all of them have one; then a node has 2k neighbours but only k successor slots, so two neighbours share a colour, and the paper's own sequence (A,B),(A,C),(A,B) makes SS-TwoHop recolour and break a virtual edge. The erroneous initiator then takes a random state, so its output changes. Repair. If there is no virtual edge u → v but there is one v → u, run the Ring-Protocol and SS-Token on it with v's virtual node as the ring initiator. With this repair we prove Theorem 3.3 (repaired_solvesSSLE). ✏️ Slips Lemma 2.1 omits two hypotheses that the paper states only in the prose: a valid output-stable configuration exists, and error-detected configurations can reach it. We prove the lemma with both hypotheses explicit (derc_lemma). The SS-TwoHop guard is garbled: it demands v.prevColor = v.color instead of u.prevColor = v.color. We use Sudo et al.'s "matching colours, different bits". "2-hop colouring" must mean "the neighbours of each node have distinct colours"; for that, 4k² colours suffice. Typos The indentation of Protocols 5–6 is lost. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.2, proof (repaired SS-EulerCycle) Lemma 3.2's proof is a sketch that uses several facts without proof. Impact. For the repaired SS-EulerCycle we prove everything Lemma 3.2 uses (multi_reach, err_reach_all). Details. The missing facts: the slot-counting argument making coherent configurations a permutation of virtual nodes (vperm), two virtual rings sharing a node, convergence of SS-Token (TokenRing.run_legit), and "an error-detected configuration reaches every configuration" (err_reach_all). Lemma 2.1 is used in the form derc_lemma. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Population protocols on a graph G (GProtocol). An interaction is an ordered pair of adjacent nodes (initiator, responder); both orders are scheduled. There are no IDs and no orientation. Randomized transitions are modelled by their support: δ p q is the set of possible outcomes. This includes the paper's RandState, random bits and random colours. Self-stabilization follows the paper. Global fairness is the standard notion of Angluin et al. SolvesSSLE: from any initial configuration, every globally fair execution reaches a valid output-stable configuration. We prove this is equivalent to reachability (solvesSSLE_iff) and to stabilization with probability 1 under any random scheduler supported on the steps (Cslib.TransitionSystem.tendsto_compl_of_reach, prob_eq_zero_of_not_reach). The Ring-Protocol of [11] is an arbitrary nondeterministic protocol with a leader output. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767413. Formalized version: arXiv 1404.4344 v4 (same text and numbering as the proceedings PDF). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The one false statement, the constant in Observation 3.2, is saved by changing that constant (⌈d⁺/2⌉ − d for d⁺ − 2d), and the max printed in Observations 3.6 and 3.8 is a typo for min. All three lower bounds of Section 4 (Theorems 4.1–4.3) and Lemmas 3.5 and 3.7 are true, and the proofs of the lower bounds needed only local repairs. The paper's main upper bounds (the spectral Theorems 2.3 and 3.3, and Table 1, which rests on them) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Observation 3.2 (SEND([x/d⁺]) is a good (d⁺ − 2d)-balancer) SEND([x/d⁺]) is not a good (d⁺ − 2d)-balancer: for d = 1, d◦ = 4, x = 3 only two self-loops get ⌈x/d⁺⌉, where self-preference with s = 3 needs three (observation_3_2_false). Impact. The correct value is about half the claimed one: it is a good s-balancer exactly for 1 ≤ s ≤ ⌈d⁺/2⌉ − d (sendRound_isGood_iff). That is still s ≥ 1 for d⁺ > 2d and s = Ω(d) for d⁺ ≥ 3d, which is all that Table 1 uses (the table also rests on Theorem 3.3, not checked). Details. When x/d⁺ is rounded up, the d original edges use up d of the e = x mod d⁺ extra tokens. Only e − d self-loops then get ⌈x/d⁺⌉, but self-preference asks for min{s, e} of them. In the smallest case the original edge gets [3/5] = 1 token and the four self-loops share the remaining two, so two self-loops get ⌈3/5⌉ = 1. Self-preference with s = 3 needs min{3, 3} = 3. The paper does not fix the tie rule; the counterexample has no tie, so it refutes every reading. Repair. We prove the exact characterisation: on a d-regular graph with d < d◦, SEND([x/d⁺]) is a good s-balancer iff 1 ≤ s ≤ ⌈d⁺/2⌉ − d. So, with halves rounded up, the paper's claim holds iff d◦ = d + 1. Because ⌈d⁺/2⌉ − d ≥ (d◦ − d)/2, this is enough for the uses in Table 1. (sendRound_isGood_iff) ✏️ Slips Observations 3.6 and 3.8 print max instead of min: the bounds on the potential drop over [t, t'], ∑_{u∈U} max{s, x_t(u) − cd⁺} (respectively max{s, cd⁺ + s − x_t(u)}), are false already on K₂ (observation_3_6_false, observation_3_8_false). Take K₂ with two self-loops per node and the good 2-balancer SEND(⌊x/3⌋), c = 1 and loads (4, 0). Node 0 drops to load 3 = cd⁺ and φ(1) drops by only 1, but the printed bound demands max{2, 1} = 2. 3.8 fails the same way, with c = 0 and loads (1, 3). Appendix B.4 actually uses min{s, ·}, and we prove the min versions (observation_3_6, observation_3_8). Observation 3.8 also prints φ_t instead of φ'_t on the right-hand side. Theorem 4.1 needs a connected graph (otherwise the diameter is infinite). Theorem 4.2 needs d < n. Proof of Theorem 4.2: the neighbour indices are written "mod d" where "mod |C|" is meant. Proof of Theorem 4.2: the paper's offset set for the circulant graph contains 0, i.e. a self-loop. Typos The introduction says that removing self-loops yields Ω(d · diam) (Theorem 4.3). Theorem 4.3 gives Ω(d · ϕ), where 2ϕ + 1 is the odd girth. The two agree on odd cycles. Every node of the shortest odd cycle through u at distance ϕ − 1 from u is such a node. No rotor-router step produces this; for example, on the 5-cycle the neighbour of u sends L − 2 and L. For ϕ = 1 every value is L and the discrepancy is 0. Repair. Replacing "or" by "and" fixes the construction, i.e. the offset becomes max{ϕ − min(b(v₁), b(v₂)), 0}. We also make two smaller fixes. The proof's "odd cycle u ⇝ v₁ → v₂ ⇝ u" is only an odd closed walk; we prove that an odd closed walk contains an odd cycle that is no longer. And u can be any vertex. (theorem_4_3) 🔧 Theorem 4.2 (stateless lower bound, d ≤ 3) The paper's clique of ⌊d/2⌋ nodes with load ℓ = |C| − 1 gives discrepancy ⌊d/2⌋ − 1, which is 0 for d ≤ 3. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a larger clique (theorem_4_2). Details. The proof needs the stateless algorithm to be anonymous: every node uses the same p◦, p₁, …, p_d, and the adversary chooses the port numbering. We formalize the theorem in that model. Repair. The formalization Model. (Model.lean) Synchronous discrete diffusion on a finite simple graph G (usually d-regular) with dl = d◦ self-loops per node, d⁺ = deg + dl. No failures, no randomness. Formalized version: the HAL deposit hal-01178651v1 (July 2015). Its numbering is that of the proceedings. There is no arXiv version. The full version cited as [6] ("Tech Report 2025, IRISA, 2015"; 2025 is the report number) is not available to us, so the proofs of Lemmas 1 and 2 ("Proof in [6]") were reconstructed. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The EA object of Figure 3 is not live: Lemma 2 (EA-Termination) and Theorem 3 are false, so the consensus algorithm of Figure 4 does not terminate and Theorem 4 is false, even in a synchronous run in which the only faulty process crashes at the start. The proof of Lemma 3 fails as well and nothing we proved repairs the algorithm, so the paper does not establish its main claim that an eventual ⟨t+1⟩bisource suffices for signature-free Byzantine consensus. Theorems 1 and 2 (CB-broadcast, adopt-commit), Lemma 1 and the safety part of Theorem 4 are correct and are proved. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 2, Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 (EA-Termination, consensus termination) Figure 3 can block forever, so EA-Termination (Lemma 2, Theorem 3) and the termination of the consensus algorithm of Figure 4 (Theorem 4) are false: in a synchronous run with n = 7, t = 2 and a coordinator that crashes at the start, no correct process ever decides (lemma2_false, theorem4_termination_false). Impact. The paper does not establish its main claim that an eventual ⟨t+1⟩bisource suffices for signature-free Byzantine consensus. A local repair unblocks this run, but its correctness is open (see Lemma 3 below). Details. A correct process that returns at line 4 never executes line 5, so its timer[r] is never set. It then broadcasts EA_RELAY[r] only if it receives EA_COORD[r] from the coordinator (lines 15–19). If coord(r) is faulty and silent, these processes never relay. The processes that did not return at line 4 can then wait at line 6 forever for n − t relays. Counterexample (n = 7, t = 2, m = ⌊(n−(t+1))/t⌋ = 2): Process p₁ = coord(1) crashes at the start. Three correct processes propose true and three propose false. The run is synchronous (all delays ≤ 1), so every correct process is a ⟨t+1⟩bisource. CB[0] returns each process its own proposal (three estimates true, three false). CB[1] (EA round 1) gives aux = true to five processes and false to the sixth. Two processes see five true messages first and return at line 4. The other four see a mixed first five, set their timers and relay ⊥. Only 4 < n − t = 5 relays are ever sent, so the four wait forever at line 6 of round 1. The two others wait forever inside the CB of AC_OBJECT[1], which has only two AC_PROP messages, fewer than t + 1 = 3. So in a run of Figure 4 where every correct process invokes EA_propose(1, −), four invocations never return, and no correct process ever decides. The paper's proof of Theorem 4 relies on EA-Termination in exactly this situation ("it follows from the EA-Termination and AC-Termination properties that they all terminate the first round"). Repair. Set the timer before returning at line 4, so that every correct process relays. With it, the same run decides (repaired_blocking_run_decides). We do not know whether the repaired algorithm is correct, because of the next item. ❌ Lemma 3 (EA-Eventual agreement; unestablished) The proof of Lemma 3 ignores processes that return at line 4: in a round of exactly the kind the proof chooses, one correct process returns true at line 4 while the others return the coordinator's false (lemma3_proof_fails). Impact. Refutes the proof, not the statement (Lemma 3 needs infinitely many such rounds); whether Lemma 3 holds, with or without the repair above, is open. It also leaves the repaired algorithm unproven. Details. The proof picks a round r > 2δ coordinated by the bisource p_ℓ, with F(r) ⊆ C, and concludes that every correct process returns the coordinator's value w "after executing lines 7–10". Processes that return at line 4 never reach line 7, and they may return a different value. Lean witness, for the EA object alone: n = 4, t = 1, a synchronous run. Round 15 has coord(15) = p₃ correct and F(15) equal to the set of correct processes. The coordinator is a bisource with X⁻ = X⁺ ⊆ F(15), so it is a round of exactly the kind the proof chooses. The Byzantine process RB-broadcasts EA_PROP1(false) consistently and sends EA_PROP2[15](true). Process p₁ returns true at line 4. The coordinator champions its own false, which p₂ and p₃ return. ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 3: Claim C uses p_k ∈ X⁻_ℓ ⊆ F(r), but the chosen round only guarantees X⁺_ℓ ⊆ F(r) ⊆ C. Choose instead r with X⁻_ℓ ∪ X⁺_ℓ ⊆ F(r) ⊆ C. Such rounds exist infinitely often: |X⁻ ∪ X⁺| ≤ 2t + 1 ≤ n − t because both sets contain ℓ. Our lemma3_proof_fails round satisfies the stronger choice. This point was not formalized further. Typos Claim C says the timer is set "at line 8"; it is set at line 5. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4, CONS-Agreement (use of EA-Validity and AC-Obligation) The proof applies EA-Validity and AC-Obligation in round r + 1, whose premises say that all correct processes propose v, although some correct processes may never reach that round; Theorem 2 even assumes that each correct process invokes AC_propose(). Impact. Statement true; both properties have to be restated for the correct processes that invoke the object. Repair. We state and prove both properties in that form, which Figures 2 and 3 satisfy, and the proof then goes through (theorem2, lemma1, Fig4.agreement). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Abstract layer, mirroring the paper's modular proofs (Basic, CB, AC, EA, Consensus): n processes, a faulty set B with |B| ≤ t < n/3, time ℕ. RB-broadcast is a primitive given by its four properties, over time-indexed delivery traces (RBSpec). CB, AC and EA are specified by their properties on what correct processes observe (CBSpec, ACSpec, EAValidity). Figures 1 and 2 are given as rules on traces; all "pick any" choices are adversarial. They are proved to meet their specifications. Figure 4 is proved safe from the object specifications, and live assuming the EA specification. The proof of Theorem 4 uses that cb_valid sets only grow, and that rounds take time (otherwise CB[0]'s "never updated after round r₀" can fail). Neither is stated. Storage-Cost Lower Bounds for Shared Memory Emulation — PODC 2016 Viveck R. Cadambe, Zhiying Wang, Nancy Lynch. Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds on the Storage Cost of Shared Memory Emulation. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933118. Formalized version: arXiv 1605.06844 v2; numbering follows it. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The paper claims bounds that make "no assumption on the structure of the algorithm", but with reliable FIFO channels, also in the paper's I/O-automaton reading, a gossip-free, atomic, live streaming relay with 36 states per server, independently of |V|, keeps the value in the reader's incoming channels and refutes all six bounds (Theorems 4.1, 5.1, B.1 and Corollaries 4.2, 5.2, B.2). The proofs assume, without saying so, that servers never send messages to an idle reader; with that assumption added (ReaderQuiet), Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2 and the Singleton-type Theorem B.1 without gossip hold, and no bound with gossip is proved. Theorem 6.5 and non-FIFO channels were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorems 4.1, 5.1, B.1 and Corollaries 4.2, 5.2, B.2 (storage lower bounds, FIFO channels) All six bounds are false with reliable FIFO channels: a gossip-free, atomic, live relay emulation keeps the value in the reader's incoming channels, so its servers need only constant state (1 state, or 36 in the I/O-automaton version), independently of |V| (not_theorem41, not_theorem41_ioa, relay_counterexample, stream_counterexample). Impact. The paper's main results fail as stated. They hold under the unstated assumption that servers never send to an idle reader (ReaderQuiet): Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2 and the counting form of Theorem B.1 without gossip are proved then. Non-FIFO and multi-reader versions are not refuted. Details. The storage cost counts only server states. Channels and client states are free. Here is the relay algorithm for 2f < n and any value set V. Write number t with value v sends W t v to all servers. It returns after n − f acks. A server that receives W t v forwards F t v to the reader and acks A t to the writer. A server that receives the read query Q j answers D j. Its local state never changes. The reader always records the largest write index it has seen in an F message, with its value. Read j sends Q j to all servers. It returns the recorded value after n − f answers D j. By FIFO, when the reader gets D j from a server, it already got every F that server sent earlier. Quorum intersection then gives regularity, in fact atomicity. Liveness holds with up to f server crashes and any client crashes. There is no gossip, and |S_i| = 1 for every server. So the left-hand sides of all six bounds are 0 while the right-hand sides are positive. Lean instance: n = 5, f = 2, V = Fin 4. The theorems assume regularity, so the counterexample is more than they need. (not_theorem41, not_corollary42, not_theorem51, not_corollary52, not_theoremB1, not_corollaryB2; the algorithm: relay_counterexample) Where the proofs break: in Section 4.3.1 "the readers and the channels from and to the readers do not perform any actions" during α, and Lemma 4.8(a) concludes that reader channels are the same at both critical points. If a server sends to the reader during α, the write cannot complete without that channel taking the message. Then the reader-side state at Q₁, Q₂ is not determined by the server states, and Claim 4.9 fails. Appendix B (Theorem B.1) has the same gap: "all channels are empty" ignores what the live reader already received. This is a false statement, not a proof gap. I/O-automaton reading (formalized). In the multi-send relay above, one server step receives W t v and sends two messages. In the paper's I/O-automaton model each send is a separate output action, so a server would have to store the pending F t v. The streaming relay (Stream.lean) respects this restriction (IOASends: an input step of a server sends nothing, a spontaneous step sends at most one message). The writer streams the bits of its values to each server, one bit at a time, waiting for an acknowledgement before sending the next bit. A server's state is (pending bit, pending ack, pending answer, turn), 36 states in all. Its spontaneous steps take turns forwarding the bit to the reader, acknowledging, and answering queries. The reader reassembles B-bit blocks per server and keeps the newest complete one. It sends one outstanding query per server and re-queries after a stale answer. It is proved atomic, live (2f < n) and gossip-free. With n = 5, f = 2, V = Fin 16 → Bool (|V| = 2^16), all six bounds fail for it. (not_theorem41_ioa, not_corollary42_ioa, not_theorem51_ioa, not_corollary52_ioa, not_theoremB1_ioa, not_corollaryB2_ioa; the algorithm: stream_counterexample) Scope. Both counterexamples need FIFO channels. The paper says only "reliable, asynchronous", and reliable FIFO is the standard channel of Lynch's I/O-automaton framework, which the proofs use. They also use the theorems' single reader. See Not formalized. below for the other channel and reader settings. Repair. Theorem 4.1 holds when servers do not push to an idle reader. We add ReaderQuiet: if the reader takes no step, no server has sent it anything. It follows from "servers send to the reader only when processing a reader message" (readerQuiet_of_repliesOnly), which ABD-style algorithms satisfy. With it, the paper's proof goes through. We prove |V|(|V|−1) ≤ (∏_{𝒩}|S_i|)·∑_{𝒩}|S_i| for every 𝒩 of at least n − f servers, which is slightly stronger than the paper's ∏·(N−f)·max. We also prove the logarithmic form, Corollary 4.2, and the counting form |V| ≤ ∏_{𝒩}|S_i| of the Singleton-type Theorem B.1 without gossip. (theorem41_count, theorem41, corollary42, theoremB1_count) ❌ Theorem 5.1, proof (Definition 5.3, Section 5.3.2) Definition 5.3 "delivers all messages" between servers, but with gossip this need not terminate, and at R₂ the servers other than s, s' also receive messages that s, s' send during delivery, so they need not be in the same state as at R₁, and the claim that all channels are empty is unjustified (also in Appendix B.3). Impact. This step is broken independently of the reader issue, and no version with gossip is proved: our repair of Theorem B.1 needs NoGossip for the same reason. With FIFO channels the statement is false anyway. This gap is not formalized. ✏️ Slips Lemmas 4.4/4.6 (writer-crash step assumes lossy channels from crashed clients): after a critical point, the valency executions delay the writer's messages "indefinitely", justified as "indistinguishable from a fair execution where the write client fails before sending the messages", but those messages were already sent. With channels reliable even from crashed processes, liveness does not guarantee the read terminates, so the step needs channels from crashed processes to be lossy. Our model (CSLib ChannelFailures) does not require them to deliver, which matches the paper's use (exists_canon_ret, exists_crit). N − f ≥ 1 is implicit (we assume f < n). The definition of critical points (Lemmas 4.6, 5.6, Definitions 4.7, 5.7) ranges over {0, 2, …, M−1} instead of {0, 1, …, M−1}. Typos The hypothesis f ≥ 2 of Theorem 4.1 is never used. The counting argument works for every f, and Corollary 4.2's total-storage bound needs only f ≥ 1 (we assume 1 ≤ f < n). In Theorem 4.1's proof, Case II says the read in γ "should return v₂" because Q₂ is 2-valent. It actually follows from Lemma 4.5 together with Q₂ not being 1-valent. P₁ = P^{(v₁,v₁)} in Section 4.3.2 should be P^{(v₁,v₂)}, and "Definition 6.8" in Case (II) of Theorem 5.1 should be Definition 5.3. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing, CSLib/Podc Cslib.ChannelFailures: deterministic processes, reliable FIFO channels, and a step receives one message (or is an invocation or a spontaneous tick) and sends any list of messages. The I/O-automaton restriction for servers is the predicate Stream.IOASends. Client states are not counted, so clients may buffer outputs for free. Nodes: n servers, one writer, one reader (Node n). The object is CSLib's register V v₀. The environment is SWSR (EvOk). Crash failures are not events. A crashed process takes finitely many steps, and channels out of a crashed process need not deliver. Fairness: correct processes step infinitely often, and channels between correct processes deliver everything. Safety IsRegular is Lamport regularity of every finite execution, via a reads-from index per read. IsAtomic is CSLib linearizability. Liveness Live A f is the paper's: in every fair execution with at most f server failures and any number of client failures, every operation of a non-crashed client returns. Storage: StateBound A S says server i's state always lies in the finite set S i. Cost is log₂|S i|, with maxStorage and totalStorage. NoGossip says servers never send to servers (Theorem 4.1's hypothesis). ReaderQuiet is our repair hypothesis. Only deterministic algorithms are covered (the paper allows nondeterministic IOAs). The counterexample is deterministic, so the refutation is unaffected. Main results in Lean. Broadcasting in Noisy Radio Networks — PODC 2017 Keren Censor-Hillel, Bernhard Haeupler, D. Ellis Hershkowitz, Goran Zuzic. Broadcasting in Noisy Radio Networks. PODC 2017. DOI 10.1145/3087801.3087808. Formalized version: arXiv 1705.07369 v1 (full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The formalized results all hold, for every constant p ∈ (0, 1): the star gap (Lemmas 15 and 16, Theorem 17: with receiver faults, adaptive routing on the star has throughput Θ(1/log n), coding has Θ(1), so the coding gap is Θ(log n)) and the sender-fault transformation for routing (Lemma 25). The proof of the routing lower bound in Lemma 15 does not work and had to be replaced by a new coupling argument, and the upper-bound half of Lemma 15 relies on an independence that the paper never justifies. Much of the paper's main point was not checked: the broadcast algorithms of Section 4, the worst-case gap, and Lemma 26, where we noticed a gap but did not decide it. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 15: Pr(Hᵢ ≥ t) = (1/2)^t should be (1/2)^{t-1}; the domination still holds. Lemma 25: "sends k'₀ = k₀x messages in (τ-ε)^{-1}(1-p)^{-1}(1+η) rounds" is missing the factor k'₀, and the closing "k'₀(τ-ε)(1-p)(1+η)^{-1} rounds" has the exponents inverted. Lemma 15 for p = 0: the model allows p ∈ [0, 1), but with p = 0 the star has throughput 1, not Θ(1/log n). We read "with receiver faults" as p > 0. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 15, impossibility half (Ω(k log n) rounds for routing on the star) The proof is internally inconsistent: it proves E[Xᵢ] ≥ (log n)/4, then uses E[Xᵢ] ≤ (log n)/4, and applies Chernoff bounds to variables that are not sums of independent indicators. Impact. Statement true; the argument is replaced by a coupling proof (star_prob_delivered_le, star_routingRounds_ge). Details. The proof first proves E[Xᵢ] ≥ (log n)/4, where Xᵢ is the number of broadcasts of mᵢ. A few lines later it uses "since E[Xᵢ] ≤ (log n)/4". The thresholds change mid-argument ((log n)/16, then (log n)/8, then (log n)/16) and do not follow from "(k log n)/4 rounds". It applies Chernoff to Xᵢ, which is not a sum of independent indicators (this is the "Chernoff on a non-sum" from triage). It applies Chernoff to S = Σ Sᵢ without independence of the Sᵢ under an adaptive schedule. That Chernoff step concludes exp(-Ω(E[S])), which is useless because E[S] ≤ k/n^c is tiny. This is legitimate for every adaptive schedule because each round reads a fresh column (sum_couple). With fewer than ⌈k/2⌉·T rounds, more than k/2 messages are sent fewer than T times. Each such message reaches all n leaves with probability (1 - p^T)^n, independently of the other messages. A union bound over the C(k, ⌊k/2⌋+1) candidate sets of messages finishes the proof. Synchronous radio network on a finite simple graph with source s. A listening node hears a neighbour iff that neighbour is its unique broadcasting neighbour. There is no collision detection. Faults. Every node flips an independent coin per round, clean with probability 1 - p. With receiver faults, the receiver's coin decides whether it receives a transmission it hears; with sender faults, the sender's coin decides, and noise still collides. The faultless model sets all coins clean. Routing. Messages are Fin k. An adaptive routing schedule is a function round → knowledge state → action of every node (Definition 14). Nearly cubic synchronous Byzantine agreement — PODC 2013 Dariusz R. Kowalski, Achour Mostéfaoui. Synchronous Byzantine Agreement with Nearly a Cubic Number of Communication Bits. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484271. Formalized version: the authors' final version on HAL (hal-01151136, 16 pp.); there is no arXiv version. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The protocol of Section 4, the contribution named in the title and abstract, does not solve Byzantine agreement: with n = 7, t = 2 (so t < n/3) and binary values, two Byzantine processes make the correct processes decide differently, whatever the default value v0, so Theorem 2 (agreement) and Lemma 5 are false. No repaired protocol with t + 1 rounds and this bit bound is proved or known to us. Lemmas 1–4, Theorem 1 (validity) and the bit count of the basic protocol hold. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Protocol of Section 4: Theorem 2 (agreement) and Lemma 5 The protocol violates agreement for n = 7, t = 2: Byzantine b₁ sends 0 to three correct processes and 1 to the other two, Byzantine b₂ reports b₁'s value in round 2 as 0 to the first group and as 1 to the second, and then the first group decides 0 while the second decides the default v0 = 1 (not_solves_BA, theorem_2_false); in this run the whole tree has a common path covering (Lemma 4), but the root is not common (lemma_5_false). Impact. The paper's algorithm, the contribution named in the title and abstract, is not a Byzantine agreement protocol, so its O(n³ log n) bound is not established. Lemma 5 is the only route from Lemma 4 to agreement, so Theorem 2 has no proof; the run shows it is false. Validity holds (theorem_1). Details. Run (correct 0..4, Byzantine b₁ = 5, b₂ = 6, inputs 0,0,0,1,1). Round 1: b₁ sends 0 to A = {0,1,2} and 1 to {3,4}; b₂ sends 1 to all. Round 2: both Byzantine processes echo the correct inputs truthfully and report b₁'s value to each receiver as that receiver got it. Round 3: they report no suspicion and echo the round-2 arrays as each receiver saw them. At the node b₁ every correct process sees the same top set: {0,…,4, b₂}. The correct children echo 0,0,0,1,1. b₂'s echo is 0 in A (strict majority 4/6: newval(b₁) = 0) and 1 at 3, 4 (tie 3/6: newval(b₁) = ⊥) (newval1_b1). At the root, A sees four 0s among seven children and decides 0. Processes 3, 4 see three and fall back to v0 = 1 (decide_exec). With v0 = 0 the same run with all values flipped works. b₂'s round-2 equivocation is detected only at the end of round 3 = t + 1 and is never reported. b₁'s round-1 equivocation is detected by 3, 4 after round 2 and reported in round 3. But newval(b₁ k) reads k's reports about b₁ only through the echoes of round t + 1 = 3, which carry round-2 arrays, not suspicion sets. So the masks that should remove 3, 4 from the top set of b₁ are all ⊤. The proof of Lemma 5 fails at the level-1 node b₁, all of whose children are common (children_b1_common, node_b1_not_common). It claims that the correct processes in the top set "do not suspect p_j" and hence "reported the same value cval(xk)". But membership of xk in the top set only says that k reported no suspicion of j by round t. A suspicion created by a round-l equivocation is reported in round l + 2, outside that window when l = t − 1. So correct members of the top set can echo different values, and a Byzantine member of the top set then decides the strict majority differently at different processes. ✏️ Slips §4.1, decoration example: "when val(x) of some node x = yjk is set to ⊤, this means that p_k reported that it suspects p_j": ⊤ means "does not suspect" (as the bullets say). §4.2, intuition paragraph: "for the nodes of level 1 and level 2, val(x) is a proposed value"; by the bullets of §4.1, level-2 val is a suspicion bit. This is harmless: val of an internal node is never used in the evaluation. Proof of Lemma 5: "n − 2t > t + 1" should be "n − 2t > t" (n − 2t ≥ t + 1). §6: "each process … relays (n − 1)t suspicions" ignores that Byzantine processes may report up to n − 1 suspicions each. The relayed amount is still O(nt) (at most about 2nt). Typos Proof of Lemma 5: the induction hypothesis gives "a child xℓ or one of its ancestors is common", while the proof uses "xℓ is common". Harmless: the ancestors of xℓ are x and the ancestors of x, whose commonness is the claim. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous rounds; n processes Fin n; static Byzantine set of size ≤ t. Reliable point-to-point channels, where the receiver knows the sender; no signatures. Each process also receives its own message. The protocol is deterministic, and the adversary chooses every Byzantine message per receiver and per round, knowing everything. The protocol (Protocol.lean) follows §4.1–4.2 literally. It has one message record (Msg): proposal, round-2 echo array, suspicion set, round-3 echo of arrays, echo of suspicion sets. The echo confirmation uses threshold n − t, counting the receiver's own echo and Byzantine echoes. A process suspected in an earlier round is treated as ⊥. Suspicion sets are cumulative. The EIG decoration (val1, cval2, valB, leafVal, cvalB) and the bottom-up evaluation (nvB, newval1, decision) follow the bullets of §4.1–4.2. Labels are lists of distinct ids in reverse order. Executions (Exec): families of views in which correct senders send out of their own view. Bridge.lean defines the protocol as a CSLib LockStep.Protocol on the complete graph. It shows that every reliable lock-step run is an Exec with the same decisions (execOf, decides_iff). The counterexample is replayed as a lock-step scenario (not_solves_BA), so the refutation is stated in CSLib's standard model. Values: arbitrary V with decidable equality for the positive results; Bool for the counterexample, which covers both choices of v0. Main results in Lean. Lemma 3, Theorem 1 and Lemma 4 use n > 3t. For t = 0 the level-1 nodes are leaves and newval = val (newval1). Not formalized. The incremental protocol of §6 (O(n³ log n) total bits) is only sketched in the paper. It uses the same information, so the run above is expected to break it too. Other readings of §4 (Python simulation in simulation/, not in Lean). The run also violates agreement if a process discards, at decision time, all messages of every process it ever suspected. It does not if a process also drops from a top set the children whose last id it suspects itself, or takes the majority among non-⊥ echoes only. A different attack with n = 10, t = 3 breaks agreement under all eight combinations of these readings. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The counterexample is checked by kernel evaluation (decide +kernel, no native_decide) on the actual protocol functions. The scenario is a CSLib lock-step run, so the hypotheses are satisfiable. The lock-step model is CSLib's Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/LockStep/ (Solves, atMost, BA). The Python simulator in simulation/ is not part of the Lean development.

DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405725. Formalized version: arXiv 2002.11378 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All three contributions survive. Algorithm 2, the detectable CAS implementation that the abstract presents among the main contributions (Lemma 2), is not linearizable: a crash-free run of two processes each executing Cas(v₀, v₀) breaks it, and Algorithm 1's initialization is inconsistent, yet one local change each saves them, and we prove the fixed versions. Theorems 1 and 2 (the first assuming |V| ≥ N values), Lemmas 3–8 and Algorithm 3 are proved, Theorem 2 after a few-line repair of its last step. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 2 (Algorithm 2, detectable CAS) Algorithm 2 is not linearizable: two processes both running Cas(v₀, v₀) while the value is v₀ give the crash-free history inv a, inv b, res a true, res b false, which has no linearization (alg2_not_durLinDet). Impact. Algorithm 2 is one of the paper's main contributions; Cas(v, v) is a legitimate operation that the paper never excludes, and the run consists of the first operations of the two processes. A local fix of the algorithm is proved wait-free, durably linearizable and detectable (alg2fix_durLinDet). Details. Both processes read C = ⟨v₀, vec⟩. The first hardware CAS succeeds and flips its own bit of vec, so the second one fails. That process returns false, although the value was v₀ the whole time. No crash is needed. The proof says "the CAS fails only if another process performed a successful CAS … hence the value … must be other than old", which overlooks successful CASes that do not change the value. Repair. Cas(v, v) just reads C and persists and returns val = v. We prove the fixed algorithm wait-free, durably linearizable and detectable. (alg2_not_durLinDet; fix alg2fix_durLinDet) 🔧 Algorithm 1 (Lemma 1; initialization R = ⟨v_init, 0, 0⟩) The initialization is inconsistent: with 1-based ids it is under-specified, and if process 0 is a real process a run with 2 processes and 1 crash has a read return v_init after a completed Write(v₁) while the only Write(v_init) "failed" (alg1_not_durLinDet). Impact. The paper's ids are 1-based ("for i = 1 to N", p1, …, pN), so "process 0" is fictitious, and the counterexample applies only to the 0-based reading. But then line 2 writes the entry A[p][0][·], which is not part of A[N][N][2]. Initializing R = ⟨v_init, 0, 1⟩ fixes it (alg1fix_durLinDet). Details. The proof's key observation is that q writes with the same toggle index again only after completing a write with the other index. This fails for the fictitious initial write, because T_0 = 0 and process 0's first write uses toggle 0. Counterexample with 2 processes and 1 crash: Process 0 starts Write(v_init) and passes line 6 (CP = 1). Process 1 completes Write(v₁). Process 0 executes line 7, rewriting the initial triple ⟨v_init, 0, 0⟩. Process 1 completes a Read, which returns v_init. The system crashes. Process 0's Write.Recover sees the old triple and A[0][0][1] = 0, so it returns fail. A read after a completed Write(v₁) thus returns a value whose only write "failed". Repair. Initialize R = ⟨v_init, 0, 1⟩. We prove the fixed algorithm wait-free, durably linearizable and detectable for all n and all value types. (alg1_not_durLinDet; fix alg1fix_durLinDet) ✏️ Slips Definition 1 (auxiliary state via NVM): "a write is made to a non-volatile variable accessible by Op in-between two successive invocations" is satisfied by the operation's own writes (e.g. Ann.result := r), which would make the conclusion of Theorem 2 trivially satisfied. The intended (and needed) notion, stated in the abstract, is a write made outside the operation, by the system or the caller; we model it as a hook aux applied at invocation. Theorem 2 ("Let Op be a recoverable operation"): read universally, the statement is false, since a register read, for instance, needs no auxiliary state. Op is the witness of double perturbation, as the proof's opening says, and we prove the theorem in that form (theorem2). Section 3, description of line 20 of Algorithm 1: recovery is said to detect a write between the two reads of R "if and only if" q's toggle bit is 1, but the "only if" direction is false. q may complete a whole write with the other toggle between p's lines 1 and 2; then the bit is 0 although a write occurred, and recovery returns fail. Only the "if" direction is used, and the proof states exactly that (alg1fix_durLinDet). Proof of Lemma 2: "Cas.Recover simply re-invokes Op (line 41)", but line 41 returns fail. Typos Section 5, description of Algorithm 3: MD is written for the array MR. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2 (last step) "Executing Op_q starting from E₁ returns u ≠ v" does not follow from linearizability, because the second Op_p is pending in E₁ and could be linearized first. Impact. The theorem holds with a few-line repair (theorem2). Repair. The contradiction is obtained instead from the linearization of execution D, where the single Op_p must precede Op_r. (theorem2) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Model.lean, self-contained). Asynchronous processes P communicate through non-volatile shared memory, under the private-cache model with system-wide crashes. A crash resets the local state of every running process to the start of its recovery function; idle processes stay idle. A step is either an arbitrary atomic transformation of the whole shared memory, or an access to the process's own private NVM. Hence the lower bounds hold for any primitives, which is stronger than the paper. The algorithms use only single-variable read/write/CAS steps. At an invocation the system or caller may write the invoker's private NVM (aux: auxiliary state via NVM, e.g. Ann_p.CP := 0). Operations receive exactly the abstract arguments, so there is no auxiliary state via arguments. Correctness (DurLinDet) is durable linearizability plus detectability, as one condition: every finite execution has a sequential order that contains every operation that returned a value (with that value), contains no operation whose recovery returned fail, may contain pending operations, and respects real-time order. fail is only returned by recovery functions. Sanity check against CSLib (LinBridge.lean): let h be a history without crashes and fail responses that records a well-formed CSLib history α, with identifier ι (p, k) for the k-th operation of p and ι injective on the invoked instances. Then a list of invoked instances is a CSLib linearization (IsLinearization) of α iff its renaming by ι is a DLin of h from O.init. Hence h has a DLin from O.init iff α is linearizable (dLin_iff_isLinearization, exists_dLin_iff_exists_isLinearization). Progress. ObstructionFree: from every reachable configuration, a solo process completes. WeakOF (Definition 2): the same, but only when all others are idle. BoundedSteps is a syntactic wait-freedom certificate. Deterministic processes; no randomness. The adversary chooses the schedule and the crashes. Lower bounds for colouring sparse graphs — PODC 2018 Pierre Aboulker, Marthe Bonamy, Nicolas Bousquet, Louis Esperet. Distributed Coloring in Sparse Graphs with Fewer Colors. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212740. Formalized version: arXiv 1802.05582 v4; numbering follows it. Only the lower bounds of §2 are formalized (Observation 2.4, Theorems 2.5, 2.6, 1.5). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Only the lower bounds of §2 were checked, not the paper's main result, the polylog-round 6-colouring algorithm. There Theorem 2.6 is false as stated for every odd k ≥ 3: the k × k grid can be 3-coloured (even 2-coloured) in (k-1)/2 < k/2 rounds, and changing one constant saves it. The asymptotic statements (Ω(√n) for planar bipartite graphs, Theorem 2.5, Theorem 1.5) are correct; we prove them with explicit constants, Theorem 2.5 with exactly the paper's bound (only that exact bound took a new argument), and the non-colourability facts the paper cites (Gallai, Fisk) for the graphs used. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 2.6 (3-colouring the k × k grid needs k/2 rounds) Theorem 2.6 is false for every odd k ≥ 3, k = 2t + 1: in t < k/2 rounds a node can count the nodes at distance exactly t, which determines x + y mod 2, so the grid can even be 2-coloured (theorem_2_6_false_odd, theorem_2_6_false_3, …, theorem_2_6_false_11). Impact. The error costs one round: the asymptotic content (Ω(√n)) is unaffected, and the "in particular" part (Ω(√n) rounds for planar bipartite graphs) is true. The correct bound from the paper's method is 2r + 3 ≤ k, which we prove (theorem_2_6); for odd k it is tight. Details. The statement: "No distributed algorithm can 3-color the rectangular k × k grid in the plane in less than k/2 rounds." In the (2t+1) × (2t+1) grid, with a, b the distances to the nearest horizontal and vertical side, the number of nodes at distance exactly t is t + 1 + a + b if a + b < t (values ≤ 2t), 2(a + b) + 2 if a + b ≥ t and a, b < t (even values ≥ 2t + 2), 2t + 1 + 2b if a = t > b (odd values) and 4t at the centre. So "output 0 or 1 according to this count" is a proper 2-colouring in t < k/2 rounds. Already for k = 3: in one round a node knows its degree, and colouring by degree (2 and 4 vs 3) works. The algorithm is a genuine t-round LOCAL algorithm (CSLib's IsLocal), and ignores identifiers. It is designed for the grid, which the statement allows: like Observation 2.4, from which the paper derives it, Theorem 2.6 is about colouring one fixed graph under every identifier assignment (and nodes know n = k²). The proof, as written, gives less: balls of radius < k of G_{2k+1,2k+1} and Observation 2.4 give r ≤ k - 2 for the (2k+1)-grid, i.e. 2r + 5 ≤ N for side N. Repair. The sharp form of the same argument gives 2r + 3 ≤ N (theorem_2_6), which is optimal for odd N. ✏️ Slips Observation 2.4: "each ball of H is isomorphic to some ball of G" must be read with rooted isomorphisms (the centre must go to the centre), otherwise the argument fails. Every use in the paper is rooted, and with that reading it is correct (observation_2_4). Typos Theorem 2.5 speaks of H_k, which is only defined for even k (Figure 2). Theorem 1.5's graph is only given by a picture ("versions … clearly exist"); we give an explicit family. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 2.5 (H_{2ℓ} needs ℓ rounds) The proof applies Observation 2.4 to H = G_{5,2ℓ+1} (Klein bottle) and G = H_{2ℓ}, but G_{5,2ℓ+1} has 10ℓ + 5 vertices, more than H_{2ℓ} (10ℓ), violating the hypothesis |V(H)| ≤ |V(G)|. Impact. The stated bound r < ℓ holds (theorem_2_5), but saving it takes a different graph, beyond the cited Gallai result, and a sharper indistinguishability principle. Details. Also, "balls of radius < ℓ" combined with Observation 2.4 (balls of radius r + 1) only gives r ≤ ℓ - 2. Repair. We use the Klein bottle grid G_{5,2ℓ} (same size as H_{2ℓ}) and a sharper form of the indistinguishability argument: only the views of the two endpoints of each edge must be realised by one identifier assignment. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous LOCAL model, deterministic, unique identifiers: the node set of a network is the identifier type V with |V| = n (so n is known). An algorithm is A : SimpleGraph V → V → β (the colour output by each node); it is r-round (BallLocal r A) if a node's output only depends on the subgraph induced by its closed r-ball, identifiers included — the paper's own description. This gives nodes slightly more than r real rounds, so the lower bounds are slightly stronger; they transfer to CSLib's Cslib.Local.IsLocal r (BallLocal.of_isLocal). DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538444. Formalized version: arXiv 2203.02553 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. We checked only Section 2.1, the synchronous approximate-agreement algorithm APA built on signature-based crusader broadcast; the clock-synchronization results (Sections 3 and 4), the paper's main point, are not formalized. Lemma 7, Lemma 8, Theorem 9 (2 rounds, (ℓ, ℓ/2, ⌈n/2⌉−1)-secure) and Corollary 2 (2⌈log₂(ℓ/ε)⌉ rounds) are all true, apart from a degenerate corner of Corollary 2. The one real error is the induction step of Lemma 8, which a few lines repair. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Corollary 2 (round count): for ℓ ≤ ε the count 2⌈log(ℓ/ε)⌉ is zero or negative, and undefined for ℓ = 0. Zero rounds suffice there (corollary_2). Corollary 2 and Figure 4 (repetition of APA): repeating the algorithm needs signatures tied to the instance. Figure 4 signs only b_v, so without a session id an old signature of an honest dealer can be replayed, and CB validity fails. The paper's "(an instance of) Algorithm CB" implies separate signing domains; our tokens carry the iteration number (corollary_2). Lemma 7's proof: the upper indices are off by b. The retained maximum is the (n − f)-th smallest value in both lists, not r̃^{n−(f−(b−1))} and r^{n−(f−b)}. The inequalities used are correct. Definition 6 and Algorithm CB (Figure 4) are stated for binary inputs b_v ∈ {0, 1}. APA uses them for real values. Signatures work for any message, and we formalize CB on reals directly. Typos Lemma 7's proof writes the lists with lengths n − k and n − k + 1 instead of n − b and n − b + 1. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 8 (induction step written backwards) The induction step concludes x ∈ I_w ⊇ Ĩ_w, where Ĩ_w is the interval with the extra ⊥, but Lemma 7 gives the opposite inclusion, and the step goes from a k-execution to some (k+1)-execution instead of covering every one. Impact. The step as written proves nothing, but the lemma holds with a repaired induction (lemma_8). Details. The induction is on the number k of ⊥ values received by honest nodes. The paper starts from a k-execution and replaces one value by ⊥. Lemma 7 says that a ⊥ enlarges the interval, so the correct step is x ∈ I_w ⊆ Ĩ_w. To cover every (k+1)-execution, one must start from an arbitrary (k+1)-execution and remove a ⊥ (honest w, faulty dealer d). The ⊥ must be replaced by the value the other honest nodes got from d (any value if all of them got ⊥). Only then does the k-configuration still satisfy crusader consistency, so that the induction hypothesis applies. The closing sentence "this construction applies for any inputs … the claim follows for all executions" leaves this out. Repair. The induction runs over configurations of CB outputs that satisfy validity and crusader consistency. A direct argument via order statistics of the common values would also work. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous lock-step rounds (CSLib Cslib.Byzantine.LockStep) on the complete network of n = |P| nodes. Static Byzantine set of at most f nodes (atMost f). Reliable channels. Deterministic protocol. No randomness. Ideal signatures as CSLib tokens (LockStep.Auth). A token (d, j, v) is d's signature on "my value in iteration j is v". Honest nodes are Unforging (proved: alg_unforging). The adversary (Scenario.AuthValid) is rushing and eavesdropping. It can send any token signed by a corrupted node, or any token an honest node has emitted in this round or earlier. This is the paper's "rushing adversary that cannot forge signatures". Corollary 2 "repeats the algorithm" with fresh CB instances. This needs signatures tagged with the iteration number (a session id). Without the tag, the adversary can echo an honest dealer's signature from an earlier iteration and make honest nodes output ⊥ for an honest dealer, which breaks CB validity. Our tokens carry the iteration number. alg f K runs K iterations of APA, two rounds each (the two rounds of Algorithm CB). All n CB instances run in parallel. After round 2K every node decides its last value. CB at node w for dealer d: output ⊥ if d's token is invalid or missing, or if an echo carries a valid signature of d with a different value; otherwise output the signed value. A node counts its own received token as one of the echoes, which is the paper's "send to all nodes" including itself. Specification (Definition 1): AASpec ℓ ε. If the honest inputs have range ≤ ℓ, then every honest node decides, decisions lie between two honest inputs, and honest decisions are pairwise ≤ ε apart. Secure t ℓ ε A T adds unforgeability of A and termination within T rounds against all admissible adversaries. The combinatorial layer (APA.lean) assumes only the CB properties of Definition 6 (IsCrusader). It applies to any CB implementation. Main results in Lean. PODC 2019 (brief announcement). DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331568. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv 1905.08733 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Algorithm 2 is not linearizable as printed, and Theorem 3 (Consistency), Lemma 3 and Theorem 4 (Update Stability) are false: a five-process execution with majority quorums lets two queries learn the incomparable states {u₁} and {u₂}, although u₁ completed before u₂ was invoked. A one-line repair of the VOTE handler restores Theorems 1–5 and linearizability at no cost to updates or message size, which we prove for CRDTs with the causal history the paper assumes. Lemmas 1, 2, 4, Corollary 1 and Theorems 1, 2, 5 hold, and so does the Section III-E reduction (Theorems 1–5 ⇒ linearizability); finite-writes termination was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Algorithm 2 (linearizability), Theorem 3, Theorem 4 and Lemma 3 Algorithm 2 is not linearizable, and Lemma 3, Theorem 3 (Consistency) and Theorem 4 (Update Stability) are false: with five processes and majority quorums, one query learns {u₂} by vote while another learns {u₁} by consistent quorum, although u₁ completed before u₂ was invoked (Cex.not_linearizable, paper_false). Impact. The paper's main claim fails for the protocol as printed, and the flaw is in the protocol (the VOTE handler), not only in the proofs. Lemmas 1, 2, 4, Corollary 1, Theorems 1, 2, 5 and the Section III-E reduction hold, and a one-line repair of the VOTE handler restores Theorems 1–5 and linearizability. Details. Take five processes p₀…p₄, majority quorums, a G-set, and only incremental prepares; no message is lost, some are only late. A query C raises the round numbers of p₀, p₁, p₃, p₄ to 1. Query A (at p₀) gets ACK((2,A), ∅) from p₀ and p₁. Update u₁, issued at p₄, is merged at p₀, p₁, p₂ and completes on their three MERGEDs. Query B reads {u₁} from p₀, p₁, p₂ and learns it by consistent quorum. Update u₂ is applied at p₃ only. A's PREPARE reaches p₂, p₃, p₄, which all move to round (2, A). The round numbers coincide because of step 1. A takes the quorum {p₀, p₁, p₃} with states ∅, ∅, {u₂}, all in round (2, A), and sends VOTE((2,A), {u₂}). p₂, p₃, p₄ are still in round (2, A) and answer VOTED, so A learns {u₂} by vote, although p₂ and p₄ hold u₁. So {u₁} and {u₂} are incomparable, which refutes Theorem 3 and Lemma 3. Since u₁ precedes u₂, Theorem 4 fails too. For the G-set, A returns {u₂} after u₁ completed and u₂ was invoked, so the history has no linearization. (Cex.lemma3_false, Cex.theorem3_false, Cex.theorem4_false, Cex.not_linearizable, paper_false) Both proofs confuse the ACK quorum with the VOTED quorum. The proof of Lemma 3 applies condition C1, which holds only on Q₁ ∩ Q₂ (here {p₀, p₁}), to the voter a = p₂ ∈ Q₁ outside Q₂. It also tacitly assumes that a later PREPARE cannot get the same round number at all acceptors. The proof of Theorem 4 says "∄Q: a.r = r for all a ∈ Q, as all a ∈ Q_u updated their round". But the acceptors of Q_u that receive the PREPARE after the MERGE do hold round r, and their payloads (with u₁) are not part of the proposed LUB. The flaw is in the protocol, not only in the proofs: a VOTED certifies that the acceptor's round is unchanged, not that its payload is ⊑ the proposal. The schedule respects the paper's own reading of line 47 too: the voters' payloads changed before they received A's PREPARE, not "in the meantime". The same flaw is in arXiv v1 (2019), whose handlers and proofs (Lemma 3.6, Theorem 3.9) are identical in the relevant lines. The non-linearizability needs queries that can tell which updates are included. On the paper's own G-counter with the sum query, this particular execution is linearizable, although the same schedule still yields the incomparable learned vectors e₄ and e₃ (not formalized). Repair. An acceptor answers VOTE(r', s') only if, in addition, its payload before the merge is ⊑ s' (Variant.fixed). Then every learned state was, at some moment, the exact payload of every acceptor of a quorum. Consistency follows from monotonicity alone, and Lemma 4's Paxos-style round argument is no longer needed. Update stability follows because a quorum acquired u₁ before u₂ existed. We prove Theorems 1–5 and linearizability for the repaired protocol. (fixed_theorem3, fixed_theorem4, fixed_linearizable) ✏️ Slips Line 13 tests sᵢ ≡ s', and the paper defines ≡ as query equivalence. The proof of Lemma 2(i) needs s' ⊑ a.s, i.e. equality, so we use equality. The causal history C(s) is treated as a function of the state, which is not well defined for every CRDT. Also u ∈ C(u(s)) is too weak for Theorem 1. We assume a causal-history map with C(s₀) = ∅, C(u(s)) = C(s) ∪ {u}, C(s ⊔ t) = C(s) ∪ C(t) and Shapiro et al.'s C(s) = C(t) ⇒ s ≡ t. The G-set has one. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous message-passing model Cslib.AsyncMP: unordered channels with arbitrary delays, crash-stop. Safety concerns finite executions, so a lost message is one that is never delivered. Histories are CSLib Labels, and linearizability is CSLib's IsLinearization w.r.t. the CRDT's sequential specification CRDT.spec (updates apply the command, queries return cmd_q(s)). Every process is a proposer and an acceptor (alg V QS). Clients are the processes themselves, with one pending operation per process. Each handler is atomic. The quorum system QS is an arbitrary pairwise-intersecting family of sets. The CRDT is arbitrary (CRDT: join semilattice, inflationary updates, queries). The theorems mentioning "includes u" use a causal-history map H. Proposer behaviour is generous, which makes the positive results stronger: the internal action advance may act on all ACKs received so far, as soon as they contain a quorum; retry n lets a pending query abandon its attempt at any time and restart with an incremental or arbitrary fixed prepare, which models NACK-triggered retries; the local acceptor counts towards the MERGED quorum.
