Space Bounds for Reliable Storage — PODC 2016 Alexander Spiegelman, Yuval Cassuto, Gregory Chockler, Idit Keidar. Space Bounds for Reliable Storage: Fundamental Limits of Coding. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933104. Formalized version: arXiv 1507.05169 v1 (the only arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The main lower bound (Theorem 2, Corollary 2: unbounded storage, or a time when f + 1 objects each hold D bits of one write) is proved, after several repairs, only in the paper's own storage model ("every stored bit belongs to one write"), not for "any reliable storage algorithm": Theorem 1 ("every write adds at least log₂|U_s| bits") is false as stated, and it does not justify that model. Algorithm 2 (Section 3.1, the safe erasure-coded register) is not safe as written when k ≤ f, e.g. for replication with n = 3, f = 1 (Lean counterexample), and with the reader decoding the largest qualifying timestamp, Corollary 3 is proved. The adaptive algorithm of Section 5 was not checked, and whether the bound holds for algorithms that code across writes is open. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 1 ("every write adds at least log₂|U_s| bits") Theorem 1 (a write of u_s ∈ U_s adds at least log₂|U_s| bits) is false: with |U₁| = 5, |U₂| = 3 and an object that stores the minimum each time (⌈log₂ 5⌉ = 3, then ⌈log₂ 15⌉ = 4 bits), the second write adds one bit, less than log₂ 3 (theorem1_false). Impact. The per-write property is lost: the cumulative bound of Lemma 1 is what is true in general (theorem1_cumulative), and it says nothing about a single write. The paper's main use of Theorem 1 is the storage model of Section 4 (next item). Details. With padding, a write can add no bits at all. The proof subtracts two lower bounds, which is invalid. Its induction hypothesis ("the object stores exactly log₂(|U₁|⋯|U_{s−1}|) bits") assumes minimal storage. The statement holds only for minimal encodings and power-of-two set sizes, the simplification made in Lemma 1's proof. ⚠️ Section 4 storage model ("each stored bit is associated with a particular write") The paper adopts this model "without loss of generality" on the strength of Theorem 1, but neither Theorem 1 nor its correct cumulative version justifies it, so the abstract's lower bound for "any reliable storage algorithm" is proved only for algorithms that do not code across writes. Impact. The main lower bound (Theorem 2, Corollary 2) holds in the paper's own model (theorem2, corollary2), which covers replication and per-value erasure coding. Details. Lemma 1 concerns one object that must keep all its inputs recoverable from its own bits. A register emulation may discard old values, spread a value over several objects, or store functions of several values (e.g. v₁ ⊕ v₂). Section 4's bookkeeping (C⁺, F(t), Observation 1, Lemma 3) depends on this attribution. Our black-box model makes it hold by construction: values are opaque, and stored data are blocks, each a fixed function of one written value, which clients only copy. Re-encoding another client's value is excluded as well. 🔧 Algorithm 2 (Section 3.1, line 16) and Lemma 9 (safety for k ≤ f) Algorithm 2 is not safe when k ≤ f: with replication (k = 1, n = 3, f = 1) a read with no concurrent write may return the stale value of an earlier write, because line 16 lets the reader decode any timestamp with k pieces (Safe.not_stronglySafe, Safe.not_weakRegular). Impact. A local fix to the reader: decoding the largest qualifying timestamp makes Algorithm 2 wait-free and strongly safe with at most n stored pieces, so Corollary 3 holds (Safe.corollary3). Details. Replication is explicitly allowed by the paper. Write w₁ stores on objects 1 and 2 and returns. Then w₂ reads objects 1 and 2, stores on 2 and 3, and returns. A later read hears from objects 1 and 2. Both timestamps have one piece, so the reader may return w₁'s value. This violates safety, since the read has no concurrent write. Lemma 9's proof misses this case. For k > f a stale timestamp cannot collect k pieces. The Lean counterexample uses the "smallest qualifying timestamp" reading of line 16. Repair. The reader takes the largest qualifying timestamp; then Corollary 3 is proved (Safe.corollary3). 🔧 Observation 1 (under-specified storage measure) C⁺(t) counts writes whose bits are in base objects or in other clients, so Observation 1 (storage ≥ |C⁺(t)|) holds only if the storage also counts copies of other writers' data held by clients, which the paper does not say. Impact. We use that measure in the hypothesis of Theorem 2 (Alg.storage, obs1). The conclusion of Corollary 2 is about base objects only. ✏️ Slips Theorem 3 / Corollary 4 (Section 5, not formalized): "with at most c < k concurrent writes the storage is bounded by (c + 1)D/k bits" is false as written, since the initial configuration already stores (2f + k)D/k bits. Lemma 12 has the intended (2f + k)(c + 1)D/k, and it assumes c < k − 1. Theorem 2 (number of clients): the bound needs at least S + 1 clients, S concurrent writers and a reader, while the paper only says Π is finite. The assumption is in the opening of Section 4 and in the abstract ("no bound on the concurrency level"); we prove the theorem with S + 1 clients (theorem2, theorem2_run). Lemma 12's proof writes ts' ≥ ts₁ > ts₁, meaning ts' ≥ ts₁ > ts₂. Typos Lemma 12's proof cites itself (meant Lemma 11). Corollary 5 says "WF-termination" for FW-termination. In Observation 2's proof, |B| = N − f should be n − f. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 2 (adaptive choice of encoders) The proof says that choosing adaptively among m encoders forces log₂ m extra bits, which is false: two encoders of a 4-element set into 2 bits, chosen adaptively, decode without an extra bit (lemma2_no_extra_bits). Impact. The lemma is trivially true: an adaptive choice of encoders is one fixed function (lemma2). 🔧 Lemma 3 (copies of a write's bits) The proof ignores copies: a client may read another writer's bits and spread them over several objects. Impact. The lemma holds in the black-box model (inv_exec, lemma3). Repair. The claim holds because Ad never lets an RMW touch an object of F(t). A batch of D bits is frozen in its object the moment it is stored, and smaller batches never add up to D. Our invariant states exactly this. 🔧 Observation 2 (reads returning a completed write) The proof says "no value satisfying weak regularity can be returned", which ignores that the read may return the value of an earlier completed write concurrent with w, not only one in C(t), so the argument works only at the first completion. Impact. Corollary 1, the only use, applies it at the first completion, where this does not matter. Repair. Alg.reader_restore concludes that the objects of B hold D bits of some write of the history, which covers both cases. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous fault-prone shared memory (Section 2.1). Deterministic clients C (finite) trigger arbitrary atomic RMWs on base objects N. A triggered RMW stays pending until an exec event applies it and delivers the response, and a client may have several pending RMWs. Taking effect and responding are one event. This only restricts the runs, which makes the hypotheses weaker and the lower bound stronger. Crash failures of clients and of at most f base objects. Failures are not events: a failure pattern enters the fairness predicate Fair (crashed clients take finitely many steps, crashed objects execute finitely many RMWs, correct clients are scheduled infinitely often, RMWs of correct clients on correct objects eventually take effect). Lock-freedom and weak regularity (MWRegWeak) are as in Section 2.2, quantified over all runs and all value assignments. No randomness. f < n/2 is not needed for the lower bound. Black-box storage. A write carries no value; write w has value val w for an arbitrary value assignment. Data are blocks (w, j) of sz j ≥ 1 bits with contents enc j (val w), where enc is the algorithm's code (e.g. erasure-code pieces or full replicas). Blocks only flow: they are stored by RMWs from the client's holdings, carried back by responses, and created only by their writer. A read's output depends only on the contents of the blocks it holds. D = ⌈log₂|V|⌉; F(t) = objects holding D bits of one write. Storage = bits in base objects plus copies held by clients other than the writer. Proof structure as in the paper: the adversary Ad (Definition 1) runs S writes. The information-theoretic step (restore): a reader that, for every value assignment, returns the value of one of finitely many writes holds D bits of one of them. Main results in Lean. Network Constructors — PODC 2014 Othon Michail, Paul G. Spirakis. Simple and Efficient Local Codes for Distributed Stable Network Construction. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611466. Formalized version: arXiv 1309.6978 v2 (full version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 10 is false: Protocol 6 (Global-Ring) does not construct a spanning ring, but nothing depends on it and the paper's own 2RC (Theorem 11) gives the spanning ring with fewer states. The other correctness claims checked hold: Theorems 3, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12 (after a typo fix in Protocol 8, and with a new argument), the state bound of Theorem 7, and Theorem 13 for c ≥ 3. The running times and the universality half of the paper were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 10 (Protocol 6, Global-Ring) Protocol 6 does not construct a spanning ring: for n = 6 a globally fair execution switches forever between spanning lines and a spanning ring, because the closing rule (l, q₁, 0) → (l', q₁', 1) can also join two different lines (GlobalRing.globalRing_not_constructs). Impact. The protocol is correct for n ≤ 5 (exhaustive model checking), so n = 6 is the smallest counterexample. No repair of Protocol 6 is proved. Nothing else in the paper depends on Theorem 10, and the separate Protocol 7 (2RC), with 6 states instead of 9, constructs a spanning ring (TwoRC.twoRC_constructs). Details. The proof says the closing rule applies "whenever one endpoint is in state l and the other is in state q₁" of the same line. But an l endpoint of one line can also meet the q₁ endpoint of another line, since every pair of agents may interact. Then the two lines are joined, and two blocked nodes sit next to each other in the middle. Later merges can leave a blocked q₁'' as an internal node of degree 2. Such a node is never unblocked, because its only unblocking rules need an active edge to an l'/l''. Concrete run on n = 6: Form two lines, 0–1 and 3–4, with leaders at 1 and 4. (l, q₁, 0) on agents 4 and 0 joins the two lines. The leader of line 0–1 (agent 1) absorbs agent 2. Its endpoint 2 closes onto 3. The result is a ring 0–1–2–3–4–0. Agents 0 and 3, both q₁' and not adjacent, meet: by (x', y', 0) → (x'', y'', 0) both become q₁''. The pair 4 (l'), 3 (q₁'') reopens the edge {3, 4}, and agent 4 (now l) absorbs the last agent 5. From there the system stays inside a closed set of 8 configurations, which the scheduler can visit forever. This set alternates between spanning lines (path 2–1–0–4–5 with agent 3 hanging at 2 or at 5) and the spanning ring 0–1–2–3–5–4–0, and agent 0 stays q₁'' forever. Under global fairness every one of these configurations recurs, so the output never stabilizes. 🔧 Theorem 13 (Protocol 9, c-Cliques): c ∈ {1, 2} The theorem claims every positive c, but Protocol 9 does not make sense for c ∈ {1, 2}. Impact. With c ≥ 3 and Q_out = states of completed components the theorem holds for every n (Cliques.cliques_constructs). Details. For c ∈ {1, 2} indices go out of range, and for c = 2 there are two contradictory rules for (l₀, l₀, 0). ✏️ Slips Protocol 8 (kRC, Theorem 12): the rule (l_{k+1}, l_i, 1) → (l_k, l_{i−1}, 0) for 1 ≤ i ≤ k produces the non-state l₀ when i = 1, and if l₀ is kept as a dead state the protocol fails (k = 3, n = 5: a K₄ plus an isolated l₀, found by the model checker). Protocol 7 has (l₃, l₁, 1) → (l₂, q₀, 0) at the same place. We read l₀ as q₀; with this fix Theorem 12 holds for all k ≥ 2 and n ≥ k + 1 (KRC.kRC_constructs). Theorem 6 (Cycle-Cover): the paper leaves Q_out unspecified, and with Q_out = Q the claim is false: for n = 4 the protocol can stop at a triangle plus an isolated q₀. With Q_out = {q₂} the statement holds: the output stabilizes to a cycle cover on at least n − 2 agents (CycleCover.constructs_cycleCover). Waste 2 does occur, for example at n = 5 (CycleCover.waste_two_attained). Theorem 13 (c-Cliques): with the unspecified Q_out = Q the leftover n mod c agents form an extra star in the output. The statement speaks of the completed cliques only, so we take Q_out = states of completed components. Theorem 11 needs n ≥ 3, which is left implicit (for n ≤ 2 there is no spanning ring); proved for n ≥ 3 (TwoRC.twoRC_constructs). Typos Protocols 7 and 8 list rules for both orientations of some pairs with different outcomes, e.g. (l₁, l₂, 0) and (l₂, l₁, 0). This contradicts the convention of Definition 1 but is harmless when read nondeterministically. Protocol 9, rule (l'_i, l'_j, 1) → (l'_{i−1}, l'_{j−1}, 0): for i = 1 or j = 1 it would produce the non-state l'₀. This case is unreachable: our invariant shows it never occurs. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 12 (kRC, proof) The paper's proof is a single sentence ("almost the same ideas as Theorem 11") and misses that a k-regular component may have bridges. Impact. Statement true (after the typo fix above); proved with two extra ideas that do not occur in the proof of Theorem 11 (KRC.kRC_constructs). Details. The component's leader must first walk to a cycle edge before opening. Otherwise the component splits and nothing is gained. Also, two k-regular components are joined by (l_k, l_k, 0) and must each drop a cycle edge. 🔧 Theorem 6 (Cycle-Cover, waste 2, proof) The paper's justification of "waste 2" is a single sentence: it overlooks leftovers such as an isolated q₀ and never rules out a lone q₁ hanging on a cycle. Impact. Statement true with Q_out = {q₂} (CycleCover.constructs_cycleCover). Repair. A counting invariant, and the handshake lemma to rule out a lone q₁ hanging on a cycle. 🔧 Theorem 13 (c-Cliques, proof) The paper's proof is a sketch: it does not treat the release of sub-followers (f_j) or why merging terminates. Impact. Statement true for c ≥ 3 (Cliques.cliques_constructs). Repair. Our proof lets a partial leader of maximal index absorb the others. 🔧 Theorem 7 (state bound for stars) The proof argues that a one-state protocol that activates edges "ends with a global clique", overlooking protocols that also deactivate edges, where the output never stabilizes. Impact. Statement true; our proof covers this case (Star.star_needs_two_states). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Network constructors as in Section 3.1, in the shared library Podc/Computability/Distributed/NetworkConstructors/. Agents form any finite type V with n = |V|; the interaction graph is complete. A configuration consists of agent states and symmetric binary edge states. Initially all agents are in q₀ and all edges are inactive. In each step the scheduler picks a pair of distinct agents and an orientation, and the deterministic δ : Q × Q × {0,1} → Q × Q × {0,1} is applied. This is the paper's "C → C' via encounter uv". It covers both the (a,b,c)/(b,a,c) convention and the random choice when a = b. The adversary is arbitrary subject to global fairness, CSLib's Run.GloballyFair: a configuration that occurs infinitely often has all its successors occur infinitely often. "Constructs T" means: in every globally fair execution from the initial configuration, the output graph is eventually constant and satisfies T. The output graph is the set of agents in output states plus the active edges among them. No randomness. The uniform random scheduler and the expected-time bounds are not modelled. We exhibit an inductive invariant of the reachable configurations and a closed set of output-stable target configurations. We then show that this set is reachable from every configuration satisfying the invariant. Under global fairness on a finite configuration space this is equivalent to construction (CSLib globallyFair_iff_reach). Tightness of the waste in Theorem 6 for n other than 5. Replication (Theorem 14) and Section 6 (universality, Theorems 15–19). Trust. The listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: globally fair executions exist (Protocol.exists_fair_execution), and the hypotheses of Theorems 11–12 are satisfiable (examples in TwoRC.lean and KRCMerge.lean). The counterexample for Theorem 10 is checked by decide on 6 agents. It works for every choice of Q_out (the paper gives none for Protocol 6) and also refutes the theorem under the uniform random scheduler, since the trap is reached with positive probability. One proof (Cliques.Inv.interact, the invariant step of c-Cliques) raises maxHeartbeats to 1000000. Before proving, every protocol was model-checked exhaustively for small n (bottom strongly connected components of the configuration graph). Optimal Mobile Byzantine Fault Tolerant Distributed Storage — PODC 2016 Silvia Bonomi, Antonella Del Pozzo, Maria Potop-Butucaru, Sébastien Tixeuil. Optimal Mobile Byzantine Fault Tolerant Distributed Storage. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933100. Formalized version: the full version, research report HAL hal-01348830v2 (Feb 2017, 42 pp); numbering follows it. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. Both "optimal" regular-register protocols are wrong at the paper's own parameters, and a read with no concurrent write returns a never-written value: in the CAM model (Theorems 8/9, for 2δ ≤ Δ < 3δ and δ ≤ Δ < 3δ/2) the extra liars are faulty servers that send a fake reply just before the read starts, delivered during the read, and in the CUM model (Theorems 11/12, for 2δ ≤ Δ < 5δ/2 and δ ≤ Δ < 5δ/4) the faulty and cured servers that the paper itself counts already outnumber the threshold #reply_CUM. No corrected protocol is proved, so the optimality claims have no matching upper bound. The lower-bound proofs (Theorems 3–6) compare executions that the reader can tell apart, because replies are authenticated; we repair Theorems 3 and 5 in the paper's own lower-bound model. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorems 8 and 9 (the (ΔS, CAM) protocol, Section 5) A read with no concurrent write returns a never-written value: for 2δ ≤ Δ < 3δ, n = 4f + 1, #reply_CAM = 2f + 1, the 3f servers hosting an agent during (t − δ, t + 2δ) all report a fake pair with the highest sequence number, and for δ ≤ Δ < 3δ/2, n = 5f + 1, #reply_CAM = 3f + 1, 4f such servers do (theorem9_false_k1, theorem9_false_k2, theorem9_false). Impact. The CAM protocol violates even safe-register validity, in a read with no concurrent write, at the parameters of Table 1. So the claimed tight bounds n ≥ 4f + 1 and n ≥ 5f + 1 for the CAM model have no proved upper bound. Lemma 7, the counting lemma behind the proof, is true (lemma7) but counts the wrong time window. Details. The paper bounds the liars of a read [t, t+2δ] by MaxB̃(t, t+2δ), "as if each message to/from them is delivered instantaneously" (Section 5.2; Corollary 3 states the resulting majority). But in the round-free synchronous model (Section 2) a message sent at time τ is delivered at any time of (τ, τ + δ]. So a server that hosts an agent at some τ ∈ (t − δ, t) can send a reply that arrives during the read. The reader's reply_i is reset at t, but replies carry no read identifier and the reader accepts all of them (Fig. 24, lines 01, 07–09). The window (t − δ, t + 2δ) has length 3δ, so it can meet ⌈3δ/Δ⌉ + 1 agent periods. That is 3 for 2δ ≤ Δ < 3δ (3f ≥ 2f + 1 liars) and 4 for δ ≤ Δ < 3δ/2 (4f ≥ 3f + 1 liars). The agents sweep disjoint blocks of f servers. Each liar sends one reply {⟨v′, N + 1⟩}, where N is the number of writes so far. select_value returns, among the pairs with at least #reply_CAM occurrences, the one with the highest sequence number, which is the fake pair. The Lean statement quantifies over all other replies whose sequence numbers are at most N. The result holds for any tie-breaking rule of select_value and for every n ≥ 3f (resp. 4f) with these thresholds. Scope. The attack needs only what the system model allows: a delay of at most δ on the faulty servers' messages. No foresight is needed either: a faulty server may send the fake reply to every client repeatedly while it hosts the agent, and any read starting less than δ later receives it. If one instead postulated that faulty servers' messages are delivered instantly, the CAM attack would not apply (the CUM attack below would). Repair. None proved. Counting the liars over (t − δ, t + 2δ) suggests #reply_CAM > (⌈3δ/Δ⌉ + 1) f and n ≥ #reply_CAM + 2f, i.e. n ≥ 5f + 1 for 2δ ≤ Δ < 3δ and n ≥ 6f + 1 for δ ≤ Δ < 3δ/2. This is not verified, and it would give up the claimed optimal thresholds. ❌ Theorems 11, 12 and 13 (the (ΔS, CUM) protocol, Section 6) The CUM read is fooled even without replies sent before the read: for 2δ ≤ Δ < 5δ/2 (#reply_CUM = 3f + 1) 3f faulty and f cured servers, and for δ ≤ Δ < 5δ/4 (#reply_CUM = 5f + 1) 4f faulty and 2f cured servers, report a fake pair with the highest sequence number (theorem12_false_k1, theorem12_false_k2, theorem12_false). Impact. The CUM protocol fails at the parameters of Table 3 (n = 5f + 1, 8f + 1), so the tightness claim of Theorem 13 is false as well. This refutation does not depend on the delay argument of the CAM item: the proof of Theorem 11 itself counts "up to 4f" (resp. 6f) non-correct servers that can reply with non-valid values, and then claims that #reply_CUM = 3f + 1 (resp. 5f + 1) exceeds this. It does not, once these servers all report the same pair. Details. The cured liars are those allowed by the paper's Lemma 18. A server cured at time c may answer a read with a non-valid value until c + 2δ. The agent leaves an entry ⟨⟨v′, sn′⟩, 2δ⟩ in W_i, and conCut(V_i, Vsafe_i, W_i) returns it (Fig. 27, line 11), since sn′ is the newest. In the counterexample the cured server receives the read request during (t, t+δ] and before c + 2δ, and replies at once. Every lying reply is sent during the read. The faulty liars are the servers hosting an agent during the read [t, t + 3δ]: 3f (resp. 4f). The cured liars are the servers whose agent left at most 2δ before the request reaches them: f (resp. 2f). ⚠️ Theorems 3–6 (lower bounds, Sections 4.5–4.6) The executions E₁, E₀ are not indistinguishable: they use the same agent schedule, so the reader receives 1 from s₀ in E₁ and 0 from s₀ in E₀; only the multisets of values coincide, while replies are authenticated. Impact. As written, the proofs establish nothing for a reader that looks at senders. Theorems 3 and 5 hold in the paper's own lower-bound model with a corrected pair of executions (theorem3, theorem5). The claim for arbitrary protocols remains unproved, and Theorems 4 and 6 (CUM) were not formalized. Details. Section 4.4 fixes the model of the lower bounds. A correct server replies once, when the request reaches it; faulty and cured servers do not reply correctly; faulty servers may send anything. The paper's E₁ of Fig. 5 is fine. E₀ must use a different schedule: the agent visits s₀, s₄, s₃ instead of s₁, s₂, s₃. In general, label the servers by blocks of at most f: A₁, B₁ (faulty in E₁ before and during the request time), A₀, B₀ (same in E₀), and C (faulty right after, in both). Every server is then either honest in one execution and impersonated, with the same delivery time, in the other, or (C) heard with both values in both. So the reader's full view — senders, values and delivery times — is the same, for every read duration and every decision rule. That gives n ≤ 5f for δ ≤ Δ < 2δ and n ≤ 4f (no C) for Δ ≥ 2δ. The cure duration γ plays no role. In this model correct servers reply only once, so "waiting more does not help" is true. For general protocols — e.g. the paper's own, where cured servers reply again once correct — it is not proved. ✏️ Slips Lemma 6 (also Lemma 13): MaxB̃(t, t+T) = (⌈T/Δ⌉ + 1) f is false when (⌈T/Δ⌉ + 1) f > n, e.g. for n = 6 = 5f + 1, f = 1, δ = Δ = 1, T = 10 it claims 11 affected servers out of 6 (lemma6_false). The paper uses it only for T ∈ {δ, 2δ, 3δ}, where the bound is below n. The correct value is min(n, (⌈T/Δ⌉ + 1) f) (lemma6); the hypotheses δ ≤ Δ < 3δ, T ≥ δ are not needed. Theorem 12 states the hypothesis n ≥ 2(k+1)f + 1, which contradicts Table 3 (n ≥ (3k+2)f + 1) and Theorem 4 (no protocol for n ≤ 8f when δ ≤ Δ < 2δ). The counterexamples need only 4f resp. 6f servers, so they refute both readings. Lemma 7, proof: minC̃oR(t, t+2δ) = n − (⌈2δ/Δ⌉ + 1) f should read ⌈δ/Δ⌉; the numbers used (5f + 1 − 2f) are those of ⌈δ/Δ⌉ = 1. Lemma 8, proof: n − 2f = 3(k+1)f + 1 − 2f = (k+1)f + 1 should start from n = (k+3)f + 1. Theorem 6, proof: the two multisets listed for E₁‴, E₀‴ are identical; the second should be the first with the values swapped. Figure 25, line 02 (CUM maintenance): Expired(timer) ∧ timer > 2δ read literally never removes an entry with timer ≤ 2δ; the prose says the entry is deleted when the timer expires or has a non-compliant value. Typos Theorem 6, proof: "we consider directly n ≤ 5" (for 5f) and n ≤ 6 (for 6f), correct for the case f = 1 that the proof treats. Section 6, select_value: the CUM version is worded "If there are more pairs with the same occurrence", unlike the CAM version; the proof of Theorem 11 fixes the same reading. Corollary 2 ends with "□ Lemma 2", Theorem 5 with "□ Theorem 3". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Real time; n servers Fin n; f mobile Byzantine agents moving simultaneously at the times t₀ + iΔ (ΔS). A schedule gives, for each period i ∈ ℤ, the at most f servers hosting an agent (Schedule); affected is the paper's B̃[a, b]. Round-free synchrony: every message delay is in (0, δ], chosen by the adversary. Protocol attacks (ReadAttack.lean): only the reader is modelled. A read invoked at t collects the triples ⟨j, ⟨v, sn⟩⟩ of all replies delivered in (t, t + D] (collected) and returns any pair allowed by select_value (SelectValue). Replies of faulty servers must be sent while faulty (ByzReply); in CUM a cured server may also lie, when the request reaches it, during 2δ after being left (CuredLiar, LyingReply, the paper's Lemma 18). Edge Dominating Sets in Port-Numbered Networks — PODC 2010 Jukka Suomela. Distributed Algorithms for Edge Dominating Sets. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835783. Formalized version: the author's version (http://users.ics.aalto.fi/suomela/doc/eds.pdf, 10 pages, same numbering as the proceedings; there is no arXiv version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. All results are formalized and hold as stated: the lower bounds 4 - 2/d (even d) and 4 - 6/(d+1) (odd d) for d-regular graphs (Theorems 1, 2), their bounded-degree consequence 4 - 1/k (Corollary 1), and the matching algorithms (Theorems 3, 4, 5). The lower bounds are proved in a slightly stronger form than stated. The only labeled mistake is a division by |D*| = 0 on edgeless graphs, a degenerate case. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips §7.8 divides by |D*|, which is 0 for an edgeless graph (degenerate case). We prove the integer form 2k·|D| ≤ (8k − 2)·|D*| instead (card_le_of_props). Typos §7.7, case c(v) = 3/2: "d_G(v) − 2 other nodes x1, x2 in addition to v" should read "in addition to s and t". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic synchronous message passing in anonymous port-numbered networks (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/PortNumbering/Basic.lean). A PNGraph has degrees and an involution p on ports (0 … deg v − 1); loops and multi-edges are allowed, so the quotient graphs of the covering arguments are PNGraphs too. Initially a node knows only its degree. Each round it sends one message per port and receives one per port, indexed by its own port numbers. Messages and local computation are unbounded. An algorithm runs for T rounds, and then every node outputs a set of its ports. The selected edge set is outEdges; Consistent is the paper's requirement that both endpoints select the edge. The problem is posed on simple graphs (IsSimple, underlying SimpleGraph toSimpleGraph). IsEDS is an edge dominating set, edgeDomNum the minimum size. Approximates A T G α means: consistent, an EDS, and |D| ≤ α·γ'(G). Lower bounds are stronger than in the paper. They hold for every algorithm and every running time T that outputs an EDS on the one graph G. Consistency is not assumed. Upper-bound algorithms are written as local processes. Fast Distributed Almost Stable Matchings — PODC 2015 Rafail Ostrovsky, Will Rosenbaum. Fast Distributed Almost Stable Matchings. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767424. Formalized version: arXiv 1408.2782 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 4.1 is true with the paper's constants: for every maximal-matching subroutine, the deterministic algorithm ASM outputs a matching with at most ε|E| blocking pairs, and all lemmas of §§3–4 hold. But the proof of Lemma 4.4, on which Theorem 4.1 rests, has a real gap: it overlooks men who become bad while inactive, and we closed it with a different charging argument that gives the same bound. Theorem 4.7 (O(ε⁻³ log⁵ n) rounds given an O(log⁴ n)-round subroutine) is also true, as an explicit round count (no CONGEST message semantics); the randomized variants were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Display (1) in Lemma 4.3 has the rank differences reversed (it should be P^m(p(m)) − P^m(w) < 2deg(m)/k). Algorithm 3 has every processor test |Q| ≥ 2^i. Only the men can be meant, as §3.4 and §4.2 say: women and inactive men must still react to proposals and rejections. Theorem 2.7 states log⁴ n rounds, while [6] gives O(log⁴ n), the form used in the proof of Theorem 4.7. Typos The proof of Lemma 4.2 ends with "ε-blocking" for "(2/k)-blocking". In §3.1 the men's quantiles are described as sets of "men". P^v(∅) = deg v + 1 in Definition 2.3 is introduced only inside the proof of Lemma 4.3. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 4.4, proof (men who become bad while inactive) The proof bounds the men who end bad with Lemma 4.5, which counts only men active in the iteration, but a man can be displaced and become bad while inactive (Example.bad_while_inactive). Impact. Statement true, with the paper's bound 4δ|E|; repaired by a different charging argument (sum_bad_card_le, lemma_4_4). Theorem 4.1 is unaffected. Details. The proof charges each man who is bad at the end to the set B_i of men that became bad in outer iteration i with |Q^m| < 2^i. But a man can be matched when he leaves the active set and be displaced later. An active man proposes to his partner, she accepts the better proposal and rejects him. He then never proposes again and stays bad with a nonempty list. The application of Lemma 4.5 does not cover such men. The construction of the sets H_i and inequality (2) are not justified either. Concrete run (5 men, 5 women, k = 2, ℓ = 1, iterations 0–2, greedy maximal matching): In iteration 1, man 3 displaces man 0, who ends the iteration unmatched with |Q| = 4. In iteration 2 only man 0 is active. He proposes to woman 3 and displaces man 2, who is inactive (|Q| = 3). Man 2 ends bad without ever having been bad while active. We found no such run with the paper's parameters (ℓ = 16k/ε) by random search. Those parameters make bad active men rare, but the argument does not rule such runs out. Repair. The number of unmatched men never increases. Hence the inactive men displaced in iteration j are at most the bad active men at the start of iteration j, i.e. at the end of iteration j − 1, and each has |Q| < 2^j. A per-man potential (2^j if matched, |Q^m| if not) shows that inactive men gain nothing else. This gives ∑_{m bad} |Q^m| ≤ ∑_i 2^{i+1} b_i, where b_i is the number of bad active men at the end of iteration i. With Lemma 4.5 this yields Lemma 4.4's bound 4δ|E| for every δ > 0 (the paper needs δ ≤ 1/2). (sum_bad_card_le, lemma_4_4) 🔧 Lemma 4.5, proof (monotonicity of good active men) "The number of matched players can only increase, hence the number of good players can only increase" is applied to the active men, although individual active men can lose their partners. Impact. Statement true; a small missing step (card_bad_act_le, lemma_4_5). Repair. The count needs two facts: inactive men are never newly matched, and the number of matched men equals the number of matched women, which is monotone. (card_bad_act_le, lemma_4_5) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous, deterministic, no failures. Men M and women W are arbitrary finite types with symmetric incomplete preference lists. The communication graph is the set E of mutually acceptable pairs. The state is updated once per ProposalRound, through local rules. A man stores Q, p and A; a woman stores her partner. Each node's update depends only on its own state, one-bit PROPOSE/ACCEPT/REJECT messages from its neighbours, and its own partner in M₀. There is no formal CONGEST message-passing semantics. MaximalMatching (Theorem 2.7) is a black box MMOracle: any function returning a maximal matching of every bipartite graph, with a round count. All results hold for every oracle, so for every deterministic subroutine. The parameters are the paper's: k = ⌈8/ε⌉, ℓ = ⌈2k/δ⌉ with δ = ε/8, and outer iterations 0, …, ⌊log₂ n⌋, where n bounds the degrees. A general version holds for any k, ℓ, L. The paper does not give the rounding of the quantile sizes deg v / k; we use ⌈k · rank / deg⌉. Theorem 4.7 is proved for an explicit round count: ASM is run with a round counter that charges 3 one-bit rounds per ProposalRound plus the subroutine's T rounds (local steps are free). The counter ends at (L+1) · ℓ · k · (3 + T) (stageC_asm), which is O(ε⁻³ log⁵ n) for T = O(log⁴ n). This is a cost accounting, not a CONGEST execution: message sizes and the subroutine's implementation are not modelled. Main results in Lean. Weak Models of Distributed Computing, with Connections to Modal Logic — PODC 2012 Lauri Hella, Matti Järvisalo, Antti Kuusisto, Juhana Laurinharju, Tuomo Lempiäinen, Kerkko Luosto, Jukka Suomela, Jonni Virtema. Weak models of distributed computing, with connections to modal logic. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332466. Formalized version: the full journal version, arXiv 1205.2051 v3 (Dec 2013); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both linear orders hold as stated: SB ⊊ MB = VB ⊊ SV = MV = VV ⊊ VVc (1) and the same for the constant-time classes (2), together with every numbered result on the way (Theorems 4, 8, 9, 11, 13, 17, Lemmas 5, 6, 15, 16, Corollaries 3, 7, 10, 12, 14, 18). The two simulation proofs (Theorems 4 and 8/9) ignore nodes that have already stopped: a stopped node sends the empty message m0, so the simulating node cannot receive the extra information it needs from it, and a local change to each simulation closes this with the claimed running times. The modal-logic characterisation (Theorem 2) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 17, proof: the step "there are nodes u, v with t(u) < t(v) and t(v) maximal; this means S(u) = 0" is loose: S(u) = 0 needs a neighbour of larger type. Connectivity, which the paper invokes, gives an edge whose endpoints have different types, and its smaller endpoint outputs 0 (thm17_mem). In Theorem 11, Π(G) is undefined for stars with k ≤ 1: they are stars, but not k-stars with k > 1. We leave the output unrestricted there. Typos Lemma 6's consequence silently uses order k = 2 (the pair u, w itself). Theorem 11, proof: the algorithm tests "the set of messages {1}", but the received set also contains m0 when Δ > 1; the padding is notational, and the algorithm works when m0 is ignored. In Theorem 17 the local type is defined through out-ports (p((v, i))), but a node can only learn the in-port version (p⁻¹((v, i))). Under consistency the two agree, which is all the proof uses. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorems 8 and 9 (Multiset simulation; stopped neighbours) The simulating algorithm B sorts the full message histories received from neighbours, but a neighbour w that has stopped sends m0, so u no longer receives w's history and cannot place w's m0 in the sorted order. Impact. Statements true; repaired with a small extra mechanism, same time T (theorem8, theorem9). Details. B "augments each outgoing message with the full message history" and sorts the received histories lexicographically. But once a neighbour w of u has stopped in A, its copy in B has stopped too and sends m0. Repair. B stores at each node the multiset H of the full histories received so far. In each round it sets H' = R + (H − R.map dropLast).map (· ++ [m0]), where R is the multiset of histories actually received. So the stopped neighbours' histories are extended by m0; this update is exact for multisets. The paper's refinement P₀ ⊇ P₁ ⊇ … of compatible port numberings is replaced by a single port numbering p*: it copies the out-ports of p₀ and sorts the in-ports by the time-T histories of B's own run, so it is not circular. We show by induction that A on p* follows B on p₀ exactly, using that truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order. Time T is kept, as claimed. (theorem8, theorem9) 🔧 Theorem 4 (Set simulation; "all messages received are distinct") The proof's claim "now all messages received by a node are distinct" is false: stopped neighbours and padding all deliver m0. Impact. Statement true; repaired locally with running time T + 2Δ + 1 = T + O(Δ) (theorem4). Repair. The non-m0 messages are pairwise distinct by Lemma 6, so the number of m0s is Δ − #(distinct non-m0 messages), and the multiset of A's messages can be rebuilt from the set. Our Set algorithm runs C_Δ for 2Δ + 1 rounds and then simulates A. (theorem4) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Model.lean) Deterministic synchronous anonymous networks. There are no identifiers, no randomness and no failures; each node initially knows only its degree. Graphs are finite simple graphs G : SimpleGraph V, [Finite V]; deg v is Nat.card of the neighbour set. A port numbering is literally the paper's p : P(G) ≃ P(G) with A(p) = A(G), where Port G = Σ v, Fin (deg v) (ports are 0-based). It is not required to be an involution; Consistent means p ∘ p = id. A state machine Machine Δ Y has stopping states Y and arbitrary intermediate states and messages, with m0, z0 : ℕ → Y ⊕ Z, μ and δ : Z → (Fin Δ → M) → Y ⊕ Z. The execution is the paper's §1.3 verbatim: the received vector is ordered by in-port and padded with m0, and stopped nodes send m0 and keep their state. Multiset/Set/Broadcast are the paper's conditions on δ/μ. An algorithm is a sequence (A_Δ). "Solves Π in time T" quantifies over all Δ, all finite G ∈ F(Δ) and all (resp. all consistent) port numberings. Constant time means T(Δ, n) = T'(Δ). The 14 classes VVc … SB, VVc1 … SB1 are defined from these. Output sets Y are arbitrary types: the equalities hold for every Y, and the separating problems use Bool. Bisimulation (Bisimulation.lean) is defined on the paper's relations R(i,j), R(i,*) and R(*,*) = E. Instead of Theorem 2 (modal-logic characterisation, not formalized), we prove directly that bisimilar nodes run through identical states for every algorithm of the matching class; Corollary 3 follows. Lemma 5 is stated for rounds t ≥ 4; it holds for t ≥ 3 (PortNumbering.lemma5'). Main results in Lean. Recoverable Mutual Exclusion with Constant Amortized RMR Complexity — PODC 2020 David Yu Cheng Chan, Philipp Woelfel. Recoverable Mutual Exclusion with Constant Amortized RMR Complexity from Standard Primitives. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405736. Formalized version: the conference version (10 pages); proofs deferred to the full version were not used. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The algorithm of Figure 1 is correct: mutual exclusion, critical-section re-entry (wait-free), starvation freedom, wait-free recovery and wait-free recovery to exit are all proved. The RMR bound "O(m) when m passages begin" fails under the paper's literal definition of a passage, but holds in the DSM model when every crash also starts a passage, a one-clause change to the definition. The bound in the CC model, proved only in the full version, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorems 1–2 (RMR bound "O(m) when m passages begin") Under the paper's literal definition of a passage, a single process that calls Enter() once and then crashes in the critical section over and over begins one passage but incurs unboundedly many RMRs (Literal.rmr_literal_unbounded). Impact. The intent is evident: with the usual RME convention that a crash ends a passage and the recovery starts a new one, the bound holds (rmr_bound). Details. The paper says a passage "begins when [the process] calls Enter() and ends when the process crashes or when it finishes its following Exit() call". Read literally, the steps of Recover() belong to no passage. Take one process: it calls Enter() once and reaches the critical section. It then crashes in the critical section over and over, and each time Recover() line 20 sends it straight back in. Every round executes D.FAI() (line 15). This is an RMR in the CC model (a non-read operation), and in the DSM model for every process whose segment does not hold D (with n ≥ 2, pick such a process and keep the others idle). Repair. We prove at most 25·#Enter() + 76·#crashes RMRs in the DSM model, counting only crashes outside the remainder section (rmr_bound). ✏️ Slips Lemma 2.1 (19) and Lemmas 2.4–2.6 omit the fairness hypothesis. Lemma 2.1 is stated for "any run" and (19) assumes only finitely many crashes, but take two processes and no crash: process false gets ticket 1 and grants it to itself (W = (1,true)), then stops taking steps; process true gets ticket 2 and busy-waits forever with Token stuck at 0 (Lemma2_1_19.lemma2_1_19_false). These lemmas are only used in the starvation-freedom proof, where fairness holds, and there the paper's argument goes through. Typos Section 1, definition of a super-passage: "begins when the process calls Enter() and when it completes its following Exit() call" should read "and ends when". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, deterministic algorithm, processes of any finite type. Shared objects: FAI counters C, D; CAS objects (with read/write) A[1..∞], W[p], Exit[p], Token. A[c] is empty / claimed q / skipped (0 / q / −1). One shared-memory operation per step. The local code after it is merged into that step, and the recursive Move_Token() calls are tail calls (a jump to line 34). The program counter carries the local variables. Individual crash–recovery. Any process may crash at any time. Outside the remainder section a crash resets its local state and starts Recover(); in the remainder section it does nothing. Shared memory (NVM) is never lost. Executions are arbitrary schedules ℕ → {step p, crash p} (an adversarial scheduler, no randomness). Liveness assumes finitely many crashes and fairness: a process outside the remainder section keeps taking steps. A step in the CS is the call of Exit(). RMRs (DSM only): W[p] and Exit[p] live in p's segment. Every access to C, D, Token or A is charged as an RMR, which is an upper bound for every placement. Ghost state (ticket owners, c_{p,t}, crash credits, lost tickets) is computed alongside the execution and never read by the algorithm. Main results in Lean. Linear-in-Δ lower bounds in the LOCAL model — PODC 2014 Mika Göös, Juho Hirvonen, Jukka Suomela. Linear-in-Δ lower bounds in the LOCAL model. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611467. Formalized version: arXiv 1304.1007 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 1 is proved for deterministic LOCAL algorithms: no algorithm finds a maximal fractional matching in o(Δ) rounds, explicitly t ≥ ⌊Δ/2⌋ − 1. The whole chain is formalized (the unfold-and-mix lower bound in the EC model, the homogeneous order on the free group, the Ramsey step, and the identifier-elimination Lemmas 6–7) and every checked statement is true, but one step of the Section 4 proof (equation (3)) is justified by an induction hypothesis that does not apply, and needs a short nested induction. The randomized extension (Appendix B) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 7: the radius 2t + 1 is too small for t = 0. The radius occurs only inside the proof, not in the statement of Lemma 7. For t ≥ 1 the neighbours of the nodes of B_{t+1}(v) lie in B_{2t+1}(v) and the argument works. For t = 0 they do not, and the saturation indicator A* needs radius ≥ 1 to see its own edges. But for t = 0 the hypothesis of the lemma (a 0-round algorithm finding a maximal FM) cannot hold: such an algorithm already fails on a 3-node path (not_hasRunTime_zero). We use radius 2t + 2 throughout. Typos In the proof of Lemma 6, "τ_t(U_G, ≺, v) ≅ τ_t(U_G, ≺, v)" should end with u. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Equation (3) (Section 4.3, unfold-and-mix step) The paper justifies τ_i(GG, ĝ) ≅ τ_i(GH, h) "by our induction assumption" τ_i(G, g) ≅ τ_i(H, h), which does not apply because GH is not a lift of H. Impact. Statement true; repaired by a nested induction (Inv.step_core). The paper's idea is right, but the step as written is a gap a careful referee would flag. Details. The paper reduces (3) to the "critical case" g* = g. GG is a lift of G, but in GH the colour-c edge at h leads into the copy of G − e, and walks can cross that edge several times by going around loops. So τ_i(GH, h) ≅ τ_i(H, h) needs its own argument. Repair. The formal proof inducts on the radius r ≤ i + 1, simultaneously for all nodes of the G-half (GG vs GH) and of the H-half (HH vs GH). (Inv.step_core) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic LOCAL with unique identifiers. Take n = 4, t = 1, node 1 faulty, K = V, and a consensus thread that is correct (all correct electors output 1, after 1, 2 and 2 rounds). All nodes start together, nobody is strong, and the inputs are 1, 0, 0. Rounds are counted from 0 (round 0 is the first round of Algorithm 7; an elector whose consensus run took τ ≥ 1 rounds sends elect in round τ). Round 1: elector 2 sends elect(1). The faulty node sends elect(1) only to nodes 2 and 3, so nodes 2 and 3 vote 1 in round 2. Node 4 has one elect and does not vote yet. Round 2: the faulty node sends vote(1) only to node 4. Node 4 now has n − t = 3 votes and returns 1 without ever having voted. Nodes 2 and 3 are stuck at two votes and return their own inputs 1 and 0 at the timeout. Formalized version: arXiv 1503.06702 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The resilience-boosting construction (Theorem 1) and the main result Theorem 3 are verified: f = n^{1−o(1)}, O(f) stabilisation time, O(log² f / log log f + log c) state bits, with only constants corrected in §4.3; Corollaries 1 and 2 are verified for the network sizes the constructions produce (Corollary 1 only for n = 3f+1). The one loss is the time constant of Theorem 2, verified only in the weaker form 2^{2^{O(1/ε)}} f, and neither Corollary 2 nor Theorem 3 depends on it. Section 5 (the pulling model) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 2 (time bound unestablished) The proof of Theorem 2 uses a per-step cost h^k, but Theorem 1 gives (2m)^k = k^k, so the claimed O(2^{2^{1/ε}} f) time is not established (theorem2). Impact. We prove the weaker bound 2^{2^{O(1/ε)}} f and do not know whether the claimed one holds. Corollary 2 (constant ε) is unaffected (corollary2). ✏️ Slips Theorem 1 for n = 1: with f = 0, k = 3 its precondition F < (f+1)⌈k/2⌉ = 2 allows F = 1 on N = 3 nodes, but no 1-resilient counter on 3 nodes exists (theorem1_as_stated_false, construction_fails). So F < N/3, which the phase king needs, does not "follow from the preconditions of Theorem 1" (§3.4) here. The base counter exists (one node incrementing its counter). We prove the impossibility by an FLM-style covering argument on an infinite line of node copies. The paper's construction also fails concretely: the Byzantine node echoes each correct node's own phase-king register back to it. Every correct node then sees its own value N − F = 2 times and the other correct value only F = 1 time, so whatever instruction it executes it keeps counting on its own, and the two correct counters stay apart forever. Nothing downstream breaks: for n ≥ 2 with f < n/3 the claim F < N/3 is right, §4.1 and Corollary 1 use n = 1 but explicitly replace the hypothesis by F < N/3, and for n ≥ 3 the theorem holds exactly as stated (boost, theorem1_paper, theorem1_of_three_le). The bit count S(B) = S(A) + ⌈log(C+1)⌉ + 1 is an upper bound, not an equality. The instruction min{j : z_j > F} does not define the empty case (we use ∞). §3.3 defines majority for vectors of length kn with threshold kn/2, but uses it for vectors of length n and k. c_k for c_{k−1} (Lemmas 2–3, §3.5); u + (β−1)c_{i−1} for u + βc_{i−1} (Lemma 1); mod c for mod C (Lemma 5); π_F(x) = d for π_F(x) = e (§2); "fewer than f" for "at most f" faulty nodes (§3.1); (3f+2)(2m)^k for 3(f+2)(2m)^k (Corollary 1). Typos "Checking I₃ℓ₊₂" for I₃ℓ₊₁ and "some any non-faulty node" (proof of Lemma 4). Corollary 1 is stated for every n > 3f but proved only for n = 3f+1. Theorems 2 and 3 produce counters only for special network sizes. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 §4.3 (computation of n/f) With the stated R_p = 2k_p iterations, n/f = 2^{8·2^P−6}, not 2^{2(2^P−1)}; the paper's value corresponds to R_p = 2·2^{P−p} and drops a factor 4. Impact. Statement true: still log(n/f) = Θ(k_1), so f = n^{1−O(1/log log f)} survives (thm3N, theorem3_asymptotic). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/SyncCounting/Model.lean, shared). Complete network of nodes V, synchronous lock-step rounds. A deterministic algorithm is (X, g, h). Each round, every node broadcasts its whole state and moves to g i m, where m is the received state vector. Its output is h i s ∈ Fin c. Static Byzantine set F. A Byzantine node may send arbitrary, different states to different nodes. Arbitrary initial states: an execution is any sequence x : ℕ → V → X such that every correct node's next state is g i m for some m that agrees with the current states on the correct nodes (IsExec). Amortized Communication Complexity of Byzantine Broadcast — PODC 2023 Jun Wan, Zhuolun Xiang, Atsuki Momose, Ling Ren, Elaine Shi. On the Amortized Communication Complexity of Byzantine Broadcast. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594596. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (9 pages; no arXiv version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The honest-majority protocol (Algorithm 4), which the abstract presents as achieving optimal amortized linear communication, is not a correct multi-shot Byzantine broadcast: its Validity and Lemma 3 ("an honest leader's epoch always succeeds") fail in a concrete run with n = 6, f = 2, and no repaired protocol is proved. Consistency (Lemmas 1, 2, Theorem 1) is correct and proved, and the dishonest-majority protocol (Algorithm 5.2), which the paper presents as a generalization, satisfies Validity (Lemma 4) and Consistency (Lemma 5) only under a corrected reading of how TrustCast is invoked; read literally, both lemmas fail. The communication-complexity analyses were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Algorithm 4 (Validity) and Lemma 3 (an honest leader's epoch succeeds) In step (8) (Query-1) a node may query an honest helper v that accuses the leader in the same round, then accuse v in Query-2, so an honest node gets a corrupt-proof and all its epochs are skipped: with n = 6, f = 2 the honest sender's value is never committed (not_validity) and an honest leader's epoch fails (not_lemma3). Impact. The protocol that the abstract presents as achieving amortized linear communication is not a correct multi-shot Byzantine broadcast. Fixing it needs a protocol change, not a local edit, and no repaired protocol is proved. Consistency (Lemmas 1, 2, Theorem 1) is correct and proved. Details. In step (8), a node u without a commit-proof sends query₁ to the smallest node v that "has not accused L_i". An honest v that also lacks the commit-proof accuses L_i in the same round, so u cannot know this. v has nothing to send in Respond-1, and in Query-2 u accuses the honest v. Together with the Byzantine nodes' accusations this produces a corrupt-proof thsig(accuse, v) of an honest node. From then on, every honest node skips every epoch led by v, in every slot. The proof of Lemma 3 fails exactly at this point: "if L_i does not have a commit-proof … then L_i must have also accused the epoch's leader, and u would not have sent query₁ to L_i". Concrete run: n = 6, f = 2, ε = 1/6, G_ε = K₆ (a valid (n, 2ε, 1−2ε)-expander). Nodes 5 and 6 are Byzantine; node 5 sends slot 1 and node 1 sends slot 2 (paper numbering). In epoch 0 of slot 1 the Byzantine leader runs the protocol correctly but sends the commit-proof only to node 4. Nodes 1, 2, 3 accuse the leader; three accusations are too few for a corrupt-proof. Nodes 2 and 3 query node 1, and node 1 queries node 2; none of them has the commit-proof. In Query-2, nodes 2, 3, 5, 6 accuse node 1, which gives the n − f = 4 accusations of a corrupt-proof. Node 4 then answers the query₂s and slot 1 completes. In slot 2 the honest sender node 1 broadcasts true, and every honest node has committed slot 1, so sequentiality allows the invocation. Epochs 0 and 1 of slot 2 are led by node 1 and are skipped by every honest node. The honest leader of epoch 2 (node 2) proposes its arbitrary value false, which everybody commits. By consistency, no honest node ever commits true in slot 2, so Validity fails (not_validity). In the same run, slot 2's epoch 1 has an honest leader and nobody commits in it, so Lemma 3 fails (not_lemma3). The skip condition ("runs the following steps if it has neither committed in slot k, nor received thsig(accuse, L_i)") does not say when it is evaluated, so we checked three readings. Validity fails when "committed" is checked at the start of the epoch (with the corrupt-proof checked at the start of the epoch or at every step). Read literally, both conditions are checked at every step, so a node that holds a commit-proof has already committed and never answers queries. Rounds 8–11 then cannot disseminate anything, and Lemma 3 fails in the same run, already in slot 1. ❌ Algorithm 4, Respond-1 condition 2 Respond-1 condition 2 ("u is the smallest node v has not accused") ignores the Query-1 filter "has not accused L_i", so a helper chosen past a smaller node that had accused L_i refuses to answer and gets accused although it is honest. Impact. A second mismatch, independent of the one above: the helper cannot evaluate the querier's view of who accused L_i, and no fix is proved. This is not formalized; it comes from our analysis of the protocol in prose. 🔧 Lemmas 4 and 5 (Algorithm 5.2, how TrustCast is invoked) Read literally, TrustCast(G_u, n, k) maintains the shared trust graph only in rounds 1..n of slot k, and then with n = 3, f = 1 Lemma 5 fails in slot 1 and Lemma 4 in slot 3 (literal_consistency_fails, literal_validity_fails). Impact. Both lemmas hold for every slot of the multi-shot execution with maintenance in every round and evidence of every slot (validity, consistency). The proof of Lemma 5 already assumes such maintenance. Details. Algorithm 5.2 invokes TrustCast(G_u, n, k), whose rules run in rounds 1..n of the slot and only consider proposals of slot k. The trust graph, however, is shared across slots. Read literally, equivocation evidence that one honest node receives in round n reaches the others when it is no longer processed, and the honest trust graphs diverge forever. Concrete run: n = 3, f = 1, Byzantine sender in slots 1 and 2, honest sender in slot 3. In slot 1 one honest node commits ⊥ and the other commits a value, so Lemma 5 fails (literal_consistency_fails). In slot 2 an honest node accuses an honest node, so TrustCast's integrity fails (literal_integrity_fails). In slot 3 an honest node commits ⊥ although the sender is honest, so Lemma 4 fails (literal_validity_fails). Running graph maintenance in every round is not enough: equivocation evidence must also persist across slots (slotLocal_validity_fails). The proof of Lemma 5 uses transferability in the Dolev–Strong rounds, i.e. graph maintenance after round n. Repair. Run graph maintenance in every round and keep the equivocation evidence of every slot (the charitable Reading). ✏️ Slips The skip condition of Algorithm 4 does not say when it is evaluated; read literally, a node holding a commit-proof never answers queries, so the check must be made at the start of the epoch. Consistency is proved for all three readings (theorem1); the failure of Validity under that reading is the first mistake above. The definition of equivocation requires the two proposals to carry the same certificate C. Taken literally, a leader escapes detection by attaching different certificates. We use "two proposals with different values". The expander definition ("for any set S of αn vertices, the number of neighbours of S is more than βn") does not say whether S counts among its neighbours. It must: no graph has more than n − |S| = (1 − 2ε)n neighbours outside a set of 2εn vertices, so the exclusive reading admits no (n, 2ε, 1 − 2ε)-expander at all. We assume only the weaker form |S ∪ N(S)| > βn. K₆ in the counterexample satisfies even the stronger form |⋃_{v∈S} N(v)| > βn. Typos The proof of Lemma 2 refers to a "Leader setup" round; this is Collect. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Algorithm 4, Model.lean). Lock-step synchrony. A message sent in round r is available from round r+1, and multicasts include the sender. n nodes Fin n and a static Byzantine set F with |F| ≤ f. The paper's adaptive adversary only matters for the positive results; for the deterministic protocol it is no stronger than a static adversary that may send anything. A signed atom of an honest node may be used once some honest node has sent it (rushing, eavesdropping adversary). A threshold signature may be used once n − f of its shares may be used. Unbounded-Concurrency Objects — PODC 2011 Yehuda Afek, Adam Morrison, Guy Wertheim. From Bounded to Unbounded Concurrency Objects and Back. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993823. Formalized version: the authors' copy of the PODC paper (11 pages, with proofs; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All three results hold: Algorithm 1 is a wait-free linearizable unbounded-concurrency swap, n-consensus objects for all n (with registers) give no unbounded-concurrency consensus, and the iterator stack has infinite consensus number but cannot solve unbounded-concurrency consensus. The proof of Lemma 15, the core of the iterator-stack impossibility, does not work as written and needed a redesigned construction; a few other proofs skip a case or a step. The composed claim of swap "from 2-consensus objects" was not checked, because F&A and snapshot are atomic base objects here. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips §4 overview: process P₀ "with depth 0" captures the root, but in Algorithm 1 max_depth starts at 1, so depths start at 1 and the root is never captured. The pseudocode and the proofs do not depend on this. §4.1 says Line 9 looks at accessed nodes "of depth ≤ depth_i"; the pseudocode (and the proofs) use all nodes of depth ≤ maxdepth_i. Theorem 9's proof: "some P_i that returns before P_j starts is ordered before P_j" should read after. Lemma 13's proof: "each step in L₁ but the last keeps the system in a bivalent state" fails for an arbitrary extension L₁ reaching a q-valent state. It holds if L₁ stops at its first q-valent state, and the proof does not use the remark (lemma_13). Lemma 14's proof: "In e_P (where I[m+1] is initially 1)" should be 2. Lemma 15's proof: "o_P = write(v_P) and o_P = write(v_Q)": the second is o_Q. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 15 (the two critical operations are not writes to the same iterator stack) The construction that keeps the victim R from ever deciding can stall, and its last step can fail; the lemma is true and we prove it with a repaired construction (lemma_15). Impact. Statement true; the impossibility half of Theorem 11 (no_consensus_iterator_stack) is fully proved. Details. The paper introduces new processes one by one and runs each one "until (1) it reads from O using an iterator i ∈ T, or (2) it is about to write to O". Two problems: A process stopped at (1) is frozen forever, even if its read cannot tell the two executions apart (for instance a read of an iterator that has already run off the end of V). An algorithm can make every new process start with such a read. Then every new process is frozen at once, no write happens, and R never moves. The claim "if only (1) occurs, eventually all iterators in T become invalid … a contradiction" is false: nothing forces the frozen readers to read different iterators. After the two writes the paper schedules R's read and says it "returns the value in V[k]". But any process may read any iterator, so the frozen readers may have advanced R's own iterator. Two writes shift V by two, and R's iterator may then point at v_P or v_Q again. Repair. Freeze a new process only at a distinguishing read, i.e. a read whose iterator points into the two entries holding v_P, v_Q. Such a read changes the memory identically in both executions. Keep writers pending and execute two writes together. Re-check R after every frozen read: if its own read is no longer distinguishing, let it move. Each distinguishing read strictly decreases the potential Σ (w + 3 − pos) over all iterators while no write is executed, so each unblocking phase ends (unblock, round, false_of_rel15). Executing writes one at a time would not obviously work: an algorithm could alternate writes with reads of R's iterator and keep R blocked forever. 🔧 Lemma 1 (Algorithm 1: no capture in the right subtree of an unrecorded node) The proof finds a node u with v_l < u < v_r that was accessed early and concludes that u lies in the right subtree of v or of v_l; it misses the case u = v. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma1_paper, state form lemma1). Details. The case u = v is excluded because the capturer of v records v in accessed (Line 5) before it starts blocking nodes, hence before P_i tries v_r. Also, the step "Lemma 1 implies wait-freedom of the capturing phase" leaves termination implicit. It holds because successive capture attempts at a fixed depth d move strictly right among the 2^d nodes of that depth (waitFree). 🔧 Lemma 5 and Theorem 9 (Algorithm 1: the chain) Lemma 5's proof only shows that the input of the process with the largest captured node is not returned (not that it is the only one), and Theorem 9 asserts without argument that Lemmas 4–8 make ⇝ a chain. Impact. Statements true; repaired (lemma5, theorem9_complete, linearizable). Details. Uniqueness follows by counting: n processes, n−1 non-⊥ returns, each value returned at most once (Lemma 7). The chain is built by induction along the order of captured nodes: the process with the next larger captured node returns the value of the current one. The linearization is the increasing order of captured nodes. The paper proves linearizability for complete executions only. We extend it to all finite executions by finishing the pending operations with solo runs (wait-freedom). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, deterministic processes, wait-freedom. Uses the CSLib-staged arrival model Cslib.SharedMemory.Arrival (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Arrival/). Processes are ℕ, and each one performs a single invocation with its input; every step is one atomic operation on one base object. Unbounded concurrency: every infinite schedule is allowed, so infinitely many processes may arrive and stay active. Bounded concurrency (Theorem 12): the number of started-but-unreturned processes stays below a bound that depends on the execution and is unknown to the algorithm (Alg2.BoundedConcurrency). There is no randomness and no failure model beyond asynchrony (a process that stops taking steps has crashed). The impossibility results assume agreement, weak validity and wait-freedom. All Byzantine Agreement Problems Are Expensive. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662780. Formalized version: arXiv:2311.08060v2 (numbering follows it). Companion of On the Validity of Consensus (PODC 2023, ValidityConsensus). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result holds: every non-trivial Byzantine agreement problem needs Ω(t²) messages, even in synchrony, and we prove it for every t < n with the explicit bound t² ≤ 32 · #messages, with or without signatures (the paper proves the weak-consensus bound even against omission faults; we also get the omission version for every non-trivial problem). Lemma 1's proof covers only t divisible by 8 and is repaired by rounding its parameters. The solvability characterization (Theorem 4) is proved too, but Lemma 10 and the unauthenticated half of Theorem 4 are false for n = 2, t = 1, and one added condition corrects them. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 10 and Theorem 4 (unauthenticated), n = 2, t = 1 Lemma 10 (unauthenticated-solvable with n ≤ 3t ⇒ trivial) and the unauthenticated half of Theorem 4 are false for n = 2, t = 1: weak consensus, a non-trivial problem, is solvable there by "exchange proposals; decide the common value if they agree, a default otherwise" (lemma10_counterexample, theorem4_unauth_as_stated_false). Impact. The lower bound and the authenticated half of Theorem 4 are unaffected, and we prove corrected statements (trivial_of_solvableSync, theorem4_unauth'). Details. Theorem 4 says a non-trivial problem is unauthenticated-solvable iff CC holds and n > 3t. Both statements rest on the cited FLM-style fact that weak consensus needs n > 3t. With two processes and one fault, every faulty execution has a single correct process, so Agreement constrains only fault-free executions. The same idea solves interactive consistency. The FLM argument needs three non-empty groups of size ≤ t, i.e. n ≥ 3. Repair. Lemma 10 holds for 3 ≤ n ≤ 3t. A non-trivial problem is unauthenticated-solvable iff CC holds and (n > 3t or n ≤ 2). (trivial_of_solvableSync, theorem4_unauth') Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 1 (the "without loss of generality" step) Lemma 1 is proved only for t ≥ 8 divisible by 8: for other t the group sizes t/4 and t/2 must be rounded, and t = 1 admits no group of size ≥ 1 of the required kind. Impact. Statement true for every t < n; repaired (omission_lower_bound, omission_lower_bound_sq, one_message). Repair. We prove a parametric bound (⌈β/2⌉·σ messages) and choose parameters for every t. For t = 1 we add a separate zero-message argument: without any messages each process decides as in isolation, which contradicts Agreement in a mixed fault-free execution. (omission_lower_bound, omission_lower_bound_sq, one_message) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchrony. The shared partially synchronous Byzantine model, restricted to runs with gst = 0. Delays lie in [0, δ]; δ = 0 is the paper's lock-step round model. n deterministic processes, at most t < n statically Byzantine, authenticated links. Optional ideal signatures (unforgeable tokens). Every lower bound is proved with signatures. The lower bounds hold for every δ; Algorithm 1 is stated for δ = 0. Omission model. A lock-step execution is the inputs plus a set of omitted message batches. A fault set is admissible if every omitted batch has an endpoint in it, so the paper's swap_omission (Lemma 15) is just another admissible fault set for the same execution. Omission executions are simulated by Byzantine runs, so the omission lower bounds transfer. Message complexity. Messages sent by correct processes to others from time 0. Omitted messages count, and self-messages do not. Results are stated as "some valid run has ≥ … messages within finite time". Remarks. Algorithm 1 (Lemma 6) needs lock-step rounds. It assumes that a fault-free execution is determined by the proposals. That fails if the adversary may choose delays in [0, δ] with δ > 0. This is harmless: the paper's model is lock-step, and we prove Theorem 3 directly in the omission model for every δ. The proof of Theorem 5 assumes "without loss of generality n = 2t"; we prove it for every n ≤ 2t. "Without loss of generality, the default is 1" before Lemma 4 is made explicit. Asynchronous Byzantine Approximate Consensus in Directed Networks — PODC 2020 Dimitris Sakavalas, Lewis Tseng, Nitin H. Vaidya. Asynchronous Byzantine Approximate Consensus in Directed Networks. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405724. Formalized version: arXiv 2004.09054 v1 (the only version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result (Theorem 4) holds: asynchronous approximate Byzantine consensus on a directed graph is solvable iff the graph satisfies 3-reach, and the paper's Algorithm BW + Filter-and-Average, implemented message by message, solves the problem under 3-reach, after local fixes to the message sets and covers (the paper is inconsistent about whether a stored path ends at the receiver), to FIFO-Receive, to the update rule ((max − min)/2 must be (max + min)/2) and to several proof steps (Theorems 10, 11, 14, 18, Lemma 8). We prove this end to end in one asynchronous message-passing model with FIFO links, with the known input range [0, K] that Section 4.6 assumes added to Definition 1 and Theorem 4. The paper does not assume FIFO links: necessity in the FIFO model is the stronger statement, but sufficiency over non-FIFO links, and hence the end-to-end theorem there, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Definitions 4, 9 and Appendix E (message sets; the algorithm never makes progress) The paper is inconsistent about whether a stored path ends at the receiver, and under either reading Algorithm BW never makes progress, e.g. with paths ending at v the set {v} is an f-cover of everything v holds, so Verify fails in every thread forever (RoundExec.never_verifyLit). Impact. Algorithms 2, 3 and Appendix E must change. With the fix below the algorithm works and Theorem 4 holds. Details. Paths stored by v end at v (Definition 9). An f-cover (Definition 4) may contain any ≤ f nodes, so {v} covers every message v holds. Then Algorithm 2 (Completeness) never holds: take Fw with v ∈ Fu ∪ Fw, so that v ∉ S_{Fu,Fw}. FIFO-Receive-All always includes v's own COMPLETE(Fv), so Verify fails in every thread forever. Algorithm 3 would trim everything. Paths end at the sender (Appendix E). Then no stored path has ter(p) = v, so no message set is ever full for (A, v) (Definition 9), and Maximal-Consistency never fires. The intent is evident from the paper: thread sets satisfy Fv ⊆ V \ {v} (line 5), covers in Lemma 8 (Eq. (1)) avoid v, and footnote 5 says the same. The Lean counterexample for the first reading (RoundExec.never_verifyLit) is proved in the abstract round model RoundExec for every round execution, including the fault-free one on K₄ with f = 1. It is not proved for an operational run of the literal algorithm. (RoundExec.never_verifyLit, not_completenessLit, not_isFALit) Repair. A node never suspects itself: paths end at v, and v is never in a cover. 🔧 Appendix F (FIFO-Receive) Appendix F defines FIFO-receive by receipt along any path, under which a forged copy on a Byzantine path would satisfy the condition, while Theorem 10 needs FIFO order along the specific path c → v. Impact. The printed rule does not give what Theorem 10 uses. Theorem 10 is proved from the per-path guarantee (theorem10). Repair. We use per-path FIFO-receive with counters (fifoCR). ✏️ Slips Algorithm 3, line 5. The update x_v[r+1] = (max O' − min O')/2 breaks validity: all inputs 1 give 0 (minus_update_invalid). It must be (max + min)/2, and the proofs' inequalities are those of (max + min)/2. It also appears in the proof of Lemma 15 and in Appendix G. Definition 1 and Theorem 4 (known input range). Section 4.6 states explicitly that the inputs lie in [0, K] with K known to all nodes, and the termination argument needs this, but the assumption is missing from Definition 1 and Theorem 4. We prove Theorem 4 in that setting with 0 < ε < K; for K ≤ ε the problem is trivial. The necessity also holds for arbitrary real inputs. (theorem4, threeReach_of_solves) Cliques. In a clique, 1-reach always holds, not "iff n > f". 2- and 3-reach also hold for n = 1. n = 1. 3-reach holds vacuously and source components may meet F₁ ∪ F₂, which the sufficiency proofs implicitly exclude. Consensus is trivial there (trivAlg_solves). After output. Nodes must keep relaying after they output; the paper does not say so. Typos U[r+1] − μ[r+1] ≤ (U[0] − μ[0])/2^r should be /2^{r+1}; the stated bound is still true. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorems 10, 11 and 14 (common values for the trimming cover) The proofs use the common values R_{F_lo} for the trimming cover F_lo, but R_W is defined only for W ≠ F_t, and F_lo = F_t is possible. Impact. Statements true; repaired (theorem10, pair_le). Details. For f = 0 the index set is empty. When the cover is F_t, any other W works. (theorem10) 🔧 Lemma 8, Case II The proof claims the f+1 paths into z "trivially" have no f-cover outside S, but {z} covers them. Impact. Statement true: the argument works only because the relevant F' avoids z. Lemma 8 also holds without its extra hypotheses. (completeness_eventually) 🔧 Theorem 18 (necessity) The proof uses inputs 0 and ε, which are still "within ε", and its executions are not fully specified. Impact. Statement true: inputs 0 and 2ε (any two more than ε apart) fix this, and we construct the replay explicitly. (threeReach_of_solvesOn) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A finite node set with a known directed graph G (Mathlib Digraph; self-loops ignored). Deterministic event-driven algorithms, reliable FIFO links with arbitrary finite delays. A static set of ≤ f Byzantine nodes that may deliver arbitrary messages to their out-neighbours at any time (full-information adversary). Fairness: every non-empty link between correct nodes is eventually served. Specification (SolvesOn I): for inputs in I, decisions of correct nodes are within ε and between two correct inputs at every time (all event sequences), and in fair runs every correct node decides. Links are FIFO in Lean but not in the paper. For necessity this is a strengthening: impossibility with FIFO links implies impossibility without them. For sufficiency it is a restriction: bw_solves and theorem4 are proved only for FIFO links. FIFO-receive does use counters as in Appendix F, but the delivery argument (chan_inv, eventually_received) is stated for FIFO channels. We have not proved that the algorithm also works over non-FIFO links. The algorithm is implemented as a full-information state machine (input + history). Every "upon …"/"for the first time" condition of Algorithm 1 is evaluated on prefixes of the history, and a node runs outRound K ε rounds. Structure of the sufficiency proof. RoundModel.lean describes one round by what correct nodes have received over time, plus the guarantees of RedundantFlood and FIFO-Flood (RoundExec). The paper's Lemmas 6–15 and Theorem 16 are proved at this level. Operational/ proves that every fair run of the real algorithm yields such rounds (mkRound). No field of RoundExec is assumed.
