Speculatively Stabilizing Mutual Exclusion — PODC 2013 Swan Dubois, Rachid Guerraoui. Introducing speculation in self-stabilization: an application to mutual exclusion. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484246. Formalized version: arXiv 1302.2217 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The protocol results stand: SSME is self-stabilizing for mutual exclusion under the unfair distributed daemon (Theorem 1), and under the synchronous daemon it stabilizes within ⌈diam/2⌉ steps (Theorem 2, by a new proof), which is optimal for SSME. But the optimality bound of Theorem 4 (no protocol stabilizes in fewer than ⌈diam/2⌉ synchronous steps), which the abstract stresses as a result of independent interest, is false under the paper's own Specification 1 and holds only for protocols whose privileged reads the process's own state, as in SSME. The claim that SSME is speculatively stabilizing was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 4 (lower bound ⌈diam/2⌉ for every protocol) Theorem 4 is false when privileged_v reads the neighbours of v, as Specification 1 allows: on the complete graph K_n (n ≥ 2, diam = 1) a token-passing protocol has mutual exclusion from time 0, while the theorem claims at least ⌈1/2⌉ = 1 step (theorem_4_false). Impact. The abstract's claim that ⌈diam/2⌉ is optimal "even if asynchronous stabilization is not required" is false in the paper's own model: on every graph whose radius is ⌈diam/2⌉ (every tree, complete graph, star, odd square grid, …) some protocol needs only ⌈diam/2⌉ - 1 steps. The bound holds when privileged_v reads only v's own state, as in SSME, so SSME is still optimal among such protocols (theorem_4, conv_time_ssme). Details. Specification 1 lets privileged_v be "a predicate over variables of v and possibly of its neighbours". The proof of Theorem 4 only makes the t-balls around u and v agree with earlier configurations. A predicate that reads the neighbours needs the (t+1)-balls. Complete graph K_n: take registers in ℤ_n. Process v is privileged iff the sum of all registers is v, and a privileged process increments its register. Exactly one process is privileged in every configuration, and the privilege goes round-robin. So mutual exclusion holds from time 0 under the synchronous daemon, and even under the unfair one (theorem_4_false). Star K_{1,n-1} (n ≥ 3, diam = 2): a pointer held by the centre does the same under the synchronous daemon (theorem_4_false_star). General construction: pick a centre z of eccentricity R and a BFS tree rooted at z. Process z increments a clock modulo n, every other process sets c_v := c_parent(v) + 1, and privileged_v ≡ (c_parent(v) = id_v). After R - 1 synchronous steps every clock within distance R - 1 of z equals c_z, so mutual exclusion holds from time R - 1 on (theorem_4_false_centre). Whenever the radius is ⌈diam/2⌉, this beats the claimed bound by one (theorem_4_false_of_radius). Repair. If privileged_v reads the ball of radius r around v, the bound is ⌈diam/2⌉ - r (theorem_4_radius). For r = 0 this is the paper's bound (theorem_4). For r = 1 it is tight on all graphs of radius ⌈diam/2⌉. Optimality of SSME among protocols whose privileged reads only the own state is not affected, since SSME's privileged reads only r_v (conv_time_ssme). 🔧 Lemma 4 (registers at time D after a non-legitimate start) Lemma 4 is off by one step: on C₅ (n = 5, D = 2, K = 29) with registers (10, 10, 10, 12, 11), process 0 holds 12 at time D, outside the claimed set init ∪ {K-D, …, K-1} ∪ {0, …, 2D-1} (lemma_4_false). Impact. Only the lemma is false; its corrected version still gives Case 2 of Theorem 2, which holds (lemma_4_corrected, theorem_2). Details. The lemma claims that if γ₀ ∉ Γ₁, every register at time D = diam lies in the set above. In the counterexample, the incorrect edge 2–3 resets at step 0 and its neighbours reset at step 1. Process 0 is at distance exactly D from the incorrect edge, keeps incrementing, and holds 12 at time D = 2. The proof assumes that the reset wave reaches a process at distance i ≤ D from the RA-enabled set by time i; it only acts there one step later. Repair. From time D + 1 on, every register is ≤ t or ≥ K - D - 1 (lemma_4_corrected). This still gives Case 2 of Theorem 2, because the only privileged value ≥ K - D - 1 is that of the process with identity n - 1. ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 4, first sentence: it claims that some process is RA-enabled whenever γ₀ ∉ Γ₁, which fails when all registers are negative. The corrected lemma covers this case with no new idea (lemma_4_corrected). Lemma 5 is false under the paper's formal definition of a protocol (an arbitrary set of global actions, so the next state may depend on far-away processes); it holds for protocols given by local deterministic rules (lemma_5). Implied assumption: the paper uses guarded local rules everywhere else, so we state the lemma for local rules. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Definition 5 and Lemmas 2–3 (islands) Islands (Definition 5) are ill-defined, and the proof of Lemma 2 uses the false step "same island and dist(u, v) ≤ D ⇒ d_K(r_u, r_v) ≤ D", so Lemmas 2–3 are not established as stated. Impact. The statements we need hold: Case 1 of Theorem 2 is proved with a new argument that needs no islands (cone, no_two_priv_early), and Theorem 2 stands (theorem_2). Details. An island is "a maximal set I ⊊ V all of whose internal edges are correct". This requires neither connectivity nor registers in stab, and it excludes I = V, which leaves a process uncovered when all registers are in stab but a chord is incorrect. With the intended reading (components of the correct-edge graph), the proof of Lemma 2 still uses the step above. It is false, because the path realising dist(u, v) may leave the island. Case 1 of Theorem 2 also mixes up island depth (a maximum over the island) with the depth of u. Repair. We prove Case 1 with a light cone (cone): if u is privileged at time i ≤ D, every process within distance i-1-j of u is allCorrect at time j, and the registers in the cone differ from r_u by at most the distance, as integers. The equality case i = D needs one extra observation that the paper does not make: a process that moves at step 0 is a local minimum (no_two_priv_early). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Atomic-state model with CSLib's daemons (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SelfStabilization/Daemon.lean). The protocol is the local rule next : (V → ℤ) → V → ℤ (rules NA, CA, RA with exclusive guards). Unfair distributed daemon: IsUnfairRun (any nonempty set of enabled processes moves; no fairness). Synchronous daemon: all enabled processes move. Executions are sequences ω t = (configuration, activated set). MutualExclusion = Specification 1: at most one privileged process in every configuration, and every process is privileged and activated (executes its critical section) infinitely often. Graph: any connected simple graph with n ≥ 2 processes. Identities: any injective id : V → {0, …, n-1}. Registers are integers restricted to the clock cherry(n, K) by SValid. Deterministic, no failures besides the arbitrary initial configuration. Strongly Linearizable Snapshots and ABA-Detecting Registers — PODC 2019 Sean Ovens, Philipp Woelfel. Strongly Linearizable Implementations of Snapshots and Other Types. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331632. Formalized version: arXiv 1908.10826 v1 (full version, 51 pp.); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The one mistake of substance is the specification of the first DRead, which wrongly forces every process's first DRead to report "no write"; for the natural specification, one condition away, Theorem 1 holds: Algorithm 2 is a lock-free strongly linearizable ABA-detecting register from n + 1 registers of O(log n + log |D|) bits. Observation 4 (Algorithm 1 is not strongly linearizable) holds, and Theorem 25 (Algorithm 3, the snapshot, is strongly linearizable) and its lock-freedom (Theorem 32) are proved with atomic S and R. The paper's main claim of a bounded-space snapshot, which needs a merely linearizable S, and Theorem 3 (simple types) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Section 3 (specification of the first DRead) and Theorem 12 The specification makes a process's first DRead return "no write", but Algorithms 1 and 2 return true for it, so in the sequential execution DWrite_p(x); DRead_p() the read returns (x, true) and Algorithm 2 is not even linearizable for the literal specification, for every n ≥ 1 (not_linearizable_literal). Impact. A mis-stated definition with evident intent: read literally, Theorem 12 is false, but with the natural specification Theorem 1 holds and is proved (theorem1). Algorithm 3 is unaffected: it only uses the flag of a DRead that follows a DRead of the same SLscan. Details. Section 3 defines DRead_q() to return a = true iff "q performed an earlier DRead_q() and a DWrite was performed since q's last DRead_q()". So a first DRead must return false. In Algorithm 2 a first DRead after any DWrite reads A[q] = ⊥ ≠ (p, s), sets changed, and returns true. The proof misses it because Lemma 8 only compares two consecutive DReads and Theorem 10 never treats the first one. Repair. The specification "a DWrite since q's last DRead_q() or since the beginning". This is the PODC'15 ABADetection formalization's abaObj, and Theorem 1 is proved for it. ✏️ Slips Observation 6(b) reads "A[p] = s throughout [t, t']", while the intended statement, used in Lemma 7, is "A[q] = (p, s) throughout [t, t']". The intended statement is true. The paper takes it from a thesis without proof; we prove it as an invariant of GetSeq (protBy_getSeq, protBy_of_wInv). Typos Lemma 8 refers to "the loop-guard on line 53" (line 41 is meant). Theorem 12's proof cites "Theorem 11" (Lemma 11 is meant). Lemma 11's case (ii) cites Q-2 instead of Q-1. Observation 6(a) says "at least n" GetSeq calls where the queue gives n + 1. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl): n processes Fin n, deterministic programs, atomic base objects, arbitrary scheduler. Executions are label lists, and a response is a separate step after the operation's last access. Strong linearizability is CSLib's Impl.StronglyLinearizable (a prefix-preserving linearization function). Lock-freedom is Impl.LockFree (every infinite execution with infinitely many steps has infinitely many responses). ABA-detecting register: abaObj (Fin n) V v₀ (value domain V with ⊥ = v₀; DRead carries the reader, and only q may invoke dread q). Algorithm 2 runs on n + 1 registers over V × Option (Fin n × Fin (2n+2)). The arbitrary choice on line 11 is any pick avoiding the excluded values (PickSpec); theorem1 uses pickMin. Snapshot: CSLib's snapObj n over ℕ (0 = ⊥; update_p(x) only on component p, x ≠ 0). Algorithm 3's lock-freedom is proved with a lexicographic potential: pending update work, stale scanner views, R ≠ S, scanners heading for the line-51 write, and steps left in the current iteration. The paper instead derives it from the amortized bound of Section 4.4. Algorithm 3 runs on an atomic snapshot S and an atomic ABA-detecting register R over vectors. The paper's S may be any linearizable snapshot (that gives bounded space), and R may be Algorithm 2 (by composability). Neither substitution is formalized: CSLib has no composition theorem. The linearization function R-1/R-2 is the paper's. It does not look at where S's operations take effect, so we expect the proof to transfer to a linearizable S, but this is not checked. Hardness of Hub Labeling in Sparse Graphs — PODC 2019 Adrian Kosowski, Przemysław Uznański, Laurent Viennot. Hardness of exact distance queries in sparse graphs through hub labeling. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331625. Formalized version: arXiv 1902.07055 v3; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The hub-labeling lower bound holds as stated: Lemma 2.2 for the weighted layered graph H_{b,ℓ}, the pass-through and distance part of Lemma 2.2 for the degree-3 graph G_{b,ℓ}, Theorem 2.1 (i)–(iii) and Theorem 1.1 are proved, all with explicit constants. One step of the proof of Lemma 2.2 is false: the claim that G_{b,ℓ} preserves all distances of H_{b,ℓ} between levels; only the special case the theorem needs is true, and it needs a new potential argument. The Sum-Index reduction and the Ruzsa–Szemerédi upper bound (Sections 3 and 4) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 2.1, inequality (1): |S*_v| ≤ diam(G)·|S_v| is off by one, since a single hub at distance diam gives a subtree of diam + 1 vertices. The factor should be diam + 1; the loose second inequality absorbs this (card_hubPathSet_le). Proof of Theorem 2.1 (iii), counting of triplets: it prints z = 2x − y and x = 2z − y; from y = (x+z)/2 the right formulas are z = 2y − x and x = 2y − z (card_triples_le_sum). Typos "path of length w(e) − 2b + −2" should be w(e) − 2b − 2. "V = ⋃_{r=0}^{2ℓ} V_i" has a mismatched index. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 2.2 for G_{b,ℓ} (distances preserved between levels) The proof asserts dist_G(u, v) = dist_H(u, v) for all u ∈ V_i, v ∈ V_j with i < j, which is false already for b = 1, ℓ = 2, j = i + 1 (dist_claim_false). Impact. Lemma 2.2's use is fine: Theorem 2.1 only needs the case u = v_{0,x}, v = v_{2ℓ,z} with z − x even, and there the conclusion is true; we prove it by a different argument (lemma_2_2_G). Details. To transfer Lemma 2.2 from H_{b,ℓ} to G_{b,ℓ}, the proof asserts that dist_G(u, v) = dist_H(u, v) for all u ∈ V_i, v ∈ V_j with i < j. For j = i + 1 it cites "the construction". This is false. The mechanism: in G, a walk can enter the in-tree T_w^in of an upper vertex w through one leaf and leave it through another leaf without visiting w. That saves up to 2b steps. The corresponding H-walk u → w → u' must pay both full edge weights. Counterexample: b = 1, ℓ = 2 (A = 24), u = v_{0,(0,0)}, v = v_{1,(0,1)}. Every H-walk from u to v needs at least 3 edges, one of them changing coordinate 2, so it weighs ≥ 3A + 1 = 73. G has a walk of length 71: u → v_{1,(0,0)} → in-tree of v_{2,(0,1)} (leaf 0, root, leaf 1) → v_{1,(0,1)}. (dist_claim_false) The vertex-cut argument for j > i + 1 inherits the same gap. For the pair the theorem needs, d_G = d_H = 2ℓA + Σ_k (z_k − x_k)²/2, and every shortest G-walk passes through v_{ℓ,(x+z)/2} (lemma_2_2_G). Repair. The repaired proof uses potentials, not a walk-by-walk comparison with H: An integer function on V(G) changes by at most 1 per edge. It is 0 at v_{0,x} and ℓA + Σ_k (j_k − x_k)² at v_{ℓ,j}. Coordinates not yet "reached" carry a correction term 2(s−1)|d| − d², and the potential interpolates linearly along trees and paths. The slack A = 3ℓs² ≫ s² + b absorbs the turnaround shortcuts. The level reflection of G gives the same bound from v_{2ℓ,z}. V_ℓ separates the bottom from the top. Summing the two bounds gives Lopt + 2 Σ_k (j_k − m_k)² for a walk through v_{ℓ,j}, with m = (x+z)/2. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Pure graph combinatorics; there is no distributed model, randomness or adversary. H_{b,ℓ} is a SimpleGraph on Fin (2ℓ+1) × ([0,s−1]^ℓ) (s = 2^b, A = 3ℓs²). It has integer weights A + Σ_k (u_k − v_k)², which is the paper's A + (j_c − j'_c)² on edges. Walk weight wlen coincides with CSLib's Walk.wlength, and wdist is CSLib's weighted distance. G_{b,ℓ} is built exactly as in the paper: in- and out-trees as heaps, and every H-edge of weight w becomes a path of w − 2b − 2 edges. Coordinates are 0-indexed. A hub labeling (SimpleGraph.IsHubLabeling) asks for a common hub on a shortest path (d(u,w) + d(w,v) = d(u,v)) only for reachable pairs. This is the paper's definition on connected graphs and a weaker hypothesis in general, so the lower bounds are slightly stronger. Throughout, b, ℓ ≥ 1, as in the paper ("positive integers"). The Multi-Agent Rotor-Router on the Ring — PODC 2013 Ralf Klasing, Adrian Kosowski, Dominik Pająk, Thomas Sauerwald. The Multi-Agent Rotor-Router on the Ring: A Deterministic Alternative to Parallel Random Walks. PODC 2013. DOI 10.1145/2484239.2484260. Formalized version: the full version HAL hal-00735113v2 (September 2014, 28 pp.); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The proofs of Theorem 3.2 (worst case Θ(n²/log k)) and Theorem 3.5 (best-case upper bound O((n/k)²)) are broken and nothing we proved repairs them; neither statement is refuted, but neither is established here. Of the range the paper claims, only the best-case lower bound stands: Theorem 3.7 (cover time Ω((n/k)²) for every start set) is true, and we prove it with a new argument and explicit constant, for n ≥ 8k instead of n ≥ 440k². The delayed-deployment technique (Lemmas 2.1–2.3, the slow-down lemma) is correct on every graph, while Theorem 3.4 and the return-time result (Theorem 4.1) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 3.2, proof (worst case Θ(n²/log k), Phase B and final bound) The deployment and its analysis use the misprinted identity (4) of Lemma 3.1 (g_i ≈ 2 a_i a_k k⁴ a₁, S_{j+1} = S_j + ⌈k⁴ a₁ a_k⌉ + 12k), and the last step goes from B₁ ∈ Θ(n²/a₁) with a₁ = Θ(1/H_k) to Θ(n²/log k), although that would really be Θ(n² log k). Impact. The worst-case bound of the abstract is not established. The statement is not refuted and looks true with the corrected lemma, but Theorem 3.2 is not formalized here. Details. The two errors cancel: with the corrected identity the computation gives Θ(n² a₁) = Θ(n²/log k) as claimed. But the Phase B deployment itself is defined with the step ⌈k⁴ a₁ a_k⌉, so a correct proof needs a redefined deployment, with steps of about 2k⁴ a_k / a₁. That deployment is not in the paper, and we did not check that the proof works with it. Repair. None proved. It needs the corrected lemma (lemma_3_1_corrected) and a reworked deployment. ❌ Theorem 3.5, proof (best-case upper bound O((n/k)²)) The deployment is inconsistent: an agent "returns to q_i" after each step, but q_i's pointer then points left, so the next step cannot start "to the right"; also, two of the q_i may coincide, and two agents on one node then leave in opposite directions. Impact. The best-case upper bound of the abstract is not established; Theorem 3.5 is not formalized here. Details. Simulation with hill-climbing over pointer initializations finds cover times ≤ 1.25 (L+1)² for gaps L ∈ {3, 5, 8} and up to 32 agents (16 for L = 8), so the statement looks true. Repair. None proved. A rigorous proof needs the domain-size dynamics. 🔧 Lemma 3.1 (the sequence a_i, identity (4)) No sequence satisfies (1)–(4) for any k ≥ 2: summing (4) a_i · a₁ = 2/a_i − 1/a_{i−1} − 1/a_{i+1} over i = 1..k telescopes to a₁ Σ a_i = 1/a₁, so (3) Σ a_i = 1 forces a₁ = 1, which is impossible (lemma_3_1_false). Impact. The intended identity is a_i / a₁ = …, which is what the lemma's own construction gives (a_i = 1/(c b_i), a₁ = 1/c²). The fix is a one-symbol change visible in the lemma's proof, but a later proof, that of Theorem 3.2, reasons with the wrong version. Details. The telescoping uses 1/a₀ = 0 (property (1), a₀ = +∞) and a_{k+1} = a_k (property (2)). The right-hand sides sum to 1/a₁ + 1/a_k − 1/a_{k+1} = 1/a₁. Only (1)–(4) and positivity are used; (5) and (6) are irrelevant. Repair. With the intended identity, all six properties hold for every k ≥ 2 (lemma_3_1_corrected). ✏️ Slips Lemma 2.4, first property: in a deployment where no two agents ever share a node, a domain need not be a sub-path. On the 6-ring, agents on 0 and 3 with pointers 0→1, 1→2, 2→1, 3→2 swap along the edge {1, 2} in round 2, giving the agent that started on 0 the domain {0, 2} after round 2 (lemma_2_4_false; both agents are stopped afterwards). The intended hypothesis also excludes agents passing each other on an edge, as the proof of Theorem 4.1 says explicitly ("no two agents meet or pass each other on an edge"). Alternatively a swap can be re-read as two bounces, since agents are indistinguishable. A label-free form of the domain picture holds in the undelayed system for every initialization (pattern_invariant). The lemma is stated without proof and is used by Lemmas 2.5–2.9, which are not formalized. Abstract and Theorem 3.2: Θ(n²/log k) is meaningless for k = 1, which the abstract includes ("1 ≤ k < n^{1/11}"). Proof of Lemma 2.1, equation (4) (and the recurrence in the proof of Lemma 2.2): the arrivals up to round t + 1 must use the exits e_v(t + 1), not e_v(t) (cf. equation (2)). The lemma is unaffected. Lemma 2.8: "holds for 2n² consecutive time steps t, …, t + n² − 1". Proof of Lemma 3.6: step (a) uses windows of length r(n/k) and step (c) jumps by r(n/k), while step (b) and the definition of good vertices use r(n/(10k)). Typos Proof of Lemma 2.1: the notation switches between port_v(u) and port_u(v). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 3.7 (best-case lower bound Ω((n/k)²)) The proof rests on Lemmas 2.5/2.6, whose proofs are sketches, and it misstates its own tools. Impact. Statement true; proved with a new argument and explicit constants (theorem_3_7): for n ≥ 8k, every start multiset has a node v such that, with all pointers pointing away from v, the ring is not covered before time n²/(8192 k²). Details. The proof initializes "in each node the pointer points away from the closest agent". It needs the opposite, the negative initialization of Lemma 2.5, where an agent entering a new node is sent back; concludes "by Lemma 2.1", which only gives upper bounds on the undelayed cover time. A lower bound needs the left inequality of Lemma 2.2/2.3; needs Lemmas 2.5/2.6 at scale n/(20k) instead of 22k: Lemma 2.5 is stated with the constants 22k and 11k, Theorem 3.7 applies it with initial interiors n/(20k) and needs the scaled conclusion Ω(n/k), and the proof of Lemma 2.5 only supports a loss of 11k (the "minimum configuration" 22k, 22k − 11, …), i.e. M − 11k ≥ M/2; argues that the unexplored stretch "will be explored by agents having domains of sizes at least Ω(n/20k), so it takes Ω(n²/400k²)". This is not derived from anything proved. Repair. We use a rotor-router potential instead of domains. For h : ZMod n → ℤ, Φ_h = 2 Σ_u pos(u) h(u) + Σ_v h(pointer target of v). Every release of an agent from v changes Φ_h by exactly h(v+1) + h(v−1) − 2h(v) (potential_run). With pointers pointing away from v, the pointer part can only grow for radially non-increasing h (ptr_term_ge). This gives two inequalities: hit lemma (hit_lemma, parabola (R − d)²): reaching v from distance > R costs R² agent-rounds within distance R of v; scale step (scale_step, bump of radius 2R): R² N_R(s) ≤ 2R² N_{2R}(0) + Σ_{s'<s} N_{2R}(s'), where N_R counts the agents within distance R of v. Iterating over the radii 2^m R₀ (multiscale) and choosing v by counting (exists_good_center, which replaces the good vertices of Lemma 3.6) gives n² < 8192 k² T at any covering time T. Lemma 2.5 is not needed. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graph and rotors (RotorGraph, Model.lean): finitely many nodes; node v has deg v ≥ 1 outgoing arcs in a fixed cyclic order (multi-arcs allowed). A configuration (Config) is the number of indistinguishable agents per node and a port pointer per node, as in Section 1.3. Rounds: synchronous. In a round with delays d, node v keeps min(pos v, d v) agents. It releases the others one by one along consecutive arcs starting at the pointer, and the pointer advances by the number released (step). A delayed deployment D gives the delays of every round (more stopped agents than present means all stop); undelayed is R[k]. Ring (ring n, Ring.lean): ZMod n, port 0 to v + 1, port 1 to v − 1. The initial pointers are arbitrary or adversarial as each statement says; no randomness (Section 3.3 on random walks is not covered). Labelled model (lstep, Domains.lean): used only for Lemma 2.4, since domains need agent identities. Agents on the same node are released in index order. Main results in Lean. TetraBFT — PODC 2024 Qianyu Yu, Giuliano Losa, Xuechao Wang. TetraBFT: Reducing Latency of Unauthenticated, Responsive BFT Consensus. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662783. Formalized version: arXiv 2405.02615 v2 (April 2026); its numbering is the same as v1's. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Termination (liveness after GST) in Theorem 1 is false for the protocol as specified: after GST the view change can deadlock forever, both with reliable channels (n = 7, f = 2) and in the paper's lossy pre-GST model (n = 4, f = 1). It survives only in a weaker form: we prove that the protocol terminates once its echo rule is repaired, but only on reliable channels, which the paper's constant-storage model does not allow; agreement and validity hold in every run. The storage, communication and latency claims and the multi-shot protocol were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Section 2 model and §3.2 (no retransmission); Theorem 1, termination In the paper's own model, where messages before GST may be lost, n = 4, f = 1 already deadlocks: timers fire once per view and nothing is resent, so view-change messages lost before GST are never replaced (Lossy.termination_fails_lossy). Impact. Termination fails in the model the paper insists on ("with constant storage, we must allow the loss of messages during asynchrony"), and no result here saves it there: our termination theorem below assumes reliable channels. Details. This deadlock comes from the lack of retransmission, not from the echo guard: the repaired echo rule deadlocks there too. Repair. None proved. The likely fix adds retransmission to the repaired echo rule. 🛠️ Theorem 1, termination proof (view synchronization) The proof only cites Lemmas 2, 4, 5, which assume all correct nodes are in a good view after GST; the paper never proves view synchronization, and the 9Δ timeout justification assumes that every node echoes. Impact. The statements of Lemmas 2, 4 and 5, the core of the liveness argument, are correct (Lemma 4 with its implicit hypotheses made explicit), and so is the 9Δ budget of a view. What is missing is the step that brings the correct nodes into such a view. Repair. For the repaired echo rule on reliable channels we prove that views synchronize, with timeout T ≥ 8δ + 9, the discrete form of 9Δ, and round-robin leaders (sync_window, fixed_termination). 🛠️ Sections 1 and 5, Appendix B (mechanized check) The TLA+ specification ShowsSafeAt has only item 2(b)iiiA of Rule 3 and omits item 2(b)iiiB, so the Apalache check covers a stricter vote-1 rule than the protocol of Section 3. Impact. The paper's mechanized safety check does not cover the protocol it presents, and it covers only n = 4. Repair. Our Lean proof of agreement covers the full Rule 3 for all n > 3f (tetra_agreement). 🔧 Theorem 1, termination (view-change echo rule of §3.2) After GST the view change can deadlock forever: a node that has already echoed a higher view never echoes the view it is itself entering, so with n = 7, f = 2 (reliable channels) correct nodes end split between views 1 and 2 and no one ever decides (Deadlock.termination_fails). Impact. The liveness half of Theorem 1 is false for the protocol as specified, even on reliable channels; agreement and validity hold in every run, and on reliable channels the protocol terminates with a repaired echo rule (fixed_solvesConsensus). Details. The rule is: on timeout, send ⟨view-change, v+1⟩; on f + 1 view-change messages for v', send ⟨view-change, v'⟩ "if it has not sent a view-change message for view v' or any higher view"; on n − f of them, move to v'. Timers fire once per view and nothing is resent. The guard lets a node that has already echoed a higher view refuse to help the others reach the view it is itself entering. Counterexample (n = 7, f = 2, Byzantine nodes 0 and 1 lead views 0 and 1, Δ = 1, timeout 9Δ): Nodes 2–5 move to view 1 together; node 6's copies of their messages are delayed until GST + Δ. Nodes 2–5 time out in view 1. Node 5 alone reaches view 2, with one Byzantine view-2 message. Node 5 times out in view 2. Its view-3 message and two Byzantine ones make node 6 echo view 3. Only then does node 6 receive the view-2 messages, and it enters view 2. Because it has already sent view 3, it never sends view 2. Nodes 2, 3, 4 now see 4 < n − f view-2 messages and 2 < f + 1 view-3 messages forever. From time 41 nothing is in transit and no timer is pending, so no correct node ever decides (Deadlock.termination_fails, with timeout 9Δ; the same schedule rescaled deadlocks with timeout 17 = 8δ + 9, the bound of the repair theorem below: Deadlock17.termination_fails; both runs use reliable channels and satisfy CSLib's Run.Valid). The same pattern works for every f ≥ 2 (informal). Repair. Echo every view ≥ the current one that was not echoed yet. For reliable channels we prove that this repair works: with timeout T ≥ 8δ + 9 and round-robin leaders, the repaired protocol solves consensus (fixed_solvesConsensus). ✏️ Slips Lemma 4 leaves its hypotheses implicit: a correct leader, and proof messages from all correct nodes. The statement is true with these hypotheses made explicit (Execution.lemma4, follower_determines_safe). Lemma 8 (d)ii: "either m or m' satisfies Rule 4 Item 3" should be "neither". Section 6's proof says "vote-4 for block s − 4" but Fig. 2 gives s − 3. Typos Lemma 8 (d)iii writes the view as v̄ and then v̂. Theorem 1's agreement proof says "i decides val_j" where val is meant. A few spelling slips ("quadrati", "whooping", "struture"). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 7 (wrong step in the proof) The proof asserts that once a correct node decides val in view v, every correct vote-1 in view v is for val, but with a Byzantine leader a synchronous run with n = 4 has correct node 1 decide true in view 0 while correct node 3 votes vote-1 for false in view 0 (Lemma7.lemma7_proof_claim_false). Impact. Statement true; Lemma 7 follows from Lemma 6 instead (Execution.lemma7). 🔧 Lemma 2 (choice of quorum) The proof picks the "last view with a vote-3" among a quorum that may contain Byzantine nodes with fake reports. Impact. Statement true; the argument works when the quorum is the set of correct nodes (Execution.lemma2). 🔧 Theorem 1, validity The validity proof is circular as written. Impact. Statement true; we prove it by induction over time (tetra_validity). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's partially synchronous Byzantine model (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync). Nodes are Fin n, at most f are Byzantine, and 3f < n. Channels are authenticated, there are no signatures, and Byzantine nodes may equivocate. Time is discrete, and each node takes one deterministic step per tick. Run.Valid f δ: reliable channels, with delivery by max(send, GST) + δ. LossyValid is the paper's model, where pre-GST messages may be lost. tetra prm (Protocol.lean) is §3.2 written as a state machine. It covers timer, echo, view change, proof/suggest reports, the proposal (input if Rule 1 shows it safe), vote-1 (Rule 3), vote-2/3/4, and the decision. Rules 1–4 are verbatim (Defs.lean). Reports come from the full vote history; constant storage is not modelled. The flag prm.fixEcho switches to the repaired echo rule, which is not in the paper. Safety is first proved for abstract executions. These are the votes cast by correct nodes, subject to four guarantees: one vote per phase and view, quorum behind each vote, Rule 3 on honest reports, quorum behind a decision. A refinement then shows that every run of tetra prm is such an execution, with no timing assumption, so safety holds in asynchronous runs too. The counterexamples are concrete runs evaluated by decide +kernel through a memoised simulator (simHist, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/PartialSync/Sim.lean). A quiescence lemma extends them to infinite time. Main results in Lean. Linearizability: A Typo — PODC 2021 Gal Sela, Maurice Herlihy, Erez Petrank. Brief Announcement: Linearizability: A Typo. PODC 2021, pp. 561–564. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467944. Formalized version: full version arXiv:2105.06737v2 (numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✅ Correct. Every claim we formalized holds as stated. Under the original Herlihy–Wing definition (2.2), linearizability is neither local nor nonblocking, while the amended definition (4.1) is both (Theorems 5.1, 5.2). Linearization points are equivalent to 4.1 (Claim 1) but not to 2.2, and the inclusions of Figure 6 hold and are strict. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Purely combinatorial, Herlihy–Wing style, with no implementations. A history is a finite list of events inv p x o / res p x r over several objects. Well-formedness, H|p, H|x, extensions and complete(H) follow the paper. Operations are identified explicitly as (process, object, index). The paper identifies operations of H, H', complete(H') and S only implicitly, through equivalence. Sequential specifications are arbitrary per-object sets of histories. They may be nondeterministic or partial, and are not required to be prefix-closed; hnil is assumed only where needed. Definitions 2.2, 4.1 and 7.1 are stated literally (LinearizableHW, Linearizable, LinearizableLP). In 7.1, linearization points are gaps between events, which is equivalent to distinct real-valued points. The Section 3 counterexamples use concrete instances: 0/1 register values and queue values 1, 2. Implicit assumptions made explicit. The "only if" direction of locality (Theorem 5.1) needs the empty history to be legal for every object. This follows from the paper's prefix-closed specifications, provided they are non-empty (left implicit in the paper). "Total operation" (Section 3.3, Theorem 5.2) is read relative to the sequential specification: from every legal complete sequential history, some response makes the operation legal. Proof remarks. We did not formalize the paper's own proof of Theorem 5.1 (the Herlihy–Wing minimal-cycle argument). Theorem 5.1 (locality) is proved by a different route: Give each object's operations the running-maximum linearization points from Claim 1. Points of different objects never coincide. Merge all objects' operations by point. The result respects the real-time order of H. Main results in Lean (namespace Podc2021.LinearizabilityTypo; general theory in Cslib.SharedMemory.HerlihyWing). Fair Leader Election for Rational Agents — PODC 2018 Assaf Yifrach, Yishay Mansour. Fair Leader Election for Rational Agents in Asynchronous Rings and Networks. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212767. Formalized version: arXiv 1805.04778 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The attacks on A-LEADuni, the paper's main focus, hold: Lemma 2.4, the success characterization (Lemmas 3.3–3.5), Lemma 4.1 (honest origin), Theorem 4.2 (k ≥ √n), the Cubic Attack (Theorem 4.3, Lemmas 4.4–4.5), Corollary 4.6 (ε < 1 − 1/n) and Claim D.1 (k < n/2) are proved. But Theorem 7.2 (no resilient FLE on k-simulated trees) is proved only for n = 2, its status for n ≥ 3 is open, and the claimed equivalence of Fair Leader Election and Fair Coin Toss (Theorem 8.1) has a wrong step and no repair. The resilience side was not checked: Theorem 5.1 (∜n-resilience) and Section 6 (PhaseAsyncLead) are not formalized. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 7.2 for n ≥ 3 (no resilient FLE on k-simulated trees) The proof's Lemma F.3 and Corollary F.4 treat b, which "simulates the rest of the tree", as a processor of the model, but it is not one, so Theorem 7.2 is unestablished for n ≥ 3; we prove it for n = 2 (Trees.thm_7_2_two). Impact. For n ≥ 3 the theorem is neither proved nor refuted, and n = 2 is only the two-party case, none of the claimed generalization to trees. The attacks on A-LEADuni (Sections 3–4) are unaffected. Details. The super-node's behaviour toward the leaf depends on how the leaf's messages interleave with internal events. So neither "a assures o in P_a ⇒ a assures o in P" nor "b is a dictator" transfers. Also, for a super-node, termination under every fair schedule does not bound the number of messages (ping-pong until a third processor's message arrives), and Lemma F.2 needs such a bound. The same issue affects connected fibres in Corollary F.4. Repair. For n = 2 only. We prove Lemma F.2 itself, for two processors, in a generalized form: arbitrary output sets, finite inputs, and no message bound needed, since it follows from finite inputs (Trees.lemma_F2). With Trees.not_resilient_of_assures (see the next item) this gives Theorem 7.2 for n = 2, all 1 ≤ k ≤ 2, ε < 1/n. ❌ Theorem 8.1, first direction (also the last step of the proof of Theorem 7.2) The step Pr(coin = 0) ≤ Σ_{i even} Pr(leader = i) is wrong, because the parity coin can succeed while the election fails: processors may output different leaders of the same parity. Impact. The claimed equivalence of Fair Leader Election and Fair Coin Toss is not established. Theorem 8.1 is neither repaired nor formalized; its status is unknown, not refuted. Details. The last step of the proof of Theorem 7.2 goes through this coin toss (leader parity), and it also covers only even n. Repair. For the use in Theorem 7.2 only. We replace the coin-toss step by a direct lemma: a coalition that forces the leader into a proper subset breaks ε-k-resilience for every ε < 1/n and every n (Trees.not_resilient_of_assures). ⚠️ Lemma 4.1 (adversarial origin) Lemma 4.1 is stated for every coalition whose segments have length ≤ k − 1, but its attack deadlocks when the origin is an adversary: only the origin wakes up spontaneously and every adversary just forwards, so nobody ever sends and the outcome is FAIL (lemma_4_1_attack_deadlocks). Impact. Unestablished for an adversarial origin; the statement is probably still true with a modified attack. We prove the lemma for an honest origin, which is all Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 need (lemma_4_1). 🔧 Theorem 7.2 at the boundary ε = 1/n For n = 2 and ε = 1/n Theorem 7.2 is false: K₂ is a 1-simulated tree, and the protocol in which one processor draws a bit and both output it is ½-1-resilient (Trees.thm_7_2_boundary_false). Impact. An edge case of the stated range ε ≤ 1/n: every FLE protocol is (1 − 1/n)-resilient (see Corollary 4.6 under Slips), and for n = 2, 1 − 1/n = 1/n. For n ≥ 3 and ε = 1/n the status is open. Repair. The condition ε < 1/n, under which we prove the case n = 2 (Trees.thm_7_2_two). ✏️ Slips Claim D.1 claims Pr(outcome = j) ≤ 1/n for every consecutive coalition, but for n ≥ 3 the block of all processors except the origin forces any outcome by the attack of Lemma 4.1 (claim_D_1_false). That block leaves one honest processor; its segment has length 1 ≤ k − 1. The proof needs the honest segment to be longer than the coalition (the text says "length k > l", meant as l > k), and the introduction presents Appendix D as a proof of the result of Abraham et al. for k < n/2. The claim is not used elsewhere. We prove it for 2k + 1 ≤ n and any position of the origin (claim_D_1). Consequence: A-LEADuni is 0-1-resilient for n ≥ 3 (isResilient_aLead_one). Corollary 4.6 is stated for 0 ≤ ε ≤ 1 − 1/n, but every FLE protocol, in particular A-LEADuni, is (1 − 1/n)-k-resilient for every k (corollary_4_6_boundary_false): no deviation can raise an expected rational utility by more than 1 − 1/n, since the deviation gets at most max u and the honest run already gets (1/n)·Σ u ≥ max u / n. Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 themselves use the strict ε < 1 − 1/n, and we prove the corollary for ε < 1 − 1/n (corollary_4_6). Lemma 3.3 says "the execution succeeds iff conditions 1–3", but outcome also needs the adversaries to terminate with the same output, which conditions 1–3 do not control. The intended reading is "all honest processors terminate with the same valid output"; we prove it, and its version for every fair schedule (lemma_3_3, lemma_3_3_run). Also, "sends n messages" should be "at least n", and the sums are over the first n messages. Definition 7.1 asks for a graph homomorphism f with {(f(x), f(y)) | (x, y) ∈ E} ⊆ E_T. A tree has no loops, so every connected fibre is a singleton (Trees.IsKSimTreeLiteral.card_fiber_le_one). The next sentence describes the intended notion (a partition into connected parts of size ≤ k whose quotient is a tree), which we use. The Section 7 remark "Every graph can be simulated by a tree of size 2 with parts of size ≤ ⌈n/2⌉" is false: K₁,₃ has no such partition. Claim F.5, which uses a star, is fine (not formalized). Appendix A: the origin starts with round = 1. It then validates its (n−1)-th incoming message against d₁ and sums only n − 1 values, so the honest run aborts whenever d₁ ≠ d₂. The verbal description (validate the n-th message) is what we formalize. Appendix C: in the Cubic Attack the zeros are sent only when count == n−k−lᵢ after incrementing count. This never happens if n − k − lᵢ = 0, and the attack deadlocks (e.g. n = 4, k = 2, l = (2, 0)). Following the text, we send them at wake-up. Proof of Theorem 4.3: Σ_{i=1}^{k'−1}(k'−1)i is written (k'−1)k'(k'+1)/2; it is (k'−1)²k'/2 (harmless). Proof of Lemma 4.4: "since l₁ = maxᵢ lᵢ" does not follow from the relaxed conditions l_k ≤ k−1, lᵢ ≤ lᵢ₊₁ + k − 1; the lemma holds anyway, and our liveness proof does not use it. Typos Proof of Lemma 3.3: the case analysis swaps the numbering of conditions 1 and 2. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous unidirectional ring of n processors (Fin n, origin 0), with reliable FIFO links. Processors are deterministic and event driven: a processor is a function of its received history (shared model Cslib.UniRing, Podc/Computability/Distributed/UniRing/Basic.lean). Every processor may send at wake-up (honest normal processors send nothing then). Schedules are oblivious sequences of processors; fair = each one scheduled infinitely often. We prove that on a unidirectional ring the schedule does not matter (terminates_iff, outcomeUnder_eq). Randomness: honest secrets d i uniform in Fin n; probabilities by counting. Messages are values in Fin n. Outcome v iff all processors (adversaries included) terminate with output v; otherwise FAIL. Coalitions of size exactly k run arbitrary deterministic strategies (Def. 2.2). Rational utilities, ε-k-resilience (Def. 2.3), ε-k-unbiasedness and FLE are as in Section 2, for every fair schedule. Deterministic deviations suffice for all negative results. Our positive results (Claim D.1 and its corollaries) are proved against deterministic deviations only (see differencies.md, item 5). Section 7 (Tree*.lean, namespace Podc.FairLeaderElection.Trees) uses a general asynchronous model on a graph. Processors see the arrival order across their links, links are FIFO, schedules are sequences of directed links, and fair = every directed edge infinitely often. Protocols need not be symmetric; random inputs come from finite sets, uniformly. Two-party protocols are the unidirectional ring of size 2. Main results in Lean. Actively Dynamic Networks — PODC 2020 Othon Michail, George Skretas, Paul G. Spirakis. Distributed Computation and Reconfiguration in Actively Dynamic Networks. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405744. Formalized version: arXiv 2003.03355 v1 (full version with Appendices A–D); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Lemma 3.1 is false for GraphToStar as printed: on the 4-node line with increasing IDs a pulling committee jumps onto a committee that is merging away in the same phase, it then merges into a follower, the committees stop being stars, and the output is not a spanning star. So Theorem 3.8 for GraphToStar, the first of the three distributed algorithms announced in the abstract, is not established, and neither is the distributed Ω(n log n) bound (Theorem 6.4). The basic subroutines (Propositions 2.1, 2.2, up to a small slip in the bound ⌈log d⌉ ≤ log n), the centralized lower bounds (Lemmas 6.1, 6.2) and the matching centralized upper bound on the line (Theorem 6.3, line case) hold and are proved, while the other two algorithms (Sections 4–5) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Lemma 3.1 (GraphToStar solves Depth-1 Tree), hence Theorem 3.8 On the line 0 - 1 - 2 - 3 with IDs increasing along the line, a pulling committee jumps onto a committee that is merging away in the same phase, the committees stop being stars, and the output is not a spanning star (GraphToStar.lemma_3_1_breaks, line4_terminates_wrong). Impact. Theorem 3.8 (O(log n) time, O(n log n) activations for GraphToStar), the first of the three distributed algorithms announced in the abstract, is not established. The bug needs only a pulling chain of length 3, so it occurs on most inputs: it showed up in about 9% of random connected graphs with up to 9 nodes in our committee-level simulator. Details. Phase 1: every committee selects its right neighbour. C(2) pairs with C(3) and enters merging. C(1) and C(0) selected committees that themselves selected, so they enter pulling. C(3) was selected and enters waiting. Phase 2: by the pulling rule, C(1) jumps to 3. C(0) jumps to 2, the leader C(1) activated an edge with in phase 1. But in the same phase C(2) merges into C(3), so node 2 is now a follower of 3. Phase 3: "the leader of C(2)" did not activate an edge in phase 2, so C(0) enters merging. Phase 4: C(0) merges into node 2. Now node 0's leader is 2, whose leader is 3. The committee invariant ("each committee is a star around its maximum-ID leader") is broken, and the network is not a spanning star (0 hangs at distance 2 from 3). When the target merges away, redirect the pointer to the absorbing leader (a potential neighbour through the former leader, so this costs one extra round). MemSnap — PODC 2024 Prasad Jayanti, Siddhartha Jayanti, Sucharita Jayanti. MemSnap: A Fast Adaptive Snapshot Algorithm for RMWable Shared-Memory. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662820. Formalized version: the proceedings version (no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result, Theorem 7.3, holds: MemSnap (Algorithm 1) is a linearizable, wait-free checkpointable object, with at most 9 shared-memory steps per operation, for every set of updaters and every family of RMW primitives, and we prove it by the paper's own route, meta-configuration tracking. Lemma 7.2 as printed is false: the third disjunct of the set Q (Figure 2) lacks the condition x_μ = X, and with that condition, which the paper's prose states, the lemma holds and gives P ≠ ∅. Lemma 7.1 (the Forwarding Invariant I₁) holds as stated, but its induction needs a local strengthening of I₁; the paper omits the proofs of both lemmas, and we supply them. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 7.2 (Figure 2, the set Q): as printed, the third disjunct of Q lacks the condition x_μ = X, so in an execution with one component, two updaters and the scanner Q contains a possibility that no linearization realizes and Q ⊆ P fails (Counterexample.lemma_7_2_false, Counterexample.not_tracked). The paper's prose states the condition, the fix is local, and no published proof uses the wrong version. Adding x_μ = X makes the lemma true, and P ≠ ∅ follows as the paper says, so Theorem 7.3 stands (lemma_7_2_fixed). For a component j with B[j].seq ≠ X, the third disjunct of Q allows p.snap[j] = a_μ for every process μ at line 12 whose CAS would succeed (b_μ = B[j]). It does not ask that the CAS make B[j].seq equal to X. If μ read X before the latest click (x_μ < X), then a_μ can be stale. Counterexample: one component, initially 0; updaters ν, μ; scanner σ. ν starts update(write 1) and finishes forward. μ starts an update and reads B = (0, 0). σ clicks (X = 1). μ reads X = 1 and A = 0; it is now at line 12. ν writes A = 1 and returns. σ clicks again (X = 2) and is at line 2. Q now contains the possibility val = 1, snap = 0, click linearized (S = ∅, third disjunct with witness μ). No linearization realizes it: ν's write returned before the second click was invoked, so the snapshot holds 1. Hence it is not in P, and Q ⊆ P fails. The text before the lemma says the third disjunct is about "a successful CAS at Line 12 that will cause B[j].seq to become equal to X". Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 7.1 (I₁ is an invariant, but not an inductive one; proof omitted in the paper) Part (6) of I₁ covers a process in its second forward iteration only at line 9, so from an unreachable state satisfying I₁ a successful CAS can break Part (7), and an induction on I₁ alone fails. Impact. Statement true; we extend Part (6) and add a few shape facts (FInv), and then I₁ follows (lemma_7_1). Details. Once such a process μ has read b_μ = B[i] and is at lines 10–12, no part of I₁ records that every process μ' poised with b_μ' = B[i] has x_μ' ≥ x̂_μ. Then a successful CAS of such a μ' with x_μ' < x̂_μ would break Part (7). The non-inductiveness is argued by hand, not in Lean. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory (CSLib Impl/IsLinearization), arbitrary adversarial scheduler (a crashed process is one that is never scheduled again; wait-freedom covers it), deterministic processes, no randomness. Any type P of processes (possibly infinite) with a designated scanner σ. σ only clicks and observes; every other process only updates (Allowed). Components: any type K (the paper has [1, m]). Component words: an arbitrary deterministic sequential specification W (any RMW primitives with any responses: read, write, CAS, F&A, FAS, …). Base objects: A[i] (a W-word that also supports read), B[i] (a CAS word over (val, seq) pairs, the paper's double-word CAS), and X (a read/write register over ℕ, so counters are unbounded). Every primitive access is one atomic step. Algorithm 2 is a deterministic ghost run arun next to Algorithm 1. Minimalist Leader Election — PODC 2025 Robin Vacus, Isabella Ziccardi. Minimalist Leader Election Under Weak Communication. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733559. Formalized version: arXiv 2502.12697 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All main results hold: Theorem 2 (for every fixed p ∈ (0,1), BFW elects a unique leader almost surely, and w.h.p. within O(D² log n) rounds), Theorem 3 (O(D log n) rounds for p = 1/(D+1)) and Section 3 (flow conservation, Ohm's law, and "there is always a leader"). The paper's anti-concentration proof of the O(D² log n) bound fails at Lemmas 14 and 17, and we replace it by a new martingale/Lyapunov proof. Lemma 19 (used for Theorem 3) is false as stated for small D (K₂, P₃), Theorem 3 still holds with a window of 2D+3 rounds, the "almost surely" claim needed a separate argument, and knowing D only up to a constant factor was checked only for upper bounds on D. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 19 (elimination within 2D+1 rounds, used for Theorem 3) Lemma 19, read per configuration in round t as its proof does, is false for small D: on K₂ (D = 1) with both nodes in B• in round t = 1, neither node loses leadership before round t + 4 > t + 2D + 1, whatever the coins (lemma19_fails_K2, lemma19_fails_P3). Impact. Theorem 3 is true: with windows of 2D+3 rounds it holds with explicit constants (elim_window, theorem3, theorem3_whp). Details. On the path u–w–v (D = 2) the earliest elimination is in round t + 2D + 1, not before it. Both counterexamples hold for every coin field and are proved in Lean. The proof of Lemma 19 has two further gaps: P(v does not beep by itself in [t, t+2D+2]) = (1−p)^{2(D+1)} is wrong if v is in B• in round t (the probability is then 0). In the case N_t(u) = N_t(v), the "self-beep of u between t and t+D+1" may be the beep in round t itself. That beep is already counted, so u does not get ahead of v. Repair. We shift the coin windows (coins of u in rounds t+2..t+D+2, all coins of v in rounds t..t+2D+2) and use windows of length 2D+3. Theorem 3 then holds with explicit constants: P(no single leader from round k(2D+3) on) ≤ n²(127/128)^k (elim_window, theorem3, theorem3_whp). ✏️ Slips Lemma 12 as stated only gives a beep of v in some round s ≤ t + dis(u,v), but Lemma 19 needs it to happen after round t. Its proof does give s > t, and we prove that version (lemma12). Lemma 14 is stated for the chain started in W, but its proof needs the stationary start. The lemma is applied (in Lemma 15) only to the stationary copy. Not formalized; our proof of Theorem 2 does not use it. Lemma 21 should read P(Σ_{i≤n} W_i ≥ k) = P(Bin(k−1,p) ≤ n−1), not P(Bin(k,p) ≤ n): for n = 1, k = 2, p = 1/2 the two sides are 1/2 and 3/4. The form used in Lemma 14 is correct. Not formalized. Typos Proof of Lemma 19, case N_t(u) = N_t(v): "N_s^beep(u) ≥ 1" should read N_s(u) > N_s(v). Proof of Lemma 17, last bound: the display ends with ≤ 1/n², while the lemma states n^{−4}, which is what the chosen A gives and what the union bound in Theorem 2 uses. The Discussion (§5) cites "Theorem 1", which does not exist; Theorem 2 is meant. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 14 (proof of the anti-concentration bound) The proof of Lemma 14 claims P(Z ≥ EZ + k(2p+1)) ≥ 1/2 for a binomial Z, which is false. Impact. This is the first step of the chain (Lemmas 14, 15, 17) behind Theorem 2's O(D² log n) bound. The statements are true. We prove that bound by a different route (see "The formalization") (theorem2_time, theorem2_whp). Details. A binomial's median is within 1 of its mean, so the probability in Lemma 14's proof is < 1/2 (for p = 1/2, k = 1, t = 100 it is 0.333). Any smaller constant works instead; this repair is not in Lean. 🛠️ Lemma 17 (proof of P(σ_{u,v} > AD² log n) ≤ n^{−4}) The proof applies Lemma 15, which bounds P(|Δ| < d), where it needs a shifted interval |Δ + δ| ≤ D. Impact. The gap is fixable and the statement is true, but that repair is not in Lean; the O(D² log n) bound is saved by the same different route (theorem2_time, theorem2_whp). Details. The proof also conditions only on E_{k−1} instead of the whole past, and it uses Lemma 15's "d large enough" although D may be 1. 🔧 Theorem 2 ("almost surely") The proof only bounds the probability of two leaders in round AD² log n by n^{−2}, and that does not give probability 1. Impact. Statement true; proved by a separate argument (theorem2_ae, theorem2_tail). Repair. Each window of 2D+3 rounds has a good event of positive probability (1−(1−p)^{D+1})(1−p)^{2D+3}, and that event eliminates one of any two given leaders. (theorem2_ae, theorem2_tail) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous beeping model on a finite connected SimpleGraph; anonymous, uniform nodes. A listening node hears a beep iff some neighbour beeps. BFW has 6 states: a phase W/B/F and a leader bit (Figure 1). No failures, no adversary. The only randomness is the W• → B• coin. The execution is a deterministic function of a coin field c : ℕ → V → Bool. Section 3 is proved for every coin field, i.e. for every rule deciding W• → B•, as the paper remarks. Probabilistic results use i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) coins on ℕ × V (Measure.infinitePi). Events are tracked by the finite set of coins they depend on (Determined); events on disjoint coin sets are independent. Initial configuration: Eq. (2), i.e. all nodes waiting and at least one leader. This is more general than the paper's all-W• start. D is any upper bound on all distances (the diameter, or more). Swiper — PODC 2024 Andrei Tonkikh, Luciano Freitas. Swiper: a new paradigm for efficient weighted distributed protocols. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662799. Formalized version: arXiv 2307.15561 v2 (contains the appendix proofs). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The weight restriction and qualification bounds (Theorem 2.1, Theorem 2.2, Corollary 2.3) that the protocols rely on hold, but the weight separation bound of Theorem 2.4 and Swiper's construction for it fail, and keeping that problem linear in n took a new rounding offset and a new analysis. The protocol transformations of Sections 4–6 were checked only in the combinatorial core of Theorem 4.2. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Theorem 2.4; Appendix A.2; Section 3, "Robustness" for weight separation The claimed bound T ≤ (α+β)(1−α)/(β−α)·n is false (ws_upper_bound_false), because case 2 of Appendix A.2 substitutes 1−γ for γ without changing the rounding offset, so Swiper's own construction violates it too (swiper_ws_counterexample, swiper_ws_family_exceeds_bound). Impact. The weight-separation guarantee does not hold as stated, and the algorithm's guarantee fails even under a disjoint-sets reading of Problem 3; the authors' public solver returns invalid tickets when the bound binds. The weight restriction and qualification results (Theorems 2.1, 2.2, Corollary 2.3) are unaffected. Details. The bound fails for α = 1/20, β = 1/10, 8 parties of weight 14 and 13 of weight 1 (n = 21): every solution needs T ≥ 63 > 59.85. Here W = 125. Each weight-14 party alone is heavy, all 13 unit parties together are heavy, and light sets contain at most 6 unit parties. If at most 6 unit parties hold tickets, those (light) and all unit parties (heavy) have equally many tickets, a violation. Otherwise any 6 ticketed unit parties hold ≥ 6 tickets, so each weight-14 party needs ≥ 7 and the unit parties together ≥ 7: T ≥ 63 > 59.85. (The optimum is exactly 63; for this family OPT/n → α/β², here 5 versus the claimed 2.85.) This instance compares a set of unit parties with a superset of it, which the paper's Problem 3 allows. Under a "disjoint S₁, S₂" reading it would not be a counterexample, but the three-party instance below refutes the proof and Swiper's guarantee under either reading. The proof rounds t_i = ⌊w_i s + γ⌋ with γ = (α+β)/2. Case 1 (t(S₁) ≥ γT) is correct; case 2 is claimed "analogous by substituting 1−γ for γ and 1−β for α". That would also require changing the rounding offset from γ to 1−γ, which is not done, so the argument works only for γ = 1/2. Redone honestly, case 2 gives max(γ², (1−γ)²)·n instead of γ(1−γ)·n. On three parties w = (1, 1, 15) with α = 1/20, β = 1/10, the paper's s yields t = (0, 0, 7), which is invalid, and every valid member of its rounding family has T ≥ 14, while the bound is 8.55. The two unit parties (weight 2 > βW = 1.7) are heavy yet ticketless, so they tie with S₁ = ∅ (disjoint sets). The authors' public solver (DCL-TelecomParis/swiper, commit f1d7a3d) hard-codes this bound and silently returns invalid tickets when it binds: weights (2, 14) with α = 1/20, β = 1/10 give tickets (0, 5), although party 1 alone is heavy (checked by running it). Repair. T ≤ ⌈(1−d²)/(2d)·n⌉ with d = β − α, using rounding offset (1−d)/2 (ws_upper_bound). It keeps all α < β, linearity in n and the shape n/(β−α) with numerator below 1. It is symmetric under (α, β) ↦ (1−β, 1−α), as the problem is (the paper's bound is not). It beats the paper's bound when α+β is near 1 and is weaker when α+β is small. ✏️ Slips Appendix A.2, case 1: the complement bound writes βWs for (1−α)Ws; as printed it fails for α+β > 1 and does not yield the next line, which matches (1−α). The §4.1 random-beacon example writes (1−αn)T ≥ ⌈αn T⌉, which is false in general (αn = 1/2, T = 3). The inequality (1−αn)T ≥ αn T of the proof of Theorem 4.2 and integrality of ticket counts give the conclusion (isBlunt_of_isWR). Non-Equivocation in Synchronous Agreement — PODC 2020 Mads Frederik Madsen, Søren Debois. On the Subject of Non-Equivocation: Defining Non-Equivocation in Synchronous Agreement Systems. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405731. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (no arXiv version; the online appendix with the full proofs was not available to us). Numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Under strong non-equivocation interactive consistency (IC) takes 1 round for any n, t, and under weak non-equivocation it takes exactly t + 1 rounds and n > 2t processes, for n ≥ 4. Local conditions repair everything: the impossibility of Theorem 6.1 needs n ≥ 4, majorities must be for genuine values, and the authenticated Byzantine model needs one more case. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 6.1 for n ≤ 3 (impossibility for n ≤ 2t under weak non-equivocation) Theorem 6.1 claims that no algorithm solves IC under weak non-equivocation for n ≤ 2t, but for n = 2, t = 1 and n = 3, t = 2 IC is solvable (theorem_6_1_false_n2, theorem_6_1_false_n3). Impact. In that range the theorem contradicts the paper's own Theorem 4.2. For n ≥ 4 the four-run argument is correct (n = 1 is trivial), so the bound n > 2t stays tight there. We prove the exact threshold: IC is solvable under weak non-equivocation iff n > 2t or n ≤ 3 (theorem_6_1, icSolvable_wne_iff). Details. When at most one process is correct, only its own entry is constrained. So these cases reduce to t = 0, resp. t = 1, which Algorithm 2 solves. The proof needs four non-empty groups O, Q, R, S, i.e. n ≥ 4. The paper contradicts itself here: its own Theorem 4.2 ("solvable for any n > 1 if t ≤ 1") covers n = 2, t = 1, which lies inside "n ≤ 2t". "WLOG n = 2t" with groups of size t/2 hides this, and it does not fit odd t either. 🔧 Lemmas 4.7 and 4.8; Algorithm 2, line 8 (when v ranges over V ∪ {⊥}) Under the reading in which ⊥ counts as a value, Lemma 4.7 ("no consistent majority for ⊥") and Lemma 4.8 fail for n = 3, t = 1, two rounds, and a reading of line 8 of Algorithm 2 that allows v = ⊥ breaks agreement (lemma_4_7_false, literal_line8_fails). Impact. Algorithm 2 is not wrong as printed: line 9 returns v into a vector of values, so the type-consistent reading is v ∈ V; under it the lemmas hold (lemma_4_8 for Maj) and the algorithm is correct (theorem_5_1). Details. The paper uses V inconsistently: line 2 of Algorithm 2 says "⊥ ∉ V", but Lemma 4.7 concludes "v ≠ ⊥" for v ∈ V, so there ⊥ counts as a value. The proof of Lemma 4.7 claims that Q contains a correct process that reported ⊥. That process may be the decider p itself, and by the convention σ(p|p|q) = σ(p|q) its "report" is the ⊥ it received. Instance: n = 3, t = 1, two rounds, and the faulty q = 2 omits everything to 0 but otherwise behaves correctly. Then {0, 2} is a consistent 2-majority for ⊥ at 0, since the only admissible route is 0|2. At 1, {1, 2} is one for v. Lemma 4.8 is false on the same instance: two correct processes have 2-majorities for different values. Its proof appeals to Lemma 4.7, which is the failing step. A reading of line 8 that allows v = ⊥ then breaks agreement: 0 returns ⊥ and 1 returns v. 🔧 Section 7.2 (definition of the authenticated Byzantine model) As printed, σ(w'|p|w) ∈ {σ(p|w), ⊥} for correct p forgets the ⟨⊥⟩ convention of Definition 2.1, so with k ≥ 2 rounds it excludes crash executions and Fig. 4's "Omission ⊆ AB" fails (silentσ_not_authByzLiteral). Impact. The intent is clear: with the intended model (absent, p's report, or ⟨⊥⟩) all Fig. 4 relations hold (authByz_of_omission). Details. The printed condition compares with what p received. A correct process that observes an omission reports ⟨⊥⟩ ≠ σ(p|w) = ⊥. (Our first attempted repair, without ⟨⊥⟩, fails for k ≥ 3; this concerns our repair, not the paper.) ✏️ Slips In Definitions 3.1 and 4.1, r = p must be excluded. Otherwise the convention σ(p|p|w) = σ(p|w) forces faulty processes to relay truthfully. In Algorithm 1, line 5 r must range over processes other than p and q. Otherwise line 6 returns ⊥. Typos Definition 4.3: q ∈ Q is stated in the text ("including q") but missing from the formula. Section 3 has a truncated sentence ("a faulty process q may receive v from"). Section 4.1 cites Definition 2.1 for weak non-equivocation, where Definition 4.1 is meant. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The paper's framework, formalized directly (Model.lean): n synchronous processes (Fintype P) with reliable channels run the full-information relay protocol of Pease–Shostak–Lamport for k rounds. The outcome is a message map σ : List P → Option V (none = ⊥). σ (p :: q :: w) is what q told p in round |w| + 1, and σ [p] is p's private value. Only routes without consecutive duplicates are constrained. ⟨⊥⟩ is a distinguished ordinary value (OmitVal). A fault model is a predicate on (rounds k, static faulty set F, σ). We define: byzantine = Definition 2.1 only; wne = Definition 2.1 + Definition 4.1; sne = Definition 2.1 + Definition 3.1; omission, crash, authByz (§7.2, Fig. 4). An algorithm is a deterministic function A p (view k σ p) q. Here view is p's local view of the first k rounds. SolvesIC M k t A requires validity and agreement of IC for every admissible σ with |F| ≤ t; termination is implicit (decision after k rounds). Impossibility results quantify over all such algorithms. Their runs are built as families of full-information executions in which a faulty process imitates the correct behaviour of another "world" towards everybody it does not omit (ExecSys, FLM-style). So it never equivocates. Line 20 of Algorithm 2 is made a deterministic choice, and the recursion bottoms out at t = 0, not at t = 1. Main results in Lean. The "algorithms can / cannot solve agreement" reading of the §7.2 examples (only their fault-model memberships are proved). The consensus column of Table 1. Example (3) of §7.2 deduces "t ≥ 2, n ≥ 5" from an algorithmic criterion ("general-omission algorithms cannot solve agreement"), which we did not formalize. As a pure fault-space separation, a smaller witness exists: a single faulty process lying consistently about its own value (n = 3, t = 1) is in weak NE ∩ AB but not in Omission (sne_inter_authByz_not_le_omission). This reinterprets the claim; it does not refute it. The paper's proof of Theorem 5.1 was not compared with ours: it is only sketched, and its hard case (one correct process has a consistent majority and another has none) is deferred to an appendix (Lemma C.1) we could not access. The theorem itself is proved in full (psl_correct): every member of Q \ {q} gets value v in the recursive vector, which gives ≥ t votes. Any competing value with ≥ t votes comes from a correct process (only t − 1 faulty ones remain). By weak non-equivocation of q's first-round message it equals v. This also covers v = ⟨⊥⟩. The paper's proof of the Section 6 round lower bound is in the same appendix; we proved the bound independently and did not compare the two. Trust. No sorry. Algorithm 2 and the Section 3 algorithm satisfy the solvability hypotheses (theorem_5_1, sne_solvesIC). The model is self-contained (Mathlib, plus the shared vote counting Finset.countEq of Cslib/Foundations/Data/Finset/Quorum.lean). ABA Prevention and Detection — PODC 2015 Zahra Aghazadeh, Philipp Woelfel. On the Time and Space Complexity of ABA Prevention and Detection. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767403. Formalized version: arXiv 1507.02722 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The lower bounds hold for linearizable implementations: Theorem 1(a) m ≥ n − 1 for bounded registers (checked for deterministic implementations only), Theorem 1(b) t·m ≥ n − 1, Theorem 1(c) 2t·m ≥ n − 1, and Corollary 1 for LL/SC. The repairs are local: the WeakRead()/WeakWrite() condition is reworded and the proof of Lemma 2 gets one more case. The upper bounds of Theorems 2 and 3 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Section 2 (the WeakRead()/WeakWrite() correctness condition) The paper claims that linearizable ABA-detecting registers satisfy its WeakRead()/WeakWrite() condition, but read literally even the trivial atomic implementation violates it (weakSpecLiteral_not_of_linearizable_concurrent, weakSpecLiteral_not_of_linearizable_later_read). Impact. An under-specified definition, not a false theorem: the lower-bound proofs use the condition only through Observation 1, which we prove directly from linearizability (separates_aba, separates_llsc), so all lower bounds hold for linearizable implementations. Details. Section 2 requires that "a WeakRead() r by p returns True iff there is a WeakWrite() w that happens before r and every other WeakRead() by p happens before w". Read literally, this fails twice. Take a DRead() concurrent with a DWrite(). If it is linearized after the write it returns True, but no write happens before it. Take the sequential history DWrite(); DRead() → True; DRead() → False. "Every other WeakRead() by p" includes the later read, which does not happen before the write, so the first read would have to return False. Both histories are executions of the trivial atomic implementation, which is linearizable and wait-free. Read literally, the condition cannot be met by any implementation in which a reader can complete two reads after a write: in DWrite(); DRead() the read must return True, and in the extension DWrite(); DRead(); DRead() the same read must return False (informal argument, not formalized). So lower bounds "for the literal condition" are vacuous. The appendix proof of Observation 1 shows the intended meaning ("every earlier WeakRead() by p", reads not concurrent with writes), and the proofs use the condition only in situations that linearizability does determine. Repair. We drop the condition and prove Observation 1 (and Observation 2 for LL/SC) directly from linearizability (separates_aba, separates_llsc). The abstract theorems (card_le_of_separates, ..._wcas, ..._regOrCas) apply to any implementation of any object for which clean and dirty configurations are distinguishable, i.e. to any repaired weak condition that implies Observation 1; no such condition is formalized. ✏️ Slips Lemma 2 derives |WCov(C′,R) ∩ P′| ≤ t′ and then only ≤ t, where < t′ and < t are needed and follow from the induction hypothesis. Lemma 2 does not state that σ is (P ∪ {q})-only and invocation-free, but Lemma 3 uses both. Lemma 3 has index typos: λ′ repeats αᵢ₊₁ where αᵢ₊₂ is meant, and Dⱼ′ = Conf(Dᵢ′, λ′αⱼβⱼ) should end in βᵢ. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 2, Case 1 (the "first process z ∈ P" on V) The proof takes "the first process z ∈ P that executes a step on V in Exec(C,β)", but no such process need exist. Impact. The lemma stands; repaired with a simple extra case (lemma2). Details. Here q is poised to read or CAS an object V. If no process of P accesses V and q's CAS would succeed, no two-step schedule λ hides it. Repair. If q's step does not change V, it is hidden anyway. If it is a successful CAS, case (c) holds directly with σ = β, because no process of P covers V. (lemma2) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model: n processes (Fintype P), atomic base objects, and executions as label lists inv/tau/ret. The adversary is an arbitrary scheduler; there are no crashes beyond processes stopping. Processes are deterministic. For Theorem 1(b),(c) and Corollary 1 this is the paper's setting. For Theorem 1(a) (and Observation 1) the paper allows nondeterministic implementations with nondeterministic solo-termination. We assume determinism and obstruction-freedom, which is the same progress condition for deterministic implementations. Our Theorem 1(a) is therefore weaker than the paper's: a space lower bound for a smaller class of implementations, excluding randomized ones. The paper's proof looks like it carries over (schedules would carry the coin flips), but CSLib's model has no nondeterminism, and this is not checked. The paper's w.l.o.g. "no CAS(x,x)" is unnecessary: such a step can be treated as a read. Implemented objects: the ABA-detecting register abaObj (DRead carries the reader) and CSLib's LL/SC object llscObj. Single-writer use is expressed by the hypotheses that the writer w0 may invoke DWrite(x) and each reader p may invoke DRead(). Executions in the proofs use only these operations; the implementation may allow more. Correctness is linearizability. Base objects: bounded registers register (V i) with Finite (V i) (Theorem 1(a)); bounded writable CAS objects wcasObj V with Finite V, where Read/CAS return the old value (Theorem 1(c), Corollary 1(b)); for "registers and CAS objects" (Theorem 1(b), Corollary 1(a)), writable CAS objects whose Write/CAS usage is restricted per object (RegOrCas). Step complexity ≤ t (StepBound): every operation, complete or not, performs at most t base-object accesses in every execution. Wait-freedom is assumed as in the paper. The proofs are generic. The only property of the implemented object they use is Separates: clean and dirty configurations are distinguishable by the reader (Observations 1/2). It is stated for a writer round ws ([DWrite(x)], resp. [LL(), SC(x)]) and proved from linearizability for both objects. Main results in Lean (namespace Cslib.SharedMemory.ABADetection). Common.lean has the finishing round γᵢ and the clean/dirty bookkeeping. CasDefs.lean has successful schedules (Succ), WCov/CCov and Budget. Not formalized. The paper's remark that the lower bounds also hold for the weak condition itself: no repaired condition is formalized. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The model comes from CSLib (SharedMemory/{Model,History,Covering,Solo,Progress}, Objects/LLSC). Contention Resolution with Predictions — PODC 2021 Seth Gilbert, Calvin Newport, Nitin Vaidya, Alex Weaver. Contention Resolution with Predictions. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467911. Formalized version: arXiv 2105.12706 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The entropy lower bound without collision detection (Theorem 2.4) and the perfect-advice lower bounds (Theorems 3.3–3.7) hold, but the proofs of Theorems 3.3 and 3.7 are wrong and were replaced by new arguments. The collision-detection entropy bound (Theorem 2.8) and the upper bounds with predictions and randomization were not checked, and the randomized lower bounds assume Newport's bound [18], as the paper does. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 (advice of "at most b bits"): the definitions say the advice has "no more than b(n) bits", and with strings of variable length ≤ b both theorems are false (theorem_3_3_false_variable_length, theorem_3_5_false_variable_length). For b = 1 the strings ε, 0, 1 tell three players who transmits, although 1 < log₂ 3 (Theorem 3.3). With collision detection, the same three advice values select one of three groups of three players, and each group is resolved in two rounds (players 1, 2 of the group transmit; after silence player 3, after a collision player 1). So n = 9, b = 1, t = 2 < log₂ 9 − 1 (Theorem 3.5). Both theorems are true for the fixed-length advice f_A : P(A) → {0,1}^b of Section 3.1 (theorem_3_3, theorem_3_5), which we treat as an implied assumption of the model section: we read "at most b bits" as "a b-bit string". The proof of 3.5 itself feeds variable-length histories into 3.3; padding to b + t bits repairs that step. Theorems 3.6 and 3.7 (upper halves of the Θ bounds): they are false for long advice, since every algorithm needs at least one round while the claimed bounds tend to 0 (theorem_3_6_upper_false, theorem_3_7_upper_false). For b(n) = ⌊log₂ n⌋ − 1 < log n, log n / 2^{b(n)} → 0 (3.6). For b(n) = ⌈log₂ log₂ n⌉ − 1 < log log n along n = 2^{2^j+1}, log log n − b(n) → 0 (3.7). Table 2's Θ(log n − b) has the same issue. It is a missing 1 +: the correct forms are Θ(1 + log n / 2^b) and Θ(1 + log log n − b), and the paper itself treats the O(1) regime only for b ≥ log log n. The lower halves are unaffected. RF-construction appends 2^j where the range index j is meant. The tightness text after 3.4 writes n/q for n/2^q. The last display of 3.7 writes O(log log n) − b(n) for a lower bound. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 3.3 (the "strongly selective" claim) The proof claims that the first-round transmitter sets V(s) form an (n, n)-strongly selective family, which is false: for n = 2, V(0) = {0}, V(1) = {0,1} solve the problem but nothing isolates 1 in {0,1} (not_stronglySelective_example). Impact. The theorem stands with an unchanged bound, on a new argument (theorem_3_3, via Cslib.card_le_of_forall_exists_card_inter_eq_one). Details. Correctness only says that some participant of each P is isolated, not every one. So Theorem 3.2 [5] does not apply. Repair. A parity argument over GF(2): a family meeting every nonempty set in exactly one point has at least n members (Cslib.card_le_of_forall_exists_card_inter_eq_one). 🛠️ Theorem 3.7, lower bound (wrong direction of Jensen) The proof bounds the cost E[2^T] of simulating a collision-detection algorithm without collision detection by 2^{E[T]}, but Jensen gives E[2^T] ≥ 2^{E[T]}, so the step "if t < log t', we get a no-CD algorithm faster than t'" does not follow. Impact. The claimed Ω(log log n − b) stands, with half the paper's leading constant (theorem_3_7_lower, theorem_3_7_lower_bits). Details. Simulating a collision-detection algorithm that takes T rounds costs 2^T rounds without collision detection. What the paper's argument gives is E[2^T] ≥ c log n / 2^b (theorem_3_7_lower_exp). Repair. Markov's inequality and independent restarts of the first 2t rounds give c log₂ n ≤ 2^b · 2^{2t+1}, i.e. t ≥ (log₂(c log₂ n) − b − 3)/2 (theorem_3_7_lower, theorem_3_7_lower_bits). 🔧 Lemma 2.5 (code not uniquely decodable) The proof applies the Source Coding Theorem to the code x ↦ (r, d), which writes r in log r bits without a delimiter and so is not uniquely decodable. Impact. The lemma's idea stands: a positive integer of mean μ has entropy at most log(μ + 1) + log e. Repair. A Gibbs inequality against a geometric distribution (sum_negMulLog_le_of_card_fiber_le). 🔧 Lemma 2.7, case 1 (mean is not median) The step "success within the first μ_i rounds with probability < 1/2 contradicts expected time μ_i" is false (T = 1 w.p. 0.49, T = 2 w.p. 0.51). Impact. Repaired with a direct bound (UniformAlg.expTime_ge), used in Theorem 2.4. Repair. If all rounds before R succeed with probability < ε and Rε ≤ 1/2, then E[T] ≥ (R+1)/2 (UniformAlg.expTime_ge). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Channel: single hop, synchronous rounds, n potential players Fin n. An adversary picks a nonempty participant set P. The problem is solved in the first round with exactly one transmitter. With collision detection everybody (transmitters included) learns "collision" vs "silence"; without it every unsuccessful round is silence. Advice: f P, the same for all participants, from an alphabet A; b bits means A = Fin b → Bool. Deterministic algorithms: advice → common feedback history → id → transmit? (DetAlg). This is fully general, since before success all participants see the same feedback. Randomized algorithms: private coins, not necessarily uniform. No-CD players draw independent transmission schedules ℕ → Bool from arbitrary laws; CD players draw strategies List Bool → Bool. Expected times are in ℝ≥0∞; worst case over P. Uniform algorithms (Theorem 2.4): a probability sequence p_r; the number of participants is drawn from a distribution on {2, …, n}; success events are independent with probability k p_r (1 − p_r)^{k−1}.
