Bayesian Ignorance — PODC 2010 Noga Alon, Yuval Emek, Michal Feldman, Moshe Tennenholtz. Bayesian Ignorance. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835785. Formalized version: the full version of May 9, 2010 (17 pp., with appendix; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The numbered results we checked hold: Observations 2.1–2.2, Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 ("ignorance is bliss"), 3.6, 3.7, 3.8, Proposition 4.1, Lemma 4.2 and the reduction of Lemma 3.5. Rosenthal's potential fails with the paper's ∞ costs but works on connecting profiles, which saves existence of equilibria and Lemma 3.8, and the other mistakes are local proof repairs. Lemma 3.4, the online lower bound behind Lemma 3.5 and the directed variants of Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 End of Section 2; proof of Lemma 3.8 (Rosenthal's potential for Bayesian NCS games) The claim that Q(s) = ∑_t p(t) ∑_e c(e) H(|{i : e ∈ s_i(t_i)}|) is a Bayesian potential is false under the paper's definitions, where actions are arbitrary edge sets and an agent whose set misses her path pays ∞. Impact. The identity holds between profiles in which every agent connects her terminals, which is what the paper evidently means (in the NCS literature strategies are paths). Existence of equilibria and Lemma 3.8 (best-eq^P ≤ H(k) · opt^P) survive with that restriction (exists_isBayesEq, lemma_3_8), although the proof of Lemma 3.8 takes a global minimiser of Q, which is the empty profile. Details. A deviation from a connecting edge set to a non-connecting one raises the agent's cost by ∞ but changes Q by a finite amount, so C_i(s) − C_i(s') = Q(s) − Q(s') fails. The global minimiser of this Q is the all-empty profile (Q = 0), in which every agent with a non-trivial type pays ∞; it is not an equilibrium. Lean counterexample on the one-agent, one-edge network 0 → 1: RosenthalCounterexample.no_finite_bayesPotential (no finite-valued function is a Bayesian potential) and RosenthalCounterexample.empty_minimises_not_isBayesEq. Repair. The per-state Rosenthal identity between two connecting profiles (payment_add_potential_update) gives the potential identity between feasible profiles (every agent connects whenever possible); a minimiser of Q over feasible profiles is a Bayesian equilibrium (isBayesEq_of_isMin, exists_isBayesEq). For Lemma 3.8, minimise Q over feasible profiles; turn an optimal profile into a feasible one without changing it on the support of the prior; the case of an unreachable destination of positive probability (opt^P = ∞) is trivial. ✏️ Slips The appendix proofs of Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7 are swapped: the "proof of Lemma 3.6" shows worst-eq^P/worst-eq^C = O(1/k), which is Lemma 3.7's claim, and the "proof of Lemma 3.7" shows Ω(k), which is Lemma 3.6's claim. Each is proved by the other's construction (lemma_3_6, lemma_3_7; the two constructions are worstConstructionA and worstConstructionB). In the "3.6" game every Bayesian equilibrium costs 3/2 + ε while the underlying game with agent k+1 at v has a Nash equilibrium of cost k+2, so worst-eq^P ≤ 3/2 + ε and worst-eq^C ≥ (k+2)/2. In the "3.7" game a Bayesian equilibrium costs k + 2 while worst-eq^C = O(1). "Unique" equilibria in the proofs of Lemmas 3.2, 3.3 and the appendix are unique only up to zero-cost edges and strategies at types of probability 0. In Lemma 3.3 agents may add zero-cost edges (z, y_j); the equilibrium cost 1 + ε is unique, which suffices. The "Alternatively" conditional form of Bayesian equilibrium in Section 2 is not equivalent to the ex-ante one when an agent's ex-ante cost is ∞; the equivalence holds when the cost is finite (Cslib.GameTheory.BayesianGame.IsBayesEq.cond_le). Proof of Lemma 3.7: the unique Nash equilibrium when agent k+1 stays at u has agents 1, …, k buy the edge (u, w), not (u, v). Proof of Lemma 3.7: the cost of an agent under s is 1 + 2/k − 1/k², not 1 + 2/k − 2/k². The chosen range 2/k − 1/k² < ε is exactly what the correct value needs. Typos Proof of Lemma 3.2: the prior is not said to be uniform, and u_ℓ, u_p are written for v_ℓ, w_p. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.3 (the equilibrium analysis on Anshelevich's graph) The proof never fixes ε, and it replaces the argument that s is the Bayesian equilibrium by "by induction on i". Impact. The lemma stands; repaired (Lemma33.lemma_3_3, Lemma33.worstEqP_le). Details. Agent i joins (x, z) only if ε < 1/(2i+1), so the claimed equilibrium needs ε < 1/(2k−1); for larger ε it is not an equilibrium. The induction must also rule out agents buying other agents' direct edges. Repair. For ε(2k − 1) < 1 we show by strong induction on the agent index that every Bayesian equilibrium has all agents on (x, z), using that no agent buys a positive-cost edge she does not need (not_isBayesEq_of_removable); hence worst-eq^P ≤ 1 + ε. Every Nash equilibrium of the state where agent k stays at x costs ≥ H(k−1) (hnum_le_stateCost). 🔧 Appendix, "Proof of Lemma 3.6" (uniqueness of the Bayesian equilibrium) The uniqueness claim is only argued against the all-via-v profile; profiles with some agents on each route have to be excluded too. Impact. The bound on worst-eq^P needs all equilibria; it stands, since a simple share comparison excludes the mixed profiles (triA_socialCost). 🔧 Lemma 3.2, proof "Agent i buys the right edge with probability 1/m" should be 1/(m+1) (a point lies on m+1 lines), and K(s) = m(1 − 1/m) forgets agent k's edge and holds only as a lower bound. Impact. The conclusion Ω(k) is unchanged (Lemma32.lemma_3_2). Repair. The correct bound is opt^P ≥ 1 + m²/(m+1) ≥ k − 1. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A Bayesian game: finitely many agents, finite action and type spaces, a common prior p on type profiles, pure strategies s_i : T_i → A_i, ex-ante costs C_i(s) = ∑_t p(t) C_{i,t}(s(t)), pure Bayesian equilibria (no profitable unilateral deviation in ex-ante cost) and pure Nash equilibria of the underlying complete-information games. No randomness other than the prior; no dynamics. Costs are ℝ≥0∞-valued (the NCS cost is ∞ when an agent's edge set misses her path); expectations are finite sums with 0 · ∞ = 0. opt, best-eq, worst-eq are ⨅/⨆ over ℝ≥0∞ (an empty best-eq is ∞, an empty worst-eq is 0; Bayesian NCS games always have an equilibrium, exists_isBayesEq). NCS games on an abstract network (step e u v, non-negative edge costs) covering directed and undirected (multi)graphs; types T_i = V × V, actions A_i = 2^E, fair cost sharing, as in the paper. Ratios are stated multiplicatively (worst-eq^P ≤ k · opt^C), asymptotic claims with explicit constants and explicit vertex counts. Section 4 uses its own model with strictly positive real costs and distributions in stdSimplex, as in the paper. Main results in Lean. A Modular Approach to Shared-Memory Consensus — PODC 2010 James Aspnes. A modular approach to shared-memory consensus, with applications to the probabilistic-write model. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835802. Formalized version: the author's full version of May 14, 2011 (18 pp., with proofs; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. The author's erratum (ratifiers are Gafni's adopt-commit objects) only fixes credit. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The only mistakes are two slips in intermediate sentences: the composition lemmas (Lemmas 1–3, Theorem 4), the safety of the conciliator/adopt-commit consensus construction, the multi-valued adopt-commit object (Theorems 8 and 10), the quorum optimality via Bollobás's theorem (Theorem 9) and the new probabilistic-write conciliator (Theorem 7: agreement probability (1 − e^{−1/4})/4, 2⌈lg n⌉ + 5 individual work, O(n) expected total work) all hold as stated. The paper's end-to-end consensus result was not fully checked: the probabilistic part of Section 4 (termination with probability 1, the expected-cost bound, Theorem 5) is proved only conditionally, because the per-stage bound "a reached conciliator fails with probability ≤ 1 − δ" is a hypothesis, not derived from Theorem 7 (see Model). Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips §5.2: "the loop is never executed for more than ⌈lg n⌉ + 1 iterations" should be ⌈lg n⌉ + 2 (= ⌈lg 2n⌉ + 1): the write probability 2^k/(2n) reaches 1 only at k = ⌈lg n⌉ + 1. For n = 1 the loop runs twice (attempts_tight). The paper's bound 2⌈lg 2n⌉ + 3 = 2⌈lg n⌉ + 5 uses the right count and is attained. §6.1, sentence before Theorem 8: the prose condition "R_{v′} includes some register written in W_v that is not written in W_{v′}" is not sufficient, since it does not exclude R_v ∩ W_v ≠ ∅, and then a process sees its own write and convergence fails. The precise condition is printed in Theorem 8, and we follow it (AC.theorem8_safety). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Adopt-commit objects (Theorems 8 and 10) use CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl). Processes are deterministic and there may be any number of them, even infinitely many. Memory consists of atomic multi-writer registers, and the scheduler chooses an arbitrary interleaving. A crash is a process that stops taking steps. Safety (validity, coherence, convergence) is proved for every finite, possibly partial, one-shot execution (Impl.Solves). Termination is CSLib's wait-freedom, and individual work is the number of register accesses of an operation. Deciding objects and composition (Section 3) are modelled by the input/output pairs of their executions (DObj). Executions may be partial; inputs are P → Option V and outputs P → Option (Decision × V). (X; Y) combines an execution of X with an execution of Y whose participants adopted from X. Composition is also built operationally on CSLib Impls, together with a projection theorem (SeqCompose.lean, ComposeBridge.lean). Theorem 7 (probabilistic-write model) uses a separate model with one register r : Option V and n processes. The k-th write attempt of a process takes effect with probability min 1 (2^k/(2n)). The coin is flipped when the scheduled write step is taken. The adversary is any function of the full history, including all coins flipped so far, and of the current configuration. It may also idle or stop processes. This is at least as strong as the paper's location-oblivious adversary. Executions are Mathlib PMFs. The probabilistic termination of the consensus construction (Section 4) is formalized abstractly. The deterministic part is proved for executions: if a conciliator's outputs agree, every process commits in the next adopt-commit object. The probabilistic part is a lemma about measures. It assumes that a reached conciliator stage fails with probability at most 1 − δ (μ(E (k+1)) ≤ (1 − δ) μ(E k)) and that the cost of an execution is bounded stage-wise by constants T(A), T(C), and derives termination with probability 1, at most 1/δ expected stages, and the cost bounds. No probabilistic semantics of composed randomized objects is built, so these hypotheses are not discharged for any concrete conciliator, in particular not for Theorem 7's (whose agreement bound is proved for a single, stand-alone instance with fixed inputs). Theorem 5 and the Section 4.1 termination claim are therefore verified only modulo this step, which the paper also treats informally. Main results in Lean. Theorem 8. The paper's timing argument is right. We prove it with an invariant on configurations, AC.Inv. Its key clause is Inv.k2: suppose p is executing line 10 with preference v and has read a set S ⊆ R_v of registers as 0. Then no process with input ≠ v that read ⊥ from proposal has a register of S in its write quorum. Once S = R_v, the hypothesis W_w ∩ R_v ≠ ∅ for w ≠ v shows that every writer of proposal has input v. Termination needs finite (in Lean: uniformly bounded) quorums, which the paper takes for granted. Theorem 7 is proved with a potential function (a submartingale) instead of the paper's "all-failures path" argument. This avoids the cases the paper skips: the index t with ∑_{i ≤ t} pᵢ ≥ 1/4 may not exist, because the adversary may stop scheduling, and the min 1 cap in 2^k/(2n). The paper's two estimates appear in the proof as attemptProb_le_sum and one_sub_sum_le_prod. Section 4. The paper's "with probability 1 some Cᵢ produces agreement" requires each conciliator's δ-guarantee to hold conditionally on the history at the moment its first participant arrives. Its "for any adversary strategy" naturally covers this, but we keep it as the hypothesis of stages_prob. Not formalized. Theorem 6 (CoinConciliator from a weak shared coin; "does not give any new results"), the noisy/priority schedulers of §4.2, the cheap-collect variant (§6.2 item 4), the Θ lower bound in the abstract's "lg m + Θ(log log m)" (the upper bound and the optimality among quorum systems are proved), and the abstract's end-to-end consensus bound for the probabilistic-write model (O(log m + log n) individual work, O(n log m) total work): it combines Theorems 7 and 10 through Section 4, whose probabilistic step is only assumed (see Model). Open points: termination with probability 1, the E[T(U)] bound and Theorem 5 are proved only under the per-stage failure hypothesis, and it was not checked that Theorem 7 gives this hypothesis conditionally on the history with adaptively chosen inputs. Our cost hypothesis also bounds stage costs by constants, so conciliators with only an expected O(n) total-work bound (a Wald-type argument) are not covered. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: concrete executions of the binary AdoptCommit, one committing and one adopting (Quorums.lean); the bit-vector and middle-layer quorums satisfy the hypothesis of Theorem 8 (bit_hWR, mid_hWR); the middle-layer family attains Bollobás's bound; for Theorem 7, an adversary under which disagreement has positive probability (Impatient.disagreement_prob_pos). Broadcasting Time in Dynamic Rooted Trees — PODC 2022 Antoine El-Hayek, Monika Henzinger, Stefan Schmid. Brief Announcement: Broadcasting Time in Dynamic Rooted Trees is Linear. PODC 2022, pp. 54–56. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538460. Formalized version: the brief announcement (BA, arXiv:2211.11352) states the result. The proofs come from the full version (FV), Asymptotically Tight Bounds on the Time Complexity of Broadcast and its Variants in Dynamic Networks, ITCS 2023, arXiv:2211.10151v2. The lower bound is due to Zeiner, Schwarz and Schmid (DAM 2019) and appears as FV Figure 5. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both bounds of BA Theorem 3.1, ⌈(3n−1)/2⌉ − 2 ≤ t*(𝒯ₙ) ≤ ⌈(1+√2)n − 1⌉, are proved for all n, and there are no false statements. The BA's upper bound is one round sharper than what FV's proof gives, and a recount of FV's pigeonhole recovers that round. FV's proofs also have small slips. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips FV Lemma 3.3 is stated for t₁ ≤ t₂ but used in Lemma 3.5 with t₁ = t₂ + 1 (round 1). That extra case is trivial (lemma_3_3). Typos In FV Lemma 3.5, the in-degree formula has x where r_t is meant. The final comparison in FV Lemma 3.5 is not the actual pigeonhole threshold, although the inequality used is still sufficient. FV Lemma 3.2 (ii) carries an unnecessary hypothesis t ≤ t'. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 BA Theorem 3.1 (upper bound ⌈(1+√2)n − 1⌉) BA Theorem 3.1 (and FV's abstract) states ⌈(1+√2)n − 1⌉, but FV Theorem 3.6 only proves the bound ⌈(1+√2)n⌉, one round weaker. Impact. Statement true; the same argument proves it after a recount of the pigeonhole in FV Lemma 3.5 (theorem_3_1, theorem_3_6). Details. The pigeonhole in FV Lemma 3.5 has slack. Take R = n + m − 1 rounds with m = ⌈√2 n⌉. The edge count is at least m(m+1)/2 + (n−1)m, and this exceeds the threshold (n−1)(n+m−1) iff m(m+1) > 2(n−1)². Repair. Optimizing m gives the slightly sharper m + n − 1 for the least m with m(m+1) > 2(n−1)², about (1+√2)(n−1) (advBroadcastTime_trees_le_of_sq_lt). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n processes, synchronous rounds, no failures and no randomness. Communication is full-information flooding. An oblivious message adversary picks each round's communication graph from 𝒯ₙ: rooted out-trees on Fin n with a self-loop at every node (treesWithLoops). A tree is a root plus parent pointers reaching it (RootedTree); every CSLib rooted spanning tree (SimpleGraph.RootedTree) of a graph on Fin n is one (RootedTree.ofGraphRootedTree). Information flow after t rounds is the relational product G₁ ∘ ⋯ ∘ Gₜ. Broadcast has happened when some process reaches all others. broadcastTime is an sInf and advBroadcastTime is a ⨆. Their junk values (0 if never or unbounded) are harmless: the upper bound is also stated per sequence (broadcasts_trees: every sequence of trees has broadcast by then); the lower bound is witnessed by an explicit sequence that has not yet broadcast. The empty product is the identity. This only matters for n = 1, where t* = 0. Main results in Lean (namespace DynamicRootedTrees). Restorable Shortest Path Tiebreaking — PODC 2021 Greg Bodwin, Merav Parter. Restorable Shortest Path Tiebreaking for Edge-Faulty Graphs. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467913. Formalized version: arXiv 2102.10174 v4; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result is proved in full: every graph has a consistent, stable, f-restorable replacement-path tiebreaking scheme, generated by antisymmetric tiebreaking weights (Theorems 2, 19, 20, 23). So are the C₄ impossibility of symmetric restorable schemes (Theorem 37) and the correctness of the preserver, labeling and +4-spanner applications, after local repairs: one constant in Corollary 22's union bound, the minimum in Theorem 23's proof, and the connectivity hypothesis of Definition 17, which Theorem 2 already prints. The sizes of the applications for f ≥ 1, Theorem 27 and all running-time and CONGEST claims were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Definition 17 and Theorem 19 (missing connectivity hypothesis): Definition 17 asks for a replacement path for every nonempty fault set F and every pair s, t, and does not require that s and t remain connected in G \ F. When F cuts s from t, no replacement path exists. So no scheme is restorable on any graph in which some F with |F| ≤ f separates two vertices: any graph with a bridge (f ≥ 1), and any disconnected graph with an edge. Read literally, Theorem 19 fails, e.g., on the single-edge graph K₂, which does have ATW functions (theorem19_literal_false). Theorem 2 states the correct hypothesis ("an s ⇝ t path remains"). We add it to Definition 17 (IsRestorable) and prove Theorem 19 (theorem19). The proof of Corollary 22 says "path lengths change by < 1/(2n)". That is the per-edge change; a path changes by < 1/2, as in Theorem 20's proof (isATW_of_coeff). The first bullet of Theorem 23's proof says a non-shortest path is "at least 1 less" than a shortest path, where "at least 1 more" is meant (theorem23). Theorem 21 (isolation lemma) is stated for a set of paths but needs distinct edge sets: a path and its reverse always tie. In the only use all paths go from s to t (Cslib.Isolation.card_not_uniqueMin_le). The proof of Theorem 30 says "restorable f-RPTS" where an (f+1)-restorable (f+1)-RPTS is needed (theorem30_correct). The proof of Lemma 32 omits replacement paths that contain no clustered vertex. In the missing case every edge of the path is in H (lemma32_correct). Appendix B (Theorem 27, not formalized) has several slips, none affecting the asymptotics: the bipartite weights should be 1 + (λ−j)/n⁴; Observation 1(c) states N(f, d) = 2^f · d² where ≤ is meant; labels are undefined for the last copy at each level, so only a constant fraction of the bipartite edges is forced. Typos Appendix B: v* is never defined. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Corollary 22 (union bound over s, t, F) The proof bounds the number of choices of (s, t, F) with |F| ≤ f by n^{f+2}, but there are about n² · |E|^f, up to about n^{2f+2} (paper_count_false). Impact. Statement true after changing the constant W in the proof; it still gives O(f log n) bits per weight (corollary22). Details. Already K₄ with f = 1 has 16 · 7 = 112 > 4³ choices with ordered pairs (84 > 64 excluding s = t). With the paper's W = n^{f+4+c}, the union bound therefore only gives about n^{f−c}, not n^{−c}. Repair. W = n^{2f+4+c} repairs the bound and keeps O(f log n) bits per weight. We prove the correct bound n² · N_f · |E| / (2W+1) with the isolation lemma. The final arithmetic (choice of W, O(f log n) bits) is not stated in Lean. (paper_count_false; repaired: corollary22) 🔧 Corollary 22 (signed weights in the isolation lemma) Applying the isolation lemma to signed directed weights needs that all shortest s ⇝ t paths cross each edge in the same direction and that the weight distribution is symmetric under negation; the proof does not say so. Impact. Statement true; the two facts are added at this step (corollary22, via tau and a sign flip). 🔧 Theorem 23 (deterministic weights) The uniqueness argument picks the minimum-ID edge of π₁ \ π₂ instead of the whole symmetric difference. Impact. Statement true; repaired (theorem23). Details. The proof also speaks of arbitrary paths, ignoring lengths; the ±2r(e) terms of oppositely traversed edges are harmless for large C. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graphs and faults. A finite undirected unweighted graph G : SimpleGraph V. Edge faults F : Finset (Sym2 V) (deterministic, arbitrary). G \ F is G.deleteEdges F and distances are edist. Paths. Selected paths are walks of G (G.Walk s t). A replacement path is IsShortestIn F: it avoids F and is a shortest walk of G \ F. Schemes. A scheme π : Finset (Sym2 V) → ∀ s t, Option (G.Walk s t) selects π(s, t | F). Weights. G* has dart weights 1 + r(u,v) (wstar). Our IsATW reads Definition 18 with lightest walks; IsATWPath reads it with lightest simple paths. The two are proved equivalent. Randomness. Only in Theorem 20 (uniform product measure on [-ε, ε]^{Sym2 V}) and Corollary 22 (uniform {−W,…,W}^{Sym2 V}, counting form). Not modelled. No distributed or computational model is formalized; running times, bit lengths and the CONGEST results are outside the formalization. Main results in Lean. Silence — PODC 2018 Guy Goren, Yoram Moses. Silence. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212768. Formalized version: arXiv 1805.07954 v1 (the only version, with Appendices A–D); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The Silent Choir Theorem, the lower bounds of Theorem 3 and the three matching AC protocols (STEALTH, D2, D1f1) hold, and so do the Appendix D bounds and protocol. The protocol proofs treat the consensus sub-protocol as a black box, which does not work: saving them took a concrete max-floodset consensus and a new argument across six lemmas. The rest needs local changes: Theorem 3 lacks the bound for D = 1, which "completely characterize" needs, and Appendix D's 1-bit encoding of huh? does not say how it is decoded. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 §4.2, "completely characterize" (Theorem 3 for D = 1) §4.2 says the three protocols make the bounds of Theorem 3 tight, but for f = 1 and D = 1 Theorem 3 gives only M ≥ n, while D1f1 uses n² − n. Impact. The claim is incomplete, and true after adding the missing bound: if all processes decide by time 1, then M ≥ n(n − 1). It follows from the Silent Choir Theorem (theorem3_D1). ✏️ Slips §4.2, STEALTH and D2: self-messages are under-specified. Under readings the text allows, STEALTH violates Commit Validity: if process 0 checks only "n − 1 first-round messages", ignoring its own vote, then with v₀ = 0 and no failures everyone commits (Stealth.literal0_not_solvesAC, Stealth.literalErr_not_solvesAC). Separately, suppose a choir member that sent err but received none still commits. With n = 3, f = 1, v₂ = 0, and process 0 crashing in round 3, process 1 commits. Both runs violate Commit Validity. Fig. 3 (D2) has the same self-message ambiguity. These are under-specified descriptions, not wrong protocols: the intended reading is "sent or received", as the D2 prose says, and we verify that reading (Stealth.solvesAC, D2.solvesAC). Lemma 2 and Corollary 2 fail when the receiver i has crashed by time m: a crashed i "receives nothing", but its state is ⊥ and it knows nothing (corollary2_literal_false). Counterexample: n = 3, f = 1, S = {1, 2}, φ = (v₁ = 1 ∨ v₂ = 1). Process 0 crashes in round 1, and every value is 1. We prove both results for an i that is alive at time m; Lemma 1 is unaffected (lemma2, corollary2, lemma1). The D1f1 prose (§4.2) says "all[1] message in the second round" where it means the third round. Theorem 2's proof says "k_y < ℓ − 1" where it needs k_y ≤ ℓ − 1. Typos Theorem 3(c)'s proof says "chain from j" where it means "from i". Fig. 1 sends all[1] to {0, …, f} instead of {1, …, f}. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ STEALTH, D2, 1.5D (consensus used as a black box; Lemmas 5, 8, 9, 11, 17, 18) The protocols call B.1.Consensus(f − 1), which tolerates only f − 1 crashes, but the Commit Validity proofs (Lemmas 5, 9, 17) need its Validity in runs where f crashes can happen during the consensus, and the Agreement proofs (Lemmas 8, 11, 18) never check the f − 1 bound. Impact. Statements true; repaired with a concrete max-floodset consensus (Stealth.solvesAC, D2.solvesAC, MidRound.OnePointFive.solvesACMid). Details. The bad runs include e.g. v_j = 0 with nothing failed earlier. Repair. With a concrete max-floodset everything works. Its validity holds for any number of crashes. When the inputs are mixed, a crash happened before the consensus, so its f rounds contain a round with no crash. 🔧 Appendix D, 1.5D (the 1-bit encoding of huh?) The paper sends huh? as "quiet to {i+1..i+f}, 1 to the rest" but never says how a receiver decodes it, and the natural decoding that ignores silence from a predecessor breaks Agreement (MidRound.OneBit.oneBit_not_solvesACMid). Impact. The encoding is under-specified: a decoding that also reads silence from a predecessor as huh? makes the 1-bit protocol correct (MidRound.OneBitFixed.solvesACMid); with huh? as a separate message 1.5D is correct as well (MidRound.OnePointFive.solvesACMid). The appendices appear only in the arXiv version. Details. Decoding "a 1 from a non-predecessor means huh?" (silence from a predecessor ignored). Agreement fails. Counterexample: n = 5, f = 2, all values 1. Process 4 crashes in round 1 reaching only processes 1 and 2; process 3 crashes silently in round 2. Processes 1 and 2 commit at time 1½ and halt, while process 0 runs the consensus alone and aborts. Decoding that also reads "no all[1] from a predecessor" as huh?. The 1-bit protocol is correct. 🔧 Lemma 11 (D2 agreement) The process c_j that received j's vote need not "send j's id to all": if it committed, it is silent in round 3. Impact. Statement true: agreement then follows from the biased-to-1 property instead (D2.solvesAC). 🔧 Lemma 18 (1.5D agreement) "This correct process will start the consensus protocol with v̂ = 1" assumes that it takes part in the consensus, which is not shown. Impact. Statement true: any uncommitted process that later decides reaches everybody with its huh? (MidRound.OnePointFive.solvesACMid). 🔧 Theorem 2 (Silent Choir) A process h ∈ S_j^r(m−1) may already have crashed in r before it is reached, and the paper's r′ makes h crash later, so h behaves differently in r′. Impact. Statement true; fixed by keeping h's earlier crash (silent_choir). Details. Messages to crashed processes count in chains, so this can happen. Full list of differences, including modelling choices: differencies.md. The formalization Model (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SyncCrash/Model.lean in CSLib, built on CSLib's LockStep). Network and timing: a complete network, synchronous rounds; round t + 1 runs from time t to time t + 1. Protocols are deterministic and history based: the local state is (initial value, received inboxes). The state becomes ⊥ after a crash. Crashes: a run is given by its inputs and its crash pattern. A process crashing in round c ≥ 1 reaches an arbitrary subset reach p in round c and nothing afterwards. γ_f allows at most f crashes. Decisions are taken at the start of a round from the current state; crashed processes do not decide. Knowledge is semantic: K_i φ holds iff φ holds in every admissible run where i has the same state. Messages are counted with Set.encard, so runs with infinitely many messages are included. There are no self-messages; protocols read their own state instead, and counts agree with the paper's. AC (Defs.lean): Decision, uniform Agreement, Commit Validity and Abort Validity on every admissible run. The common case is the nice run, where all values are 1 and nobody fails. Appendix D (MidRound.lean): the same runs, with mid-round decisions. Such a decision is performed only if the process finished its sending phase. Consensus inside the protocols: max-floodset (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SyncCrash/Floodset.lean). Main results in Lean (namespace Papers.PODC2018.Silence). Minimum Weight Cycle in CONGEST — PODC 2024 Vignesh Manoharan, Vijaya Ramachandran. Computing Minimum Weight Cycle in the CONGEST Model. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662801. Formalized version: the PODC paper's Theorems 1.2.A and 1.4.A. Their proofs are deferred to the full version arXiv:2308.08670v3, which in turn defers them to the companion paper arXiv:2205.14797v2 (Near Optimal Bounds for Replacement Paths and Related Problems in the CONGEST Model, §3.1.1–3.1.2, Lemmas 13–14, Figures 4–5). We formalize those proofs. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both checked lower bounds hold as stated: computing a (2 − ε)-approximation of the minimum weight cycle (MWC) needs Ω(n / log n) CONGEST rounds, both in directed graphs (weighted or unweighted) and in undirected weighted graphs, even on networks of constant diameter. The proofs need two local repairs: the cited constructions are disconnected, so the "constant diameter" part is not proved there, and Lemma 14's argument covers only the heavy weight w = 2, not the large w that the (2 − ε) claim needs. The sublinear-round algorithms, the paper's other main part, and the lower bounds for larger approximation factors were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips All in the companion paper's proofs; none affects a result. The directed proof decides "by checking if the minimum cycle has length at least 4". Every cycle has length at least 4; the test should be "at least 8" (or "greater than 4"). The undirected proof likewise says "weight at least 6" where it should be "> 6" (or "≥ 8"). Both proofs say "the cut has 4k edges". The graphs as constructed have 2k cut edges (our graphs with a hub have 4k). This is harmless. In Lemma 14 the case list of 4-cycles leaves out the all-heavy cycles r_i r′_j r_p r′_q on Bob's side. They weigh 4w, like the listed ℓ_i ℓ′_j ℓ_p ℓ′_q. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Thm 1.2.A, 1.4.A ("even on graphs with constant diameter") The constant-diameter part is not proved: the graphs of Lemmas 13 and 14 in the cited proofs can be disconnected (for S_a = S_b = ∅ they are perfect matchings). Impact. Statements true; repaired with a hub vertex, on diameter-2 networks and for every n (dComap_ediam, uComap_ediam, theorem_1_2_A, theorem_1_4_A). Details. The companion paper adds a sink vertex with an arc from every vertex to get diameter 2, but only for its replacement-path bound, not for MWC. For directed MWC the same sink works, since a sink lies on no cycle. For undirected weighted MWC it must be done with care. A hub joined to all vertices by unit-weight edges creates triangles hub–ℓ_i–r_i of weight 3, below the gap 2w + 2, and the reduction fails. Repair. We add a hub whose edges weigh 2w. Then every cycle through the hub weighs at least 4w, and the bound holds on diameter-2 networks. We also add pendant padding vertices so that every n is covered, not only n = 4k. 🔧 Lemma 14 (the heavy weight w needed for (2 − ε)) The proof bounds cycles with at least 6 edges by "at most as many light edges as heavy edges", which for heavy weight w gives only 3w + 3 for a 6-cycle, below the needed 4w once w > 3. Impact. The lemma is true; the proof needed a parity step (uGraph.weight_ge). Details. For (2 − ε)-approximation, the paper changes the heavy weight 2 to a large w and says one must then tell cycles of weight 2w + 2 from cycles of weight 4w. Its argument: the graph is bipartite and the light edges form a matching, so a cycle has at most as many light edges as heavy edges. With w = 2 this gives weight at least 9. Repair. Light edges are the only edges between Alice's side L ∪ L′ and Bob's side R ∪ R′, so every cycle has an even number of light edges. A 6-cycle therefore has at most 2 light edges and weighs at least 4w + 2. (uGraph.weight_ge) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous CONGEST, deterministic (Cslib.Congest.Algorithm). Node IDs are the vertex names, and the vertex type V is arbitrary with |V| = n. Messages have exactly B bits per edge, direction and round. Nodes have unbounded local computation. There are no failures. The network is the underlying undirected unweighted graph (§1.1). Node v's input is the weights of its incident arcs in both directions (directed case, WDigraph.view) or of its incident edges (WGraph.view). Weights lie in {0, …, W}. MWC is the minimum weight of a simple cycle, ∞ if there is none (Def. 1.1). Simple cycles are periodic sequences of distinct vertices, of length ≥ 2 (directed) or ≥ 3 (undirected). Output convention (ApproxOutput): every node outputs none or an estimate. At least one node outputs an estimate, and every estimate e satisfies MWC ≤ e ≤ α · MWC. The paper's own algorithms meet this, and it is the weakest convention its lower bounds claim ("even when only one node is required to know the weight"). The hypothesis is weaker than "solves MWC". The directed algorithm need only be correct on unweighted digraphs whose underlying network has diameter ≤ 2. The undirected one need only be correct on weighted graphs of diameter ≤ 2, with W ≥ W₀(α). So the theorems cover weighted and unweighted algorithms and the constant-diameter claim. Bounds are explicit: n ≤ 32 · B · T + 12, i.e. T = Ω(n / B) = Ω(n / log n) for B = Θ(log n). Set disjointness on k² bits is embedded into graphs with n = 4k + 1 + p nodes and 4k cut edges. The deterministic bound CC(DISJ_K) ≥ K is proved in CSLib. Randomized versions (the paper: "all our lower bounds hold for randomized algorithms") use private random strings per node. They are conditional on the randomized communication lower bound for set disjointness (Razborov / Kalyanasundaram–Schnitger), which enters as the hypothesis RandDisjLB δ κ (private-coin protocols with nonempty finite uniform coin spaces) and is not formalized. Asynchrony-Resilient Sleepy TOB — PODC 2024 Francesco D'Amato, Giuliano Losa, Luca Zanolini. Asynchrony-Resilient Sleepy Total-Order Broadcast Protocols. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662779. Formalized version: arXiv 2309.05347 v2 (6 May 2024); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Algorithm 1 as printed is not the protocol the paper means, which is Malkhi–Momose–Ren's protocol [MMR] with latest unexpired votes: its input rule lets a Byzantine VRF winner erase the lock, and the printed algorithm then violates safety even with no asynchrony at all. With the one-word fix taken from [MMR] and from the paper's own proofs, all checked statements are true, namely Lemma 1 (the extended graded agreement and clique validity), Lemmas 2–3, Theorem 1's safety and the main Theorem 2 (π-asynchrony resilience for π < η), and two proofs need short repairs. Liveness (Theorem 1's second half) and healing (Theorem 3) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Algorithm 1, lines 6–7 (input rule of GA_{v,1}) With the printed rule "highest-VRF proposal not conflicting with L_{v-1}", a Byzantine VRF winner can propose a strict prefix of the decided log and erase the lock, so Algorithm 1 as printed violates safety even with no asynchrony (algorithm_1_literal_unsafe, theorem_1_false_for_literal_algorithm, theorem_2_false_for_literal_algorithm). Impact. The paper presents Algorithm 1 as [MMR]'s protocol, whose rule is "extends L_{v-1}, else input L_{v-1}", and its own proofs reason with that rule; with this one-word fix all checked statements, including Theorem 2, are true. Details. arXiv v1 says "not conflicting" too, three times. The printed algorithm also has no fallback when no proposal qualifies. With the printed rule, the winning proposal may be a strict prefix of the decided log, and then the lock is lost. Counterexample: 4 processes, process 3 Byzantine, everyone always awake, all messages delivered at once, η = 2. All honest processes vote [1] in view 1 and decide [1] in round 3. The Byzantine process then wins the VRF with the proposal [] (the genesis log), which does not conflict with L_1 = [1], so every honest process votes []. In view 3 an honest proposal [2] = b‖C_2 wins, and [2] is decided in round 7. So Lemma 3 fails (round-3 voters do not extend the decided [1]), Theorem 1's safety fails (with π = 0), and Theorem 2 fails ([1] ∈ D_ra for ra = 3, π = 1). All of the paper's hypotheses hold in this execution: η-sleepiness 3 > 2/3·4 in every round, Equations 4 and 5, π < η. The view-1 votes [1] come from a Byzantine view-0 proposal that wins the lottery. Shifting the run by one view gives a variant in which the Byzantine process wins only once (not formalized). The paper defers the protocol's correctness to [MMR]'s proof, and its own proofs use the step "outputs Λ with grade 1, hence votes for an extension of Λ", which holds in odd rounds only under the "extends" rule. Repair. We formalize the [MMR] rule (Exec.Follows), and the printed rule only for the counterexample. ✏️ Slips Definition 4 (integrity): "there exists a well-behaved process that inputs the log" fails for every graded agreement with validity: one honest process with input [1] outputs [] with grade 1 (integrity_literal_false). The intended property, as in [MMR] and the proof of Lemma 1, is that some honest input extends the log. That is what we prove. Algorithm 1, line 1, for v = 1 refers to GA_{0,2}, which does not exist (view 0 only proposes). We start decisions at round 3 and leave round-1 votes unconstrained. In the proof of Theorem 2, |H_ra \ H_{ra+π+1}| should be |H_ra \ B_{ra+π+1}|. In the proof of Lemma 2, the latest votes in M0 are "from rounds no later than ra" only up to later honest votes, which also extend Λ. Typos In the proof of Lemma 2, |S_r' ∪ P0| should be |O_r' ∪ P0|. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3 (base case) The proof says that once some process decides Λ, "by graded consistency" every process of H_r votes for an extension of Λ, but graded consistency only gives Λ grade ≥ 0 elsewhere (graded_consistency_insufficient). Impact. Statement true; repaired with [MMR]'s argument (Exec.Follows.decision_lock). Details. Bounded divergence allows a second, conflicting and longer grade-0 log, which would become L_{v-1}. Example: 7 honest processes (5 vote [1], 2 vote [2,5]) and 2 Byzantine processes voting [1] to p and [2,5] to q. Then p outputs [1] with grade 1, while q's longest output is [2,5]. In the paper's own network model, all honest receivers of a synchronous round receive the same messages, so their tallies agree and the conclusion also follows directly. Only the cited justification is insufficient. Repair. Integrity of GA_{v-1,2} makes every output extended by an honest GA_{v-1,2} input. Those inputs are grade-1 outputs of GA_{v-1,1} and pairwise compatible by its uniqueness. So no output of GA_{v-1,2} conflicts with Λ, and the longest one extends Λ (Exec.Follows.decision_lock). 🔧 Lemma 2 and Theorem 2 (clique validity applied outside its hypotheses) Lemma 1 requires H' ⊆ H_r ∪ H_{r+1} and concludes only for receivers in H', but the proof of Lemma 2 applies it to H' = H_ra \ B_r', which contains processes asleep at both r' and r'+1. Impact. Statements true; a more general form of clique validity covers both uses (clique_validity). Details. The proof of Theorem 2 needs the conclusion for every receiver of the synchronous round ra+π+1 and redoes the argument by hand. Repair. The proof of clique validity in fact only needs H' disjoint from B_r, and works for any receiver whose initial votes contain the clique's votes. We prove this general form (clique_validity) and derive the paper's form from it (lemma_1_clique_validity). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n processes, synchronous rounds 0, 1, 2, … with sleepiness: O_r is awake at round r, and B_r ⊆ O_r is Byzantine with a growing adversary (B_r ⊆ B_{r+1}; Byzantine processes never sleep). H_r = O_r \ B_r, and the receivers of round r are H_{r+1}. Signatures are modelled by message senders. There is no randomness: VRF proposals are abstracted adversarially. In odd rounds an honest vote is any extension of a longest output L_{v-1}, which covers every proposal that can win the VRF lottery, so safety holds for every outcome. Messages are (sender, round, log). Each q ∈ H_t (t ≥ 1) sends one vote per round. Byzantine processes send arbitrary sets of messages with arbitrary round tags, including back-dated ones. rcv p r (messages received by the end of round r) only grows. In a synchronous round, every receiver has every message sent so far. In the single asynchronous period [ra+1, ra+π] delivery is arbitrary. Expiration: the GA of round r is tallied from the latest received votes with round tag in [r-η, r]. A sender whose latest votes equivocate is discarded. Grade 1 means more than 2m/3 votes for extensions, an output means more than m/3, and β = 1/3 throughout. We prove that this tally is an instance of the extended GA of Figure 3, with M0 = latest votes from [r-η, r) and P0 = O_{r-η,r} (Exec.tally_eq_ga_M). This is the correspondence claimed in Section 3.3, so Lemma 1 transfers verbatim (Exec.isGA, Exec.clique). Figure 3 is modelled as an abstract one-shot instance (ExtGA). Each receiver has initial votes M0 from P0. Honest senders send only their input, absent senders send nothing, Byzantine senders send anything. Round-r votes override M0, and equivocations are discarded. Main results in Lean. The paper states Equations 1–2 as the synchronous-round assumptions but uses η-sleepiness (Equation 3) throughout: Lemma 2's base case needs it in round ra, Lemma 3 in rounds ≤ ra, and Theorem 2 in rounds ≥ ra+π+2. This is not a mistake: Section 3.3 works in the η-sleepy model, and Equations 1 and 2 imply 3 with exactly the paper's β̃ (Exec.sleepy_of_churn_of_failure, betaTilde_identity). Footnote 7's equivalences hold (Exec.footnote_7). Not formalized. Liveness: Theorem 1's liveness half, which is probabilistic via the VRF and deferred to [MMR], and Theorem 3 (healing), which has a two-line informal proof. Also the necessity of β̃ claimed in Figure 1's caption. Safety under the original (non-expiring) MMR protocol is not treated separately: it is the case η = 0. Trust. No sorry. The listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: theorem_2_hypotheses_satisfiable exhibits an execution of the modified Algorithm 1 that satisfies every hypothesis of Theorem 2 and contains a decision before the asynchronous period. The model is self-contained in this folder (Mathlib only). Tally.lean (logs, faithful tallies, graded-agreement counting) is marked as a CSLib candidate.

Distributed Approximation on Power Graphs — PODC 2020 Reuven Bar-Yehuda, Keren Censor-Hillel, Yannic Maus, Shreyas Pai, Sriram V. Pemmaraju. Distributed Approximation on Power Graphs. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405750. Formalized version: arXiv 2006.03746 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Every checked statement is true: the centralized 5/3-approximation for G²-MVC (Theorem 12, Lemmas 13–16), Lemma 6, the combinatorial core of the (1+ε)-approximation (Theorem 1, Lemmas 2–5), Corollary 17, and the Ω̃(n²) CONGEST lower bounds for exact G²-MWVC and G²-MVC (Theorems 20 and 22, Lemmas 21, 23, 24, with the [CKP17] family lemma proved from scratch). The one serious flaw sits in a side result that nothing depends on: the proof of Corollary 17 applies Theorem 12 to a graph that is not a square, where Algorithm 2 really is only a 2-approximation, and a new accounting saves the 5/3 bound. The CONGEST round complexities and the G²-MDS half of the paper were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 6: the claim |I| < n/α fails for the path 0–1–2–3 with r = 2, where I = {0, 3} is independent in G² and |I| = 2 = n/α (lemma_6_strict_false). The non-strict bound |I| ≤ n/α follows from the paper's own argument and is all the lemma needs (card_mul_le_of_indep, lemma_6). Lemma 6's second sentence (the (1 + 1/⌊r/2⌋)-approximation) needs r ≥ 2; for r = 1 it divides by 0. Theorem 12, degree-3 case: the three disjoint edges are {y₁,z₁}, {y₂,z₂}, {x,y₃}, not {x,y₂}. The distributed description of Phase I calls vertices with "at least 1/ε" neighbours in R candidates; the pseudocode, Lemma 2 and Lemma 5 need "more than 1/ε". Theorem 1, case ε > 1: "a G²-MIS has at most n/2 vertices" fails for n = 1. Theorems 20 and 22: V_B = V(G) \ V_B should be \ V_A. Typos Lemma 5 writes Sᵢ = N(vᵢ) ∩ R for N(cᵢ) ∩ R. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Corollary 17 (the proof misapplies Theorem 12) The proof runs Phase I of Algorithm 1 with ε = 1/2 and then applies Theorem 12 to the remaining graph G²[U], which is not a square, and Algorithm 2 really is only a 2-approximation there (corollary_17_proof_gap). Impact. The corollary is true: the overall 5/3 bound holds with a different accounting (induced_bound, corollary_17). Details. The proof says the leader "locally uses Theorem 12 to compute a 5/3-approximation for the remaining graph" G²[U]. Theorem 12 only covers squares G². G²[U] is just an induced subgraph of a square, and every graph is one. The proof of Theorem 12 also breaks there: Lemma 13 (3) needs the G-midpoint of every blue edge to lie in V1, but now the midpoint can lie in S. Concrete run: take vertices a₀..a₃, b₀..b₃ and midpoints wᵢⱼ ~ aᵢ, bⱼ. Phase I picks a₀, …, a₃ and ends with U = {aᵢ, bⱼ} and G²[U] = K₄,₄. That graph is triangle-free and 4-regular, so Algorithm 2 goes straight to part 3. Part 3 may output all 8 vertices (both ends of a perfect matching), while 4 vertices suffice (corollary_17_proof_gap). Repair. A midpoint in S has at most two neighbours in the triangle-free remainder, so it pays for at most one blue edge, just like a triangle vertex. Lemma 5 charges S at ratio 3/2, the same as part 1 charges triangles. So Lemma 14 (4) becomes s₁ + |S| ≥ (3/2)|V_{R'}| and the 5/3 computation goes through (induced_bound, corollary_17). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graphs are finite SimpleGraphs. G.power r joins distinct vertices at G-distance ≤ r (Podc/Foundations/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Power.lean). Vertex covers are Mathlib's IsVertexCover or a Finset covering G²[X]. Centralized algorithms (Algorithms 1 and 2) are nondeterministic transition systems (Step). Each choice the pseudocode leaves open is a nondeterministic choice, and the theorems hold for every complete run. Algorithm 2 stores only V', since E' = G²[V'] throughout, as the paper proves. Degree-0 vertices may be removed at any time in parts 1–2 (the paper removes them eagerly). Part 3 is "any 2-approximate cover". Existence of runs comes from exists_step/exists_run: the existence claims of lines 9–10 hold, and part 3 can use a maximal matching. "Polynomial time" is formalized as an n + 3 bound on the number of steps, each step being a polynomial-time check. Theorem 1 (CONGEST, O(n/ε) rounds) is formalized only in its sequential semantics with ε = 1/l: correctness and approximation, Lemma 3, and the facts behind the round count. These are: at most l neighbours in U per vertex, hence |F| ≤ ln, and at most n/(l+1) Phase-I iterations. BFS pipelining and ID symmetry breaking are not modelled. Lower bounds use CSLib's deterministic synchronous CONGEST model with B-bit messages and families of lower-bound graphs (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Congest/). Nodes know their IDs and neighbourhoods, plus their weight for Theorem 20. "Computes MVC of G²" is formalized, as in [CKP17]/Theorem 19, as deciding the threshold predicate "H² has a cover of size (weight) ≤ W'". The deterministic bound is unconditional, because CSLib proves CC(DISJ_K) ≥ K. The randomized versions assume CC^R(DISJ_K) ≥ κK (real κ > 0, private coins from nonempty coin spaces) as a hypothesis. There are also versions that need correctness only on connected networks (H_{x,y} is disconnected only for x = y = 1). Main results in Lean. Remarks. Two routine details the paper leaves implicit. In the degree-2 case of Theorem 12, the edges {z,y₁} and {x,y₂} are disjoint only because z ≠ y₂, which holds because the graph is triangle-free; the paper does not say so. Classification of distributed binary labeling problems — PODC 2020 Alkida Balliu, Sebastian Brandt, Yuval Efron, Juho Hirvonen, Yannic Maus, Dennis Olivetti, Jukka Suomela. Brief Announcement: Classification of Distributed Binary Labeling Problems. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405703. Formalized version: the full version arXiv 1911.13294 v3 (48 pages); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Everything we checked holds as stated: Observation 3.2 (the four equivalent problems), Theorems 8.1–8.3 (families V and VI have deterministic complexity Θ(n)), proved for every number of nodes, Lemma 10.4 (every problem not of type I–IV relaxes to a forbidden-degree or bipartite sinkless-orientation problem) and Lemmas 10.8–10.9 (FDSO(s) is a fixed point of round elimination). The proofs of Theorems 8.1 and 8.2 need short local changes, and the proof of Theorem 8.3 has an orientation going the wrong way. The complete classification itself was not checked, since Sections 6, 7, 9 and 11, Theorem 10.11 and the completeness of Table 2 are not formalized. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proof of Theorem 8.3: it roots the tree at a leaf and orients all edges towards it, which gives a non-root node of degree k exactly k − 1 incoming edges and violates the constraints of the hardest VI.b problem W = 010⁺, B = 0⁺10 for k ≥ 3. With the paper's convention (an X-edge points from black to white), every relevant node must have exactly one incoming edge. Orienting away from the leaf, every non-root node has one incoming edge, and the leaf root is irrelevant (viHard_exists, theorem_8_3). The same slip appears in the sentence "it is always possible to orient a tree towards a root" about the Theorem 8.2 problem. Proof of Lemma 10.4, case 1010: the case B = 0⁺ (type II.b) is not mentioned; the lemma's hypothesis excludes it. Proof of Lemma 10.8 (2): "configurations consisting of δ labels" (and Z₁ … Z_δ) should read d. Proof of Lemma 10.9, items (1)–(2): "black" and "white" (and d, δ) are swapped in the description of the output problem; the proof itself uses the right constraints. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 8.2 ("at most a single vertex has all edges outgoing") This intermediate claim of the proof is false for general trees, and so is the claimed equivalence with the "oriented tree problem", though both hold on the instances the reduction actually uses. Impact. Statement true; repaired by running the mirroring argument directly on caterpillars (dirR_mono, Caterpillar.viEasy_lower). Details. Only relevant nodes (white degree d, black degree δ) must have at most one incoming edge. Nodes of other degrees can absorb several incoming edges, so in a general tree many nodes can be sources. The claim does hold on the instances the reduction uses: a path whose nodes are all relevant, with leaves attached. Repair. Our proof runs the paper's mirroring argument directly on those caterpillars and never uses the general claim. 🔧 Theorem 8.1 (upper bound, only subdivided regular trees) The proof only treats subdivided d-regular trees ("it is sufficient that V.a is solvable on any d-regular tree"), but on a general bipartite tree black nodes of degree ≠ 2 are not edges of an underlying tree. Impact. Statement true; a solution always exists (va_exists). Repair. Root the tree at a node of degree ≤ 1 and use the parity of ⌊dist(r, u)/2⌋ at white nodes u. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Problems and solutions. A binary labeling problem is Π = (d, δ, W, B) with d, δ ≥ 2, W ⊆ [0, d], B ⊆ [0, δ]. An instance is a finite tree G with a proper 2-colouring f (white/black). A solution is an edge labelling, symmetric on edges. White nodes of degree exactly d must have X-degree in W; black nodes of degree exactly δ must have X-degree in B. All other nodes are unconstrained (§3.1, §3.6). Computation. Deterministic, synchronous, fault-free LOCAL with unique identifiers. The nodes of every instance are the elements of a fixed finite type V, so n = |V| is known, and node names serve as identifiers. A T-round algorithm is a function of the radius-T view (CSLib's Cslib.Local.IsLocal: edges at distance < T, inputs at distance ≤ T). The colour is a local input. A T-round message-passing algorithm is (T + 1)-local in this sense (it also learns the degrees at distance T), which only shifts the constants. White and black algorithms. In a white algorithm every edge gets the label written by its white endpoint; a black algorithm is symmetric (§5). WhiteSolvable Π V T means some T-round white algorithm solves Π on every tree on V with every proper 2-colouring. No port numbers. With identifiers, port numbers can be derived from the IDs. For the lower bounds, assuming them absent is without loss of generality: an algorithm correct for all port numberings is correct for the ID-induced one. Identifiers. The identifiers are exactly the n nodes rather than a poly(n) range. This only restricts the instances, so the lower bounds become stronger. The upper bounds gather the whole tree in n rounds. Randomized results. §10.3–10.4 and §11 are not formalized. Lemmas 10.8–10.9 are the purely combinatorial round-elimination step: output problems, maximal configurations, renaming. Main results in Lean (namespace Podc.BinaryLabeling). Safety-Liveness Exclusion in Distributed Computing — PODC 2015 Victor Bushkov, Rachid Guerraoui. Safety-Liveness Exclusion in Distributed Computing. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767401. Formalized version: the authors' full version with proofs (EPFL Infoscience record 207929, 19 pages); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 4.4 (when a weakest excluded liveness property exists) and Lemma 4.8 are correct, and Theorem 4.9 ("a strongest non-excluded liveness property must be Lmax") holds, with a locally repaired proof, if processes take steps only while they execute an operation. That is the convention of the paper's prose, but its formal I/O-automaton model does not impose it, and there the theorem is false even with Lmax = wait-freedom. The (l,k)-freedom theorems of §5 follow from the cited (im)possibility results once "progress" for TM is read as the authors' earlier work defines it; those cited results, the TM model and Lemma 5.4 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 §3.2 (the order on liveness properties) The claim "L₁ is weaker than L₂ iff L₂ ⊆ L₁" is false: for reactive implementations, wait-freedom and wait-freedom plus the never-fair history inv₀ (with p₁ idle forever) are ensured by exactly the same implementations (weaker_iff_subset_false). Impact. All proofs of the paper use ⊆, and we formalize every result with ⊆. With the paper's semantic definition, strongest and weakest properties are determined only up to equivalence: "it should be Lmax" in Theorem 4.9 then holds only up to equivalence. 🔧 §5.1 (the remark on LF_l ∪ OF_k, also "a union" in the Introduction) "LF_l ∪ OF_k is the set of all executions that ensure (l,k)-freedom" is false: only ⊆ holds (lkFree_imp_lf_or_of), because two correct processes, one of them stepping and progressing alone, give an execution that is 2-obstruction-free but not (2,2)-free (lf_union_of_not_iff). Impact. The remark is not used: all results rest on Definition 5.1. ✏️ Slips Theorem 4.9, implied assumption: in the paper's I/O-automaton model, which lets a process take steps while it executes no operation, Theorem 4.9 is false even for Lmax = wait-freedom: for two processes, a safety property S meeting all the paper's assumptions has a strongest non-excluded liveness property strictly weaker than wait-freedom (theorem_4_9_false_waitFree). §2 describes processes as running their algorithm when invoked, and every implementation in the paper does so. For such reactive implementations Theorem 4.9 holds (theorem_4_9), and Corollaries 4.10–4.11 follow from the cited impossibilities (corollary_4_10). Whether this is an implied assumption is a borderline call; see the details below and differencies.md. Theorem 4.9, proof: it ignores the case where every process crashed in h, in which there is no correct pending process to answer. Such a history has no well-formed extension, so the assumption on Lmax puts it into Lmax (core_subset_Lmax). Theorem 4.9 with no invocations: the empty history is then fair for every reactive implementation, so an Lmax omitting it makes the theorem fail. We assume [Nonempty Inv]. Definition 5.1 and Theorem 5.3: read literally, Definition 5.1 makes Theorem 5.3 false. If "good" responses are those that do not abort, a TM that aborts every commit request is opaque and (n,n)-free, and if they are commits, a correct process that never invokes tryC makes every (1,k)-freedom unimplementable (argued, not formalized). The intent can be recovered from §4 ("the set of 'good' events is restricted to commit events") and from the authors' [4], which exempts parasitic processes. With that reading, the cited results give Theorem 5.3. We formalize it from those results, taken as hypotheses (theorem_5_3). §4.1, example before Corollary 4.5: some histories listed in F₁ (e.g. propose₁(v) · v₁ · propose₂(v')) are never fair, because correct idle processes must keep invoking. For n ≥ 3, F₁ must also crash the other processes. The corollary is unaffected. §5.3: the second requirement of S says the transactions "should be aborted in h". This is not prefix-closed; "none of them commits" is meant. §2: input-enabledness is stated for every state at which pᵢ is "not pending". Read literally, this includes unreachable states and the crashed state, where nothing may be enabled. We require it along executions (see differencies.md). Details (Theorem 4.9 with idle steps). S contains every well-formed history except those in which p₀ receives a response after p₁ crashed before p₀'s first invocation without ever having invoked. S is prefix- and limit-closed, every invocation can be answered sequentially, and every history of S is a history of an implementation ensuring S, namely Is. The implementation Is has a single-writer register (counter, flag) written by p₁. p₁ increments the counter at every step, also while idle (a heartbeat), and sets the flag in each operation. On its first invocation p₀ reads the counter, then waits until the counter changes or the flag is set. Either event proves that p₁ was alive after p₀'s invocation, or had invoked. Later invocations of p₀ are answered at once. Two facts make the counterexample work: In every valid implementation ensuring S, the histories Y are fair (Y_subset_fairH). In these histories p₁ crashes, possibly after invoking, p₀ invokes and waits forever, and nobody responds. The reason: if the inputs of Y are applied without internal steps, the state is the one reached after crash₁ · inv₀, because p₁'s inputs touch only p₁'s local state and the crash erases it. From that state S forbids any answer to p₀. Every other fair history of Is is wait-free (Is_fairH_subset). So WaitFree ∪ Y is the strongest non-excluded liveness property (isStrongestNonExcl_waitFree_Y), and it is not wait-freedom. The proof breaks at its claim "because A_I' is input-enabled, every history h' with a single response and h'|pᵢ = invᵢ · resᵢ is a history of A_I'". This needs the other processes' invocations and crashes to commute with pᵢ's run. That fails as soon as pᵢ waits for an idle process. Is is valid but not reactive (Is_not_reactive). Repair (Theorem 4.9). We assume that processes take no step while idle, and repair the proof (see Proof gaps). theorem_4_9 holds for every class of reactive valid implementations that contains the two trivial implementations of the paper's proof. One example is the reactive implementations from registers. The hypotheses can be met (nonvacuous_4_9). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4.9 (proof, reactive implementations) The proof derives invₗ · resₗ ∈ S from h · resₗ ∈ S, which does not follow. Impact. Statement true for reactive implementations; repaired (core_subset_Lmax, theorem_4_9). Details. For consensus, propose₂(1) · propose₁(0) · decide₁(1) satisfies agreement and validity, but propose₁(0) · decide₁(1) violates validity. The paper's second and third steps pick the response resₗ in opposite orders. Repair. We use the characterization Setting.isStrongestNonExcl_iff: a strongest non-excluded property is Lmax ∪ core, where the core is the set of histories fair for every implementation ensuring S. It then suffices to show core ⊆ Lmax. Take a core history h. The silent implementation ensures S, so h has no response, and every process is pending or crashed at its end. If all processes crashed, h has no well-formed extension, so the assumption on Lmax puts h into Lmax. Otherwise take a pending correct p_l and its invocation x. First choose r with inv_l x · res_l r ∈ S (the paper's assumption on S), then an implementation I' ensuring S with this history. The one-shot responder that answers r ensures S: each of its histories is a history of I' by the frame lemma Run.frame, which uses reactivity. Yet h is not fair for the responder. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, n processes, crash failures (any number), deterministic adversary (scheduler and environment), no randomness. An implementation is the paper's composition A_{I₁} × … × A_{Iₙ} × A_B (Impl). Each process has a local state, or the crashed state. The base objects have a state. Invocations, responses and crashes touch only their process's local state. Internal steps of a process may access the base objects. A_B may have internal actions. Fairness is the paper's (§3.2), and fairH I is fair(A_I). Histories are finite or infinite sequences of inv/res/crash events. Well-formedness also forbids events after a crash. Valid implementations (Impl.Valid) have an initial state, produce only well-formed histories, and are input-enabled along executions. Reactive implementations (Impl.Reactive) take no step of a process that is not pending. Safety and liveness properties follow Definitions 3.1–3.2. The paper's assumptions on S and Lmax are SafetyAssumptions and LmaxAssumptions. The class of admissible implementations, e.g. "from registers", is a parameter 𝓒. Sections 3–4 are proved in an abstract setting (Abstract.lean) and instantiated in the model (setting). Section 5 works on what Definition 5.1 sees of a fair execution: the correct, infinitely-stepping and progressing processes. The cited (im)possibility results are hypotheses. Main results in Lean. The Complexity of Robust Atomic Storage — PODC 2011 Dan Dobre, Rachid Guerraoui, Matthias Majuntke, Neeraj Suri, Marko Vukolić. The Complexity of Robust Atomic Storage. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993816. Formalized version: the EPFL accepted version (infoscience record 208945, 10 pages, proofs included; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both lower bounds hold in the round model of [1] (see Model below): two-round reads are impossible when S ≤ 4t and R ≥ 4 (Proposition 1), and with three-round reads the write needs more than min {R, k} rounds when S ≤ 3t + ⌊t/t_k⌋ (Lemma 1, Lemma 2, Proposition 2; Ω(log t) rounds at optimal resilience). The run constructions of Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 are correct, and the one gap, in the step to Lemma 2 and Proposition 2, where scaling the blocks by c = t/t_k works only when t_k divides t, is closed by changing the block sizes. The matching upper bounds of §5, and so the optimality of four read rounds, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 2: "solving for k" derives t ≥ t_k ⇒ k ≤ ⌊log ⌈(3t+1)/2⌉⌋, while the proof needs the converse; both directions hold (tseq_le_iff). §4, proof of Lemma 1: "the state of {B_l, C_l} at the end of Δpr_1" should be Δpr_l. Typos §3, general step of Proposition 1: the index expressions (σ_{((j mod 4)/j)(k−i−1)}, footnote 3) are hard to parse; Fig. 1 gives the intended runs. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Proposition 2 and Lemma 2 (scaling Lemma 1 to t ≥ t_k) "By carefully choosing c = t/t_k" (Proposition 2), and "this is valid even with R ≥ k readers and t ≥ t_k faults" (Lemma 2): multiplying the blocks of Lemma 1 by c needs an integer c, so the argument covers only t_k ∣ t. Impact. Statements true; repaired by another block-size assignment (exists_fits). Details. For t = c·t_k + d with 0 < d < t_k, uniform scaling by c = ⌊t/t_k⌋ gives 3c·t_k + c objects with c·t_k faults, fewer than the claimed 3t + c objects. Lemma 2 is the case S = 3t + 1, and it relies on the same step. Repair. The construction of Lemma 1 only needs upper bounds: every set of objects that is malicious in some run, or skipped by a terminated round, has at most t objects (Fits). The blocks B_k, C_k and B_{k+1} never lie in a common such set. So we take c times the paper's sizes, add d objects to each of these three blocks, and get 3t + c objects (exists_fits, write_lb_general, lemma2, proposition2). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing between one writer, readers Rd (R = card Rd) and objects Obj (S = card Obj). At most t objects are malicious; there is no authentication. Objects never communicate with each other or with clients other than by replies, and clients do not message each other. Clients are one-shot. Deterministic protocols (Proto): objects reply as a function of their log; writes take exactly K rounds and reads exactly N rounds. In each round a client sends to all objects, which process a client's round messages in FIFO order. The round may terminate once S − t objects replied, and the scheduler decides when. This is the round model of [1]. The paper's own Definition 1 is more restrictive for the adversary: a round may end without the reply of s_i only if s_i is faulty or faulty in some indistinguishable run. So the Lean theorems are formally weaker than the paper's (a protocol cannot wait for extra replies after spotting a faulty one). The paper's runs satisfy its condition: in a symbolic replay of all runs, every terminated round has a run with the same client view in which the skipped objects and all forgers so far are at most t. This check is not in Lean. A malicious object may overwrite its state at any time (forge), which is the Byzantine behaviour used in all proofs. Atomicity is the paper's §2.2 definition, for histories with one write. Proto.Atomic P t ⊥ quantifies over all runs and all malicious sets of size ≤ t. Restricting the runs (one-shot, forging-only Byzantine) only strengthens the impossibility results. Operations take a fixed number of rounds (K for writes, N for reads); adaptive round counts are not representable. Proposition 1 is proved for N = 2, Lemma 1/2 and Proposition 2 for N = 3; "at most N" follows by padding with no-op rounds, which is not formalized (writes: every fixed K up to the bound is covered). Proof method. Each construction is run with a protocol-independent label protocol whose messages are (instance, round) labels (Sim.lean, Label.lean). A label run is checked to be canonical: every terminated round sees its canonical transcript T (i, q). A canonical label run maps to a run of an arbitrary protocol with the same schedule (sim). So every read instance returns the same value in all runs, and the atomicity chain is short. The paper's runs were first replayed symbolically in Python (all k ≤ 8); this found no error in the constructions. Main results in Lean. The matching upper bounds of §5 (built from other papers' algorithms and transformations) and the secret-value model. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: Sanity.atomic_one_object exhibits an atomic protocol in the same model (one object, t = 0), so Proto.Atomic is satisfiable outside the theorems' ranges. Proposition 1 is proved for every S ≤ 4t directly, without the resilience bound S ≥ 3t + 1. Lemma 1 is proved also for k = 1, which the paper takes from [1].

Wait-Free Runtime Verification of Linearizability — PODC 2023 Armando Castañeda, Gilde Valeria Rodríguez. Asynchronous Wait-Free Runtime Verification and Enforcement of Linearizability. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594563. Formalized version: arXiv 2301.02638 v3 (Nov 2025, full version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All main results hold: the impossibility of runtime verification (Theorem 5.1), the impossibility of predictive runtime verification (Theorem A.1, under the black-box reading of the model), the predictive verifier for DRV and every O ∈ GenLin (Theorem 8.1) and self-enforced implementations (Theorem 8.2). Lemma 7.4 is false as stated: it fails for pending operations that no view has seen yet, and the proofs of Lemmas 8.1/8.2 routinely meet such operations, but their statements are still true once the comparison is made with a prefix, and we prove them that way. The progress and step-complexity claims were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 7.4 (tight execution vs. its sketch) Lemma 7.4 claims that every tight execution E is equivalent to its sketch X(λ_E), but this fails when a pending operation has written to N and no view has seen it yet, i.e. its N.Write comes after every N.Snapshot (lemma_7_4_false). Impact. The proofs of Lemmas 8.1 and 8.2 meet such operations routinely. The statements of Lemmas 8.1/8.2, and all main results, are true; we prove them with a prefix comparison. Details. Such an operation is missing from X(λ_E). Example: a process completes one operation, then invokes a second one and writes it to N. The proofs of Lemmas 8.1 and 8.2 apply Lemma 7.4 to executions in which such operations are normal: the execution F of Lemma 8.1, obtained by removing snapshot steps, and T(E'|A*) in Lemma 8.2. Repair. Compare with a prefix: truncate at the last relevant snapshot and use prefix closure. (Exec.sketch_mem_of_tight, Exec.cut_mem_of_sketch, sketch_isAStarHist) 🔧 Claim 7.2 (for all implementations) Claim 7.2 is stated for all implementations, but it fails for abstract ones (sets of histories). Impact. It holds for A*, the only implementation it is used for. ✏️ Slips Theorem 8.2 (2) needs O ≠ ∅. Theorem 8.2 (3) states the direction of similarity backwards. Proof of Lemma 7.3: "E and T(E) are equivalent" should be E' and T(E). Proof of Lemma 8.2: H should be a prefix of X(τ''). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 8.1 (order equality) The proof of Lemma 8.1 claims ≺_{F'} = ≺_{T(E')}, where only ⊆ holds. Impact. Statement true; only ⊆ is needed for similarity (Exec.sketch_mem_of_tight). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Histories. We use CSLib's single-object Herlihy–Wing histories. Linearizability is CSLib's amended definition (Sela–Herlihy–Petrank), which is the paper's Definition 4.2. Similarity (Def. 7.1) is defined literally (Obtain, Similar) and shown equivalent to a semantic form (similar_iff_simS). GenLin (Def. 7.2) means closed under prefixes and similarity. Impossibility. n ≥ 2 asynchronous processes run a verifier with the structure of Fig. 2. Lines 03–05 and 08–12 are atomic transitions on an arbitrary shared memory, so any base objects are allowed, of any consensus number. They may read a global clock. The environment chooses operations; each process chooses each operation at most once. The input A is an abstract implementation: a prefix-closed set of well-formed histories. It answers within this set. Executions are infinite and fair: each process runs infinitely many iterations. There are no crashes; wait-freedom is reflected in the atomic blocks. The verifier does not depend on A (black box). thm_5_1_nonuniform and trivialVerifier_predictive treat the other reading. Positive part. An execution of V_O (Fig. 10) running A* (Fig. 7) over a black-box A is given by: the operations each process invokes; A's responses, which must form a history of the prefix-closed set 𝒜; injective times of the 8 steps of each operation: A* invocation, N.Write, A invocation, A response, N.Snapshot, A* response, M.Write, M.Snapshot + test. Snapshots are atomic and return everything written before them. Executions of A* alone have 6 steps per operation. Histories of A*, of A, of the tight execution T(E) and of V_{O,A} are timed histories (TimedHist.lean); their list versions are obtained by sorting by time. The sketch X(τ) of Section 7.3.3 is the timed history XTH τ. Infinite executions (thm_8_1_inf). A process may block forever inside A. The two standing assumptions are hypotheses: a process that took its N.Snapshot also writes M; tests occur at arbitrarily late times. Reading of Section 3. Section 3 says the black-box requirement is "modeled as conceptually V_O taking A as its input". The intended reading is that one verifier works for every A (∃V ∀A), which is what we formalize. If V_O could depend on A, Definition 6.1 would be trivially solvable (Impossibility.trivialVerifier_predictive, a remark). Main results in Lean. A Combinatorial Topology Approach to Arrow's Theorem — PODC 2022 Sergio Rajsbaum, Armajac Raventós-Pujol. A Distributed Combinatorial Topology Approach to Arrow's Impossibility Theorem. PODC 2022, pp. 471–481. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538433. Formalized version: the PODC version; no arXiv version exists. For the proofs that the PODC version defers (Prop. 4.1, Thm. 4.2, Section 4.2) we used the full version, A Combinatorial Topology Approach to Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (MPRA 120023, 2024; Social Choice and Welfare, 2025). Numbering is the PODC one unless marked "full version". Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The topological proof of Arrow's theorem stands after small repairs: Arrow's theorem (Thm. 2.1), its topological form (Thm. 2.2), the index lemma, the orientability of N_I and the index-lemma proof of the base case are all correct. The promised characterization of domain restrictions does not hold as printed: Theorem 4.2 is false, and the corrected characterization of the full version (Theorem 6), which we verified, needs critical triples. The claim that every subdomain admits a non-dictatorial map, in Prop. 4.1 and Thm. 4.2, holds only for subdomains in which every pair of alternatives stays free. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, "moreover" sentences (subdomains) "Every domain contained in one of these maximal domains admits a non-dictatorial map" is false, e.g. for the one-profile domain {(ABC, ACB)}, where unanimity forces F(R) ∈ {ABC, ACB}, one voter's preference (prop41_moreover_false, thm42_moreover_false). Impact. A missing hypothesis: non-dictatoriality is not inherited by subdomains that lose a vertex of N_I. The sentence holds for subdomains in which every pair of alternatives stays free, and the rest of Prop. 4.1 is correct (prop41_moreover_of_pairFree, thm42_moreover_of_pairFree). 🛠️ Theorem 4.2 (domain restrictions, two critical profiles) Theorem 4.2 is false whenever the blue edges of the two removed critical profiles share a vertex, e.g. for R₁ = (BAC, ACB), R₂ = (CBA, ACB) every unanimous IIA map on N_I \ {R₁, R₂} is dictatorial (thm42_counterexample, thm42_not_admits_of_adjacent). Impact. Section 4's characterization needs a new statement; Arrow's theorem and its topological proof are unaffected. Details. The theorem considers n = 2, |X| = 3, and two critical profiles R₁ ∈ C₁, R₂ ∈ C₂ with different blue edges, and claims that N_I \ {R₁, R₂} admits a non-dictatorial unanimous IIA map. When the two blue edges share a vertex (12 of the 30 choices), the antiunanimity profile spanned by the two edges is still in the domain, and it forces dictatorship. In the explicit instance the remaining profile is (BCA, ACB). Repair. The statement is true for disjoint blue edges (critical pairs) (thm42_admits_of_disjoint, thm42_maximal).
