Formalized version: arXiv 2102.13242 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Every theorem we formalized holds: Theorem 14 (linearizable SWMR ⇒ write strongly-linearizable), Theorems 10/12/13 and Corollary 11 (Algorithm 2 is write strongly-linearizable but not strongly linearizable; Algorithm 4 is linearizable but not write strongly-linearizable), Theorem 6 (with merely linearizable registers a strong adversary keeps Algorithm 1 running forever) and Theorem 7 (if R1 is write strongly-linearizable, Algorithm 1 terminates with probability 1 — in fact at most one coin sequence defeats any given strong adversary). The proof of Theorem 14 (Lemma 67) is wrong; we prove the theorem with a different construction. The gaps in the proofs of Theorems 7, 10 and 12 are closed by local changes. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 17 says "line 37" for line 34; Claims 17.1/17.3 say "round 2" in the general case. Typos Algorithm 3 (Theorem 10) is ambiguous on ties: two pending writes can have equal partial timestamps (e.g. both [0, ∞, ∞]). Harmless — only "w_i last in B_i" is used; we order the rest by process id. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 14 (Lemma 67, Appendix E) Claim 67.1 wrongly asserts that an incomplete write that is not last in f(H) must be read by some read of H, so the construction f* of Lemma 67 fails (lemma67_construction_fails). Impact. Theorem 14 is true; we prove it with a different construction (swmr_writeStrongLin). Details. From an arbitrary linearization function f the paper builds f* by deleting the last operation of f(H) when it is an incomplete write. But the next operation may be a pending read, linearized with an added response (Definition 2 allows it). Counterexample, on the atomic SWMR register: in G the writer completes write 1 and invokes write 2, and a reader invokes a read; f(G) = write 1, write 2, read. In the extension H the read returns 1 and f(H) = write 1, read. Then f*(G) = f(G), f*(H) = f(H), and the writes write 1, write 2 of f*(G) are not a prefix of the writes write 1 of f*(H) (lemma67_construction_fails). The claim also tacitly assumes distinct written values. Repair. Take, for each history, a linearization with the fewest operations of the writer; restricting a linearization of an extension to the operations of the prefix shows this number is monotone, so the write sequences are prefixes of each other (swmr_writeStrongLin, for any set of SWMR histories — shared memory, message passing or hybrid). 🔧 Theorem 7 (Lemma 19 is too weak) Lemma 19 ("for each round j, with probability ≥ 1/2 nobody enters round j + 1") only bounds the probability of an infinite game by 1/2, not by 0. Impact. Theorem 7 is true, in a stronger form: at most one coin sequence defeats a given strong adversary (Thm7.forever_subsingleton, theorem7). Details. The proof does give the needed conditional statement (the adversary's order of the two round-j writes is fixed before the round-j coin is flipped). Repair. Against a fixed (deterministic) strong adversary, the round-j coin that lets the game go on is determined by the history before it is flipped, so at most one coin sequence keeps the game alive (Thm7.forever_subsingleton), which has probability 0 (theorem7). 🔧 Theorems 10 and 12 (Lemma 42, Case (b)) Lemma 42 Case (b) uses "r starts after w completes" where only "w writes Val[-] before r starts" is available. Impact. Statements true; the gap is filled (Alg2.alg2_writeStronglyLinearizable). Repair. Fixed via Lemma 40. Shared memory (Sections 4–6): CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl): n processes (Fin n), atomic base registers Val[i] (single-writer by the code), deterministic programs, one base-object access per step; wait-free, no failures needed. Write strong-linearizability is CSLib's strong linearizability restricted to a set of operations (Impl.IsStrongLinFunFor RWOp.isWrite): only the write subsequence must be prefix-monotone. Details. Lemma 1 says: in any solution in which low processes decide at once, a process i that becomes low at m with a single low value v, hidden capacity ≥ k − 1, and k hidden processes j_b that are high at m − 1 must decide v at m. In the counterexample i has input 2, two processes x, y have input 0, a process z crashes in round 1 sending nothing, and j₁, j₂ have input 2. All four hypotheses hold for i at time 1 with v = 0 (⟨z, 0⟩ and ⟨j₁, 1⟩ witness HC ≥ 1). The protocol: a low process decides its input at time 0; at time 1, a high process that missed a round-1 message and whose only low value is 0 decides its smallest high value, and every other process decides its minimum. It solves 2-set consensus for t = 1: whoever misses a message knows the unique faulty process, so 0 is held by correct processes and only one more value can be decided. Here i decides 2. The proof fails in the "changes": when j_{b'} (b' > b) has decided v, process j_b must get no message carrying v in round m. Time vs. Cost of Deterministic Rendezvous — PODC 2014 Avery Miller, Andrzej Pelc. Time versus cost tradeoffs for deterministic rendezvous in networks. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611473. Formalized version: arXiv 1508.02471 v1 (the only version; same text as the proceedings copy we have). Numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both main lower bounds hold (Theorem 3.1: cost E + o(E) forces time Ω(EL); Theorem 3.2: time O(E log L) forces cost Ω(E log L)), and so do Propositions 2.1 (Cheap) and 2.2 (Fast) as stated. The cost bound of Proposition 2.3 (FastWithRelabeling) needs a new constant, (8w+6)E, which keeps Corollary 2.1 (cost O(E), time O(L^{1/w}E)). The proof of Theorem 3.2 relies on the false Fact 3.11, and 10 sectors instead of 6 get around it. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Proposition 2.3 (FastWithRelabeling, cost 2·w(L)·E) The cost bound 2·w(L)·E is false: on the oriented 3-ring (E = 2) with L = 2, w ≡ 1 and simultaneous start at nodes 0 and 1, the agents first meet at time 4 with cost 6 > 2wE = 4 (prop_2_3_cost_false). Impact. The time bound (4t+5)E is true, and the correct cost bound (8w+6)E is still O(E) for constant w, so Corollary 2.1 survives, although its proof quotes the false 2cE (prop_2_3_cost_repaired, cor_2_1). Details. FastWithRelabeling runs Algorithm Fast on the new t-bit labels (here t = 2, labels 01 and 10). Its schedule starts with an exploration (T[1] = 1) and doubles every bit of M(ℓ'). With simultaneous start, both agents explore in segment 1 in lock-step, which in an oriented ring cannot produce a meeting. So 2E is spent before anything distinguishes the agents, and at least one more move is needed. The failure is not specific to w = 1: agents whose new labels share a leading 1 explore in lock-step for 5 segments (cost 10E > 4E for w = 2), and a simulation of the oriented 5-ring with simultaneous start gives worst-case cost 44 > 2wE for w = 2, 3 (E = 4). Repair. Each agent explores in at most 4w+3 segments, so the true bound is (8w+6)E (prop_2_3_cost_repaired, cor_2_1). ✏️ Slips The abstract, Section 1.3 and Section 3 say that simultaneous-start Cheap has "cost exactly E". Agents may finish earlier or meet before finishing, so it is "at most E", as Section 2 says (Upper.cheapSim_bounds). Facts 3.6–3.8 (proof of Theorem 3.1) need F > 3φ, which the paper leaves implicit in φ = o(E) (thm_3_1_explicit). Fact 3.7's index range is off by one: it is stated for i ≤ ⌊L/2⌋ - 1 but refers to α_{i+1} (LBCost.step). Proposition 2.2's proof mixes τ ≥ 1 with 0 ≤ τ ≤ E, an off-by-one in the round numbering (Upper.prop_2_2). Typos Proposition 2.2's proof says "i ∈ {2,…,m}" for "i ∈ {1,…,m}". Corollary 2.1 uses t' = c L^{1/c} as if it were an integer. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3.2 (Fact 3.11) Fact 3.11 is false: on the ring with n = 12, x moving +1,+1,+1,-1 from node 0 and y moving -1,-1,-1,+1 from node 6 have all partial surpluses ±1, yet both are at node 3 after round 3 (Fact311.fact_3_11_false). Impact. Fact 3.15 is not established as written; the rest of the proof of Theorem 3.2 stands with different constants (thm_3_2_core, thm_3_2). Details. The proof cuts the ring into 6 sectors of size n/6 and time into blocks of n/6 rounds, and it tracks the sector of each agent only at block boundaries. Fact 3.11 claims that partial surpluses of absolute value at most 1 keep x inside P_{j-1} ∪ P_j ∪ P_{j+1}. In mid-block, however, an agent at the end of P_{j+1} can step into P_{j+2} and return. In the counterexample Agg_x = (1,0) and Agg_y = (-1,0). The vectors come from a correct 2-label algorithm and survive trimming (Fact311.V_correct, Fact311.mx_ge_four). Fact 3.15 (distinct labels have distinct progress vectors) uses Fact 3.11 on every zero run. Repair. Blocks and sectors of size ⌊n/10⌋. Two agents with equal progress vectors then stay within distance < 5⌊n/10⌋ ≤ n/2 relative to their antipodal starts. This also removes the assumption 6 ∣ n. The rest of the argument is the paper's, with different constants. (thm_3_2_core, thm_3_2) 🔧 Theorem 3.2 (Fact 3.16, count of vectors) The count of {-1,0,1}-vectors with at most k non-zero entries forgets the factor 2^i for signs. Impact. Only constants change (thm_3_2_core). 🔧 Theorem 3.1 (Fact 3.1, witness) Fact 3.1's shifted start p'_B = p_A + forward(A) + 1 + back(B) uses B's solo extent instead of its extent during the execution. Impact. The fact itself is true (LBCost.back_le_phi). Details. With B's solo extent the segments can overlap around the ring; the extent within the execution works. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Upper bounds (Section 2, Segments.lean). Nodes form an arbitrary type V. EXPLORE is any walk that visits all nodes within E rounds from every start (Explore V E). The paper only uses this property; no graph or port structure is needed, so the bounds hold more generally. Synchronous rounds; one agent wakes at time 0 and the other δ ≥ 0 rounds later (adversarial). A sleeping agent waits at its start node and can be found there. Labels are distinct integers in [1, L]. The algorithms are deterministic segment schedules (Cheap, simultaneous-start Cheap, Fast, FastWithRelabeling). Time is the first meeting time, counted from the earlier wake-up. Cost is the number of moves of both agents before it. Lower bounds (Section 3, Ring.lean). The network is the oriented ring ZMod n with E = n - 1, and the agents start simultaneously. An algorithm is a behaviour vector V : Fin L → ℕ → {-1,0,1} per label, exactly as in the paper. This loses no generality: before meeting, an agent's observations (degree 2, entry port) are determined by its own moves. Meeting means the same node at the end of the same round. "Time" and "cost" are worst-case over distinct labels and distinct start nodes; m_x (procedure Trim) is mx. These restrictions only strengthen lower bounds, as in the paper. No randomness, no faults. Main results in Lean (namespace Podc.RendezvousTimeCost). The memory discussion of Section 1.2, the remarks about alternative wake-up models in the Conclusion, and the general reduction from port-labelled-graph agents to behaviour vectors. The paper states that reduction in one sentence; we take behaviour vectors as the model. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: Simultaneous-start Cheap in the ring is correct with cost ≤ E and time ≤ (L−1)E (RingCheap.thm_3_1_tight). So the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1 are satisfiable and its Ω(EL) is tight. Approximate Agreement on Trees and Block Graphs — PODC 2026 Marc Fuchs, Diana Ghinea, Zahra Parsaeian, Joel Rybicki. Round and Resilience-Optimal Approximate Agreement on Trees and Block Graphs. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815967. Formalized version: arXiv 2502.05591 v5; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The reductions are correct: AA on trees reduces to real-valued AA plus gradecast (Theorems 3 and 5), and AA on block graphs reduces to AA on trees (Theorem 8); we proved them in the synchronous lock-step model with the black boxes as hypotheses. The resilience c ∈ [1/3, 1/2) with signatures rests on a refuted protocol (Theorem 7), and the block-graph round bound R_TreeAA(4·D(G)) on the unproved Lemma 15; both are unestablished, not refuted. The cited real-valued AA protocols and Fekete's lower bound construction were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 7 (authenticated RealAA, t = c·n, c ∈ [1/3, 1/2)) For small D/ε the protocol RealAA^PKI of Theorem 7's proof runs Theorem 10 (Theorem 3.1 of [25], PODC 2022), which is false for t ≥ n/3, so it fails already for n = 3, t = 1, D = 1, ε = 1/2 (AA.theorem_3_1_sync_false). Impact. Theorem 7 is unestablished, not refuted: its statement (existence of some protocol) is probably still true. Corollaries 3 and 5 depend on Theorem 7; our reductions use RealAA as a black box and are unaffected. Not formalized. Details. For constant D/ε the proof uses Theorem 10, i.e. Theorem 3.1 of [25] with t_a = 0. That theorem is false in synchronous networks when n ≤ 3t. This project's formalization of [25] has a run with n = 3, t = 1, t_a = 0 in which the honest values stay at 0 and 1 forever (Papers/PODC2022/HybridApproxAgreement/, AA.theorem_3_1_sync_false). With n = 3, t = 1 (c = 1/3), D = 1, ε = 1/2 the test log₂((1−2c)/c) + log₂log₂(D/ε) > 0 fails, so RealAA^PKI runs exactly that broken protocol and the honest outputs 0 and 1 are not ε-close. Repair. Proposed, not proved in Lean: run the Proxcensus-based RealAA₁^PKI for a constant number R of iterations with (c′R)^R ≥ D/ε. ❌ Lemma 15 (D(T) ≤ 2·D(G) for a minimum-diameter clique tree) The proof says that if a longest path passes ≥ 4 consecutive cliques sharing a vertex, then "replacing them by a star strictly decreases the diameter", but another longest path may survive the change. Impact. The lemma is unestablished, not refuted, and not formalized. Theorem 8's bound R_TreeAA(4·D(G)) and Corollaries 4 and 5 rest on it; we state Theorem 8 with the round bound of the tree protocol on T_S and prove D(T_S) ≤ 2·D(T). Details. Counterexample to this step: the path x₀ … x₆ with two pendant vertices at x₃. Exhaustive enumeration (scripts/lemma15_check.py) finds minimum-diameter clique trees (diameter 5) whose longest path has the separators x₁, x₂, x₃, x₃, x₃. The final counting is also off by one, and |P_G| ≤ D(G) is justified only by "P_G is a path" (it holds because such a path is a shortest path in a block graph). Repair. Sketch, not proved in Lean: the statement is believed true; compare with the clique tree in which the cliques at each cut vertex form a star. ✏️ Slips Theorem 2's round bound: for 1 < D/ε < 2 the bound 7 log₂δ / log₂log₂δ + 3 is below 3 rounds, i.e. below one iteration, and at D/ε = 2 it divides by zero (theorem2_bound_degenerate). The arithmetic is correct for D/ε > 2 (theorem2). Theorem 8's bound silently assumes R_TreeAA is monotone; blockGraphAA_solves is stated with the rounds on T_S, which avoids this. §4.1 says "the k := D(P) vertices of P", but there are D(P)+1. The proof of Lemma 6 claims k_max ≤ D, but in fact k_max ≤ D+1; the inputs are still D-close. The proof of Theorem 3 writes R_RealAA(|V(T)|,1) where the statement has 2·|V(T)|. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 13, Case 3 (validity on block graphs) For a clique output c that does not contain the party's input v_in, the proof says the output (the vertex of c closest to v_in) is the separator between c and its neighbour towards the honest clique c_b, but it is the separator towards the party's own clique. Impact. The case as argued picks the wrong separator; validity on block graphs still holds (blockOut_spec). Details. Example: the path x₀–x₁–x₂–x₃ with cliques {x₀x₁}, {x₁x₂}, {x₂x₃}. Take honest inputs x₀ (this party) and x₃, and the tree output {x₁x₂}. The party outputs x₁, while the separator towards {x₂x₃} is x₂. Repair. By the tripod property of trees, c lies between the own clique and one of the two honest cliques, and Lemma 12 puts the correct separator on a shortest path. (blockOut_spec) 🔧 Lemma 12 (Appendix D, clique-tree edge separator) The proof assumes the first clique of the walk lies on c's side, and asserts without justification that some walk vertex lies in both cliques of the crossing edge. Impact. Both steps are closed in a few lines (sep_mem_support, sep_btw). Repair. Our proof is an induction along the walk with the invariant "every clique containing the current vertex is on c's side". (sep_mem_support, sep_btw) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Proof remarks. The proofs of Lemma 3 (Euler tour) and Theorem 3 are sketchy but correct. Properties 3–4 of Lemma 3 are argued informally; Theorem 3's validity step k* ∈ [i_min, i_max] needs the unstated remark that the short-path party's own projection index is at most k*. Lemma 3.1 does not need |V(T)| > 1. (subtree_iff_indices, exists_median_between, treeAA0_spec) Model. CSLib's synchronous lock-step Byzantine model (Cslib.Byzantine.LockStep) on the complete network, with n = |P| parties. Protocols are deterministic and history-based, and channels are reliable. A static adversary corrupts at most t parties (atMost t) and sends arbitrary messages; this covers rushing. The paper allows adaptive corruption. Our reductions never use static-ness, but adaptivity is not modelled. Ideal signatures are the abstract CSLib tokens (Auth), and every theorem holds for arbitrary token structures. This covers both of the paper's settings: t < n/3 unauthenticated (Auth.none), and t < n/2 with PKI. Black boxes are hypotheses on lock-step protocols. SolvesAuthWithin … pre spec R means: the spec holds and all honest parties decide within R rounds, in every admissible run whose inputs satisfy pre. Gradecast (Def. 4): one protocol per sender, run in parallel. Gradecast snd is the shared Problem.Gradecast (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/Specs.lean) with grades Fin 3; gradecast_iff unfolds it. RealAA (Def. 1, ε = 1): the shared Problem.ApproxAgreement (termination, range validity, ε-agreement; realAA_iff unfolds it), only required for D-close inputs (pre = Close D), matching R_RealAA(D, ε). Sequential composition ("wait until round R ends") is Protocol.seq in Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/LockStep/Sequential.lean. Phase 2 starts at round R for everybody. Graphs are Mathlib SimpleGraphs. The hull ⟨S⟩ is the union of all shortest paths between vertices of S (hull, via Btw a w b := d(a,w)+d(w,b) = d(a,b)). A block graph is a graph whose distinct maximal cliques share at most one vertex, given together with a clique tree (IsCliqueTree); chordality is the existence of the clique tree, as in the paper. The root v_start is an arbitrary fixed vertex. Main results in Lean. Improved Tradeoffs for Leader Election — PODC 2023 Shay Kutten, Peter Robinson, Ming Ming Tan, Xianbin Zhu. Improved Tradeoffs for Leader Election. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594576. Formalized version: arXiv 2301.08235v4. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The tradeoff Ω(log n/(log f(n)+1)) of the abstract, Theorem 3.11 (Ω(n log n) messages for time-bounded algorithms, with explicit bound (n/2) log₂ n) and the algorithms of Theorems 3.10 and 3.15 (with explicit constants) hold after local changes. Theorem 3.8 is one round too strong, and its k-round message bound is only proved as Ω(n^{1+1/k}). The Las Vegas, adversarial wake-up and asynchronous results were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 3.8 (the + 1 and the "consequently" clause on k-round algorithms) Theorem 3.8 is off by one round: with f(n) = n, the one-round algorithm in which every node sends its ID to everybody and the maximum ID wins sends n(n − 1) ≤ n·f(n) messages, but the claimed bound T(n) > (log₂ n − 1)/(log₂ f(n) + 1) + 1 exceeds 1 for every power of two n ≥ 2 (theorem_3_8_as_stated_false). Impact. The proof gives the bound without the + 1 (theorem_3_8_corrected). Only the one-round case is refuted; for T ≥ 2 the stated bound is unproved. The claim that k-round algorithms need Ω((n/2)^{1+1/(k−1)}) messages rests on the false bound and is unestablished, not refuted: whether the stronger exponent holds is open. The corrected bound only gives Ω(n^{1+1/k}) (rounds_messages_tradeoff). That bound (e.g. Ω(n^{3/2}) instead of Ω(n²) for 2 rounds) still improves polynomially on Afek–Gafni, but no longer matches the O(n^{3/2}) 3-round algorithm of Theorem 3.10. Details. The paper claims: at most n·f(n) messages imply T(n) > (log₂ n − 1)/(log₂ f(n) + 1) + 1. The broadcast algorithm runs in T = 1 round, for every ID universe, while with f(n) = n the claimed bound is (log₂ n − 1)/(log₂ n + 1) + 1 > 1. The cause is an index slip. The communication graph G_r only contains messages of rounds < r, but the proof applies Lemma 3.9 with r = T, so the messages of the last round are never accounted for. The induction step of Lemma 3.9 also builds G_{r+1} from the messages "sent during round r+1". Repair. Running the induction one round further gives the corrected bound T > (log₂ n − 1)/(⌈log₂ f⌉ + 1), in fact log₂ n ≤ (⌈log₂ f⌉ + 1)·T. (theorem_3_8_corrected) 🔧 Theorem 3.8 (log₂ f vs. ⌈log₂ f⌉) Theorem 3.8 is stated with log₂ f(n), but the proof uses blocks of size 2^{(⌈log₂ f⌉+1)(r−1)}, and its last inequality, 2^{σ_T} ≤ 2^{(log₂ f + 1)(T − 1)}, goes the wrong way when f is not a power of two. Impact. The printed form is unproved, not refuted, when f is not a power of two; the tradeoff Ω(log n/(log f + 1)) is unaffected. Repair. We prove the version with ⌈log₂ f⌉. (theorem_3_8_corrected) 🔧 Definition 3.5, Lemma 3.6, Corollary 3.7 (terminating components) Definition 3.5 ("in every restricted prefix E ∈ Exec_r(X) all nodes of X have terminated") holds vacuously when Exec_r(X) is empty, so Lemma 3.6 fails already for n = 2 with three singletons, and so does Corollary 3.7 (lemma_3_6_literal_false). Impact. The definition must be read existentially. The proof of Lemma 3.6 uses that reading, under which both results hold and suffice for Theorems 3.8 and 3.11 (not_disjoint_isolable, exists_universe_no_isolable_pow). Details. The full definition reads "X forms terminating components if, for some r, in every restricted prefix E ∈ Exec_r(X) all nodes of X have terminated". Exec_r(X) is empty when some node of X must send on more than |X| − 1 ports. For the broadcast algorithm every set of fewer than n IDs is then "terminating". Lemma 3.6 claims at most n/2^ℓ disjoint terminating 2^ℓ-sets. The proof of Lemma 3.6 actually uses the existential reading: some isolated execution of X exists. 🔧 Algorithm 1 (Theorem 3.15, nodes must stop) Algorithm 1 must stop nodes after they select a leader; otherwise later ID blocks keep broadcasting and the message bound fails. Impact. A missing case in the pseudocode; with it the result holds, with explicit constants (SmallIds.electsBy, SmallIds.terminatesBy, SmallIds.msgBound). Details. The assumption d ≤ n is not needed. 🔧 Lemma 3.14 (quantifiers) "Every execution prefix in Exec_{r_i}(I)" is stronger than what the construction provides, since the round r_I depends on the chosen execution. Impact. One adversarial execution per set suffices for Lemma 3.13 (level_step). ✏️ Slips Algorithm 1 for n = 1: the rule "select when receiving messages" never fires (SmallIds.electsBy). Theorems 3.11 and 3.13 drop the n log₂ n IDs that Corollary 3.7 removes: Lemma 3.14 needs n T'^{log₂ n − 1} + n log₂ n IDs for the single-send algorithm, whose time is T' = nT (Lemma 3.12). We prove Theorem 3.11 with n log₂ n + n^{log₂ n} T^{log₂ n − 1} IDs (theorem_3_11). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.14 (merging) The merging step wires the two clusters by independent maps g, h, so a node can receive two new links and keep capacity 2^i − 2, not the claimed |D|/2 − 1. Impact. Property (a) does not follow from the printed construction; the lemma holds with a different wiring (merge). Details. The ports opened by C are wired into C' by an arbitrary one-to-one map g, and those opened by C' into C by an independent h. Repair. Wiring along one perfect matching C ↔ C'. (merge) 🔧 Lemma 3.14 (counting) "U_i contains many pairwise disjoint sets" is not preserved by |U_i'| ≥ |U_i|/T. Impact. Property (c) does not follow as printed (level_step). Repair. The pigeonhole must be applied to a disjoint subfamily. (level_step) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Proof remarks. Theorem 3.10: up to n^{1/(k−1)} survivors can remain after the last two-round iteration, and the final all-to-all round selects the maximum; its cost is within the claimed bound. The referee counts ⌈n^{i/(k−1)}⌉ can exceed n − 1 for small n, so the algorithm caps them. Lemma 3.14, absorbing phase: how the first |C|/2 − 1 new ports are kept inside C is left implicit; we track capacity per node (absorb). Model. (Model.lean) Synchronous clique of n = m + 1 nodes, KT0: a node initially knows only its ID and n. Each node has m ports, and the adversary chooses the port mapping (IsPortMap: per node a bijection of ports onto the other nodes). Nodes are identified with their IDs, and the ID assignment I is an n-subset of the ID universe U. Deterministic algorithms (Algorithm m): the initial state depends on the own ID; in each round a node sends at most one message per port, computed from its state; LOCAL (unbounded messages); simultaneous wake-up. Executions are also defined for partial port mappings (run, Valid). These are the paper's restricted execution prefixes. Any compatible full port mapping yields the same prefix (run_eq_of_extends), which formalizes the adversary wiring unused ports adaptively (augment). Lower bounds assume only ElectsBy A U T: in every execution, after round T exactly one node outputs "leader". Uncoordinated Beeps — PODC 2020 Fabien Dufoulon, Janna Burman, Joffroy Beauquier. Can Uncoordinated Beeps tell Stories? PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405699. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (there is no arXiv version). The extended version [7], which contains the omitted proof of Theorem 1, was not used. Numbering follows the proceedings. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. The coding-theory core of the paper (Section 3) holds: Definitions 2 and 3 of uncoordinated superimposed (USI) codes are equivalent (Theorem 1), a USI(h,k)-code decodes every uncoordinated transmission scenario with conflict at most k (Theorem 2), and Sidon sets give USI(h,k)-codes of length at most 8h²(k+1)² (Theorems 3, 5, 7, Lemma 6, Corollary 8). What needs correcting is a typo in Lemma 4, the wording of Definition 4 and degenerate cases. The beeping simulation of Sections 4–6, which carries the paper's algorithmic claims (2-hop beeps, 2-hop desynchronization, message passing), was not formalized, so this verdict does not cover it. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 4 takes differences "mod l" and is false as stated: D = {0, 1, 3} is a (4, 3) Sidon set, yet 1 ≡ 1 − 0 ≡ 0 − 3 (mod 4) comes from two different pairs (lemma_4_mod_false'). This works even if a pair and its reverse count once. The sets of the paper's own Theorem 3 fail too, for ordered pairs: for p = K = 3 the Erdős–Turán set is D = {0, 7, 13}, a (14, 3) Sidon set since 14 ≤ 2p², and 7 − 0 ≡ 0 − 7 (mod 14) (lemma_4_mod_false). The lemma itself ends "i.e., D is a Golomb ruler", and the proof ignores the "mod l" and proves the integer statement (non-zero integer differences are distinct), which is all Lemma 6 needs. We prove that version (lemma_4). Definition 4's "all pairwise sums of elements in D are different" must include the sums d + d: under the weaker reading D = {0,1,2} is a Sidon set, but its codeword 111 overlaps its own shift by 1 in two positions, and Lemmas 4 and 6 fail (lemma_6_needs_strong_sidon). The results stand, because the Erdős–Turán sets satisfy the strong reading, which we use. Lemma 6 needs t ≠ t'. The surrounding text says "two" shifted words, so this is clearly intended. (lemma_6) Theorem 1 needs codeword length l ≥ 1. For l = 0 no shift is admissible, so Definition 2 holds vacuously while Definition 3 fails. (theorem_1_length_zero) Theorems 5 and 7 need K ≥ 1. Otherwise "USI(1, K−1)" is meaningless. Corollary 8 uses Theorem 3, which needs an odd prime in [K, 2K]. For K = h(k+1) = 1 none exists. This case is trivial (D = {0}). Theorem 10's last step, f(Δ_up² + Δ_up + 2) ≤ f(Δ_up+1)², needs Δ_up ≥ 1 (arithmetic check only; Section 4 is not formalized). Footnote 4 ("σ̄(c,t₁) ≠ σ̄(c,t₂) iff t₁ ≠ t₂") fails for the all-zero codeword. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Binary words of length n are Fin n → Bool, with 0-based positions (paper position i is our i−1). Shifted words σ(x,t), extended shifted words σ̄(x,t) of length 3l−2, and superpositions (bitwise OR over a Finset) are defined literally. A "set of codeword–shift pairs" is a Finset (Word l × ℤ), compared as pairs. Theorem 2 uses an uncoordinated transmission scenario (Scenario). The model is the beeping model with uncoordinated starts on a static graph G with finitely many nodes, global rounds in ℤ, and a wake-up round wake v per node. Local round r_v ≥ 1 is global round wake v + r_v − 1. Each node starts a finite set of codeword transmissions (codeword, global start round), each at or after its wake-up. A node beeps in a round iff one of its transmissions has a 1 there, so concurrent schemes are OR-ed. H_v records whether v or a neighbour beeped. The conflict at (v, r) is the number of distinct (codeword, start) pairs started in N(v) within l−1 rounds of r, as in the paper's proof. The theorem is quantified over all graphs, wake-up patterns and transmission sets. It does not need the hypothesis r_v ≥ 1. Sidon sets are Finset ℕ with the strong Sidon property (sums d + d included). Main results in Lean (namespace Podc.UncoordinatedBeeps). Section 4 (BEEP2H/LISTEN2H, Algorithms 1–3, Lemma 9, Theorem 10, Lemma 11, Theorem 12), Section 5 (2-hop desynchronization, probabilistic) and Section 6 (local message broadcast). Open remark on Algorithm 3, a suspicion and not a confirmed error; it was not checked in Lean or against Lemma 11 in depth. Algorithm 3 tests history windows H[r−l−(i−1), r−1−(i−1)], which can start at local index ≤ 0, before the node's wake-up. The paper does not define these bits, and Lemma 11 does not cover such windows. Suppose the missing bits read as 0 and c₁[1] = 0, which Theorem 7 allows because it fixes no partition. Then a node u that wakes one round after a neighbour w started c₁ would "decode" that c₁ and relay it. A neighbour v of u would then record a 2-hop beep of w in a round when the path v–u–w was not yet awake, contradicting Definition 5 and Remark 2. Either of two local fixes would close the gap: choose c₁ to contain the position of the Sidon element 0, or decode only windows that lie inside the awake period. Theorem 10's base case ("no node starts transmitting c₂ in rounds 1 to l") suggests that windows outside the awake period are not meant to be decoded. Trust. No sorry. State Complexity of Population Protocols — PODC 2021 Philipp Czerner, Javier Esparza (arXiv v3 adds Jérôme Leroux). Lower Bounds on the State Complexity of Population Protocols. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467912. Formalized version: arXiv 2102.11619 v3 (July 2022); numbering follows it. v3 has the double-exponential bound for leaderless protocols (Ω(log log η)). The PODC version (= arXiv v2) claims only a triple-exponential bound and proves it differently (rejection certificates). That proof is not formalized. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both lower bounds stand: Theorem 5.9 gives η ≤ 2^((2n+2)!) and BB(n) ≤ 2^((2n+2)!) for leaderless protocols, and Theorem 4.5 gives η < F_{ℓ,ϑ}(n) for protocols with ℓ leaders. Local changes save them: BB_L must fix the number of leaders, Lemma 5.8's hypothesis must be strict, and the proofs of Theorem 4.5, §5.3 and Corollary 5.7 need repairs that leave the final bounds unchanged. That the bound with leaders is non-elementary was not checked: it rests on the cited Lemma 4.4 at level F_ω, and we prove only that some admissible F exists. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Definition 1 (BB_L does not fix the number of leaders) Read literally, BB_L(4) does not exist: a 4-state protocol with η leaders decides x ≥ η for every η (not_bddAbove_BBLSet, majority4_computesGe). Impact. Evident intent: a fixed number ℓ of leaders, as in Theorem 4.5, whose bound F_{ℓ,ϑ}(n) depends on ℓ. With that reading the claims about protocols with leaders hold and follow from Theorem 4.5 (theorem_4_5_ctrlChainBound). Details. Definition 1 defines BB_L(n) as the largest η such that some protocol with at most n states and any leader multiset computes x ≥ η. Take states A, B, a, b with L = η·A and input state B. The transitions are AB ↦ ab, Ab ↦ Aa, Ba ↦ Bb, ab ↦ bb, and identity on the other pairs; B, b output 1. This protocol decides #B ≥ #A, i.e. x ≥ η. So with 4 states every threshold is computable, and literally read, "a bound on BB_L(n)" (§4), "the inverse of a non-elementary function for protocols with leaders" (abstract) and "Ω(α(η)) for protocols with leaders" (§6) are false. The intended reading (a fixed number of leaders, or leaders counted in the size) is also the one of the cited O(log log η) construction of Blondin et al. and of the follow-up by Leroux (PODC 2022, "with a fixed number of leaders"). 🔧 Lemma 5.8 (concentration hypothesis must be strict) Lemma 5.8's proof needs ξ·C(Q\S) < i, but its hypothesis "C is 1/ξ-concentrated in S" only gives ξ·C(Q\S) ≤ i, so the lemma as stated is unestablished, though not refuted (lemma_5_8 proves the strict version). Impact. Theorem 5.9 is unaffected: there the configuration is in fact 1/(ξ3^n)-concentrated, which gives the strict inequality. Details. With equality, the pigeonhole step "|J| > C(S)" fails. ✏️ Slips The proof of Lemma 5.8 swaps S and Q \ S: it writes C(S) where it means C(Q\S). The case "if x ∉ S take θ empty" should read "if x ∈ S, take j = 1, θ = 0, C' = x": an empty θ gives j = 0, which is useless for Lemma 5.2. P'_k in Example 2.1 has k+2 states, not k+1. Lemma 4.4 writes v_{g(n)} for v_{i_{g(n)}}. Typos Lemma 4.2's proof says "for every 2 ≤ i ≤ k". Theorem 4.5 states η < F but its proof ends with η ≤ i_k ≤ F; strictness is immediate from k < ℓ. The outline in §1 still says that Section 5 gives a triple exponential upper bound, a leftover of the PODC version; v3 proves a double exponential one. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4.5 (condition 2 of Lemma 4.1 never established) The proof applies Lemma 4.1 with D_b := C_ℓ − C_k, but never shows its condition 2, b·x →* D_b. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a variant of Lemma 4.1 (lemma_4_1', theorem_4_5). Details. The two configurations C_k ≤ C_ℓ lie in the same basis element B + ℕ^S. Lemma 4.2 only gives C_k + b·x →* C_ℓ, which is not the same thing: b input agents alone, without the leaders, need not reach D_b. Repair. A variant of Lemma 4.1 with condition 2 replaced by B + D_a + b·x →* B + D_a + D_b. Pumping still works, because C_k + λ b·x →* C_k + λ D_b by induction. (lemma_4_1', theorem_4_5) 🔧 Theorem 4.5 (indices when applying Lemma 4.4) The sequence of Lemma 4.2 starts at C_2 while Lemma 4.4 starts at v_0, so Lemma 4.4 cannot be applied with (ℓ, ϑ) as printed. Impact. One constant changes and the shape of the bound is untouched (theorem_4_5). Repair. Apply Lemma 4.4 with either δ = ℓ + 2 or a chain two elements longer; we use g = ϑ + 2. 🔧 §5.3 (unstated assumption that every state is coverable) The text says "Recall our assumption that for every state q there is an input i_q with IC(i_q) →* C_q ∋ q", but this assumption is never stated, and it is not WLOG for Lemma 5.1(ii) as used. Impact. Theorem 5.9 holds without the assumption (lemma_5_1_ii, lemma_5_3, lemma_5_4). Details. π may contain transitions whose pre-states are not coverable. Repair. We work with the set of coverable states (Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4) and strengthen Lemma 5.1(ii) to require saturation only on the pre-states of transitions in the support of π. In Theorem 5.9 these pre-states are coverable, because π is the Parikh vector of a real execution. (lemma_5_1_ii, lemma_5_3, lemma_5_4) 🔧 Corollary 5.7 (the wrong linear system for Lemma 5.8) Corollary 5.7 sets up "|Q|−1 equations on |T| variables", but Lemma 5.8 needs to decompose i and C together with π. Impact. The final bound of Theorem 5.9 is unchanged; we use the right system (with our own Pottier-type constant, see the Model). Details. The decomposition requires the |Q| inequalities Σ_t π(t)Δ_t(q) + [q = x]·i ≥ 0 on |T|+1 variables, which is also what the exponent of ξ = 2(2|T|+1)^{|Q|} suggests. We use that system. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Population protocols in the multiset (Petri-net) style of the Esparza group (Podc multiset model, Cslib.PopulationProtocol.Transition, MStep, MReach, FiresSeq, FlowEq). A Protocol Q has a transition relation T ⊆ Q²×Q² that is total on pairs, a leader multiset L, one input state x, and an output map O. IC(i) = L + i·x, and inputs satisfy i ≥ 2. The scheduler is the paper's fairness: if a configuration is reachable infinitely often, it is visited infinitely often. This is CSLib's Run.GloballyFair; no randomness. ComputesGe η says that every fair execution from IC(i), i ≥ 2, eventually has consensus output [η ≤ i]. computesGe_iff proves the paper's reachability characterization ("every reachable configuration can reach SC_{[η≤i]}"), and all later proofs use it. Cited results. Rackoff's bound is proved: g(n) ≤ 2^{2(2n+1)!} for covering sequences. Pottier's theorem is replaced by a proved, weaker Hilbert-basis bound (2M)^(2^e−1). This changes the intermediate constant ξ but not the final bound 2^((2n+2)!). Lemma 4.4 (Figueira et al.) is used as a hypothesis property CtrlChainProp. We prove that admissible functions exist (by compactness and Dickson's lemma), but not that they lie at level F_ω. Lemmas 4.1 and 5.2 get the extra hypothesis b ≥ 1. In the paper it is implicit: D_b is called a configuration, and configurations have at least two agents, so condition 2 already forces b ≥ 2. We work with arbitrary multisets, and then b = 0 must be excluded: with b = 0, D_b = 0, π = 0, all hypotheses hold for a = 2 and any stable configuration reachable from IC(2), viewed as the basis element (C, ∅), while η ≤ 2 fails for any protocol deciding x ≥ 3. Both applications in the paper have b ≥ 1. (lemma_4_1_b_zero_false, lemma_5_2_b_zero_false: counterexamples to the relaxed reading) Main results in Lean. Zigzag Causality — PODC 2017 Asa Dan, Rajit Manohar, Yoram Moses. On Using Time Without Clocks via Zigzag Causality. PODC 2017. DOI 10.1145/3087801.3087839. Formalized version: arXiv 1705.08627 v1 (extended version with the appendix); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Theorem 4, the "Visible Zigzag Theorem" (knowledge of a timed precedence ⇔ a σ-visible zigzag of sufficient weight), which the abstract presents as a main contribution, is false in its "only if" direction for general nodes, so the characterization of knowledge survives only in a weaker form. The "only if" direction does hold when one endpoint is a basic node of σ's past, which covers both coordination tasks (Early: θ₁ = σ; Late: θ₂ = σ), so the paper's characterization of optimal coordination (Protocol 2) keeps its basis. Theorems 1 and 2 (zigzag sufficiency and necessity), Theorem 3 for flooding full-information protocols and the "if" direction of Theorem 4 are proved; Protocols 1 and 2 themselves were not formalized. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 4 ("only if" direction, Visible Zigzag Theorem) In a 4-process flooding full-information system a node s knows θ₁ --0--> θ₂, yet every s-visible zigzag from θ₁ to θ₂ has weight ≤ −1 (Counterexample.theorem_4_false, Counterexample.theorem_4_counterexample). Impact. A false statement about the paper's main structural result. The "if" direction is correct, and necessity holds when one endpoint is a basic node of σ's past, which covers both coordination tasks of Protocol 2. Details. Take processes i, j, k, l with channels i→j, i→k, k→j, j→l. All lower bounds are 1; U_ij = U_jl = 2 and U_ik = U_kj = 1. Processes run a flooding full-information protocol (FFIP). Let s be an i-node that just received an external message, and set θ₁ = ⟨s, ijl⟩, θ₂ = ⟨s, ikjl⟩. s knows θ₁ --0--> θ₂. The chain i→k→j reaches j exactly 2 units after s. The direct message i→j arrives after 1 or 2 units. If both arrive at t+2 they arrive at the same j-node, so the two chains coincide from then on and θ₁ = θ₂. Otherwise θ₁ ≤ t+3 ≤ θ₂. No s-visible zigzag has weight ≥ 0. The past of s contains only i-nodes, since i has no incoming channel. The potential timer(ρ) + τ(q) on nodes ⟨ρ, q⟩, with τ(ij) = 2, τ(ik) = 1, τ(ikj) = 2, τ(ijl) = 4, τ(ikjl) = 3, is compatible with all bounds. It bounds every fork and every junction of such a zigzag, so its weight is at most τ(ikjl) − τ(ijl) = −1. The knowledge comes from a case split over runs (merge at j or a gap of at least 1), and neither case is visible to s. Where the proof breaks: Lemma 18.5, case (2). In the "fast run" the chain of θ₂ can merge with the chain of θ₀ = θ₁. The resulting time difference is the weight of a fork whose head is a node on θ₁'s chain. That node differs from θ₂ in the actual run r, so no zigzag in r ending at θ₂ results. Repair. Necessity holds when θ₁ or θ₂ is a basic node in the past of σ with positive time; the other endpoint can be any σ-recognized node. That is exactly the shape used in Protocol 2. Our proof builds a fast run as in Definition 24 and replaces the longest-path lemmas 10–16 by a maximum over visible zigzags, bounded with Theorem 1. (Sys.visible_zigzag_necessity_basic, Sys.visible_zigzag_necessity_early, Sys.visible_zigzag_necessity_late) ✏️ Slips Theorem 3 and Lemma 4 assume nothing about the protocol, but Theorem 3 is false for a full-information protocol that does not flood: there B learns of μ_go from the absence of a message, without a message chain from the go-node σ_C (CounterexampleFIP.theorem_3_false_for_FIP). The paper's standing FFIP assumption (Section 2.2) covers this hypothesis, and we prove Theorem 3 and Lemma 4 for FFIPs (Sys.thm3_late, Sys.thm3_early, Sys.lemma4). The proof uses Lemma 3 (needs full information), and the proof of Lemma 4 uses that a node outside the past still sends to every neighbour (flooding). The counterexample: D sends to C and B; C replies to B unless it has just received μ_go, in which case it sends "go" to A. The delays are exact, so the reply would reach B together with D's message. B performs b when it gets D's message without a reply. This implements Late⟨a --0--> b⟩. A run in which C receives an extra external message together with μ_go looks the same to B but does not contain σ_C, so K_σ(σ_C·A --0--> σ) fails. Lemma 12 is false as stated: a σ-recognized node with a longer path may itself lie in the past, before the boundary node. The lemma is only used for nodes outside the past, where it holds. (Not formalized: our proof replaces Lemmas 10–16.) Definition 3 says ⟨σ, p⟩ appears if σ appears and p is a path. That presupposes flooding and a non-initial σ, since initial nodes never send. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 4 (sender still initial) The induction step treats the r-node of the sender at time t_µ as if it sent the message in r, which fails when the sender is still initial at t_µ in r. Impact. Statement true for FFIPs; repaired (Sys.lemma4). Repair. An extra invariant: a process activated in the constructed run was already activated in r. 🔧 Lemma 18 (chain leaving the past) The proof assumes that the chain of θ₀ leaves past(r, σ) with its first message, and its case analysis misses deliveries inside the past. Impact. Repaired in the proof of the corrected Theorem 4 ("only if"). Repair. The zigzag starts with a fork rooted at the last past node of the chain, and from there the chain is delayed to its upper bounds. 🔧 Theorem 4 ("if" direction) The proof says "wt(Z) depends only on the pattern", but joinedness depends on the run. Impact. Statement true (Sys.visible_zigzag_sufficiency): we show joinedness is preserved for σ-visible zigzags. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Bounded communication model without clocks, as in Section 2. Time is ℕ. The network is a directed graph with bounds 1 ≤ L ≤ U per channel. Processes are deterministic and event-driven: they act only when something is delivered, and initial states never send. A local state is the initial state followed by the batches received: the internal messages (sender, content) and the external messages of each activation. Time is not recorded. At most one message per channel per activation. The environment (Sched) chooses the initial state in G₀, the delivery time of every message within [L, U], and the external deliveries (each external message at most once). Local states are computed from these choices, so every schedule satisfying the bounds is a run of R(P, γ). Full information means the message content determines the sender's local state. A flooding FFIP additionally sends to all out-neighbours at each activation. Concrete FFIPs exist; contents are encoded injectively into ℕ. Knowledge K_σ φ is truth in all runs in which the basic node σ appears (bridge to CSLib's IndistSystem.K: Sys.knows_iff_K). There are no failures and no randomness. Main results in Lean. Deterministic Lower Bound for Dynamic Balanced Graph Partitioning — PODC 2020 Maciej Pacut, Mahmoud Parham, Stefan Schmid. Brief Announcement: Deterministic Lower Bound for Dynamic Balanced Graph Partitioning. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405696. Formalized version: the 3-page brief announcement (no arXiv version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 2.1 (every deterministic online algorithm for the learning model is Ω(kℓ)-competitive, k ≥ 3, ℓ ≥ 2) holds, even with a slightly better constant: ((k-2)(ℓ-1)-2)/2 instead of ((k-2)(ℓ-1)-4)/2. The adversary in the paper does not work as written: it assumes that the algorithm always keeps the revealed ground sets together, and it gets stuck when the pivot is the one node of B's home cluster outside B, but two local additions repair it. Theorem 2.2 (PPL is O(kℓ)-competitive) and Lemma 3.1 have no proof in the paper and we prove both, while Theorem 3.2 (ALG3 is O(ℓ)-competitive) has no proof in the paper and is not formalized, so this verdict does not cover it. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips In the final count of the proof of Theorem 2.1, B contributes |B| - 1 = k - 2 to Σ(|C*| - 1), but the proof subtracts k - 1. This only weakens the bound, and the printed ratio follows (theorem_2_1_paper). Typos The proof of Theorem 2.1 stops at < ℓ + 3 isolated nodes, while < ℓ + 2 suffices, because B's home cluster has no isolated node. This only weakens the bound. The pigeonhole step needs only ℓ isolated nodes, not ℓ + 1. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2.1 (the algorithm is assumed to keep every ground set in one cluster) The proof says "Any competitive algorithm under the learning model maintains a perfect partition of ground sets", but a deterministic algorithm may split a revealed ground set, for example by moving a node of B away for a while, and nothing in the proof covers this. Impact. Statement true; repaired with repair requests (theorem_2_1). Repair. Whenever the algorithm's current configuration splits a ground set, the adversary requests a split pair, which costs the algorithm at least 1 (it pays for the request or migrates). The adversary moves on to the next pivot step only when all ground sets are back together. Between two such moments the algorithm migrates at least two nodes (LB.two_le_dist; this also covers an algorithm that moves B instead of the pivot). If the algorithm never puts the ground sets back together, the repair requests alone make its cost large enough. (theorem_2_1) 🔧 Theorem 2.1 (the pivot step is undefined when the pivot is z) If the pivot is z, the node of B's home cluster that is not in B, the required "ground set of the same origin residing in a different cluster" does not exist, and following the text the construction stops after O(1) swaps. Impact. Statement true; repaired by making z part of the first pair (LB.grow_shape). Details. The paper does not control z: during the requests inside B the algorithm may move z away, so x₀ ≠ z, and later choose z as a new pivot. Then the only other ground set with z's origin is B itself, and B is in the same cluster as z. Following the text literally, the adversary would request (z, b) with b ∈ B. That request is internal, and B ∪ {z} then fills the cluster, so no pivot is left. Repair. Make z part of the first pair {x₀, y₀}. In our adversary B is never requested before the first pivot step, so x₀ = z, and y₀ comes from another cluster. Every later pivot then has an origin other than B's home cluster. With k ≥ 3 it always has a partner of the same origin (LB.grow_shape). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Not a distributed model: online algorithms against an adaptive adversary. n nodes, ℓ clusters (Fin ℓ) of capacity k. A configuration V → Fin ℓ is balanced if every cluster has at most k nodes; with n = kℓ this means exactly k. There is no resource augmentation. Serving request (u, v) costs 1 if the configuration in which it is served separates u and v. Migration costs α ≥ 1 per moved node. Before serving a request the algorithm may repartition. A deterministic online algorithm (OnlineAlg) is a map from the requests revealed so far to a balanced configuration. Adaptivity of the adversary is automatic. OPT (optCost) is the minimum over all balanced offline schedules starting in the initial configuration. Learning model, finite form (IsLearningInput): the requests admit a perfect partition. Static form (IsStaticLearningInput, Section 2): an infinite sequence that admits a perfect partition, in which every communicating pair communicates infinitely often. The lower bound is proved in both forms. Theorem 2.2 needs the static form (see below). Lower-bound instance: nodes Fin ℓ × Fin k (cluster of origin, index), initial partition Prod.fst. A lower bound for one instance is a lower bound for the problem. Competitive ratio: the paper leaves the notion implicit. In the learning model every sensible algorithm has bounded total cost (PPL pays at most 2(n-1)α·n), so no lower bound is possible if the additive constant β may depend on α. Theorem 2.1 holds for strict competitiveness, or for β independent of α (letting α → ∞). We prove c ≥ ((k-2)(ℓ-1)-2)/2 - β/(4α) for every (c, β)-competitive algorithm with c ≥ 0 (theorem_2_1_competitive, theorem_2_1_omega). Main results in Lean. This brief announcement omits these proofs; we supply them. Theorem 2.2 (PPL is O(kℓ)-competitive), with ratio 2(kℓ-1) in the static learning model (theorem_2_2, theorem_2_2_kl). PPL never pays for a request. While D = dist(init, P*) for a perfect partition P*, every configuration PPL visits is within D of init. Each repartition merges two components, so there are at most n - 1 of them, and each costs at most 2αD. Any offline algorithm with finite cost ends in a perfect partition and pays at least αD. This uses "pairs communicate forever": on a finite sequence OPT may simply pay for the requests (one request: OPT = 1, PPL ≥ 2α). Section 2 makes "communicate forever" part of the model, so this does not contradict Theorem 2.2. Lemma 3.1 (k = 3: a repartition needs at most two swaps; K3.lemma_3_1, K3.lemma_3_1_closest). For clusters of size 3, if a balanced configuration respecting the merged components exists, one exists at distance at most 4 (two swaps). The hard case is when a and b are singletons sitting next to pairs. A counting argument then finds a cluster made of three singletons (K3.exists_triple). Not formalized. Theorem 3.2 (ALG3 is O(ℓ)-competitive for k = 3): the paper gives no proof and does not fully specify ALG3's phases. The matching Ω(ℓ) lower bound for k = 3 in the general model is theorem_2_1_general with k = 3. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: theorem_2_1_static builds static learning inputs, so the hypothesis of Theorem 2.2 is satisfiable. PPL is a concrete OnlineAlg (ppl). The model (Model.lean) is self-contained on top of Mathlib. The generic online-algorithm and cost definitions are a CSLib candidate.

Pareto-optimal (unbeatable) consensus — PODC 2013 Armando Castañeda, Yannai A. Gonczarowski, Yoram Moses. Brief announcement: Pareto optimal solutions to consensus and set consensus. PODC 2013, pp. 113–115. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv 1311.6902 v1, Good, Better, Best! — Unbeatable Protocols for Consensus and Set Consensus; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The main results hold: Opt0 is an unbeatable consensus protocol (Thm. 2), OptMaj is unbeatable for t > 0 (Thm. 3), Opt_min-k is unbeatable (Thm. 4), and U-Opt0 is an unbeatable uniform consensus protocol deciding by f + 1 / f + 2 (Thm. 5). Saving them takes a new inner induction for Lemma 15, the core of Theorem 5, and one added condition each for Lemma 10 (the core of the k-set part; the same lemma as Lemma 1 of the authors' PODC 2016 paper), Lemma 6 and Corollary 1 (HMW's P0opt is beatable, which needs t ≥ 2). The uniform k-set protocol U-PROT_min-k (Thm. 6) was not formalized, so this verdict does not cover it. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 10 (the core of the k-set part) Lemma 10 is false as stated: with n = 6, k = 2, t = 1, V = {0, 1, 2}, a 2-set consensus protocol in which low processes decide at once can make process 0 decide 2 at time 1 even though all five conditions hold for it with v = 0 (lemma10_false). Impact. Lemma 11 and Theorem 4 stand: the proof goes through with an extra hypothesis that holds wherever Lemma 10 is used (lemma11, theorem4). Details. This is Lemma 1 of the authors' PODC 2016 paper, with the same five conditions. The "changes" in the proof suppress messages carrying v to j_b, which may need more than t crashes. The counterexample and the repair are in UnbeatableSetConsensus. (lemma10_false, theorem4) Repair. Add the hypothesis "every process alive and low at m − 1 crashes in round m". (Podc.UnbeatableSetConsensus.lemma1) 🔧 Lemma 6 when d = t (missing hypothesis) Condition (b), "K_i(K_j ∃v held at m − 1) for at least t − d processes j", holds vacuously when i knows of d = t failures, even if v occurs nowhere, so Lemma 6 is false then (lemma6_literal_false). Impact. Recoverable from its proof: the proof sketch counts "processes knowing ∃0, including i itself", so it assumes K_i ∃v. We prove Lemma 6 with "K_i ∃v and ((a) or (b))" (lemma6). All uses in the paper are consistent with this version. Details. Example: n = 3, t = 1, all inputs 1, process 2 crashes in round 1 sending nothing. At time 1, process 0 knows of one failure, so (b) holds for v = 0, but K_0 ∃correct(0) is false. The remark on time t + 1 after the lemma repeats the error. (lemma6_literal_false; repaired: lemma6) 🔧 Corollary 1 ("P0opt of [HMW] is not unbeatable") for t ≤ 1 Corollary 1 holds only for t ≥ 2 (or n ≤ t + 1): for t ≤ 1 (and n ≥ 3), P0opt makes exactly the same decisions as Opt0, so it is unbeatable by Theorem 2 (p0opt_sameDecisions, p0opt_unbeatable). Impact. One condition on t saves it: the paper's own example ("one failure seen in each of the first two rounds") needs t ≥ 2. As a refutation of HMW's general claim, the corollary is correct (corollary1). Details. We read P0opt as the paper describes it: decide 0 on K_i ∃0; decide 1 after a round in which no new failure became known. (corollary1; for t ≤ 1: p0opt_sameDecisions, p0opt_unbeatable) ✏️ Slips Lemma 15, last case: "j fails at (r', m) before sending any messages" must mean that j's round-m + 1 message reaches only i, and "known by ⟨i, m⟩ to fail" should read ⟨i, m + 1⟩. Contribution 3 (§1) says "P0opt, which was claimed to be beatable is not unbeatable"; it should say "claimed to be unbeatable". Typos Two different results are numbered "Corollary 1" (§3 and Appendix C). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 15 (inner induction) The inner induction on |C_i \ Z_i| does not decrease in Case II: the new process j does not see ⟨k, m⟩ and may consider more processes possibly alive, so C_j can be larger than C_i. Impact. Statement true; proved with a different induction (lemma15_part1, lemma15_part2). Details. The induction hypothesis is also applied to j without checking that j knows ∃0 for the first time at m and does not know ∃correct(0) at m. The base case needs z ∈ C_i argued. The counting argument for Part 1 ("fewer Case II than Case I invocations") is not needed. Repair. We prove Lemma 15 by an induction on n − |Z_i|. Case II followed by Case I becomes one step x ~_i x' ~_j x'': in x'', k has received z's message, Z_i has grown by k, and the induction hypothesis is applied to i itself. The number of failures in these runs never exceeds F⟨i, m+1⟩ + 1 ≤ t. The base case becomes "⟨z, m⟩ hidden" (Case C). (lemma15_part1, lemma15_part2, ic, ic_caseII) 🔧 Theorem 2 (derivation in §3) Theorem 2's proof says a process deciding 1 must know never-known(∃0), but by Agreement this is only a precondition for correct deciders. Impact. Statement true (theorem2). Repair. The proof works by making i correct in the run that contains the hidden path (exists_run_of_hiddenPath). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous message passing, crash failures, at most t crashes. Theorem 5 and the uniform lemmas assume t < n, as in the paper's model. A run (adversary) is CSLib's SyncCrash.Run: inputs, crash round, and the set reached in the crashing round. The model, views and hidden nodes are those of the companion formalization Papers/PODC2016/UnbeatableSetConsensus (same authors, same model), which this folder imports. Full-information protocols: a protocol is a decision rule that depends only on the view (SameView, i.e. CSLib's FIIndist). A process decides at the first time its rule fires while it is alive. The companion's theorem1_lockStep shows that this covers all deterministic protocols (Coan). Consensus is nonuniform 1-set consensus with inputs {0, 1}. Uniform consensus requires that all deciders, faulty ones included, agree. Unbeatability (Def. 1): P solves the problem, and every solution Q with Q ⪰ P satisfies P ⪰ Q. Domination compares decision times per process and per adversary. Knowledge K_i φ (Def. 2) is truth in all admissible runs where i is alive at m with the same view. K_i ∃v is "v has been seen" (Lemma 1/KoP via decided_mem_vals). K_i(Maj = v) is characterized explicitly (knows_maj_iff). ∃correct(v) means "some correct process knows ∃v at time m". No randomness. Lemma 17, case F⟨i, m⟩ = t: it suffices that only z carries 0. The paper makes every hidden process at m − 1 carry it. Lemma 2: the proof needs P0 to decide at the first time K_i ∃0 holds, which is true because first knowledge happens by time f + 1 ≤ t + 1. Main results in Lean. Namespace Podc.ParetoOptimalConsensus. Beyond Alice and Bob: MaxIS inapproximability in CONGEST — PODC 2020 Yuval Efron, Ofer Grossman, Seri Khoury. Beyond Alice and Bob: Improved Inapproximability for Maximum Independent Set in CONGEST. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405702. Formalized version: arXiv 2003.07427 v2; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorems 1 and 2 hold, conditional on the Chakrabarti–Khot–Sun communication lower bound as in the paper, but the paper's proof miscounts the cut, which has Θ(log³ k) edges, not Θ(log² k), and so only gives Ω(n/log⁴ n) and Ω(n²/log⁴ n). Saving them takes a redesigned ingredient: a code over a constant-size alphabet in the same construction, which even improves the bounds to Ω(n/log² n) and Ω(n²/log² n) rounds. The t-party framework (Theorem 5, Corollary 1) and the combinatorial heart of the paper (Properties 1–3, Claims 1–7, Corollary 2, Lemmas 1–3) are correct. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Definition 5 reads w(I) ≥ OPT/γ; it should be w(I) ≥ γ·OPT (IsApprox). As written, no (1/2+ε)-approximation could exist. Corollary 1 needs a strict gap: with Definition 6 a γ-approximation may output weight exactly γβ in both cases, so it does not decide the gap predicate. We require hi < γ·lo, and since Lemmas 2 and 3 hold for every ε, one uses ε/2 (corollary1). Typos In the proof of Claim 6 the weight is written t(4ℓ+α) instead of 4tℓ + 2tα. The proof of Lemma 3 has a sign error (4t log k − 2t log k/log log k), drops a factor t in 2αt, and drops the constants of Claim 7 (t² for 3t³). Its bounds ≥ 4(t−1) log k and ≤ 3(t+2) log k still hold for k ≫ t. Step (4) of Claim 4 sums 2ψ over i ≠ j ∈ [t], but step (6) counts unordered pairs. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorems 1 and 2 (the cut is miscounted) The proofs use |cut(G_x̄)| = t² log² k, but the construction of Section 4 has Θ(t² log³ k) cut edges, so the argument as written only gives Ω(n/log⁴ n) and Ω(n²/log⁴ n) rounds (paper_cut_edges). Impact. Both theorems are true: the same construction with a constant-size alphabet proves them, and even improves the bounds to Ω(n/log² n) and Ω(n²/log² n) (theorem1, theorem2). Details. C^i_h and C^j_h are joined by a complete bipartite graph minus a perfect matching. That is (ℓ+α)(ℓ+α−1) edges for each of the ℓ+α positions h and each pair i<j. So the cut has exactly (t choose 2)·q²(q−1) edges, q = ℓ+α ≈ log k, which is Θ(t² log³ k). Corollary 1 then gives only Ω(k/(log³ k · log n)) = Ω(n/log⁴ n) (resp. Ω(n²/log⁴ n)). Changing ℓ, α does not help: with Reed–Solomon codes the alphabet has size at least the code length, and the cut is at least (log k/log log k)³. Repair. The construction never needs the alphabet to be as large as the code length. Take a code over an alphabet of constant size Q = 4^D (D ≈ 2t/ε), with length M = log₂ k and pairwise agreement ≤ M/D; such a code exists by Gilbert–Varshamov. Give heavy nodes weight M. All claims go through with the same proofs, and the cut has t(t−1)/2 · M · Q(Q−1) = O(log n) edges. Corollary 1 then gives T·B·log n = Ω(n) (resp. Ω(n²)), so T = Ω(n/log² n) (resp. Ω(n²/log² n)) for B = O(log n). This implies the paper's claims. (theorem1, theorem2) 🔧 Lemma 3 (the choice of t) The proof of Lemma 3 picks t = 3/(4ε) − 1, which is too small: for ε = 1/8 and t = 5 the gap ratio between Claims 6 and 7 is 0.9 > 0.875 (= 3/4 + ε). Impact. Statement true; any t ≥ 3/(2ε) + 3 works (lemma3, lemma3_paper). Details. The gap between Claims 6 and 7 has leading terms 3(t+1)ℓ versus 4tℓ, with ratio 3/4 + 3/(4t). For t = 3/(4ε) − 1 this ratio exceeds 3/4 + ε. With the paper's own simplified bounds 3(t+2) vs 4(t−1) it is even 21/16 > 1 at ε = 1/8. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous CONGEST (CSLib Cslib.Congest.Algorithm). The node set V is fixed and its names are the IDs. In each round a node sends B bits on every edge and direction. A node's input is its weight; randomized algorithms also give each node a private uniform random string. The output is one bit per node: membership in the independent set. ApproxMIS A γ T ε: on every graph with node set V and weights in {0,…,n}, after T rounds the output is an independent set of weight ≥ γ·OPT with probability ≥ 1−ε. Weights must be bounded: with unbounded weights no algorithm with bounded T·B could exist, and the theorems would be vacuous. The paper's instances have O(log n)-bit weights. Multi-party communication is the number-in-hand blackboard model (Definition 1). Protocols are trees in which the designated player writes one of m symbols, costing ⌈log₂ m⌉ bits. Randomized protocols have private coins. Promise pairwise disjointness uses the Chakrabarti–Khot–Sun promise: pairwise disjoint, or uniquely intersecting. Hypothesis. The CKS bound (Theorem 3) is assumed as PPDLowerBound c. It says that every private-coin protocol with error ≤ 1/3 and nonempty coin spaces writes at least c·k/(t log₂ t) bits. This is implied by CKS (public-coin, binary). Everything else is proved. The lower bounds are for infinitely many n, namely the sizes of the families. They hold against algorithms that may depend on V. Main results in Lean. The generic claims (claim5_generic, claim7_generic, card_code_le) hold for any code with pairwise agreement ≤ a. They serve both the paper's Reed–Solomon parameters and the repaired constant-alphabet instance. The base cases of Claims 2 and 5 use ℓ ≥ 1 and the inductive step of Claim 5 uses α ≥ 1; both are implicit in ℓ ≫ α ≥ 1, and the paper fixes k, α, ℓ as positive integers. Reductions and Extension-Based Proofs — PODC 2021 Kayman Brusse, Faith Ellen. Reductions and Extension-Based Proofs. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467906. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (no arXiv version; the "full version" cited for Sections 5–7 was not available). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. We prove Theorem 1 (an augmented extension-based impossibility proof transfers from T to S along a reduction) and the transfer of §8 only for reductions (R₁, R₂) in which R₂ needs no communication, i.e. each process applies a function to its own output of S, with R₁ an arbitrary NIS-solvable task. Two steps of the paper's proof fail as written, and the general case, where R₂ needs the NIS composition A₂ ∘ (A ∘ A₁) of Section 6 whose correctness the paper defers to a full version, was neither proved nor refuted; Section 5 was not checked either. The Section 4 claim (extension-based ⇒ augmented extension-based) and the cited fact "NIS-solvable ⇒ IS-solvable" are proved. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 1 ("Why the prover wins", first case) The step "if the values output in D₀γ' did satisfy the specifications of S, then the values output in C would satisfy R₂ ∘ S ∘ R₁" fails when the prover reaches C before every process has finished A₁, because D₀ then gives those processes arbitrary inputs. Impact. Theorem 1 was not refuted, but it is saved only for R₂ without communication: the repair, choosing D₀ canonically, is proved in that case (theorem1_local, step_queryA1, ucan_mem). Details. D₀ is any initial configuration of A compatible with C₀γ₁, so its inputs are only fixed for processes that finished A₁. If the prover reaches C before every process has finished A₁, D₀'s input vector need not be an output vector of R₁ (it need not even be an input vector of S). A valid S-output for that input vector then tells nothing about T. The step is correct only for final configurations, but the paper's prover also wins by reaching partial configurations that already violate T. Repair. 𝒫 keeps the A-part with canonical inputs: the outputs of a fixed completion of the A₁-part (toA, ucan). After every simulated step of A₁, not only the last one, 𝒫 re-reaches this configuration by a chain of queries from the start of its phase. We also handle the infinitely-many-phases case by a potential argument, since "𝒫_T can only end a finite number of phases with A₁/A₂-only steps" needs one. (theorem1_local, step_queryA1, ucan_mem) ⚠️ Theorem 1 (assignment queries, enumeration of C₂) The assignment-query step enumerates "the initial configurations C₂ of A₂ such that there is a P'-only schedule from C₂ that results in a configuration satisfying f", which ignores the steps of A₂ that other processes, possibly outside P, already took during γ. Impact. Such a step can be necessary for f, so the filter can drop the right g, and the prover then answers None although a schedule exists. Correct answers to assignment queries are proved only for R₂ without communication (assign_sound, assign_complete). Repair. The later exhaustive search over μ₂ makes the filter unnecessary: enumerating all g repairs this. We proved this only in the local case, where 𝒫 enumerates every g with h ∘ g = f. Typos "Suppose R₂ ∘ S ∘ R₂ is a reduction" (§1) and "R₁ ∘ S ∘ R₂" / "R₂ ∘ S ∘ R₂" (§7, "Why the prover wins") should read R₂ ∘ S ∘ R₁. In §3, "if δ(s'ᵢ) ≠ ⊥ then pᵢ outputs δ(sᵢ). If δ(sᵢ) = ⊥ …" should read δ(s'ᵢ) in both places. In §7, Ending phases, α'(ϕ) is written for α'(φ). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. NIS model. Full-information non-uniform iterated snapshot model: asynchronous and wait-free, n = a finite type P of processes (any n), deterministic, no randomness. A protocol is its decision function δ on full-information states. A state is init i x, upd s (the paper's s·1) or scan s v, which stores the pre-scan state s together with the paper's (i, v). A configuration is the vector of states; the memory is determined by the states. Crashes are processes that stop being scheduled. Every input vector over the input type is an initial configuration; the task constrains only the runs from its input vectors. Game. A prover is a deterministic strategy: a function of the history. The protocol is a decision function together with arbitrary correct answers to assignment queries; these answers are adversarial and may depend on the history. Each query response carries the new configuration and the outputs of all processes. Reached configurations. In a phase these are reinit base u (the paper's C₀' α(φ)) plus the query responses. endPhase C requires C to be a response of the current phase. Winning. The prover wins if all its moves are legal and one of these holds: it reaches a configuration whose partial outputs cannot be extended to a valid output vector; there are infinitely many phases; from some point on, every move is a query from the previous response (an infinite chain). An infinite last phase that is not eventually one chain is a loss. This is the rule "finitely many chains and assignment queries per phase". Reductions. The paper's definition (IsReduction), with the implicit well-formedness made explicit: outputs of each task are inputs of the next one. Theorem 1 is proved under the extra hypothesis LocallySolvable R₂ h. R₁ only needs to be NIS-solvable: the paper's "w.l.o.g. A₁ is an IS protocol" is proved (exists_isIS_of_solves, which needs finitely many inputs, as in the paper). Main results in Lean. Message Reduction in LOCAL — PODC 2019 Shimon Bitton, Yuval Emek, Taisuke Izumi, Shay Kutten. Message Reduction in the LOCAL Model is a Free Lunch. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331582. Formalized version: arXiv 1909.08369 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The size bound of Theorem 1.2 and Lemma 4.7 is false for algorithm Sampler as written: |S| is Õ(n^{1+δ+ε}), not Õ(n^{1+δ}) (ε = 1/h), but the corrected size equals the message bound the paper already uses, so the abstract's spanner (constant stretch, O(n^{1+ε}) edges and messages, O(1) rounds) survives. The stretch analysis holds: we prove the deterministic core of Theorem 4.6 (stretch 2·3^k − 1), Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5, and the probabilistic core of Lemma 4.3 for one node, including the adaptive trials. The LOCAL implementation (Section 5) and the message-reduction scheme (Theorem 1.3) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 1.2 and Lemma 4.7 (spanner size Õ(n^{1+δ})) Sampler as written can put ≈ n^{11/6} edges into S for k = 1, h = 2 on K_n, so |S| = Õ(n^{1+δ}) fails with probability ≥ 1/8, not n^{−c}; the true bound is Õ(n^{1+δ+ε}) (theorem_1_2_size_false, first_trial_large). Impact. Theorem 1.2 holds after this change of the size bound, which gives up its separation of size from messages: the corrected size equals the message bound the paper already uses. Capping F_v at the threshold inside a trial would also work, but we did not prove that. The paper does not rely on the separation: the abstract's spanner survives, and Theorem 1.3 / Lemma 6.1 set ε = δ and only need |S| = Õ(n^{1+2δ}). Details. In every trial of Cluster_j, every node samples s_j = c² n^{2^j δ + ε} log³ n edges and keeps one edge per queried neighbour in F_v. The test |F_v| < c n^{2^j δ} log n (Pseudocode 2, line 4) is made only between trials, so the last trial can add up to s_j edges. The proof of Lemma 4.7 counts O(n^{2^j δ} log³ n) edges per trial and node, dropping the factor n^ε. Counterexample: k = 1, h = 2 (δ = 1/3, ε = 1/2), G = K_n, any constant c ≥ 1. In the first trial of level 0 every node draws ≈ c² n^{5/6} log³ n of its n − 1 edges, and all distinct draws enter S. A node hits at least s/2 distinct neighbours on average, and an edge is counted at most twice. So, by a reverse Markov argument, with probability ≥ 1/8 this single trial already puts ≥ n·s/8 ≈ n^{11/6} edges into S. For all large n this exceeds C · n^{4/3} · log^D n, for any C, D. (theorem_1_2_size_false, first_trial_large) Repair. The correct bound is |F_v| < τ_j + s_j (Setup.card_F_lt). Summed over the levels (with Lemma 4.1) this gives |S| = Õ(n^{1+δ+ε}), the same as the message complexity (size_exponent). ✏️ Slips V' = ⋃_{1≤j≤k−1} V'_j (before Lemma 4.5) should range over 0 ≤ j ≤ k, as the proof of Theorem 4.6 uses ("any node in G_k is unclustered"). As printed, {C(v) | v ∈ V'} is not a partition of V. Theorem 1.2 allows h = 0, but ε = 1/h. Typos The prose says a node joins a center in N̂_j(v) (an edge of F_v); Pseudocode 2, line 19, uses any edge of F = ⋃ F_u. The stretch proof works with either rule; we formalize the pseudocode. The proof of Lemma 4.5 speaks of a spanning tree of "height" 3^j − 1; its induction bounds the diameter, which is what the lemma states. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 4.3 (volume classes miss volume 1) Class x is defined by |E_j(v,u)| ∈ (n^{xε}, n^{(x+1)ε}], which excludes neighbours with a single edge, so at level 0 (simple G_0, where these are all neighbours) the maximum class need not carry m_i/2h of the volume. Impact. Statement true; with the classes [n^{xε}, n^{(x+1)ε}) the proof goes through (Setup.lemma_4_3_node). Details. We also needed the unstated α ≥ 6 for ⌊(β−1)α/β⌋ ≥ α/3; it holds for the paper's α. Lemma 4.3 is proved for one node, with the 2h adaptive trials and the union bound made explicit (Setup.lemma_4_3_node). The paper's "abuse of probabilistic arguments" is harmless here: each trial fails with probability ≤ |N|(1 − θ)^s conditionally on any history. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The centralized algorithm of Sections 3–4 (Sampler, Cluster_j) on a finite simple graph G_0. The distributed implementation (Section 5: synchronous LOCAL with unique edge IDs, broadcast-convergecast in clusters) and the simulation scheme (Section 6) are not formalized. Stretch (Hierarchy.lean): a Run G k is any outcome of the coins, given by merge maps, center marks and the edge sets F_a of all levels, subject to the postconditions of Pseudocode 2. Level-j nodes are identified with their root vertex, and the multigraph G_j is represented by the original edges between clusters. So parallel edges are exactly the paper's E_j(a, b). Theorem 4.6 is proved for every run that satisfies the conclusions of Lemmas 4.2/4.3 (every node light or with a queried center; every level-k node light). This is the paper's own split into "whp facts" and a deterministic argument. Randomness: finite uniform sample spaces with probabilities by counting (CSLib uprob). Lemma 4.3 (Lemma43.lean) models one node v with an arbitrary multigraph neighbourhood (volumes 1 ≤ vol u < b^L). The L adaptive trials draw from the current X_v. Each sample is a uniform number in Fin M, M = (vol N)!, decoded into an exactly uniform edge of the current X_v (uprob_decode). The bound is unconditional over the whole adaptive process. Size counterexample: the first trial of Cluster_0 on a simple graph. Every node samples s of its incident edges uniformly with replacement; we count the query edges, which all lie in S.
