Small Buffers on a Path (AQT) — PODC 2019 Avery Miller, Boaz Patt-Shamir, Will Rosenbaum. With Great Speed Come Small Buffers: Space-Bandwidth Tradeoffs for Routing. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331614. Formalized version: arXiv 1902.08069 v1 (the only version, with the appendix); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The space-bandwidth tradeoff survives, but only in the number n of nodes: we prove Theorem 4.1 (space ℓ n^{1/ℓ} + σ + 1 when ρℓ ≤ 1) for HPTS with the levels of each phase in decreasing order, and the abstract's O(ℓ d^{1/ℓ} + σ) upper bound in the number d of destinations is proved nowhere. Lemma 4.8 is false for HPTS as printed, and the one-line change of the level order repairs it. PTS/PPTS on paths and trees (Propositions 3.1, 3.2, 3.5, B.3) and the lower bound (Theorem 5.1) are proved. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Abstract and introduction (the O(ℓ d^{1/ℓ} + σ) upper bound in terms of destinations) The abstract and introduction claim O(ℓ d^{1/ℓ} + σ) space for d destinations (and O(log d) space when ρ ≤ 1/log d), but the paper never proves it: Theorem 4.1 is in terms of the number n of nodes. Impact. The tradeoff is established only with n in place of d; the d-form is not refuted. The hierarchy is built on node indices, so the d-form does not follow directly; our sharper form gives only min(ℓ n^{1/ℓ}, d) + σ + 1 (theorem_4_1, Run.occ_le_keys). The lower bound in terms of d follows from Theorem 5.1, since d ≤ n. Not formalized. 🔧 Lemma 4.8 (Algorithm 3, order of the levels in a phase) Lemma 4.8 is false for HPTS as printed: Algorithm 3 runs the levels of a phase in increasing order, while the proof needs (and says) decreasing order, and with m = ℓ = 3 and 27 nodes a node's badness does not decrease over a phase (lemma_4_8_false_alg3, lemma_4_8_false_indexing). Impact. With the levels of each phase in decreasing order (a one-line change to Algorithm 3) we prove Lemma 4.8 and Theorem 4.1 (lemma_4_8, theorem_4_1), and Theorem 4.1 only claims that some algorithm "HPTS" achieves the bound, so this variant proves it. For Algorithm 3 as printed, Theorem 4.1 is unverified (see Not formalized.). Details. Algorithm 3 works at level λ = t mod ℓ and accepts new packets when λ = 0, so a phase runs the levels 0, 1, …, ℓ−1. The indexing in the statement of Lemma 4.8 (rounds t+1, …, t+ℓ) gives 1, …, ℓ−1, 0. The proof assumes the opposite: "levels are activated in decreasing order over the course of a phase". In the round of level λ, a bad packet can be traded for a bad packet at a lower level (Case 2 of Claim 2). If that lower level was already processed in this phase, the badness does not decrease. Counterexample (m = ℓ = 3, 27 nodes, no injections): node 8 holds two packets to 15, node 9 one packet to 15, node 10 two packets to 20 and one packet to 15. Node 10 has badness 1: a bad level-2 packet with intermediate destination 18. The rounds at levels 0 and 1 do nothing. At level 2, node 8 sends a packet to its intermediate destination 9, where it becomes pre-bad at level 1. ActivatePreBad then pushes node 9's level-1 packet into node 10, which is busy forwarding at level 2. Node 10's badness stays 1, for both orders 0,1,2 and 1,2,0. Here badness follows Definition 4.5 restricted to intermediate destinations w_k > i (see the slips below; the fix to Algorithm 5 line 5 listed there plays no role in this instance). Read literally, Definition 4.5 also counts node 8's bad level-2 packet at node 10, although that packet never crosses node 10; then node 10's badness drops from 2 to 1 in this instance. But the literal definition breaks the first step of the proof of Theorem 4.1, B(i) ≤ ξ(i) + 1: with m ≥ 6, three packets injected at once at node 0 for node 1 (σ = 2) give B(5) = 2 and ξ(5) = 0. The restricted definition is the one the proof needs. This is a false lemma, and the proof of Theorem 4.1 rests on it. Repair. With levels in decreasing order (ℓ−1, …, 0) we prove Lemma 4.8 and Theorem 4.1 (space ℓ n^{1/ℓ} + σ + 1 when ρℓ ≤ 1) (lemma_4_8, theorem_4_1). 🔧 Lemma 5.4 (used in Theorem 5.1) Lemma 5.4 counts the β-stale packets at the end of round t by the load of [F(t+1)+1, F(t)] in round t+1, but such a packet may already be delivered then and occupy no buffer. Impact. Theorem 5.1 is true: we prove load ≥ ((ℓ+1)ρ−1)(m−1)/(4(ℓ+1)) − 1 against every protocol (theorem_5_1, exists_load_ge), which with n ≈ (ℓ+1)m^ℓ is the paper's Ω(((ℓ+1)ρ−1)/ℓ · n^{1/ℓ}) up to constants. Repair. We count them in round t, where they are still fresh and hence undelivered by Lemma 5.3 (card_becomeStale_le_sum_load). Theorem 5.1 then follows by a global telescoping count, which replaces Lemma 5.5. (theorem_5_1, exists_load_ge) ✏️ Slips Definition 4.5 (badness): the sum must be restricted to intermediate destinations w_k > i, as in Definition 3.3. Without the restriction, the first step of the proof of Theorem 4.1 fails (see the Lemma 4.8 item). Formalized with this fix. Definition B.4 / the PPTS-tree badness (Appendix B.2, Proposition 3.5) sums B_k(v) over all destinations, and with that definition the step "B(v) ≤ ξ(v) + 1" fails: inject 3 packets at a child of v with destination v; then ξ(v) = 0 but B(v) = 2. Restricting to destinations above v (as Definition 3.3 does on the path) repairs it; the statements are true (Tree.prop_3_5, Tree.prop_3_5_depth). Algorithm 5 line 5 should read i < w_k: activating the empty pseudo-buffer at w_k itself would block the pre-bad run of a packet arriving at w_k one level lower. Formalized with this fix. Claim 2, item 1 should say j > λ, not j < λ. Propositions 3.2 and 3.5 omit ρ ≤ 1 (added). The construction of Theorem 5.1 needs (ℓ+1)m^ℓ + 1 nodes, not (ℓ+1)m^ℓ ("destination n"). Section 4.1 says I_{j,r} has m^j nodes and I_j = {I_{j,r} : r ∈ ⟨m^j⟩}, and Algorithm 3 line 6 ranges over r ∈ ⟨m^{ℓ−λ}⟩; it should be m^{j+1} nodes and r ∈ ⟨m^{ℓ−j−1}⟩ (as in the definition of I_{j,r} and in Algorithm 5). The phase boundaries in Section 4.2 (rounds (φ−1)ℓ … φℓ−1) and in Lemma 4.8 (t+1 … t+ℓ) disagree. Algorithm 2 line 2 uses an undefined w_d. The proof of Lemma 2.5 writes ℓ·s + 1 for ℓ(s−1) + 1. The proof of Theorem 5.1 writes /2k for /2ℓ. Typos Definition 2.1 writes N_T(v) for an interval I. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Claim 2, item 3 (badness never increases in a round) The proof of Claim 2 is not a proof: item 3 is argued through events (a)–(c) and Cases 1–3, which do not account for each unit of badness. Impact. Claim true; replaced by a new argument (Bad_low_le, Bad_lam_le, phase_decreasing). Repair. Within a level-(λ−1) block, the nodes active at level λ form a suffix. A lower-level pseudo-buffer can gain a bad packet only at the first node of that suffix. So for every node i, the lower levels gain at most one unit of badness, and only when i is active at level λ, where it loses one unit (Lemma 3.4). (Bad_low_le, Bad_lam_le, phase_decreasing) 🔧 Lemma 4.8 (end of the proof) The final step of the proof ("hence B^{s+}(i) = B^s(i), as desired") is garbled and does not prove a strict decrease in the phase. Impact. Statement true for levels in decreasing order (lemma_4_8). Repair. A short induction over the levels, in decreasing order, replaces it (phase_decreasing). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous rounds on the directed path 0 → ⋯ → n−1. Each edge carries one packet per round. A round is an injection step followed by a forwarding step, and buffer occupancy is measured between the two. Deterministic and centralized, with no failures. Adversaries are count functions A t a b (round, source, destination), (ρ,σ)-bounded on every buffer and every interval of rounds (Cslib.AQT.IsBounded, staged in Podc/Computability/Distributed/AQT/Basic.lean), with real ρ ≥ 0 and σ. Upper bounds. Configurations count the packets per node and destination. HPTS is formalized for n = m^ℓ (hptsStep): FormPaths in closed form (fpAct), then ActivatePreBad for levels λ−1, …, 0. The packet a pseudo-buffer sends is chosen arbitrarily (ValidSel), so every priority rule is covered. A Run uses one level per round according to a schedule, and new packets are accepted in batches at phase starts: the ℓ-reduction reduce A ℓ. Pending packets are not counted, as in the paper. PPTS and PTS are HPTS with ℓ = 1, m = n, accepting packets in their injection round. Trees. A finite forest given by a parent map (Tree.DTree). Packets move towards ancestors, and destinations are ordered by a topological index. Algorithm 6 is formalized both as the loop and in closed form (Tree.act). Lower bound. Arbitrary offline protocols: any trajectories that move each packet at most one hop per round towards its destination, with at most one packet per edge per round (LowerBound.Execution). The adversary lbAdv is a finite packet family. Injecting "ρm packets per phase" at once would not be (ρ,1)-bounded, so it spreads the injections at rate ρ, a routine reading of the paper's "during the phase". Main results in Lean. Optimal EBA with Omission Failures — PODC 2023 Kaya Alpturer, Joseph Y. Halpern, Ron van der Meyden. Optimal Eventual Byzantine Agreement Protocols with Omission Failures. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594573. Formalized version: arXiv 2305.06271 v1 (full version with appendix); numbering follows it. Targets: §6 (Prop. 6.1, Thm. 6.3, Prop. 6.4, Thms. 6.5–6.6, Cor. 6.7). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Correctness of P0 (Prop. 6.1) and the concrete results hold for t ≤ n − 2: P^min and P^basic implement P0 (Thms. 6.5, 6.6), and P0 is safe (Prop. 6.4) once the definition of a 0-chain is repaired. The general "safe ⇒ optimal" (Thm. 6.3) is proved only with an extra hypothesis, which holds in the two concrete contexts, and against one-shot competitors, so both protocols are optimal in that sense (Cor. 6.7) and the general claim is neither proved nor refuted. The full-information protocol of Section 7, which settles the open problem of the abstract, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 6.3 (safe ⇒ optimal in every EBA context) The proof takes the first round k in which P and a strictly dominating P' differ, for an agent i that "may be faulty", and has three gaps, so the general claim is neither proved nor refuted (Context.thm_6_3 proves it with an extra hypothesis). Impact. Unestablished in general; our extra hypothesis NFConsistent holds in γ_min and γ_basic, so Cor. 6.7 (t ≤ n − 2) is fully established for one-shot competitors. Whether Thm. 6.3 holds in every safe EBA context is open. Agents that can detect their own faultiness are the risk. Details. The agent i may be faulty. Safety (1) yields a run where all preferences are 1 and i has the same state. The contradiction ("P' decides 0 against Validity") needs i to be nonfaulty there. EBA imposes nothing on faulty agents. A case is missing. The case "P decides at k, P' does not" is never treated. Repeated decisions. "All agents have the same state up to time k − 1" fails if P' performs decide again after deciding. The spec allows this, and faulty agents may do it freely. Repair. We prove Thm. 6.3 for one-shot competitors under one extra hypothesis, NFConsistent: an undecided agent's local state also occurs, with the same preferences, in a run where that agent is nonfaulty. The hypothesis holds in γ_min (trivially) and in γ_basic (by swapping the roles of i and a nonfaulty agent). (Context.thm_6_3, Context.thm_6_3_lit) 🔧 Proposition 6.4 (definition of 0-chain, condition (c)) With the paper's 0-chains, Prop. 6.4 is false already for n = 3, t = 0, no failures and preferences 0, 1, 1: at time 1 agent 2 knows that somebody just decided 0 but not who, so it has received no 0-chain, and safety condition (1) fails for P^min (Counterexamples.prop_6_4_lit_false; every n ≥ 3, t ≤ n − 2: prop_6_4_lit_false_gen). Impact. A one-clause fix of a definition with evident intent: with "i_{m'} knows that some agent has just decided 0" Prop. 6.4 holds (prop_6_4_min, prop_6_4_basic), and Thm. 6.3 with the paper's definition still follows. Details. Condition (c) of a 0-chain asks that i_{m'} knows that i_{m'−1} has just decided 0. In the minimal context an agent only learns that somebody just decided 0, not who. In the example, at time 1 agent 2 has jd = 0. In the run with preferences 1, 0, 1 it has the same local state, so it does not know that agent 0 decided. Hence it has received no 0-chain. Yet every run in which it has this local state contains a preference 0. This breaks safety condition (1) for P^min, the unique implementation of P0 there. The same failure-free example works for every n ≥ 3, t ≤ n − 2. It also refutes the main-text claim that "K_i(⋁_j jdecided_j = 0) holds iff i receives a 0-chain". The proof of Prop. 6.1 reaches the paper's definition by an invalid step: from K_i(⋁_j jdecided_j = 0) it concludes K_i(jdecided_j = 0) for some j. ✏️ Slips Corollary 6.7 is stated for all of γ_min,n,t, i.e. for every t < n, but for t = n − 1 the protocol P^min_{n−1} implements P0, is an EBA protocol and strictly dominates P^min (Counterexamples.cor_6_7_min_false, cor_6_7_min_false'). A 0-chain reaching time n − 1 would need n agents besides the undecided agent, so P0 already decides 1 at time n − 1 = t, one round before P^min does; in the failure-free all-1 run the decisions are at n − 1 vs n. Cor. 6.7 is derived from Thms. 6.5/6.6, which assume t ≤ n − 2, and with that hypothesis it holds (cor_6_7_min, cor_6_7_basic). Proposition 6.1 is stated for every EBA context, whose failure model may drop messages of nonfaulty agents, but Agreement and termination in t + 1 rounds need F ⊆ SO(t), the only model the paper uses (Context.prop_6_1 assumes it). Section 5: the update rule of jd sets both jd = 0 and jd = 1 if a 0-message and a 1-message arrive in the same round. This never happens for implementations of P0; we set jd = 0. Typos Proof of Thm. 6.5: I should be the system of P^min, not of P0; jdecided should be deciding; "(Note that t′ = m.)". Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Proposition 6.4, safety (1) in γ_basic In γ_basic the proof's all-1 run with "the same adversary" fails: an agent that decided 0 in r sends (init,1) in r' and changes the counts #1. Impact. The repaired statement is true (prop_6_4_min, prop_6_4_basic). Repair. We also silence each faulty agent from the round in which it decides 0 (ZeroBiased.allOnes). 🔧 Theorems 6.5 and 6.6 (decide-1 case) The proofs show only one of the two conditions needed for P0 to decide 1: they do not show ¬K_i(⋁_j jdecided_j = 0) in the decide-1 case. Impact. Statements true; the missing fact follows from safety (1) (ZeroBiased.not_knows_jDecided, thm_6_5, Basic.thm_6_6). An EBA context (Context) is an information-exchange protocol plus a failure model. Local states are (⟨time, init, decided, jd⟩, x), and the core part is updated exactly as §5 prescribes. Messages have a tag 0/1/none (the sets M⁰, M¹, M²). A run is determined by its initial global state (Config: pattern, preferences, initial extra state). The Impact of Cooperation in Bilateral Network Creation — PODC 2023 Tobias Friedrich, Hans Gawendowicz, Pascal Lenzner, Arthur Zahn. The Impact of Cooperation in Bilateral Network Creation. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594588. Formalized version: arXiv 2207.03798 v2 (full version with appendix); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Every statement we checked is true, and the proofs of Lemmas 2.4 and 3.5 are saved by local changes: this covers Lemma 2.4, Lemma B.1, Proposition 3.1, Corollary 3.2, Lemmas 3.3–3.5, Theorem 3.6 (trees in BSwE have ρ ≤ 2 + 2 log α), and Propositions 3.8 and 3.9 (stretched binary trees give the matching Ω(log α) lower bound for BGE). The paper's most significant result, the constant Price of Anarchy for 3-BSE on trees, was not checked, and neither were the bounds for general networks and the refutation of the conjecture of Corbo and Parkes. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips The proof of Lemma 2.4 misstates dist_{C_n}(u) for odd n as (n-1)(n-2)/4 instead of (n²-1)/4; the bound derived from it uses the correct value. The proof of Lemma 2.4 says "if every node in G' has degree 2, then G' is isomorphic to C_n", which ignores disjoint unions of cycles. Those are disconnected and excluded by the penalty M. The definition of the Bilateral k-Strong Equilibrium must require a nonempty coalition; otherwise the empty coalition "improves" vacuously and no graph is in BSE. With M only required to exceed α n³, disconnecting is not always worse when α is tiny (e.g. n = 3, α = 0.01, M = 1: an agent of the triangle drops both edges). This never matters under the paper's standing assumption α ≥ 1. Typos Proposition 3.9 says "for sufficiently large η". The paper's proof (with k = ⌈α/η⌉) needs a threshold that depends on γ; η^γ ≥ 512 suffices (prop_3_9). The statement also holds with the γ-independent threshold η ≥ 512 (prop_3_9_uniform): if η^γ < 512, the claimed bound is below 1 ≤ ρ, and a complete binary tree of the right size is in BGE. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 2.4 (the explicit α-range for odd n) The proof claims C_n is in BSE for (n+1)(n-1)/4 - (n-1) < α < (n+1)(n-1)/4 when n is odd, but for (n-1)²/4 < α < (n²-1)/4 the cycle is not even in RE (as for C_5 with α = 5; C5_not_BSE, cycle_odd_not_BSE, cycle_not_RE). Impact. Statement true: with the right end (n-1)²/4 the range is still nonempty and of order n², so Lemma 2.4 as stated, "for some range of α ∈ Θ(n²)", holds (cycle_BSE, lemma_2_4). For even n the paper's range is correct. Details. The proof cites [14] for Remove Equilibrium on this range. But an agent on C_n who drops one of its two edges saves α and loses only n(n-1)/2 - (n²-1)/4 = (n-1)²/4 in distance. C_5 with α = 5 lies inside the claimed range (2, 6). 🔧 Lemma 2.4 (path case) The proof's path case assumes that "one of the end nodes must be part of the coalition", which is unjustified: the edge may have been dropped by the other endpoint, and then both end nodes can stay outside. Impact. Statement true (cycle_BSE, lemma_2_4). Repair. Our proof avoids the case analysis by counting distance levels: every coalition member of degree ≤ 1 in a path, and every member of degree 2, is not better off (cycle_BSE, lemma_2_4). 🔧 Lemma 3.5 (case α ≥ n/2) The proof starts with "if α ≥ n/2, the claim holds by definition of the 1-median r", but |T_u| ≤ n/2 ≤ α does not give |T_u| ≤ α/(ℓ(u)-1) once ℓ(u) ≥ 3. Impact. Statement true; the case split is unnecessary: the swap argument of the main case (u swaps its parent edge for an edge to r) works for every α (lemma_3_5). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Model.lean) A static, one-shot game; no distributed model and no randomness. Agents = vertices of a finite type V, n = |V|. A state is the created graph G (SimpleGraph V). The paper does the same: in equilibrium nobody pays for an edge that is not built. cost(u) = α · deg(u) + ∑_v d(u,v), where d is the hop distance and M is the distance between disconnected agents. Theorems assume the paper's α ≥ 1 and M > α n³ (M ∈ ℕ). Solution concepts are exactly the paper's: RE (one agent drops one edge), BAE, PS, BSwE (u replaces uv by uw, and both u and w must strictly gain), BGE = PS ∧ BSwE, k-BSE (coalition moves: dropped edges touch Γ, added edges lie inside Γ), BSE = n-BSE. log is log₂ (Real.logb 2), as is standard; Lemma 3.4, Theorem 3.6 and Proposition 3.9 are stated with it. ρ(G) = cost(G) / cost(OPT), where cost(OPT) is the infimum over all graphs on V. We prove cost(OPT) = 2(n-1)(α+n-1) for α ≥ 1 (lower bound socialCost_ge, star optCost_le_star). Trees: layers and subtrees are metric, T_u = {x | d(r,x) = d(r,u) + d(u,x)}. A 1-median minimizes the distance cost (IsMedian, IsSubMedian). The k-stretched complete binary tree is an explicit graph on Σ ℓ : Fin (dk+1), Fin 2^⌈ℓ/k⌉ (stretchedTree d k). Main results in Lean. Forget-IT — PODC 2026 Ittai Abraham, Sourav Das, Yuval Efron, Jovan Komatovic. Forget-IT: Optimal Good-Case Latency For Information-Theoretic BFT. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815965. Formalized version: the proceedings version (11 pages). The full version [3] (Cryptology ePrint) was not available, so the proofs were rebuilt from the proof sketch of §4.2. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The title's good-case latency of 3δ holds, and so do non-triviality and agreement (Theorem 2), even in a fully asynchronous model with crash–recovery. The stronger robust good-case latency (Theorem 3, first item, also in the introduction and Table 1), the paper's distinctive claim over TetraBFT, is false under the paper's own definition, and we proved no robust variant: a run in which GST is the moment a correct leader enters its view can still take 14 message delays to decide. Termination after GST in general, view length, O(n²) messages per view and O(1) persistent storage were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 3, first item (robust good-case latency 3δ; also introduction and Table 1) The claim is false under the paper's own definition: correct processes that entered the leader's view during the asynchronous period and timed out there never vote in it, so with n = 4, f = 1 a run in which GST is the moment a correct leader enters its view decides only at GST + 14 ticks instead of GST + 3 (RobustLatency.robust_latency_counterexample). Impact. This is the paper's distinctive claim over TetraBFT; the title and abstract only claim (non-robust) good-case latency, which holds (good_case_latency). Agreement and the 3δ good-case latency are unaffected; the plausible intended version is not proved. Details. §3 defines T_rgc over the executions in which "GST coincides with a correct leader entering its view". Nothing stops the other correct processes from having entered that view earlier, during the asynchronous period, and from having timed out there. After the timeout (line 65, vc[V] = true) they never send vote-1 in that view (line 37). So the leader's proposal cannot gather a quorum, and the decision waits for the leader's own timeout and a further view. Concrete run: n = 4, f = 1, Δ = 2 ticks, one message delay after GST = one tick. Process 0 leads view 1 and is Byzantine; process 1 leads view 2 and is correct. All messages to process 1 are delayed until GST = 21. Processes 2 and 3 finish view 1 with the help of Byzantine SAFE echoes and enter view 2 at tick 11. They time out there, so vc[2] = true by tick 19. At GST process 1 receives f + 1 echo-3 for view 1 and enters view 2 (line 80). It proposes, but nobody votes. The processes decide only in view 3, at tick GST + 14, where the claim promises GST + 3. The run is a valid run of CSLib's partially synchronous model: start at 0, no drift, no crashes, reliable delivery by max(τ, GST) + δ. It is therefore an execution of the paper's model, and the facts are checked by evaluation (RobustLatency.robust_latency_counterexample, others_timed_out, decides_later). The run also misses the weaker bound 3Δ = 6 ticks. The claim stays false if δ is read as the maximum delay δ(E) over the whole execution (§3, Responsiveness). Then a crash–recovery of processes 2 and 3 before GST plays the role of the timeout: line 53 sets vc[2], and every delay can be small (informal argument, differencies.md). The termination sketch has the gap that causes this: it says every correct process "enters view V (line 85)" on the leader's prepare, which ignores processes already in V. The intended notion is probably "the whole view lies after GST". We did not prove the claim for that version. Even then it needs δ < Δ or favourable tie-breaking: with δ = Δ the first entrant's 3Δ timer (line 45) can fire just when the vote-1 quorum arrives, and then it never locks. As written, though, the claim is false. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 2, agreement sketch (number of vote-2 senders) The sketch claims that a decision implies that "at least 2f + 1 correct processes" broadcast the deciding vote-2, but only f + 1 are guaranteed. Impact. Statement true, even in a fully asynchronous model with crash–recovery (agreement). Repair. f + 1 correct senders are enough: any 2f + 1 senders meet them (base). 🔧 Theorem 2, agreement sketch (induction over views) The sketch treats the views after the decision as if all correct processes entered V_dec + 1 together, but in an asynchronous run processes may lock or echo in V_dec after others have moved on. Impact. Statement true (agreement); the sketch's argument goes through after the repair. Repair. The induction must be stated as an invariant that holds as soon as the f + 1 lockers are fixed, even before they lock (Hyp/Concl in Safety.lean, concl_reach). With this repair the sketch's argument goes through unchanged: guards, the three echo-1 triggers, the SAFE wildcard, and the second-echo mechanism. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Safety (Spec.lean, Safety.lean): Algorithms 1–3 are written as guarded actions, one per pseudocode rule (Defs.lean). These run in an asynchronous transition system with n = 3f + 1 processes and a static set of at most f Byzantine processes; the paper notes that adaptive corruption is equivalent here. Channels are authenticated, there are no signatures, and Byzantine processes may send anything. Correct processes receive any message ever broadcast by a correct process, at any time. They may lose received and accepted messages (volatile state) and may run the recovery procedure at any time. Timers may fire at any time. This covers every execution of the paper's model: partial synchrony, lossy links before GST, crash–recovery, constant persistent memory. Timing (Protocol.lean): forgetIT prm K is the protocol as an Algorithm of CSLib's partially synchronous model (Cslib.Byzantine.PartialSync). Time is discrete and every correct process takes one step per tick. Delivery between correct processes is reliable, by max(τ, GST) + δ. Clocks are drift-free, processes start at 0, and there are no crashes. In a step, a process receives, then runs K passes over the rule candidates, executing every enabled one. Timers expire after 3Δ ticks (line 45) and 4Δ ticks (line 65). One message delay is δ + 1 ticks, and Δ ≥ δ + 1 is the paper's δ ≤ Δ. Every run of this algorithm is an execution of the asynchronous system (run_reach), so safety transfers. Persistent memory is kept as unbounded per-view arrays. Every rule reads only the three-view window or the guard of the view being entered, and views only grow, so this is equivalent to the paper's window. Remark on non-triviality (not an error). Non-triviality is required only when GST = 0, and that restriction matters. Because of the SAFE wildcard, cert(echo-3, f+1, V, v) holds for every value once f + 1 SAFE echoes arrive. A leader resolving line 80's "for some v" adversarially may then propose a value nobody proposed, so weak validity without the GST clause is not guaranteed by the pseudocode. Our implementation tries SAFE first. Main results in Lean. Termination after GST in general (view synchronization; the sketch has the gap described in the Theorem 3 item, but in the counterexample the protocol still decides in the next view), view length 7Δ, message complexity O(n²), the O(1) memory bound, optimistic responsiveness, the corrected robust-latency claim. The full version [3] was not available, so we judged the proceedings sketch only. CSLib candidates. foldl_pres/foldl_progress and quorum_of_all (Latency.lean). Trust. No sorry. All listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; the counterexample is checked with decide +kernel through CSLib's memoised simulator (simHist). Non-vacuity: the good-case theorem and the counterexample run show that decisions do happen; the agreement hypotheses are only n = 3f + 1 and |F| ≤ f.

Distributed Graph Algorithms with Predictions — PODC 2025 Joan Boyar, Faith Ellen, Kim S. Larsen. Brief Announcement: Distributed Graph Algorithms with Predictions. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733530. Formalized version: the brief announcement; the proof of Theorem 4.1 is taken from the full version, arXiv 2501.05267 (Lemmas 4 and 5 there). Verdict: ✅ Correct. Theorem 4.1 (every deterministic component-size bounded MIS algorithm needs (n − 5)/2 rounds on an n-node line) holds, by the paper's own Ramsey proof, and so do the 3-round pruning algorithm, the round bound n of the Distributed Greedy MIS Algorithm, consistency, and the η + 3 round bound of "pruning, then greedy on every error component". The same Ramsey argument applied directly to MIS gives the slightly better bound (n − 4)/2. The framework's asymptotic definitions and the generic compositions of Section 5 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous, fault-free, deterministic LOCAL. Nodes are named by distinct identifiers (the convention of CSLib's Cslib.Local), so comparisons of identifiers are comparisons of node names. Lower bound (Line.lean, LowerBound.lean). A T-round algorithm is any function f : SimpleGraph ℕ → (ℕ → Lab) → ℕ → β with Cslib.Local.IsLocal T f: the output of a node depends only on the edges at distance < T and the labels at distance ≤ T. An n-node line is an injective placement id : Fin n ↪ ℕ; the label of a node holds the identifiers of its left and right neighbours (so after T rounds a node knows the identifiers up to distance T + 1, and the orientation). The algorithm may depend on n (nodes know n), and must be correct for every placement of arbitrary natural identifiers, i.e. its round count does not depend on the identifier domain. Every component-size bounded algorithm is such an algorithm, and algorithms that ignore the orientation or see less are special cases, so the lower bound covers them. The *_bounded variants show that identifiers below an explicit D(n, T) already suffice ("d is a sufficiently large function of n"). Algorithms (Algorithm.lean, Greedy.lean, Main.lean). CSLib's locally-iterative model (Cslib.LocallyIterative.Algorithm): in each round a node updates its state from its own state and the set of its neighbours' states. A state holds the identifier, the prediction bit and the status (active / output 1 / output 0). pruneAlg = prune rule, then "output 0 if a neighbour output 1"; greedyAlg = local-maximum rule in odd rounds, "output 0" rule in even rounds; predAlg = pruneAlg.seq 3 greedyAlg. Graphs are finite (Fintype V), identifiers linearly ordered. The error measure η is the paper's: the maximum number of nodes of an error component, i.e. a connected component of the subgraph induced by the nodes the pruning algorithm leaves active (eta). Main results in Lean. Paper Lean File Thm 4.1 (= full version Lemma 5): MIS on the n-line needs ≥ (n − 5)/2 rounds theorem_4_1 LowerBound.lean Full version Lemma 4: 3-colouring the n-line needs ≥ (n − 3)/2 rounds (any finite colour set) lemma_4, lemma_4_bounded LowerBound.lean Full version Lemma 5, reduction MIS (T rounds) → 3-colouring (T + 1 rounds) misToColour_isLocal, misToColour_solves LowerBound.lean Ramsey step of Lemma 4 exists_homogeneous_window LowerBound.lean Sharper bound ≥ (n − 4)/2 (not in the paper) mis_lowerBound_sharp, mis_lowerBound_bounded LowerBound.lean Full version Thm 3: finite Ramsey theorem for k colours Cslib.exists_homogeneous_finite Podc/Foundations/Combinatorics/HypergraphRamsey.lean §3: I ∪ neighbours is an extendable partial solution; agrees with the prediction pruneSet_extendable, pruneSet_agrees, isMIS_union_of_extendable Main.lean, Basic.lean §3: the variant initialization (larger I) is extendable pruneSet'_extendable, pruneSet_subset_pruneSet' Main.lean §3: state after the 3 pruning rounds pruneAlg_status Main.lean §3: consistency (correct prediction ⇒ η = 0, output = prediction after 3 rounds) predAlg_consistent Main.lean §4: Distributed Greedy MIS terminates within n rounds (within the component size), output is an MIS greedy_round_complexity, greedy_decided, greedy_isMIS Main.lean, Greedy.lean §5: pruning + greedy terminates within η + 3 rounds with an MIS (η-degrading) predAlg_terminates, predAlg_correct Main.lean the algorithm is a LOCAL algorithm predAlg_isLocal Main.lean Remarks. Theorem 4.1 is not tight in its constant (a remark, not a mistake: the paper's bound is true). Applying Ramsey directly to the MIS outputs gives three consecutive middle nodes with the same output: all three in the MIS contradicts independence, none in the MIS contradicts maximality. This needs a window of 2T + 5 nodes and gives T ≥ (n − 4)/2. The paper's detour through 3-colouring (Lemma 5 of the full version) loses one round. (mis_lowerBound_sharp) Lemma 4 of the full version holds for any finite number of colours, not only 3: the Ramsey argument never uses the number of colours. (lemma_4) Round counting of the pruning algorithm (proof remark). The paper's third round only tells the remaining active nodes that the neighbours of I have terminated. With the usual "send, receive, compute" round convention (CSLib's locally-iterative model) this message is part of the next round, and 2 rounds suffice. This is a counting convention, not an error: we prove the paper's 3 (round 3 is idle in our model). Not formalized. The framework definitions (consistent/robust/smooth as asymptotic notions), the generic compositions of Section 5 with black-box algorithms (2f(η)-degrading composition with a clean-up algorithm, the fault-tolerant parallel composition), the coloring-based algorithms and the cited results ([2], [7], [8]). Of the generic compositions, only the round arithmetic was read. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity of Theorem 4.1: exists_mis_algorithm gives an n-round MIS algorithm for n-node lines (parity of the distance to the left end), so the class of algorithms is not empty and the bound is tight up to a factor 2. Models come from CSLib (Cslib.Local.IsLocal, Cslib.LocallyIterative); the k-colour Ramsey theorem was added to the staged Podc/Foundations/Combinatorics/HypergraphRamsey.lean (CSLib candidate). State Complexity of Protocols With Leaders — PODC 2022 Jérôme Leroux. State Complexity of Protocols With Leaders. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538421. Formalized version: arXiv 2109.15171 v2 (March 2022); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The main result holds as printed: Theorem 4.3 is proved for every protocol of finite interaction-width, n ≤ (4 + 4·width + 2|ρ_L|)^(|P|^((|P|+2)²)), and so are Corollary 4.4 (the Ω((log log n)^h) lower bound for h < 1/2) and Examples 4.1 and 4.2. The proof of Lemma 7.3, on which Section 8 rests, is broken: it took a new argument, which gives Lemma 7.3 only with a weaker constant (the weak Pottier bound instead of Pottier's), and re-derived constants in Section 8, which are still enough for Theorem 4.3's bound. Lemmas 5.2–5.4, 6.2, 7.1, 7.2 and Theorem 6.1 are proved as stated, Lemma 6.2 with a short repair of its proof. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Lemma 7.3 (Pottier step) The proof reads the variables β(a) of system (1), one per displacement a ∈ A of a simple cycle, as counts β(e) of edges e, so the claim "#Θ'(e) > 0 if #Θ(e) ≥ k" is not established, and the length bound misses a factor |S|. Impact. Proved with a weaker constant (the weak Pottier bound), which is still enough for Theorem 4.3's bound (lemma_7_3). The lemma with the paper's constant is neither proved nor refuted (see Not formalized.). Details. The proof reads β(e) for edges ("Σ_H β(e) = #Θ(e)") and builds Θ' with "#Θ' = β'". That is a type error: different cycles with the same displacement are merged, so the system no longer knows which edges a solution uses. The length is also off: |Θ'| counts edges, but ‖β'‖₁ counts cycles. Each cycle has up to |S| edges, so the proof gives |Θ'| ≤ |S|·(|E|+d)(1+2|S|‖T‖)^(d(d+1)), not the stated bound without the factor |S|. Repair. We prove Lemma 7.3 with variables indexed by the cycles themselves. This works with the weak Pottier bound (Cslib.exists_small_decomposition), whose constant does not depend on the number of variables. The constant becomes K = (2|S|M)^(2^d−1), with k > ‖Δ(Θ)|_Q‖₁·|S|·M·K and |Θ'| ≤ (|E|+d)·|S|·K. Section 8 goes through with this constant (ℓ = h^(2^d+2d+4), k = d·h^(2^d+1), threshold h^(2d+5)·ℓ). The final exponent still fits under |P|^((|P|+2)²), so Theorem 4.3 is unaffected. (lemma_7_3) ✏️ Slips Section 8: Theorem 6.1 is applied to P' = P \ {i}, so it gives (d−1)‖α‖∞ ≤ b, not d‖α‖∞ ≤ b. The weaker bound suffices, because the sum is over R' ⊆ P'. Section 8: "Δ(Θ)(p) = μ(p) − η'(p) − Δ(π)(p)" should read α'(p) instead of η'(p). The following estimate only works with α'. Section 8: "α'(i) = ρ_L(i) + (n−1) − Δ(σ)(i)" has the wrong sign; the bound ≥ n − h holds anyway. Section 8: Lemma 7.3 is used with its hypothesis ‖T‖∞ > 0 without checking it. We avoid the issue with M = 1 + ‖T‖∞. Lemma 7.3's proof: Pottier's decomposition is a multiset, not a "set H". Typos Section 8 writes "d = |Q|" (meaning |P|), "the (n > i) predicate" (meaning (i ≥ n)) and "a cycle θ on x|_Q" (meaning α|_Q). The proof of Lemma 7.3 writes Δ(Δ) for Δ(Θ) and swaps α'/β' in one sentence. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 6.2 (bound on the restricted reachability set) In the case where every β reachable from ρ_n has β(p) < λ_{n+1} on R_n, the proof asserts that the T|_{Q'}-reachability set of ρ_n|_{Q'} has at most sλ_{n+1}^{d−n} elements, but the case hypothesis is about the full net T. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_6_2_step). Details. In the restricted net T|_{Q'} the places p_1, …, p_n are unconstrained, so the case hypothesis does not apply directly. Repair. Suppose an R_n-place reaches λ_{n+1} in T|_{Q'}. A shortest such path stays in a set of at most sλ_{n+1}^{d−n} configurations, so it is that short. It then lifts to T by Lemma 5.2, since ρ_n(p_j) ≥ λ_n ≥ sλ_{n+1}^{d−n}‖T‖. That contradicts the case hypothesis. (lemma_6_2_step) 🔧 Section 8, "#Θ(e) ≥ ℓ for every e" The decomposition of a path into a multicycle Θ and an elementary path π gives #Θ(e) ≥ ℓ − 1 (or ≥ ℓ − |S| for a short path), not #Θ(e) ≥ ℓ. Brokering with HTLCs is NP-hard — PODC 2021 Eric Chan, Mohsen Lesani. Brief Announcement: Brokering with Hashed Timelock Contracts is NP-Hard. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467952. Formalized version: the 4-page proceedings version (no arXiv version exists). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The reduction from Knapsack to minimum leader sets in flower graphs is right in spirit, and two local changes make it correct (theorem_4_1_repaired): double all weights and the capacity first, and read the number of levels m with the parenthesis in its intended place. Lemma 4.2 (and the forward half of Lemma 4.4) is false for the construction as printed, while Lemma 4.3 (for V ≥ 2) and the backward half of Lemma 4.4 hold. What is checked is the combinatorial correctness of the reduction: its polynomial running time and NP-hardness as a complexity class are not formalized. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 4.2 (and the forward half of Lemma 4.4) for instances with a weight-1 item When some item has weight 1, the "bitcoin pump" contracts (yᵢ, b) carry min_w(X) − 1 = 0 B, so for the satisfiable instance (v, w) = (1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2), V = 2, W = 2 the flower graph has no adequate leader set for any number of levels m (lemma_4_2_false_minW_one, paper_minW_one). Impact. The construction cannot work on such instances. They are ordinary Knapsack instances, weight-1 items are not a degenerate case, the paper reduces from Knapsack in general, and it gives no way to handle them. A new first step, doubling all weights and the capacity, repairs the reduction (theorem_4_1_repaired). Details. The y-parties are the broker's only bitcoin source besides the supplier: each yᵢ, 2 ≤ i ≤ m, pays (min_w(X) − 1) B. With min_w(X) = 1 they pay nothing, so the flower graph is adequate only if all items fit into the knapsack, whatever m is. The instance above is satisfiable (the first two items) and meets all the paper's assumptions; even every single item fits. But Σ_w(X) = 4 > 2 = W. The intended formula for m (see the slips) divides by zero here. The amount min_w(X) − 1 cannot simply be raised: Lemma 4.3's proof needs it to be below every weight. Repair. Double all weights and the capacity first (theorem_4_1_repaired). ✏️ Slips Lemma 4.2, number of levels (all weights ≥ 2). The printed m = ⌈Σ_w(X)/min_w(X) − 1⌉ + 1 has a misplaced parenthesis. It equals ⌈Σ_w(X)/min_w(X)⌉, which is too small: for the satisfiable instance (v, w) = (1, 2), (1, 2), (1, 4), V = 2, W = 4 (which meets all the paper's assumptions) m = 4 and the broker gets at most 4 + 3·1 = 7 < 8, so the flower graph has no adequate leader set at all (lemma_4_2_false). The broker b starts with nothing and must pay every item contract (b, xᵢ) = wᵢ B, so it must receive Σ_w(X) bitcoins in total. Its only bitcoin income is W from the supplier s and min_w(X) − 1 from each of y₂, …, y_m. So Σ_w(X) ≤ W + (m − 1)(min_w(X) − 1) is necessary for any leader set to be adequate, whatever the schedule (budget_of_adequate). The intent is m = ⌈Σ_w(X)/(min_w(X) − 1)⌉ + 1: writing ⌈x − 1⌉ + 1 instead of ⌈x⌉ makes no sense otherwise, and the proof's "left with at least Σ_w(X) B" holds exactly for that reading. The reduction is correct for every m ≥ 1 that satisfies the budget (lemma_4_4_of_budget, theorem_4_1_of_budget), in particular for the intended m, whenever all weights are ≥ 2 (theorem_4_1_fixed). Lemma 4.3's proof assumes that no single item has value ≥ V, justified by "otherwise the Knapsack problem is trivial", but an item with vᵢ ≥ V and wᵢ > W does not make the instance trivial. The lemmas are true under the stated assumption (lemma_4_3, satisfiable_of_adequate). Without it, Lemma 4.3 and the backward half of Lemma 4.4 fail even for the paper's own m: take the items (2, 20), (0, 10) with V = 2 and W = 12. The instance is unsatisfiable, yet {b, x₁} is adequate: x₁'s 2 E start the whole chain, which then releases the supplier's bitcoins. This example was checked by hand, not in Lean. The reduction first has to discard items with wᵢ > W, and then answer "yes" directly if some remaining item has vᵢ ≥ V. Lemma 4.3 also needs V ≥ 2. With V = 1, the assumption vᵢ < V forces all values to be 0; then (b, y₁) = 0 E and {b, z₁} is adequate although the instance is unsatisfiable. This case is degenerate. The reduction needs positive weights, which the paper never states: a weight-0 item can be funded for free and min_w(X) − 1 is meaningless. This is standard for Knapsack (theorem_4_1_repaired). Lemma 4.2's proof says "after repeating this process m times", but only the m − 1 parties y₂, …, y_m send bitcoins; the + 1 in the intended m pays for this (adequate_of_satisfiable). In Lemma 4.3's proof, {b, y₁} and {b, y_{m+1}} give b no bitcoins, not min_w(X) − 1; this is harmless. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A transaction graph is a multigraph of contracts. Each contract e has a sender, a receiver, an asset and an amount, and each party has an initial endowment own p a (TxGraph, Model.lean). Contracts are created one at a time, under the HTLCP rules with brokering of §§2–3. A leader may create its outgoing contracts at any time. A follower may do so only once all its incoming contracts exist. In both cases the sender must tentatively own the amount: its endowment, plus what it received on created incoming contracts, minus what it already escrowed. This is the paper's master-contract bookkeeping. Adequate L: some order of creations creates every contract ("the set L can create all edges"). The model is asynchronous, with no failures and no adversary: everybody conforms, and the broker chooses the order. Secret release and triggering are not modelled; the paper's notion of adequacy concerns only edge creation. A minimum leader set is an adequate set of minimum cardinality (IsMinimumLeaderSet). A flower graph (IsFlower) has a broker b incident to every contract, with contracts to and from every other party. Only b is a broker, and every other party owns exactly what it sends. In the paper's graphs b starts with nothing (brokerOwn); the paper's case analysis assumes this throughout. flower K m c is the construction of Figure 2, parameterized by the number of levels m and by the bitcoin amount c on the contracts (yᵢ, b), 2 ≤ i ≤ m. paperFlower K is the paper's choice, c = min_w(X) − 1 with the printed m. The construction is a flower graph (Flower.isFlower). Knapsack has natural-number values and weights. Main results in Lean. Polynomial running time of the reduction, the closing remark that Knapsack stays NP-hard for polynomially bounded weight ratios, and NP-hardness as a complexity class. We verify the combinatorial correctness of the reduction: K is satisfiable iff {b, s} is a minimum leader set, iff minimum leader sets have size 2. Also not formalized: the example of Figure 1, the counterexample without the vᵢ < V assumption (hand-checked only), and the step that discards overweight items. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The hypotheses are not vacuous: lemma_4_2_false and lemma_4_2_false_minW_one exhibit instances meeting all assumptions (V ≥ 2, vᵢ < V, positive weights), and theorem_4_1_repaired holds for all such instances. The model is self-contained (Mathlib only). The two generic tools Adequate.first_hit and Reachable.batch' are possible CSLib candidates if another token-game model needs them.

Fast Concurrent Data Sketches — PODC 2019 Arik Rinberg, Alexander Spiegelman, Edward Bortnikov, Eshcar Hillel, Idit Keidar, Lee Rhodes, Hadar Serviansky. Fast Concurrent Data Sketches. PODC 2019 (brief announcement). DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331567. Formalized version: arXiv 1902.10995 v2 (Dec. 2019; the PPoPP 2020 text). The PODC 2019 publication itself is a two-page brief announcement; Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 are stated identically in v1 (Feb. 2019, proofs in its Appendix A), v2 and the journal version. v2 defers its proofs to "the full paper"; the proofs we checked are those of the journal version (ACM TOPC 9(2), 2022), Sections 6–7. See differencies.md for version differences. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 hold: the generic algorithms are strongly linearisable with respect to SeqSketch_{Nb} and SeqSketch_{2Nb}, for every composable sketch, provided the threads' initial hint is the empty sketch's hint (Algorithm 2 hard-codes 1, which is right for the Θ sketch but not in general). The simulation behind Theorem 1, the paper's main correctness result, does not preserve histories, so Theorem 1 took a new direct invariant proof; we prove both results in a stronger form, which is the one the error analysis needs. The error bounds of Section 6 check out algebraically, with the order-statistic moments of §6.1 taken as hypotheses. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 (Algorithm 2's initial hint 1) Algorithm 2 starts with hint_i = prop_i = 1, which breaks Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 for general composable sketches: an exact counter whose calcHint always returns 2 and with shouldAdd(h, a) = (h ≠ 1) meets all requirements, but drops every update forever (parSketch_hint_one_not_stronglyLinearizable). Impact. For the paper's Θ sketch, 1 is exactly the empty sketch's Θ, so only the generic claim is affected. With "initial hint = hint of the empty sketch" both results hold (lemma1, theorem1). Details. The pre-filtering requirement of Section 5.1 only constrains shouldAdd(h, ·) for hints h produced by calcHint(). So the first batch of every thread is filtered with a hint about which nothing is assumed. With the counter above and N = b = 1, two completed updates followed by two queries returning 0 is an execution with no linearization in SeqSketch_{Nb}. Repair. We prove both results with "initial hint = hint of the empty sketch" (more generally, any hint that filters harmlessly on every stream). (lemma1, theorem1) 🔧 Section 5.3 (exactness of the sequential Θ sketch, off by one) "The sequential Θ sketch answers queries with perfect accuracy in streams with up to k unique elements" holds for Algorithm 1 only up to k − 1 distinct hashes: with exactly k, the initial 1 is evicted and the estimate becomes (k−1)/Θ, for every k (thetaSketch_query_exact, thetaSketch_query_of_le; smallest instance thetaSketch_not_exact_k). Impact. A remark motivating eager propagation; nothing depends on it. The same off-by-one appears in "Θ is 1 during the first k updates". Typos Update threads are indexed 0 ≤ i ≤ N (t₀ is the propagator). hint_i and prop_i are declared int but carry real Θ values. Section 6.1 has a broken reference, "the RSE bound of Lemma ??". Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 1 (simulation by ParSketch) Section 5.2 announces a proof of Theorem 1 by simulating N OptParSketch threads with 2N ParSketch threads, and the full version carries it out, but the mapping does not preserve histories. Impact. Statement true; the simulation is not repaired, and we prove Theorem 1 directly instead, by a separate invariant argument (theorem1). Details. An update that fills a buffer returns in OptParSketch while the simulating ParSketch update still waits at line 125, and in the first round line 225 is mapped to line 125 of a thread with no pending operation. 🔧 Definition 2 vs. Section 6 (what "strongly linearisable w.r.t. SeqSketch_r" gives) Definition 2 is weaker than what Section 6 uses: an r-relaxation may drop queries and may place an operation after arbitrarily many operations that follow it (isRelaxation_drop, isRelaxation_future). Impact. The algorithms satisfy the stronger property Section 6 needs; we prove Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 in this form (lemma1_pastOnly, theorem1_pastOnly). Details. An r-relaxation may drop up to r operations altogether, including queries, which may then return anything. It may also put an operation after arbitrarily many operations that follow it in H': U, q is a 1-relaxation of q, U for every list of updates U. So "strongly linearisable w.r.t. SeqSketch_r" does not by itself give the model of Section 6 ("a query misses up to r of the updates preceding it"), on which the error bounds rest. Repair. In the witnessing relaxation no query is dropped, and a query is preceded only by operations that precede it in the linearization. (lemma1_pastOnly, theorem1_pastOnly) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous shared memory: an interleaving of atomic accesses to base objects. The paper assumes a weaker memory with fences, but its proofs also reason with atomic steps. No failures. The scheduler is arbitrary; we prove safety only. Processes: N ≥ 1 update threads, the propagator t₀ (started by a never-returning propagate operation), and any number of query threads. The propagator scans the threads round-robin. Base objects: the composable global sketch is atomic (merge, snapshot, calcHint). The paper requires its snapshot/merge to be strongly linearisable and treats them as atomic steps. There are also local sketches (update, read, reset), atomic registers prop_i : Option Hint (none = 0), and for OptParSketch registers cur_i. Sketches are derandomised, as in Section 4 (coins fixed by an oracle). A Composable sketch carries the paper's requirements as hypotheses: merge of summaries summarises the concatenation; snapshots answer like the sketch; shouldAdd(calcHint(S), a) = false ⇒ a can be removed from any extension of the stream summarised by S. Everything is generic in the sketch. SeqSketch is the set of histories of the sequential sketch. SeqSketch_r is Definition 2, taken literally. Strong linearisability w.r.t. a set of histories (Definition 1) is a prefix-preserving map from executions to linearizations in that set (Impl.HStronglyLinearizable). The witness is the paper's l (updates at invocation, queries at their snapshot). The relaxed history is the paper's f (visibility points), computed by a ghost run. Main results in Lean. Weakest Failure Detector for Eventual Consistency — PODC 2015 Swan Dubois, Rachid Guerraoui, Petr Kuznetsov, Franck Petit, Pierre Sens. The Weakest Failure Detector for Eventual Consistency. PODC 2015. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767404. Formalized version: arXiv:1505.03469v1 (full version with the appendix; numbering follows it). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The sufficiency half of the main result holds: Ω implements eventual consensus (Lemma 2), and EC and ETOB are equivalent (Theorem 1); both proofs needed the same small repair. Local changes save the rest: Lemma 3 is false because the paper's ETOB algorithm (Algorithm 5) is not stable over non-FIFO links, and sequence numbers on promotions fix it, while Theorem 3 (EC ⇔ EIC, appendix) is false if EIC-Agreement is read literally, and holds among correct processes. The necessity half of the main result (Lemma 1, a CHT-style extraction) is not formalized, so this verdict does not cover it. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 3 (Algorithm 5 does not implement ETOB) Algorithm 5 is not stable over non-FIFO links: an older, shorter promotion from the leader can arrive after a newer one and shrink d_i, so with two processes, no crashes and a leader stable from time 0, ETOB-Stability fails for every τ (Alg5.lemma_3_false). Impact. Breaks the paper's ETOB algorithm and the §5 claim that it gives TOB when Ω is stable from the start. The sufficiency half of the main result rests on Lemma 2 and Theorem 1, which hold. Adding sequence numbers to promotions repairs it (Alg5Fixed.lemma_3_fixed, Alg5Fixed.tob_of_const_leader). Details. On receiving a promotion from its current leader, a process sets d_i := promote_j. Links are reliable but not FIFO. Counterexample: two processes, no crashes, Ω outputs process 0 everywhere from time 0, and the application broadcasts 0, 1, 2, …. The adversary delivers promotion b followed by the delayed promotion b − 1 infinitely often, with all delays bounded. ETOB-Stability then fails for every τ. The proof's step "d_i(t₁) = promote_j(t₃), d_i(t₂) = promote_j(t₄), hence prefix" silently assumes t₃ ≤ t₄, i.e. FIFO delivery. The same run refutes the §5 TOB claim. Repair. The leader numbers its promotions, and a process adopts a promotion only if its number is larger than the last one it adopted from that leader. The repaired algorithm implements ETOB from Ω in every environment, and TOB under a leader that is stable from the start. 🔧 Lemma 3 (proof, the choice τ = τ_Ω + Δt + Δc) The proof uses a "longest communication delay Δc" and a longest local timeout Δt, which need not exist in an asynchronous run, where delays are finite but unbounded. Impact. The step that gives every process a promotion after τ is not justified; it is replaced in the repaired algorithm (Alg5Fixed.lemma_3_fixed). Repair. Take instead the maximum, over the finitely many correct processes, of the first adoption of a promotion of the final leader after τ_Ω. 🔧 Theorem 3 and Lemma 4 (EC ⇔ EIC, literal EIC-Agreement) Under the literal, uniform reading of EIC-Agreement, EIC cannot be implemented with Ω at all, already with 3 processes and at least one correct (EICImpossible.not_solvesEIC), and Algorithm 6 violates it concretely (Alg6Counterexample.not_EICAgreement). Impact. Appendix result. With agreement among correct processes, Lemmas 4 and 5, and hence Theorem 3, hold, with the printed Algorithms 6 and 7 (Alg6.lemma4, Alg7.lemma5). Reading it among correct processes is a plausible intent, but the paper words it exactly like the uniform EC-Agreement, so as printed the statement is false. Details. The paper requires that "no two processes return infinitely different values", and it defines a process's response as its last response, so a crashed process keeps its response forever. Two processes run solo, respond to instance 0 with their own, different proposals, and crash, and nothing can change their last responses afterwards. EC, by contrast, is implementable with Ω. In Algorithm 6 a faulty process decides true and crashes while the correct one decides false forever, even though the EC box satisfies EC. Typos Lemma 3's proof (ETOB-Total-order) says "p_i and p_j receive at least one message of type promote from p_j"; the leader there is p_k. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Algorithm 2 (ETOB's usage assumption) ETOB is specified only for distinct broadcast messages, but two processes that propose the same v to instance ℓ both broadcast (ℓ, v). Impact. Local fix: broadcast (p_i, ℓ, v) (ETOBtoEC.tobHist_distinct, ETOBtoEC.ec_of_etob). 🔧 Lemma 2 and Theorem 1, ETOB → EC (uniform agreement) Both proofs pick k as the first instance invoked after the stabilization time of Ω (resp. ETOB), but Ω and ETOB constrain only correct processes, while EC-Agreement covers all processes. Impact. Statements true; repaired (Alg4.agreement, ETOBtoEC.ecAgreement). Details. A faulty process that is still alive after that time can return a different value. Repair. Also choose k after every faulty process has crashed, which is possible because P is finite. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing with crash failures and failure detectors, following CHT / Jayanti–Toueg (Podc/Computability/Distributed/MessagePassing/FailureDetectors/Model.lean). The set of processes P is finite. In each step a process receives one message in transit, a time-out (λ), or an input; it queries the failure detector and broadcasts at most one message. Links are reliable and not FIFO. Failure patterns are monotone. An admissible run delivers every message to every correct process, and each correct process takes infinitely many time-out steps. Ω is the set of histories that eventually output the same correct process at all correct processes. All positive results hold for every failure pattern, so they hold in every environment. Transformations treat the black box adversarially. Its responses or outputs are input events chosen by the scheduler, and the box is constrained only by the hypothesis that its history meets the spec whenever it is used properly. This covers every implementation of the box. DOI 10.1145/2767386.2767407. Formalized version: the journal version Computing k-Atomicity in Polynomial Time, SIAM J. Comput. 47(2), 2018 (DOI 10.1137/16M1056389, authors' copy, complete proofs). All statements, numbering (Theorem 3.5, Lemma 3.8, Algorithms 1–3, Lemmas 4.2–4.5, 5.5–5.10, …) and the input ranges are those of the journal version; the PODC 2015 extended abstract is not openly available and was not consulted, so its numbering and wording may differ. Verdict: ✅ Correct. Every checked statement holds as written: the normalization procedure (Theorem 3.5), the graph characterization of k-atomicity (Lemma 3.8), the correctness of GPO for histories satisfying Assumption 4.1 (Lemmas 4.2–4.5, Theorem 4.10, for every k ≥ 2), and the correctness of CGS for arbitrary histories with distinct written values (Lemmas 5.5–5.7, Theorem 5.8), plus the size bounds of the configuration graph (Lemmas 5.9–5.10), which concern the graph built by CGS on its inputs 2 ≤ k ≤ n. The proofs go through with only routine additions. The running-time bounds (second part of Theorem 4.10, Theorem 5.11) are not formalized, so the polynomial-time half of the paper's point is not covered. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Typos Lemma 4.5, P(x)-(c) asks for b ∈ B_x[k-1-j] for all 0 ≤ j ≤ i, which mentions the nonexistent set B[0] when i ≥ k-1. Such edges cannot occur once P(x)-(a) holds, so only j with k-1-j ≥ 1 matter. The phrase "for any value v" there binds an unused v. The proof of Lemma 4.4 says "since we are considering k > 2"; for k = 2 the same argument works with the range 1 ≤ y < k-1 empty. Lemma 5.7 attributes distinctness of the induced sequence to Corollary 5.6; it actually comes from Lemma 5.5. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. No execution model is involved. A history on one register is a finite set of operations, each an interval [s op, f op] with s op < f op and natural-number times. <_H is f a < s b. Writes are indexed by the values they write (V) and reads by R, with val : R → V. This builds in Assumption 3.2 in the form of the abstract ("all values written are distinct"), so w(v) is well defined. A k-atomic total order is a strict total order on operations that extends <_H, in which each read's dictating write precedes it with fewer than k writes in between. Unique event times (DistinctTimes) are never needed: every result holds for arbitrary natural-number times. The algorithms are deterministic functions or propositions. GPO is computable: its outer loop runs |V| times, each step is the identity once U = ∅, and ties between equal finish times (impossible in the paper's model) are broken by a linear order on V. CGS is a classical proposition (decision only, no implementation). Proof remarks. Lemma 3.8 needs Assumption 3.4, which the paper assumes throughout. With only Assumption 3.3 it fails; we found a 6-operation counterexample by brute force for k = 1, but did not formalize it. Our proof of the "if" direction is shorter than the paper's three stages: each read is placed right after the last write that must precede it (opKey). GPO uses several invariants the paper leaves implicit: B[i] ⊆ U, |B[i]| ≤ i after each successful iteration, and the bound "an unplaced G_R-successor of a value placed d steps ago forces d ≤ k-1". These are the fields of Inv. Lemma 4.4 (YES ⇒ k-atomic) does not need Assumption 4.1; only Lemma 4.5 does. In Claim 4.9 the swap with z is shown to be topological by a short case analysis, which the paper leaves out. Lemma 5.5's proof establishes "distinct values, no inversion" and then needs a linear-extension step to reach "subsequence of a topological ordering". We supply it (Good.exists_topoOrder_sublist). Range of k. The abstract and Section 1 announce the algorithms "for any k ≥ 3" (the new range: k ≤ 2 was solved before), while the inputs of Algorithms 2–3 and Section 7 say 2 ≤ k ≤ n. Both ranges are correct: GPO is correct for k ≥ 2 (theorem_4_10) and CGS even for k ≥ 1 (cgs_iff_kAtomic). Lemma 5.10 is about the graph G_C "computed at line 11 of the algorithm" (§5.3), so k ≥ 2. Its edge bound indeed needs max(m,k) ≥ 2 (card_edges_le): for m = k = 1, n_w sequential writes and no reads give n_w(n_w-1)/2 configuration-graph edges. The vertex bound holds for every k ≥ 1. Theorem 3.5: the paper processes the values one at a time; the moves do not interact, and we formalize the simultaneous version. The k-atomic total orders of H and of its normalization coincide (normalize_isKAtomicOrder_iff, no hypotheses). Main results in Lean. All in namespace Podc.KAtomicityVerification.History. A Paradox of Eventual Linearizability in Shared Memory — PODC 2014 Rachid Guerraoui, Eric Ruppert. A Paradox of Eventual Linearizability in Shared Memory. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611484. Formalized version: the EPFL Infoscience copy of the PODC paper (10 pages, with the appendix proving Proposition 11); no arXiv version. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Eventually linearizable objects cannot implement any non-trivial linearizable object (Theorem 12, Proposition 14), they make consensus easy (Proposition 16), and an eventually linearizable non-blocking fetch&increment can be turned into a linearizable one (Lemma 17, Proposition 18). This needs only the implied assumption that operations are total, which the paper's model leaves out although every type it uses is total, and a local repair of one wrong step in the proof of Lemma 17. The claim that eventually linearizable objects do not boost the consensus power of registers (Proposition 15) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Partial operations: Lemma 6 (prefixes of t-linearizable histories). Lemma 6 is false for types whose operations are not applicable in every state: the paper's δ ⊆ Q × OP × RES × Q may leave an operation without a transition (lemma6_false_partial). The lemma and its proof are correct for total types (TLinearizable.prefix, tLinearizable_take_self), and every type the paper uses is total. So are its other uses of totality ("a prefix of length at most t is trivially t-linearizable", "any permutation yields a legal sequential history"). Counterexample: take a one-bit object whose operation use is only enabled once enable has set the bit. Process 0 runs use (events 1–2), then process 1 runs enable (events 3–4). With t = 2 the history is 2-linearizable: the order enable, use is legal, and use responded among the first two events, so its response is unconstrained. The prefix of length 2 is not 2-linearizable: it contains only use, which must be linearized and cannot be applied in the initial state. The proof breaks when it completes the early operations "with the responses they would have if executed in that order". Partial operations: Theorem 12 and Proposition 14 (base objects that never respond). Both need base objects whose operations always have a legal response (total types with an initial state), which the paper never states. Every base object in the paper is total, and the proof of Theorem 12 presupposes it. With it added (theorem12, prop14), both results hold. The model only says a programme "can invoke an operation on a base object and await a response". If a base type has an operation with no transition, no response to it is weakly consistent, so the caller waits forever. An implementation of any type whose operations all start with such a call never responds. It is therefore linearizable, and it is vacuously obstruction-free: no process takes infinitely many steps. So item 4 of Theorem 12 holds for every type, while item 1 fails for registers. This is argued in prose, not as a Lean counterexample. Partial operations: Lemma 8, "if" direction (weak consistency is local). The proof inserts the process's operations on other objects "with responses as dictated by the objects' sequential specifications", which needs total operations. The statement is true even without totality (weaklyConsistent_iff_restrict): for each other object, take the weak-consistency witness of the process's last operation on it, and concatenate these witnesses (they are on different objects) before op's own witness. Claim 1 in the proof of Proposition 18 applies Lemma 17 with t = ℓ₀ = 0, outside its hypothesis t > 0. Lemma 17 holds for t = 0 (lemma17). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 17 (fetch&increment: t-linearizable prefixes ⇒ t-linearizable) In the real-time case op₂ ∈ A₄, the proof's claim that in a t-linearization of the prefix with all responses ≤ v "all the slots of E prior to slot v are filled using operations of A₁ and operations of A₄" is false. Impact. The statement stands, with a repaired proof (lemma17). The hypothesis t > 0 is not needed. Details. An operation of A₂ ∪ A₃ that is still pending in that prefix, and later returns a value > v, can occupy an E-slot below v. Example with t = 1: x, z and y are invoked at positions 0, 1, 2, and y returns 1 at position 3. Later x returns 2, and z never returns. The paper's prefix ends at y's response, and x(0), y(1) is a 1-linearization of it. Slot 0 is in E and holds x ∈ A₃. Repair. Take instead a prefix containing op₁'s response and the responses of all late operations invoked before op₂. In any t-linearization of it, the E-slots below v hold operations of A₁ ∪ A₄ invoked before op₁'s response (count_free_le). With finitely many processes the bound |E| ≤ |A₁| + |A₄| then follows from the prefixes alone. The t₀-linearization is needed only for |A₁| ≤ |E|. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Histories (Section 3) are finite or infinite timed sequences ℕ → Option Ev. An operation is named by the position of its invocation, and a response event names the operation it answers. Positions without events are allowed. On gap-free histories, "the first t events" are the positions < t. Sequential histories are ℕ-indexed (possibly infinite), and legality is per object. Weak consistency (Definition 1), t-linearizations (Definition 2) and eventual linearizability (Definition 3) are transcribed literally. Implementations (Section 3) are asynchronous, with deterministic processes of arbitrary (infinite) state. A process may stop forever (crash). Executions are infinite label sequences; a finite execution is one that is eventually idle. The environment invokes arbitrary operations. Each step writes its event at its own position, so t counts steps. Eventually linearizable base objects (Theorem 12, Propositions 14 and 16): a base access is an invocation step plus a later response step of the same process, so base objects are wait-free. The adversary chooses the response values. An execution is admissible iff every base object's history is eventually linearizable for its type. Base types are total, with initial states (needed for wait-freedom). Linearizable base objects (Proposition 18) are atomic: one step applies a transition of a possibly nondeterministic total type. The implementation fixes the initial states of the base objects; Proposition 18's A' uses the states of the stable configuration C₀, as in the paper. Progress conditions: wait-free (a process taking infinitely many steps completes each of its operations), obstruction-free (likewise, if from some time on only it steps), non-blocking (if an operation is pending and steps continue, some operation completes). There is no randomness and no failure detector. Main results in Lean. Limited-Use Atomic Snapshots — PODC 2012 James Aspnes, Hagit Attiya, Keren Censor-Hillel, Faith Ellen. Faster than Optimal Snapshots (for a While). PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332507. Formalized version: the journal version Limited-Use Atomic Snapshots with Polylogarithmic Step Complexity, J. ACM 62(1):3, 2015 (author copy), together with the authors' erratum to it; numbering follows the journal version. The proceedings version has the same Algorithm 2 (its Lemmas 1–3 and Theorem 4). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The 2-component max array of Algorithm 2, the paper's key tool, is not linearizable as published in either version, an error the authors found and published in their erratum, which we confirm in Lean for k = 3; with the erratum's fix (an embedded MaxScan in MaxUpdate1) it is linearizable for every tree shape, but proving this takes a new linearization and criterion. Over atomic max arrays, Algorithm 3 is a linearizable (b−1)-limited-use snapshot with O(log² b log n) Updates and O(log b) Scans, and so is the multi-writer version (Theorem 5.1); the corrected max array keeps these bounds, and Theorem 4.2 needed new linearization points, because the paper's ones are wrong, a flaw not in the erratum. Joining the two halves is informal here, and Section 6 was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Theorem 3.4 (Algorithm 2, linearizability of MaxArray_{k×h}) Algorithm 2 is not linearizable: with k = 3 (balanced tree, m = 2) and three processes, a slow MaxScan returns (1, 0) although MaxUpdate1(r, 1) completed before MaxUpdate0(r, 1) started (alg2_not_linearizable). Impact. The authors found this error and published it in their erratum; we confirm it in Lean. The max array is the paper's key tool. The snapshot is left unproved as published, because the proof of Theorem 4.2 uses Theorem 3.4, but it is not refuted. The erratum's correction is linearizable (alg2_fixed_linearizable, for every tree shape). Lemma 3.5 is correct for Algorithm 2 as published (lemma_3_5), but it is not the cost of the corrected algorithm (lemma_3_5_erratum): MaxUpdate1 goes from O(log h) to O(log k log h), and Algorithm 3's O(log² b log n) per Update absorbs this. Details. The execution is the erratum's: p₀ starts MaxScan, reads r.second = 0 (line 11) and r.switch = 0 (line 12), then pauses. p₁ runs MaxUpdate1(r, 1) to completion. p₂ runs MaxUpdate0(r, 1) to completion. It goes left at the root and sets the switch of the left child. p₀ resumes: it propagates its stale 0 into r.left.second, follows the new switch and returns (1, 0). A linearization that lets the scan see 1 in the first component must put MaxUpdate0 before it, and by real-time order also MaxUpdate1. The Lean execution (badExec, 17 labels) is checked by decide. The non-linearizability proof is a short argument on an arbitrary candidate linearization. The proof of Theorem 3.4 orders scans among themselves and each update against the scans, but never orders MaxUpdate0 against MaxUpdate1. The PODC 2012 version has the same Algorithm 2 and proof. Repair. Line 9.5 of the erratum: MaxUpdate1 performs a MaxScan after its WriteMax. We prove this version linearizable (alg2_fixed_linearizable) with a new history-level criterion for max arrays (exists_isLinearization_maxArr). Each update goes immediately before the first scan that may see it, or last if there is none. ✏️ Slips The erratum says the embedded MaxScan is added to MaxUpdate0(r, v) "after its WriteMax(r.second, v)". That line belongs to MaxUpdate1, which is what its own step-complexity paragraph uses (alg2_fixed_linearizable). The proof of Theorem 5.1 says "op is always linearized after it performs Line 2". An operation can be linearized at another process's Update between its ReadMax and its WriteMax of GetTS. What the proof uses, that op is linearized after it begins, still holds (Snapshot.MW.theorem_5_1). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4.2 (linearization points of Section 4.1) Linearizing an Update at the first WriteMax(root.mr, ptr ≥ d) (d its own root pointer) is wrong, because another process may carry the new value to the root inside a smaller pointer c < d, and a Scan reading c returns the value before the Update is linearized (Snapshot.Counterexample.paper_linearization_points_fail, 3 processes). Impact. The statement stands, with repaired linearization points (Snapshot.theorem_4_2). Details. The false step is "if there is no Update by process j linearized before op, then count_j = 0". Repair. Linearize an Update of process j with counter m at the first WriteMax(root.mr, c) with (root.seq[c])_j ≥ m. 🔧 Lemma 4.1 The proof does not justify that the parent's index at the invocation is at most the sum of the children's components (it follows from the monotonicity of seq along max-array states). Impact. The statement stands, with the step added (Snapshot.lemma_4_1). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous wait-free shared memory, CSLib Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl. Processes are deterministic and scheduled arbitrarily; a crash is a process that stops taking steps. There is no randomization. Linearizability is CSLib's (amended Herlihy–Wing). Algorithm 2 is flattened over an arbitrary binary tree T : Shape. The leaves are the values of the first component, and the split m at a node is the size of its left subtree. This covers the balanced m = ⌈k/2⌉ and every unbalanced choice. The switches are atomic 1-bit registers. The MaxReg_h objects second are atomic max registers, as the paper uses them in Theorem 3.4; their access cost ch is a parameter of the step bounds. Algorithm 3 is modelled over atomic max arrays, an atomic MaxReg at the root and register arrays, for any binary tree with the processes as leaves. Algorithm 4 is modelled over an atomic single-writer snapshot and an atomic timestamp max register. CSLib has no composition theorem. "Algorithm 3 over the corrected Algorithm 2" therefore follows from the two linearizability results only by locality of linearizability, informally. The bound b is not needed for linearizability with unbounded objects. Instead, limited_use shows that with at most b − 1 Updates every pointer and index stays < b. Main results in Lean. Wait-free Queue with Polylogarithmic Step Complexity — PODC 2023 Hossein Naderibeni, Eric Ruppert. A Wait-free Queue with Polylogarithmic Step Complexity. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594565. Formalized version: arXiv 2305.07229 v1 (the PODC paper plus Appendix A with the deferred proofs); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Fig. 4 is not linearizable as printed: line 13 never sets the super field of leaf blocks, and line 78 reads the wrong node's blocks, and with either error the queue fails (Lean counterexamples). With both lines repaired as the paper's own proofs intend, the queue is linearizable (Theorem 18) and wait-free (Corollary 23), and Lemmas 9–17, 20 and 21 hold. The O(log p) bound for enqueues and null dequeues is proved, but the O(log² p + log q) bound for the other dequeues was checked only in parts, and the bounded-space version was not checked. Formalized version: arXiv 2502.05889 v2 (full version with appendix; numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The solvability characterizations (Theorems 2–7) are proved for every k ≥ 2, in both directions; for the degenerate k = 1 all their "only if" directions are false. The proof of Theorem 2's necessity does not cover k = 2 and the reduction in Lemma 13 is invalid, but both statements hold, by short arguments on groups that keep the paper's cover and split-brain ideas. The sufficiency directions were checked only relative to Theorems 8 and 9 and the cited broadcast protocols, which are hypotheses here. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorems 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, "only if" directions for k = 1. For k = 1 every "only if" direction is false: with one party per side, bSM is solvable with no communication on every network and against every adversary, since each party outputs the only party on the other side (theorem2_only_if_false_k1, bSM_solvable_k1, bSM_solvableAuth_k1). The paper never assumes k ≥ 2, and all characterizations hold for every k ≥ 2, in both directions. For example, Theorem 2's claim that k = 1, tL = tR = 1 is unsolvable (since 1 ≥ k/3) is false. Theorems 6 and 7 are worded as "if" only, but the introduction and §5.2 claim and argue necessity too; Lemma 13 and Corollary 5 fail for k = 1 in the same way. Corollary 1 says "if tL < k/2"; it should be tR < k/2, since in a one-sided network L relays through R. The proof of Theorem 4 says "one of the conditions tL < k/3, tR < k/2"; the second should be tR < k/3. Lemma 5's proof: "c1 must decide to match party v2" should be v1. The proof of Theorem 8 writes n − 2tL for k − 2tL. The proof of Theorem 7, case tR = k, tL < k/3, invokes Theorem 4, which needs tR < k/2. The statement is true: the protocol ΠbSM of Lemma 9 only uses L–R edges, so it also works on the one-sided network and settles the case. The implicit requirement that BA/BB outputs are non-⊥ on runs without omissions (Theorems 8/9) is needed and is made explicit. Typos The proof of Theorem 4 cites "Corollary 2"; it should be Corollary 1.
