The formalization Model (CSLib, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/LockStep/). 2k parties Fin k ⊕ Fin k (L, R) run deterministic protocols in synchronous lock-step rounds over a fixed network (fully, oneSided, bipartite) with authenticated point-to-point channels. There is no randomness. Static Byzantine adversary with at most tL corruptions in L and tR in R. Byzantine messages are arbitrary functions of round, sender and receiver, which covers rushing. The paper claims adaptive security for its protocols; we prove only static security. Authenticated setting: ideal unforgeable signatures as abstract tokens, with a rushing, eavesdropping adversary (the strongest standard one, so the impossibilities hold a fortiori). A party's output is its first decision. bSM/sSM are specs on inputs, the honest set and honest decisions. Impossibilities are proved directly for all k ≥ 2 by group-level FLM covers, for every network (Lemma 7/13: every network without L–L edges). This subsumes the paper's "small n + scaling" route. Every result of the paper is formalized and proved: the impossibilities (Props. 6, 14, 19, Thm. 17, Cor. 18, Thm. 20), Algorithms 2 and 4 (Theorems 9, 12) and the universal construction (Algorithms 5, 6, Theorems 28, 32). The proof of Theorem 32 is broken in two places, and we saved it with a new proof of the flattened algorithm, using our own potential function. Our Theorem 32 covers one fixed resolution of the ∥ interleavings, not all of them. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Props. 14, 19, Thm. 17, Cor. 18, Thm. 20 (implicit n ≥ 2): all these impossibility results fail with a single process, which can keep the abstract state locally and leave shared memory constant, e.g. a wait-free, perfectly history-independent 3-valued register with no base objects at all (prop14_needs_two_processes). The results hold with at least two processes, and we assume a reader and a changer c ≠ r with suitable access rights. Prop. 6 is not affected: its proof uses a single process, and constant memory gives distance 0. Lines 6R.1 and 18R.1 read "wait until Load(announce[i]) ∉ R"; it must be ∈ R. o_change for o_read in Prop. 14; X_i for R_i in Thm. 17; α for β in Prop. 6 ("state(H(α)) = q₂"). "t executions" for t + 1 in Lemma 38. In the history-independence proof of Theorem 12, "for any other index j ≠ v, A[v] = 0" should be A[j] = 0. Typos Theorem 20's proof cites Lemma 16 for Lemma 38. Formalized version: the proceedings version (no arXiv full version exists); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The lower bounds proved in the body (Lemmas 5–6, Theorem 8, Corollary 9) and the Section 4.1 upper bound hold, and the proofs of Lemmas 6 and 7 need only local changes. The bound "n + k − 2 for n ≤ 2^(k−1)+2" in the abstract, introduction and conclusion drops the body's conditions: it fails for k = 1, n = 3, and some cases of it are unproved. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Abstract, introduction and conclusion (range of the n + k − 2 bound): the bound "n + k − 2 when n ≤ 2^(k−1) + 2" is stated without the body's k ≥ 3 and n > 2. Observation 3 (start configuration not p₀-idle): a scanner's solo Scan may return the old value V of a pending Update of p₀ that has not taken a step, although the execution is V-absent (prose counterexample only, not in Lean). The scan may be linearized before the pending update. Yet the execution is V-absent, because the only p₀-idle configuration reached during αα' is the one after the update. The paper applies Observation 3 only from C₀α_j, which is p₀-idle, so the proofs are unaffected. We prove a correct version (scan_resp): a scan returns the value after some number of p₀'s operations that is at least the number of operations completed before the scan was invoked. In the proof of Lemma 6, "V₁ contains a 1 in every component" should be "in its k-th component", which is all the argument uses. In the proof of Lemma 1, "these final n collects" should be u + 1. Impact. Statement true; we avoid I' altogether and work with stages (reduce_stage, see the Model). Repair. The missing step is short: otherwise p_j would run solo forever in I. 🔧 Lemma 6 (only m = k treated) Lemma 6's proof treats only m = k. Impact. Statement true; the same argument covers m ≤ k (lemma6). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, CSLib Cslib.SharedMemory: deterministic processes P (n = |P|), invocation, steps and response as separate labels, no crashes. Base objects B : ι → ObjSpec (m = |ι|). Fast-write MWMR impossibility — PODC 2020 Kaile Huang, Yu Huang, Hengfeng Wei. Fine-grained Analysis on Fast Implementations of Distributed Multi-writer Atomic Registers. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405698. Formalized version: arXiv 2001.07855 v6; numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The main result, Theorem 1 (no multi-writer atomic register with one-round-trip writes and two-round-trip reads, for t ≥ 1, W ≥ 2, R ≥ 2), is true; we prove it for every algorithm in the paper's round-trip model, with a simpler construction that needs no sieving, because §4 is not a proof. The fast-read (W2R1) algorithm of §5.2 / Appendix A is not atomic: with S = 4, t = 1, one reader (so R < S/t − 2 holds) and two writers, a read that starts after write(1) has returned can return the initial value. So the sufficiency half of the claimed tight condition for W2R1 is lost, as we proved no repaired algorithm; its necessity half (§5.1) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ §5.2 / Appendix A (the W2R1 algorithm, Algorithms 1–2; MWA2 / Lemma 5) The algorithm is not atomic: with S = 4, t = 1, R = 1, W = 2, a read that starts after write(1) has returned can return the initial value 0 (W2R1.w2r1_not_linearizable). Impact. The sufficiency half of the claimed tight condition for W2R1 (R < S/t − 2) is not established; Theorem 1 is unaffected. Details. Initial value 0. Both writers query and see timestamp 0, so w₁ writes (1, w₁) (value 1) and w₂ writes (1, w₂) (value 2). (1, w₁) reaches s₀, s₁, s₂ and write(1) returns. Then the read starts, and (1, w₂) reaches s₀, s₁. The read hears from s₀, s₂, s₃. (1, w₂) occurs in only one reply, so it is not admissible. (1, w₁) occurs at s₀ and s₂, but at s₀ its updated set is just {w₁}. The server's current value there is (1, w₂), so the reader is never recorded with (1, w₁). The intersection is {w₁}, and degree 2 fails. The read returns 0 although write(1) completed before it started. Lemma 5 claims that (k, wᵢ) is "admissible with degree 2" because the read sees it at S − 2t servers. It forgets that the updated sets must also contain the reader. In the single-writer algorithm this holds because the writer's value is always the current one. With several writers a concurrent larger value hides it. The counterexample holds both for the literal line 20 (record the reader only for the values in its valQueue) and for the single-writer-style reading (also record it with the server's current value). The second reading is the one that matters: under the literal one the algorithm already fails with a single writer, because a first read is never recorded with a new value, so a completed write(1) seen at only S − 2t = 2 of the read's servers is never admissible. (W2R1.w2r1_not_linearizable) ❌ Appendix A (Lemmas 2 and 6, Corollary 1, hence Lemma 7 / MWA3) Even on correct runs, Lemma 2, Lemma 6 and Corollary 1 are false (model checking, not in Lean), so the proof of MWA3 (Lemma 7) does not stand either. Impact. Nothing in Lean replaces these lemmas, so the part of the atomicity proof they carry is unsaved. Details. With concurrent writers a smaller (k, wᵢ) can be invoked after a read has seen a larger value. Scripts and traces: scripts/. ❌ Algorithms 1–2 and Lemma 8, case (ii) (MWA4; no per-reader read counters) The pseudo-code has no per-reader read counters, unlike the single-writer original, and Lemma 8's case (ii) is wrong: a late read request can cause a new–old inversion (model checking, not in Lean). Impact. Adding the counters survives a bounded search, but that variant is neither proved nor refuted, so no fix counts. Details. A third reading of line 20 records the reader with every value the server holds. It defeats the execution of the first item, but it fails too, with S = 5, t = 1, R = 2 and a single writer. There a late (stale) read request records r₂ with a value r₂ never saw, so r₁ returns the new value and a later read of r₂ returns the old one. Only that reading plus per-reader read counters survived our exhaustive search at S = 4 (and a non-exhaustive one at S = 5, R = 2). Scripts and traces: scripts/. Typos "One round-trip skips server s" (§3.1) does not say whether the request or the reply is delayed. Our repair of Theorem 1 needs the reply variant for R₂⁽¹⁾ (see the Theorem 1 item below). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 1 (§4, "sieve-based construction" in the crucial-info model) §4 does not prove what §3 needs: the assumption that the first round-trip R₂⁽¹⁾ of the second read does not change the value returned by the first read R₁ is argued only in a "crucial-info model" whose steps do not follow for a general algorithm. Impact. Statement true; repaired by a simpler construction that needs no sieving (theorem_1, zigzag). Details. §3.3 uses the assumption when it claims that R₁ returns the same value in β'₀ as in α_{i₁−1} ("appending R₂ should not change the return value of an existing read"). But in β'₀, R₂⁽¹⁾ reaches every server before R₁⁽²⁾, so R₁ has not finished. §4 then argues in a "crucial-info model": a server only holds the order "12"/"21" of the two writes, and a first round-trip can only flip it. The "affected" servers are sieved out, and at least 3 servers are said to remain. A general algorithm's servers can store arbitrary information, so none of these steps follows. Repair. The first round-trip of R₂ is blind: it is r₂'s first action, so its messages are fixed. Include R₂⁽¹⁾ (between R₁⁽¹⁾ and R₁⁽²⁾) in every execution of chain α. In chains β, γ let r₂ ignore the reply of the critical server in round one, while its request is still delivered. Then R₁ behaves exactly as in chain α, and the zigzag chain of §3.4 goes through unchanged. (theorem_1, zigzag) 🔧 §3.2 (chain α and real time) α₀ is "W₁ precedes W₂" and α_S is "W₂ precedes W₁", and each αᵢ is described as identical to α₀ except for swapped arrivals. But from α₂ on, the writes must be concurrent (two servers see W₂ first, yet W₁ waits for S − 1 acknowledgements). Impact. Statement true; all chain elements are concurrent in our proof. Repair. The end values come from sequential executions with the same server logs (ret_seq). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous, reliable, unordered message passing between clients and n servers (Fin n), as CSLib Cslib.AsyncMP.Protocol. Servers do not talk to each other. Up to t servers may crash, so a client proceeds once it has n − t replies of the current round-trip. The scheduler chooses when, possibly after more replies arrived. Our counterexample executions are crash-free; t only matters through the quorum size. All W1R2 algorithms (W1R2Alg). A server replies immediately, by an arbitrary function of its log (all messages it processed, with senders), the sender and the message. This covers every deterministic server and is the paper's full-info model (§4.1). A write sends one arbitrary message per server (a function of the writer's state, the value and the server) and returns after n − t replies. A read does two such round-trips. Its round-two messages and its result are arbitrary functions of the replies, which are seen in arrival order. Clients have arbitrary local states between operations. Writers only write and readers only read. Atomicity is CSLib linearizability of every reachable history (Protocol.Linearizable) for register V v₀. Deterministic algorithms (as in the paper). Space Complexity of Fault-Tolerant Register Emulations — PODC 2017 Gregory Chockler, Alexander Spiegelman. Space Complexity of Fault-Tolerant Register Emulations. PODC 2017. DOI 10.1145/3087801.3087824. Formalized version: arXiv 1705.07212 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main results hold: the lower bound of Lemma 1 and Theorem 1, kf + ⌈kf/(n−(f+1))⌉(f+1) registers, is proved, and so are Theorems 3 and 5–7, after local repairs of the proofs of Lemmas 1, 3 and 7 and Theorem 1. Theorem 4 is false for dense domains such as ℚ and needs a condition on the value domain, Theorem 8 read literally (fixed k) contradicts Theorem 3 and needs a change of quantifiers, and Algorithm 2's writer mapping has an off-by-one. Theorem 2 is proved by a different, direct argument; the max-register/CAS upper bounds of Table 1 are not formalized. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 4 (CAS max register, Algorithm 1, wait-freedom) Theorem 4 is stated for "some domain of ordered values V" but is false over ℚ: a write-max(1) can loop forever while another process completes ever larger writes below 1 (MaxRegisterCAS.ratImpl_not_waitFree). Impact. The paper explicitly claims an arbitrary ordered domain, but its use with timestamps (over ℕ) is unaffected: Theorem 4 holds over ℕ (theorem4_nat), and Lemma 5 (linearizability) and lock-freedom hold over every linear order. Details. Over ℚ, the other process completes write-max(1 − 1/(j+2)), j = 0, 1, …, each between the first process's read and its CAS. The proof's "assume w.l.o.g. there are k values between v′ and v" is an unstated hypothesis, which holds for the timestamps the paper uses but not for the stated domain. Repair. The exact condition for wait-freedom is that no interval [v₀, c) contains an infinite increasing sequence (MaxRegisterCAS.waitFree_iff). 🔧 Theorem 8 (no emulation adaptive to point contention) Read literally (k fixed, M may depend on the algorithm), Theorem 8 is false: Algorithm 2 (Theorem 3) uses finitely many registers, so it is adaptive with a constant M (theorem8_false_as_stated). Impact. The intended version (bound independent of k) holds (Alg.theorem8). Details. The proof only shows that consumption grows by f over each of the k writes. Repair. True version: no M independent of k works. For every M there is a k such that every k-register emulation has a sequential run with more than M registers in use. (Alg.theorem8) ✏️ Slips Theorem 3 (Algorithm 2, Appendix D: writer-to-set mapping): client c_i, 1 ≤ i ≤ k, writes to the register set R_⌊i/z⌋, an off-by-one that overloads a set, and then Algorithm 2 is not even WS-Safe (Alg2.Counterexample.not_seqSafe_paperMapping, not_wsRegular_paperMapping, on our formalization of Algorithm 2). The intent is evident: the paper says each set serves (|R_j|−(f+1))/f clients. With j = ⌊(i−1)/z⌋, the mapping the paper's own counting describes, the algorithm is wait-free and WS-Regular with exactly kf + ⌈k/z⌉(f+1) registers, so Theorem 3 holds (Alg2.theorem3_wsRegular, Alg2.theorem3). With 1-based i, R_0 gets z − 1 writers, a later set gets one writer more than it is sized for, and when z | k, client c_k maps to a set R_m that does not exist. Smallest case: n = 4, f = 1, k = 3, so z = 2. Clients c_2 and c_3 share the overflow set R_1, which has 2f + 1 = 3 registers a, b, c on servers 0–2. A failure-free sequential run goes as follows. c_2 writes 1 to a and b, and its write to c stays pending. c_3 writes 2 to c and a, and its write to b stays pending. Then c_2's old write lands on c. A read that hears from servers 1–3 sees at most timestamp 1 and returns 1. So the counting of Lemmas 6/7 ("⌊(|R_j|−(f+1))/f⌋ writers per set") fails for the paper's own mapping. The max-register specification "highest written value or v₀" needs v₀ = min V. Lemma 1 says "k failure-free runs r_i, 0 ≤ i ≤ k". Typos Lemma 2.11 writes δ⁻¹ for δ. Algorithm 2's initial state ⟨⟨⟨0,1⟩, v₀⟩, …⟩ is ill-typed. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3 (the crash run) The crash run "crashes Q_i ∪ M_i immediately after r". But in the adversary run, reads on these servers keep responding (Definition 3.3(a)), so the two runs differ for c_i. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Alg.round_main). Repair. The servers must crash at the stabilization time. In our version the adversary freezes reads too, and its run is then itself fair (Alg.round_main). We simplified the adversary to G_i = F \ F_i, which removes M_i. We also replaced the paper's Lemma 4 by a stronger core statement (Alg.fresh_resp): after a complete write of a new value, the newly written, previously uncovered registers span more than f servers. 🔧 Lemma 1(b) (the final extension) The final extension "by Definition 3.3(a)" until F is uncovered does not exist if c_i keeps writing to F after it returns. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Alg.lemma1_step). Repair. One has to stop scheduling c_i and let only its pending writes respond (Alg.lemma1_step). 🔧 Theorem 1 (last step) The last step applies Lemma 1 to G, the servers with many registers. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405723. Formalized version: the 10-page proceedings version (there is no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Proposition 4 (binary consensus + window registers in M₂), on which the placements of binary consensus and window registers rest, is proved only for algorithms whose objects are all allocated at set-up, because its proof ignores the run-time allocation of M₂; the rest of that proof also needs real repairs (partition invariant, counting, last step). The other formalized claims hold: the impossibility results for window registers in MA₃ (Lemmas 8–9, Proposition 5), the finite-memory reduction (Lemma 4) and the two consensus algorithms (Algorithm 2 for Theorem 3, Algorithm 3 for Proposition 3). The hierarchy as a whole was not checked: the universal construction (Theorem 1), stated without proof in the paper, the placements as such and Section 8 are not formalized. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Proposition 4 (run-time allocation is ignored) In M₂ processes may allocate finitely many fresh objects at run time, and the γ step's pigeonhole over the m − i set-up objects fails when p covers an object it just allocated. Impact. Only the static version is proved: our theorem covers algorithms whose (finitely many) objects are all allocated at set-up (Prop4.not_consensus). We believe the statement for M₂ is true, but nothing we proved saves it. Details. The γ step runs p "until it covers an object not in {x₁, …, xᵢ}", which may be an object p just allocated. The natural repair is to stop only at set-up objects and to treat objects allocated inside a class as private to that class. It needs a model of references and allocation that we did not build. Typos Definition 3: "node′ = listₙ" should be nodeₙ, and "a value v precedes a value v" should end with v′. Proposition 4 uses "separable" for "partitioned" and indexes i ∈ {0, …, m−1} for a sequence starting at 1. "it is is" (Definition 6); "if if" (Definition 3); "multi-treaded" (Figure 1). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Proposition 4 (the partition invariant is too weak for the merging step) Definition 4 only asks that the restriction of α to each class be a valid execution, which does not imply that the restriction to a merged class gives its members their real local states. Impact. Repaired with a stronger invariant, for the static model (Prop4.Inv, Prop4.Inv.block_memEq). Details. Equality of the shared memory (condition 3 of Definition 4) is required for one process p only. After a block β, the classes of the l·i processes of Φ are merged. The new class's restriction is an interleaving of several classes, which could now read each other's writes. Validity for each class alone does not imply that the merged restriction gives its members their real local states. What makes it work is that every block overwrites all objects of Xᵢ: windows are written l > k times, and consensus objects are decided on the common value b. Repair. We prove the invariant for every union of classes, together with "objects outside Xᵢ are untouched everywhere" and "consensus objects of Xᵢ are initial or decided b". After each block, the memory of any restriction containing the block equals the real memory. (Prop4.Inv, Prop4.Inv.block_memEq) 🔧 Proposition 4 (the end of the proof) The final paragraph says two processes "are about to write … to the last register" (in C(α_{i+1}), which should be C(α_m)) and decide differently, which by our analysis does not follow from the construction. Impact. Repaired, for the static model (Prop4.iteration, Prop4.not_consensus). Details. The w.l.o.g. "registers first/last" assumption is unnecessary. Repair. The correct end reuses the argument of the γ step. In the last stage Xₘ is the whole memory, so the solo run of p must decide. Another class then performs a block, and its representative runs solo and decides an input of its own class, which contradicts agreement. (Prop4.iteration, Prop4.not_consensus) 🔧 Proposition 4 (the counting) The coverage after j scheduling steps is uᵢ − l·j, not uᵢ − j, since each step consumes l covering processes per object; likewise "uᵢ − v = 2 l u_{i+1}" should be uᵢ − l·v. Impact. Repaired with our own thresholds, for the static model (Prop4.not_consensus). The paper's uᵢ already fit the corrected counts. Every step is one atomic operation on one object. A finite execution is a schedule List ℕ, an infinite one a sequence ℕ → ℕ. Classifying Trusted Hardware via Unidirectional Communication — PODC 2021 Naama Ben-David, Kartik Nayak. Brief Announcement: Classifying Trusted Hardware via Unidirectional Communication. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467948. Formalized version: arXiv 2105.10566 v1 (full version, 11 pp.); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The paper set out to split trusted hardware into two power classes, but the Claim of §4.1 is false: a simple echo protocol implements unidirectional rounds over sequenced reliable broadcast (SRB) for every n > 2f, so the separation "shared memory ⊋ unidirectionality ⊋ SRB" (Fig. 1, abstract) collapses, and with the Claim of §4.2 unidirectionality and SRB are equivalent for n > 2f. The positive claims hold: Theorem 1 in an eventual form, the §3.2 claim (SWMR objects give unidirectionality) as stated, and the Appendix A claim. The §4.2 construction is safe with the conflict check described in the text; Algorithm 3's pseudocode omits that check and then violates agreement. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Claim of §4.1 (SRB cannot implement unidirectional rounds for n > 2f, f > 1) The claim is false: a simple echo protocol over SRB implements unidirectional rounds for every n > 2f; the formal claim is refuted for n = 5, f = 2 (claim_4_1_false, srb_implements_unidirectional). Impact. The paper's separation "shared memory ⊋ unidirectionality ⊋ SRB" (Fig. 1, abstract) collapses: with the Claim of §4.2, unidirectionality and SRB are equivalent for n > 2f. The appendix "corner case" f = 1 is not special. The classification in the abstract and §1 does not follow from the paper. Details. Counterexample protocol (Echo.echoProtocol). In round r, each process SRB-broadcasts its signed message. Whenever it delivers some process's round-r message, it SRB-broadcasts an echo of it, i.e. relays the signed message. It ends round r once it has delivered echoes of its own message from n − f distinct senders. It has received q's message if it delivered q's message or any echo of it. Why it works. Take two correct processes p, q. Their echo-sender sets have n − f elements each, so they share a sender s (possibly Byzantine), because n > 2f. SRB delivers s's messages to everybody as prefixes of a single sequence. Whichever of echo(p), echo(q) comes first in that sequence has been delivered by both p and q before they ended the round. Liveness. The ≥ n − f correct processes echo everything. Within the paper's model. The protocol uses only what the paper itself assumes and uses: transferable signatures (§2), relayed signed messages counting as "received", and waiting for messages from n − f processes — exactly the ingredients of the paper's own Appendix A protocol for f = 1. Definition 2 puts no other constraint (e.g. wait-freedom) on how rounds end. What breaks in the paper's proof. Scenario 1 asserts that C₂ "must eventually start the next round since they are receiving all messages sent by correct processes". This is unjustified: a round may wait until its own messages have been echoed by n − f processes. In Scenarios 1–3, C₁ and C₂ do not end the round until their delayed messages reach Q, and then the scenarios are no longer indistinguishable. Lean. We prove that the echo protocol satisfies Definition 2, plus integrity and liveness in every fair execution, against any SRB adversary with unforgeable signatures, for every n > 2f (Echo.echoProtocol_implements). ✏️ Slips Algorithm 3 (pseudocode of the L1 rule, agreement). As printed, it violates agreement (property 2 of SRB): with n = 3, t = 1 and a Byzantine sender, two correct processes deliver different messages with the same sequence number (Alg3.pseudo_disagreement). The text of §4.2 says a process builds an L1 proof only if it sees t+1 copies of its own value "and no other value", and the Lemma 3 Case 1 argument uses this check; the pseudocode (lines 29–39, validateValue) merely ignores conflicting copies. With the text's rule, agreement (Lemma 3 Case 1) and Lemma 4 are proved (Alg3.agreement), so the construction itself is not affected. Counterexample (n = 3, t = 1). The sender 0 is Byzantine; it sends m to 1 and m' to 2. In the forwarding round, 2 hears 1 (so unidirectionality holds), but 1 does not hear 2. Each of 1 and 2 has two copies of its own value: its own and 0's. Under the printed rule both build L1 proofs. Result. Process 0 builds L1 proofs for both values. So {1, 0} is an L2 proof of m and {2, 0} is an L2 proof of m', and the correct processes 1 and 2 deliver different messages with the same sequence number. Claim of §4.2 (which unidirectional round Algorithm 3 uses). Definition 2 only relates messages sent in the same round, but Algorithm 3 uses "the unidirectional round" for every (sender, sequence number) instance without saying which round. Processes handle instances at different paces, and may skip one after seeing an L2 proof, so a single round sequence cannot be aligned across processes. A separate round instance per (sender, sequence number), which tagging provides, settles it; our Alg3 model assumes this. Theorem 1 (SRB implements TrInc: exact vs eventual interface). Theorem 1 is stated for the exact TrInc interface, where CheckAttestation returns true for every attestation previously output, but over SRB this holds only once the attestation has been delivered. The result holds in the eventual form, which is exactly what the paper's proof shows (property (1)). We prove consistency between checkers, non-equivocation (one valid attestation per counter), soundness (property (2)) and completeness for increasing counters (property (1)). Proof of Theorem 1 (implementation of Attest). Attest never returns null for a non-increasing counter; the returned "attestation" is simply never valid (TrInc.attest_nonincreasing_invalid). k is never incremented. The attestation omits prev, which is determined anyway (TrInc.accepted_prev). Typos validateL1Prf is defined twice; the second definition should be validateL2Prf. maybeDeliver(val) takes no parameter. key == k refers to an undefined key. Lemmas 2 and 3 speak of last[p]; the code has next_p. "line ??" in Lemma 2. checkL2Proof is called without a proof argument. Lemma 2 needs a process to count its own copy, otherwise n = 2t + 1 correct processes only produce t copies from others. §3.1 says "but using" for "by using". Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Claim of Appendix A (reliable broadcast gives unidirectionality for f = 1) The proof ignores a Byzantine member of Q and assumes w.l.o.g. that all of Q sees the same value. Impact. The claim stands, with the same protocol and a different case split (AppendixRB.appendix_claim). Details. "All processes in Q must receive at least one of p or p''s messages in phase 1" is false for a Byzantine member of Q. "W.l.o.g. they receive p's value" ignores that different members of Q may see different values. "Valid phase-2 messages must contain n − 1 values" contradicts the protocol's check m ≥ 2. Repair. If n ≥ 4, Q contains a correct process. If n = 3, the m ≥ 2 check and the non-equivocation of reliable broadcast force the Byzantine member's phase-2 message to contain p's or p''s value. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Round layer spec (Rounds.lean, Definition 2). A system exposes, for each process, the list of completed rounds; entry r holds the round-r messages received before the round ended. Messages are chosen by an arbitrary adaptive client (round-r message = function of earlier receipts). ImplementsUnidirectional requires four properties: completed rounds never change; Definition 2 for all correct p ≠ q; integrity: a message "received" from a correct q is q's real round-r message; liveness: every correct process completes every round in every fair execution. SRB systems (SRB.lean, Definition 1). Asynchronous; a set F of Byzantine processes, |F| ≤ f; one SRB instance per process. SRB properties 2–4 mean the deliveries of correct processes are prefixes of one log per sender. A Byzantine sender appends arbitrary messages to its log. Signatures are unforgeable and transferable. A message declares the signed messages it relays, and a Byzantine process may relay (q, m') only if q is Byzantine or m' is in q's log. Protocols are arbitrary deterministic message-driven state machines with arbitrary message and state types. Scheduling is arbitrary. Fairness is exactly SRB properties 1 and 2. Fair executions exist for every protocol (round robin, SRBProtocol.rrExec_fair). SWMR shared memory (SWMR.lean, §3.2). Every access (append-write of the own object, read of one object) is an atomic step under an arbitrary interleaving. Byzantine processes overwrite their own objects arbitrarily; there is no bound on |F|. Fairness: correct processes take infinitely many steps. Fair executions exist. Theorem 1 (TrInc.lean) is proved at the level of the SRB log of one sender. A correct checker's delivered messages form a prefix of that log; the stored attestations are a function of that prefix. Claim of §4.2 (Alg3.lean) and Appendix A (AppendixRB.lean) are formalized at the level of the end-of-round data: §4.2: who forwarded what, who heard whom before compiling L1 proofs, and who issued L1 proofs; Appendix A: phase-1/phase-2 senders and phase-2 contents, with one common content per sender (reliable broadcast). These capture the safety arguments of Lemmas 3–4 and the Appendix exactly. Liveness (Lemmas 2 and 3 Case 2) is formalized only through its counting core. Main results in Lean. LCLs on Trees Without Knowledge of n — PODC 2026 Alkida Balliu, Sebastian Brandt, Fabian Kuhn, Dennis Olivetti, Timothé Picavet, Gustav Schmid. The Distributed Complexity Landscape on Trees Depends on the Knowledge About the Network Size. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815947. Formalized version: arXiv 2605.12787 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 1 holds as stated: if the nodes know nothing about n and IDs are arbitrary natural numbers, k-hierarchical 2½-colouring needs Ω(n) rounds for every k ≥ 1. The paper's induction has a gap, because the parity surgery needs the induction hypothesis in the modified graph Ĝ but the hypothesis is stated only for the lower bound graph G; the fix runs the induction over a class of graphs closed under the surgery. We checked only Theorem 1: Theorem 2, Theorems 3–7 and the landscape as a whole, which is the paper's main point, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proof of Theorem 1, choice of z: property 2 ("u, v at distance at least 2T_i + 1") does not guarantee a node z at distance > T_i from both. The chosen u, v (at distance T_i + 1 from the two ends) are about 0.8 ℓ_i apart, so such a z exists. Typos T_i = ℓ_i/10 need not be an integer. The proof uses "distance exactly T_i + 1" and round counts ≤ T_i; we use ⌊ℓ_i/10⌋. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 1, property 4 of the induction (parity surgery) The parity surgery applies the induction hypothesis in the modified graph Ĝ, but the hypothesis was proved only for runs on the lower bound graph G. Impact. Theorem 1 stands, but not by a local edit: the induction has to be restated and proved again over a class of graphs closed under the surgery (claim, hostOK_hat, emb_hat_child). Details. The induction claims properties 1–4 "by running A on G", where G is the k-hierarchical lower bound graph. To show property 4 for a level-i path, the proof removes a path node z (with its subtree) and joins its two neighbours. This gives Ĝ. Then u and v keep their colours, but the parity of their distance changes, "thus the produced 2-colouring cannot be proper". That step needs the u–v path to be properly 2-coloured in Ĝ, and hence needs that no node on it outputs E. Constraint 4 rules out E only if all lower-level neighbours output D in Ĝ. The algorithm is run afresh on Ĝ, and Ĝ is not a k-hierarchical lower bound graph (one level-i path is one node short), so the induction hypothesis says nothing about it. Lower-level nodes next to the cut can see the change. Repair. Prove the claim for every level-j component of the lower bound graph embedded in any tree of a suitable class (a "host"). The class must be closed under the surgery and the levels of the 2½-colouring problem must stay the designed levels in it (claim, hostOK_hat, emb_hat_child). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic synchronous LOCAL model on finite trees. A network (Inst) is a finite tree whose nodes are natural numbers: the node names are the unique identifiers. There is no bound on the ID space, and no other input; in particular n is unknown. An algorithm (Alg) is given extensionally by the round time I v in which node v stops and its output out I v. Locality (Alg.IsLocal): whether v has stopped by round t, and its output if so, depend only on the edges incident to nodes at distance ≤ t from v (CSLib Cslib.Local.GAgree … (t+1)). This is one hop more than a node learns in t LOCAL rounds, so more algorithms are local and the lower bound is (slightly) stronger. Ω(n) is Knuth's: there are ε > 0 and n₀ such that for every n > n₀ some n-node tree has a node that runs for ≥ εn rounds. The algorithm only has to be correct on trees of maximum degree ≤ Δ, for any Δ ≥ 3. The hard instances have maximum degree 3. Main results in Lean. Lemma 5.3 claims that in a graph of maximum degree Δ whose degree-Δ vertices are independent, some matching covers all degree-Δ vertices. It fails for Δ = 0: a single isolated vertex has degree Δ and no matching covers it (lemma_5_3_false_of_zero). Algorithm 2 uses the lemma only for Δ ≥ 8, and for Δ ≥ 1 the lemma holds (lemma_5_3_matching): Hall's theorem gives every degree-Δ vertex its own neighbour using only "maximum degree ≤ Δ", and the independence hypothesis then makes the chosen edges pairwise disjoint. Proof of Theorem 2: "for Δ < 7 apply Lemma 5.1 … otherwise, for Δ ≥ 8" leaves out Δ = 7. Lemma 5.1 covers it. Lemma 5.2 says "the maximum degree of DG is 2" where "at most 2" is meant. Proof of Theorem 3: the step "sequentially identifies edges connecting two vertices of degree Δ and colors them using any color from the other party's palette" is correct only if degree means the current degree in the remaining graph. With the current-degree reading, the one Algorithm 2 uses and the one we formalize (exists_deferral), the deferred edges form a maximal matching and one colour of the other palette suffices. If it means the degree in the party's graph, all such edges are deferred at once and they need not be colourable with Δ colours: take Alice holding a triangle with Δ = 2. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Two-party, edge-partition model (Section 3.1). The vertex set (Fin n for the protocols), n and Δ are public. Alice holds A : SimpleGraph V, Bob holds B, with Disjoint A B, and G = A ⊔ B has maximum degree ≤ Δ (ValidInput). This is more general than the paper's "maximum degree exactly Δ". Each party outputs colours for its own edges. The outputs are correct if the combined colouring is a proper edge colouring with colours < k (SolvesEdgeColoring). Colourings are maps Sym2 V → ℕ. Deterministic protocols, no randomness. Zero communication (Theorem 3): each output is a function of that party's own edge set. One round (Theorem 2): a OneRoundProtocol where both parties simultaneously send a bit string and then output (the paper's footnote 1 convention). Cost is the total number of bits. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733527. Formalized version: arXiv 2505.17891 v1 (extended version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The gather part of the paper holds after local repairs: Lemma 3.2 is true (the 30-process system of Figure 1 satisfies B³ and makes the quorum-replacement gather, Algorithm 2, miss a common core), and the new constant-round asymmetric gather (Algorithm 3) is correct, with Lemmas 3.3–3.8 holding once Definition 3.1, line 62 and the proofs of Lemmas 3.5 and 3.7 are fixed. The claim in Appendix A that the quorum-replacement pattern reaches a common core within log n − 1 rounds is false, but it is an unproved side remark about the approach the paper rejects, and nothing depends on it. The DAG consensus protocol of Section 4 is not formalized, so that part of the paper's point was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Appendix A, "common core in log n − 1 rounds" (also "would require log n rounds", §3) The quorum-replacement pattern does not reach a common core in log n − 1 rounds: for n = 8 (log₂ 8 − 1 = 2 rounds) a fault-free B³ system has a run with no common core after 2 rounds (log_rounds_claim_false, two_rounds_five_processes). Impact. An unproved side remark about the gather the paper rejects; Lemma 3.2 and the new gather (Algorithm 3) are unaffected. We proved no corrected round bound. Details. Appendix A says that, by quorum consistency, the common core "can be obtained in log n − 1 rounds" of receiving messages from a quorum and sending them on. Counterexample: 8 processes with single quorums {1,2,4}, {3,4,5}, {1,4,5}, {1,5}, {1,3,4}, plus three processes that copy the first quorum. The quorums pairwise intersect, so the canonical fail-prone system satisfies B³. All processes are correct and each one hears exactly its own quorum. After 2 rounds no quorum lies inside every output. After 3 rounds a common core does exist. The first five processes alone already defeat 2 rounds (5 < 2³), so the §3.2 heuristic "3 rounds suffice below 16 = 2⁴ processes" does not carry over to 2 rounds. Rounds are counted as the paper counts them: "the 3 rounds of Algorithm 2", which waits for a quorum three times. With the floor reading, ⌊log₂ 30⌋ − 1 = 3, the claim is refuted by the paper's own Figure 1. 🔧 Definition 3.1 (asymmetric gather, no termination) Definition 3.1 has no termination property, so a protocol that never ag-delivers satisfies it. Impact. Lemma 3.8 and the text clearly intend that every maximal-guild member ag-delivers, and Algorithm 3 does. Adding the property is enough: we prove termination too (termination, lemma_3_8). 🔧 Algorithm 3, line 62 (delivery trigger) Line 62 ("upon receiving DISTRIBUTET from a quorum, ag-deliver U") counts raw receptions, also those with T ⊄ Sᵢ that line 60 has not incorporated, so U may lack the core. Impact. One added condition fixes the pseudocode, and Lemma 3.8 is proved for it (lemma_3_8). Repair. Count only DISTRIBUTET messages already incorporated by line 60, that is, those with T ⊆ Sᵢ. We model this reading (QualT). ✏️ Slips §2.4: "2f − 1 processes" should be 2f + 1. Lemma 3.5: the statement's "the processes of Qᵢ receive DISTRIBUTES before sending DISTRIBUTET" only makes sense for the correct members of Qᵢ. We prove that version. Line 148 of Algorithm 6 commits with "a quorum Q ∈ Qⱼ for some Qⱼ ∈ ℚ", a quorum of any process. The text says a quorum of pᵢ, and Lemma 4.2's intersection argument needs that. Not checked in Lean. Typos §3.2 says "3 rounds, fewer than 16 processes", then "n rounds, fewer than 2ⁿ processes". These two statements do not match: 2³ = 8. §3.2 says Algorithm 2 gives a common core "after four rounds". Elsewhere it speaks of three rounds; "four" presumably also counts the input broadcast, as DAG-Rider's 4-round waves do. With that count the "log n − 1" claim is off by even more. Lemma 4.3 writes strong_path(u, v) from round 1 to round 4, so the direction is reversed. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.5 (wise vs. maximal-guild process) The proof goes "all quorums contain a wise process (Lemma 7 of Alpos et al.), so a wise process sent CONFIRM; apply Lemma 3.4", but Lemma 3.4 needs a maximal-guild member, and a wise process need not be one. Impact. The lemma stands for the correct members of the quorum (see Slips), with one replacement fact (lemma_3_5, exists_candidate). Repair. A quorum Q of a guild member g meets g's quorum inside the guild, so Q contains a guild member. 🔧 Lemma 3.7 (possibly Byzantine intersection process) The proof picks a process in Qᵢ ∩ Qⱼ and uses that it put Sᵢ into its T, but that process may be Byzantine. Impact. The lemma stands, with a one-line change (lemma_3_7). Repair. Both pᵢ and pⱼ are wise, so consistency against the actual faulty set gives a correct process in the intersection. 🔧 Lemma 3.2 (Appendix A, "easy way to observe" no common core) The argument is a non sequitur: "every S set has an element in [16,30]" plus "every U misses some element of [16,30]" does not imply that no S lies in all Us. Impact. The conclusion is still true; checked directly (fig1_no_core). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous message passing in CSLib-style Cslib.Byzantine.AsyncBroadcast (staged in Podc/). Interleaving semantics, authenticated channels, Byzantine faults with adaptive corruption (stronger than the paper's static faulty set F). The faulty set of an execution is the set of processes corrupted at some time, and wise processes and guilds are defined relative to it. No randomness. Asymmetric trust (new, Podc/Computability/Distributed/AsymmetricQuorum.lean): fail-prone systems F i, B³, asymmetric quorum systems (consistency + availability), kernels (all sets meeting every quorum of i), wise processes, guilds, the maximal guild. The asymmetric reliable broadcast of the inputs is a val message. For Byzantine senders its consistency and totality towards the guild are hypotheses on the execution (RBC). These are exactly the guarantees of the primitive of Alpos et al. that the paper uses. Validity and integrity for correct senders follow from the model. Algorithms 2 and 3 are given by their handler guards. Liberal choices (e.g. which received T sets go into U) only add behaviours, so the safety results transfer. Liveness uses weak fairness: messages between correct processes are delivered, and a correct process whose guard for a message holds forever sends it. Lemma 3.2 and the round claims: an explicit fault-free run of the r-round quorum-replacement gather (r = 3 is Algorithm 2) is reachable, with all processes ag-delivering. All processes form the maximal guild. Every possible core S (a set with a pair for each member of a quorum) misses some output. In a fault-free run every arb-delivery order can happen, so these runs are genuine. Algorithm 3: results hold for every nonempty guild G with RBC for G, in particular for the maximal guild (as in the paper). Main results in Lean. Local Advice and Local Decompression — PODC 2024 Alkida Balliu, Sebastian Brandt, Fabian Kuhn, Krzysztof Nowicki, Dennis Olivetti, Eva Rotenberg, Jukka Suomela. Brief Announcement: Local Advice and Local Decompression. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662805. Formalized version: the full version Distributed Computation with Local Advice, arXiv 2405.04519 v2 (22 Aug 2025); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The 3-colouring result holds: every 3-colourable graph of maximum degree Δ can be 3-coloured in O(Δ⁹) rounds with 1 bit of advice per node (Theorem 30), and Lemmas 31–34 hold, including the Lovász-Local-Lemma step of Lemma 32. Theorem 5 (advice algorithms can be made order-invariant), on which the ETH lower bound rests, also holds, but its proof ignores that LOCAL nodes know n and it took a new Ramsey argument; the rest is slips: the cited Lemma 1 is false in the corner d = 0, and the decoder's description has a typo. The other main results (sub-exponential growth, balanced orientations, Δ-colouring and the ETH bound itself) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 1 (symmetric local lemma, cited) for d = 0. With the condition e·p·d ≤ 1, one event of probability 1 depends on no other event and satisfies e·1·0 ≤ 1, yet it always occurs (lemma_1_as_stated_false). This is a degenerate corner of a cited textbook result: the standard condition is e·p·(d+1) ≤ 1, and the only use (Lemma 32, d ≤ 48Δ⁸, p ≤ 1/(144Δ⁸)) satisfies it as well (used instead: Cslib.Probability.exists_forall_not_of_symmetric). Decoder of Theorem 34 (page 42, "receive color 1"). The decoder takes x as the smallest identifier "among all nodes in the (30Δ³)-hop neighborhood of w in C(u) that receive color 1", but no node of C(u) has colour 1; it must be "receive bit 1". The intent is evident from the overview of Appendix D and the proof of Theorem 34; that proof drops the qualifier altogether ("the smallest-ID node among all nodes in the neighborhood"). Typos The existence of a greedy 3-colouring of a 3-colourable graph is used but not shown. It is easy: take a proper colouring with minimal colour sum (exists_isGreedy). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 5 (order-invariance: the proof ignores the knowledge of n) The paper's LOCAL model (Section 3.1) gives every node n, but the proof treats A as one map from labelled radius-T views to outputs and then runs it on a padded graph H with N ≫ n nodes, where it behaves as the different map A_N. Impact. Theorem 5 stands with a new core step, and the resulting A' does not even depend on n (theorem_5). Details. The proof colours s-subsets of identifiers by that map and takes an infinite monochromatic set I. Then it runs A on a graph H made of many copies of G, with N ≫ n nodes and N chosen after I. If A reads n, the behaviour on H is that of A_N, and I was built for the wrong map. Repair. For each M, apply finite Ramsey on {1, …, N_M} with N_M = (R(M) + M)! to A_{N_M}. That gives a homogeneous M-set whose behaviour is one of finitely many types. By pigeonhole one type F* occurs for infinitely many M. For a graph with n nodes take such an M ≥ n + s; then n | N_M, so H can be exactly N_M / n copies of G. (theorem_5) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. 3-colouring (Theorems 30, 34; Lemmas 31–33). Deterministic synchronous LOCAL with unique identifiers and no failures. The nodes of every graph are the elements of a fixed finite linearly ordered type V, and the order is the identifier order. An R-round algorithm is a function SimpleGraph V → (V → Bool) → V → Fin 3 whose output at u depends only on the radius-R view of u (CSLib Cslib.Local.IsLocal: edges at nodes at distance < R, labels at distance ≤ R). The advice is one bit per node, and the algorithm knows the degree bound Δ. The paper's colours 1, 2, 3 are 0, 1, 2. Components of G_{2,3} and distances dist_C are those of the graph H23 G φ on V, where colour-1 nodes are isolated. Nodes in different components are at distance ⊤, so the per-component ruling sets R_C merge into one set R. Theorem 5. Identifiers are natural numbers. An instance is a finite node set Vs ⊆ ℕ, a graph on ℕ with edges inside Vs, and node inputs from a finite alphabet. The algorithm A : ℕ → SimpleGraph ℕ → (ℕ → In × (Fin β → Bool)) → ℕ → Out gets the number of nodes n as first argument, and each A n is T-local. The paper's "identifiers in {1,…,poly(n)}" is abstracted as any admissibility predicate that accepts every {1,…,N}. "Component-wise defined" means: a valid solution restricts, along an isomorphism onto a union of components, to a valid solution. The graph family must be closed under disjoint unions of copies. The conclusion is stronger than the paper's: A' is order-invariant, does not know n, and works for arbitrary identifiers. Randomness appears only inside a proof (Lemma 32): the LLL on a uniform finite product space, where probabilities are counts. Main results in Lean. The MBroadcast Abstraction — PODC 2023 Mathilde Déprés, Achour Mostéfaoui, Matthieu Perrin, Michel Raynal. Brief Announcement: The MBroadcast Abstraction. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594569. Formalized version: the brief announcement (Theorems 1, 2, Property 1). For the converse direction we used the algorithm and proof of the extended version (DISC 2023, Send/Receive Patterns Versus Read/Write Patterns in Crash-Prone Asynchronous Distributed Systems, Algorithm 2 and App. A), since the brief announcement gives no algorithm for it. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Every result we checked holds: Property 1, Theorem 1 (Algorithm 2 builds MBroadcast from causal message delivery when t < n/2), Theorem 2 (Algorithm 3 builds a linearizable, terminating MWMR register on top of MBroadcast, for any number of crashes), and the converse (MBroadcast, even a FIFO and reliable version, from atomic SWMR registers, for any number of crashes). The only flaw is the abstract's wording of mutual ordering, "p delivers first m and then m′": read literally (p delivers both messages), this property is too weak, and then Property 1 and Theorem 2 are false. Everything holds under the wording of Section 3, with the reading the paper itself uses elsewhere for "deliver m′ before m". Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Abstract and Section 1, paraphrase of mutual ordering (the meaning of "before"). The main text says "it is not possible that p mdelivers m before m′ and p′ mdelivers m′ before m". The abstract paraphrases it as "it is not possible for p to deliver first m and then m′ while p′ delivers first m′ and then m". The pattern MP1 of the full version is also drawn with both processes delivering both messages. The results need the stronger reading: "when p mdelivers its m, it has not (yet, or ever) mdelivered m′". This is the reading of the paper's own FIFO and causal properties ("no process mdelivers m′ before m"), of Property 1 ("p′ cannot return … before it has mdelivered m") and of the introduction ("p′ does not ignore p"). We formalize the strong reading (DelivBefore). Under the literal reading both claims fail. Take two processes. p₀ writes 1 with Algorithm 3: it mbroadcasts synch and write(1, ⟨1, p₀⟩), mdelivers both itself, returns, and crashes. Then p₁ reads: its synch and its write-back of (0, ⊥) are mdelivered only by p₁ itself, and the read returns 0. No process mdelivers both messages of a pair, so the literal mutual ordering holds vacuously. Validity and no-duplication hold too, and Global CS-termination is respected since p₀ is faulty. Yet Property 1 fails, and the history "write(1) completes, then read() returns 0" is not linearizable (property1_false_weak, alg3_weak_not_linearizable). Distributed Computing with Rules of Thumb — PODC 2011 Aaron D. Jaggard, Michael Schapira, Rebecca N. Wright. Distributed computing with rules of thumb. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993870. Formalized version: arXiv 0910.1585 v2 (Distributed Computing with Adaptive Heuristics, the ICS 2011 / full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The main impossibility result, Theorem 4.1, is true for deterministic, self-independent, stationary bounded-recall reaction functions (the version restated and proved in Appendix F) and for non-stationary 1-recall ones, and Examples 4.2 and 4.3 are correct. Its announced extensions to randomized reaction functions and to non-stationary k-recall with k ≥ 2 are not established, and the game-theoretic application (Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.2, Theorem B.2) holds only for equilibria that are fixed points of the best-response map. The other applications of Section 5 and Sections 6–8 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 4.1 for randomized reaction functions (not formalized) The main text and the end of Appendix B.1 say Theorem 4.1 also holds for randomized reaction functions, but the paper never defines convergence of randomized dynamics (every realization, or almost surely) and gives no proof. Impact. The claim is neither proved nor refuted: the proof in Appendix F treats deterministic functions only, and nothing we proved covers the randomized case. We formalize deterministic reaction functions. ⚠️ Corollary 5.2, Theorem B.2 and Theorem 5.1 (best-response dynamics) With "consistent tie-breaking" a pure Nash equilibrium need not be a stable state, so a 2×2 game with two pure equilibria, one weakly dominated, has best-response dynamics that always converge (corollary_5_2_false, theorem_5_1_false). Impact. The game-theoretic application fails as stated; Theorem 4.1 is unaffected. What is true, and what we prove, is the statement for two equilibria that are fixed points of the best-response map; this is automatic when best responses are unique (corollary_5_2, corollary_5_2_of_unique). Details. Corollary 5.2 says that if a game has two pure Nash equilibria, then best-response dynamics with consistent tie-breaking can fail to converge asynchronously. Counterexample: a 2×2 game. Player 0 gets 1 unless it plays y against x, so x weakly dominates y. Player 1 gets 1 iff it matches player 0. The pure equilibria are (x,x) and (y,y). Break ties towards x. Then player 0 always plays x, player 1 copies player 0, and every fair dynamics converges to (x,x). The proof applies Theorem 4.1 to the Nash equilibria, but (y,y) is not a fixed point of the tie-broken best-response map, so it is not a stable state. The same example refutes Theorem 5.1 ("all bounded-recall self-independent dynamics can oscillate"). ⚠️ Theorem 4.1 for non-stationary reaction functions The main text says Theorem 4.1 holds "even if nodes' reaction functions are not stationary", but the valency proof of Appendix F does not cover this case; we repair it for 1-recall (theorem_4_1_oneRecall), and for k-recall with k ≥ 2 it remains open. Impact. The stationary version (the one Appendix F restates and proves) holds. The non-stationary claim is established for 1-recall and unestablished, but not refuted, for k ≥ 2. Details. The valency argument (Appendix F) builds a fair run in which every history is bivalent, meaning at least two limits are still possible. For stationary functions such a run cannot converge: once the run sits at a limit c for k steps, c is a fixed point, so only c remains reachable. For non-stationary functions this step fails. A run can converge to c while every history stays bivalent, because c may be reproduced only at the time steps at which the run happens to activate the nodes. Appendix F.7 (Theorem F.14) avoids the problem by quietly changing what a stable state is ("a vector of actions and a time after which it is a fixed point"). That is not the notion of Section 3, and the proof also assumes finite action spaces. Appendix F.8 extends it to k-recall only by a sketch. A brute-force search over small periodic systems found no counterexample for k ≥ 2. Repair. The FLP-style extension lemma holds for non-stationary k-recall. Non-convergence follows once the limit of every fair dynamics is eventually absorbing (not_convergent_of_absorbing). We prove that absorption property for 1-recall functions with arbitrary action spaces: a node that deviates infinitely often could be made to oscillate fairly (absorbingAfter_of_oneRecall, theorem_4_1_oneRecall). ✏️ Slips Section 3, "stable state" (unfair schedules). Section 3 calls a a stable state when some (s⁰, σ)-dynamics converges to a, for a schedule σ that need not be fair, and with this literal reading Theorem 4.1 is false (stableState_literal_reading). Take the system in which every node always plays x. It is historyless, self-independent and convergent, but the unfair dynamics that only ever activates node 0 converges to (x,y). "Stable state" must mean the limit of a fair dynamics, as the paper's remark that in the historyless case the stable states are exactly the fixed points shows; we use it. Typos Section 3 types f(i,t) : H_t → Δ(A_i), but the dynamics applies f(i,w+1) to s⁰ ∈ H_w. The input is H_{t−1}. Section 3 writes s(t) = a for a history s(t); it means the last profile. "Safe" (Appendix F, Example 4.2) is used for "convergent". In the proof of Lemma F.12, case e = e_i, e' = W, "the second color equality" should be the first one. Lemma F.13's "activate v first" suffices only for 1-recall. For k-recall v must be activated k times, as F.8 notes. Def. F.4 defines a "fair extension" as an arbitrary finite extension; the fairness actually used is the one in the proof of Lemma F.8. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Appendix F.6–F.7 (act-and-tell translation) The act-and-tell translation lets W reveal an empty set of reactions, and the "number of time steps" argument then counts steps with an empty activation set, which Section 3 forbids. Impact. One condition closes the gap: we only allow W when something is pending, and the extension lemma still holds (System.exists_bivalent_after). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Model.lean) Finitely many nodes ι (a Fintype). Node i has an arbitrary action type A i, so infinite action spaces are allowed. A history h ∈ H_w, w ≥ 1, is stored as the current profile plus the earlier ones, most recent first. h.time = w. Reaction functions are deterministic: F.f i t h is node i's action at time step t after the history h. A schedule σ : ℕ → Finset ι activates the nonempty set σ t at absolute time t. The (s⁰, σ)-dynamics F.run s⁰ σ starts at time w + 1 with any initial history. Activated nodes react simultaneously, so the model is synchronous lock-step with an adversarial asynchronous activation pattern. There are no failures and no randomness, and monitoring is perfect. Fair σ: every node is activated infinitely often. Convergent: for every initial history and every fair schedule, the profile is eventually constant. IsStableState a: some fair dynamics converges to a. Restrictions, as in Section 3: SelfIndependent: the reaction depends only on the other nodes' actions. HasRecall i k: on histories with at least k entries, the reaction at each time step depends only on the k most recent profiles. Stationary i k: one function of the k most recent profiles for all time steps. Historyless: Stationary i 1. Proof structure. Valency.lean: the stable colouring F.lims h P, the set of limits of fair dynamics from h whose next activation set contains P. It also proves that two histories differing only in node j's actions become equivalent after j is activated alone k times. FLP.lean: the act-and-tell model, in which e_j adds j to the pending set and W reveals a nonempty pending set. It proves the extension lemma exists_bivalent_after (Lemmas F.8 + F.12) for non-stationary k-recall functions. We prove it directly in this model rather than through the abstract IoD framework. Bivalence.lean: an initial bivalent history (Lemma F.13 and its F.7/F.8 variants), and segments. Concat.lean: concatenation of segments into a fair schedule (the iteration of Theorem F.9). Formalized version: arXiv 2106.01036 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The centralized result of Section 2 holds: for every ε ∈ (0,1) and integer κ ≥ 2, Algorithm 1, with the wrong variable of line 18 corrected, builds a (1+ε, 30(34 log κ/ε)^{log κ − 1})-emulator with at most n^{1+1/κ} edges (leading constant 1), in every order of consideration, and it is ultra-sparse (n + o(n) edges) for κ ≈ log n · log log n. CC vs. DSM complexity separation — PODC 2011 Wojciech Golab. A complexity separation between the cache-coherent and distributed shared memory models. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993822. Formalized version: arXiv 1109.5153 v1 (full version; numbering follows it). Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The main result holds: the signaling problem has an O(1) RMR solution in the CC model (Section 5), but no deterministic terminating read/write solution with O(1) amortized RMR complexity in the DSM model (Theorem 6.2), and we proved both, and the separation, in Lean. The construction in the proof of Lemma 6.10 does not preserve the regularity invariant, so saving the lower bound took a weaker invariant and changed rounds. Corollary 6.14 drops the word "terminating", which its own proof assumes, and its extension to CAS and LL/SC was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Lemma 6.10 (regularity invariant, Definition 6.6 condition 3) The construction in the proof of Lemma 6.10 does not preserve condition 3 of regularity (the last of several writers of a variable is finished), so Lemma 6.10 as stated is unestablished: neither proved nor refuted here. Impact. Theorem 6.2 is unaffected: a variant of Lemma 6.10 with a weaker invariant (SoleW) is proved and is all that Theorem 6.2 needs (Algorithm.lemma_6_10). Details. Condition 3 requires: if a variable v has several writers and the last one is p, then p is finished. In the erasing case, the paper removes conflicts only with variables "already written by active processes". A kept unstable process may still write a variable previously written by a finished process. Example: a rolled-forward process r wrote a shared flag G, and in a later round an unstable process writes G as its next RMR. The result violates condition 3. Finished processes cannot be erased, and such writers need not be a constant fraction, so erasing them is not an option either. Under condition 3 the claim "for each process we add at most one edge" is also wrong. A variable whose last writer is finished may have many active earlier writers (the processes left behind by a roll-forward), and a new write to it conflicts with all of them. Repair. We replace condition 3 by a weaker one: after erasing the (active) last writer of v, the last writer of v is not active (SoleW). This condition is preserved by every step of the construction. It gives out-degree ≤ 1 for the write conflicts (≤ 2 together with touching). It is all that Lemma 6.13 and the roll-forward need: erasing active processes reverts every variable to a value written by a finished process (SoleW.erase_writer_not_mem, Algorithm.round). ✏️ Slips Corollary 6.14 omits "terminating". It claims the DSM lower bound for "any deterministic algorithm", but without termination it fails: an algorithm whose Poll() busy-waits forever on the caller's own module solves the problem with no RMRs at all (corollary_6_14_needs_terminating). The corollary covers "any deterministic algorithm" using reads, writes and CAS or LL/SC. In the counterexample Poll() busy-waits forever on a variable in the caller's own module and Signal() returns at once. Specification 4.1 only constrains calls that return, so this algorithm solves the problem, yet no execution has an RMR in the DSM model. The algorithm uses only reads, so it is also a "reads, writes, and CAS" algorithm. The corollary's own proof starts from "some deterministic terminating algorithm", and the fix is one word. Theorem 6.2 is unaffected. Proof of Lemma 6.10: "|Fin(H_{i+1})| ≤ |Fin(H_i)| + 1 ≤ i" should end with i + 1. Proof of Lemma 6.12: "erase all active processes except ⌊N^{1/3^c}/2⌋ unstable ones" should say stable. Lemma 6.13: "at most k processes participate in H" and "RMRs incurred in H" should say H′. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 6.13 and the roll-forward of Lemma 6.10 (termination in unfair histories) Stable processes "complete any pending call to Poll()", s's Signal() "must eventually terminate" and the rolled-forward process completes its Poll(), but the histories in question are not fair, because the other active processes are stopped in mid-call, so termination does not apply directly. Impact. Erasing the other active processes first makes the solo runs legitimate (Algorithm.final_stable). Repair. Our proof runs s solo in the history where all stable processes are erased: there every other participant has terminated. It never needs the pending polls. We prove: for each stable p, s's solo Signal() accesses p's module or a variable last written by p. Otherwise p's next Poll() would return true after a run without any signal (Algorithm.final_stable). 🔧 Lemma 6.13 (one RMR per stable process) "s performs one such RMR for each stable process" needs the sets "p's module ∪ variables last written by p" to be pairwise disjoint over the stable processes p, which the paper does not say. Impact. A missing step: the disjointness follows from conditions 2 and 3 of regularity (Algorithm.final_stable). 🔧 Lemma 6.13 (choice of s) The paper's choice "a process whose module is not written" does not guarantee that s is outside Par(H). Impact. One extra condition on s, available by the same count for N large (Algorithm.final_stable). 🔧 Theorem 6.2 (the constant k) The theorem promises a constant k, but in the branch of the proof that goes through Lemma 6.11 the paper's k = c + ⌊N^{1/3^c}/2⌋ is not constant. Impact. The theorem holds: using only c² + 1 unstable processes there gives k ≤ c² + c + 1 in every branch (theorem_6_2). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory with N processes Fin N, deterministic programs and atomic reads and writes of variables V. Algorithm has the shape of Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl specialised to registers. Each variable lives in one process' module (home, the DSM placement chosen by the algorithm). An execution is a list of events that record what each step did: invocation, read with the value read, write, or return. Valid means every event is a legal step of its process and every read returns the last written value. Recording the accessed variables and values makes the erasing argument (Lemma 6.7) a statement about filtering a list (Algorithm.valid_erase). There are no crashes. A process that stops in mid-call is a prefix; a process that terminates stays idle forever. Which call an idle process makes next is chosen by the environment. DSM RMR: an access to a variable outside the process' own module (rmr). CC RMR: the paper's loose definition (ccRMR). A read is free if the process read the variable before and no other process has written it since; every other access costs one. Specification 4.1 is required only in executions with at most one call to Signal() (one signaler). Waiters may stop after any number of polls. Participants are processes with at least one event, invocations included. Both choices make the lower bound stronger. Termination follows Section 2: in every fair infinite history every call completes (Algorithm.Terminating). The proof uses only a weaker solo form (SoloTerminating), which we derive from it. The lower bound is existential over executions: the adversary chooses the schedule and which procedures are called. Theorem 6.2's quantifiers are implicit (standard asymptotic convention; not counted as a mistake). The statement fixes A (hence N) and quantifies "for any constant c". For a fixed N the claim is false: a signaler that writes all N per-process flags makes at most N − 1 RMRs per history, so c = N violates it (easy example, not formalized). The intended reading is the standard one: c is independent of N, and the claim holds for all N ≥ N₀(c). The proof says "if N is large enough", and we formalize exactly that. Main results in Lean. Space-Optimal Naming in Population Protocols — PODC 2018 Janna Burman, Joffroy Beauquier, Devan Sohier. Brief Announcement: Space-Optimal Naming in Population Protocols. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212791. Formalized version: the full version, LRI research report HAL hal-01790517v3 ("Space-Optimal Naming in Population Protocols", 21 pp., also DISC 2019); the 2-page brief announcement has no proofs. Numbering follows the full version. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All formalized propositions hold, for P ≥ 2: the impossibilities (Propositions 1, 3, 4, Theorem 11), the sink property (Proposition 6), Lemma 2 and the protocols of Propositions 12, 13 and 14. The proof of Theorem 11, the subtlest result, has a real gap, and we replace it with a different adversary argument; the summary in Table 1 and the introduction leaves out that without a leader, symmetric naming is impossible for n = 2 agents whatever the number of states. Propositions 16 and 17 and the with-leader cells of Proposition 12 were not checked, so the classification is checked only in part. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Table 1 and §1 (no leader, global fairness, symmetric rules: "P + 1 states"). The summary says naming without leader under global fairness is possible with P + 1 states, but with n = 2 agents no symmetric leaderless protocol, with any number of states, names them (not_solvesGlobal_of_card_two, not_solvesWeak_of_card_two). From a uniform configuration of two agents, both orientations of the only pair apply (s, s) → (s', s'), so every reachable configuration is uniform. This holds under any fairness. Only the summary is affected: Proposition 13 itself states the restriction n > 2 and is correct (prop13_solvesGlobal). Since the model asks for one protocol that works for all n ≤ P, this table cell (and "the norm is P + 1 states" in §1) holds only for populations of at least 3 agents. Propositions 3, 4 and Theorem 11 are false for P = 1 (one state, at most one mobile agent: naming is trivial). All our statements assume P ≥ 2. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 11 (no P-state symmetric naming of non-initialized agents under weak fairness) The proof builds the execution e by alternating segments from the two indistinguishable worlds C⁻ˢ/C (Lemmas 8–10) but never shows that e is weakly fair, and then lets e end in a stable C* through a segment with an idle s-agent that the construction does not provide. Impact. The theorem holds, but the paper's construction cannot be patched locally: it takes a different adversary argument (thm11, thm11_paper). Details. Lemmas 9/10 transfer segments in which the plus world's s-agent stays idle. Every segment the construction produces ends with that agent being reduced. A final segment reaching a named C* (which contains s) can be transferred only if the s-agent was idle there, and nothing ensures this. For Protocol 1 under global fairness the leader must meet the s-agent before it can finish. Also, with arbitrarily initialized mobile agents the "hidden agent" construction of C₁ and C₁⁻ˢ is not needed: both are initial configurations. Repair. Let m be the sink and s ≠ m. Two reduced configurations with the same leader state are related (Rel) if, as multisets, plus + {m} = minus + {s} and minus has no s. A reduced step of the minus world can always be mirrored in the plus world; the roles swap exactly when the minus world creates s (mirror). By weak-fairness correctness, every reachable reduced configuration reaches a named one by reduced steps (exists_rreach_injective), so a driving minus world eventually creates s (drive). The adversary always lets the minus world drive. When the actual execution is the minus world, it first performs the pair that weak fairness requires next; otherwise it follows the other world until the roles swap again. This execution is weakly fair and has two m-agents infinitely often, so it never names the agents (thm11_core, built with exists_weaklyFair_of_phases). 🔧 Proposition 4 and Lemma 2 (stabilized configurations taken as terminal) Lemma 2 and Proposition 4 take for granted that a stabilized configuration is terminal, i.e. that no continuation can change a name, and under weak fairness stabilization of one execution does not give this. Impact. One added fact lets the paper's mirroring go through: correctness implies that a closed named configuration is reachable from every reachable configuration (exists_stablyGood_of_weaklyFair). Repair. Our proof of Proposition 4 mirrors the leader's interactions in a closed named configuration (prop4_core). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic population protocols on the complete interaction graph, CSLib's Cslib.PopulationProtocol.Protocol with labelled configurations. Asynchronous, no failures, adversarial scheduler. Weak fairness: every unordered pair of agents interacts infinitely often (CSLib's WeaklyFair). Global fairness: CSLib's GloballyFair on labelled configurations. No randomness. Symmetric protocol: δ q p = (δ p q).swap (IsSymmetric). Leader protocols (LeaderProtocol L Q) have separate rules for mobile–mobile, leader–mobile and mobile–leader interactions and are encoded as a CSLib protocol on L ⊕ Q with agents Option A (none is the leader). The leader's state set L is arbitrary, even infinite; it must be finite only for global fairness. Naming: the names name (state) of the mobile agents are eventually constant and pairwise distinct (SolvesWeak / SolvesGlobal, for every fair execution from the allowed initial configurations). The name is an arbitrary function of the state; for P-state protocols it is shown to be injective (Lemma 2). Initializations: arbitrary (Set.univ, initArb), uniform ({fun _ => q₀}, initUniform), initialized leader with arbitrary mobile agents (initLeader), arbitrary leader with uniform mobile agents. "For every population size n ≤ P" is quantified over finite agent types. The impossibilities use only the sizes actually needed (P, or P - 1 and P), which makes them stronger. Main results in Lean. The k-Bakery — PODC 2010 Robert Danek. The k-Bakery: Local-Spin k-Exclusion Using Non-atomic Reads and Writes. PODC 2010. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835707. Formalized version: the author's 9-page copy (no arXiv version); the proofs the paper omits (Theorem 9, the CC part of Lemma 7, Theorem 10) are taken from Danek's PhD thesis (Toronto, 2010, Chapter 5: Figures 5.3, 5.5, 5.6, Theorems 5.9, 5.20, 5.33). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The non-atomic algorithm of Figure 3 — the variant named in the title — violates k-exclusion: with safe registers, 3 processes and k = 1, two processes end up in the critical section together (NonAtomic.counterexample), and no repair is proved. The two algorithms for atomic reads and writes are correct: Theorems 8 and 9 (k-exclusion, starvation freedom with up to k − 1 crashes, k-FCFS, FIFE, Θ(N) RMRs per passage in the DSM and CC models) are fully proved. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 10 (Figure 3, non-atomic reads and writes) Figure 3 does not satisfy k-exclusion: for N = 3 processes y, p, r and k = 1 there is a legal execution with safe registers after which y and p are both in the CS (NonAtomic.counterexample). Impact. The title's claim of a k-exclusion algorithm with non-atomic reads and writes is refuted for the paper's algorithm. The atomic results (Theorems 8 and 9) are unaffected. The thesis' Theorem 5.33 (same algorithm, Figure 5.6) is false for the same reason. Details. Ticket is a safe register too (the paper duplicates Want and Capture, but not Ticket), so a read of Ticket[r] that overlaps a write of r may return any value, even 0. Line 44 keeps an old capture value Capture[r][p], written in an earlier passage of r, until p's ticket catches up with it. The execution (246 steps): y starts its first passage and begins writing Ticket[y] := 1; meanwhile r chooses its ticket, its read of Ticket[y] returns 100, so r gets ticket 101. y (ticket 1) goes through the CS and leaves. Then r goes through the CS; at line 45 it captures y and p with Capture[r][·] := 101. r starts a second passage and stops in the middle of writing Ticket[r] := 102. y starts its second passage; its read of Ticket[r] returns 0, so y gets ticket 2 and enters the CS (all announcements it sees are larger). p starts its first passage; its read of Ticket[r] returns 0, so p gets ticket 3. p cannot remove y (whose pair (2, y) is smaller), but it reads the stale Capture[r][p] = 101 > 3, leaves the loop as captured, and enters the CS too. The thesis' proof breaks at Lemma 5.21 ("if Cp → Cq then tp < tq"): "the value that q reads from Ticket[p] is no smaller than tp" fails when p is rewriting Ticket[p] in a later passage (step 4–5: C_r → C_p but t_p = 3 < t_r = 101). Lemma 5.24 then allows a capture by a stale value, and the induction of Lemma 5.25 ("r was CS-qualified earlier, so r violates the lemma earlier") no longer applies, because the processes that block p started their passages after r's passage. Scope. The counterexample uses one particular legal schedule, foreach loops in increasing index order (the paper leaves the order open), and the safe-register semantics the paper states ("if a non-atomic read and write access the same variable concurrently, then the read returns an arbitrary value"). It does not depend on crashes. Repair. Not formalized. Making Ticket an atomic or at least a regular register (a read overlapping a write returns the old or the new value) restores Lemma 5.21, since tickets only grow; whether the rest of the thesis' proof then goes through was not checked. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, N processes of a finite linearly ordered type P (ids break ticket ties). Figure 2 is one transition system with a flag fife: false is the unshaded algorithm (Theorem 8), true the full algorithm (Theorem 9). One shared access per step; the program counter carries the local variables. The adversary schedules processes and picks the next index of every foreach (any order). Crash failures: a process crashes iff it takes finitely many steps and stops outside the NCS; a process resting in the NCS forever is not faulty; a scheduled process in the CS leaves it (so "the CS is finite" for non-faulty processes). No fairness assumption beyond this. Executions are infinite schedules (every process always has an enabled step); safety is also proved for all reachable configurations. Deterministic algorithm, no randomness. RMRs: DSM with Ticket[p], Want[i][p], Capture[i][p] in p's module; CC write-through / write-invalidate caches (cached), reads miss iff no valid copy, every write is an RMR and invalidates the other copies. Figure 3: separate model (NonAtomic.lean) with safe registers: writes take two steps (begin, end), a read overlapping a write returns an adversary-chosen value. This is a sub-model of the paper's interval semantics, so its executions are legal executions of the paper's model. Main results in Lean. Safe s q v r says that q cannot get priority over the pair (v, r) before its next ticket; the set U s v r of unsafe processes only shrinks while v ≤ Ticket[r].
