Partial Reversal Acyclicity — PODC 2011 Tsvetomira Radeva, Nancy Lynch. Brief Announcement: Partial Reversal Acyclicity. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993880. Formalized version: the full version, MIT technical report MIT-CSAIL-TR-2011-022 (April 14, 2011, 20 pp.), whose numbering we follow. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result holds: Gafni–Bertsekas Partial Reversal keeps the graph acyclic in every reachable state (Theorem 5.5), and the proof via the parity-based variant NewPR and the two simulation relations is formalized in full. The only real repair is a changed case condition in Lemma 5.3 (b), which keeps the paper's one-or-two-step scheme. Invariant 3.2's "exactly one of the two parts" fails only for an isolated node, where both parts hold. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Invariant 3.2, "exactly one" of the two parts: for a node without neighbours, both parts hold in every reachable state, so "exactly one" is false (Counterexamples.inv_3_2_exactlyOne_false, two nodes and no edges). "At least one part" holds for every node and "exactly one" holds for every node with a neighbour (PR.inv_3_2, PR.inv_3_2_exactlyOne). Only "at least one" is used later (Corollaries 3.3, 3.4), so nothing else is affected. The case is degenerate whether or not G is assumed connected: for connected G it only occurs in the one-node graph V = {D}. The proof of the base case says "if u is a source, part 1 does not hold because the direction of the edges to all out-nbrs is out". This presumes out-nbrsᵤ ≠ ∅. For an isolated node, list[u] = ∅ and both parts are vacuous. The paper does not assume that G is connected; it only says that nodes need not have a path to the destination. Proofs of Invariant 3.2 (Case 2), Lemma 5.1 (Part 2, Case 2) and Lemma 5.3 (Part 2, Case 2) say that every neighbour of u that takes a step adds itself to list[u]. Only those that reverse their edge to u do: a sink v with u ∈ list[v] ≠ nbrsᵥ keeps that edge. The other neighbours change neither list[u] nor u's edges, so the arguments go through unchanged. Typos §4.2 says Invariants 4.1, 4.2 and Theorem 4.3 conclude "that PR maintains acyclicity"; they are about NewPR. Proof of Lemma 5.1, Part 2, Case 2: "In NewPR, all nodes in T take a step one at a time" should be OneStepPR. The proof also writes R for R0. Proof of Theorem 5.2: the last step should be (s'', reverse(S), s'), not reverse(u). Proof of Lemma 5.3, Part 1: "We prove that t.G' = s.G'" should be t'.G' = s'.G'. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 5.3 (b) (simulation OneStepPR → NewPR), Cases 1 and 2 of Part 1 The step "s.list[w] ⊆ in-nbrs_w (odd parity), so by Corollary 3.4 s.list[w] = in-nbrs_w" fails when s.list[w] = ∅ = out-nbrs_w, and then the prescribed single reverse(w) of NewPR reverses nothing while OneStepPR reverses all of w's edges (Counterexamples.lemma_5_3_paper_step_fails). Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_5_3_b) by choosing the matching sequence differently. Theorems 5.4 and 5.5 stand. The counterexample needs a connected component without the destination. The paper never assumes that G is connected, so it allows such graphs. Details. The even case is symmetric. Corollary 3.4 gives list[w] = in-nbrs_w or list[w] = out-nbrs_w. Together with list[w] ⊆ in-nbrs_w, the second option only gives list[w] = out-nbrs_w = ∅; it does not give list[w] = in-nbrs_w. The counterexample is a related pair of reachable states. G'init is the single edge 0 → 1, and the destination 2 is isolated. s is the initial state of OneStepPR. t is reached in NewPR by reverse(1), reverse(0) (dummy), reverse(0), so it has the initial orientation and counts (2, 1, 0). Then (s, t) ∈ R, node 1 is a sink, t.parity[1] is odd and s.list[1] = ∅ ≠ nbrs₁. The paper prescribes one reverse(1), which reverses out-nbrs₁ = ∅, while OneStepPR's reverse(1) reverses the edge {0,1}. Repair. If the set that NewPR would reverse (in-nbrs_w for even parity, out-nbrs_w for odd) is nonempty, OneStepPR reverses exactly that set, and one step suffices. Otherwise OneStepPR reverses all of nbrs_w, which is then the other set, and NewPR takes a dummy step followed by a real one (NewPR.exists_steps). Claim 5.4 is proved as in the paper, from Invariants 4.1 and 4.2 (claim_5_4_even, claim_5_4_odd). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. As in the paper, the whole system is one I/O automaton (no message passing, no failures, no randomness): each automaton is a step relation, and "reachable" means reachable from the unique initial state. There is no fairness, since only safety (acyclicity) is claimed. The initial directed graph G'init is primitive: Network.init u v means "initially u → v, i.e. u is left of v". It is required to be acyclic (Relation.TransGen init irreflexive). G is its underlying undirected graph, and nbrs, in-nbrs, out-nbrs are derived from it. The node type V is arbitrary. The destination D is a field Network.dest. No node D ever steps, and no result depends on it. The state has a direction variable dir[u,v] ∈ {in, out} for every ordered pair; only pairs that are edges matter. s.G' is arcs N s.dir: u → v iff {u,v} ∈ E and dir[u,v] = out. PR's action reverse(S), with S a nonempty set of sinks and D ∉ S, is given in closed form (PR.effect). It equals the paper's for each u ∈ S loop whenever S is an independent set, which holds in every reachable state. OneStepPR is reverse({u}). NewPR reverses in-nbrsᵤ or out-nbrsᵤ according to the parity of count[u]. Simulating PR by OneStepPR (Lemma 5.1 (b), Theorems 5.2 and 5.5) assumes a finite node set ([Finite V]), because reverse(S) becomes |S| single steps. Everything else holds for arbitrary V. "Left/right" of the paper's planar embedding is only used for neighbours, so it is the relation init. Theorem 4.3's "rightmost node of the cycle" argument is reorganized. All nodes on a cycle have the same count (Invariant 4.2 (d)). By Invariant 4.1, every arc between two such nodes then goes the G'init way (even count) or every arc goes the reverse way (odd count), so the cycle would be a cycle of G'init or of its reverse. Proof remarks. Invariants 4.1 and 4.2 are derived from a single inductive invariant per edge (NewPR.EdgeInv: equal counts, or the left node one ahead with even count, or the right node one ahead with the left count even). This replaces the paper's case-by-case induction, which we checked by hand and found correct. The proofs of Section 4 use, without stating it, the analogue of Invariant 3.1 for NewPR (dir[u,v] = in ↔ dir[v,u] = out). It holds (NewPR.consistent_of_reachable). Main results in Lean. Constant Amortized RMR Abortable Mutex — PODC 2019 Prasad Jayanti, Siddhartha Jayanti. Constant Amortized RMR Abortable Mutex for CC and DSM. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331592. Formalized version: arXiv 1809.04561 v1 (full version with all proofs); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main results hold for Algorithm 1 as printed: mutual exclusion, starvation freedom, O(1) amortized RMRs per attempt in both the CC and DSM models, O(1) worst-case Exit, Fast Abort and O(n) space. The new fairness property AFCFS is false as defined, because the definition forgets passages that end with an abort, and one added condition gives a corrected version that holds. The distance function of the starvation proof misses the case of line 11, the invariant of Theorem 4.1 is true but needs an extra conjunct to be inductive, and a constant in the proof of Lemma 5.3 changes from 4 to 5. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 4.2 (AFCFS) As defined, AFCFS fails whenever p aborts the last attempt of its passage: if p completes its doorway and then aborts for good, a later process p' splices out p's node and enters the CS although p never enters the CS in that passage (afcfs_literal_false, a 13-step run with n = 3). Impact. Only the new fairness notion is affected; the algorithm is as fair as intended. Under the paper's definition no starvation-free abortable lock can satisfy AFCFS: a process that leaves after its doorway would block every later process forever. The evident fix is local, and we prove it: p' does not enter the CS before p enters the CS or the Abort section (theorem_4_2). Details. A passage ends with a successful attempt "or the last attempt" (j = k). If p's last attempt is aborted and p never returns, the passage consists of aborted attempts only, and the A-precedence relation is based on the doorway of that last attempt. The failure needs the strict reading of "p' does not enter the CS before p enters the CS" (p' must wait for an entry of p that never comes). Under the weaker reading "if both enter, p enters first", the definition already says what is intended and Theorem 4.2 holds. Three things show the intended exception: the airline analogy ("people behind you occupy your original position"), the paper's proof (it only orders processes while they are in Q, and "leaves Q from any position" includes aborting), and the fact that the strict reading cannot be met by any starvation-free abortable lock. AFCFS is the paper's own new definition and the abstract lists it, but the fix only adds the missing case "unless p's passage ends with an abort", the proof reasons with the intended version, and the algorithm is unchanged. Repair. theorem_4_2 assumes that p is at line 3 at time T (it has just completed lines 1–2) and that p' begins a passage at a time t' ≥ T (PassageStart: p' is in the Remainder, and its last step, if any, completed the Exit section). It concludes that whenever p' is at line 7, p was at line 7, 9, 10 or 11 at some time in between. The proof keeps p ahead of p' in the queue (before_step) and uses I10. 🔧 Definition 4.1 / Lemma 4.4 (the digit function f misses line 11) Equation (1) gives no value of f at line 11, so δ(p) is undefined when the prefix leader q_m is an aborted process at line 11 (marked node, about to wake its successor), a case the proof of Lemma 4.4 itself lists. Impact. This is a local fix. With f(11) = 4, the only value between f(10) = 5 and f(1) = 3, Lemma 4.4 and Theorem 4.5 hold (lemma_4_4_part1, lemma_4_4_part2, theorem_4_5). ✏️ Slips Figure 1, I7: *mynode_p should be *mynode_{q_i}; I9: go_{q₁} should be &go_{q₁}. Lemma 4.4 should exclude an aborting step of p itself, after which δ(p) is undefined. Appendix C, Lemma 5.3, lines 3, 7, 9: the proof writes α_CC(11) for α_CC(9). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4.1 (the invariant I is not inductive) The induction step for line 3 (case 3, splicing out an aborted predecessor) fails from a configuration satisfying I in which the new predecessor's node still holds the spliced process's go-address, after which I7 fails (paperInv_not_inductive: n = 3, Q = [r, x, π], r at line 3 with *a_r = &go_x, x aborted at line 11, π at line 3). Impact. The statement is true: I holds in every reachable configuration (theorem_4_1). The appendix's "the rest of the invariants continue to hold since they are unaffected" is the gap. Repair. We add one conjunct (Loc.x1): an aborted queue member at line 1, 10 or 11 never has its own go-address in its predecessor node, since it erased it at line 9. With this conjunct the invariant is inductive (inv_step), and it implies I verbatim (paperInv_of). An exhaustive model check of all 11 413 reachable configurations for n = 2, plus random runs for n = 3, 4, agrees. 🔧 Lemma 5.3 (CC constant for lines 8 and 11) The proof claims α_CC(8), α_CC(11) ≤ 4, but the write *v ← true also invalidates go_q in q's cache, which adds one more unit of potential, so the true bound is 5. Impact. The statement ("bounded by a constant") is true (lemma_5_3, with exact per-line bounds 0, 1, 2, 5). The bound 5 is attained for n = 2. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory with n processes Fin n, deterministic, no crashes, and an arbitrary scheduler (any schedule σ : ℕ → Fin n × Bool). Processes that have not "joined" yet are processes that stay in the Remainder section. The shared objects support Fetch&Store, read and write. One step is one shared-memory operation plus the local actions after it, as in the paper. Line 1 is the Remainder section and line 7 is the CS. Abort signal: a step carries an abort flag that is used only at lines 4–6. An aborting step there jumps to the Abort section and executes line 9 in the same step. This follows the paper's convention that a step is one shared-memory operation plus any local actions, and a jump is a local action. Lemma 4.4 also holds when the jump is attached to the preceding operation instead. It would fail only if the jump were a separate, memory-free step, which the paper's convention rules out; see differencies.md. Starvation freedom assumes a fair schedule: every process outside the Remainder eventually takes a step. The process under consideration never aborts. RMR cost models: DSM: an arbitrary placement of variables with go_p in p's partition. CC: per-process caches. Reads hit or miss; every Fetch&Store or write costs 1 and invalidates all copies. Caches start empty. Main results in Lean. Why Extension-Based Proofs Fail — PODC 2020 Dan Alistarh, James Aspnes, Faith Ellen, Rati Gelashvili, Leqi Zhu. Brief Announcement: Why Extension-Based Proofs Fail. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405743. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv 1811.01421 v3 (August 2020, NIS model, the model of the brief announcement); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The limitation result stands for the provers we checked: for every k ≥ 2, no extension-based prover whose infinite chain is eventually played alone can refute every wait-free k-set agreement protocol in the NIS model, for any number of processes and any finite input set. The adversary of Section 5 is saved only by a new output-query rule with a stronger invariant, because its answers none are not shown to stay correct after later subdivisions, and Lemma 4.13, whose proof ends with an unjustified inequality, needs a new carrier argument. Provers that interleave an infinite chain with finitely many others belong to the paper's class but were not checked (see Not formalized.); nothing about them is shown false. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips §5 defines X_t(a) as the set of descendants in all levels V_r, r ≤ t. The adversary instead adds sets of vertices of G_t to X_t(a). Invariant 6 only makes sense for the vertices of G_t: a non-terminated vertex of a lower level is not a vertex of G_t. Theorem 5.7, Cases 1 and 2 of output queries: the Q-only schedule "from C that results in process p_i being in state v = (i, {u})" exists only if no process has updated S_{t+1} in C, which the paper never states (invariant 3 allows 2t + 1 steps). The schedule exists for the paper's own adversary, so this is a missing justification, not an error. The paper's strategy keeps a stronger, unstated invariant: after every response, active processes are at levels < t, and processes at level t are terminated (invariant 2 and the query rule). So nobody has written to S_{t+1} in a reached configuration. A schedule that brings p_i to u can be cut to the causal past of u, and then p_i p_i gives (i, {u}). If some process had written to S_{t+1}, as invariant 3 permits, p_i's scan would return (i, τ) with |τ| ≥ 2. That vertex can be adjacent to vertices that have not seen y. Our adversary is different and uses its own construction (oq_some_of_unprot): in Lean, undecided states are active, so p_i runs alone, round after round, until no other process has written to the next snapshot object. Each new state stays unprotected (unprot_round), and the next solo state is safe (safe_solo). Case 1 and the start of phase 2: "each vertex in X_t(y) is adjacent to a vertex in T_t(b)" drops invariant 6's alternative v ∈ N_t(y). The dropped case is covered, since T_t(y) is far from N_t(y). Typos Lemma 5.5's proof writes χ(N_t(a), Δ) and χ(T_t(t), δ) for χ(N_t(a), δ) and χ(T_t(a), δ). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 5.7 (adversary, output queries answered none; Lemma 5.5, invariant 6) The adversary answers none by looking only at the vertices of G_t, although its promise covers all future Q-only executions from C, and Lemma 5.5 asserts without proof ("by the definition of χ") that invariant 6 survives a subdivision. Impact. The correctness of the adversary, hence the proof of Theorem 5.7, is not established as written. We prove the theorem with a modified rule for output queries and a stronger invariant (not_hasEBProof_setAgreement, oq_spec). This repair holds for every prover; only interleaved infinite chains remain unchecked (see Not formalized.). Details. After t is incremented, X_{t+1}(a) contains the new descendants (i, τ) of the recorded vertices. A carrier τ may mix a vertex u of Case 3, which is adjacent to T_t(b) only through another clique, with vertices of other processes. Then (i, τ) has seen a, so it is not in N_{t+1}(a). It is adjacent to a terminated vertex only if some clique contains τ and a terminated vertex, which need not exist. The paper gives no argument that such vertices are protected. This matters twice. Later in phase 1, the adversary terminates a vertex with a whenever this keeps the invariants, and it uses invariant 6 to argue that this vertex is not in X_t(a). In phase 2, it outputs a at every vertex of F' that is not adjacent to a terminated vertex. Either step could make a vertex in X_t(a) output a, contradicting an earlier none. Repair. For a query (C, Q, y) our adversary considers the Q-descendants of C at all levels, in the protocol where all undecided states stay active (oq). If one has already output y, it returns a schedule to it. Otherwise, if some undecided descendant with at least t rounds has seen y and is not adjacent to a vertex terminated with another value, it lets that process run alone until it is ahead of everybody. It then subdivides and terminates the next state with y. That state is safe (safe_solo); the paper's Cases 1 and 2 are special cases. Otherwise it answers none. Then every undecided descendant is protected: it has not seen y, or it is adjacent to a vertex terminated with another value (RecOK). Protection survives later terminations (adj_transfer, which keeps an edge alive by restricting an execution to the causal past of its two endpoints). A safe vertex is never protected, so no later termination contradicts a none (AInv.terminate, dstar_none). 🛠️ Lemma 4.13 (subdivision increases distances) The last inequality, "distance(A, A'∩C) + 2 + distance(B'∩C, B) > distance(A, B)", does not follow from the preceding decomposition of shortest paths, which only gives the reverse inequality (the points of A'∩C and B'∩C closest to A and B need not be adjacent). Impact. The lemma is one of the paper's main technical tools. Its statement is true; proved by a different argument (Far.subdiv_succ, far_layer_succ). Repair. We use a carrier argument. Every vertex of G_{t+1} has a carrier in G_t, and the carriers of adjacent vertices lie in a common clique. Mapping a walk of G_{t+1} to its carriers gives a walk of G_t that is no longer. If the image walk uses an edge between two active vertices, their carriers are nested, so one step can be saved. The same argument gives Lemma 4.11 directly (Far.subdiv). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. NIS model (shared with the PODC'21 companion ExtensionBasedReductions). Asynchronous, wait-free, deterministic, full information. n processes form any finite type, and each process updates and then scans each snapshot object S_1, S_2, … at most once. A protocol is its decision function δ, consulted after each scan. There is no randomness, and crashes are processes that stop being scheduled. Extension-based proofs. A prover is a deterministic strategy on the history. It uses queries (C, q), output queries (C, Q, y) and phase ends, as in §3. Output queries may name any set Q (the paper requires Q active), which only helps the prover. The protocol may answer correct output queries adversarially. The prover wins if all its moves are legal and it reaches a violating configuration, or plays infinitely many phases, or from some point on plays one infinite chain of consecutive queries. Task. k-set agreement setAgreement X k: every input vector over a finite set X is allowed, and the outputs are inputs, with at most k distinct values. The paper's case is X = {0, …, k} and n > k. Graphs G_r. Defined semantically: two states are adjacent if they belong to different processes and occur together in a reachable configuration (Adj). The paper's N_r(a) is replaced by the set Uset of vertices that have not seen a, which is its vertex set by Lemma 5.3. The adversary's partial protocol treats undecided states as active (AState.term). Main results in Lean. The completion at the start of phase 2 assigns values on all states with t + 1 rounds, not only on F'; states outside F' are never reached by the prover. Not formalized. Section 3's example (the FLP-style valency proof is extension-based). Lemmas 4.4–4.9 and Corollary 4.9: connectivity is not needed, and the χ-construction is replaced by the semantic graph. Lemma 5.3 is avoided by working with Uset. Provers that interleave several chains, one of them infinite (differencies.md, item 8). Our proof of Lemma 5.6 (IsChain.false) assumes that the adversary state changes only through the chain's own queries, so it would need to be generalised. This case is not formalized. The paper's invariant 6. Open: whether it can actually fail after a subdivision. We neither proved nor refuted it, and we did not try to build a prover that triggers the scenario of the first proof gap. Trust. It also has the restriction lemma (exec_restrict), truncation to a level (trunc) and keeping a causal past (exists_sched_restrict). 3-colouring grids in Online-LOCAL — PODC 2024 Yi-Jun Chang, Gopinath Mishra, Hung Thuan Nguyen, Mingyang Yang, Yu-Cheng Yeh. A Tight Lower Bound for 3-Coloring Grids in the Online-LOCAL Model. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662794. Formalized version: the conference version (everything formalized here is fully proved there; full version arXiv 2312.01384). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Theorem 1.1 (Ω(log n) for grids) and Theorem 1.3 (Ω(√n) for cylinders and tori) are proved, with explicit constants, together with Lemmas 3.3–3.6. No proof step fails, and the only labeled mistake is that Theorem 1.3 as stated omits that √n must be odd, which its proof assumes; read as a bound for all large n, it is false for even √n. The results on k-partite graphs (Theorems 1.5, 1.8, 1.10) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 1.3 (and the abstract): the theorem claims locality Ω(√n) for 3-colouring √n × √n toroidal and cylindrical grids with no condition on n, but for even √n these graphs are bipartite and the O(log n) Online-LOCAL algorithm for bipartite graphs (the one behind Corollary 1.2) applies, so it is false if Ω is read "for all large n". The proof picks √n odd, and the correct reading is "for √n odd" (or "infinitely often"); we prove the general a × b form with b ≥ 3 odd (theorem_1_3_cylinder, theorem_1_3_torus). Outside the proof, only §2.1 (odd-column cylinders/tori are not bipartite) and the closing remark of §3.3 (the Ω(a) bound for a × b grids needs b odd) mention parity. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (CSLib, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Local/OnlineLocal.lean, following §2.2 of the paper). Deterministic algorithms View ι → L; the algorithm may depend on n and the host graph arbitrarily. The input is an identifier placement pos : ι ≃ V on the host grid/cylinder/torus and a reveal order listing every node once. When vᵢ is revealed the algorithm sees the subgraph induced by B({v₁,…,vᵢ}, T) with identifiers and the reveal sequence, and irrevocably labels vᵢ. Correct = proper for every placement and every order. The identifier space has exactly n elements (the paper allows poly(n)): this weakens the adversary, so the lower bounds are stronger. The adversary chooses only pos and the order; re-embedding is derived from an indistinguishability lemma (label_eq_of_agreeOn), not assumed. T = 0 is allowed (the paper assumes T ≥ 1). Colours Fin 3, our 2 is the paper's 3. Grids are Mathlib's pathGraph/cycleGraph box products. Main results in Lean. Bounded Timestamping from Standard Primitives — PODC 2023 Benyamin Bashari, Ali Jamadi, Philipp Woelfel. Efficient Bounded Timestamping from Standard Synchronization Primitives. PODC 2023. DOI 10.1145/3583668.3594601. Formalized version: the 45-page full version with appendices (University of Calgary report). There is no arXiv version. Numbering follows the full version. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The algorithm of Figures 1–2 is not linearizable: Lean checks a sequential execution with 3 processes in which isEarlier(1, 0) gives the wrong answer, so Lemmas 6, 8 and 9 and Corollary 10 are false and Theorem 1 is not established by it. A simple repair (a separate link for helpMoveTS) blocks our attack, but we did not prove it correct, so the paper's main point is not saved. What stands is Section 6 (bounded FAI from bounded FAA), with a slightly better bound, and the constant step complexity (Lemma 12): every operation takes at most 2κ + 107 base-object steps, independently of n. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 1 and Corollary 10 via Lemma 6 (linearizability of Figures 1–2) The algorithm is not linearizable, because the helpMoveTS() coroutine shares its LL/SC links with the process's other LL()s: with n = 3, κ = 4 a sequential execution makes isEarlier(1, 0) return false (alg_not_linearizable), and Lemma 6 is false (lemma6_false). Impact. Lemmas 6, 9 and 8 and Corollary 10 are false for Figures 1–2, and Theorem 1 is not established. A simple repair (a separate link for helpMoveTS) blocks our attack, but we did not prove it correct. Section 6 and the constant step complexity (Lemma 12) are unaffected. Details. The cause is reusable: a helpMoveTS() call spread over several operations shares its LL/SC links with the rest of the process's code. Line 23 executes helpMoveTS() κ steps per helpActiveCluster() call, so one call is spread over several operations of the same process. Those operations perform their own LL()s on TS entries: isEarlier lines 35/37/44/45/50, helpUpdateTS line 9, conditionalReset line 29. With one link per process and object, which is the paper's LL/SC definition in Section 3, such an LL() renews the link that the coroutine later checks with VL() (line 65) and uses for SC() (line 73). Distributed Computations in Fully-Defective Networks — PODC 2022 Keren Censor-Hillel, Shir Cohen, Ran Gelles, Gal Sela. Distributed Computations in Fully-Defective Networks. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538432. Formalized version: the PODC paper, with the proofs of the full version arXiv 2205.11148 v1. Numbering follows the PODC paper; arXiv numbers in brackets. Verdict: ✅ Correct. We found no mistakes, but the paper's main result (Theorem 2) is only partly verified. The simple-cycle simulator (Algorithm 1, Theorem 4, Lemma 5, [Theorem 6]) is proved correct (safety, liveness under fair scheduling, no starvation and quiescence), the two-party impossibility (Theorem 3) holds as stated, Robbins cycles exist exactly in the 2-edge-connected graphs, and for the Robbins-cycle simulator (Algorithm 3, Theorem 6 [Theorems 10, 12]) safety and deadlock freedom are proved: single token holder, global consistency, consistent rotations, and the simulation of π. Its liveness under fairness is not formalized, nor are the distributed construction of the Robbins cycle (Section 5), the binary encoding and the complexity bounds. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Network. Asynchronous; every channel is fully defective, so only the existence of a message matters and a link is a pair of pulse counters. Channels are not FIFO. Nodes. Deterministic. A wait until is a blocking receive on the named direction or edge. Robbins cycles. For Algorithm 3, a node reads one pulse at a time from a channel it waits on. Channels are counters per ordered pair. A node's rotation is stored as the position of its occurrence 0. Rings. Algorithm 1 runs on the oriented ring ZMod n, for every n ≥ 1, including n = 1, 2. A node knows its two neighbours. The simulated protocol π (Protocol.lean): deterministic, event-driven and asynchronous; it may send to any node. It is a black box. Every message delivered to π is processed after an arbitrary delay, and its outputs are enqueued at once. Messages are encoded by any injective map into the positive integers (unary lengths). Simulation. At every reachable configuration of the simulator there is a reachable configuration of π over the noiseless network with the same states and the same local transcripts at all nodes. Its in-transit messages are exactly those sent but not yet processed. Liveness. Executions are infinite (stutters allowed) and weakly fair: every node step, and every π processing step, that stays enabled is eventually taken. In such executions every message sent by π is eventually processed. A round-robin scheduler is weakly fair, so the hypotheses are satisfiable. Theorem 3. Two deterministic event-driven parties with any message alphabet. The adversary rewrites every delivered message. Executions are fair; outputs are irrevocable. Main results in Lean. Proof remarks. The paper's proofs are informal, real-time inductions over epochs; the formal proofs need some invariants that the paper uses without stating them. Three points are only implicit in the paper and needed real work: Why the token is caught (Lemma 5(1)). The paper says the token travels "until it reaches a node v with a non-empty Q_v, which must exist". Two invariants make this precise. First, a request pulse of the current token phase implies a node with a non-empty queue: the initiator keeps its message until it captures the token. Second, the released token has not passed such a node. Together they bound the token's hops by n. (Inv2, progress_step) Lemma 11 [full version] is a sketch ("we can now repeat the proof of Lemma 5"). The formal invariant for Algorithm 3 needs facts the sketch does not mention. The token always lies in segment 0 of every node (RobbinsSim.Inv.rot; the paper states this one). At most one token, data or end pulse is in transit, and the ghost variable wv names its channel. A node still in its data phase cannot read a request pulse of the next epoch at its occurrence 0 (RobbinsSim.EndStage.read). Implicit model conventions. Several conventions are only implicit. A wait until is a blocking receive: pulses from other directions stay buffered. Unary payloads must be positive. Fairness is needed for liveness. Theorem 3's proof also needs a fair execution to exist; we prove that a round-robin schedule gives one (TwoParty.Protocol.rr_isFairExec). Not formalized. These parts are not formalized: liveness and no starvation of Algorithm 3 under fairness (only deadlock freedom is proved); the binary encoding (Algorithm 2, Lemmas 8–9), which was only model-checked; all communication-complexity bounds (CC_init, CC_overhead, Lemmas 7, 9, 13, 14, 19); the distributed construction of a Robbins cycle (Section 5: Algorithms 4–6, Theorem 15); the reduction from networks with a bridge to Theorem 3; [Remark 1] (the derived noiseless scheduler is FIFO; our noiseless model is non-FIFO) and [Remark 3] (broadcast). Hence Theorem 2 is covered only for a given Robbins cycle, not for the preprocessing phase. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: a weakly fair execution of the simulator exists (Cycle.roundRobin_fair), and so does a fair two-party execution (TwoParty.Protocol.exists_fairExec); there is a concrete Robbins cycle (triangleRobbinsCycle). Before the proofs, we model-checked Algorithms 1, 2 and 3 exhaustively on small rings and Robbins cycles. This includes repeated edges and nodes with three occurrences. No violation was found. The checkers are in modelcheck/ and are not part of the Lean development. The content-oblivious model is new: CSLib's ContentOblivious rings have two ports per node and nodes that act only on start-up or on consuming a pulse, while the simulators need environment events (π enqueues messages at any time), spontaneous steps (line 1 fires on a non-empty queue) and, for Robbins cycles, arbitrary degree. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733516. Formalized version: arXiv 2505.00665 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Theorem 8, the primary result, holds in full: Algorithm 1 is a linearizable, wait-free auditable MWMR register whose audits report exactly the effective reads, and whose writes and reads are uncompromised by curious readers; we prove it, and the register is even strongly linearizable. The proof of Lemma 7 misses two effects of the removed reader and takes a new simulation, while Lemma 38 and the other statement mistakes are slips. Linearizability and wait-freedom of the max register and the snapshot extensions were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Section 3.2, Termination (the bound m + 1) The claim that the repeat loop (lines 9–14) terminates after at most m + 1 iterations is off by one: m failures caused by readers, one caused by a concurrent visible write, then the exiting iteration give m + 2. Impact. One constant changes and writes stay wait-free: alg1_waitFree is proved with a potential that allows m + 2. The bound itself is not formalized. ✏️ Slips Lemma 38 (max-register extension, at the initial value w₀). With natural-number nonces, even fresh ones, a reader with no w₀-effective read can still learn that writeMax(w₀) occurred, so Lemma 38's "no writeMax has input w" in some indistinguishable execution fails for w = w₀ (lemma38_false, all nonces; lemma38_false_fresh, fresh nonces). The paper never fixes the nonce domain. Impact: Theorem 8 is unaffected. With nonces in ℕ the failure is confined to w = w₀: any other pair the reader knows, it has fetched (which makes its read effective), and ℕ has no largest nonce. writeMax(w₀) does not change the abstract max register, and the paper's own use (Algorithm 3, version numbers ≥ 1) never invokes it. The claim: in Algorithm 2, for every value w and reader p_j, either p_j has a w-effective read, or some execution indistinguishable to p_j has no writeMax(w). The proof replaces (w, N) by (u, N'), where u is "the largest input smaller than w" and N' > N. It fails because no input smaller than w = w₀ exists. Counterexample (values and nonces in ℕ, initial pair (0, 0), one reader, two writers): writer A runs writeMax(0) with nonce 2, so R becomes (1, (0,2), ·); writer B runs writeMax(1) with nonce 1, so R becomes (2, (1,1), ·); the reader runs one read, fetching (2, (1,1), ·) and returning 1. The reader has no 0-effective read. Yet in every execution it cannot distinguish from this one, it fetches the same triple. R.seq grows by one per change and R.val strictly increases, so the pair stored at sequence number 1 lies strictly between (0,0) and (1,1). That pair is (0, N) with N ≥ 1, or (1, 0). (1, 0) reuses the initial nonce and is excluded by freshness. So a writeMax(0) occurs in every such execution. The reader learns that 0 was written without reading it. Claim 4, Lemmas 3, 5 and 6 (no writer, one value). These results fail without writers or with a single value: a read is then v₀-effective as soon as it is invoked, and an audit invoked right after the invocation does not report it, so Lemma 5 fails; Lemma 6's proof needs a value v' ≠ v. We assume a writer and two distinct values, and "multi-writer" implies the first (claim4, lemma5, lemma6). Lemma 5 also needs the audit to be invoked after α. An audit already running when the read becomes effective may miss it. The proof ("linearized after the read is effective") shows this is the intended reading. Appendix B: q_x reads x − 1, not x, from SN. Appendix B: V[x−1] and B[x−1] are finalized by A_x, not V[x] and B[x]. Algorithm 2, line 30: continue must restart at line 26, since mval is undefined otherwise. Typos Algorithm 1, line 22: lsa ← sn should be lsa ← rsn. Line 21 uses bits for the audit's rbits. Lemma 19 has "for x > 1" where it means x ≥ 1. Claim 4's proof has "x > prev_val" where it means prev_sn. Lemma 7's proof has the garbled "only changes the kth tracking bit of R unchanged to, say, b". Lemma 25 lists the σ_ℓ lines inconsistently. Impact. The statement holds, even in a stronger form: in the indistinguishable execution p_k invokes nothing at all (lemma7, read_uncompromised, core remove_reader). The paper's construction does not give it; it takes a new simulation. Details. A direct read also runs SN.compare&swap(sn−1, sn) (line 5). If that step is the one that moves SN, removing it changes the values of SN that p_j reads later. A writer's R.compare&swap may fail only because p_k inserted itself into the reader set. Without p_k it would succeed earlier, and the executions diverge. Repair. The writer poised at line 15 takes over p_k's successful SN step. Writer loop iterations whose compare&swap fails in α are dropped. These iterations start and end in the same local state and only write V/B, which readers never read. Asynchronous shared memory in CSLib (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl) with deterministic processes. Crashes are modelled by processes that stop taking steps; this matches the paper's honest-but-curious attacker. Processes: m readers, any type W of writers and any type Au of auditors. Store-collect over an abstract MAC layer — PODC 2022 Lewis Tseng, Qinzi Zhang. Brief Announcement: Computability and Anonymous Storage-Efficient Consensus with an Abstract MAC Layer. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538462. Formalized version: the 3-page brief announcement (no arXiv version); numbering as there. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Theorem 1 holds: MAC-SC (Algorithm 1) implements a regular store-collect object in the single-hop abstract MAC layer with any number of crashes, and we prove it in a model where stored values carry sequence numbers, which is how the paper says uniqueness is obtained. The mistakes are implied assumptions on the handler priority and on sequence numbers, plus one wrong word. Wait-freedom under the repaired priority rule, the stacked constructions and the anonymous consensus algorithms, which the announcement only mentions, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Abstract: "all of the algorithms are wait-free" (MAC-SC under assumption (iii)). Under assumption (iii) as stated (the handler has priority over the main thread), the adversary can keep a node's message queue non-empty forever, so with two nodes a Collect₀ never returns (Starvation.mac_sc_not_wait_free). Impact: a missing implied assumption. Assumption (iii) is really needed for Theorem 1, but the fix is local and can be read off the proof of Theorem 1, and under it the main thread cannot starve. A reader who takes the paper's asynchrony literally gets a non-wait-free algorithm. Section 2 says the handler processes queued messages one by one and "has a priority over the execution of the main thread". So line 1 or line 4 of an operation can run only when the handler's queue is empty. Take two nodes. Node 1 runs Store₁ operations forever. In every round, its new message reaches node 0 before node 0's handler has processed the previous one. Node 0's queue then always holds one or two messages and is never empty. In this infinite execution nobody crashes, every broadcast is delivered and acknowledged, and node 1 completes one operation per round. Node 0's handler processes every message it receives, within two rounds. Yet node 0's Collect₀ never executes line 4 and never returns. Theorem 1, proof sketch: the merge. The merge A ∪ B keeps "the newer value from each node". The paper calls this well defined because values are unique and operations sequential. But a node cannot compute it from unique values alone, because a stale view can arrive after a newer one. It needs the sequence numbers that the paper mentions as the way to make values unique. We tag every stored value with the index of its store operation and merge by that index; Theorem 1 is unaffected (theorem_1). Theorem 1, proof sketch of Property II: delivery. The sketch says that when a mac-broadcast completes "all the fault-free nodes have received the broadcast message". What is needed, and what the MAC layer gives, is "every node not crashed yet". The node of the later collect may crash after that collect returns, so it need not be fault-free. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Assumption (iii) is necessary for Theorem 1 (not an error; the paper does assume it). Suppose the main thread may read view_i while delivered messages are still queued. Node 0 completes Store₀(7), and its message waits in node 1's queue. Node 1 then invokes Collect₁ and returns ∅. This violates Property I(i). The proof sketch of Property I ("node i has not received any message from j's mac-broadcast") and of Property II both use (iii) silently. (theorem_1_needs_priority) Property I(ii)'s "we can prove by contradiction" is left to the reader. The argument needs the merge to never replace an entry by an older one, which again relies on sequence numbers. Model (Model.lean). Asynchronous, single-hop abstract MAC layer, deterministic nodes, any number of crash failures. Nodes form an arbitrary type ι (possibly infinite); the algorithm never uses n. Events: client invocation (only at an idle node, so at most one pending operation); lines 1–2 / 4–5, which compute currentView and start mac-broadcast; delivery of a broadcast to any node, at most once per node, even after the sender crashed; one handler step, which pops the first queued message and merges it (lines 7–8); the acknowledgment, enabled once every node that has not crashed yet has received the message; the return (lines 3/6); crash. Any interleaving is allowed. Handler priority (prio = true): lines 1/4 may run only when the node's queue is empty. Histories are lists of inv i n o / ret i n r events, where operation (i, n) is the n-th operation of node i. The real-time order is the order in the list. Regularity (Regular = RegularI ∧ RegularII) transcribes the paper's two bullets and ⪯. A view maps each node to an optional (index, value) entry. Theorem 1 is quantified over all finite executions (Reach true c h), so it covers every prefix of every infinite execution. Main results in Lean. Wake Up and Join Me! (energy-efficient maximal matching in radio networks) — PODC 2021 Varsha Dani, Aayush Gupta, Thomas P. Hayes, Seth Pettie. Brief Announcement: Wake Up and Join Me! An Energy-Efficient Algorithm for Maximal Matching in Radio Networks. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467950. Formalized version: arXiv 2104.09096 v2 (full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Algorithm 1 outputs a maximal matching w.h.p. (Lemma 5.4), but the neighbour-assignment result rests on Theorem 6.3, whose normalisation does not terminate and takes a new argument. Theorem 6.5 claims maximum load at most k, while the true bound is k + 1, attained on disjoint copies of P₃ whenever the matching subroutine succeeds, and its coverage bounds hold only by a changed count. The energy bound of Theorem 1.1 for Δ ≥ 2, the paper's main cost claim, and the running time were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 6.5 (maximum load of the neighbour assignment) Algorithm 4 with parameter k does not have maximum load at most k: on disjoint copies of the path P₃ with k = 1 the load is 2 whenever both matching calls succeed, which happens with high probability (theorem_6_5_load_false, exists_run). Impact. The true bound is k + 1 (theorem_6_5_load), and the polylog-factor claim of the abstract survives. The proof never discusses the load, and the bound k is part of the claim. Details. Algorithm 4 calls the maximal matching subroutine k + 1 times: once in line 1 and once in each of the k loop iterations. Each call gives a vertex at most one new partner, so it adds at most one vertex pointing to it. Hence the load is at most k + 1, and this is attained. Take a path ℓ — c — ℓ' and k = 1. The first call matches c with one leaf ℓ. In the iteration, ℓ' is the only unassigned vertex and c its only neighbour, so every maximal matching of the cross graph matches them. Then c is re-assigned to ℓ', while ℓ still points to c, so c has load 2. With c disjoint copies (n = 3c) this happens in every execution where both calls succeed. By the paper's own Theorem 1.1 that has probability 1 − O(1/n²), so the claimed property fails with high probability. ✏️ Slips Theorem 1.1 for Δ = 1 (energy bound). For Δ = 1 the energy bound 2C (log n)(log Δ) is 0, but a node is matched only in a round in which it sends or listens, so on any graph with an edge the event of Theorem 1.1 is empty (theorem_1_1_delta_one). With the usual convention log Δ ≥ 1 this disappears. The energy part of Theorem 1.1 is not formalized otherwise. In the proof of Lemma 5.4, "first bad round: Δ(t) ≥ 1/(2r(t))" should read Δ(t − 1). The proof of Lemma 5.6 switches from d(v, t−1) to d(v, t) inside an expectation conditioned on M(t−1); a case split on d(v, t−1) is intended. The energy computation of Theorem 1.1 has r(T) for 3r(T). Typos T = CΔ log n need not be an integer. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 6.3 (the normalisation does not terminate) The proof redirects f(f(v)) to a load-0 vertex v, "repeated … to all leaves in turn", but at a leaf of a star with a bidirected edge r ↔ x₁ this just moves the leaf to x₁ and cycles forever. Impact. The statement holds with a new argument (theorem_6_3, exists_cover_of_naf), and the proof of Theorem 6.5 uses it. Details. The claimed final shape also contains leaves and misses "double stars". Repair. Apply the move only where f(v) is not on a 2-cycle and v has load < L. Each move strictly decreases |{v : f³(v) ≠ f(v)}|. When no move applies and L ≥ 2, a counting argument gives f³ = f, so every component is a 2-cycle with leaves. Labelling in-neighbours injectively by 1..L then yields L matchings. 🔧 Theorem 6.5 (coverage: a false intermediate claim) The proof claims that after k iterations at most (1 − 1/(2L+2))^k (1 − ε) n vertices of S ∪ R remain unassigned, which fails because the cross-graph matchings may keep picking unassigned vertices outside S ∪ R (proof_6_5_step_false). Impact. The coverage bounds hold with a change to the bookkeeping (theorem_6_5_coverage_exp, theorem_6_5_full_coverage). Details. Example: the star K_{1,9} with a partial NAF on 3 vertices of load 2. After 7 iterations a vertex of S is still unassigned, although the bound is (5/6)^7 · 3 < 1. Repair. Count all assigned vertices. Each call assigns at least |S \ A|/(2L+2) new vertices, and this gives the stated coverage (1 − ε)(1 − e^{−k/(2L+2)}) and the "in particular" claim for k ≥ (2L+2) ln n. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graph theory (Section 6). G is a finite simple graph. A NAF is f : V → V with G.Adj v (f v). A matching cover is k Mathlib matchings (Subgraph.IsMatching) whose vertex sets cover V. Theorem 6.3 assumes no isolated vertices; otherwise neither NAFs nor covers exist. Radio model (Sections 2.3, 4, 5). Synchronous rounds of three timesteps, no collision detection: a listener receives iff exactly one neighbour sends. IDs are unique (they are the vertices). Algorithms 2–3 are implemented message by message (Radio.lean). In each round a node draws a role: recruit with probability r(t)/2, accept with probability r(t)/2, sleep otherwise. Matched nodes ignore their role. All draws are independent. Probability. Executions of T rounds are paths Fin T → V → Role with the product law (Chain.lean). One-round statements (Lemmas 5.2, 5.6) condition on the current matching M(t−1). Lemma 5.1 holds for every role sequence, which is stronger than "with probability one". Algorithm 4. The maximal matching subroutine is a black box. An execution is a sequence of maximal matchings: the first of G, the later ones of the assigned–unassigned cross graph. Theorem 6.5 is proved for every execution in which all calls succeed; the probability wrapper 1 − O(k/n²) is Theorem 1.1's. log is ln. Main results in Lean. K-set agreement bounds in closed-above round-based models — PODC 2020 Adam Shimi, Armando Castañeda. K-set agreement bounds in round-based models through combinatorial topology. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405752. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version; the full version arXiv 2003.02869 v2 (same statements, proofs in the appendix) was used for the proofs. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The general lower bounds, Theorems 5.4 and 6.11, are the paper's new topological results, and they are false: for the closed-above model generated by a single star (n ≥ 2), Theorem 5.4 claims that (n-1)-set agreement is impossible in one round, but consensus is solvable there. The claimed tight (n − s) bound for unions of stars does not follow either, since its γ^dist computation is wrong. All upper bounds (Theorems 3.2, 3.4, 3.7, 6.3–6.5, 6.7, 6.9, Corollaries 3.5, 3.8, Lemma 6.2) are correct, and the intended versions of Theorems 5.1 and 6.10 (k < γ(G), γ(G^r)) hold, by a short combinatorial argument instead of topology, but Theorem 5.1 is the bound the paper takes from prior work. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorems 5.4 and 6.11 (general lower bounds, one and multiple rounds) Theorem 5.4 is false for the closed-above model generated by a single star, for every n ≥ 2: it gives l = n − 2, so it claims (n−1)-set agreement is impossible in one round, but consensus is solvable there (theorem_5_4_false). Theorem 6.11 is false by the same example: products of stars are stars, so S^r = {G^r} with G^r a star, l = n − 2 for every r ≥ 1, and consensus is still solvable (theorem_6_11_false). Impact. The paper's main lower bound for general closed-above models fails, and its multi-round extension with it; only the trivial bound "impossible for k < max_{G∈S} γ(G)" follows for general S (not_solvable_of_lt_domNum). The symmetric specialization (Corollary 5.5) loses its derivation, but is not refuted. Details. Take S = {G}, where G is the star with center c: c sends to everybody, and the other processes send nothing. For a single graph, γ^dist({G}) = γ^eq(G) = n, because a set dominates the star iff it contains c. A non-dominating set P of size t hears only itself, so max-cov_t = t, M_t = n − t, and l = min(n − 2, n − 2) = n − 2. But every process hears c in every graph of ↑G, so "decide c's input" solves consensus in one round (Theorem 3.2 with γ(G) = 1). For n = 3 the theorem claims that 2-set agreement is impossible. Where the proof breaks (Appendix B of the full version). Let the input facets φ_0, …, φ_t differ at a set P of t processes. The proof says ⋂ C_{G_i}(φ_i) is "either empty or a pseudosphere". It then uses the bound for the non-empty case only. When P contains a process heard by everybody, the intersection is empty. Lemma 4.17 needs it to be (l − t)-connected, and an empty complex is not. More conceptually, for a single graph γ^dist quantifies over all sets of a given size. So it reduces to the equal-domination number, while the tight single-graph bound (Theorem 5.1) is governed by the ordinary domination number γ(G) ≤ γ^eq(G). The theorem is stated for general (non-symmetric) closed-above models, so Corollary 5.5 is not refuted by this example. ❌ Section 5 and Appendix G (γ^dist(S) = n − s + 1 for unions of s stars) The computation γ^dist(S) = n − s + 1 for the symmetric model of unions of s stars is wrong: for s = 1, n ≥ 3 we have γ^dist(S) ≤ n − 1 (distDomNum_stars_le, distDomNum_stars_ne). Impact. The claimed "tight" lower bound (n − s) for stars, and the proof of Theorem 6.13, do not follow from Theorem 5.4 even where that theorem might hold. Theorem 6.13 itself is not refuted. Details. The argument picks one graph whose centers avoid P. But Definition 5.2 asks for min(i, |S|) distinct graphs. For s = 1 and n ≥ 3, a set of n − 1 processes misses only one possible center, so any two distinct stars include one whose center it contains. Hence γ^dist(S) ≤ n − 1 < n. 🔧 Section 3.2 (covering numbers of a star) Section 3.2 says that "every covering number of a star equals 1"; in fact cov_i = i (star_cov_eq). Impact. The conclusion drawn there still holds: n − cov_i = n − i ≥ γ^eq − i, so covering numbers do not improve the bound (star_example). The claims about the second graph of Figure 1 are correct (figure1_example). ✏️ Slips Theorem 5.1 (k ≤ γ(G) should be k < γ(G)). Theorem 5.1 says k ≤ γ(G), which for k = γ(G) contradicts Theorem 3.2 (theorem_5_1_false). The text after Theorem 3.2 states the intended k < γ(G). We prove the corrected statement (theorem_5_1). Theorem 6.10 (γ(G) − 1 should be γ(G^r) − 1). Theorem 6.10 is false as written: for the directed 3-cycle, γ(G) = 2, so it claims consensus is impossible in any number r > 0 of rounds, but after 2 rounds everybody has heard everybody (γ(G²) = 1) (theorem_6_10_false). The intended γ(G^r) is recoverable from Theorem 6.3 and Appendix E. We prove it (theorem_6_10); together with Theorem 6.3 it shows that γ(G^r) is tight (obliviousSolvable_up_iff). Definition 6.1 reads "(u,v) ∈ Π ⟹ ∃w …"; it should read "(u,v) ∈ E ⟺ ∃w …". Typos Definition 6.8 uses "keq−dom(G)" for γ^eq(G). Appendix C writes "max-cov_t({G}) = t" in the second case, which should be "> t". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n = |α| processes (any Fintype), synchronous communication-closed rounds, no crashes. Each round's directed communication graph is chosen by an oblivious adversary from ↑S = {H | G ≤ H for some G ∈ S} (closed-above model). Graphs are Cslib.HeardOf.Graph α, with self-loops implicit (Hears), as the paper assumes. One-round algorithms are full information: a decision map applied to the vector of received inputs (Cslib.HeardOf.msgs). r-round algorithms are oblivious (Definition 2.5): flood the known (process, input) pairs and apply a decision map to them after r rounds. These pairs are exactly the inputs of the in-neighbours in the product G₁ ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ G_r (known_eq_msgs). k-set agreement: every decision is some process's input, and at most k distinct values are decided. Deterministic algorithms, no randomness. Inputs: the upper bounds use any nonempty linearly ordered V (the paper assumes a total order). The lower bounds (Theorems 5.1, 6.10) assume at least n input values (α ↪ V); the paper does not fix the input set. The counterexamples work for every V. The combinatorial numbers (γ, γ^eq, cov_i, γ^dist, max-cov_i, M_i, l, covering sequences) are defined literally as in the paper, with sInf/sSup over ℕ. Main results in Lean. The combinatorial-topology part: Section 4 (pseudospheres, nerve lemma, Lemma 4.17, Theorem 4.12), Corollary 5.5 (lower bound for symmetric models) and Theorem 6.13 (stars). These are neither proved nor refuted; their proofs depend on the flawed argument of Theorem 5.4. A brute-force comparison of Corollary 5.5 with the paper's own upper bounds over all graphs with n ≤ 4 found no conflict. No sorry; all listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The model reuses Cslib.HeardOf (Graph, Hears, msgs) from Cslib/Computability/Distributed/DynamicNetworks/HeardOf.lean. The corrected Theorem 5.1 is proved directly. Validity forces each process to decide an input it has heard. With pairwise distinct inputs, the processes whose inputs are decided then form a dominating set, so at least γ(G) values are decided. Partially Replicated Causally Consistent Shared Memory — PODC 2018 Zhuolun Xiang, Nitin H. Vaidya. Brief Announcement: Partially Replicated Causally Consistent Shared Memory. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212790. Formalized version: arXiv 1703.05424 v3 (full version, …: Lower Bounds and An Algorithm); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The paper's necessary and sufficient condition survives: the edge-indexed timestamp algorithm achieves replica-centric causal consistency (Theorem 3), and tracking every edge of the timestamp graph is necessary (Theorem 1). Both take new arguments: Lemma 4, on which the correctness proof rests, is false (also in its only well-typed reading), and the executions in the proof of Theorem 1 had to be redesigned. Footnote 2's claim that the algorithm satisfies Constraint 1 of the lower-bound section is also false, but it is a side remark nothing is derived from, and the paper's third contribution, the timestamp-size lower bound, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Footnote 2 (the algorithm satisfies Constraint 1) Footnote 2's claim that the algorithm's timestamp is a function of the causal past (a set of updates) is false: on six replicas, two executions give replica 0 the same causal past but different τ₀[e_25] (Footnote2.footnote_2_false). Impact. The lower bound of Section 4 (which assumes Constraint 1) does not apply to the paper's algorithm in general. Nothing is proved in place of the footnote. Details. Take six replicas with X₀ = {e,b}, X₁ = {a,b}, X₂ = {a,c}, X₃ = {c,d}, X₄ = {e,d}, X₅ = {c,e,d}. Replicas 2, 3, 4, 5 write once each. In both executions replica 0 ends up with the same causal past (all four updates). In one, 2's update reaches 0 through 5, which tracks e_25; in the other, only through 4, which does not. So τ₀[e_25] is 1 vs. 0. 🛠️ Lemma 4 (Appendix B, timestamps along causal chains), and with it the proofs of Lemma 5 and Theorem 3 Lemma 4 (if u' from k to i with timestamp T' happened before u from j to i with timestamp T, then T[e_ki] ≥ T'[e_ki]) is false even when e_ki ∈ E_j, its only well-typed reading, on five replicas (Lemma4.lemma_4_false, Lemma4.not_lemma4Statement). Impact. The correctness proof of Theorem 3 rests on it, through Lemma 5, but Theorem 3 is true: we prove it by a new argument (chain_main, lemma_5, theorem_3_safety). Safety is not violated in the counterexample. Details. When e_ki ∉ E_j, T has no such entry, and the proof of Lemma 5 nevertheless applies the lemma there. Even when e_ki ∈ E_j it fails. Take five replicas with X_A = {f,e,b}, X_B = {e,a}, X_C = {a,g}, X_D = {g,b}, X_I = {f,a,g}. A writes f (u', delayed on its way to I), then e. B applies e and writes a; C applies that and writes g; D applies that and writes g (u). Then u' ↪ u and e_AI ∈ E_D (triangle D, I, A). But e_AI ∉ E_C (X_C ⊆ X_I, so condition (iii) fails on every loop through C), so C drops the information and T[e_AI] = 0 < 1 = T'[e_AI]. Safety is not violated: B's and C's updates also go to I and must be applied first. The lemma's proof also assumes that causal chains form simple loops. Repair. We replace it by a strong induction on the length of a causal chain a ↪ v₀ ↪ ⋯ ↪ v_m = u. If a replica repeats, or an intermediate update also goes to the receiver i, the chain gets shorter (the latter by safety of earlier steps). Otherwise, either every replica on the chain tracks e_ji and the counter reaches u's timestamp, or the chain closes with i into a simple loop that is not a (p_q, e_ji)-loop. Each of the three failing conditions of Definition 6 then exhibits an update sent directly further down the chain, which again shortens it. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 1 (necessity of tracking every timestamp-graph edge) In Case 2 applying u₁ also brings j's whole causal past into i's graph, so the two graphs differ in more than updates on e_ji, and Case 3 delays all other messages "indefinitely", which breaks its liveness arguments. Impact. The statement holds for every deterministic metadata algorithm and every quiescent state R₀ (Necessity.theorem_1), with redesigned executions. Details. Also, in Case 3 an earlier update on the path l₁ … l_s may already reach k, and in Case 3.2 the execution without u₀ loses j's causal past. Repair. Both executions share a first update u_A of j, which k applies, and one execution adds a second update u_B. Every relay applies all updates sent to it (liveness forces this). The critical message is the first path update stored at k. The two executions are compared by an explicit simulation. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Peer-to-peer architecture with R replicas (ι), registers Reg, and replica i storing X i. Asynchronous, reliable, non-FIFO channels, no failures, deterministic replicas. The scheduler (delivery order, delays, client writes) is adversarial. Liveness is under weak fairness: an update that stays applicable is eventually applied. "Receive" is merged into "apply": an update can be applied at any time after it was issued, if the predicate of Step 4 holds. Values and reads are omitted (irrelevant to Definition 5). ↪ (Definition 4) is defined through a ghost set pre per update: the updates applied at the issuer before it was issued. Theorem 1 quantifies over all deterministic metadata algorithms (Necessity.Alg). A replica keeps metadata, attaches it to its updates, and decides when to apply a received update from its metadata, the sender, the register and the attached metadata only (Section 2). The decision may see sender and register, which enlarges the class. The class assumes deterministic replicas whose metadata changes only when they write or apply an update (not on receipt). The paper's model (Section 2) does not discuss other algorithms, and its proofs assume this. Main results in Lean. Interplanetary and Relativistic Distributed Computing — PODC 2025 Siddhartha Jayanti. On Interplanetary and Relativistic Distributed Computing. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733563. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Algorithms are state machines per processor (Def. 4.1). A step is (π, σ, e, σ') with δ_π(σ, e, σ') (Def. 4.2). Events may be sends (π, send, m, π') or receives (π', receive, m). The model is asynchronous, with arbitrary (possibly infinite) step sets and arbitrary processor sets. An execution is a set S of steps with a relation on the subtype ↥S. The conditions that do not depend on the order are message validity and at-most-once delivery (MsgValid). The conditions that depend on the order are: per-processor steps form a rooted, consecutively permissible sequence (ProcSeq: a strict total order with finitely many predecessors), and messages are oriented forward (MsgForward). Classical execution: the order is induced by an injective time map S → ℝ (CP1, CP2). Computational execution: ◁ = TransGen(program order ∪ message edges) as a fixed-point equation (A1–A3). Relativistic execution: the order is induced by an injective map into an abstract Spacetime. That structure has a strict causal order (RP1), real time coordinates for each frame that refine it (RP1), world lines that are chains (RP2), and one body at rest whose world line is parametrised by frame time (the physical fact used in Lemma 6.6). Messages go forward in ≺ (RP3). Instance: Minkowski spacetime ℝ × ℝᵈ with c = 1. Causal order: ‖Δx‖ ≤ Δt. Inertial frames have velocity ‖v‖ < 1, and frame time is t − ⟪v, x⟫ (the Lorentz time up to the factor γ_v). This is a precise universal condition, the quiescent-convergence clause of eventual counters [2]. It holds vacuously when there are infinitely many increments, so WEC_COUNT contains such words. The proof of Lemma 5.3 assumes instead that every word of the language has finitely many incs ("eventually every process always picks read operations"). Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Abstract, Section 1.2 and Conclusion (scope of the binary-consensus result) The abstract says binary consensus objects "are not more powerful as far as helping solving approximate agreement faster is concerned", but Theorem 4, the only supporting result, gives a bound one round below the IIS bound whenever 1/ε ≤ n ≤ 2^⌈log₂ 1/ε⌉ (for n = 4, ε = 1/4: 1 round versus 2). No numbered statement is false, and Theorem 4 itself is correct as stated (theorem4_log); the test&set half stands for n ≥ 3 (theorem3_log). Details. Read literally, the abstract's claim fails for n = 2, where consensus solves the task in one round; the body states the qualifiers it needs. The conclusion says binary consensus is not useful "at least when n ≥ 1/ε". Theorem 4 covers only algorithms whose consensus inputs depend on the process id and the round. Its bound min(⌈log₂ n⌉ − 1, ⌈log₂ 1/ε⌉) matches the IIS bound only for n > 2^⌈log₂ 1/ε⌉ (e.g. n ≥ 2/ε). ✏️ Slips Theorems 1 and 2: the speedup proofs use two model properties that the paper never states: a round of some processes extends to a round of all of them with the same views for the early ones (P^(1)(τ') ⊆ P^(1)(τ)), and a box called solo returns a value determined by the caller's input ("b_i = B_t(a_i)"). Both hold in all the paper's models, so every application is correct. We make them explicit hypotheses (Model.Extendable, Model.SoloDet) and prove them for IIS, iterated snapshot, IIS + test&set and IIS + binary consensus. Section 2.2: solvability keeps the complex-based definition after the carrier-map requirement on Δ is dropped; read literally with faces, the liberal task of Definition 4 would not be liberal. The proofs use exact participation throughout (Solves). The claims are applied to 3^k ε and 2^k ε beyond Definition 3's range ε ≤ 1 (we prove them for every ε ≥ 0). Typos Claim 4's proof (and Corollary 2's) says P^(1)(σ) for the protocol complex P^(1)(τ) of the local task. The proceedings version of Theorem 1's proof mixes ρ'/ϱ'. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4 (iteration of Claim 6) Claim 6 assumes |S| ≥ 5, and the proof of Theorem 4 applies it to every S_k but only checks |S_{t−1}| ≥ 3. Impact. The statement is true; the missing inequality holds (theorem4_aux). Repair. Claim 6 in fact needs no size hypothesis, and we iterate with the cleaner invariant "|S| ≤ 2^(t+1) or 1 ≤ 2^t ε". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n asynchronous wait-free processes P (any finite type, decidable equality), iterated full-information protocols (Algorithms 1 and 2): in round r every participant writes its view to a fresh memory, optionally calls a fresh black-box object, and reads. One round is a pattern (who sees whom, box answers) admissible in the model for the participating set and box inputs (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/IteratedModel/Basic.lean). Models: IIS (iis, the chromatic-subdivision condition of Section 2.2), iterated snapshot (isnap), IIS + test&set (iisTS: the winner is a process of the first concurrency class), IIS + binary consensus (iisBC: the proposal of such a process wins), all in Cslib/Computability/Distributed/IteratedModel/Patterns.lean. Crash failures: a task is solved if, for every input simplex σ and every execution in which exactly id(σ) participates, the decisions form an element of Δ(σ). Crashes mid-execution are faces of such executions (Model.Extendable). Deterministic processes, adversarial scheduler, no randomness. Tasks are relations Δ(σ) without carrier-map assumption; approximate agreement on the grid {0, 1/m, …, 1} is scaled to integers {0,…,m} with ε = e/m. The paper drops the carrier-map requirement on Δ but keeps the complex-based definition of solvability, under which the liberal task of Definition 4 would not be liberal. We use the standard reading: the processes of σ participate exactly. Main results in Lean. Topology of Randomized Symmetry Breaking — PODC 2021 Pierre Fraigniaud, Ran Gelles, Zvi Lotker. The Topology of Randomized Symmetry-Breaking Distributed Computing. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467936. Formalized version: the conference version (numbering follows it). For the proofs it defers we used the full version arXiv:2105.11713 v1. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Eq. (2), the paper's formal knowledge equation for message passing, mis-models the model described in words (Section 2.1: every node may send a message to each other node; port numbers "may assist in breaking symmetry"), and read literally with it the "if" direction of Theorem 4.2 is false. Adding the sender's port saves both directions of Theorem 4.2 in the standard port-numbering model that the prose and the full version's proof use, and a few lines replace the misapplied zero–one law in Lemma 3.2, so the framework and both leader-election characterizations stand. The informal Theorem 5.1 was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Eq. (2) (message-passing knowledge) and Theorem 4.2, "if" direction Eq. (2) never lets a receiver learn the port number at the sender's end, and in that model the "if" direction of Theorem 4.2 is false for n₁ = 2, n₂ = 3 (theorem_4_2_if_false, theorem_4_2_counterexample_explicit): the correct condition becomes the blackboard one, some nⱼ = 1. Impact. In the standard port-numbering model, which the paper's prose (Section 2.1) and the full version's proof use, Theorem 4.2 holds in both directions (theorem_4_2_if_twoSided, corollary_4_4_standard). Theorem 4.1 (blackboard), Lemma 3.2, Lemma 3.5, Lemma 4.3 and Corollary 4.4 hold in both models. Details. By Eq. (2), the knowledge Kᵢ(t) = (Kᵢ(t-1), Xᵢ(t), K_{πᵢ(1)}(t-1), …, K_{πᵢ(n-1)}(t-1)) only records what lies behind each of my ports. The paper says that sending the whole history is without loss of generality, but no party ever learns the port number at the other end of a channel. Counterexample: n = 5 and two sources, with parties 0, 1 on source 1 (n₁ = 2) and parties 2, 3, 4 on source 2 (n₂ = 3), so gcd = 1. Each party numbers its ports in increasing order of the other parties. Then parties 0 and 1 see the sources (1, 2, 2, 2) behind their ports, and parties 2, 3, 4 see (1, 1, 2, 2). This partition by sources is equitable, so by induction parties with the same source have identical knowledge at every time, whatever the random bits. Nobody is ever alone, and leader election fails with probability 1. More generally, for any configuration in which every source feeds at least 2 parties, some port numbering is equitable in this sense. So in the model of Eq. (2) the worst-case characterization is "some nⱼ = 1", exactly as in the blackboard model (worstCase_iff, worstCase_algorithm_iff). The paper's prose model (Section 2.1) lets every node send a message to each other node, and the full version's proof of the "if" direction (CreateMatching) sends ACKs back through a chosen port. This is the standard port-numbering model. Its full-information knowledge also records the sender's port, so the "without loss of generality" step leading to Eq. (2) is wrong. Repair. In the standard model Theorem 4.2 is true, and we prove the "if" direction with a short argument instead of the full version's sketch. Once the sources' bits differ, the knowledge partition stabilizes within n rounds. In a stable partition, a fixed port p with back-port q maps each class injectively into any other class, so all classes have the same size m. Each source is a union of classes, so m ∣ gcd = 1. (theorem_4_2_if_twoSided, corollary_4_4_standard) ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 3.2: "Kᵢ(t) is included in Kᵢ(s+t)" is not literally true. The property actually needed is that knowledge at s+t determines the knowledge of the run that starts with the same window, which we prove for both models (lemma_3_2, lemma_3_2'). Proof of Lemma 4.3 (full version): as printed, "port j of party i goes to ((i+j) mod g + ⌈i/g⌉g + ⌈j/g⌉g) mod n" connects a party to itself whenever 1 < g < n (e.g. n = 4, g = 2: port 2 of party 1). With floors ⌊i/g⌋, ⌊j/g⌋ it is a valid port numbering (checked by script for n ≤ 12), and the argument goes through. The lemma is true; we use other constructions (lemma_4_3, lemma_4_3_standard). Typos In the proof of Lemma 3.2, "independent whenever |s − s'| > t" should read ≥ t. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.2 (zero–one law) The proof applies Kolmogorov's zero–one law to E = ⋃ₛ E_{st}, which is not a tail event (it contains E₀). Impact. The statement is true, and a direct counting argument replaces the step (lemma_3_2, lemma_3_2'). Details. The zero–one law is also not needed: disjoint windows are independent, so Pr[no E_{st}, s < m] = (1-p)^m → 0. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Parties and sources. n anonymous fault-free parties, synchronous rounds, k independent uniform bit sources. A configuration is α : Fin n → Fin k (not required to be surjective), and nⱼ = load α j. Probability. All 2^{kt} source realizations of length t are equiprobable. Pr[P(t) solves O | α] is the fraction of them whose global state solves O (probSolves). No measure theory is used. Full-information knowledge is given by types defined by recursion on time. Blackboard (Eq. (1)): BBKnow (t+1) = BBKnow t × Bool × Multiset (BBKnow t). Message passing (Eq. (2)): MPKnow (t+1) = MPKnow t × Bool × (Fin (n-1) → MPKnow t), for a port numbering π i : Fin (n-1) ≃ {j // j ≠ i} chosen by the adversary. Both are instances of FullInfoModel: knowledge is local, cumulative, and shift-refining. Tasks and solvability. A task is a set of output vectors. Definition 3.1 says a global state solves O if some decision map f on knowledge values has f ∘ K ∈ O. Definition 3.3 (eventually solvable) says probSolves → 1. Consistency projections of a single facet are represented by the name sets of their simplices, so a name-preserving simplicial map between them is an inclusion. Uniform algorithms. Since per-facet solvability lets f depend on the facet, we also prove that, for leader election in both models, one uniform decision rule applied one round later achieves the same probability. The positive results are therefore algorithmic. Standard port model. We additionally state Lemma 4.3 and Corollary 4.4 in CSLib's standard port-numbering model (Cslib.PortNumbering: port-dependent messages, receivers learn the sender's port). There they hold for all deterministic algorithms, even ones that read the whole random stream of their source in advance. For the "if" direction of Theorem 4.2 we use the full-information knowledge of this model: Eq. (2) with the sender's port added, TSKnow (t+1) = TSKnow t × Bool × (Fin (n-1) → Fin (n-1) × TSKnow t) (tsModel). Main results in Lean.
