Bounded-Size Registers — PODC 2024 Carole Delporte-Gallet, Hugues Fauconnier, Pierre Fraigniaud, Sergio Rajsbaum, Corentin Travers. The Computational Power of Distributed Shared-Memory Models with Bounded-Size Registers. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662789. Formalized version: the conference paper, with the proofs of the full version arXiv 2309.13977 v1 (Sections 4–5 there = Sections 3–4 of the conference paper). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 1.1 (bounded registers are not universal when n/2 < t < n) is proved, together with the two results it cites (Lemma 2.1, FLP for read/write memory; Lemma 2.2, wait-free ε-agreement), and so is Algorithm 1 (two-process ε-agreement with 1-bit registers, Proposition 5.1). Theorem 1.2 (3-bit registers are universal for two processes) is proved from the Biran–Moran–Zaks characterization, which the paper cites: its "only if" direction (solvable with unbounded registers ⇒ connectivity and covering) is assumed as the hypothesis BMZ Δ; the rest (BMZ conditions ⇒ Algorithm 2 with 3-bit coordination registers solves the task) is proved. All repairs are local, namely Algorithm 2's parameters and a few missing proof cases, while Theorems 1.3–1.5, which include the t < n/2 and iterated results, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Algorithm 2 (full version), resolution The pseudocode calls A_{L/2} with ε = 1/(L+1) and then indexes the node Y_{dL}, while the text and Lemma 5.8 use ε = 1/L; dL is not an integer as printed, and L/2 need not be one either. Impact. Nothing else in the construction changes, and Theorem 1.2 holds. Repair. We use resolution 1/L with odd L = 2k+1 and call Algorithm 1 with parameter k, so the decision indexes the path node directly (alg2). ✏️ Slips In Section 5.2.4, "for every j ∈ {1,…,L}, Y_j ∈ Δ(X)" should read j ∈ {0,…,L−1}, as in Section 5.2.2; the last step of Lemma 5.8 repeats the index range (PathSystem.legal). In the proof of Theorem 1.1, w_ℓ is taken "after each process has decided", but a process may crash. The word w_ℓ should be the register contents at the end of E_ℓ (not_solves_epsAgreement). Claim 3.1's "D ⊆ O_ℓ' for some ℓ' ≠ ℓ" fails for D = {0}, ℓ = 0. This is harmless, since singletons are handled separately (solves_binConsensus_of_not_claim). Proposition 5.1 says "for every k ≥ 0", but for k = 0 the loop is empty and r is undefined. Algorithm 2 only needs k ≥ 1, which we assume (alg1_solves). In the proofs of Lemmas 5.1 and 5.4 the registers R1/R2 are swapped. The caption of Figure 1 says "1-bit registers are universal (Theorem 1.2)"; Theorem 1.2 says 3 bits (which is what is proved: Algorithm 1's ternary input register plus its 1-bit register). Typos |W| = … should be |W| ≤ …. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Claim 3.1 and Theorem 1.1 (inputs of the absent processes) The inputs of p_{n−t+2}…p_n are never fixed: the reduction to consensus uses the validity of ε-agreement, which only applies when all n inputs are equal, while consensus fixes only the inputs of p₁…p_{n−t+1}, and the final step needs E_{2i} and E_{2j} to agree on everything that p_{n−t+2}…p_n can observe, including those processes' own inputs, which the paper calls "arbitrary". Impact. Statements true. The proof works because p_{n−t+2}…p_n never take a step, so their inputs do not matter; the paper does not say this. Repair. In the validity argument those inputs are set to the common value (solves_binConsensus_of_not_claim). Everywhere else they are fixed the same way in all executions E_ℓ (not_solves_epsAgreement). 🔧 Lemma 5.8 (Algorithm 2, one process deciding) Lemma 5.8 assumes that both processes decide, yet Theorem 1.2's proof concludes correctness from it, so the case where one process decides and the other crashes is not treated. Impact. Statement true. This is exactly the case where the covering condition is needed. Repair. Solo decisions are legal too (covering condition); we prove that case (alg2_safe). 🔧 Lemma 5.5 (Algorithm 1, case k = 1) Lemma 5.5's case "I_j read as ⊥" says the other process decides at line 17 with r_j = 2, which is wrong for k = 1. Impact. Statement true (alg1_solves). Repair. For k = 1 the other process completes the loop and decides at line 14 instead. The value is the same, so the statement holds. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The asynchronous read/write shared-memory model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SWMR/Basic.lean). Processes are deterministic state machines with arbitrary state spaces, and there is no randomness. Each process owns a bank of SWMR atomic registers. A step is one read of any register, one write to an own register, or an irrevocable decision; processes may keep stepping after deciding. The adversary picks the inputs and the schedule. Crash failures: in an infinite schedule a process is faulty iff it takes finitely many steps. t-resilient solvability (Alg.Solves A t T) means two things. Every finite execution's decisions are legal. In every infinite execution with at most t faulty processes, every correct process decides. Wait-free is t = n − 1. "Registers of at most f(n) bits" means that the register bank of each process has at most 2^{f(n)} contents. This allows several registers per process, so the impossibility is stronger than the paper's. Unbounded registers (positive side of Theorem 1.1): one register per process holding a List ℚ. Two-process tasks (Theorem 1.2) are relations Δ on full input/output vectors over all input pairs In × In (the paper allows an arbitrary input set I). The model is a new, self-contained one. CSLib's shared-memory Impl framework (registers as base objects, Task, WaitFree, valency) has no crashes or t-resilience, and CSLib's FLP/ folder is Völzer's message-passing model. So neither could express t-resilient solvability or the register version of FLP. A bridge (an Alg as an Impl (taskObj In Out) over the registers P × K, plus a t-resilient fairness predicate on CSLib's InfExec) is left for the CSLib migration. Algorithm 1 uses, per process, a write-once input register (Option Bool, ⊥ = none) and a 1-bit register. Algorithm 2 additionally has the write-once task-input register. These are the paper's special input registers; the coordination registers hold 3 bits. Main results in Lean. Decision Power of Weak Asynchronous Models — PODC 2021 Philipp Czerner, Roland Guttenberg, Martin Helfrich, Javier Esparza. Decision Power of Weak Asynchronous Models of Distributed Computing. PODC 2021. DOI 10.1145/3465084.3467918. Formalized version: arXiv 2102.11630 v2 (full version with appendix); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Only Section 3 was checked, not the paper's main point, the characterizations of Sections 4–6. In Section 3 all the impossibility results hold: Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, 3.4 and 3.5 and Corollaries 3.3 and 3.6, which we prove directly for all three selection constraints (liberal, exclusive, synchronous). The one heavy repair concerns the explicit cutoff β + 1 of Lemma 3.4 for exclusive automata, which nothing else depends on (Proposition C.3 uses only some cutoff, and the paper's class-level results go through [16]); the rest is local. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 3.5's proof concludes that "K := m(|Q|−1) + 2 is a valid cutoff", but its argument needs L_G(q) ≥ (m−1)|Q| + 2, the bound printed one line earlier, and K is smaller than (m−1)|Q| + 2 whenever m > |Q|. The proof shows that adding a leaf with label q preserves acceptance when L_G(q) ≥ (m−1)|Q| + 2, which is what the pigeonhole step needs. The lemma only claims that some K exists, so it is unaffected. We use K = B + 3 with B = max(m_Y, m_N)·|Q| + 1 (lemma_3_5). In Lemma 3.5's proof, "the fact that MinPre*(C) is upward-closed" should read Pre*(C). Typos In Lemma 3.4's induction step, "⌈Q_{G(t+1)}⌉_β" should be ⌈·⌉_{β+1}. In Lemma 3.2's proof, "C_t(v) = C_t(f(v))" should be C'_t(v) = C_t(f(v)). In Lemma 3.5's proof, states and labels are identified ("L_G(q)" for a state q). The definition of a covering does not say that H must be connected and have at least three nodes. This is implicit in the graph convention. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, 3.4 (exclusive selection) The paper "generally assumes exclusive selection", but the proofs of Lemmas 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4 use non-exclusive schedules and rely, for exclusive selection, on the selection-independence theorem of [16], which does not give the explicit cutoff β + 1 of Lemma 3.4. Impact. Statements true; we prove all three lemmas directly for every selection constraint, including Lemma 3.4 with the cutoff β + 1 for exclusive selection (lemma_3_1, lemma_3_2, lemma_3_4). Details. The non-exclusive schedules: the proofs of Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4 run the automaton synchronously (as a DA$ automaton); the proof of Lemma 3.1 selects all copies of the nodes chosen by ρ_G and ρ_H at the same time. None of these is an exclusive schedule. The theorem of [16] relates classes of automata, so on its own it does not give the explicit cutoff β + 1 of Lemma 3.4 for an exclusive automaton. Repair. Lemma 3.1 alternates G-steps and H-steps. Every lifted selection is then the set of copies of a single node, which is independent and can be executed one node at a time. Sequentialising the paper's simultaneous selection would also work, since it only changes states at the junction nodes, which the distance argument already discards. Lemma 3.2 executes the fibre f⁻¹(v) one node at a time. Lemma 3.4 uses stars instead of cliques, with the schedule "all leaves (one at a time), then the centre". 🔧 Lemma 3.5 (stable acceptance) "An analogous argument shows that the same holds for acceptance" requires a second cutoff m', for the set of configurations that can reach a non-accepting configuration. Impact. Statement true; we take max(m, m') (lemma_3_5). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/DistributedAutomata/, staged for CSLib). Input graphs. LGraph Λ is a finite labelled simple graph. Admissible k encodes the paper's convention (connected, at least 3 nodes) plus a degree bound k : ℕ∞, where k = ⊤ means arbitrary graphs. Machines. A Machine has a counting bound β ≥ 1. Its transition function δ q N is applied to neighbourhood counts cut off at β (view). It has accepting and rejecting states Y, N. Halting means that Y ∪ N is absorbing. Steps and schedules. In step, the selected nodes move simultaneously. A schedule is ℕ → Set V. Selection and fairness. The selection constraint is liberal, exclusive or synchronous. Fairness is adversarial or pseudo-stochastic, exactly as in §2: every node is selected infinitely often, and under pseudo-stochastic fairness every finite sequence of permitted selections occurs infinitely often. Acceptance. Acceptance is by stable consensus. Consistent k is the consistency condition on admissible graphs. Accepts means that some fair run accepts. The complexity proof of Lemma 3.5 (early-stopping coloured ruling sets) does not work as written and would lose the optimal bound, so saving it takes a redesign of the colouring step of Algorithm 3 with a new induction on levels. Theorem 3.1 (CarefulWalk) and Proposition 3.2 hold as stated, the other repairs are local, and the cited lower bound behind "optimal" was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Lemma 3.5 (1) (running time of the early-stopping coloured ruling set) The recurrence T_i ≤ max(O(R·i), T_{i-1}) + O(R·i) for the commitment round of level V_i only gives T_i = O(R i²), not the claimed "by induction T_i ∈ O(R·i)" (lemma_3_5_recurrence_gap). Impact. We do not know whether the printed Algorithm 3 meets the bound. With the colouring step changed the bound holds (ES.rule, ES.colLe_isLocal), and so does Theorem 1.1. Left unrepaired, Theorem 1.1 would only give O(D (log* ℓ_min)²). Details. T_i = 1+2+⋯+i satisfies the recurrence with equality. The +O(R·i) comes from the (deg+1)-list colouring (line 11), run with Lemma 2.1 in Θ(R log* n_i) = Θ(R i) rounds. It starts only after all lower levels have committed, because the lists depend on their colours. Line 4's "wait Θ(R·i) rounds" is therefore also unjustified. Repair. Keep the membership computation as in the paper: membership of level i is decided after 816 R i rounds, because the chain through lower levels only adds O(R) per level. Split the colouring into two parts: Linial's colour reduction on G^{9R-1}[N_i], where N_i is the set of new ruling-set nodes of level i. It does not need the lower levels' colours. A sweep over the resulting 4096 classes, in which each node takes the least colour in [17] not used within distance 9R-1. This costs O(R) rounds after the lower levels' colours are known. Then colours of level i are fixed after 40000 R i rounds, and Lemma 3.5 holds with κ₃ = 40001 (ES.rule, ES.colLe_isLocal). 🔧 Lemma 4.5 (T_{α,L} + 7L) The proof places the ZWalk(8R_α) of SearchingWalk between rounds T+5L and T+6L, but it lasts 32R ≤ 2L rounds and can end at T+7L, so the argument only gives T_{α,L} + 8L (lemma_4_5). In the case R_β > R_α the extra delay τ then gives T+τ+5L+24R_β < T+8L rather than T+7L. ✏️ Slips Lemma 3.5 (2) ("if outside S, v knows the members of S at distance ≤ R-1") is false for the final ruling set S: a node of a higher level can join S within R-1 of v after v committed, if it is at distance ≥ R from v's ruling-set neighbour. It holds only for S_T at v's commitment round T. What v knows at commitment time is S_T ∩ N^{R-1}(v), which contains at least one node by part (3). That is all Algorithm 5 needs (it only needs some known ruling-set node). Our interface ColRuling.knows is stated this way. N^k(v) is defined as an open neighbourhood (distance in [1, k]). Line 4 of Algorithm 5 and the proofs of Lemmas 4.4–4.7 need closed balls. Typos Lemma 4.7 uses "the first bit where the colours differ"; any differing bit works. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 3.4 (iteration count of the greedy extension) The claim that a node w with locally maximal b_w lies within 2R-3 of v is not justified, and "N^{3R-4}(v) contains at most 6 ruling-set nodes, therefore 6 iterations suffice" is off by one. Impact. Statement true; the algorithm's 6 iterations are enough (gIter_spec). Details. A hill-climbing argument can end farther away (up to 3R-4). With the paper's count one would need 7 iterations. The correct count is that at most 2 added nodes lie on each side of v, at distance in [R, 3R-3]. So 5 iterations suffice and the algorithm's 6 are enough. The same argument gives 3 iterations, against Algorithm 3's 4 (gIter_spec). Full list of differences (modelling choices, constants, imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The line is ℤ, with an injective labelling ℓ : ℤ → ℕ. Time is synchronous rounds. The second agent wakes up τ rounds after the first; τ is arbitrary and unknown. A sleeping agent sits at its start node and can be found there (delayed τ b t = b (t - τ)). The agents are deterministic and identical, with no communication. They know neither D nor τ, neither positions nor orientation. Frame model (Algo, Line.lean). An agent cannot see the orientation of the line, but it knows the port it entered by, so it can keep walking straight or turn back. We therefore describe an algorithm by its trajectory pos μ t in the agent's own frame: start node 0, port 0 at the start is +1, and μ is the labelling read in that frame. The algorithm is causal: the move in round t+1 depends only on the labels of the nodes visited by round t. The adversary picks the start nodes, the delay, the labelling and both frame orientations ε = ±1. This model allows fewer algorithms than raw port numbers, which an algorithm could exploit, and every frame algorithm is implementable with ports. So our upper bounds hold in the paper's model. Rendezvous means being at the same node in the same round (thm_1_1). The variant with simultaneous edge-crossing detection (MeetOrCross) is used for Algorithm 5 itself, as in the paper. Early stopping means the radius depends on the node's own label. Algorithms on the unoriented line commute with the isometries of ℤ (IsEquivar); this is what lets both agents simulate the same ruling set. log* is lstar n = Nat.logStar n + 1, the paper's convention log* ≥ 1 (with ⌊log₂⌋). Distinct Gathering under Round-Robin — PODC 2026 Fabian Frei, Koichi Wada. Distinct Gathering and the Virtue of Self-Consistency. PODC 2026, pp. 239–246. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815962. Formalized version: the 8-page proceedings version. The announced full arXiv version (ref. [17], "arXiv:xxxx.xxxxx") could not be found, so the proceedings version is all there is; it gives only proof sketches. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Only the impossibility results were checked, and they are correct: Theorem 4 (no algorithm gathers 3 robots from distinct positions under Round-Robin) and Theorem 1 (no algorithm gathers n ≥ 3 robots from arbitrary positions, even with a shared unit length) are proved in Lean, in a stronger form that also holds with rigid movement and a common chirality. The one mistake is that Conjecture 3 is printed with "Gathering" instead of "Distinct Gathering". The paper's main positive results, Theorem 5 (n ≥ 4) and Theorems 6 and 7 (self-consistency), were not checked, because their algorithms and proofs appear only in the unavailable full version. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Conjecture 3 (§3) is printed as "every algorithm that solves Gathering under RoundRobin is a rapid-gathering algorithm", which by the paper's own Theorem 1 is vacuously true for every n ≥ 3, so the claim in §1 and §4.1 that Theorem 5 disproves it fails as printed (conjecture_3_as_stated). Distinct Gathering is meant: §3 states Conjecture 3 after Défago et al., Conj. 1, the sentence before it speaks of "any algorithm solving this problem", meaning Distinct Gathering, and Definition 5 starts from distinct positions. For n = 3 the intended version holds vacuously by Theorem 4 (conjecture_3_distinct_three), which agrees with the paper's remark "confirming Conjectures 2 and 3 in this case". The disproof for n ≥ 4 rests on Theorem 5 together with Défago et al., Thm. 16, and was not checked. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/MobileRobots/Model.lean, namespace Cslib.MobileRobots). n point robots in the plane ℂ. They are oblivious, anonymous and uniform, and the algorithm is deterministic. An algorithm is any function from the snapshot to a trajectory (Finset ℂ → (ℝ → ℂ), target = value at 1). The snapshot is the set of robot positions in the robot's local frame, with the robot at the origin, so there is no multiplicity detection. Variable disorientation: at every activation an adaptive adversary picks the frame, a similarity v ↦ a·v or v ↦ a·conj v with a ≠ 0 (scale, rotation, mirror). The theorems take a frame restriction frameOK. Theorem 4 needs only that all orientation-preserving similarities are allowed. Theorem 1 needs only that all rotations with the true unit length are allowed. Scheduler: centralized, one robot per step, so each Look-Compute-Move cycle is atomic. IsRoundRobin means a fixed order of all n robots, repeated forever; every order is allowed. Movement: an abstract Movement model fixes which stopping points the adversary may choose. The only requirement is that reaching the target is always allowed. Instances are Movement.rigid and Movement.nonrigid δ: stop at any point once the travelled arc length (eVariationOn) is at least δ. Both impossibility theorems hold for every movement model, which covers the paper's default (non-rigid, with δ known or unknown). Problem: Solves n A sched frameOK M init means every legal execution from an initial configuration satisfying init eventually stays gathered. Gathering uses init = True; Distinct Gathering uses init = Injective. The counterexample executions never gather, not even for a moment. Main results in Lean. From Few to Many Faults: Optimal Adaptive Byzantine Agreement — PODC 2026 Andrei Constantinescu, Marc Dufay, Anton Paramonov, Roger Wattenhofer. From Few to Many Faults: Optimal Adaptive Byzantine Agreement. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815964. Formalized version: arXiv 2505.19989 v3 (17 Jun 2026); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 3.1 (synchronous BA, t < n/2, O(n·f) messages, O(f) rounds) holds for the paper's protocol SyncBA against a static adversary, with the quadratic fallback (Momose–Ren) taken as a black box, once the proofs of ViewByzantineAgreement sign the view. Theorem 3.3 (Ω(t²) expected messages in asynchrony) holds, in fact almost surely, and Theorem 3.8 (committee assignment) holds, and we also prove the disperser existence the paper only cites; each needed one local repair of its proof. The partially synchronous and QAB protocols were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Appendix B.1 (ViewByzantineAgreement: key/lock/commit proofs must sign the view) The pseudocode forms proofs as tcombine((KEY, value), ρ) without the view, so a Byzantine leader can replay a key proof under a larger claimed view, bypass the lock check, and get commit proofs for two values. Impact. The protocol is unsafe as written, but the intent is evident and the fix is local (sign the view): the paper's proofs speak of "a key proof with view number view3" and "a commit proof contains a view number". Theorem 3.1 holds with the fix. Details. A party stores key ← (v, view, proof), and the key phase compares the claimed view of a proposed key with the view of its own lock. With unsigned views, a Byzantine leader can re-use a key proof for v₂ from view 3, claim it is from view 9, and pass the lock check of parties locked on v₁ in view 5. Lemma B.2 then fails, and two values can get commit proofs. Repair. Our statements key b v, lock b v, commit b v include the view (Stmt, key_after_commit). ✏️ Slips SyncBA (Appendix B.3), line 30 sets the fallback input to v_in, which may have become ⊥; we use the original input, as the proof of Theorem B.14 says. This only matters when the honest inputs are not unanimous. Theorem 3.8 for f̂ = 0: the construction has M = 0 committees, so every party is vacuously blocked. The paper uses f̂ ≥ 1 only. Typos SyncBA (Appendix B.1): whether a party that already has a commit answers RunRetrieval is ambiguous. Lemma 10.1 needs every honest party to answer an honest leader's retrieval. We take "a party is active in a view iff it had no commit when suggesting". Then an honest leader that runs the retrieval sees every honest party active, since otherwise it would have received a commit. Theorem 10.5 says f < ⌊(n−t−1)/2⌋, Theorem 7.2 says f ≤; ≤ is what holds. The Section 7 overview says a party accepts if its lock has a lower view than the proposed key (strict), while the pseudocode of Appendix B.1 rejects only a strictly smaller key view. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3.3 (asynchronous Ω(t²) lower bound, Markov step) The proof claims ⋂_{p∈C} E_pᶜ ⊆ {M ≥ t²/2}, but with |C| = t/2 parties each receiving more than t/2 messages one only gets M > t²/4. Impact. Statement true, even stronger: the bound holds almost surely (Async.theorem_3_3, Async.lower_bound_general). Details. So P(⋃ E_p) ≥ 1/2 and "P(E_p) ≥ 1/t for some p" are unjustified. Positive probability is enough for the final contradiction, so the theorem survives. The proof also silently assumes t even (|C| = t/2). Its "decides within time T" step has no meaning in an asynchronous model. Repair. No probability estimate is needed: the Final-setup argument applies pointwise to almost every random string. Hence a.s. every p ∈ C receives more than t/2 messages, and M ≥ (⌊t/2⌋+1)(⌈t/2⌉+1) ≥ t²/4 almost surely. We replace "decides within time T" by "decides before receiving any message" (Async.no_init_decision). 🔧 Theorem 3.8 (committee assignment; Theorem 6.2 used outside its range) The proof takes a disperser with N = n left and M = 4c_d·f̂·log n right vertices, but Theorem 6.2 is stated only for M ≤ N, which fails once f̂ is close to n / log n. Impact. Statement true; repaired by proving the disperser existence directly, for all N, M (theorem_3_8, exists_disperser, theorem_6_2). Repair. We prove the disperser existence by a union bound, for all N, M. This gives Theorem 3.8 for every n, f̂ with explicit constants: (4f̂+1)(⌈log₂ n⌉+1) committees, at most 2(⌈log₂ n⌉+1) committees per party, and at most 4f̂ blocked parties. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Theorem 3.1. CSLib's synchronous lock-step model (Cslib.Byzantine.LockStep) on the complete network of Fin n; one round is one Δ. The adversary is static and Byzantine, with f ≤ t < n/2 parties, rushing, and sends arbitrary messages. Signatures are ideal tokens (LockStep.Auth): the adversary may forge only Byzantine signatures, and may replay any signature an honest party has emitted. A k-threshold signature is a set of at least k partial signatures on one statement. We count messages, not bits; a party gets its own messages by self-delivery, which is not counted. The protocol syncBA is deterministic and defined as a local state machine (SyncBA/Defs.lean). Stage A runs ViewByzantineAgreement with the synchronous retrieval for n views of 11 rounds each, round robin, so every party leads once, then the HELP / PROOF / FALLBACK / LOCK rounds. Stage B runs the fallback among the parties holding a fallback certificate. The fallback is a hypothesis (Fallback): an unforging authenticated BA protocol for t faults, deciding within Rfb rounds, in which every honest party sends at most mfb messages whatever the others do. This is the paper's Theorem B.15 ("even if not all honest parties join"). Theorem 3.3. Message-driven asynchronous message passing. All randomness, a PKI and any setup are one random element ω, with no measurability assumed. The scheduler sees only metadata: who sent to whom, which messages were delivered, who decided. Faults are static, at most t parties, which run the code but whose links need not be fair. These are Byzantine behaviours, so a Byzantine-resilient protocol satisfies our requirement Solves. The weak adversary and scheduler make the lower bound stronger. Theorem 3.8. Pure combinatorics; log n is ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1. Complexities. O(n·f) / O(f) are meant with the convention f ≥ 1 (footnote 2); we state O(n(f+1)), O(f+1). Weaker than the paper: Theorem 3.1 is proved against a static adversary. The paper claims a dynamic one. Generalized CAS and a space-efficient universal construction — PODC 2026 Vassos Hadzilacos, Myles Thiessen, Sam Toueg. Generalized Compare-and-Swap and Space-Efficient Universal Constructions for the Infinite-Arrival Model. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815968. Formalized version: arXiv 2605.19237 v1 (full version with appendices); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorems 4 and 5 for Algorithm 1 hold: it is a linearizable, wait-free universal construction for any (possibly infinite) set of processes, its space is at most 4 plus the number of processes that have participated, and an operation takes O(c) steps, where c is the point contention when it obtains its timestamp. The flaws are local steps of the counting argument: a non sequitur in the induction of Lemma B.2.14, repaired by a pigeonhole argument, and an additive constant in the proof of Theorem B.2.15. Algorithm 2 (Theorem 6), the paper's second construction, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma B.2.6 uses Proposition B.2.5 ("not pending ⇒ complete") also for Noop, which is not an operation execution. The case is easy: no process ever writes Noop into A. We treat it separately (OpStart.old_out). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma B.2.14 (counting periods; inductive step) The inductive step concludes "o' = o_{3n+2} = o_{3n+3} = o_{3n+4} for some o' ∈ O_n" from the set not growing, which is a non sequitur: the three new operations can be three different elements of O_n. Impact. Statement true; repaired by a pigeonhole argument (OpStart.it_le). Details. The lemma bounds the number of non-initial periods of an operation o by 3|S(o)|. The proof shows |{o₁,…,o_{3n+1}}| ≥ n+1 by induction, where oᵢ is the operation identified by the i-th period. In the inductive step it assumes the set did not grow, so o_{3n+2}, o_{3n+3}, o_{3n+4} all lie in O_n. It then applies Proposition B.2.13 to four periods identifying one operation. Repair. Proposition B.2.13 says that no operation is identified by four periods. So each operation of S(o) is identified by at most three periods, and pigeonhole gives at most 3|S(o)| periods. In Lean we count differently. A rise of an operation τ is a step after which τ is done and not in A. Every operation rises at most 3 times, because its owner writes it into A at most twice after it is done (Trace.card_RE_le). Every non-initial period contains a rise of an operation of S(o), and disjoint periods give distinct rises (OpStart.useful, OpStart.it_le). 🔧 Theorem B.2.15 (number of iterations) At most 3c disjoint periods allow up to 15c + 4 complete non-terminal iterations after the first, not 15c, so the total is 15c + 6 iterations, not 15c + 2. Impact. Statement true: linearity is unaffected. We prove that an operation completes at most 15|S(o)| + 5 iterations and takes at most 105c + 44 memory steps (step_bound). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory (CSLib Impl, Cslib.SharedMemory). The processes form an arbitrary type P, possibly infinite: this is the infinite-arrival model with unbounded concurrency. The adversary chooses the schedule. A crash is a process that stops taking steps. There is no randomness. Base objects. C is a fetch&increment object, initially 1. A is a GCAS object (Podc/.../Objects/GCAS.lean) on triples (time, op, ptr), compared lexicographically as in footnote 2; this needs a linear order on operations. S is a CAS object. The dummy cell holds (0, ⊥). Further cells are CAS objects with arbitrary initial contents, handed out by a memory manager in the order 0, 1, 2, …. Since Algorithm 1 never frees cells, every allocation order has this form up to renaming. The target type T is a deterministic sequential specification (CSLib ObjSpec). Each line that accesses a shared object is one step, and local computation is merged into steps. Line 2 is a step only when the process allocates. Line 16 returns the response read on line 5. Correctness notions are CSLib's Linearizable and WaitFree. The point contention is the number of processes with a pending operation. The space is the number of static objects (C, A, S, the dummy cell) plus the number of allocated cells. Proof method. Linearizability is a state invariant (Invariant.lean, about 30 clauses) over the algorithm augmented with ghost variables (Ghost.lean). The linearization is the order of the successful CAS operations on S, as in the paper. The step bound follows the time-based arguments of Appendix B.2 on Traces. A trace is an execution indexed by time, with ghost records of when each line of the current iteration was executed. exists_trace turns any finite execution into a trace. Main results in Lean. Energy-Efficient Distributed Agreement — PODC 2025 Hugo Mirault, Peter Robinson. Brief Announcement: Towards Energy-Efficient Distributed Agreement. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733554. Formalized version: the brief announcement, with the algorithms and proofs of its full version arXiv 2506.12282 v1 (cited as [12] for the omitted proofs; Algorithm 1/Lemmas 1–4 of the BA = Algorithm 2/Lemmas 2–5 there, Theorem 2 of the BA = Theorem 6 there). arXiv v2 is a different, later paper (OPODIS 2025, with Meir and Peleg) with a redesigned binary algorithm; it is not formalized here. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The paper has two results of equal weight, and only one survives. The multi-value result (Theorem 1) holds: Algorithm 1 solves crash consensus in f + 1 rounds with 2 + 2⌈f(f+1)/n⌉ awake rounds per player and O(f³ + nf) messages, although its proof needs one repair and Lemma 2 is false as literally stated. The binary-consensus result (Theorem 2) is not established: the algorithm behind it, sketched in the BA and given as Algorithm 3 in the full version, violates agreement, e.g. for n = 5, f = 3, although the claim itself is existential and so not refuted. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 2 (binary consensus algorithm) The binary consensus algorithm (sketched in the BA, Algorithm 3 of the full version) violates agreement: for n = 5, f = 3, a chain of single-recipient crashes makes the non-faulty p₀ decide 1 and p₁ decide 0 (algorithm3_violates_agreement, algorithm3_violates_agreement_7_4, algorithm3_violates_agreement_9_7). Impact. Theorem 2 is existential, so it is not refuted but unestablished; Theorem 1 (multi-value consensus) is unaffected. Details. Take n = 5, f = 3. Committees (JoinCommittees(3, 3)): C₁ = {p₁,p₂,p₃}, C₂ = {p₄,p₀,p₁}, C₃ = {p₂,p₃,p₄}, and T = ⌈4/√5⌉ = 2. Only p₂ has input 1. The run goes as follows. Round 1: p₂ crashes, and its message reaches only p₃ ∈ C₁. Round 2: p₃ (now active) crashes, reaching only p₄ ∈ C₂. Round 3: p₄ relays 1 to C₃ = {p₂,p₃,p₄}. All other members of C₃ have already crashed, so the adversary does not need to crash anyone in this round. Round 4 = f + 1: p₄ broadcasts and crashes, reaching only p₀. With only 3 crashes, the non-faulty p₀ decides 1 and p₁ decides 0. The gap is the paper's counting argument: a relay round does not always produce a new holder of 1 or force a new crash. A message can go to a committee whose members have all crashed already, or to the relay itself. The same works for n = 7, f = 4 (three non-faulty players) and for the perfect square n = 9, f = 7. For n = s², f = n − 2, a relay chain whose receivers are taken from C₁ = C_{1+s} = … whenever possible eventually makes such a round free. A simulation (scripts/family.py) confirms this for all 3 ≤ s ≤ 12. The BA's sketch (committees "analogous" to Algorithm 1, unspecified) is affected just as much. A model check shows that for n = 5, f = 3, every choice of 3 committees of size 3 admits a disagreeing execution. In the full version, Lemma 11 (used for Lemma 12, agreement) is false: in the run above |P₄| = 3 ≤ f, yet agreement on 0 fails. The authors' later OPODIS 2025 version describes this exact attack ("crash players, one at each round, such that eventually … all the members of a committee have already crashed") and redesigns the algorithm. ❌ Full version, Section 4.1 (committee spacing, used in Lemmas 9 and 11) The full version's claim that a player in C_i is in none of C_{i+1}, …, C_{i+⌈√n⌉+1} is wrong: JoinCommittees does not guarantee it, and no assignment can once f > ⌈√n⌉, or f = ⌈√n⌉ with n not a perfect square, as in the n = 5, f = 3 run. Impact. The analysis of the binary algorithm depends on this property, and we have no replacement for it. Details. The property would need min(f, ⌈√n⌉+2) pairwise-disjoint committees of size ⌈√n⌉, i.e. more than n players. 🔧 Lemma 2 (hypothesis "alive in round i") Lemma 2 is false as stated: it assumes only that p is alive in round i (not crashed in rounds 1, …, i − 1), so p may crash in round i itself and lose its message (lemma_2_as_stated_false). Impact. Evident intent: the proof says that p "successfully sends its message to all destinations", so the intended hypothesis is "does not crash in round i". We prove that version: every decision is ≥ v (corrected lemma_2). Details. Example: n = 2, f = 1, inputs 5, 0. p₀ sends 5 to C₁ in round 1 and crashes, reaching nobody; p₁ decides δ = 0 < 5. ✏️ Slips Algorithm 1 needs f ≥ 1, since it refers to C_f. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 4 (agreement) The proof treats the first clean round t only for t = 1 and 1 < t < f + 1, missing t = f + 1, and in the main case concludes "since p does not crash" for an arbitrary alive holder p of δ, which may crash later. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_4). Repair. The repair uses two facts. After a clean round t ≤ f, all alive members of C_t hold the same value, because every one of them received every alive member of C_{t−1}, whose maximum dominates their own earlier values by Lemma 3 (mv_clean_le). And C_t has a non-faulty member, which carries this value to the end. If t = f + 1, every decider receives the values of all alive members of C_f, and Lemma 3 bounds its own value. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SleepingCrash/Model.lean, staged, CSLib candidate). Synchronous rounds 1, 2, … on a complete network of n players with unique IDs, in the sleeping model. In each round a player is awake or asleep, as a function of the round and of its state at the start of the round (an "alarm" set when it was last awake). Asleep players send nothing, receive nothing (messages to them are lost) and do not change state. Crash faults: an omniscient adversary fixes the inputs and, for at most f players, a crash round c ≥ 1 and the subset of recipients that still get the player's round-c messages. Afterwards the player sends nothing. Deterministic algorithms, no randomness. Deciders are the players that complete round f + 1. Agreement and validity are proved for all of them. Energy is the number of rounds in 1..f+1 in which a player is awake before crashing (awakeCount). Messages are counted as sent, including those lost (msgCount). Multi-value inputs come from any linearly ordered type (the paper uses integers). Main results in Lean (namespace Podc.EnergyEfficientAgreement). Distributed Download from an External Data Source — PODC 2025 John Augustine, Soumyottam Chatterjee, Valerie King, Manish Kumar, Shachar Meir, David Peleg. Brief Announcement: Distributed Download from an External Data Source in Byzantine Majority Settings. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733526. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv 2412.19649 v1 ("… in Faulty Majority Settings", the only version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The deterministic crash-tolerant Rapid Download protocol (Algorithm 7) is wrong: with k = 4 peers, n = 4 bits and f = 2 crashes, a nonfaulty peer finishes without ever learning a bit, so Lemmas 5.13 and 5.15 are false and Theorem 5.16 (time O(n + f) for any β < 1) is unestablished for f ≥ 2. The one-round lower bound (Theorem 3.6) and the simple Static Download protocol (Theorem 5.9: query-optimal, time O(nf)) are correct, after small repairs of their proofs. The paper's main point, the randomized protocols against Byzantine peers, was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Algorithm 7 (Rapid Download), Lemmas 5.13 and 5.15 Algorithm 7 does not solve Download: with k = 4 peers, n = 4 bits and f = 2 crashes (β = 1/2), a run makes the nonfaulty M3 skip bit 2 and finish with res[2] = ⊥, which refutes Lemmas 5.13 and 5.15 (Rapid.lemma_5_13_false, Rapid.lemma_5_15_false, Rapid.rapid_not_solves). Impact. Theorem 5.16 (time O(n + f) for any β < 1) is unestablished for f ≥ 2. The lower bound (Theorem 3.6) and Static Download (Theorem 5.9) are unaffected. Details. Peers M0,…,M3, lead(v) = v mod 4; M1 and M2 crash (f = 2 ≤ βk with β = 1/2). In the run below, "index" is the paper's 1-based bit index. View 1 (leader M1). M1 sends ⟨view 1, 1, b₁⟩ to all, then crashes during its second transmission, which reaches only M2. M2 now has two messages, sets I = 2 and sends ⟨view change 2, 2⟩. M0 and M3 see the silence and send ⟨view change 2, 1⟩. All three messages reach M2 in the same round, so M2 works on index 2. View 2 (leader M2). M2 queries b₂ and crashes during its first transmission, which reaches only M0; M0 sets I = 2, res[2] = b₂. M3 heard nothing, so it suspects M2 one round earlier than M0 and sends ⟨view change 3, 1⟩ to lead(3) = M3, i.e. to itself. View 3 (leader M3). M3 starts when its own message arrives. Line 8 takes the highest index among the view-change messages of that round only, which is 1. M0's ⟨view change 3, 2⟩ arrives one round later and is ignored ("for the first time", line 7). M3 sends ⟨view 3, 1, b₁⟩ twice. M0 keeps I = 2 (line 19: 1 < 2), but on the second message line 23 increments I to 3 regardless of the index carried. The skip. At this point the nonfaulty M0 has I = 3, while the nonfaulty M3 has res[2] = ⊥; this refutes Lemma 5.13. From now on every leader works on index ≥ 3. M3 downloads bits 3 and 4, finishes with I = 5 > n, and keeps res[2] = ⊥ forever, which refutes Lemma 5.15 and the correctness of Algorithm 7. The pseudocode is event-driven and does not fix initialisation or timing. We fix the round timing of the paper's own Remark 1 (also Remark 2's claim "M will work on i+1" fails here). Under the other natural timing (a view-changing peer stays idle for two rounds), a simulator finds the same index skip with n = 6, caused by different F sets instead of different detection times. With Remark 1's timing, the protocol still fails (simulation, n = 6) if a leader adopts a higher index that arrives later, as Remark 2 suggests. The theorem's f ≤ βk, β < 1 (also claimed in §1.4.3) contradicts Table 2, which marks Theorem 5.16 "#: β ≤ 1/k", i.e. f ≤ 1. ✏️ Slips Algorithm 7 never says how view 1 starts: no peer sends ⟨view change 1, ·⟩, so read literally all peers suspect the nonfaulty lead(1) after one round, contradicting Lemma 5.11. The intent is evident: we let lead(1) start view 1 at time 0. Theorem 5.9 for f = 0: T = O(nf) is literally false (it is n), and so is M = O(k²·f·n); the bounds hold for f ≥ 1. Peer IDs are [1, k] but lead(v) = v mod k ∈ [0, k−1]. Typos In §3 the letter n is both the number of peers and of bits, and Lemma 3.3 needs them equal. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3.6 (Eq. (8) in the proof of Lemma 3.4) Eq. (8) claims p(R̂(Byz)) > (1 − e⁻¹)/2 for every Byzantine set Byz, which fails, e.g., when the defective peer v(R) always lies in Byz. Impact. Statement true; we prove a derandomized version (theorem_3_6). Details. Only the average over the uniformly random Byz is bounded. That suffices once the involution Byz ↦ V \ (Byz ∪ {v(R)}) is applied per random profile R; the paper applies it to sets that depend on R. Repair. For every algorithm there are an input, a bit ℓ and a fixed set of (n−1)/2 Byzantine peers that run the algorithm on the input with ℓ flipped, with failure probability ≥ (1 − e⁻¹)/4. 🔧 Lemma 3.3 (maximizing q(i)) The claim "q(i) is maximized when p_v(i) = 1/n" is not justified. Impact. Statement true; we use 1 − x ≤ e^{−x} and pigeonhole instead (lemma_3_3). 🔧 Theorem 5.9 (query bound) The proof says each nonfaulty peer leads "at most n/γk" views, but the exact bound is (n + k − 1)/(k − f) ≤ 2n/(γk). Impact. Statement true: the exact bound still gives Q = O(n/γk) (theorem_5_9_queries, Static.theorem_5_9). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Crash part (Model.lean): synchronous DR model with k peers on a clique and a trusted source X : Fin n → Bool. A round is a query sub-round, the answers, then a message sub-round (a message to each peer, possibly oneself), followed by a local step. Protocols are deterministic state machines. Crash faults follow an arbitrary pattern: a peer crashing in round c sends its round-c messages only to an adversarial subset of peers and then stops. At most f peers crash. The adversary chooses the input and the pattern, which for deterministic protocols is the same as an all-knowing adversary. Q is the number of bits a nonfaulty peer queries. Download within T means: from time T on, every nonfaulty peer has res = X. Lower bound (LowerBound.lean): one synchronous round; n peers and n bits. Each peer has independent private coins over a finite space, and its query set, messages and output are arbitrary functions of its coins, its answers and its inbox. Each peer always skips at least one bit (A ∈ A(n−1, 1)). The adversary is the paper's weak adversary, derandomized: a fixed input, bit ℓ and set of (n−1)/2 Byzantine peers that run the algorithm honestly on the input with bit ℓ flipped. The result is stronger than with the paper's random set, and it also covers the broadcast model. Algorithm 7 (RapidDownload.lean) is encoded literally from its pseudocode, with the timing and initialisation choices listed in differencies.md. A crash-free sanity run downloads all bits. Adjacency Labeling for Power-Law Graphs — PODC 2016 Casper Petersen, Noy Rotbart, Jakob Grue Simonsen, Christian Wulff-Nilsen. Brief Announcement: Near-Optimal Adjacency Labeling Scheme for Power-Law Graphs. PODC 2016. Formalized version: full version arXiv 1502.03971 v1; numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The checked results all hold once the paper's missing definitions are filled in the only way that makes its proofs work: the upper bounds (Theorems 1 and 2), the lower bounds (Proposition 4 and Theorem 3) and the properties of P'_α (Propositions 1–3). The normalising constant C is never defined, so we use C = 1/ζ(α); Proposition 4 is false only for c large compared to n, and the repairs of Proposition 3, the Proposition 4 padding argument and the greedy construction of Theorem 3 are local. The experiments and the threshold prediction were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Proposition 4 fails when c is large compared to n: for n = 2, c = 100, one bit suffices, but the claimed bound is ⌊√200/2⌋ = 7 (prop4_false). For c ≥ (n-1)/2, S_{c,n} is the family of all graphs, which have labels of about n/2 bits, while ⌊√(cn)/2⌋ grows without bound in c. The intended regime (constant c, growing n) is fine, and we prove the bound for all c < n (prop4). Definition 2: the normalising constant C is never defined, and the proofs need C·ζ(α) = 1: Prop. 1's proof needs C·ζ(α) ≥ 1, and Thm 3's construction needs C·ζ(α) ≤ 1. This is an implied assumption (the standard normalisation of a power law); with C = 1/ζ(α) (C) all results hold. Thm 3's construction uses Σ_{i ≤ i₁} ⌊Cn/i^α⌋ ≤ n. With a small C, the class-size constraints of Definition 2 no longer bound the maximum degree by O(n^{1/α}), because the isolated vertices absorb the slack. With a large C, P'_α is empty for large n and the lower bound fails. Neither alternative was formalized. Definition 1 (n / log n with log 1 = 0) is meaningless for n = 1. Under the literal reading, with the Lean convention x/0 = 0, P'_α ⊄ P_α at n = 1. We require k ≥ 1, which is automatic for n ≥ 2. Prop. 1's proof defines k' = ⌊n^{1/α}⌋ but the integral step needs ⌈n^{1/α}⌉; with ⌈·⌉ the stated bound, including the +3, comes out exactly (prop1). Theorem 3, Phase 1 omits the requirement that the added pair be non-adjacent, so as written the loop does not terminate (exists_maximal_fill). Theorem 3 is claimed "for all n", but the construction needs n large; it is true for all large n (theorem3_proper, theorem3). Typos i₁ must be the smallest positive such integer (i = 0 qualifies trivially). "Moon's bound ⌊n/2⌋" is for fixed-length labels. For labels of length at most ℓ, counting gives ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ (moon), which suffices for every use. The paper's C' is called a constant but depends on n through i₁/n^{1/α}, which stays bounded; ours does not depend on n. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Proposition 3 (integral comparison in the wrong direction) The proof uses Σ_{i=k}^d i^{-α} ≤ ∫_k^d x^{-α}dx, which misses the term k^{-α}, and |V_i| ≤ Cn/i^α + 1 for all i, which fails for i = 2 (+2). Impact. Statement true: P'_α ⊆ P_α holds with a larger constant (prop3). Repair. The inclusion holds with C'₀ = (C/(α-1)+8)^α + Cα/(α-1) (prop3). 🔧 Theorem 3 (the greedy construction) Phase 2 claims that after greedily adding edges between unprocessed vertices of V' "at most one vertex of V' remains unprocessed", but the remaining unprocessed vertices form a clique and there can be several (targets 3, 3, 2 joined in the order ab, ac, bc leave a, b unprocessed). Impact. Statement true (theorem3_proper, theorem3). Repair. We replace each greedy loop by an edge-maximal graph (exists_maximal_fill). The remaining clique has at most i₁ vertices, so all of them are saturated by leaves (bip_phase). Parity is fixed in advance by choosing |V₁| (realize). 🔧 Proposition 4 (padding argument) The proof uses n both for the family size and for the embedded graph, so as written it covers only family sizes of the form ⌊m²/c⌋. Impact. Statement true for all c < n (prop4). Repair. Our proof embeds an arbitrary graph on ⌊√(cn)⌋ + 1 vertices directly into n vertices and applies the counting bound ⌊(m-1)/2⌋ (prop4). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Graphs are finite simple graphs on Fin n. deg, |V_i| = numDeg G i, c-sparse means |E| ≤ cn (Sparse), and log n = ⌈log₂ n⌉ (lg, the number of bits of an identifier). An adjacency labeling scheme with X-bit labels for a family F of n-vertex graphs (HasAdjLabeling n F X) is a decoder fixed for the family. The decoder is an arbitrary relation on bit lists and may depend on n. Every G ∈ F must have labels of length ≤ X such that the decoder decides adjacency of any two distinct vertices. Upper bounds construct an explicit decoder that depends only on ⌈log₂ n⌉. Lower bounds hold against arbitrary decoders. P_α (Definition 1, IsPowerLaw α C') takes the constant C' as a parameter. P'_α (Definition 2, IsProperPowerLaw α) is transcribed literally with C = 1/ζ(α). The class V₀ of isolated vertices is unconstrained, as in the paper. Theorem 3's graph uses isolated vertices for the slack instead of the paper's extra degree-≥ i₁ singletons. Definition 2 allows this. "Ω(n^{1/α}) for all n" is formalized as: there is κ > 0 such that for all large n every scheme needs κ n^{1/α} bits. Main results in Lean. Almost Stable Matchings in Constant Time — PODC 2010 Patrik Floréen, Petteri Kaski, Valentin Polishchuk, Jukka Suomela. Brief announcement: Almost stable matchings in constant time. PODC 2010, pp. 281–282. DOI 10.1145/1835698.1835765. Formalized version: the full paper Almost Stable Matchings in Constant Time, arXiv 0812.4893 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All three theorems hold with the paper's constants: truncated Gale–Shapley gives an ε-stable matching in T ≤ 4 + 2Δ²/ε rounds (also with ties), a (2+ε)-approximate maximum-weight matching in T ≤ 4 + 2Δ/ε rounds, and a constant-query estimator of the size of a stable matching. Lemmas 1–5 are true. Lemma 6 is false as stated for Δ = 1, i = 1, and the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 inherit this; it needs i ≥ 2, as in Lemmas 4 and 5, which its proof uses, and this condition changes no constant. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 6 for Δ = 1, and its use in the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 Lemma 6 claims f_i(R) ≤ γ w_i(B) for all γ > 0 and i ≥ 1 + (Δ-1)/γ, which for Δ = 1 allows i = 1, where the bound fails already on a single edge K₂ (lemma_6_false_at_one). Impact. The intent is evident: the proof combines Lemmas 4 and 5, which are stated only for i ≥ 2, and with the extra hypothesis i ≥ 2 the lemma holds (Bicoloured.lemma_6). No constant of Theorems 1–3 changes. Details. After round 1 nothing is matched (w_1(B) = 0), while every red node has a pending proposal (f_1(R) > 0). K₂ has maximum degree 1 and no isolated nodes. For Δ ≥ 2 the hypothesis forces i ≥ 2. The proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 inherit the mistake: for Δ = 1 they allow i = 1, and M_1 = ∅ is neither ε-stable nor an approximation. Repair. Add i ≥ 2 to Lemma 6. In Theorems 1 and 2, whose statements are true, choosing i = max(2, ⌈…⌉) keeps T = 2i within the claimed bounds (theorem_1, theorem_2). ✏️ Slips Proof of Lemma 5: "w({r,b}) < w_j(b)" should be ≤. The weights respect the preferences only weakly, and with w ≡ 1 equality holds. Only ≤ is needed. Typos §6.3 treats Y (the matched nodes among the first N red samples) as a binomial variable without saying that the analysis conditions on the sample containing N red nodes. The bound is correct. We prove it with a martingale (exponential-moment) argument over the sequential sampling. (card_firstHits_abs_sub_ge_le in Podc/Probability/Finite/MultiplicativeChernoff.lean) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Distributed model (Theorems 1, 2): CSLib's anonymous port-numbering model (Cslib.PortNumbering). It is synchronous and deterministic, with no failures and no identifiers. A node knows its degree, its colour (red/blue input) and T (built into the algorithm). Its ports are numbered by preference (port 0 = favourite). The graph is any simple port-numbered graph whose input colouring is proper; isolated nodes are allowed. One GS round is two communication rounds (blue turn, red turn), so T = 2i. Messages are full local states (Algorithm.ofLocal), but each node only uses the information the 'propose', 'accept', 'reject' and 'break' messages of §4 carry. The output is the port of the partner. For Theorem 1 with ties the paper's "analogous" hides nothing: the ports refine the weak preferences, and every edge unstable for the weak preferences is unstable for the refinement (theorem_1_ties). Centralised analysis: Bicoloured V is a finite bicoloured graph with strict preferences, given as ranks that are injective on the neighbours. run I i is the state at the end of round i, a global synchronous transition. dec_localRun proves that after 2i communication rounds the port-level run decodes exactly to run I i. Theorem 2: each node's input is its colour and the weights (nonnegative reals) of its edges, given per port. The node ranks its ports by decreasing weight, breaking ties by port number, and then runs the Theorem 1 algorithm. M* ranges over all matchings. Theorem 3: randomness is uniform on (Fin N → V) × (Fin K → V) (sampling with replacement, probability by counting), and the algorithm knows n. The oracle is not modelled interactively. Instead we prove the three facts the query count rests on: locality (whether r is matched in M_j depends only on the local data within distance 2j), the bound < 3(Δ-1)^{2j} on the size of such a ball, and the arithmetic bound on N + K + N·3(Δ-1)^{2j}. M is the stable matching M_∞ reached by Gale–Shapley, as in the paper's proof. Main results in Lean. Namespace Podc.TruncatedGaleShapley. Blunting an Adversary with Linearizable Implementations — PODC 2022 Hagit Attiya, Constantin Enea, Jennifer L. Welch. Blunting an Adversary Against Randomized Concurrent Programs with Linearizable Implementations. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538446. Formalized version: arXiv 2106.15554v2 (full version with appendix). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4, on which the proof of the main theorem rests, are false (Lean counterexamples), and the simulating adversary used in their proofs is not a valid adversary. Theorem 4.2 holds as stated for programs with one random step, and a weaker bound, which still gives convergence to atomic objects, holds for any number of random steps; for r ≥ 2 the stated bound remains unestablished (neither proved nor refuted here). Only shared-memory objects are covered: the application to ABD, snapshots and the other implementations of Section 5 was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4, and Theorem 4.2 (main theorem) for r ≥ 2 Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4 are false because conditioning on X biases the program's own coins, and Theorem 4.2 is unestablished for programs with r ≥ 2 random steps, since its proof is the decomposition (1)–(2) over X, which needs the two false lemmas. Impact. The stated bound holds for r = 1 (the only case used in the paper's example, Appendix A.3.1) and in a weaker form for every r; for r ≥ 2 it is neither proved nor refuted here (theorem_4_2_r1, theorem_4_2_weak). The instance below does not refute Theorem 4.2 itself. Details. Lemma 4.3 claims Prob[(P(O^k)||A → B) | X] ≤ Prob[P(O^a) → B] for every adversary A. In a two-process program with one register, one object read with a one-step preamble and two coins, an adaptive adversary with k = 2 gets Pr[B | X] = 2/3 > 1/2 (Counterexample.lemma_4_3_false). In the same instance, the adversary that overlaps only when c1 = 1 gets Pr[B | ¬X] = 1, while Prob[P(O) → B] ≤ 1/2, which refutes Lemma 4.4 (Counterexample.lemma_4_4_false). X = "every object random step picks a randomization-free preamble iteration". Conditioning on X biases the program's own coins: the adversary can decide, after seeing the first coin, whether the preamble iteration that might be chosen later overlaps the second coin. Instance: processes p, q; a register R and an object S whose read has a one-step preamble (the object is strongly linearizable, so all hypotheses of Theorem 4.2 hold, with r = 2); p: c1 := coin; R.write(c1); c2 := coin, q: S.read(); y := R.read(), B = {y = 1}. With atomic objects (and with the original object) Pr[B] ≤ 1/2 for every adversary. With k = 2, the adversary that lets q start S.read before p's write and c2 only when c1 = 0 gets Pr[B | X] = 2/3. Repair. For every r we prove Prob[O^k] ≤ Prob[O^a] + (1 − q) and Prob[O^k] ≤ Prob[O] with q = (max{0,k−r}/k)^{n−1}. The stated bound Prob[O^a] + (1−q)(Prob[O] − Prob[O^a]) is stronger whenever Prob[O] < 1. A repair of the stated bound along the lines of the paper fails when the adversary makes the choice of which iterations get spoiled at a later coin depend on earlier coins. 🛠️ Proofs of Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4 (the adversary A_O) The simulating adversary A_O built in these proofs is not a valid adversary, because its schedule depends on future coins. Impact. The simulation of P(O^k) by P(O) with unused iterations removed is saved by a new argument, which the bounds above use (Removal.opt_le_avg, prob_iter_le_prob_impl, optBX_le_prob_atom). Details. The adversary A_O chooses each object random value as the "best" one after later program coins, and remRedundant moves preamble steps relative to earlier coins, which violates the paper's own definition of an adversary. Repair. The object random choices are independent of everything the adversary sees before they are made, so they can be sampled in advance; for each advance choice the removal of unused iterations is a causal adversary against P(O) (Removal.opt_le_avg). ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.1 speaks of tail strong linearizability of a set of histories, which is not defined (the notion needs executions and control points). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 4.5 (probability of X) The proof treats the events X_i as independent with fixed probabilities, although the set of spoiled iterations depends adaptively on earlier choices. Impact. Statement true; proved by a potential argument (lemma_4_5, Clean.optNX_le). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, no failures. Objects are deterministic implementations from atomic base objects (CSLib Impl), all operations allowed; a finite set of objects is one combined object. Message-passing implementations (ABD) are not covered. Programs: one deterministic client per process with local steps, random(V) (uniform over m+1 values) and object calls. Outcomes are final client states (at least as general as the paper's return-value outcomes). Strong adversary: chooses the next process with full knowledge of the configuration (hence of all past random values). Prob[P(O) → B] (prob) is the optimal value of the resulting finite-horizon game (MDP.opt, supremum over horizons; non-terminating runs do not count), i.e. the supremum over all strong adversaries. Conditional probabilities in the counterexamples use the value of a fixed adversary. Preamble mapping = predicate "the local state is still inside the preamble" with well-formedness (PreambleWF); effect-free = preamble steps apply read-only primitives (EffectFree); tail strong linearizability (TailStronglyLinearizable) = linearizable + prefix-preserving linearization function on executions in which every pending invocation has passed its preamble. O^k (iterSem, Algorithm 2): k preamble iterations from the post-invocation local state, then one uniform choice; ghost fields record which iterations overlapped a program random step (event X). Wear Leveling in Persistent Data Structures — PODC 2022 Xialin Liu, Wojciech Golab. Brief Announcement: Towards a Theory of Wear Leveling in Persistent Data Structures. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538457. Formalized version: the 4-page proceedings version (no arXiv version). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The round-robin counter of Figure 1 is correct: it is strictly linearizable (Theorem 4.1, for unbounded words) and lock-free (Theorem 4.2), and with k words of endurance T it survives k·T FAIs (Theorem 4.3). Theorem 4.4 ("any implemented object … can guarantee endurance at most k·T") is false as stated: a test-and-set from one word of endurance 1 never wears out. It is true for fetch-and-increment, so the counter is optimal, which is all the paper uses the theorem for; only the generality, on which nothing depends, is lost. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 4.4 (endurance at most k·T for any implemented object) Theorem 4.4 is false for test-and-set: a TAS from one word A[0] of endurance 1 (CAS(A[0], false, true), Flush(A[0]), return "lost" iff the CAS failed) is strictly linearizable and lock-free in all executions, with any number of operations (theorem_4_4_false, tas_guarantees). Impact. The generality "any implemented object" is given up. The theorem is true for fetch-and-increment: the counter's k·T is optimal, which is the claim of the introduction (theorem_4_4_fai). Details. The proof says that, under sequential access, "each update operation on the implemented object must update at least one base object". This fails for objects whose updates stop changing the state. In the TAS, A[0] is written back at most once in any execution, so with k = 1 and T = 1 Theorem 4.4 promises a failure after k·T + 1 = 2 updates that never comes. The refutation holds in the model of the proof of Theorem 4.3 (wear = write-backs to persistent memory), whatever a worn-out word does (wrong values or no response). This is a false theorem, not a degenerate case: TAS is a standard object and the theorem says "any implemented object". The model cannot be changed to rescue both Theorems 4.3 and 4.4. If every operation applied to a base object counted towards its endurance (Definition 2.1 applied to the base CAS objects), Theorem 4.3 would fail instead: every FAI of Figure 1 starts with a CAS on A[0] (lines 3–5), so A[0] receives T + 1 CASes within T + 1 sequential FAIs. Repair. We prove the FAI case: every strictly linearizable, obstruction-free FAI implementation from k words has a sequential crash-free execution with k·T + 1 FAIs that writes some word back T + 1 times (theorem_4_4_fai). ✏️ Slips Definition 2.1 and Theorem 4.3: the wear model changes between the definition and the proof. Definition 2.1 counts updates invoked on an object. For the base objects, the proof of Theorem 4.3 instead counts write-backs to persistent memory, under assumptions (1)–(3) and "a failed CAS does not dirty the line". The formalization uses the proof's model; under it, Theorems 4.1–4.3 hold and Theorem 4.4 fails. Proof of Theorem 4.1, crucial claim: iter = ⌊ℓ/2^k⌋ and index = ℓ mod 2^k should be ⌊ℓ/k⌋ and ℓ mod k (with ℓ counted from 0). The rest of the proof uses the correct values. Proof of Theorem 4.2: the value of A[k−1] is read at line 12, not line 13. The CAS on A[k−1] comes k − 1 (not k) iterations later. Proof of Theorem 4.3: when FAI k·T + 1 takes effect, A[0] is written back for the (T+1)-st time. A[0] is accessed (CAS at line 5) by every FAI. Theorem 4.2 implicitly assumes finitely many threads. Its proof needs a suffix without successful CAS, and with infinitely many threads each could perform one successful CAS and then stop. Typos Theorem 4.3: "endurance at T" is missing a word. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Persistent/, staged for CSLib). Asynchronous threads (any set P; finite for lock-freedom), adversarial schedules of events: invocation, one step of a thread, spontaneous eviction of a cache line, system-wide crash. Deterministic algorithms. k words of persistent memory behind a coherent, volatile write-back cache (one word = one cache line). Reads and CAS act on the cache. A successful CAS dirties the line, a failed one does not. Flush and eviction write a dirty line back and clean it, and do nothing on a clean line. A crash reloads the cache from persistent memory and abandons all running operations. These are assumptions (1)–(3) of the proof of Theorem 4.3. Each line of Figure 1 is one atomic step. The purely local lines 3, 10, 11 are merged with the neighbouring shared-memory step. Lines 12–13 are the same states as lines 1–2. Words hold unbounded naturals. Safety = strict linearizability (Aguilera–Frølund) of the history of invocations, responses and crashes w.r.t. a fetch-and-increment counter. An operation pending at a crash takes effect before the crash or never. Liveness = lock-freedom: in every infinite schedule with finitely many crashes in which running threads keep taking steps, responses keep occurring. Wear-out: a word survives T write-backs. Every later write-back stores an arbitrary value chosen by the adversary (junk); the cache is unaffected. Definition 2.1 is HasEndurance: safe and live in all executions with ≤ N invocations for every junk, but not with N + 1 for some junk. Non-responsive wear (a worn-out word that stops answering) is not modelled. Main results in Lean (namespace Podc.WearLeveling). The paper never says how a worn-out word fails; Definition 2.1 only says it loses "safety and liveness". If a worn-out word may stop responding (e.g. the Flush that performs its (T+1)-st write-back never completes, a non-responsive failure in the sense of Jayanti–Chandra–Toueg [4]), FAI k·T + 1 never returns and the counter's endurance is exactly k·T, as stated. The same reading gives "a hardware FAI followed by a Flush provides endurance T". In the safety-only wear model formalized here (a worn-out write-back stores an arbitrary value, the word keeps responding), the exact value is k·T + 1. Definition 2.1 says endurance T means "correct in all executions with at most T updates, but not in some execution with T + 1". With k words of endurance T, the (T+1)-st write-back of A[0] happens only when all k·T + 1 FAIs have already performed their successful CAS. After that, no thread reads or CASes the memory again: the pending operations only flush and return values already computed. A lost or corrupted write therefore becomes visible only through a crash and another FAI. So the counter is correct in all executions with k·T + 1 FAIs, whatever a worn-out word stores. It fails with k·T + 2: k·T + 1 sequential FAIs, a crash, one more FAI. If worn-out words keep their old value, the last FAI returns k·T a second time. So in this wear model the exact endurance is k·T + 1, because the counter has no read operation. The paper's argument ("k·T FAIs can be invoked before any element is updated more than T times") is right in every wear model. In this wear model the counter itself also exceeds the bound k·T of Theorem 4.4 by one. How to Tame Multiple Spending in Decentralized Cryptocurrencies — PODC 2022 João Paulo Bezerra, Petr Kuznetsov. Brief Announcement: How to Tame Multiple Spending in Decentralized Cryptocurrencies. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538465. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv 2205.14076 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The lower bound (Theorem 5.1: no k-Consistent Broadcast for k below the inconsistency number k_max), and with it the advertised "the optimal spending number is precisely the inconsistency number", is false: we give trust models with k_max = 3 and k_max = 2 where 2-CB, resp. 1-CB, is implementable (for every source, with per-value Local Progress). The correct optimum of k-CB for a source s is max(1, λ_s), the maximum restricted to faulty sets containing s; we prove both bounds, but optimality for k-SAT itself was not checked, as Theorem 5.2 is not formalized. Theorem 3.6 (uniform model, with the implicit f < q ≤ n), Theorem 4.1, Lemmas 4.3–4.7 and Theorem 4.8 (Algorithms 1–2 implement k_max-spending asset transfer, safety and liveness) hold, the latter with assumptions on the correct issuers that the paper uses implicitly. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Theorem 5.1 (lower bound: no k-CB for k < k_max) and the optimality claim of §5, the abstract and the introduction Theorem 5.1 is false: with three processes, each process's only quorum being itself, and at most one failure, k_max = 3, yet "every process delivers the first value it gets from the source" is a 2-CB for every source (theorem_5_1_false). Impact. Sinks the advertised "the optimal spending number is precisely the inconsistency number". The correct optimum for a source s is max(1, λ_s), the maximum restricted to faulty sets containing s; we prove both bounds (optimal_kcb). The claim at the end of §5, "Algorithms 1 and 2 implement k-SAT with optimal k", fails for the same reason; the safety and liveness of Algorithms 1–2 (Theorem 4.8) are unaffected. Details. The proof lets a Byzantine source r ∈ F equivocate to the members of an independent set of a graph G_{F,S} with maximum independence number. But the maximum may be attained only by faulty sets that do not contain the source — typically F = ∅, when correct processes have disjoint quorums. With a correct source nothing can go wrong, and with a faulty source the relevant graphs have smaller independence number. In the smallest example (the uniform model with q = 1, f = 1), with no failures all three processes are pairwise independent, so k_max = 3. With a correct source only one value is delivered, with a faulty source only two processes are correct. A less degenerate example has four processes a, a', b, b' with quorums {a,a'}, {b,b'}, Π, Π and faulty sets ∅, {a}, {b}: k_max = 2, yet a quorum-echo algorithm is a 1-CB for every source (theorem_5_1_false'). The paper's own algorithm even beats k_max: in the three-process example (k_max = 3) every run of Algorithms 1–2 has spending number at most 2 (algorithms_beat_kmax). Only faulty issuers spend an input twice, and a faulty issuer spends it at most λ(Q, {B}) times, B the actual faulty set (spendingNumber_le_refined). In the four-process example (k_max = 2) nothing is ever spent twice (algorithms_no_double_spending_pairsT). Repair. With λ_s the largest independence number of the graphs G_{F,S} with s ∈ F, every k-CB with (per-value) Local Progress has k ≥ λ_s (lower_bound, srcInconsistencyNumber_le, the paper's gluing argument; it uses ∅ ∈ F, which follows from the standing inclusion-closure assumption), and the quorum-echo algorithm achieves max(1, λ_s) (echoAlg_isKCB). So the optimal k is max(1, λ_s), not k_max (optimal_kcb). 🔧 §5.1, Local Progress (too weak for the proof of Theorem 5.1) The proof needs Local-Progress executions in which the k processes deliver k different values, but Local Progress only promises that p delivers some value (WeakLP.theorem_5_1_needs_localProgressAll). Impact. Per-value Local Progress, which the proof evidently intends, fixes this; our repaired lower bound uses it, and the quorum-echo algorithm satisfies it (lower_bound, echoAlg_localProgressAll). Details. With three processes s, a, b, quorums Π, {s,a}, {s,b} and faulty sets ∅, {s}, the source is faulty in the only graph attaining k_max = λ_s = 2; still, an algorithm in which a and b deliver a default value on their own, and any other value only when both echoed it, satisfies Local Progress and is a 1-CB. ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.6 does not state f < q ≤ n, an implied assumption; for q ≤ f the formula's denominator is ≤ 0 and the inconsistency number is n − q + 1 (theorem_3_6_needs_q_gt_f). The formula holds under f < q ≤ n (theorem_3_6), and inconsistencyNumber_uniform gives the value for all f. Lemma 4.7 (Validity) and Accuracy in Theorem 4.8 silently assume that a correct process issues only valid transactions whose inputs it has already accepted and never issues conflicting ones, but transfer checks neither; without the input condition Validity fails (ValidityCex.validity_needs_inputs). They hold with these assumptions, which the paper uses implicitly (Setup.lemma_4_7, Setup.lemma_4_7_of_issue, Setup.accused_byzantine). Accuracy says verify-acc returns true "iff AC ⊆ F"; the "if" direction is impossible for a run-independent function (Setup.accuracy_iff_impossible), "only if" is meant. Algorithm 1 line 5 checks the REQ signature against the sender instead of the issuer. Algorithm 2 line 26 omits tx ≠ tx'. Theorem 5.2's proof writes deliver(m) for a transaction carrying m'. Typos Example 3.1 writes the fault model {{p₃}} (not inclusion-closed) and gives p₃ a quorum without p₃. The proof of Lemma 4.4 does not say why the k acceptors are distinct; it follows from No-Conflict of each history (Setup.lemma_4_4). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3.6 (proof covers only |F| = f and only the upper bound) The proof only handles faulty sets of size exactly f and never shows that ⌊(n−f)/(q−f)⌋ is attained. Impact. Statement true (with f < q ≤ n); both parts are easy and added (theorem_3_6, inconsistencyNumber_uniform). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Trust model (Q, F): a quorum map and a fault model over a finite process set; p ∈ Q for every quorum of p (SelfMem), F inclusion-closed (DownClosed) and every process has a quorum (HasQuorums) are explicit hypotheses where used. G_{F,S} is a Mathlib SimpleGraph on the correct processes; independence number = SimpleGraph.indepNum. Asset transfer (§4): transactions are an abstract type with issuer, output map and input set. Algorithms 1–2 run in an asynchronous interleaving model with a static Byzantine set B ∈ F, authenticated channels (messages may be received any number of times), unforgeable issuer signatures (Byzantine processes inject only correctly signed content), and liberal guards (a superset of the code's behaviours). Correct processes never issue conflicting transactions (HonestIssuers) where needed, as the paper assumes implicitly. Liveness is over infinite executions with reliable delivery between correct processes and weak fairness of every action (Setup.Exec.Fair); fair executions exist (Setup.exists_fair). k-CB (§5): the asynchronous Byzantine broadcast model Cslib.Byzantine.AsyncBroadcast (staged in Podc/) with adaptive corruption, weak fairness for liveness, and executions whose set of corrupted processes lies in F. Delivery is the single decision. Algorithms are arbitrary guard-based protocols (guards may read everything a process received and sent). Main results in Lean.
