Replicated List: the Jupiter Protocol Revisited — PODC 2018 Hengfeng Wei, Yu Huang, Jian Lu. Brief Announcement: Specification and Implementation of Replicated List: The Jupiter Protocol Revisited. PODC 2018. Formalized version: full version, arXiv 1708.04754 v4; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The main results hold: once clients send in-range positions, Jupiter and CJupiter behave identically (Theorem 12), are convergent (Theorem 11) and satisfy the weak list specification (Theorem 18), which settles the conjecture of Attiya et al. As written, they fail: the paper lets users insert or delete "at a position larger than the list size" (meaning at the end) and sends that position unchanged, so the OT functions of Figure A.1 violate CP1 and both protocols diverge; the fix is one line, normalising the position before sending. Several proofs of Section 5, on which Theorem 18 rests, are not real arguments, and we replace them by a different argument. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Figure A.1 with out-of-range positions (Theorems 11 and 18) With positions beyond the list size, which Section 2.3 allows and the clients send unchanged, the OT functions of Figure A.1 violate CP1 (cp1_fails), and both Jupiter and CJupiter diverge, violating Theorems 11 and 18 (jupiter_raw_counterexample, cjupiter_raw_counterexample). Impact. A local fix (one line of pseudocode) that the paper's own text supplies: normalise the position when the operation is generated (genOp); with in-range positions Figure A.1 satisfies CP1 (square) and all main results hold. The out-of-range convention is stated explicitly in the paper, so the printed protocols really diverge. Details. Section 2.3 defines Ins(a, p)/Del(p) for p beyond the list size as an insertion/deletion at the end. The clients send o unchanged (Algorithms B.5, C.5), and the OTs of Figure A.1 compare raw positions. On [x]: o₁ = Del(5) deletes x, and o₂ = Ins(b, 1) appends b. Then OT(o₁, o₂) = Del(6) and OT(o₂, o₁) = Ins(b, 1). Applying o₂; Del(6) gives [x], while o₁; Ins(b, 1) gives [b]. As a run of Jupiter with two clients: c₀ inserts x; then c₀ deletes at 5 while c₁ inserts at 1. Both final Reads see all three updates, yet c₀ reads [b] and c₁ reads [x]. This violates A_cp and hence A_weak. The violation of A_weak does not depend on the choice of the abstract execution: c₁'s final Read must see c₁'s own Ins(b, 1), nobody deletes b, yet it returns [x]. So no well-formed abstract execution complying with the run is in A_weak (cjupiter_raw_not_weak_any, jupiter_raw_not_weak_any). The paper requires that a transformed operation "inserts (resp. deletes) the element a", which only makes sense for in-range positions, and the OT literature it cites [8, 9] assumes them. Repair. We normalise the position in genOp. The user-visible result does not change; only the operation sent to the server does. ✏️ Slips Footnote 8's LCA definition (an antichain of common ancestors) does not say "lowest". Typos Appendix A says that the smaller replica id has the higher priority, while Figure A.1 shifts the insertion with the larger pr. With ids used as priorities (Figure A.1's caption), Figure 1 ends in ab, not ba. Either convention works. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemmas 23 and 24 (Theorem 26, pairwise compatibility) Lemma 24, Case 2.2 ("step ladder") and the inductive step of Lemma 23 are not real arguments. Impact. Statements true; we give a different proof (Sched.Vert.inter, Sched.compatible). Repair. The vertices of the global state space are the causally closed operation sets made of a ≺s-prefix plus operations of one client. These sets are closed under intersection, so the LCA of Lemma 23 is V₁ ∩ V₂. Along any path, the operations keep the relative order of existing elements. Two common elements of V₁ and V₂ were therefore inserted in V₁ ∩ V₂ and keep their order on both paths. 🔧 Lemma 25 (one-step claim) The one-step claim assumes the operation "does not correspond to any element of the list in v", which excludes deleting a common element, a case the induction needs. Impact. Statement true: a deletion only shrinks the common elements and keeps their order (Sched.sublist_of_subset, Sched.compatible). 🔧 Remark after Definition 19 (used in Lemma 21) The remark that lo is transitive on each list "by definition" is only true given pairwise compatibility. Impact. Statement true; transitivity follows from Theorem 26 (Cfg.GI.weak, Sched.compatible). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n clients and one server. Each client is connected to the server by two reliable FIFO channels; the system is asynchronous. An execution is any finite sequence of events: do c u (a user operation at c), srv c (the server processes the next message from c) and recv c (c processes the next message from the server). There are no failures and no randomness. The server generates no operations (as in the paper). Operation ids are (client, seq). Inserted elements are these ids (the paper's "unique elements"). The priority of an insertion is its client id. Both protocols follow the pseudocode of Appendices B and C literally. A state space is the list of its edges (each labelled by an operation whose context is the source vertex) plus the current vertex. In Jupiter, the edge of u in dimension d is the latest-added matching edge, which mirrors the array overwrite of Algorithm C.4. CJupiter's firstEdge is the edge that Compare ranks below all others. Read also generates a NOP operation that is sent around, as Do does in the pseudocode. A Del on an empty list is recorded as Del(⊥, k). An abstract execution has H = the do events in execution order. Its visibility is "the operation was processed by the replica before this event". This is a well-formed visibility relation (proved), but we do not prove that it coincides with Lamport's happened-before. Proof device: a global state space determined by a schedule (Sched.T, Sched.L). Its ranks are the server order, prophesied from the final configuration of the execution (pending operations come after the processed ones, in FIFO order). Main results in Lean. The figures' step-by-step examples (we only ran Figure 1 as a test) and the literal set equalities of Propositions 14 and 16. These are replaced by the invariants above, which are stronger for what Theorems 12 and 18 need. Proposition 9, Lemma 5 and Propositions 14 and 16 are argued by "mathematical induction" sketches, and Prop. 9's hard Case 2 (an operation inserted in the middle of a client's sequence) is only illustrated; we found no wrong step but did not check them, and prove these facts as invariants instead. The Recoverable Consensus Hierarchy — PODC 2019 Wojciech Golab. Brief Announcement: The Recoverable Consensus Hierarchy. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331574. Formalized version: the full version Recoverable Consensus in Shared Memory, arXiv 1804.10597 v2 (May 2018); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All four results hold: the two transformations (Figure 1 under simultaneous failures, Theorem 1; Figure 2 with f + 1 consensus instances under at most f independent failures, Theorem 2) and the two lower bounds (f readable test-and-set objects do not suffice, Theorem 3; f consensus objects do not suffice for generic constructions, Theorem 6). The proof of Theorem 3 rests on a restricted failure model (Assumption 1) in which its Case C is false for readable TAS, and changing one condition of that model repairs it; the multi-register reads of Figures 1–2 need only a local argument. The Θ(f) tightness for TAS was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Section 5, after Corollary 4: "2-process conventional consensus implemented using a single TAS object and no additional read/write registers" is impossible (the loser must learn the winner's input); with O(1) registers per instance, as the abstract says, the intended O(f) space bound holds. Theorem 2 sketch and Lemma 15, Case 2: "R[z] > R[j] = x" should be R[j] = x + 1. Lemma 14, Case B: "line 17 in its own iteration k_i or higher" should be k_i + 1. Typos Lemma 13: there is no condition k > 0 at line 19; the loop is simply empty. Theorem 2 sketch, validity: "at line 4" should be line 21. Lemma 9: Case 3 "reads P[j] = ⊥ at line 10" should be line 9; Cases 4–5 say p_j for p_i. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 3 (Assumption 1 and Case C) With Assumption 1 as written — p₁ crashes right after its first access to a TAS object — Case C ("p₁ has accessed T already, so T holds 1") is false when that access was a read of the readable TAS, and the restricted-model statement the proof establishes is then false (literal_assumption1_rcorrect). Impact. Statement true; repaired by counting only tas operations in Assumption 1 (theorem3, corollary4). Details. In the critical state both processes may be poised to apply tas to an object T that still holds 0 but that p₁ has already read. Then p₁'s tas is not its first access, so no crash follows (Case B does not apply), and the two tas operations do not commute (Case C's premise fails). This is not just a missing case: the algorithm A₀ (P[i] := v; read T; tas T; the winner returns v, the loser returns the other's P), with one rTAS object and two registers, satisfies agreement, validity and recoverable wait-freedom on every execution obeying the literal Assumption 1 (p₁ crashes once, after its dummy read, before any tas), so no argument confined to those executions can derive a contradiction. A₀ is of course incorrect in the real model (A₀_not_solvesP, from Theorem 3). Repair. p₁ crashes right after its first tas on each rTAS object (reads do not count). An rTAS object on which p₁ has applied tas holds 1 (Theorem3.tasInv), so Case B applies whenever the object holds 0 and Case C whenever it holds 1; there are still at most as many crashes as rTAS objects. We also supply the steps the proof omits: an initial bivalent state (biv_init), termination of the critical-state construction (exists_crit: finitely many crashes, so some process steps crash-free forever and must decide), agreement of all outputs in restricted executions although the paper's agreement is only between distinct processes (agree'), and the non-symmetric Case D in which p₂ reads and p₁ runs solo with its forced crashes (contra_a). 🔧 Lemmas 9, 10, 14 (non-atomic multi-register reads) The proofs for Figures 1 and 2 treat the two-register tests of Figure 1 (lines 2, 9, 11) and the scan of R[1..n] in Figure 2 (lines 24–25) as atomic snapshots. Impact. Statements true; the Lean proofs handle the reads one at a time (Fig1.theorem1, Fig2.lemma14). Details. Figure 1: P[i] changes only when p_i writes it and never returns to ⊥, and an idle process whose proposal is recorded implies that nobody is in lines 3–5 (used implicitly in Lemmas 9–10). Figure 2: the argument "when p_i reached line 26 no process had reached line 17 of a later iteration" holds per checked process; the invariant is "the commitment holds, or some not-yet-checked process has R ≥ k_i + 2". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's crash-recovery shared-memory model (Cslib.SharedMemory.Recoverable): asynchronous, deterministic processes, one atomic operation per step, objects with deterministic sequential specifications. A crash resets the crashed process's local state to its initial state (holding its input); shared objects are non-volatile. No randomization; the adversary chooses the schedule and the crashes. Independent failures: Ev.crash p; AtMost f = at most f crashes in total. Simultaneous failures: our event type SEv with crashAll (resets every process), arbitrarily many crashes. Binary consensus (CSLib's inputs/outputs are Bool): impossibility results are slightly stronger, algorithms slightly weaker than the paper's multi-valued ones. Specification: the paper's recoverable consensus SolvesP (agreement between distinct processes, validity, recoverable wait-freedom: a process that steps forever without crashing after time N outputs after N) for the lower bounds; the algorithms satisfy the stronger CSLib Solves (all outputs agree, also those of one process in different incarnations) resp. SolvesS. Time Bounds for Shared Objects in Partially Synchronous Systems — PODC 2011 Jiaqi Wang, Jennifer L. Welch, Hyunyoung Lee. Brief Announcement: Time Bounds for Shared Objects in Partially Synchronous Systems. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993877. Formalized version: the full version, J. Wang's MS thesis of the same title (Texas A&M, December 2011, advisor J. L. Welch); numbering follows the thesis (Chapter IV for the lower bounds). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The d + min {ε, u, d/3} lower bounds hold: for every strongly immediately non-self-commuting operation (read-modify-write, dequeue, pop; Theorem C.1) and for |OP| + |AOP| under the hypotheses of Theorem E.1. The (1 - 1/k) u bound of Theorem D.1, one of the three main results, is established only under a stronger hypothesis, which covers writes and every k = 2, and for skew ε ≥ (1 - 1/k) u; the claim that Theorem E.1 covers push/peek on a stack is false. The upper bounds of Chapter V were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ §IV.E and Table III (push and peek on a stack) The thesis says that Theorem E.1 "can be applied to push and peek on a stack" and lists d + min {ε, u, d/3} as a lower bound for |push| + |peek|, but push/peek never satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem E.1 (stack_push_peek_not_E1). Impact. The push+peek entry of Table III (and the same claim in Chapter VI) is unproved, and we have neither a proof nor a refutation of the bound itself; the theorem itself and its application to enqueue/peek on a queue are fine (queue_E1_hyps). For E.1's hypotheses, a peek after pushes behaves like a read after writes, a case the thesis itself excludes from Theorem E.1 (overwriting). Details. Hypothesis A asks that exactly one of ρ ∘ op₁ ∘ aop₁ and ρ ∘ op₂ ∘ op₁ ∘ aop₁ be legal. With op₁, op₂ pushes and aop₁ a peek, both sequences leave the element of op₁ on top, so they are legal together or illegal together (as soon as hypothesis C makes op₁, op₂ legal instances). A peek of a queue sees the first element, which is why enqueue/peek works. ⚠️ Theorem D.1 of Chapter IV (Step 1.1 of the proof) Step 1.1 asserts a single legal permutation π of the k concurrent operations that fixes the results of every later sequence of operations; correctness does not give this, and without it the runs of the proof yield no contradiction (tr_answers). Impact. Theorem D.1, a main result of the thesis (abstract), is unestablished in its stated generality; we have neither a proof nor a counterexample. We prove it under a stronger hypothesis, LastRevealing (one fixed query sequence whose results determine the last of the k operations). This covers writes with k = n (write_lastRevealing) and every case k = 2 (theorem_D1_two). Details. Correctness gives a linearization for each complete run; an algorithm may decide the order of concurrent operations lazily, depending on later operations. The proof's runs R₁ and its shifts R₂^z only imply: the answers of later queries are compatible, for every z, with some permutation that respects the real-time order of R₂^z. If |OP| is close to (1 - 1/k) u (above (1 - 2/k) u), that order only puts op_z before op_{z+1 mod k}, so op_z is not last. For the "test-and-reset" register (writes W a; T a answers whether the value is a and resets it), the writes satisfy the theorem's hypothesis (tr_nonEquiv), yet for k = 3 every query sequence has answers compatible, for every z, with a permutation whose last write is not z (tr_answers; only the last write matters, so one with op_z before op_{z+1} exists). So the hypothesis does not imply LastRevealing (tr_not_lastRevealing). We do not know whether Theorem D.1 itself fails for this object. Repair. theorem_D1: with ε ≥ (1 - 1/k) u and LastRevealing, |OP| ≥ (1 - 1/k) u. The thesis's shifts and its six-case delay check are correct (after the typo in the shift, see Slips). ✏️ Slips Theorem D.1 (clock skew): the run R₂ of the proof has skew (1 - 1/k) u, but the theorem allows any ε; the bound is established only for ε ≥ (1 - 1/k) u (theorem_D1). The proof states that it assumes the optimal skew ε = (1 - 1/n) u ≥ (1 - 1/k) u, and Chapter V makes the same assumption. For smaller ε the bound appears to fail: Algorithm 1 of Chapter V answers pure mutators (writes) after ε (not formalized). Definitions D.1, D.2, D.4: read literally, an accessor has a legal ρ with ρ ∘ op illegal, so ρ ∘ op is not equivalent to ρ and op is a "mutator". No operation type is then a pure accessor (not_pureAccessor) and Theorem E.1 is vacuous. The intended definition (Kosa) compares only legal sequences; with it (NonMutator) Theorem E.1 is proved (theorem_E1). Proof of Theorem D.1, Step 2: the shift x_i = [-(k-1)/2 + ((z-i) mod k)/k] u should read -(k-1)/(2k) (as in Step 2.2 and in the skew computation). Proof of Theorem C.1, Step 2: "messages from p_j to p_k cost δ = d - m" should be p_j to p_i. Proof of Theorem E.1, Step 1: "since aop'₁ and aop'₂ are pure mutators" should be pure accessors. §III.B.2: views require strictly increasing clock times, which rules out simultaneous receipts such as those at p_k in the run R₁ of Theorem C.1; non-decreasing times are meant. Claim B.2: for timed automata whose timers accumulate at a finite time (Zeno), a finite admissible run has no complete admissible extension; non-Zeno algorithms are meant. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem E.1 (both orders of op₁, op₂ are legal) The proof infers that ρ ∘ op₁ ∘ op₂ and ρ ∘ op₂ ∘ op₁ are both legal from immediate self-commutativity, which needs ρ ∘ op₁ and ρ ∘ op₂ legal; hypothesis C gives only one of them. Impact. Statement true; repaired by running each operation alone after ρ: a correct implementation returns a legal value, and determinism does the rest (theorem_E1). Details. We also invoke the accessors at fixed times (t + B₁ + η and m later) instead of the thesis's adaptive times; this makes the case analysis of Step 2.2a unnecessary. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Partially synchronous message passing, n processes (Fintype P), no failures, reliable channels, message delays in [d - u, d] chosen by the adversary as a function of sender, receiver and send time, drift-free clocks with offsets of pairwise difference at most ε (Cslib.TimedMP.Scenario.Admissible). Deterministic algorithms, no randomness. The adversary also chooses the clock offsets and the invocation times (one pending operation per process, WF). An algorithm is given by causal local behaviours in local clock time (Cslib.TimedMP.Algorithm): every non-Zeno timed automaton of the thesis is one. Runs exist and are unique (exists_run, IsRun.unique); shifting a run is IsRun.shift; chopping and extending is running another scenario that agrees before a causally closed cut (agree_of_cut, agree_window). Hypotheses on the algorithm, all from §III.B.4: correctness (Correct: unique responses, linearizability with the real-time order "response < invocation"), bounded operation time (TimeBound … Bop), finite runs (consequence of bounded quiescence, FiniteRuns), history-obliviousness (HistoryOblivious, same residual behaviour after two runs executing the same operations). Theorem D.1 needs only correctness and Bop. |OP| ≥ X is stated as: if every OP operation responds within B in all admissible runs, then B ≥ X. Proof remarks: Theorem C.1 holds for n ≥ 2 (the thesis assumes n ≥ 3); the ρ-prefix of every run is a fresh admissible run glued by history-obliviousness (restart), which is necessary when 2 min {ε, u, d/3} > u; where the thesis invokes an operation "immediately after" a response, we leave a small gap, since precedence is strict. At-Most-Once with Nearly Optimal Effectiveness — PODC 2011 Sotirios Kentros, Aggelos Kiayias. Solving the At-Most-Once Problem with Nearly Optimal Effectiveness. PODC 2011. DOI 10.1145/1993806.1993847. Formalized version: arXiv 1107.2990 v2 (Dec 2013, the full TCS version with all proofs); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. KK_β never performs a job twice (Lemma 4.1), is wait-free for β ≥ m (Lemma 4.3), and with up to m − 1 crashes has effectiveness exactly n − (β + m − 2) (Theorem 4.4 for f = m − 1), which for β = m is the abstract's n − 2m + 2; Theorem 2.1 (E ≤ n − f for every algorithm) holds too. Theorem 4.4 claims the same value for every f ≤ m − 1, and with fewer crashes the effectiveness can be larger, so "=" becomes "≥" there, and the proof of Lemma 4.3 needs one definition changed. The work bounds, IterativeKK(ε) and Write-All were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 4.4 (equality for f < m − 1 crashes) The theorem claims E_{KK_β}(n, m, f) = n − (β + m − 2) for every f ≤ m − 1, but with fewer crashes KK_β can be forced to perform more jobs: for m = 2, β = 4, n = 5 = β + m − 1 and f = 0 the formula gives 1, yet every fair execution performs at least 2 jobs (theorem_4_4_false_few_crashes). Impact. The lower bound E ≥ n − (β + m − 2) holds for all f ≤ m − 1 (theorem_4_4_ge), and the value is exact for f = m − 1 (theorem_4_4), which is the case the abstract's n − 2m + 2 and its comparison with the bound n − m + 1 = n − f refer to. Only the "=" for f < m − 1 is false. The paper's matching adversary crashes m − 1 processes, so its proof covers only f = m − 1. Details. With m = 2, β = 4, n = 5 and no crash, process 1 always picks the smallest available job, and process 2 always picks an element of rank ≥ 2. So process 2 never announces job 1 (u1), and process 1 performs job 1 in its first iteration (invA). Process 2's first target is job 3. While only job 1 is done, process 1 announces only jobs 1 or 2, so process 2's first check cannot fail and it cannot terminate before performing a job other than 1 (invB). By wait-freedom and fairness both processes terminate, so at least two jobs are performed (kk254_do_ge). Exhaustive model checking (kk_modelcheck.py) finds more counterexamples, also with crashes and well above n = β + m − 1: (n, m, β, f) = (9, 2, 6, 0) has E = 4 against 3, and (8, 3, 6, 1) has E = 2 against 1. Repair. Theorem 4.4 with f = m − 1 (theorem_4_4), plus the lower bound for all f ≤ m − 1 (theorem_4_4_ge). ✏️ Slips Theorem 4.4 (small n): for n ≤ β + m − 2 the formula n − (β + m − 2) is ≤ 0, the regime where the paper's guarantee is vacuous (fewer than about β + m jobs), but KK_β can be forced to perform jobs: for m = n = β = 2 and one crash the effectiveness is 1, not 0 (theorem_4_4_false_small). As long as no job has been performed, process 1 always targets job 1 and process 2 always targets job 2, so no check fails and no process can reach end before some job is done (noJob_inv); a fair run with at most one crash therefore performs a job (kk222_do_pos), and Theorem 2.1 gives E ≤ n − f = 1. Our exhaustive model checker shows the same for other small cases: n = m = β = 3 with f = 2 also has E = 1, against a formula value of −1. For n ≥ β + m − 1 and f = m − 1 the theorem holds as stated (theorem_4_4). Lemma 4.2: stated for "any finite execution", which in the I/O-automaton model is trivially true (the input stop_p is always enabled), whereas the intended statement needs at most m − 1 crashes and an extension by a step of a live process; it holds in that reading (lemma_4_2_extend). We also prove the stronger form: while fewer than n − (β + m − 2) jobs are done, no process has terminated (lemma_4_2). rank(FREE_p, TRY_p, p) is undefined when |FREE_p \ TRY_p| < p, which can only happen for β < m. The text nevertheless says correctness holds for β < m. We clamp the rank; safety holds for all β ≥ 1. Typos Fig. 1 declares TMP_p ∈ {0, …, n}, but compNext stores the rational (|FREE_p| − (m−1))/m in it. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 4.3 (wait-freedom, the set POOL_α) The proof claims that no process other than p₀ ever holds the job x₀ of rank k_{p₀} in POOL_α = J \ (J_α ∪ STUCK_α), but STUCK_α excludes only jobs of crashed processes, while a terminated process keeps its last, possibly abandoned and unperformed, job (maybe x₀) in next. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_4_3). Repair. Define POOL as the unrecorded jobs minus the next values of all processes that stop taking steps, crashed or terminated (pool). With this change the paper's argument goes through. We prove a stronger statement: KK_β has no infinite execution at all, fair or not. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory with m deterministic processes (Fin m) and atomic read/write registers (Model.lean). Each process has exactly one enabled locally controlled action per state, as in the paper's I/O automaton. KK_β is transcribed action by action from Figure 2 (kk, Algorithm.lean). FREE_p is not stored but defined as J \ DONE_p, which the paper's updates keep invariant. Crashes are fairness exemptions: a run is Fair F if every process outside F steps infinitely often or terminates. Runs may stutter, so finite fair executions (all live processes terminated) and infinite ones are both runs. This matches the paper's fairexecs_f, where at most f processes receive stop. The adversary is omniscient and online, i.e. it chooses any schedule. There is no randomness. Do(α) counts the distinct jobs of {1, …, n} performed. Effectiveness is the infimum of Do over fair runs with at most f crashes (Definition 2.4). Main results in Lean. Safety (Inv, Safety.lean) is one inductive invariant. Its core replaces the paper's case analysis on the order of events by two invariants. K: two processes that announced the same job and read each other saw it. L: a process that read next_p after p claimed the job has it in TRY or DONE, or will read it from p's line of done. Store-Collect in the Presence of Continuous Churn — PODC 2020 Hagit Attiya, Sweta Kumari, Archit Somani, Jennifer L. Welch. Brief Announcement: Collect in the Presence of Continuous Churn with Application to Snapshots and Lattice Agreement. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405709. Formalized version: the full version Store-Collect in the Presence of Continuous Churn with Application to Snapshots and Lattice Agreement, arXiv 2003.07787 v3; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The churn-tolerant store-collect algorithm CCC (Algorithms 1–3) is not regular as written: a collect returns its node's current local view, which may contain a value it never wrote back, and a later collect can miss that value — already in a 5-node system without churn or crashes, with parameters satisfying all of the paper's constraints — and no repair is proved. So Theorem 6, Corollary 7, Lemma 10 and Observation 5 are false. The other main contribution stands: the atomic snapshot built on any regular store-collect object (Algorithm 7) is linearizable (Theorem 8, with the paper's proof idea), and the churn arithmetic (Lemmas 1–3, Corollary 1) is correct up to a sign slip in Constraint (A). Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 6, Corollary 7, Lemma 10, Observation 5 (CCC is a correct store-collect implementation) A COLLECT returns LView at Line 47, but during its store-back phase the node's own server thread (Line 48) may have merged a concurrent STORE into LView; that value was never written back, so a later COLLECT can miss it: with 5 nodes, no churn and no crash, COLLECT_{p₁} returns {⟨r, 1⟩} and the subsequent COLLECT_{p₂} returns ∅, violating regularity part (2) (theorem6_false). Impact. The paper's main algorithm does not implement a store-collect object, so every application built on CCC (Section 6 under churn) inherits a broken base object. The snapshot and lattice-agreement constructions themselves are fine on top of any correct store-collect object. Details. Parameters α = Δ = 1/100, γ = 3/4, β = 3/5 (threshold 3), N_min = 2, D = 20, satisfying Constraints A–D; nodes r, p₁, p₂, a, b, all in S₀, always active. t = 1: p₁ starts COLLECT; replies from p₁, a, b (empty views); store-back of ∅ at t = 3. t = 4: r invokes STORE(1); its store message reaches p₁ at t = 6, which merges r ↦ 1 into LView (Line 48). t = 7: three store-acks arrive; p₁ returns LView = {r ↦ 1}. t = 8–12: p₂ runs COLLECT with quorum p₂, a, b, none of which has heard of r's value yet, and returns ∅. Every message carrying r ↦ 1 reaches p₂, a, b at t = 24 (delay ≤ D). Afterwards all messages are delivered, FIFO per sender; the execution is complete and admissible (ex_admissible). The counterexample works for the code with the slips of Algorithms 1–2 repaired (see Slips). With the literal stray-message handling (but S₀ nodes joined) it reaches the same violation, because no stray reply or ack reaches p₁ or p₂ before t = 12. The proof fails where it identifies view(s), defined (p. 10) as LView at the end of the store phase, with the view carried by the phase's store message (Observation 5, Lemma 10 Case II: "Qc contains a node whose LView is ⪰ view(s)"). Lemma 10 (a store phase that ends before a collect phase starts is seen by it), the key lemma of Theorem 6, is false in the same execution: the store-back phase of COLLECT_{p₁} ends at t = 7, the collect phase of COLLECT_{p₂} starts at t = 8, but view(s) = {r ↦ 1} ⋠ view(c) = ∅ (lemma10_false). Observation 5 (a node active D after a store phase starts knows its view) is false too: for the store-back phase s of COLLECT_{p₁} (starting at t = 3), node a is active throughout and at t = 3 + D = 23 its LView is still ∅ ⋡ view(s) (observation5_false). view(s) includes r ↦ 1, which p₁ received after broadcasting its store message; nothing obliges it to reach a within D of the start of s. Lemmas 7 and 8 and Case I of Lemma 10 rely on it with the same view(s). Repair. None proved (see Not formalized. below). It is not a typo: the prose ("returning LView"), the pseudocode and the definition of view(φ) agree with each other, Theorem 6(2)'s proof uses view(s) = V₁, and the journal version (Information and Computation 285, 2022) keeps the same code (its Line 51) and definition. ✏️ Slips Constraint (A): as printed, N_min ≥ 1/(Z + γ − (1+α)³) is vacuous when the denominator is ≤ 0, which Constraints (B)–(D) allow (literal_constraints_not_imply_ZNmin: α = 0.04, Δ = 0.01, γ = 0.1, β = 0.8, N_min = 1). Lemma 5 needs N_min·(Z + γ − (1+α)³) ≥ 1, which we use (ConstraintA'). Corollary 1 does not even need (A) (corollary1_of_Z_pos). Algorithm 1: is_joined is initialized to false also for the initial members S₀, so in a system consisting of S₀ no node ever answers a collect or a join. The proofs treat S₀ nodes as joined; repaired in our model (CCC.lean). Algorithm 2: the client's single counter is incremented by late collect-replies during the store-back and by store-acks after the return (which would "return" again). The proofs treat phases as separate; repaired in our model (CCC.lean). Proof of Lemma 11, Case 1: "⟨r, w⟩ ∈ W₂" should be W₁. Typos Section 5: the example α = 0, Δ = 0.21, γ = β = 0.79 is outside the model (α > 0), though the constraints hold at α = 0 (example_alpha_zero); for every α > 0 these γ, β violate (B) and (C) (not_constraintB_021_079, not_constraintC_021_079), γ = β = 0.78 works at α = 1/1000 (example_alpha_small). Lemma 10, Case I: "enter-echo" should be "collect-reply". Proof of Lemma 13: "both stores of uop_p" is imprecise. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Store-collect specification (Section 2): schedules of STORE/COLLECT invocations and responses; Regular is the paper's regularity, with "no other store occurs between" read as the usual regular-register condition (weaker reading; Theorem 8 holds under it). CCC counterexample: asynchronous message passing, reliable FIFO broadcast, message delays in (0, D], crash and churn assumptions of Section 3 (here: no churn, no crash, N = 5), integer times; a complete finite execution (every message delivered to every node, nothing happens afterwards) checked by decide in the kernel. Algorithm 1 never fires in a static run. Churn arithmetic: nodes with entry, leave and crash times, N(t) the number of present nodes, the Churn, Minimum System Size and Failure Fraction assumptions as in Section 3, plus local finiteness (finitely many nodes have entered by any time). Process p₀ runs O₀.CAS(0,1) and installs (h, 1) in X of O₀'s Z (DurEC line 10). It then crashes before forwarding. Under the stated rule p₀ may now invoke O₁.CAS(0,2) without recovering O₀. Its DurEC ECSC on O₁'s Z writes h.Val ← (2,0) (line 7). Then p₁ runs O₀.CAS(0,1): its install fails, and its FORWARD moves h.Val = (2,0) into O₀'s Z. We assume the per-process discipline, so a crashed process runs RECOVER before anything else. Under it, theorem_4_1_1 proves durable linearizability and detectability of every history. The setting has any number of processes and objects, values of any type, and individual crashes. 🔧 Algorithm 1, FORWARD (lines 14 and 16: null dereference) X starts as (null, 0), and RECOVER (which DuraCAS always runs on both W and Z) runs FORWARD even on objects that never had an install, where x.hndl.DetVal dereferences null. Impact. A missing case in the pseudocode, reached by RECOVER on a fresh object. Nothing else depends on it. Repair. "if x.hndl = null return", which we model (Model.lean). ✏️ Slips Lemma 4.4 / A.5(1): "X.hndl = h, h.Val = v" names the mover's handle h instead of the installer's h′, so as written it is false whenever another process moves; the proof reasons with h′. Definitions A.42(3), A.43(2): "the earliest time when Z.val ≠ old" must be read within the operation's interval. Lemma A.9, case 4 is a copy of case 3 (it says ECVL returns Y). AModel.lean defines DuraCAS over atomic durable EC objects, where a crashed ECSC may stay pending as an orphan. reach_aReach shows that every execution of the inlined code (DurEC over hardware CAS) is matched by an A-level execution with the same history. aReach_durLinDet redoes A.3 on the A-level model with orphans. Asynchronous shared memory (NVM) with read and CAS. Any process may crash at any time, any number of times. A crash erases the program counter and the locals; memory persists. Detectable is the two-property contract: d₂ > d₁ ⇒ the operation took effect with response true; d₂ = d₁ after a crash ⇒ no effect. Main results in Lean. For the other problems the n > 5f algorithms are cited. ✏️ Slips Read literally, "n ≤ 5f" in Theorems 1 and 7 and Corollaries 6, 8, 10 and 15 includes n = 1, f = 1, where the single process decides its input in round 0, so Theorem 1 and Corollary 6 fail (literal_theorem1_fails_n1). The paper's setting is 3f < n ≤ 5f, and our proof needs only 2f ≤ n. Typos The introduction defines communication closure as discarding early and late messages, while Section 3.2 discards only late ones; we follow Section 3.2. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Corollary 10 (broadcast; the proof covers only 4f < n ≤ 5f) The proof goes through Algorithm 3 (crusader agreement from n consistent broadcasts), which is correct only for n > 4f, so it says nothing about 3f < n ≤ 4f. Impact. Statement true for every n > f ≥ 1 by a direct argument (corollary10, corollary10_commClosed). Details. Corollary 10 claims that reliable/consistent broadcast has unbounded round complexity for canonical-round algorithms with n ≤ 5f. Algorithm 3 needs n > 4f because Theorem 9 needs two sets of n − 2f senders to intersect. Repair. The direct argument, which the introduction hints at: in the first K rounds, let every process hear n − f processes other than the correct sender (for communication-closed algorithms, deliver the sender's messages one round late). The others then have no information about the sender's input, yet validity forces them to deliver it. (corollary10, corollary10_commClosed) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (CSLib, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Byzantine/CanonicalRounds/). Asynchronous message passing, n processes, reliable FIFO links, static Byzantine faulty set of size ≤ f. Byzantine processes send arbitrary messages with arbitrary round labels. A canonical-round algorithm sends its round-r message to all and advances once it holds round-r messages from n − f distinct senders. Each message may be any function of the history; the paper sends the full history. A larger class of algorithms makes the impossibilities stronger. The first some of the decision function is the irrevocable decision. Randomness: a tape with one random number per process and round, under an arbitrary probability measure. Deterministic algorithms correspond to a fixed tape. The adversary is full-information and adaptive: a function of time and the current configuration, including all random numbers drawn so far. It is non-anticipating by construction, a subclass of the paper's adversaries, so the impossibilities are again stronger. Admissible means at most f faults, every correct process wakes up, and every link into a correct process is served infinitely often. Safety is required at every prefix of every admissible execution, for every tape. Round complexity is the smallest round by which all correct processes decide; the expected value is the integral over the tape measure. Communication-closed (CommClosed): messages and decisions factor through a view that drops late messages. The adversary of Theorems 1 and 7 works tape by tape: it forces round complexity > K (resp. non-termination) for every tape, not just in expectation. Proof remarks. In the proceedings version, Theorem 7's proof is only a sketch ("see [8]"; the arXiv full version gives it in full); it is fully formalized here. Theorem 18 uses |⌈a⌉ − ⌈b⌉| ≤ 1 for |a − b| ≤ 1 without proof, and the paper does not show that decisions lie in {1, …, R} (both proved). The proof of Theorem 14 (crusader agreement from gather, Algorithm 4) uses that an output contains at most one pair per process id, i.e. gather agreement for i = j. The paper's agreement property ("if p_i and p_j are correct") does not exclude i = j, so it covers this step, and we require agreement for all correct i, j. If agreement is required only between distinct correct processes, validity (ii) fails: n = 4, f = 1, a correct output with two different pairs of the faulty process (Gather.validity_fails_without_self_agreement). Only slips were found: filled in, the paper's proof sketches hold, covering the min-ID orientation (Theorem 2.1), Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3, and the deterministic O(log_δ n) sinkless orientation of Theorem 1.1, counted in LOCAL rounds. The CONGEST implementation, the paper's main point, was checked only for Theorem 2.1, so the CONGEST bound of Theorem 1.1 is not verified. The randomized part relies on external reductions and was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 2.2, "in particular" clause: the ball of radius ⌈log_{δ−1} n⌉ is said to contain "a node of degree δ or a cycle", but it should read "degree < δ" (lemma_2_2_clog). As printed it is false, e.g. on a path with δ = 3. "Degree < δ" is what the main statement (item (i)) gives and what Algorithm 2 uses. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic, synchronous, fault-free LOCAL with unique identifiers; every node knows n. No randomness. Round complexity is locality. An orientation algorithm A : ∀ G, Orientation G is R-local if the direction of each edge uv is the same in any two graphs that agree on all edges incident to nodes at distance < R from u, i.e. on what u learns in R rounds. Since A sees the node set V, a rule may depend on the global identifier set, slightly more than standard LOCAL. This is harmless for the explicit algorithms and makes the lower bound stronger. Theorem 2.1 is also implemented as an explicit flooding algorithm in CSLib's synchronous SET-LOCAL model, with O(log n)-bit states. CONGEST message sizes are otherwise not modelled. Graphs: Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 2.3 hold for any (even infinite) simple graph; Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 1.1 assume a finite node set. Tie-breaking in Algorithm 2 uses a fixed choice function. The proofs use only the specifications of the choices, so ID-based tie-breaking is covered as well. Main results in Lean (namespace SinklessOrientation). Is a LOCAL Algorithm Computable? — PODC 2026 Antonio Cruciani, Avinandan Das, Massimo Equi, Henrik Lievonen, Diep Luong-Le, Augusto Modanese, Jukka Suomela. Brief Announcement: Is a LOCAL Algorithm Computable? PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815908. Formalized version: the full version, arXiv 2602.21022 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The paper's main result, the separation Theorem 4.1 (an LCL Π with complexity O(log n) in uncomputable-LOCAL but Ω(√n) in computable-LOCAL, i.e. classes I < II of Table 1), was not checked: the LCL Π of Section 4 is not formalized, only the diagonalization core of Lemma 4.17 (on abstract hypotheses) and Lemma 4.18. The equivalences of Section 5 hold, in slightly greater generality: with a bound n ≤ N (or n ≤ N ≤ f(n)) uncomputable and computable LOCAL coincide (Theorem 5.3), in uncomputable LOCAL the bound does not help (Theorem 5.4 / Corollary 5.6), and critical views are decidable (Lemma 5.2). Saving them took a redesign of the paper's central tool, "maximally T-safe neighbourhoods", as "critical" views. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Definition 5.1: "maximal" vs. "safe with t+1 unsafe" coincide only if safety is downward closed, which is not shown, so "the" maximally safe neighbourhood of a node need not be unique. Our first critical radius settles it, and no theorem depends on the difference. Lemma 5.2, step 3 ("reject if ... t < T(n)") has the inequality reversed: it should be T(n) < t. Theorem 5.3's proof does not say which class "safe" ranges over. If safety ranges over all graphs, the final contradiction uses a network that need not satisfy the promise n ≤ N ≤ f(n) for the same N, and the uncomputable algorithm owes nothing there. Definition 5.1 has a class parameter 𝒢, and with the promise class the contradiction works. We prove the theorem by a different argument: for fixed N, search over the finitely many finite tables "(view, radius) ↦ output" for one that solves the problem on all legal networks. The uncomputable algorithm's table shows that the search terminates (exists_computable_of_promise). In Lemma 4.17, "do not see farther than the first k−1 layers" must also avoid the constantly many special layers near the bottom. In Lemma 4.17, "the value computed by T will equal k₀" is not true in general, but any k with the property works (Model.exists_far_of_computable). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Definition 5.1 ("maximally T-safe"; used in Lemma 5.2 and Theorems 5.3–5.4) Maximal safety of radius t depends on the unseen radius-(t+1) view, so the paper's algorithms that "grow the view until it is maximally T-safe", read literally, exceed the time bound by one round: in C₃ with T(n) = ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ they cannot stop within T(3) = 1 (maxSafe_rule_exceeds). Impact. Theorems 5.3 and 5.4 are true and proved with a corrected notion ("critical" views). Under the view-level reading the algorithms stay within T(n), but then the paper's proofs of Lemma 5.2 and Lemma 5.5 do not handle that notion. Details. t is maximally safe for v if t is safe and t+1 is not, and safety of t+1 is defined with radius-(t+1) neighbourhoods. A node that has seen only N^t(v) cannot evaluate this. Yet both algorithms "grow the view until it is maximally T-safe" and are claimed to run within T(n) rounds. Counterexample with T(n) = ⌊(n-1)/2⌋: a node of the triangle and a node of the 5-cycle have the same radius-1 view (same identifiers and ports). Radius 1 = T(3) is maximally safe in C₃, since radius 2 is unsafe because of C₃ itself. In C₅ it is not maximally safe: every network containing the radius-2 view has ≥ 5 nodes, so radius 2 is still safe. So no ball-growing rule stops exactly at maximally safe radii. Any algorithm that never stops before a maximally safe radius fails to stop within T(3) = 1 rounds in C₃ (maxSafe_not_view_determined, no_alg_stops_at_maxSafe, maxSafe_rule_exceeds); the view-level reading is sound (maxSafeView_iff, first_critical_maxSafeView). The paper's sentence "if t is maximally safe for v, then N^t(v) is maximally safe" can also be read as a property of views: maximally safe for some node with this view. Under that reading the radius-1 view above is maximally safe, also in C₅, and the algorithms stay within T(n). A view is then maximally safe iff it is safe and critical (below). The first such radius of a node is exactly its first critical radius, which is where our B stops. But then the paper's arguments do not establish what is needed: Lemma 5.2's procedure tests only safety of t, never criticality, and Lemma 5.5 does not show that A_N stops within the view. So in either reading the statements are true and the gap is in the proofs. Repair. Call a radius-t view critical if it occurs in some network G' with T(|V(G')|) ≤ t. Every node meets a critical radius by T(n), and any algorithm of locality T has already stopped there (Model.Critical, out_of_critical). Maximal safety implies criticality (MaxSafe.critical). Section 5 is reworked on this notion (Model.exists_boundFree, Model.sandwich_computable). 🔧 Lemma 5.2 (the procedure tests only safety) The procedure tests only safety of t and never that t + 1 is unsafe, so it does not decide maximal safety in either reading of Definition 5.1. Impact. Decidability holds for critical views (Model.critical_decidable). Repair. Add the bounded search for a witness network with T(n) ≤ t. 🔧 Lemma 5.2 (case split) The case "t = T(N') = C" misses t > sup T. Impact. The decidability claim stands (Model.critical_decidable). Repair. The case should read "T bounded with supremum C ≤ t", and step 1 should accept for t ≥ C. 🔧 Lemma 5.5 (inside Theorem 5.4) The proof takes the neighbourhood X_i itself as a graph, which is not a network, and then only gets that A_N stops within T(N_i) rounds, while the sandbox needs A_N to stop within the radius of X_i. Impact. Statement true; the rest of the proof of Theorem 5.4 stays (exists_boundFree). Details. X_i is not a network: boundary degree labels count unseen edges. Repair. Take N_i to be the size of a criticality witness (exists_boundFree). 🔧 Definition 3.5 (why the locality T is non-decreasing) The paper's reason, "the set of graphs with n₁ nodes is contained in the class of graphs with n₂ nodes", is false. Impact. The claim is true, for a different reason (stops_of_le). Repair. Pad with isolated nodes that have fresh identifiers (identifiers lie in [1, n^c], c ≥ 1); this does not change the views (stops_of_le). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic synchronous LOCAL, ball-growing formalism (Definition 3.5). An algorithm is A : View → ℕ → Option Out (none = ⊥). A node outputs A (view, t) at the least radius t with a non-⊥ value. Locality T means every node of every n-node network stops by radius T(n). Abstract networks (Model Net View). Networks have sizes, and views of every node and radius. The radius-t view determines all smaller ones; this is the only property used. Concrete instance (concreteModel Δ c k): the networks of Section 3. Simple graphs of maximum degree Δ, port numbering = neighbour order, unique identifiers in [1, n^c], inputs < k, full-information views (own identifier, input, degree, and the neighbours' radius-(t−1) views in port order). With unique identifiers these carry the information of N^t(v) (Definition 3.1) except the port numbers, at the distance-t nodes, of their edges towards distance-(t−1) nodes. So the concrete model sees slightly less than Definition 3.1 (as if messages were not tagged with the sender's port). The abstract theorems apply to either kind of view. The C₃/C₅ counterexample also holds for Definition 3.1 views: the ports match. Knowledge of n: a common input N with promise n ≤ N (UpperBound) or n ≤ N ≤ f(n) (Sandwich f). An algorithm is then a family A N. Problems are arbitrary validity predicates on output labellings (LCLs and beyond). Theorem 5.4 uses a finite output alphabet. Theorem 5.3 uses a computable validity check. Computability is Mathlib's Computable on Primcodable encodings of (N, view, radius). Uncomputable-LOCAL algorithms are arbitrary functions. Main results in Lean. The LCL Π of Section 4 (trees, rows, growing grids, Turing machine and consensus layers; Lemmas 4.4–4.16, Corollary 4.14). Hence Theorem 4.1 and the strictness I < II are not verified. Only the diagonalization of Lemma 4.17 is formalized, for an abstract family G_K(x) whose two properties (validity forces the halting result; the node holding x does not see the bottom) are hypotheses; whether Π really forms such a family is open. The equivalence of full-information views and Definition 3.1 balls and the direct computable O(log n) algorithm with a bound N (end of Section 2.1) are not formalized. Trust. No sorry; the listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity checks: every node has a critical radius (critical_self); the concrete model satisfies the abstract hypotheses: restriction in Concrete.lean; computability in ConcreteComputable.lean: primitive recursive well-formedness, enumeration of networks with ≤ N nodes, computable injectively coded views; a toy separation family on promised paths (SeparationToy.lean): uncomputable locality 0 (toy_uncomputable_solves) versus computable locality ≥ n − 1 (toy_computable_lower). Computable list combinators (Computable.list_foldl/map/all/any/findSome?/filterMap/flatMap/filter, Computable.nat_find) and Primrec.list_all/any, Primrec.nat_pow are shared code in CSLib Cslib/Computability/Partrec/List.lean and Cslib/Computability/Primrec/List.lean. The abstract ball-growing model (Basic.lean) is a CSLib candidate.

Consistent Refereeing: Impossibilities for Strong Linearizability — PODC 2026 Hagit Attiya, Armando Castañeda, Constantin Enea. Impossibility Results for Strong Linearizability: The Difficulty of Consistent Refereeing. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815906. Formalized version: arXiv 2506.18401 v3 (same text as the proceedings version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All theorems we formalized hold: Theorems 1, 3, 4, 5, 25, 30, Proposition 11, Corollary 12, and Lemma 14 for counters, max registers and snapshots. The proof of Theorem 30 fails in its test&set case, and closing it took a new argument. The other mistakes are one local repair in Lemma 17 and slips. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Lemma 29(2) fails in the degenerate case w = 0: the sequences it needs (|γ| = w, γ = qλ) do not exist. We use window max(w, 1) (a 0-window object is also 1-window-like), and our proof of Theorem 30 does not need Lemma 29(2) at all. Lemma 17 needs decide to be pending. This implied assumption holds where the lemma is used, and the lemma is proved with it (lemma17). The last paragraph of Theorem 25 ("We have that αβp is closed. Otherwise…") is garbled; we formalized the intended argument (theorem25). Lemma 28's test&set case calls αβq′ closed, but it is supervalent there; the case needs only αβq closed (lemma28). Typos Lemma 29's proof cites Lemma 21 instead of Lemma 27. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 30, case "all processes apply T&S to the same test&set object R" The proof claims that αβγpγ′₁q′ᵏγ′₂ and αβγ′₁q′ᵏγpγ′₂ end with the same shared memory and look the same to every other competitor q″, but if R is still unset after αβ, q wins the test&set in the first execution and q′ in the second. Impact. Statement true; closed with a different argument (const_valency_contra, theorem30). Details. q′ then takes k more steps in different local states, and so do the processes of γ′₂. These steps may write different values to other objects, and q″ can read them. So neither the memory equality nor the indistinguishability follows. Repair. Our fix does not use Lemma 29(2). Once some competitor has set R, every later referee step on R changes nothing and commutes with every competitor step. By Lemma 17 the singleton valency W(αβq·u·p) is then the same for every competitors-only extension u. Taking u in which some competitor completes more operations than that value contradicts the specification. (const_valency_contra, theorem30) 🔧 Lemma 17 (counting q's operations) q's operations are counted in αβ′ and then transferred to α′β′σ, but α′ may contain a different number of operations of q, since indistinguishability compares only states. Impact. Statement true (lemma17). Repair. Count the operations inside β′, which wait-freedom gives just the same. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl). Deterministic processes; atomic base objects with deterministic sequential specifications. Executions are label lists, and responses are separate steps. Crashes are processes that stop taking steps. P is any finite type of processes with a referee ref; all other processes are competitors. compete carries the caller's id, because objects cannot see the caller. The implementation must allow each role's operation. The contest object of Section 4 is one-shot by definition, but our model lets a process invoke operations repeatedly. Statements that hold only for one-shot use are therefore restricted, and this is not an error in the paper: Proposition 11 and Theorem 3 are proved on executions where the referee decides at most once. Theorem 3's algorithm is not linearizable with two decides. Proposition 11 also assumes an injective encoding of process ids as queue values. Theorem 4: the paper's algorithm would overflow the (n−1)-window under repeated competes. Our variant writes only on the first compete, so it is the same algorithm on one-shot executions, and it is strongly linearizable on all executions. Theorem 5 says "wait-free" and the introduction says "lock-free". On one-shot executions the two coincide: there are only finitely many operations, so both say that no such execution has infinitely many steps. We prove both (theorem5_lockFree, theorem5_waitFree). Correctness and progress are assumed only on admissible executions, which makes the impossibility results stronger. Corollaries give the versions with the unrestricted LockFree/WaitFree/ StronglyLinearizable. One-shot contest (Adm): every process invokes at most one operation, the one of its role, and the referee starts after some compete completed. Long-lived contest (LLAdm): roles are respected and the referee decides at most once. The long-lived contest is a nondeterministic specification (llSpec): decide may return any bound on all competitors' counts. Strong linearizability is taken with respect to it. Base objects are given by semantic classes (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/ObjClasses.lean, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/ObjClasses/Basic.lean): Herlihy-interfering (per state); window-like with window w (w-window registers are window-like with every w′ ≥ w); stack-like (isomorphic to a stack); read/write (every primitive is read-only or a blind write); test&set-like (every primitive sets the object to a fixed state). Proof remarks. The case analyses of Lemmas 20, 23, 27, 28 and Theorems 25, 30 omit the referee's invocation and response steps; these are routine completions in the formalization. Main results in Lean (namespace Cslib.SharedMemory.Referee). Decisive linearizability, so Theorems 3 and 13 are not covered as decisive. Theorem 13 is not formalized at all; Theorem 3 is proved only as linearizable. Lemma 14 for fetch&increment and fetch&add, and from strongly linearizable implementations. The paper's own proof of Theorem 1, which we obtain through Corollary 12. Theorem 5, stack case 4c (one push, one pop), as the paper argues it. It refers to case 4b, "conceiving the step of p_i as a push of u_i", but the two orders leave different stack shapes than in 4b (u_j·T vs s₀·T, where s₀·T is the stack in C), so the transfer is not immediate; we did not decide whether the case holds up as written. Theorem 5 itself is proved by a replacement argument covering 4b and 4c (Crit.stack_push, lockstep): Run the canonical extension (a third competitor solo, then the referee) from α·i·j and from α·j in lock-step. What is Agreement About if not Common Knowledge? — PODC 2026 Or David, Yoram Moses. Brief Announcement: What is Agreement About if not Common Knowledge? PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815934. Formalized version: the 4-page proceedings brief announcement (we found no full version on arXiv); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The paper gives no proofs; we supplied them, and knowledge of preconditions (Thm 1.2), necessity of dynamic common knowledge (Thm 1.5, Cor 1.6) and sufficiency (Thm 1.7) all hold in the generic runs-and-systems model. One clause of Theorem 1.7 ("the nonfaulty processes decide v in r iff r ⊨ θ_v") is false only in runs with no nonfaulty process. The informal converse remark after Theorem 1.7 needs one added condition: nonfaulty processes must remember their decisions. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Converse remark after Theorem 1.7 (needs memory of decisions) The remark "underlying the design of every AoN protocol is a set of facts Θ as described in Theorem 1.7" fails for a protocol whose nonfaulty processes forget their decisions (no_theta_for_forgetful_protocol). Impact. An imprecise informal claim: it holds when nonfaulty processes remember their decisions (exists_theta_of_AoN). Details. We read Θ as facts that describe the protocol's decisions; read literally, all-false Θ makes the remark trivial. Example without recall: one failure-free process learns a bit b at time 1, decides b then, and forgets b afterwards. This protocol is AoN and satisfies Agreement, Validity and Decision. Yet no local, remembered profile makes θ_v ↔ all_decide(v) even dynamically everyone-known, let alone dynamic common knowledge. (no_theta_for_forgetful_protocol) Repair. With memory of decisions, take θ_v = "some nonfaulty process decides v" and the profile 𝛅(v) (exists_theta_of_AoN). ✏️ Slips Theorem 1.7, the "iff" clause: "the nonfaulty processes decide v in r iff r ⊨ θ_v" fails in a run with N(r) = ∅, where all_decide(v) holds vacuously but θ_v need not (theorem_1_7_iff_false_without_nonfaulty). Exclusivity even forbids θ_v for two different values, while all_decide(v) holds for all of them. Counterexample: one run, every process faulty, all θ_v false; all hypotheses of Theorem 1.7 hold trivially. Assuming N(r) ≠ ∅, which most models do (f < n), repairs it (allDecide_newDec_iff). The other claims of Theorem 1.7 hold unchanged. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. The generic runs-and-systems model (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/Knowledge/Basic.lean). A system is an arbitrary type R of runs with time ℕ, and local states loc i r t for each process i. Each run has a set nf r of nonfaulty processes; the failure model is abstract, as in the paper. Facts are predicates on points; run facts are time-independent facts. K_i quantifies over all points of all runs with the same local state of i. No synchrony, communication or failure assumptions are needed, matching the paper's claim "in all models". The modalities are those of the shared indistinguishability system System.toIndist (IndistSystem.K, KN, kop, …), used also for the knowledge notions of KMO'11 and of CSLib's synchronous crash model. K_i^N φ = i ∈ N ∧ K_i(i ∈ N → φ), plus Kuznets et al.'s hope H_i. Dynamic knowledge, dynamic everyone-knows and dynamic common knowledge follow Definitions 1.3–1.4 verbatim. A protocol is its system plus decision facts decideᵢ(v). Decisions are assumed i-local: this is the paper's standing assumption that decisions depend on the local state. Theorem 1.7 has no proof in the paper. We build P_A on the same runs: it adds the local decision rule ψᵢ(v) ∧ K_i(i ∈ N → θ_v). The new decisions are outputs only and do not change local states or messages. Remarks (no error). Theorem 1.7's hypothesis ⊨ θ_v → C^N@𝛙(v)(θ_v) is equivalent to the weaker-looking ⊨ θ_v → E^N@𝛙(v)(θ_v), by the induction rule (sufficient_of_EN). The assumption that P solves A is never used. The memory hypothesis is used only to make the new decisions stable ("conscious"). Corollary 1.6 needs AoN(v) only for the decided value v, and it holds for every precondition of deciding v, as the text says (KN_CN_of_precondition). Main results in Lean. Formalized version: arXiv 2605.18171 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. With one constant corrected in Algorithm 1, Theorem 5.7 and Corollary 5.8 are verified end to end: a deterministic self-stabilising C-counter tolerating f < n/3 Byzantine faults that stabilises in O(f + 1 + log n) rounds, a bound that depends on the actual number of faults f, with explicit constants 120 f + 113⌈log₂ n⌉ for the recursion over Algorithm 8 (filtering) and Algorithm 10 (King Consensus). The other mistakes are local too, and the 8-round King Consensus of Section 6.1 (Theorem 6.5) is verified, including its message-count property. The paper's main result, Theorem 1.1 (O(f + 1) stabilisation, Section 7), was not checked, and neither were message sizes or the bit-complexity results of Section 6.2. Impact. A one-symbol fix with evident intent: with input C_v + R − 1, which the paper's own timing conventions require, everything goes through (tmpl 2), and Theorem 5.7 and Corollary 5.8 are verified. Details. Line 3 starts an instance and the loop of lines 4–9 runs its round 1 in the same round (Section 4: round 1 is computed from the input), so an R-round instance whose input is read from C_{v,r−1} outputs in round r + R − 1. Line 7 then overwrites C_v with the output and line 15 increments it. Once the clocks agree, the next instance whose correct leader is agreed upon outputs the agreed input C_{v,r−1} + R, so C_{v,r+R−1} = C_{v,r−1} + R + 1. Such instances recur every k_b rounds. This is not a question of how rounds are labelled: between reading the input and writing the output there are R updates of C_v, while the proof of Lemma 5.4 ("outputs in round r + R") needs R + 1. The paper's own Lemma 5.6 (J_ℓ has R rounds) and Algorithm 7, line 19 (input C_v + R − 1, read after the increment) use the correct timing; Algorithm 7, line 2 repeats the error (Section 7 is not formalized). The non-stabilisation proof covers any n ≥ 2, C ≥ 2 and any early-stabilizing sub-counters; the trace-level argument does not depend on k₀, k₁, X. (literal_breaks, literal_never_counts, literal_counterexample; fixed: tmpl 2) 🔧 Lemma 2.3 (Algorithm 8 vs Definition 2.2) Lemma 2.3 is proved by Algorithm 8, which gives crusader agreement over only X rounds instead of the X + 1 that Definition 2.2 asks: with n = 4, one Byzantine node, X = 1, K = 2, node 1 outputs 1 at time 4, where only ⊥ or 0 are allowed (filt_crusader_window_false). In the example both L = 0 and L = 1 collide, and 2 > ε·1 + 1. (lemma_5_5_proof_constants_fail, lemma_5_5) 🔧 Lemma 5.6 (incomplete counting) The counting argument claims "L_max > 4", which is false for the larger k_b, where L_max = 4 and the final count L_max/2 − L_max/4 − 1 > 0 becomes 0. Stranger-Free Tasks — PODC 2025 Eli Gafni, Giuliano Losa, Michel Raynal, Gadi Taubenfeld. Brief Announcement: Stranger-Free Tasks. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733545. Formalized version: the brief announcement (no full version used). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Theorem 2.1 (a stranger-free task for n processes needs n registers) and the lower bound of Theorem 3.1 (k-bounded lattice agreement needs k + 1 registers) are proved. The upper bound of Theorem 3.1 is not established: Algorithm 1 is not wait-free for any k ≥ 2, already with two processes, though it is safe and obstruction-free for every k, and wait-free for k = 1. So the claimed wait-free hierarchy is established only in the obstruction-free sense (and for k = 1). Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 3.1, upper bound (Algorithm 1, wait-freedom for k ≥ 2) Algorithm 1 is not wait-free for any k ≥ 2: with two processes whose double collects keep invalidating each other, both take infinitely many steps in a one-shot execution and never output (exists_livelock, theorem_3_1_alg1_not_waitFree). Impact. The wait-free upper bound of Theorem 3.1 (k + 1 registers, unboundedly many processes) and the wait-free "infinite hierarchy" of the abstract are not established for k ≥ 2; whether they hold remains open. Algorithm 1 is safe and obstruction-free for every k, and wait-free for k = 1. Details. §3.1 argues that "processes that keep interfering have seen sets that converge to the same value or eventually grow in cardinality past k". Counterexample with two processes a, b and k = 2, so |seen| = 2 ≤ k never triggers the early exit at line 23. Once both have seen = {a, b}, repeat forever: a does its first collect; b writes; a's second collect fails because b's triple changed; b does its first collect; a writes; b's second collect fails. Converging seen sets do not help: without helping, the double collects keep invalidating each other, as in the double-collect scan of Afek et al., which is only obstruction-free. The livelock does not depend on how line 21 is read. Replacing > k by ≥ k in line 23 would only repair k = 2. Repair. For k = 1 the claim is true, but the paper's sketch does not apply. Our argument: a process other than p can write A[2] (the second register; A[1] in the 0-based Lean code) only as its second write, and only if it read ⊥ there before anybody wrote it. So only finitely many interfering writes on A[2] exist, while every two failed iterations of p need one (theorem_3_1_k1). ✏️ Slips Remark after the proof of Theorem 2.1: the obstruction-free variant needs stranger-freedom with respect to obstruction-free algorithms, a stronger hypothesis that the paper does not state (theorem_2_1_obstructionFree). It holds for k-bounded lattice agreement, the paper's application. Typos Line 21 of Algorithm 1 (seen ∪ collect[j][3]) is a no-op as written, probably a typo for A[j][3]. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Safety argument of §3.1 (more than k + 1 participants) The argument ("unless at least k + 1 processes participate, the set will always be a subset of at least one register … k processes are not enough to obliterate all k + 1 registers") covers only runs with few participants. Impact. Statement true; repaired by a counting argument (card_union_of_obliterate, alg1_solves). Details. With more than k + 1 participants, k + 1 processes poised on distinct registers can overwrite everything after a successful snapshot, and the paper does not say why containment then still holds. Repair. It does hold, by a counting argument over "clean" writes. A clean write by a process that has completed a collect since all registers became dirty carries a seen-set of size ≥ k + 1, and each process makes at most one write without such a collect. So if all registers become clean, the union of their seen-sets is too large for a later output of size ≤ k (card_union_of_obliterate, alg1_solves). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (CSLib Cslib.SharedMemory). Asynchronous shared memory, deterministic processes, arbitrary interleavings. Atomic multi-writer multi-reader registers (any value type), one register access per step. No crashes: a process may simply stop taking steps. Wait-freedom and obstruction-freedom as usual, on infinite executions and solo runs. Process type: finite with |P| = n for Theorem 2.1 and the lower bound; arbitrary (possibly infinite) for Algorithm 1. One-shot tasks: the input/output relation must hold on every finite one-shot execution (participating = has invoked). Every process may invoke with every input. Full-information versions store (value, writer's view) in registers. The paper's remark that an algorithm and its full-information version solve the same tasks with the same registers is proved. Stranger-freedom quantifies over the full-information versions of all algorithms solving the task. Main results in Lean. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733539. Formalized version: the 4-page brief announcement (no arXiv or full version found). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main claims hold: Algorithms 1 and 2 generate (k−1)·2^w distinct identifiers from k w-bit read/write/FAI registers, and no anonymous obstruction-free implementation supports more than k·2^w + k + 1 calls. The lower-bound argument is sound, but to reach the stated count poised writes must also respect the bound of 2^w poised processes per register, and Claim 1 misses one case. "Algorithm 2 remains wait-free" must be read as wait-free for every bounded number of calls, the regime in which the paper claims correctness. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Algorithm 2 ("remains wait-free"): the paper says Algorithm 2 "remains wait-free since the object produces a finite number of distinct identifiers", but with unboundedly many calls a process can starve in the repeat loop, so this is not standard wait-freedom. The argument already relies on a bounded number of calls, which is the regime where correctness is claimed; we prove wait-freedom for every bound on the number of invocations (alg_waitFreeUpTo). Algorithm 1 is wait-free unconditionally (alg1_waitFree). §3, first variation: "since k' ≥ k/2, B ≥ k/2·2^w" with B = (k'−1)·2^w does not follow as written. It is true since k' − 1 ≥ k/2 (variation_bound). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 §4, definition of "poised" (Theorem 4.1's final count) Condition (2) of "poised" for write(x) lacks the bound "fewer than 2^w processes poised on Rᵢ" that condition (1) has for FAIs, so up to 2^{w+1} processes can be poised on one register and the argument yields only k·2^{w+1} + k + 1, not the stated k·2^w + k + 1. Impact. A local fix: adding "fewer than 2^w processes are poised" to condition (2) as well gives the stated bound k·2^w + k + 1 (theorem_4_1). The lower-bound argument is otherwise sound. Details. Condition (1) for FAIs says "fewer than 2^w processes poised on Rᵢ". Condition (2) for write(x) only forbids a second poised write(x). Under this literal definition the proof's case split is exactly the negation of "poised", and Claim 1 works with ≥ 2^w poised processes, so the argument goes through. But a register can then collect up to 2^w FAIs plus 2^w distinct writes, and the final count "at most 2^w processes poised on every register" fails. 🔧 Claim 1 (pigeonhole step) The step "one of x, x−1, …, x−f is a poised write value" fails when all 2^w poised primitives are FAIs, because then no write is poised. Impact. Statement true: the register can still be set to any x with fewer than 2^w of those FAIs (claim1 covers both cases). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory (CSLib Cslib.SharedMemory), deterministic processes, no crashes. k registers with values in Fin m, with atomic read, write v and cyclic FAI, which returns the old value (bReg m). Here m = 2^w. All results are proved for general m. The object is uidObj with the long-lived operation get() returning ℕ. Correctness (UniqueResp): distinct completed operations return distinct values. For this specification this is equivalent to linearizability. "Correct for B calls" (CorrectUpTo I B): every execution with at most B invocations satisfies UniqueResp. Anonymity (Anonymous I): the same automaton and the same initial state for all processes. It is necessary: without it, p can return ⟪p, c⟫ using no shared memory (nonAnonymous_correct). Progress: CSLib ObstructionFree for the lower bound and WaitFree for Algorithm 1. WaitFreeUpTo I N for Algorithm 2: wait-freedom in infinite executions with at most N invocations. The lower bound uses k·m + k + 2 processes (e : Fin (k*m+k+2) ↪ P), each calling get() once. The algorithms work for any set of processes, each calling get() any number of times. Algorithms 1 and 2 are one algorithm alg n d m: repeat i ← R₀.FAI() mod d until i < n; j ← R_{i+1}.FAI(); return i·m + j. Algorithm 1 is d = n = 2^x. Algorithm 2 is d = 2^⌈log₂ n⌉. Revisiting Lower Bounds for Two-Step Consensus — PODC 2025 Fedor Ryabinin, Alexey Gotsman, Pierre Sutra. Brief Announcement: Revisiting Lower Bounds for Two-Step Consensus. PODC 2025, pp. 58–61. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733541. Formalized version: arXiv 2505.03627 v2 (full version with appendices A–C; numbering follows it). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. Both main theorems hold, and we prove them as "iff" statements in one model, given n ≥ 2, e ≤ f and two values: an f-resilient e-two-step consensus task exists iff n ≥ max {2e+f, 2f+1} (Theorem 1), and an f-resilient e-two-step consensus object exists iff n ≥ max {2e+f−1, 2f+1} (Theorem 2). The upper bound for objects, however, does not follow from the paper's protocol: the object version of Fig. 1 is not wait-free, and we prove Theorem 2 with a repaired protocol that replaces the leader mechanism by rotating ballots. The proofs of Lemma 4, Lemma 5 and §B also have gaps, all of which we repaired; Lemma 4 took a new invariant. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Fig. 1 object version (§C.3, upper bound of Theorem 2; wait-freedom) The object protocol (Fig. 1 with the red lines) is not wait-free: 1B messages do not carry initial_val and a leader at line 37 can only propose its own initial_val, so a value known only to a non-leader is never proposed (Fig1.object_not_wait_free_omega, Fig1.object_not_wait_free). Impact. The paper does not establish the "if" direction of Theorem 2, but Theorem 2 itself is true: we prove it with a repaired protocol (Impl.theorem_2_upper, theorem_2). Details. Two concrete executions show this. Ω scenario, any admissible parameters. No process crashes, and Ω permanently outputs a correct l that never calls propose. Every process moves to ballot 1 before anybody invokes (the ballot timer runs from startup: "Initially it is set to 2Δ", §C.1). Later a correct r ≠ l invokes propose(v). Its Propose is ignored (bal ≠ 0), so l computes val = ⊥ in every ballot and never sends a 2A, and r never returns. (Fig1.object_not_wait_free_omega) Crash scenario, any leader election, whenever n − f − e ≥ 2 (e.g. n = 7, f = 3, e = 2, which meets the paper's bound). p proposes v, only r accepts it, and p crashes. Everyone else moves to a slow ballot. r invokes propose(w) later; line 3 is skipped because r has already voted. Each 1B quorum shows at most one vote for v, which is below n − f − e, and no leader has an initial_val, so nobody ever decides. (Fig1.object_not_wait_free) Repair. We fix lines 37–38 in the object version ("else, if initial_val = ⊥, propose the leader's own val"). We also replace Ω by clock-driven rotating ballots, so every correct invoker eventually leads a ballot after GST. The fix alone does not save the Ω version: the first scenario still applies. We prove the fixed protocol correct and two-step for n ≥ max {2e+f−1, 2f+1}. (Impl.theorem_2_upper, theorem_2) ✏️ Slips Introduction: "EPaxos uses 2f+1 = 2e+f−1 processes, Lamport requires 2f+3" holds only for even f. For odd f, EPaxos's 2f+1 equals 2e+f, and Lamport's bound is 2f+2. Typos §B.2: decide(p, 1) in σ′ should be decide(p, 0), and "F ∪ {p,q} = f" should be a cardinality. Brief announcement only (arXiv v2 is correct), lines 33 and 35: Q_f should be S. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 4 (slow-path safety) The induction on b′ claims that a process with vbal_q′ = b received its Decide from the leader of ballot b, which is false: Decide may come from a decision at a higher ballot. Impact. Statement true; we prove agreement through a "potentially chosen" invariant over all fast and slow decisions (Fig1.lemma4, Fig1.task_agreement, Fig1.object_agreement). Details. The Decide may be received before answering 1A(b′), and decided_q′ need not be the value of 2A(vbal_q′). Agreement between two fast-path decisions is never argued either. 🔧 Lemma 5 (object fast-path recovery) The proof considers the line-33 case only when v itself has > n−e−f votes in Q, but with n = 2e+f−1 v can also have exactly n−e−f = e−1 votes while another w has e votes. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Fig1.lemma5, Fig1.lemma1). Details. Counting does not exclude this case. It is ruled out by the line-35 argument: all f processes outside Q voted for v, so w's proposer did as well, and in the object version it then never proposed w. In the task version (Lemma 1) the same case is excluded by counting, and the paper skips it silently. 🔧 Lower bounds for smaller n (§B, Theorems 1 and 2 "only if") The proofs assume n = 2e+f−1 (Thm 1) and n = 2e+f−2 (Thm 2) without reducing smaller n to these cases. Impact. Statements true; we prove both bounds for every n ≥ 2, using one generic merge lemma for all the indistinguishability arguments (theorem_1_lower, theorem_2_lower, merge_task, merge_object). 🔧 Lemma 3 base case and conclusion of Theorem 1 (§B.1) "All correct processes propose 0, thus 0 is decided" does not follow from Validity, because the crashed processes propose 1. Impact. Statements true; one extra step using the paper's own Lemma 2 closes it (syncRun_decides_eq). 🔧 Continuation of σ (§B.2, Theorem 2 "only if") In §B.2 the correct processes never call propose, so wait-freedom forces no decision in the continuation. Impact. Statement true; a correct r outside {p, q} invokes propose in the continuation (theorem_2_lower). Details. Moreover, the "w.l.o.g. 1 is decided" ignores a third proposed value. The formalization Model (our own; now in CSLib as Cslib.CrashPartialSync, Cslib/Computability/Distributed/CrashPartialSync/; Model.lean here keeps Definitions 3–5). n deterministic crash-prone processes and point-to-point links, in the Dwork–Lynch–Stockmeyer partially synchronous model. Discrete time with one tick = Δ; GST is unknown. At each tick an alive process takes one atomic step. The step receives the messages delivered now, in an adversary-chosen order, together with an optional invocation (the task input at time 0, or an object propose). Processes see the clock.
