Two-shot objects solving two-process consensus — PODC 2025 Minh Tung Nguyen, Pierre Sutra. An Exact Characterization of the Two-shot Deterministic Objects Solving Two-process Consensus. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733534. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (no arXiv version found); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main result is fully formalized: a deterministic two-shot type (T, m), together with registers, solves wait-free two-process consensus iff it lies in C₁ ∪ C₁.₅ ∪ C₂. Both directions and all three algorithms hold after local repairs: a typo in Algorithm 3, and missing cases and a changed graph definition in the proofs. The one claim lost is the illustrating example "the asymmetric queue AQ is in C₁.₅", which is false (AQ is in C₂) and which nothing depends on. Mistakes in the paper ❌ §4.2.5 (the asymmetric queue AQ is in C₁.₅) The asymmetric queue, where only p₀ may dequeue, is not in C₁.₅: the paper's witness violates property (1), and no witness exists (paper_AQ_witness_fails, aq_not_C15). Impact. Illustration only: AQ is in C₂ (with the WQ witness), so it still solves consensus (aq_C2). The characterization itself is unaffected, but C₁.₅ is left without a concrete object: we proved no other example. Details. The paper's witness is queue [0], f = dequeue, f' = read, g = enqueue(1), g' = read. That witness already violates property (1): dequeue returns 0 whether or not enqueue(1) went first. Properties (3), (4) and (5) fail too; only (2) holds. No witness exists, in any state and in either role orientation. Property (1) forces g = enqueue(y). Properties (1) and (3) then force g' = read, f = dequeue and an empty queue. But then p₁ reads [y] both in gg'ff' and in fgg'f', so property (4) fails. 🔧 §4.2.5, paragraph on WQ (conditions for distinguishing fg from gf) "If fg and gf are distinguishable to p₀ then f = read(), g = enqueue(1) and the queue is initially empty" is false: for WQ, f = read, g = enqueue(y) distinguish from every state, so emptiness is not forced. Impact. Dropping the overstated conditions is enough, and the conclusion that WQ is not in C₁.₅ is proved (part of wq_C2). Details. For AQ, f = dequeue() on an empty queue also works. ✏️ Slips Algorithm 3, line 30 tests v[1][1] where v[0][1] is meant; only p₀ executes the line, and its v[1][1] is ⊥, so taken literally agreement fails in the run where p₁ runs solo first. A brute-force search (Python, not in Lean) found a 4-state object in C₂ exhibiting the failure. With v[0][1] Algorithm 3 is correct (proved in Lean, solvable_of_C2Cond), and the characterization stands. Corollary 1's "op ∈ [0, k]" should be [0, 3^k]. The proof of Lemma 2 is imprecise (its case a = 0 gives n = 3^{k-1}, which for n = 1 violates k > 0; it cites the "third" property of C₂ for the pairs of property (2)); the padding argument is formalized. The proof of Proposition 2 writes "n ≥ 2 even" where n must be odd. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Necessity proof, §6 (f and g assumed to be first accesses) At the critical configuration the paper treats f and g as each process's first call to O, and Lemma 5 / Proposition 1 use "the second call f'", which need not exist. Impact. Statement true; the missing cases are covered (KSetup.dist_of_last, KSetup.c15). Details. If f is p₀'s second call, p₀ can never touch O again, so it must distinguish fg from gf. The object is then in C₁, or in C₁.₅ with alternative (5a) and an arbitrary f'. Likewise, p₀ may decide without calling O again after fgσg'; then (5a) holds. 🔧 Proposition 2 (the graph G must be bipartite) With operations as nodes, an operation allowed to both processes merges a p₀-node with a p₁-node, so a path can switch sides there and "cᵢ ∈ m(p₀) for even i" fails. Impact. Statement true; repaired with (process, operation) nodes (KSetup.Adj, KSetup.c2_or_smaller, reduction, necessity). Repair. Using (process, operation) nodes repairs this; the reduction to fewer objects works unchanged. The "minimal number of objects" argument becomes an induction on the number of copies, which needs finitely many copies. We prove the reduced algorithm correct and wait-free. 🔧 Lemma 4 (Algorithm 3, omitted histories) Its case analysis ignores histories where the other process applies its operations on O after the decider's reads. Impact. Statement true; the Lean proof enumerates all interleavings (decide0_ok, decide1_ok). Details. k ≥ 1 is genuinely needed: with N = 1, line 23 would fire wrongly in the run g c_N f c_{N−1}. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Two deterministic processes with binary inputs; asynchronous; wait-freedom (every process taking infinitely many steps in an infinite schedule outputs). Crashes are modelled by processes that stop taking steps: CSLib Cslib.SharedMemory.Recoverable without crash events, WFConsensus. Shared objects: Read/write-like objects (ObjSpec.RWLike, which includes registers of any value type). Finitely many copies of the deterministic type O (the paper's "minimal number of objects" argument presupposes this; necessity is proved for such algorithms). Each process applies at most two operations to each copy in every execution (TwoShot), and only operations allowed by m (Allowed). Initial states are chosen by the algorithm. Solvable O m existentially quantifies over all such algorithms (Model.lean). Generalizing registers to read/write-like objects only strengthens necessity. Self-stabilizing Leader Election in Directed Networks — PODC 2024 Karine Altisen, Alain Cournier, Geoffrey Defalque, Stéphane Devismes. On Self-stabilizing Leader Election in Directed Networks. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662778. Formalized version: the full version on HAL, hal-04434345v4 (4 March 2024); numbering follows it (v1 has the same statements and algorithms). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Both characterizations hold, for leader election (Corollary 3) and synchronous unison (Corollary 5), but the unison algorithm U(K) of Theorem 5 is not self-stabilizing as printed: the bug is in the input of the third instance E of PEL. A one-line change (I_E(p) = (¬p.A.M, p.Id) instead of (¬p.A.M, p.MI.M)) repairs it, and with that change the paper's proof of Theorem 5 goes through. Everything else we checked holds: C-MAI (Theorems 1 and 2, with the bound α + MAD + 2), PEL (Theorem 3, with 3α + 3MAD + 6 rounds under the distributed unfair daemon) and the impossibility (Lemma 13, Corollary 2); the space bounds were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 5 (Algorithm 2 on top of PEL, synchronous unison) U(K) does not stabilize: every process of the source component gets E.d = 0 and increments its clock on its own, so e.g. on the 2-cycle 0 ⇄ 1 with K = 2 the clocks alternate (1, 0), (0, 1), … forever (twoCycle_paper_unison_fails, U.paper_unison_not_selfStab). Impact. The printed algorithm does not work, but a one-line change (I_E(p) = (¬p.A.M, p.Id) instead of (¬p.A.M, p.MI.M)) repairs it, and the characterization of Corollary 5 survives. Leader election (PEL, Theorem 3) is unaffected. Details. Section 5.3 and the proofs of Lemmas 16 and 19 use that in a terminal configuration of PEL, p.E.d = ‖ℓ, p‖, so the leader ℓ is "the only process satisfying E.d = 0". The paper cites Theorem 1 for this. But Theorem 1 gives p.E.d = Mind(p): the distance to the closest ancestor whose E-input equals the minimum (0, mid). That input I_E(q) = (¬q.A.M, q.MI.M) equals (0, mid) for every q with q.MI.M = mid. This includes the whole source component (Corollary 4 and Lemma 14). So all these processes have E.d = 0, and U-DAG makes each of them increment its own clock independently. Counterexample: the 2-cycle 0 ⇄ 1 with identifiers 0, 1, α = 1 and K = 2. Start from a terminal configuration of PEL with clocks (0, 1). Under the synchronous daemon the clocks alternate (1, 0), (0, 1), … forever. They are never equal, so no choice of legitimate configurations makes U(K) self-stabilizing. The paper's own example is inconsistent in the same way. In Figure 5(c), the six processes of the two triangular components have E-input (0,4), yet Figure 6 shows E.d = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 for them. Scope: we prove the failure for every network whose source component has two distinct processes (so on every strongly connected network with n ≥ 2), every K ≥ 2, every identifier assignment and every α ≥ MAD (U.paper_unison_not_selfStab; concrete instance twoCycle_paper_unison_fails). More generally, it fails as soon as two processes have only ancestors with identifiers ≥ mid (U.paper_unison_not_selfStab_gen). So if the smallest identifier lies in the source component, every process has E.d = 0, and U(K) fails on every network with n ≥ 2 (U.paper_unison_not_selfStab_of_min). An example is the dipath 0 → 1, whose source component is a single process (dipath_paper_unison_fails). Repair. With I_E(p) = (¬p.A.M, p.Id), PEL still elects mid: Lemma 15 holds for both inputs (PEL.lemma15). Moreover the leader is now the only process with E.d = 0, and E.d is a BFS distance from it (U.fixed_ed). The paper's Lemmas 16 and 19 then go through. We prove Theorem 5 for the repaired algorithm, with the claimed bound of 3α + 4MAD + 6 synchronous steps (U.theorem5, U.theorem5_time), and Corollary 5 (corollary5). ✏️ Slips Lemma 10's induction claim reads "If MinI(p) < i"; it should be "Mind(p) < i". Lemma 9 and Lemma 10 index rounds by R(i), which is undefined once the (finite) execution has ended. This is harmless: terminal configurations are legitimate. Typos Lemma 5's proof writes q ∈ F_{i+1}(q) for q ∈ F_{i+1}(p), and Lemma 8 has F_j(q) for F_j(p). Lemma 9 has a stray q in "Mdf_{R(α+1)} q(p)". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (the shared daemon library Cslib/Computability/Distributed/SelfStabilization/{Defs,Daemon}.lean, namespace Cslib.SelfStabilization, and digraph reachability Cslib/Foundations/Combinatorics/Digraph/Walk.lean). Atomic-state model on a finite Digraph V. G.Adj q p means p reads q, i.e. q is a predecessor of p. Deterministic algorithms next : (V → Q) → V → Q. A process is enabled iff its action changes its state. The hierarchical collateral compositions E ∘ A ∘ MI and U-DAG ∘ PEL are written as one such function. Distributed unfair daemon: IsUnfairRun next e S (IsUnfairExec next), where each step activates a nonempty set of enabled processes. Executions are in the paper's Ext∞ form: a terminal configuration repeats forever, so "finite" means "eventually terminal". Synchronous daemon: IsSyncExec next e, i.e. e (t+1) = next (e t). Rounds follow the paper's neutralization definition. RoundDone e S s s' says that every process enabled at s executes or becomes disabled in [s, s']. Time bounds hold for every sequence RoundBounds e S r of such boundaries, a family that contains the paper's minimal rounds (IsLeastRoundBounds). So an algorithm must work for every assignment of unique identifiers ("insensitive to its inputs"). DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662785. Formalized version: the full paper, arXiv 2405.03646 v1 (the only version); numbering follows it (BA Theorems 1 and 3 = full Theorems 1 and 3). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The algorithms are correct exactly as claimed: Algorithm 2 is a quiescently terminating leader election on oriented rings with exactly n(2·IDmax+1) pulses, the leader terminating last, and Algorithm 3 elects and orients non-oriented rings quiescently with n(2·IDmax+1) pulses (Theorem 2) or n(4·IDmax−1) pulses (Proposition 14). The lower bound holds as a worst case over ID assignments, as Theorem 17 of the full version says, once one step of its lockstep proof is repaired locally; IDs must be positive. Corollary 2 (the external compiler) and Appendix B (anonymous rings) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 3 ("any … algorithm sends at least n⌊log₂(IDmax/n)⌋ messages") is false if read for each ring and ID assignment: Algorithm 2 with IDs relabelled by the swap 1 ↔ 16 is still a correct quiescently terminating leader election, and it sends at most 3 pulses in every execution on the single-node ring with ID 16, while 1·⌊log₂ 16⌋ = 4 (theorem_3_per_instance_false). The full version's Theorem 17 states the quantifier explicitly ("for some assignment of IDs") and derives Theorem 3 from it, so the intended reading is clear from the full paper. What Theorem 17 proves, and what we prove, is the worst case: for n ≤ M, some assignment of distinct IDs from {1,…,M} has an execution with at least n⌊log₂(M/n)⌋ ≥ n⌊log₂(IDmax/n)⌋ pulses (theorem_3). IDs must be positive: the paper writes ID_v ∈ ℕ without excluding 0, but a node with ID 0 relays every pulse, so on the 1-node ring Algorithm 2 runs forever (infinite_execution_id_zero). The proofs (Lemma 5's base case, the pigeonhole in Lemma 22) silently use ID ≥ 1, and with it all results hold. The lower bound needs correctness on rings with 1 node (a self-loop) and 2 nodes (a double link). The paper uses these explicitly, but its definition of a ring ("connected graph with all degrees 2") does not literally include them. Typos Several cross-references are wrong: "Lemma 1–5" in Lemmas 6–8 and Appendix A mean the items of Lemma 5 and Lemma 24, "Algorithms 2–2" means line ranges, and Lemma 11's proof has ID_v for ID_b. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 19 / Theorem 17 (lockstep argument) The lockstep argument says that nodes with equal solitude patterns "send their first pulse in the same direction … receive and send exactly the pattern", one pulse per time step, but patterns record received pulses, so two IDs with equal patterns may still send in different batches. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Cslib.ContentOblivious.reach_sync, lemma_19, theorem_17). Details. Example: two pulses at start versus one at start and one after the first reception. Then "one pulse per time step" and "send exactly the pattern" are not literally true, and the synchronized scheduler needs to be made precise. Repair. Schedule by rounds of receptions. In round k, every node consumes the pulse at the port given by the k-th symbol of the common prefix. It is available because the sender sent it after the same k−1 receptions in its own solitude run. Count received pulses (n·s), which bound sent pulses from below. (Cslib.ContentOblivious.reach_sync, lemma_19, theorem_17) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Cslib/Computability/Distributed/ContentOblivious/Model.lean). Two-port nodes on a ring ZMod n (any n ≥ 1). The oriented ring links Port1 of v to Port0 of v+1. A non-oriented ring additionally flips the ports of an arbitrary set of nodes. Pulses carry no content, so each channel is a counter. Pulses are never lost or created. Asynchronous: at each step an adversary delivers any pulse in transit to a node that is ready to read the port it arrives at. Readiness models the pseudo-code's polling. Unread pulses stay in transit. Deterministic, event-driven nodes that know only their own ID (uniform: no knowledge of n). All nodes act at time 0. Terminated nodes never act again. "Terminates / stabilizes" is stated finitely. The number of pulses is bounded on every execution, so all executions are finite. All final configurations (no step possible) are correct. This implies the paper's statements under any fairness assumption. IDs are distinct and positive; for Algorithm 1 they only need to be positive. Main results in Lean. It covers every deterministic algorithm in the model, including ones that poll only some ports. It assumes only that maximal executions on 1- and 2-node rings end with all nodes terminated and exactly one leader. The lockstep/indistinguishability lemma (reach_sync) and the solitude characterization (reach_one) are in Cslib/Computability/Distributed/ContentOblivious/Lockstep.lean. Not formalized. Corollary 2 (simulation via the external compiler of Censor-Hillel et al.) and Appendix B (anonymous rings, randomized ID sampling); neither was checked. Trust. Before the proofs, a bounded exhaustive check of all schedules (modelcheck/mc.py: all schedules and all port assignments for n ≤ 3 and IDs ≤ 4, plus spot checks for n = 4) found no counterexample to Theorems 1, 2 or Proposition 14. The 2026 paper Efficient Counting and Simulation in Content-Oblivious Rings (Chalopin, Chang, Di Luna, Zhou) cites this paper only as prior work and claims no correction. It mentions a later terminating algorithm for non-oriented rings by Chalopin et al., which answers the open question of §6.

Fault Tolerant Coloring of the Asynchronous Cycle — PODC 2022 Pierre Fraigniaud, Patrick Lambein-Monette, Mikaël Rabie. Brief Announcement: Fault Tolerant Coloring of the Asynchronous Cycle. PODC 2022. DOI 10.1145/3519270.3538456. Formalized version: arXiv 2207.11198 v1 (the only version, the full version of the brief announcement). Numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The paper claims a wait-free 5-colouring of every asynchronous cycle C_n in O(log* n) rounds (Algorithm 3, Theorem 4.4), but neither 5-colouring algorithm is wait-free: Algorithm 2 (Theorem 3.11) and Algorithm 3 (Theorem 4.4) have executions on every cycle C_n, n ≥ 3, in which two processes take rounds forever without returning, and we proved no replacement. The 6-colour Algorithm 1 is correct: we prove Theorem 3.1, with a better bound. The Cole–Vishkin lemmas 4.1–4.3 and the safety Lemma 4.5 (the evolving identifiers of Algorithm 3 stay a proper colouring) also hold. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorems 3.11 and 4.4, Lemma 3.13 (Algorithms 2 and 3 are not wait-free) On C_3 with identifiers 0, 1, 2, if all three processes take a round at time 1, process 1 then stops, and processes 0 and 2 keep taking rounds simultaneously, then neither of them ever returns, under both Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3 (theorem_3_11_false, theorem_4_4_false), which also refutes Lemma 3.13 (lemma_3_13_false). Impact. The wait-free 5-colouring in O(log* n) rounds is not established, and no bound on the number of rounds exists for either algorithm. The correctness and palette parts of both theorems do hold. Whether some wait-free 5-colouring of C_n exists is not settled here: we refute the algorithms, not the possibility. Details. At time 1 each process writes (X, a, b) = (X, 0, 0) and recomputes: process 0 gets (1,1), process 1 gets (1,1), process 2 gets (0,1). Process 1 then crashes, or is just slow, and its register keeps showing its initial colours (0, 0). Processes 0 (the local minimum) and 2 (the local maximum) now take their rounds simultaneously, which the model explicitly allows. Each round they read the stale (0,0) of process 1 and each other's colours. Their states alternate forever between (1,1)/(0,1) and (2,2)/(0,2), and each of them always finds both of its colours in the conflict set C. In Algorithm 3 the same execution works. Process 0 is a local minimum and process 2 a local maximum, so both set r ← ∞ in their first round and never change their identifiers again; after that the algorithm runs exactly like Algorithm 2. The same pattern works on every C_n, n ≥ 3, with identifiers 0, …, n-1. Processes 0 and n-1 play the roles of 0 and 2. Their other neighbours 1 and n-2 stop after their first round (theorem_3_11_false_all, theorem_4_4_false_all). Lemma 3.13 (non-minima return), on which the termination proofs of Theorems 3.11 and 4.4 rest, fails in the same run: process 2 is not a local minimum and its set A_2 stays empty, yet it never returns. The lemma's proof claims that the neighbours' a-values are positive "by time t_4", which ignores registers that are frozen at the initial value 0. Two remarks from bounded model checking. If at most one process is activated per time step (no simultaneous rounds), Algorithm 2 terminates on all C_n with n ≤ 5. Leaving the initial colours unwritten (⊥) does not repair it. ✏️ Slips Lemma 3.3 is false as written with the open interval (t₁, t₂): a neighbour that takes a round exactly at t₂ can still conflict with p, and random simulation finds such runs on C_4. It holds for the half-open interval (t₁, t₂], which is the form we prove and use (fresh_of_conflict); it is used only inside the proof of Theorem 3.1. Theorem 4.4 assumes only a proper colouring X, but its O(log* n) bound needs identifiers in [0, poly(n)], as Section 2.1 assumes for identifiers. Typos The proof of Theorem 3.1 says "min{ℓ, ℓ'} is bounded by ⌊3n/2⌋", which is true but not what is needed: the bound used is n/2. The final bound holds. In the proof of Lemma 3.5, Y and τ should be x and t'. The proof of Lemma 4.10 uses an undefined R. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 4.5 (Algorithm 3 keeps identifiers proper) The proof's induction claim X_p ∉ {X_q, X̂_q} is not inductive on its own. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a stronger invariant (lemma_4_5, alg3_X_ne_reg, alg3_X_proper). Details. The paper's stale-read case concludes something about X̂_p where it needs the current X_p. The case X_q(T+1) = f(X_q(T), X_p(T)) omits the cases where q is a local maximum or reduces against its other neighbour. Repair. The invariant also records two things. First, a register holds an earlier state with a counter r̂ ≤ r, equal only if the identifier is unchanged. Second, if a neighbour's last step changed its identifier and r̂_q = r_p, then that step read exactly the current X_p. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (Model.lean). Network and processes. n processes on ZMod n, where the neighbours of p are p ± 1. They are asynchronous, deterministic and crash-prone. Registers. Each process owns a single-writer register, initially ⊥, that its two neighbours read. The full local state is written; the paper's algorithms write all their variables. Rounds. A round is a local immediate snapshot: write, then read both neighbours, then compute or return. A schedule σ : ℕ → Finset (ZMod n) gives the processes activated at each time. Processes activated together all write before any of them reads (Section 2.1). Activating a returned process does nothing. Faults and adversary. Crashes and slowness are schedules that stop or delay activating a process. The adversary is any schedule; no fairness is assumed. Measures. workActs counts the working activations of a process, which is the paper's round complexity. WaitFreeWithin A init K means that in every schedule every process is activated at most K times while working. ProperOutputs means that terminated neighbours have distinct outputs; OutputsIn is the palette. Inputs. A proper colouring X (X p ≠ X (p+1)), as in the theorems. For Algorithm 1, X may take values in any linear order; the theorem itself uses ℕ. Faithfulness. The model is exactly the paper's. The counterexamples use only schedules the paper explicitly allows: simultaneous rounds and a process that stops after one round. Under-specified and minor points. The pseudocode never says how a ⊥ register enters lines 11–19 of Algorithm 3. We follow the proof of Lemma 4.10: an unwritten r blocks the green light. The counterexample does not depend on this choice. Theorem 4.4 assumes only a proper initial colouring, but its O(log* n) bound needs identifiers in [0, poly(n)], as Section 2.1 assumes for identifiers. Moot, since termination fails. Lemma 4.1 is stated over the reals. We prove it over ℕ, with α = 3. Main results in Lean (namespace AsyncCycle, all imported by Main.lean). It gives the a ↔ b / order-reversal symmetry of Algorithm 1. Changes.lean: counting changes of a sequence, with the "lag" and "follow" lemmas. Activations.lean: generic facts about activations. Mex.lean: a kernel-computable mex. Not formalized. Properties 2.1–2.3: MIS impossibility, the Ω(log* n) lower bound and the 5-colour lower bound for C_3. They are reductions to cited results (strong symmetry breaking, Linial, renaming lower bounds). Lemmas 3.4–3.8, 3.14 and 4.6–4.10, which are steps of proofs we replaced or of claims that are false. The paper's proof of Theorem 3.1 leans on loose lemmas (Lemma 3.3 as written, the parity bookkeeping of Lemmas 3.4–3.8), which we did not check. We give a new, sharper proof with bound max(4, n) activations, where the paper has ⌊3n/2⌋ + 4 (theorem_3_1, alg1_workActs_le): Local extrema return within 4 activations, as the paper claims. Our argument: after the first round of a local maximum p, each smaller neighbour can cause at most one more failure of p (workActs_le_four_of_max). A non-extremal process returns within ℓ + ℓ' + 1 activations (Lemma 3.9, third term), where ℓ, ℓ' are the monotone distances to the closest local maximum and minimum. Our argument: every failed round changes the colour (Lemma 3.2), a_p changes at most ℓ times, and b_p at most ℓ' times (lemma_3_9). The parity bookkeeping with the sets A_p, B_p (Lemmas 3.5–3.8) is not needed. The terms 3ℓ + 4, 3ℓ' + 4 of Lemma 3.9 (via Lemma 3.4 for non-extremal processes). Exhaustive model checking for n ≤ 6 found no violation. Appendix A (O(Δ²) colours on general graphs). Trust. No sorry. The listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The C_3 counterexamples are checked by kernel decide (2-periodic configuration); the all-n versions are symbolic. Correctness and palette are proved for every initial colouring. modelcheck/ holds the Python model checkers used to find the counterexample and to test the bounds: exhaustive over all schedules for small n (mc12.py, lasso.py, bounds1.py, scc3.py), and random/BFS search for Lemma 4.5 (alg3.py, rand3b.py, bfs3.py). CSLib candidates: the local-immediate-snapshot cycle model (Model.lean, could be generalized to graphs), Simulation.lean, Changes.lean.

You Can Lie but Not Deny — PODC 2025 Xing Hu, Sam Toueg. You can lie but not deny: SWMR registers with signature properties in systems with Byzantine processes. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733550. Formalized version: arXiv 2504.09805 v2; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✅ Correct. We found no mistake in what we checked, the optimality result of Section 10. For 3 ≤ n ≤ 3f there is no correct implementation from SWMR registers of the one-shot test-or-set object (Theorem 29), nor of verifiable, authenticated and sticky registers (Theorem 31), and Observation 30 (test-or-set from each of these registers) also holds. The implementations for n > 3f (Theorems 14, 20, 25), the other half of the paper's main point, are not formalized and were not checked. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Typos Section 6 introduces the authenticated register as "a multivalued SWMR verifiable register". Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Byzantine/Model.lean, staged for CSLib) Asynchronous shared memory with n = card P processes, at most f of which are Byzantine. Implementations are deterministic programs (CSLib Impl). Base objects are atomic and come with access rights. Correct processes may take steps outside their operation intervals (helping). A Byzantine process applies arbitrary primitives it has the right to apply. For SWMR registers this means arbitrary writes to its own registers. Correct processes are invoked only when idle, and only with allowed operations (e.g. only the setter Sets). Byzantine linearizability (Definition 7). Some well-formed history h' uses only allowed operations, agrees with h on the correct processes, and is linearizable. Correctness (Definition 9, Impl.ByzCorrect): every finite execution is Byzantine linearizable, and correct processes complete their operations in every fair infinite execution. This holds for every set of ≤ f Byzantine processes and every invocation pattern allowed by adm (one-shot for test-or-set, unrestricted for the registers). Requiring Byzantine linearizability only for finite executions is implied by the paper's definition, so the impossibility results are at least as strong as stated. Base objects: any family of single-writer objects (only the owner changes an object, and it can overwrite it with any state). This covers SWMR registers of arbitrary value types, any number per process. Main results in Lean. Paper Lean File Definition 7, 9 ByzLinearizable, Impl.ByzCorrect Podc/…/Byzantine/Model.lean Definitions 10, 15, 21, 26 verReg, authReg, stickyReg, testOrSet (+ …Allowed) Objects.lean Observation 27, 11–13, 16–18, 22–24 tosSig, verSig, authSig, stickySig (SigTest structures) Objects.lean Lemma 28 (generalized) SigTest.validity, SigTest.unforgeability, SigTest.relay SigTest.lean Theorem 29 (generalized core) SigTest.no_byzCorrect Impossibility.lean Theorem 29 theorem29 Main.lean Observation 30 observation30, observation30_verifiable, observation30_authenticated, observation30_sticky Observation30.lean Theorem 31 theorem31_verifiable, theorem31_authenticated, theorem31_sticky Main.lean (degenerate case) authenticated_unit_byzCorrect, authenticated_unit_swmr Degenerate.lean The impossibility proof (histories H1–H3 of Figure 1) is sound. Lemma 28 has only a proof sketch in the paper; the sketch is correct, and we prove the lemma in full (SigTest.validity, SigTest.unforgeability, SigTest.relay). Degenerate value domains (implicit convention). Theorem 31 for authenticated registers is false if the value domain is {v₀}: then Read always returns v₀ and Verify(v₀) always returns true, so every operation can return immediately. The sticky register is likewise trivial for an empty domain. The paper speaks of multivalued registers throughout, which excludes these cases, so this is an implicit convention rather than an error. We make it explicit with the hypotheses v ≠ v₀ and Nonempty V. (authenticated_unit_swmr, theorem31_authenticated) CSLib candidates. Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Byzantine/Model.lean and Restrict.lean (Byzantine shared-memory model, Byzantine linearizability, replay, single-writer objects, termination ⇒ completion, history restriction); the positional linearization lemmas stAt, idx, lin_* of SigTest.lean. Not formalized. The implementations for n > 3f (Algorithms 1–3, Theorems 14, 20, 25 and their appendix proofs). The remark that n = 2 is trivial. The paper's derivation of Theorem 31 from Theorem 29 and Observation 30, which we did not check. It goes through an unstated composition property: a correct implementation of test-or-set from a verifiable register, composed with a correct implementation of the verifiable register from SWMR registers, gives a correct implementation of test-or-set from SWMR registers. The paper's Section 3.2 motivates Byzantine linearizability by exactly this use ("as if it were an atomic object"), so the step is a standard tacit assumption. For deterministic implementations it is plausible, but it is not trivial: Byzantine processes may deviate at both levels. We avoid the composition and prove Theorem 31 directly for all four objects at once (SigTest.no_byzCorrect, theorem31_verifiable, theorem31_authenticated, theorem31_sticky). The proof of Theorem 29 only uses three properties of a positive test: validity, unforgeability and relay (Lemma 28). We prove these for every "signature-like" object directly from Byzantine linearizability, so the impossibility applies to all four objects. Trust. No sorry. The listed theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: Impl.ByzCorrect is satisfiable. Observation 30 gives correct implementations for every f, and authenticated_unit_swmr gives one from SWMR registers for 3 ≤ n ≤ 3f. So the impossibility results do not follow from an unsatisfiable correctness notion. Histories and linearizations come from CSLib SharedMemory (History, LinPoints). The Byzantine execution model, replay/indistinguishability lemmas and history restriction (Podc/Computability/Distributed/SharedMemory/Byzantine/{Model,Restrict}.lean) are CSLib candidates.

Tight Bounds on Channel Reliability via Generalized Quorum Systems — PODC 2025 Alejandro Naser-Pastoriza, Gregory Chockler, Alexey Gotsman, Fedor Ryabinin. Tight Bounds on Channel Reliability via Generalized Quorum Systems. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733529. Formalized version: arXiv 2505.02646 v1 (proceedings text plus appendices); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The necessity half of the paper's characterization stands after local changes: Lemma 2, Theorem 2 (lattice agreement, MWMR registers, SWMR snapshots, and also consensus), Theorem 6 (partial synchrony) and Proposition 1 are proved for arbitrary deterministic algorithms, once the implied non-trivial value domain is named, the remark on U_f is reworded and one proof step is closed. The sufficiency half was not checked: the upper bounds (Theorems 1, 4, 5) are not formalized, and for the quorum access functions of Figure 3 we formalize the protocol and its safety only (see the table). Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Remark after Theorem 2 (U_f is not determined by F) The remark calls U_f "the largest set of processes for which termination can be guaranteed", but U_f depends on the quorum system, not only on F (Uf_not_unique). Impact. The theorems themselves are unaffected; the remark has to be read for the quorum system built in the proof. Details. With two processes and only the channel 0 → 1 reliable, both ({0},{0}) and ({0,1},{1}) are generalized quorum systems, with U_f = {0} and U_f = {1}. Termination can be guaranteed at {0} or at {1}, but not at both (Lemma 2). Repair. Every terminating set lies in U_f of the quorum system built in the proof: τ(f) ⊆ U_f (theorem_2_generic). ✏️ Slips Theorem 2 (also Lemma 2 and Theorem 6) needs a non-trivial object. It is false over a chain (e.g. ℕ): returning one's own proposal immediately is a safe, wait-free lattice agreement algorithm, yet under "one of two processes may crash" (τ(f) = the correct process) no generalized quorum system exists (theorem_2_false_of_chain). The same algorithm shows that registers, snapshots and consensus need at least two values. The proof picks two incomparable elements x₁, x₂, but the theorem is stated for any semi-lattice. With two incomparable elements (lattice agreement) or two distinct values (registers, snapshots, consensus) as hypotheses, everything holds (theorem_2_lattice_agreement, theorem_2_register, theorem_2_snapshot, theorem_6). Typos Proposition 1, ambiguous "strongly connected in G \ f". If it meant that the induced subgraph is strongly connected, Proposition 1 would be false (proposition_1_false_induced). Take processes 0, 1, 2, with only the channels 0 ↔ 1 failing, and write quorums {0}, {1} reachable from the read quorum {0, 1}. Then U = {0, 1}, but 0 and 1 reach each other only through 2. Not an error under the natural reading: the proof of Proposition 1 and the definition of U_f as a strongly connected component use mutual reachability in G \ f; with that reading everything is correct, and this is the reading we formalize (proposition_1). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 6, lower bound (finiteness of σ is not enough) For Theorem 6 the paper only argues that σ is finite, but liveness is also applied to the executions α₁, β₁, which must themselves be partially synchronous. Impact. Statement true; proved directly (theorem_6). Repair. One gluing argument proves the bound for every object with two conflicting operations, and it uses liveness only through one canonical continuation, which is both fair and partially synchronous. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model (staged shared library Podc/Computability/Distributed/MessagePassing/ChannelFailures/, namespace Cslib.ChannelFailures). Asynchronous message passing among finitely many processes, deterministic event-driven algorithms (invocations, spontaneous steps reading a local clock, receptions), FIFO channels (a restriction of the adversary, which only strengthens lower bounds). Determinism is without loss of generality: the paper's liveness is "returns in every fair execution", so a nondeterministic algorithm can be replaced by a deterministic refinement; probabilistic termination is not considered by the paper. Histories are CSLib Labels; registers and snapshots use CSLib linearizability. A failure pattern (procs, chans) enters only fairness: crashed processes stop taking steps, disconnected channels stop delivering (a suffix of their messages is lost); all other processes take infinitely many steps and all other channels between them deliver every message. This is exactly the paper's f-compliant fair execution. Finite executions are failure free; safety is required for all of them. (f, T)-obstruction-freedom and wait-freedom as in §2. Partial synchrony (§7): discrete time with GST and Δ, non-drifting clocks after GST, and a step of every correct process per time unit. The lower bounds quantify over all algorithms, message types and local states. Main results in Lean. Impossibility Results for Data-Center Routing with Congestion Control and Unsplittable Flows. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662777. Formalized version: the PODC proceedings version (no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorems 3.4, 4.2 and 4.3, the upper bound of Theorem 5.4 and all lemmas are correct, and the proofs that the paper omits as "routine" (Lemma 2.2, Lemma 3.2, Lemma 4.4, Lemma 4.6, Lemma 5.2) are also proved here. The tightness part of Theorem 5.4 is proved only for odd n: the paper reduces to odd n "without loss of generality", but for even n its construction gives only ε → 1/(n-2), which still shows that the bound becomes tight as n grows. The other gaps close locally, including the wrong rates that the proof of Theorem 5.4 computes for n = 3. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 5.4, second part (the "w.l.o.g. n odd" step) The tightness proof stacks (n-1)/2 copies of the gadget of Example 3.3 plus one extra middle "doom" switch, which needs n odd, and nothing reduces even n to odd n; for even n the same idea gives only ε > 1/(n-2). Impact. We prove the claim for odd n and the weaker bound ε > 1/(n-2) for even n ≥ 4 (theorem_5_4_tight_odd, theorem_5_4_tight_even). Whether the claim holds for even n is open. The paper's message ("the bound becomes tight as n grows") is unaffected. Details. The claim is: for every n ≥ 3 and every ε > 1/(n-1), some collection of flows has T^{T-MmF} ≥ 2(1-ε) T^MmF. For even n only (n-2)/2 gadgets fit. Other gadget shapes do not seem to help. By an informal count (not formalized): take L ≤ n-1 type-1 flows on I_1/O_1 forming chains of length ≥ 2, consecutive flows of a chain joined by a bundle of k type-2 flows, B bundles in all, every bundle on the doom switch. Then the Doom-Switch throughput is L(1 - 1/B) + 1, while T^MmF → B ≥ L/2. For even n the best ratio is max(2 - 2/(n-2), 2 - 4/n + 4/n²), still below 2(1 - 1/(n-1)). (For n = 4 a single chain of three type-1 flows gives ratio → 5/4, i.e. ε → 3/8. This beats the formalized 1/(n-2) = 1/2 but not the paper's 1/3.) ✏️ Slips In the routing of Lemma 4.6, the type-2.b flow is written (s_i^1, t_i^j). It should be (s_i^1, t_{n+1}^j). Typos Definitions 2.4/2.5 speak of "the" max-min fair allocation of every routing. Existence (water-filling) is assumed; we prove uniqueness, and our statements do not need existence. The proof of Theorem 5.4 writes T^{T-MmF} ≤ T^{T-MT} = T^MT. Only ≤ is needed, so Lemma 5.2 is not used for the bound. In (R1), "max-main" should be "max-min". Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Proof of Theorem 5.4, n = 3 (Doom-Switch rates) The proof says that under the Doom-Switch routing the type-1 flows get 1 - 2/(n-1) and the type-2 flows get 2/(k(n-1)), but for n = 3 (type-1 rate 0, type-2 rate 1/k) this allocation is not max-min fair (doom_paper_rates_not_isMaxMinFair). Impact. The statement for n = 3 is still true, trivially, because then 2(1-ε) < 1. The rates are correct for odd n ≥ 5, where k(n-3) ≥ 2 (doom_clos_isMaxMinFair). Details. The type-1 flows have no bottleneck, and giving every flow 1/(k+1) is feasible for the same routing and lexicographically larger. 🔧 Lemma 4.6, Step 2 (lexicographic principle) Step 2 argues that every routing that raises some rate must lower "a flow of equal (or no greater) rate" and concludes a*↑ ⪰ a_r↑, but never states which lexicographic principle makes this inference valid, especially when several rates change at once. Impact. Statement true; repaired, and Step 2 shows more than the paper claims (sortedRates_lt_of_forall, aStar_criterion, lemma_4_6). Repair. We prove this principle in general (the leximin criterion): if a ≠ b and every flow that gains in b is matched by a flow of no larger a-rate that loses in b, then b↑ ≺ a↑. With it, Step 2 shows that a* lex-dominates every allocation that is feasible for any routing, whether max-min fair or not. Hence the lex-max-min fair allocation is unique and equals a*. Static rate allocation; there is no dynamics, so synchrony, failures and randomness do not arise. A collection of flows is a finite type F with source and destination servers (Server n = Fin (2n) × Fin n). A routing assigns a middle switch to every flow (unsplittable flows). An allocation is F → ℝ. It is feasible if all rates are non-negative and every link's load is at most its capacity. Amnesiac Flooding: Easy to Break, Difficult to Escape — PODC 2025 Henry Austin, Maximilien Gadouleau, George B. Mertzios, Amitabh Trehan. Brief Announcement: Amnesiac Flooding: Easy to Break, Difficult to Escape. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733523. Formalized version: arXiv 2502.06001 v2 (29 Oct 2025), the full version with all proofs (Appendices A–D). Numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The termination dichotomy is fully verified: from an arbitrary message configuration, amnesiac flooding terminates iff the configuration is balanced (Theorem 5.1), iff it is reachable from the empty configuration by multicasts (Theorem 5.5), and then within 2|E| rounds (Corollary 5.1.1); the single-message fragility of Theorem 5.6 and all other Section 5 claims not listed below are proved too. But the first claim of Theorem 5.7 (uni-directional link failure) holds only for one initiator and fails for initiator sets with two nodes, the broadcast half of Theorem 5.8 (Byzantine failure) needs a different condition, the claim that any Byzantine set with a non-leaf node can break flooding is false, and the termination proof for Random Flooding is broken. The Section 4 uniqueness theorem, the paper's other half, is not formalized, so this verdict does not cover it. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Introduction, consequence of Theorem 1.5 (non-leaf Byzantine nodes) The claim that "any Byzantine set containing a non-leaf node on any network can force either non-termination or non-broadcast for Amnesiac Flooding with any initial set" (also consequence (3) of the PODC version) fails on the path 0 – 1 – 2 with I = {0, 2}. Impact. The corrected Theorem 5.8 does not restore this claim, and no repaired form of it is proved. Details. Node 1 is not a leaf, but it can force neither non-termination (the path has no cycle) nor a broadcast failure (theorem_5_8_broadcast_false). ❌ Proposition C.2 (Random Flooding, termination window) The proof's claim that if all bits are 1 for D + 1 rounds and then all 0, flooding has stopped two rounds later, fails on the 5-cycle (D = 2) from a reachable configuration with a single message (random_flooding_window_false). Impact. The statement (almost sure termination) is unestablished but plausible with a longer window (about 2n all-ones rounds); we do not formalize the probability. Details. Choosing bits that keep a single message (0,1) alive, then 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, leaves messages in flight. ⚠️ Theorem 5.7, first claim (uni-directional link failure, several initiators) The claim that for every initiator set I ⊊ V some uni-directional link failure breaks broadcast or termination fails on the path 0 – 1 – 2 with I = {0, 2} (theorem_5_7_multi_false). Impact. The claim holds for a single initiator, which is all the paper's proof covers ("the initiating node"); we prove that case and the second claim of Theorem 5.7 (theorem_5_7_singleton, theorem_5_7_second). Details. Each of the four possible failures leaves at least one of 0 → 1, 2 → 1 working, so node 1 is informed in round 1. Node 1 forwards at most one message, to a leaf, and flooding stops by round 3. Repair. For a single initiator s, fail the link from s to any neighbour b. Then either b is unreachable along working links, or there is a cycle s ⇝ b → s of working links. Around that cycle, one more message travels with it than against it, and this surplus never decreases (Lemma D.3). We prove this, and the second claim of Theorem 5.7 the same way, with a simpler proof than the paper's strong-connectivity case split. 🔧 Theorem 5.8, broadcast part (Byzantine failure) The claim that Byzantine nodes J can force a failure to broadcast iff J contains a cut vertex set fails on the path 0 – 1 – 2 with I = {0, 2} and J = {1}: {1} is a cut vertex set, but every node is an initiator or receives the message in round 1 (theorem_5_8_broadcast_false). Impact. The non-termination half of Theorem 5.8 holds; the broadcast half is true only in a corrected form (theorem_5_8_broadcast). Details. The counterexample holds whether or not Byzantine nodes must receive the message. The "if" direction also fails for one initiator if failure is counted over honest nodes only. Example: a star with centre c, the initiator s a leaf, and J = everything except s. J ⊇ {c} is a cut vertex set, but the only honest node is s. Repair. What is true, and proved, is this: the adversary can make some honest node never receive the message iff some honest node is unreachable from every initiator in G − J. For the "if" direction the adversary stays silent until flooding on G − J has died out (theorem_5_8_broadcast). ✏️ Slips Lemma 5.2 (definition of T): as printed, with T the sinks of S, the lemma is false already for a single message on an edge (lemma_5_2_as_stated_false). The proof uses the sinks of S̄, i.e. the nodes sending to all neighbours in S. We prove the lemma with the proof's T, and Lemma 5.3 from it (lemma_5_2, lemma_5_3). Section 5.2.2 (fault-model indexing): uni-directional failures act only from S_2 on (∀ i ≥ 1, S_{i+1} = A(S_i) \ X), and drops only from round k ≥ 1, so read literally the initiator's first-round messages cannot fail, and the second claim of Theorem 5.7 fails on a single edge. We let faults act from the first round, which is what the proofs use (theorem_5_7_second). Typos Lemma 5.2 reads "∀ v ∈ N(v)". Definition A.1 has an empty bullet. Appendix C refers to "Theorem C.3" (a lemma), Lemma B.6 to "Theorem B.4", and Observation C.5 to "Theorem D.5" for balance under Parrot Flooding. Two figures are both labelled "Fig. 5". Full list of differences: differencies.md. The formalization Model. G : SimpleGraph V on a finite type, in synchronous rounds. A configuration is S : Set (V × V) (IsConfig: messages along edges). One round with initiators I is step G I (A_{I,G}, Definition 3.2); af G = A_{∅,G}. Terminates G S means A_∅^k(S) = ∅ for some k. Multicast runs are runFrom G Is S, and Reachable is statement (2) of Theorem 5.5. Single-source flooding is srcRun (agrees with Hussak–Trehan's sends, mem_srcRun_iff_sends). Balance (Definition 5.4) is Balanced. It is balance (BalancedOn) along every cycle and along the closed walk c₁ ++ p ++ c₂ ++ p⁻¹ of every faux-even cycle (FEC); this walk traverses the paper's H². Pulling S back along it gives exactly S^{2,H} (Definition 5.3). BalancedOn S w says that for every position k₀ the clockwise and anticlockwise messages with heads at k₀ + 2i are equinumerous. For odd cycles this is "as many each way" (balancedOn_iff_of_odd); for even cycles it is the paper's head-parity classes. Faults: dropRun: one lost message. uniRun: a set X of failed directed links, every round. byzRun: until a round k ≥ k₀ chosen by the adversary, nodes of J send arbitrary messages along edges; everyone is honest afterwards. The paper's k₀ is twice the diameter. "Fails to broadcast" means some (honest, non-initiator) node never receives a message. Connectivity is assumed only where needed (Theorem 5.6, broadcast part). Brute force (all graphs with n ≤ 6, |E| ≤ 8) shows it is in fact "iff"; we prove the "if" as stated. Remark. The PODC version's Theorem 4.1(2) states the bound 2|E| − 3. It fails on the path with two edges: {(0,1)} needs 2 rounds (podc_bound_false). It also fails on a single edge. The full version's 2|E| holds (corollary_5_1_1), and brute force on all graphs with n ≤ 6 and 3 ≤ |E| ≤ 8 agrees with 2|E| − 3, which we do not formalize. Not formalized. The paper's proof of the hard direction of Theorem 5.1 ("balanced ⇒ terminates", Appendix A). It is informal: Lemmas A.3–A.6 bound how long a message can stay on a cycle or FEC by "new messages must collide with …" sketches, and the word combinatorics of Lemmas A.8–A.15 then show that a recurrent message's path must linger on a cycle or FEC. We did not follow it and found no specific broken step. Instead we prove the theorem differently (theorem_5_1, corollary_5_1_1, theorem_5_5): Pull the configuration back along any closed walk. The easy direction (Lemma A.1, invariance) is as in the paper. Theorem 4.1 (uniqueness). Delay-Optimal Transaction Order Fairness — PODC 2026 Zhuo Cai, Amir Goharshady. Brief Announcement: Delay-Optimal Transaction Order Fairness. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815912. Formalized version: the 4-page brief announcement (no arXiv version; the full version, HAL hal-05625798, was not used). The BA gives proof ideas only; we wrote complete proofs. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 5.1 (the feasible region θ > Δ/k, φ > 1 − h/k gives an acyclic AOF graph) is correct apart from n = 0, and its proof idea works as written. Theorems 3.1 and 5.2 (cycle constructions) are true only when the number of nodes n may be taken large: read with the model's fixed n, both are false, and for n = 4, h = 3/4 the cycles claimed by Theorem 5.2 do not exist, but their proofs ("as the number of Byzantine groups grows") show that a large n was intended, and with n large we prove both. The protocol sketch of §6 was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 5.2 (cycle construction needs many nodes) Read with the model's fixed n, Theorem 5.2 is false for the standard n = 3f + 1 = 4: with 3 honest nodes (h = 3/4), k = 1, θ = Δ > 0 and φ = 0.6 < 0.625 no Δ-synchronous profile has a cycle (theorem_5_2_fixed_n_false). Impact. The proof idea ("as the number of Byzantine groups grows") shows that a large n was intended; for all sufficiently large n we prove it (theorem_5_2, theorem_5_2_finite). Details. The theorem says that in the model (n nodes, honest fraction h), every θ ≤ Δ/k and φ < 1 − h/(k+1) admit a synchronous profile whose AOF graph has a cycle. In the counterexample all hypotheses hold, including 1 − h/k ≤ h. An edge needs ⌈0.6·4⌉ = 3 supporters, so at least 2 honest ones, more than |H|/2. The counting argument of Theorem 5.1 with k = 2 (θ = Δ > Δ/2) applies, so no Δ-synchronous profile has a cycle. The proof idea gets support "arbitrarily close to 1 − h/(k+1)" by splitting the Byzantine nodes into more and more groups, which needs n → ∞. For a fixed n, each edge of the construction loses about ⌈hn/(k+1)⌉ honest supporters and one Byzantine supporter. Repair. For all sufficiently large n with hn integral (explicitly, whenever φn + hn/(k+1) + 2 ≤ n) the rotating construction gives a cycle. (theorem_5_2_fixed_n_false; repaired: theorem_5_2, theorem_5_2_finite) 🔧 §5 and §7 ("boundary gap") §7 says the feasible and infeasible regions "intentionally leave a small boundary gap" between 1 − h/k and 1 − h/(k+1) and that closing it "would require a sharper characterization", but the gap is closed by the paper's own Theorem 5.1 (threshold_tight). Impact. A remark, not a theorem; the paper's feasible region is untouched, and the true picture is sharper than the remark says. Details. If θ ≤ Δ/k, Theorem 5.2 applies with k, and if θ > Δ/(k+1), Theorem 5.1 applies with k + 1 instead of k. So on every band Δ/(k+1) < θ ≤ Δ/k the threshold is exactly 1 − h/(k+1) (up to the large-n caveat above). ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.1 (cycle construction needs many nodes): "for any φ ∈ (1/2, 1) … there is a Δ_sync-synchronous arrival profile" with a φ-majority cycle is false for a fixed n and φ > 1 − 1/n (theorem_3_1_fixed_n_false): every vote edge then needs all n nodes, and no node can receive the transactions of a cycle in strictly increasing order, so no profile has such a cycle. The proof idea picks k > 1/(1 − φ) groups, so the intended reading lets the profile choose n ≥ 1/(1 − φ); under that reading the theorem holds (for any φ < 1, even with all nodes honest; theorem_3_1). Theorem 5.1 needs n ≥ 1; with n = 0 every pair is an edge. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A finite node type (n nodes) with an honest finset H; the rest are Byzantine. The honest fraction h is linked by |H| = h·n. A profile ts : Node → Tx → ℝ gives every node's reported timestamp for every transaction. Byzantine timestamps are arbitrary. Δ-synchrony: honest timestamps of each transaction differ by at most Δ. Every honest node receives every transaction of the profile. There is no clock skew; timestamps are real times. The three convergence theorems (interleaving, parallel with update-only-on-change, distributed with bounded staleness) hold and are formalized after local proof repairs, and so are Theorem 2's necessity examples; strong fairness is not needed in Theorem 4.1: plain fairness is enough. Two applications in the full version's Section 6, for stable marriage and shortest paths, which the abstract advertises, do not satisfy the theorems' hypotheses: Algorithm 5 (lock-free Gale–Shapley) is not monotone, although the paper says it is, and Algorithm 7 (Bellman–Ford with levels) has no common fixed point at all. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Full version §6.1 ("Algorithm 5 is inflationary and monotone") Algorithm 5 (lock-free Gale–Shapley) is not monotone: with two men who both rank w₀ first, G = (1,1) ≤ H = (1,2) but f₀(G) = (2,1) ≰ (1,2) = f₀(H) (Apps.alg5_not_monotone). Impact. The derivations "from Theorem 3 / Theorem 4 it follows that Algorithm 5 yields the man-optimal stable marriage" are invalid, and no replacement is proved, but the conclusion itself seems true. Details. Let both men rank w₀ first and w₁ second, and let w₀ prefer m₁. In G = (1,1) both propose to w₀; in H = (1,2) m₁ has moved on to w₁. Then f₀(G) = (2,1): m₀ is rejected because m₁ is at w₀. But f₀(H) = (1,2), because nobody w₀ prefers is at w₀. The test "mpref[j][G[j]] = w" looks at where j proposes now, which is not monotone in G[j]. A monotone test would ask whether j has ever proposed to w. We model-checked an over-approximation that covers the interleaving, parallel and stale-view executions: exhaustively for n ≤ 3, and for 300 random profiles with n = 4. Every reachable common fixed point was the man-optimal matching (scripts/alg5_modelcheck.py). That is evidence, not a proof. ❌ Full version §6.2 (Algorithm 7, Bellman–Ford with levels, as an instance of Corollary 4.2) Algorithm 7 has no common fixed point at all, whatever the weights and the relaxation rule, and its functions are not monotone (Apps.alg7_no_common_fixed_point, Apps.alg7_not_monotone). Impact. "From Corollary 4.2, it follows that Algorithm 7 converges to the cost of the shortest paths" has no basis. The distance components may still converge; we did not check. Details. Its fᵢ increments G[i].level whenever no vertex lags behind i. So the vertex of minimal level always changes, and no state is a common fixed point. The level component is unbounded, so the lattice is not finite either. Non-monotonicity: take one edge 0 → 1 of weight 1, G = ((0,1),(5,1)) ⊑ H = ((0,1),(5,2)). Theorem 4.1 is different: with i-local functions its commit is a join of admissible states, so it does stay inside any join-closed L (distCommit_mem). Corollaries 4.1 and 4.2 say "fᵢ : L′ → L′ monotone and deflationary". They mean deflationary on L, that is, inflationary on L′. Impact. Statement true; repaired (theorem_3_1). Repair. A round that changes nothing has no writes at all (Lemma 3.2(3)), so every read returns the committed value. 🔧 Theorem 3.1 (parallel convergence, leastness step) The proof's "all writes in round t are ≤ Y and so X ≤ Y" is circular as stated, since the writes depend on what was read in the same round. Impact. Statement true; repaired (RoundExec.commit_le, theorem_3_1). Repair. Impact. Statement true; repaired, and then strong fairness is unnecessary: plain fairness suffices (theorem_4_1_fair). Repair. Take a round after U + T, so that every coordinate of the view dates from after stabilization. Any round t ≥ U + T with i ∈ S_t works. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic functions, no failures, no randomness. The schedule is arbitrary, subject to fairness: every index infinitely often. Strong fairness (StronglyFair τ, Definition 6) is also defined. Interleaving (§2): G (t+1) = f (σ t) (G t) on any finite poset with ⊥. The general-start version works on any poset without infinite ascending chains. Parallel (§3): states are (k : κ) → β k, a finite product of finite posets (the paper: {0,…,m}ⁿ). A round (RoundExec) is given by each active process's read vector and the instant its reads end. A read returns the committed value or the value of any write, in this round, by a process whose reads ended earlier. This causality is implied by the paper's real-time description; without it, values can appear out of thin air (acausal_round_breaks_leastness). A process writes exactly the coordinates whose computed value differs from the read one (update-only-on-change), and every written coordinate commits the value of some write. This allows every read and commit behaviour the paper allows, and more. The naive rule (write everything) is the same structure with another write policy. Distributed (§4): process i owns coordinate i. The view V t i has the current own coordinate, and every other coordinate is G s j for some t − T ≤ s ≤ t (bounded staleness). Global certification via perfect hashing — PODC 2024 Nicolas Bousquet, Laurent Feuilloley, Sébastien Zeitoun. Brief Announcement: Global certification via perfect hashing. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662781. Formalized version: HAL hal-04467834v2 (same text as the proceedings brief announcement). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✏️ Slip. Theorem 4 (homomorphism to H with O(n log n' + log log M) bits) and Theorem 3 (bipartiteness with O(n + log log M) bits) are proved, with explicit constant 10, uniformly in H and M, so Conjecture 1 of Feuilloley–Hirvonen is indeed false. The only mistakes are the implied assumption M(n) ≥ n, degenerate cases, and the words "has size" in the cited Theorem 7, which should say "at most". Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorems 3 and 4, implied assumption M(n) ≥ n: the definition of a scheme asks that G satisfies P iff for every identifier assignment some certificate is accepted. If M(n) < n, no injective identifier assignment into {0,…,M(n)−1} exists, so the right-hand side holds trivially and every n-vertex graph would have to satisfy P. For example, with M(3) < 3 the triangle would have to be bipartite, and no scheme for bipartiteness exists at all, of any size (theorem_3_false_of_small_range). Every reader makes this assumption (identifiers must exist); we assume M(n) ≥ n too, and then both theorems hold. Theorem 7 (perfect hash families, cited from Mehlhorn), degenerate parameters: the claimed (k, ℓ)-perfect hash family "which has size ⌈k e^k log ℓ⌉" (for all k ≤ ℓ) does not exist for k = ℓ = 1: the bound is ⌈e · log 1⌉ = 0 in any base, but the empty family is not perfect for S = {0} (theorem_7_false_l_one). The case k = 0 < ℓ is just as degenerate: no function into the empty set exists. Theorem 7, "has size": read as "exactly this size" it fails already for k = ℓ = 2: the bound is ⌈2e² ln 2⌉ = 11 (15 with log₂), but there are only 4 functions {0,1} → {0,1} (theorem_7_exact_size_false). The paper uses the result only as an upper bound. We prove the intended statement: size at most ⌈k e^k ln ℓ⌉ for 1 ≤ k ≤ ℓ, ℓ ≥ 2 (hence also with log₂), by the counting argument (theorem_7); it gives Theorems 3 and 4. The trivial family {id} covers n = M(n) (using n ≤ M(n)). Proof of Theorem 4, size count: the O(n) bits for h are absorbed into O(n log n'), which needs n' ≥ 2; for n' ≤ 1 a trivial 0-bit scheme is used instead (isGlobalScheme_small). Typos The proof in Section 3 is labelled "Proof of Theorem 3" but proves Theorem 4. In Theorem 4, n' = |V(H')| should be |V(H)|. The verifier "reads n in the global certificate", but the certificate is a fixed-length bit string, so n must be written in a self-delimiting way. This is not discussed; unary n costs n + 1 = O(n) bits, which we use. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Global certification exactly as in Section 2 (Model.lean). The graphs are finite simple graphs on any Fintype V, with n = |V|. Identifiers are given by an injective Id : V → ℕ with values < M(n). Node u sees Id u, the set Id '' N(u) of its neighbours' identifiers, and the global certificate. The verifier is an arbitrary predicate (no computability, as in the paper). A scheme of size s and range M satisfies P V G ↔ ∀ Id, ∃ c < 2^{s(n)}, every node accepts (IsGlobalScheme). Certificates of s(n) bits are numbers c < 2^{s(n)}. This fixes the paper's "set C of size 2^{s(n)}" to {0,…,2^{s(n)}−1} for every n, so the verifier gets no information about n from the certificate for free. This is stronger than the paper's definition, where C may depend on n arbitrarily. IsGlobalScheme.toAbstract / theorem_4_paper_def give the paper's literal definition. There is no distributed execution to model: verification is one local predicate per node (radius 1). There are no failures and no randomness. The perfect hash family exists by a counting argument; the verifier picks it by choice. The scheme (Scheme.lean) is the paper's: certificate 1ⁿ0 · idx · code, with n in unary, idx the index of a hash function in the (n, M(n)) family, and code < n'^n the list L in base n'. A node accepts iff its colour L[h(Id u)] is a vertex of H adjacent to L[h(Id v)] for every neighbour v. Soundness holds for any labelling, even a non-injective one (sound): as the paper observes, perfection of h is not checked. Main results in Lean. One concrete claim in §7 about Example 1 is false: that every protocol meeting the constraint μ(φ_both | fire_A) ≥ 0.99 makes Alice believe φ_both with degree ≥ 0.9 with probability ≥ 0.9 when she fires, which fails as soon as Alice fires as a mixed action. Nothing depends on it, and it holds for Alice's belief that Bob fires, which keeps the example's message. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ §7 (claim about Example 1) The claim that every protocol with μ(φ_both | fire_A) ≥ 0.99 makes Alice's belief in φ_both reach 0.9 with probability ≥ 0.9 when she fires is false as soon as Alice fires as a mixed action: in our counterexample that probability is 0 (Example1.Mixed.section7_claim_false). Impact. The claim illustrates the results of §7 and no numbered result uses it. With φ_both replaced by "Bob fires" (the two constraints coincide), the claim holds in every protocol-generated system (JointProtocol.section7_claim_fireB); for φ_both itself it stays false. Details. §7 says: "Corollary 7.2 implies that in every protocol that satisfies this constraint [μ(φ_both | fire_A) ≥ 0.99], the probability that Alice's degree of belief that both are firing together when it decides to fire meets or exceeds 0.9 is at least 0.9" (emphasis in the paper). Corollary 7.2 needs φ_both to be local-state independent of fire_A, and that fails as soon as Alice fires as a mixed action. Counterexample (the Spec of Example 1 holds): if go = 1, Alice sends two messages in round 1 and fires at time 1 with probability 1/2; Bob fires at time 1 iff he received one of them. Then μ(φ_both | fire_A) = 0.99. But when Alice fires she does not yet know her coin (§2.2: "when the agent decides on the mixed step she does not know which of the actions … will actually be performed"), so β_A(φ_both) = 0.5 · 0.99 = 0.495. So the belief reaches 0.9 with probability 0, not ≥ 0.9. This is general: in every protocol-generated pps, β_i(φ ∧ does_i(α)) ≤ P_i(ℓ_i)(α), the probability of choosing α (JointProtocol.belief_and_does_le, cprob_belief_and_does_eq_zero). This is not a typo: the sentence names φ_both, the very fact of the constraint it applies Corollary 7.2 to, and it stresses "every protocol", while mixed actions are part of the paper's model and exactly the case §§4 and 6 warn about. Repair. The fire_B version is true in every protocol-generated system, because "j performs β" is local-state independent of every action of i ≠ j (JointProtocol.section7_claim_fireB). The paper's Lemma 4.3 does not cover this case: "Bob fires" is not past-based. ✏️ Slips Abstract: it states that the expected belief when acting equals the probability that φ holds when acting, and that a threshold 1 − ε² forces belief ≥ 1 − ε with probability ≥ 1 − ε, without the hypothesis of local-state independence, without which both are false (Fig1.theorem_6_2_needs_independence): in Figure 1 with φ = does_i(α), μ(φ@α | α) = 1 but E(β_i(φ)@α | α) = 1/2, and the belief never reaches 1. The contribution list in §1 and the theorems in the body carry the hypothesis. Lemma 4.3(b): in an arbitrary tree pps (§2.1), past-based facts need not be local-state independent, so the lemma silently needs a protocol-generated system with observable termination, and its proof is a sketch. Example: two initial states that i cannot tell apart, and i performs α in exactly one of them. The proof uses "the probability that i performs α is the same at all points with local state ℓ_i". This needs a pps generated by a joint protocol in which all participants choose independently, and runs that cannot end at different times while i has the same local state. We prove the lemma for protocol-generated systems with a fixed horizon via a Markov-property argument. It also holds for facts that additionally depend on the other agents' current actions (JointProtocol.lemma_4_3b, JointProtocol.lsi_of_indepOwnAction). Typos The proof of Theorem 6.2 cites "Theorem 4.1" for Definition 4.1, and so does the remark after Theorem 4.2. In the proof of Theorem 7.1, β_i(φ)@α | α [r] should be β_i(φ)@α [r]. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Abstract pps (PPS, Basic.lean). Finitely many runs with positive prior probabilities summing to 1, a common length per run, and the local state r_i(t) of every agent at every point, under synchrony (a local state determines the time). Facts are arbitrary sets of points, and an action is given by its fact does_i(α). Beliefs, φ@ℓ, φ@α, proper actions, β_i(φ)@α (0 off R_α), local-state independence and expected belief follow Definitions 3.1–6.1 literally. Every tree pps of §2.1 gives such a structure. Conversely, every such structure is a tree pps in which the environment's initial state fixes the run. So §§4–7 are proved in exactly the paper's generality, and slightly more: the action may be any fact. Protocol-generated pps (JointProtocol, Protocol.lean), used for Lemma 4.3(b) and §7. A synchronous system: an initial distribution over global states, participants (agents and the environment) with local states (t, loc p g), a probabilistic protocol per participant, and independent choices in every round. There is a deterministic transition function and a fixed number N of rounds. Runs are the action sequences of positive probability; this matches the paper's assumption that the environment records the history. There are no failures and no adversary: the adversary is fixed, as in §2. Examples are concrete abstract pps's: Figure 1, T̂ of Figure 2, FS, and the mixed variant. Main results in Lean. Girth Approximations in the CONGEST Model — PODC 2026 Shiri Chechik, Gur Lifshitz, Doron Mukhtar. Girth Approximations in the CONGEST Model. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815933. Formalized version: arXiv:2603.27601v1, §6 (lower bounds). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The lower bounds of §6 hold: Theorem 6.1 and its asymptotic form ((3 − ε)-approximation needs Ω̃(n^{3/5}) rounds, unconditionally) and Theorem 6.2 under the Erdős–Simonovits hypothesis, for directed and for undirected weighted graphs, deterministic and randomized, on networks of diameter O(log n). They need one corrected constant in Claim 6.2(1) and a few-line repair of the proof of Claim 6.2(2). Only §6 was checked: the upper bounds of §§3–5, the paper's algorithmic results, were not examined. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Claim 6.2(1) (weighted girth for intersecting inputs) The claim says the weighted girth equals 2q/ε · (1 + ε) = 2q + 2q/ε, but each pipe r_1 → … → r_q has only q − 1 edges, so the girth is 2(q − 1) + 2q/ε, 2 less than claimed (claim_6_2_value_lt). Impact. The reduction only needs girth ≤ 2q/ε · (1 + ε), which still holds, so Theorem 6.2 is unaffected. Details. The proof counts 2q pipe edges of weight 1. The directed Claim 6.1 counts this correctly. The cycle through a shared edge therefore weighs 2(q − 1) + 2q/ε, so the girth is strictly below the stated value. Repair. We prove the corrected upper bound and that the stated value is strictly too large. (uGraph_mwc_of_inter, claim_6_2_value_lt) ✏️ Slips §6, "Before presenting …": the paper attributes ex(n, C_{<2k}) = O(n^{1+1/k}) to Bondy–Simonovits and calls it conjecturally tight. For graphs with no cycle shorter than 2k (girth ≥ 2k) the right exponent is 1 + 1/(k−1). The cited bound is for C_{2k} alone. For k = 3, girth-6 bipartite graphs with Ω(n^{3/2}) edges exist, so O(n^{4/3}) is false. The rest of §6 uses the correct exponent (z(n^{2/5}, C_{<6}) = Θ(n^{3/5}), m = Θ(a^{1+1/(k−1)})), and "known for k ∈ {3, 4, 6}" matches the corrected exponent. (ex_bound_misquoted) Typos None of these affects a result. "The total number of vertices is n^{2/5} · n^{3/5} = n" (and n = 2aq in §6.2) ignores the about 2q tree vertices. Our parameter choice accounts for every vertex and pads to exactly n. The output convention ("each node computes an approximation") and the randomized communication bound (public coins are needed, since middle pipe nodes are simulated by both players) are left implicit. See the model below. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Claim 6.2(2) (weighted disjoint case) The proof projects a minimum cycle onto H and says this "yields a cycle in H", which fails for undirected graphs: a cycle may enter the pipe of l at both ends (two Alice edges at l_1, two Bob edges at l_q), so the projection visits l twice. Impact. Statement true; repaired for every k (uGraph_mwc_of_disj, egirth_le_card_of_stutter). Details. In general the projection is only a closed trail in H (no repeated edges, because the inputs are disjoint), not a cycle. The proof then concludes there are at least 6 input edges. The case of a cycle with no input edge at all (inside one pipe) also has to be excluded. Repair. A non-empty closed trail is at least as long as the girth. We prove the claim, for every k, with this argument. (uGraph_mwc_of_disj, egirth_le_card_of_stutter) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Synchronous deterministic CONGEST (Cslib.Congest.Algorithm) on an arbitrary node type V with |V| = n. Node names are the IDs. Messages have B bits per edge, direction and round. There are no failures. The network is the underlying undirected unweighted graph. Node v's input is its incident arcs with their directions (WDigraph.view), or its incident edges with their weights (WGraph.view). Girth (mwc) is the minimum weight (directed: length) of a simple cycle, ∞ if there is none. These are the definitions of the companion formalization Papers/PODC2024/MinWeightCycleCongest. Output convention ApproxOutput, the weakest one: every node outputs none or an estimate, at least one node outputs, and every estimate lies in [girth, α · girth]. Algorithms only have to be correct on unweighted digraphs (directed case) or on weighted graphs with positive integer weights in {1, …, Wm}, Wm ≥ kMn (undirected case), of diameter ≤ 2 log₂ n + 4. So the theorems also cover weighted directed algorithms and the small-diameter claim. Randomized algorithms give each node a private random string. Since nodes in the middle are simulated by both Alice and Bob, the simulation yields a public-coin protocol. The randomized bounds are therefore conditional on the public-coin randomized lower bound for set disjointness (Razborov / Kalyanasundaram–Schnitger), which enters as the hypothesis PubRandDisjLB δ κ. That hypothesis quantifies over nonempty finite coin spaces with κ : ℝ. It is not formalized. H is any bipartite graph of girth ≥ 2k; the paper takes an extremal one. The shortcut tree is a balanced binary (segment) tree of depth d ≥ log₂ q. Pendant padding vertices on the root make the node count exactly n. Theorem 6.2's hypothesis DenseHighGirth k is the bipartite form of the Erdős–Simonovits conjecture: for every a there is a bipartite graph with sides of size a, girth ≥ 2k and ≥ c · a^{1+1/(k−1)} edges. We prove it for k = 3 with the points–lines incidence graph of the affine plane over ZMod p and Bertrand's postulate. The cases k = 4, 6 (generalized polygons) are not formalized. Explicit bounds. Fixed parameters: q ≤ 2T + 1 or |E(H)| ≤ 2T(d + 1)B + 2 (randomized: κ|E(H)| ≤ …). Asymptotic: C · n^{k/(2k−1)} ≤ (T + 1)(B + 1)(log₂ n + 2), i.e. T = Ω(n^{k/(2k−1)} / (B log n)). The black-box communication lower bound is correct here, but not via a fixed cut (checked, not a mistake). The paper invokes Das Sarma et al. (Lemma 4.1 of [9]) "on the underlying undirected communication network consisting of the pipes and the shortcut tree". This network is not literally theirs: the inputs are edges inside layers 1 and q. Every fixed cut separating Alice's input nodes from Bob's cuts all 2a pipes, so a fixed-cut simulation only gives T = Ω(m / (aB)) = Ω(√a / B). We formalized the moving-cut simulation in general and checked it for this network. Alice's simulated set shrinks by one column per round, and per round only one arc per tree level crosses into each shrinking set, so T rounds cost 2T(⌈log₂ q⌉ + 1)B + 2 bits as long as 2T + 2 ≤ q. The black box is therefore correct here. (MovingCutFamily.simulation, gadgetFamily, card_toA_le) Main results in Lean.
