It does not matter how you define LCLs — PODC 2026 Antonio Cruciani, Avinandan Das, Alesya Raevskaya, Jukka Suomela. Brief Announcement: It Does Not Matter How You Define Locally Checkable Labelings. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815923. Formalized version: the full version arXiv:2602.18188v1 (40 pages). Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. Theorem 5.1, the graph-theoretic key of the reduction from LCLs to PN-checkable problems, is false as stated, and the version we prove needs edge-consistency for all pairs of vertices, which a PN-view verifier cannot enforce. So the main Theorem 7.1, which relies on it through Lemmas 5.4 and 5.8, is unestablished, though not refuted: a local repair with a larger r_D is plausible but not proved. Section 6 (PN-checkable → RE formalism, Lemmas 6.2–6.6) is correct up to slips. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 5.1 (graph-theoretic key of the reduction to PN-checkable problems; also Lemma 5.13 and Corollaries 5.11, 5.14, 5.16; used by Lemma 5.4, hence Lemma 5.8 and Theorem 7.1) The hypothesis compares colours only with the centre's colour inside an r-gball, but the conclusion claims all of gball_r(v) is injectively coloured, and two vertices of the gball at gadgeted distance up to 2r can share a colour: in the gadgeted K_{3,3} with r = 1, two original vertices of the same side may (theorem_5_1_false). Impact. Lemma 5.4 (soundness of the lift B → D) invokes the false theorem, so Lemma 5.8 and the main Theorem 7.1 inherit the gap and are unestablished, though not refuted. Theorem 5.1 becomes true once edge-consistency is required for all pairs of vertices; we prove that repaired version in full, with the paper's proof strategy (theorem_5_1_repaired). But in the application (Lemma 5.4) consistency is only checked inside PN-views of radius r_D. We see no reason to doubt that these results hold with the repaired theorem and a larger r_D, but this part is not formalized. Details. Condition 2 ("edge-consistent in every r-gball") requires: for every edge {v,u} and every v' ∈ gball_r(v) with χ(v') = χ(v), v' has a neighbour of colour χ(u). The hypothesis never compares a pair at gadgeted distance up to 2r. Counterexample: base graph K_{3,3}, edges expanded into 1, …, 9 A-gadgets (an injective, hence distance-2r, edge colouring), r = 1. Take an injective colouring and give the two original vertices 0 and 1 the same colour. They are at distance 2 in K_{3,3}, so at gadgeted distance 2 > r and graph distance > 2. Hence conditions 1 and 2 hold. Both lie in the 1-gball of the original vertex 3. (theorem_5_1_false) The paper's proof establishes only that the colour of the centre v and of its outer neighbours is unique in gball_r(v) (Corollary 5.14, Lemma 5.13). Corollary 5.16 then concludes uniqueness for every pair, which does not follow. Even those partial claims fail at the boundary of the gball: Lemma 5.13 is false as stated: in the gadgeted K_{3,3} with r = 1, the original vertex 1 may get the colour of the outer vertex v of the expanded edge {0,3} next to 3 (lemma_5_13_false). The idea is the same: 1 ∈ gball_1(3), but 1 and v are at gadgeted distance 3/2 > 1, so the hypothesis never compares them. The lemma is a step of the paper's proof of Theorem 5.1, whose repaired version we prove separately. Corollary 5.14 fails too, by a SAT experiment that is not Lean-checked: in the gadgeted K_4 with lengths 1, …, 6 and r = 1, a SAT search found a colouring satisfying conditions 1 and 2 in which two adjacent original vertices get the same colour. The proof of 5.14 applies Lemma 5.13 to a vertex u' that may lie outside gball_r(v). Nothing here rests on this experiment. Repair. If edge-consistency holds for all pairs of vertices, then every gball_r(v) is injectively coloured. This uses x as a distance-2r edge colouring with positive lengths; simplicity and 3-regularity are not needed (theorem_5_1_repaired). The proof follows the paper's ideas, made precise: An original vertex never shares a colour with a vertex in a triangle (Lemma 5.2/5.9; the Figure 2 case analysis). Colours propagate rigidly along expanded edges, so matched edges have equal length (Lemmas 5.12–5.13). The distance-2r edge colouring then forces two equally coloured vertices of a gball onto the same expanded edge, read in opposite directions. That is impossible: at the middle of the edge, two vertices at distance ≤ 2 would get the same colour. This does not save the local form of the theorem: Problem D would need a view radius large enough to cover every pair the argument compares; see differencies.md. ✏️ Slips Gadgeting (Section 5.1): x : E(G) → ℕ allows length 0, which the gadget construction cannot handle; we require positive lengths. Lemma 6.2 silently needs every view of C_D to have a root with 3 children. This holds for PN-views of 3-regular graphs. Proof of Lemma 6.4: (T(v→u)) ≅ (T(v∖u)) should read (T(u∖v)). Typos The remark "only original vertices are non-triangle vertices" is attributed to Lemma 5.2, but it holds by construction. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. No distributed model is formalized. The checked results are about problem definitions, graphs and colourings. Round complexities, symmetry breaking ♢(M) and the simulations of Section 3 are not modelled. Section 5: a base graph is given by an edge type with endpoint maps (Base), so multigraphs are allowed and edges have an orientation that is used only to lay out the chain. len is the paper's edge colouring x. gadget(G, x) is Base.graph on original vertices and chain positions gad e k, k < 6·len e. The paper's A-gadget vertices 1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 6 become positions 0, …, 5, so the chain is a path plus chords and reading it backwards is k ↦ 6L−1−k. Gadgeted distance uses doubled 0/1 weights. "Distance-k edge colouring" means line-graph distance ≤ k ⇒ different colours (the paper does not define it). Conditions 1 and 2 of Theorem 5.1 are IsDist2Coloring and IsEdgeConsistentIn r, taken literally. Our repaired hypothesis is IsEdgeConsistent. Section 6: PN-views up to isomorphism are canonical forms View L k (label plus multiset of child views). pnView G σ r v is the tree of non-backtracking walks. An RE problem is a pair of multiset constraints on the half-edge labels around a node and along an edge, on a 3-regular simple graph. Outcomes are PMFs over labellings. MultiKrum and an optimal notion of robustness — PODC 2026 Gilles Bareilles, Wassim Bouaziz, Julien Fageot, El Mahdi El Mhamdi. Brief Announcement: Byzantine Machine Learning, MultiKrum and an Optimal Notion of Robustness. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815914. Formalized version: arXiv 2602.03899 v1 (full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All bounds hold: MultiKrum is robust with the stated upper bound (Theorems 1, 5, 6), the lower bounds hold for n ≥ 2 (Proposition 1, Theorems 3, 4, Proposition B.1), and so does the asymptotics of the transition point (Theorem 2). The proofs of Theorem 2 and Proposition B.1 and the score values in Theorem 4 need local changes only. Display (1) of Theorem 1 prints ≥ for the upper bound, and the lower bounds fail for n = 1 under the paper's own convention 0/0 = −∞; both are slips. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 1, display (1) reads κ⋆_m ≥ (n−f)/(n−2f)·min((√2+1)², κ^>_2(m)), which is false for f = 0, m = n (theorem_1_as_written_false): MultiKrum is then the plain mean, so κ⋆ ≤ 0, while the right-hand side is min((√2+1)², 1) = 1. The theorem is announced as an upper bound and its proof proves ≤. We prove that, together with "MultiKrum is robust" (theorem_1). Proposition 1, Theorem 3 (odd n), Theorem 4 for n = 1: with the paper's own convention 0/0 = −∞, Krum on a single input is robust with κ⋆ = −∞, so these lower bounds, which all equal 0 for n = 1 (Proposition 1: κ⋆ ≥ f/(n−2f)), fail there (kappaStar_eq_bot_of_n_eq_one). They hold for n ≥ 2. Theorem 3 states no hypotheses. We prove it under Definition 2's standing assumption f ≤ n/2 (for n = 2f, κ⋆ = +∞, while the printed score s(0) is negative). FEAT as printed does not achieve what Theorem 6.6 claims (comparator-based γ-Batch-Order-Fairness), and Theorem 6.4 and Lemma 6.3 fail with it: the paper's score counts only honest replicas, and a 7-replica run with f = 2 makes FEAT output [z, m] although cmp_T(z, m) = False. If the score counts all replicas, Lemma 6.3 and Theorems 6.4 and 6.6 hold, and we prove them; Theorem 4.4 (ACC suffices) and the Ω(|T| log |T|) lower bound (Theorem 4.5, Corollary 4.6) are correct, and we prove the lower bound in a stronger form. The matching O(|T| log |T|) upper bound (Theorem 6.7, Corollary 6.8) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Lemma 6.3, Theorems 6.4 and 6.6 (score counts only honest replicas) With score(T) counting only honest replicas (§5.1), a 7-replica run with f = 2 makes FEAT output [z, m] although cmp_T(z, m) = False, so Lemma 6.3 and Theorems 6.4 and 6.6 (FEAT achieves comparator-based γ-Batch-Order-Fairness) are false (lemma_6_3_false, theorem_6_4_false, theorem_6_6_false). Impact. The output of the protocol as defined is not consistent with its own comparator. Counting all replicas in the score, a one-word change to the definition, restores all three statements. Details. §5.1 defines score(T) as the number of honest replicas whose committed local orderings include T, and replicas cannot know which replicas are honest, so this score cannot be computed by the protocol. Case 2 of the proof of Lemma 6.3 reasons as follows: z is solid and m is blank, so W(z, m) > τ_dec = τ_shaded > W(m, z). The second inequality needs W(m, z) ≤ score(m). But W(m, z) counts all committed orderings, including the Byzantine ones. Here is a counterexample with n = 7, f = 2, γ = 1 (so n > (2γ+1)f/(2γ−1) = 6), τ_dec = 5/2 and τ_solid = 5: Honest replicas 0 and 1 receive m, z, and honest replicas 2, 3 and 4 receive z, m. In round 1, replicas 0 and 1 and both Byzantine replicas commit [m, z], and replicas 2, 3, 4 commit [z]. So z is solid (honest score 5) and m is blank (honest score 2). Also W₁(m, z) = 4 > W₁(z, m) = 3 ≥ τ_dec, so the pair is decided in round 1: cmp_T(z, m) = False. FEAT finalizes FO₁ = [z]. In round 2, replicas 2, 3 and 4 commit m. Now m is newly solid, so RO₂ = [m] and FEAT outputs FO₂ = [z, m]. FEAT never compares this pair. The output violates ACC and the linear-batch-partition clause of Definition 4.1: the batches are {z} and {m}, z comes first, but cmp_T(z, m) = False. All system-model assumptions hold. Rounds after 2 commit nothing new (empty fragments), so FO₂ is the final ordering. The γ-precedence clause is not violated in this run. What fails is the claim that FO is consistent with FEAT's own comparator, and that claim is exactly what Theorems 6.4 and 6.6 state. Repair. If the score counts all replicas, the proof goes through: W(m, z) ≤ score(m) < τ_shaded. On the same run, FEAT then inserts both transactions in round 1 and outputs [m, z]. (lemma_6_3_false, theorem_6_4_false, theorem_6_6_false; repaired: Setup.lemma_6_3, Setup.theorem_6_4, Setup.theorem_6_6, contrast run cex_scoreAll_FO1) The repair uses the "loose" reading of W that the paper's proof uses; see Not formalized below. 🔧 Lemma 6.3, Case 1 Case 1 says that the head of TailList_{r−1} immediately followed z in Merged_{r−1}, which fails when round r−1 finalized nothing (ℓ = 0): then z was finalized earlier. Impact. The (repaired) statement is true; an invariant over rounds closes the gap: FO ++ TailList satisfies ACC and the last finalized transaction is solid (Setup.inv_step). ✏️ Slips Algorithm 3: after the loop while i ≤ |TailList| and j ≤ |RO_r|, the tests if i = |TailList| and else if j = |RO_r| are both false (the exhausted index is one past the end), so the remaining suffix is never appended. The prose (steps (1) and (2)) is correct, and we model the prose (List.merge). Algorithm 1 inserts the transactions that are "newly solid" or "newly shaded". Read literally, a transaction that turns from shaded to solid would be inserted twice. The prose says "newly non-blank". Rule (4) of pcmp says "both weights exceed the threshold". It should be ≥, as in rules (2) and (3). Typos The bound W(T_j, T_i) ≤ (1−γ)(n−f) + f in Lemma 6.5 implicitly takes exactly n − f honest replicas. It remains true with more honest replicas: n − γ|H| ≤ n − γ(n − f). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. n = |R| replicas: the honest set H and at most f Byzantine replicas. Every round has its own "committed local ordering up to round r" L r i, which only grows. Honest committed orderings are prefixes of the receive orders (consensus property (3)). Every transaction received by an honest replica is eventually committed by all honest replicas (property (4)). Byzantine orderings are arbitrary, and fragments may be empty. Synchrony and the consensus layer are abstracted into this round-indexed data, as the paper does. W_r(a, b) counts orderings that contain a and do not have b before it. pcmp^(r) implements rules (1)–(4) with W ≥ τ_dec written as n − f ≤ 2W. cmp_T takes the value of pcmp at the first round where it is defined. A pair that is never decided defaults to the tie-break hash; under the assumptions this never happens for pairs that matter. FEAT (Setup.run) answers every comparison with cmp_T. In the protocol, ⊥ only delays an action (deferral or waiting), and every defined answer equals cmp_T. So the only effect of timing is the order in which insertions succeed. We therefore quantify over every insertion order of the newly non-blank transactions (InsOK), and over every in-order-preserving rebalancing (AVL rotations). The score is a parameter: scoreHonest is the paper's, scoreAll is the repair. Definition 4.1 is stated for a finite list FO, with batches the strongly connected components of the comparator graph on its elements. "At least a γ-fraction of honest replicas receive a before b" is GammaPrec γ. Theorem 6.6 is proved for every round's FO_r. Lower bound: a deterministic comparison-based algorithm is a binary decision tree (Cslib.DecisionTree) over queries (i, j) of input positions. We count queries, and the expectation is over a uniformly random arrival order. Main results in Lean. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815916. Formalized version: arXiv:2605.17961v1. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The proof bounds Pr(|J| < (1−ε)n) for one k-subset by a Chernoff bound around the mean, which is e^{−ε²(1−ε/2)n/8}. It then takes a union bound over the at most 2^{2m} ≤ 2^{2cn} subsets, with c = ε³/8. (The displayed inequality also silently drops the /2 of the exponent; even then it needs ε < 0.84.) Repair. Our proof uses only second moments. Chebyshev shows that each element is bad with probability a ≤ 2/(ε²B) ≤ ε/288. The bad events are independent across elements. So the probability that ⌊εn⌋+1 elements are bad is at most C(n,t)a^t ≤ (e a/ε)^t, which beats 2^{2cn} for every ε. The formalization Model. Network. n nodes Fin n and M abstract tasks. The model is synchronous and deterministic. A task takes R rounds and is completed iff its executor does not crash during them (executor-safe, idempotent). At most αn crashes over the whole execution, α ∈ [0,1). Algorithm 1 (Algorithm.lean), iteration-level model. An iteration is a task phase of 2BR rounds plus one broadcast round of the bits s_{i,v}, so it costs 2BR + 1 rounds. Adversary. It is adaptive and arbitrary. For every node it fixes: the iteration in which the node crashes; whether the node survived that iteration's task phase; which nodes receive its last broadcast bit (any subset, as in the paper's crash model). Uniform Content-Oblivious Leader Election on Eulerian Graphs — PODC 2026 Fabian Frei, Ran Gelles, Ahmed Ghazy, Alexandre Nolin. Brief Announcement: Toward Uniform Content-Oblivious Leader Election on General Graphs. PODC 2026. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815949. Formalized version: the 4-page brief announcement (no arXiv version). Numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The combinatorial core is correct: any port pairing of a graph with all degrees even induces a unique circuit decomposition (Lemma 2), re-pairing at a node merges distinct circuits into one (Lemma 4), the merging phases of Lemma 5 end, after at most log₂ n phases, in a single Eulerian circuit with a single leader, and the pulse arithmetic of Theorem 1 gives O(|E|·IDmax). Two steps of the Lemma 5 sketch each need one added rule: in a mutually selecting pair of circuits both merges must not be executed, and the OR protocol, which we verify on an asynchronous content-oblivious ring, must say how the leader's own input is used. The election as a pulse-level algorithm was not checked: Lemma 3 with its ring-election black box, the max-ID protocol and the synchronisation of merges are not formalized. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips The intro says the "maximum-ID node on the merged circuit becomes its new leader". It is the maximum among the merged leaders (the root of the merge tree; id_le_id_top_of_top_eq). This need not be the maximum-ID node of the circuit: in Lemma 3 a node may only relay passively on a circuit and then does not take part in its election. "Eulerian" is defined as all degrees even, but a disconnected graph cannot end with a single circuit, so Lemma 5 and Theorem 1 need connectivity, which we assume (lemma5). The max-ID step of Lemma 5 (bitwise ORs over "prefix-free" encodings) needs an order-preserving prefix-free code. Otherwise it returns the lexicographically largest code, not the largest ID. Not formalized. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 5, merging phases (mutually selecting circuits) The sketch lets every circuit merge into its adjacent circuit with the largest leader ID, so two circuits that select each other are merged twice, and the second re-pairing can split the merged circuit again (DoubleMerge.double_merge_splits). Impact. Statement true; repaired by letting the larger circuit of a mutually selecting pair not merge (phaseStep_spec, lemma5). Details. In the sketch a designated node of C re-pairs one pair of C with one pair of the selected circuit C'. Two circuits often select each other; for example, if only two circuits remain, each one's only neighbour is the other. The second re-pairing then acts on two pairs that by then lie on one circuit. Take K_{2,4} (x, y adjacent to 2, 3, 4, 5) with circuits C₁ = x2y3x and C₂ = x4y5x. Merging at x (the node designated by C₂) gives one Eulerian circuit. Merging at y as well (the node designated by C₁, re-pairing as in Lemma 4) gives two circuits again, x2y5x and x3y4x. Whether this happens depends on how the pairs are labelled, which the sketch leaves open ("w.l.o.g."). So the sketch does not show that the number of circuits halves, or even decreases. Repair. The circuit with the larger ID in a mutually selecting pair does not merge. Then the merge links form a forest, every link joins two different circuits, and each merged tree contains at least two old circuits and is led by its root, the largest ID in it. We prove that the number of circuits at least halves per phase, so there are at most log₂ n phases. (The protocol must then also tell C whether C' selected C; we do not formalize that.) (DoubleMerge.double_merge_splits; repaired: phaseStep_spec, lemma5) 🔧 Lemma 5, OR protocol (the leader's own input) The sketch does not say how the leader's own input enters the OR protocol, and if "the first node with input 1" excludes the initiating leader, the protocol outputs 0 when only the leader borders another circuit (OrProtocol.literal_wrong). Impact. Under-specified; the evident fix (the leader reflects if its own input is 1) is verified on every schedule (OrProtocol.orProc_final, orProc_totalSent_le). Details. The leader ℓ_C starts a clockwise pulse that "the first node with input 1 reflects"; if the pulse completes the cycle, the leader forwards it once more and every node outputs 0. Under the literal reading, for every ring size, all executions give output 0 when only the leader has input 1, and the algorithm would stop with several circuits. Repair. If its pulse completes the cycle and its own input is 1, the leader acts as the reflector. We verify the fixed protocol in the asynchronous content-oblivious ring model for every schedule: it terminates quiescently, every node outputs the OR, and at most 2|C| pulses are sent. Also, nodes with input 1 that come after the first reflector receive a counter-clockwise pulse first and must behave like nodes with input 0, which the paper's sentence "receive a counterclockwise pulse without a clockwise one" covers. DOI 10.1145/3796701.3815941. Formalized version: arXiv 2605.04699 v1; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. All the main results hold, and we prove them without assumptions: the separation theorem (Theorem 5: throughput 5/8 − ε is achievable for large n), the two results from the literature it uses, dependent rounding (Theorem 3) and the Chernoff bound under negative correlation (Theorem 4), and also Propositions 1–4, Lemma 1, Observations 1–4 and Theorem 6. The proofs of Theorem 5 and Proposition 1 need local repairs, and the problem box of Demand-Aware Weak Direct Throughput and Proposition 3 have typos with evident intent. The running times (Propositions 5, 6) and the NP-hardness result (Theorem 7) were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips The problem box of Demand-Aware Weak Direct Throughput asks whether "the direct throughput of G … is at least κ"; it should say "weak direct throughput" (defined in §1.1). Read literally, the problem coincides with Demand-Aware Direct Throughput, and Theorem 6 would then contradict Proposition 3 for n ≥ 2. The intent is clear from the name, §1.1, Observation 4 and the proof of Theorem 6. Proposition 3 constructs M_κ but says "(M, κ) is a no-instance"; it should be (M_κ, κ). Proof of Theorem 5: "Let ε = κ − 5/8 > 0" should be ε = 5/8 − κ (since κ < 5/8). "Hence b_ij < (2n−1)κ a_ij" fails when a_ij = 0 (then they are equal; this is harmless). "b_ij < min(a_ij, d_ij)" should read b_ij < d_ij. Numerical remark after Theorem 5: by the proof's own two conditions, κ = 0.6 needs n ≥ 26068, not 26000. The other three numbers (≈ 700, 2250, ≈ 27 million) check out. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 5 (non-integer number of variables in Theorem 4) For each row the proof applies Theorem 4 "with t = n + Y_i" variables (the n rounding variables plus Y_i = ∑_j (1 − b'_ij) constant ones of weight 1), but Y_i is not an integer in general. Impact. Statement true; local fix (line_bad_prob_le). Repair. Add n constant variables of weight 1 − b'_ij ∈ [0, 1] instead. The mean, δ and the bound e^{-2nε²/3} stay the same. (line_bad_prob_le) 🔧 Proposition 1 (arithmetic) In the displayed computation 5/6 − 5ε/12 − ε²/2 is set equal to 5/6 − 5ε/6 + ε − ε − ε²/2, which is false. Impact. Statement true; the final inequality < κ(1 − ε) still holds, because ε²/2 < 7ε/12 (proposition_1). 🔧 Proposition 1 (graphs with at most one self-loop) The graphs with ≤ 1 self-loop are dismissed with "cannot host (5/6)M_κ since 1 − ε > 2/3", which is not an argument. Impact. Statement true; we repair the case analysis (two_node_bounds_rel, proposition_1). Repair. We replace the graph-by-graph reasoning with two cut inequalities that hold for every flow on two nodes: D_ab ≤ A_ab and D_ab + D_aa + D_bb ≤ A_ab + A_aa + A_bb. Proposition 1, Proposition 4 (first part) and the M₂ example follow by arithmetic. (two_node_bounds_rel, proposition_1) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. A network on Fin n is a directed multigraph given by an ℕ-adjacency matrix A. It is (2n−1)-regular if all row and column sums are 2n − 1. Arcs have capacity 1/(2n−1); equivalently, as in the paper, capacity 1 with demand (2n−1)·θ·M. A flow is a finite family of non-empty paths (walks with at least one arc, so self-demand uses a self-loop or a closed walk) with non-negative amounts. It must serve exactly the demand of every ordered pair. "Throughput of G for M is at least κ" is rendered as "G hosts θM for some θ ≥ κ". The four problems are DAThroughput, DADirectThroughput, DAWeakThroughput and DAWeakDirectThroughput. Capacity semantics. The paper charges a path once per multigraph arc it uses. Constructions (yes-instances) use the stricter rule CanRoute: a path is charged once per traversal of the pair (u, v). No-instances are proved for the weaker rule CanRouteRel: a path through (u, v) is charged once. The paper's semantics lies between the two, so both kinds of results transfer to it. Direct routing is the same under all three rules. Randomness is used only in proofs. It lives on finite sample spaces: a distribution is a non-negative weight function with total 1 (FinDist). This is not a distributed-computing model: there are no processes, failures or adversaries. Main results in Lean. Simple and Local Independent Set Approximation — PODC 2018 Ravi B. Boppana, Magnús M. Halldórsson, Dror Rawitz. Brief Announcement: Simple and Local Independent Set Approximation. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212793. Formalized version: arXiv 1803.00786 v1 (full version; numbering follows it). Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Boppana's algorithm / the Caro–Wei bound achieves a tight (Δ+1)/2 ratio (Theorem 1), and no 1-round randomized algorithm does better (Theorem 4, whose proof needed a different pair of graphs). Theorems 3, 6 and 7 and Lemmas 2–4 also hold, and everything else is a slip, such as the wrongly rounded constant of Theorem 2. Theorem 5 was not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips Theorem 2 (ratio (d̄+2)/1.657 in terms of the average degree) is false as printed: K_{24000,10000} has α = 24000 but (d̄+2)/1.657·CaroWei ≈ 23999.2 (theorem2_false). The theorem claims α(G) ≤ (d̄+2)/1.657 · CaroWei(G) for every graph. The proof ends with (d̄+2)/(4(√2−1)) ≤ (d̄+2)/1.657, but 4(√2−1) = 1.65685… < 1.657, so the inequality goes the wrong way. Because the bound is asymptotically tight on bipartite graphs with regular sides and τ ≈ 1/√2 (the paper's own extremal family), the rounded constant really fails. The smallest complete bipartite counterexample is K_{13721,5683}. The statement with the proof's own constant 4(√2−1) in place of 1.657 holds (theorem2_corrected). Lemma 5 lacks Y > 0: as stated (a > b > 0, Z − Y ≥ X > 0) it is false, since a=2, b=1, X=1, Y=−100, Z=−50 gives a smaller value at t = 0 than at t = 1 (lemma5_false). The hypothesis holds at the only use, Y = w(opt) > 0; with it we prove the lemma (lemma5). Theorem 1 at Δ = 0: a ratio (0+1)/2 < 1 is impossible on edgeless graphs (theorem1_false_zero), and Theorem 3's ratio is undefined there. The theorem holds for every Δ ≥ 1 (theorem1). Theorem 6 takes the minimum over x ≤ 1, where the expression takes negative values (theorem6_min_unbounded). The minimum should be over 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, which we formalize. "For Δ = 2, … ρ ∼ 1.657" should be ≈ 1.686 = 1/0.593 (rho_two_gt). The arXiv abstract says Boppana's algorithm is "only a Δ-approximation" on weighted graphs. The correct ratio is Δ+1, as §3 and the PODC abstract state; it exceeds Δ on K_{Δ,Δ} with weights 1, Q > Δ (boppana_weighted_not_Delta). §3 writes E[w(B)] = Σ_{v∈B} …, which should be Σ_{v∈V}. Lemma 5 is applied with t = W/X, which is undefined when V′ = ∅. Typos Eqs. (8) and (11) write w(Max) for E[w(Max)]. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 4 (1-round lower bound) The proof says no 1-round algorithm can distinguish K_{Δ+1} from a Δ-regular bipartite graph, but in the paper's model nodes know n, the two graphs have different sizes, and the view also contains the port number at the neighbour's end. Impact. The theorem is true, and the paper's argument stays with another pair of graphs (theorem4, theorem4_ratio). Repair. We use 2k copies of K_{Δ+1} versus k copies of K_{Δ+1,Δ+1} minus a perfect matching, on the same nodes, with matching port numbers at both ends of every edge. For each node v, a permutation fixing v maps its view in one graph to its view in the other, so averaging over labelings gives every node the same join probability in both graphs. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Finite simple graphs (Mathlib SimpleGraph, indepNum). "B has performance ratio ρ for Δ" (HasPerformanceRatio) means α(G) ≥ B(G) ≥ α(G)/ρ for all finite G with Δ(G) = Δ. HasTightPerformanceRatio adds that no smaller ratio holds. Boppana's algorithm: a uniformly random ordering σ : V ≃ Fin n; the output is the set of vertices preceding all their neighbours. We prove its expected size is exactly CaroWei(G). Theorem 4: synchronous message passing in CSLib's port-numbering model, one round. Nodes have unique labels from Fin N (any N ≥ n) and private i.i.d. random strings from an arbitrary distribution on a finite set. Messages and local computation are unbounded, and n, Δ, N are known. The algorithm must output an independent set with probability 1, but only on simple Δ-regular graphs with n = 2k(Δ+1) nodes. This is a weaker hypothesis than the paper's, so the theorem is stronger. Not covered: randomness with infinitely many outcomes (e.g. exact uniform reals). Weighted section: positive real weights. In Max, node v draws x_v ∈ [0,1] uniformly (product Lebesgue measure) and joins iff x_v^{1/w_v} beats all its neighbours. Lemma 2 is proved measure-theoretically. Main results in Lean. Local Computation Algorithms for Knapsack — PODC 2025 Clément L. Canonne, Yun Li, Seeun William Umboh. Local Computation Algorithms for Knapsack: impossibility results, and how to avoid them (Brief Announcement). PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733515. Formalized version: arXiv 2504.01543 v1 (full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The impossibility results (Lemma 3.1, Theorems 3.2–3.4) are true, although their proofs needed new arguments: the reductions of 3.2/3.3 break the paper's own normalisation of the profits, and Lemma 3.5 in the proof of 3.4 is not justified. The other half of the paper, how weighted sampling avoids them, is lost: Theorem 4.1 ("Algorithm 2 LCA-KP is an LCA giving access to a (1/2, 6ε)-approximate solution"), the paper's main theorem, is false, because on a Knapsack instance whose items all have the same efficiency LCA-KP answers "no" to every query, with probability close to 1. Lemma 4.6, on which it rests, is false on the same instance, and no repaired algorithm was proved. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.6 (LCA-KP is a (1/2, 6ε)-approximation LCA; ties in efficiency) On N identical items (weights 1, weight limit N/2, ε = 1/m with m ≥ 30, N ≥ m²), LCA-KP answers "no" to every query with probability ≥ 1 − ε/36, which is not a (1/2, 6ε)-approximation (Sec4.theorem_4_1_false), and no equally partitioning sequence exists (Sec4.no_eps_uniform). Impact. The main positive result is lost, even in the weakest, per-query reading of correctness; there is no local fix, and the existential claim of Theorem 1.4 is at best unestablished. The impossibility results are unaffected. Details. In normalised form every item has profit and weight 1/N. All items are small with efficiency 1, so the efficiency distribution that rQuantile samples is a point mass at 1. Suppose all quantiles are accurate, which by Theorem 4.5 happens with probability ≥ 1 − tβ ≥ 1 − ε/36. Then every 1 − kq lies in (τ, 1 − τ), and every ẽ_k = 1. So every item of Ĩ is a copy of (ε², ε²) with efficiency 1. CONVERT-GREEDY finds no index k with ẽ_k > p_j/w_j = 1, sets e_small = −1, and LCA-KP answers "no" to every query (Sec4.answerKP_uniform). This holds for any sample and any tie-breaking in the sort. The empty set is not a (1/2, 6ε)-approximation, since OPT ≈ 1/2. Even in the weakest, per-query reading of correctness, no seed-dependent (1/2, 6ε)-approximate solution agrees with each answer with probability ≥ 1 − ε. Reading > as ≥ in Line 3 of Algorithm 3 does not help: LCA-KP then answers "yes" to every item, which is infeasible. The paper never assumes distinct efficiencies, and ties are built into the design: the synthetic items of Ĩ have efficiency exactly ẽ_{k+1}. Theorem 4.1 rests on Lemma 4.6 (an equally partitioning sequence exists with probability ≥ 1 − 13ε/36). On the same instance every set A_k(I) of Definition 4.3 is either empty or contains every item, so no equally partitioning sequence of length t ≥ 1 exists and the probability in Lemma 4.6 is 0. The proof of Lemma 4.6 turns Pr[p/w > ẽ_k] ≤ kq + τ into Pr[p/w ≥ ẽ_k] ≤ kq + τ, which ignores the mass of items with efficiency exactly ẽ_k. ✏️ Slips Theorem 3.4 says "(t(n), 4/5)-LCA", which is failure probability 4/5 by Definition 2.2. The proof uses success probability 4/5, and we formalize that version. The literal version cannot follow from the paper's distribution: a 1-query algorithm that answers "yes" on a weight-3/4 item with a random hash bit succeeds with probability 1/2 > 1/5 on it. The proof of Theorem 3.4 draws (i, j) uniformly from [n]², so i = j is possible, and then the weights are ill-defined. We use distinct pairs. Theorem 2.7 states the sample complexity with Ω̃; it should be Õ. The approximation guarantee is stated inconsistently: (1/2 + ε) in Theorem 1.4, (2 + ε) in the technical overview, (1/2, 6ε) in Theorem 4.1. Algorithm 3, Lines 2–3 do not say what happens when no k satisfies ẽ_k > p_j/w_j, or when no j ≥ 1 exists. The evident reading is k = 0, the branch k < 3. Typos The "τ-approximate p-quantile" of Theorem 4.5 is never defined; its proof derives the definition. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 (the reduction leaves the paper's model) The reduction instance I(x) from OR_{n−1} has total profit |x| + β, so it violates the normalisation of Definition 2.2, and normalising it requires knowing |x|. Impact. Statements true; proved both for LCAs correct on unnormalised instances (the paper's reduction, theorem_3_2, theorem_3_3) and for LCAs correct only on normalised instances (theorem_3_2_normalized, theorem_3_3_normalized). Details. The paper's reduction only applies to LCAs that are correct on unnormalised instances. We formalize it in that setting (theorem_3_2, theorem_3_3, bound n/3 on n + 1 items). Repair. For LCAs required to be correct only on normalised instances we use a different hard family and a direct argument. The first item of a block of b = ⌊1/α²⌋ + 1 items takes the profit of the whole block. This gives the bound ⌊n/b⌋/3, still Ω(n) for fixed α. (theorem_3_2_normalized, theorem_3_3_normalized) 🛠️ Theorem 3.4 (Lemma 3.5 is not justified) Lemma 3.5's argument that the default answer to each query k must be "yes" confuses an error conditional on the query being k with the 1/5 bound, which is an average over all k. Impact. Theorem 3.4 is true with the paper's constant, by a new joint count (theorem_3_4, theorem_3_4_perQuery, LCA.count_le). Details. The argument is that answering "no" costs error 1/3 − 1/10 > 1/5. An algorithm may answer "no" on a constant fraction of the k and still meet the average bound. The lemma's hypotheses are in fact unsatisfiable (they contradict Theorem 3.4), so the lemma is vacuously true, but its proof does not show this. Repair. Let y be the fraction of default "yes" answers. The algorithm fails on a ½(1 − y) + ½(y² + (1 − y)²) − O(q/n) ≥ 7/16 − O(q/n) fraction of the hard distribution. This gives t(n) ≥ n/11 for every n ≥ 2 with success probability 4/5, the paper's constant, and t(n) ≥ n/40 − 1/5 under the per-query reading. (theorem_3_4, theorem_3_4_perQuery, LCA.count_le) 🔧 Theorem 3.4 (hard distribution outside the model) The instances have weights 3/4, 1/4 and profits 0, while Definition 2.2 requires integer weights and total profit 1. Impact. Statement true (theorem_3_4). Repair. We scale the weights to 3, 1 with weight limit 4 and use profits 1/n. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Knapsack instance on n items (Instance): real profits, natural-number weights, weight limit K. WellFormed means non-negative profits and weights ≤ K. Normalized additionally requires total profit 1, as in Definition 2.2. Randomized LCA (LCA): a PMF over random seeds. For each weight limit, seed and query there is an adaptive query tree over the item oracle i ↦ (p_i, w_i) that outputs yes/no. Since the answer is a function of (instance, seed, query), the LCA is stateless, parallelizable and query-order oblivious by construction (Definitions 2.2–2.4). Complexity is the worst-case number of item queries per answer (QueryBound, the paper's t(n) as query complexity). Correctness is formalized in two readings. Per-query (Correct): there is a seed-dependent solution C r such that each single answer agrees with it and C r is valid with probability ≥ 1 − δ. Global (CorrectStrong): the set of "yes" items is valid with probability ≥ 1 − δ. Global implies per-query. Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 and the refutation of 4.1 use the weaker per-query reading, so they hold in both. Theorem 3.4 is proved in both readings. Lower bounds quantify over all randomized LCAs with arbitrary seed spaces. The easy direction of Yao's principle is an averaging lemma (sum_mul_probReal_le). Section 4: LCA-KP (Algorithm 2 with Algorithm 3) is modelled as a function of one run's random data: the sample R, the rQuantile outputs ẽ_k, and the sorting order of Ĩ. The only property of rQuantile used is the accuracy guarantee of Theorem 4.5. The probabilistic statement takes as hypothesis that each run is accurate with probability ≥ 1 − ε/36, which is what Theorem 4.5 with β = ε²/36 and t ≤ 1/ε calls gives. Main results in Lean. Strong and Hiding Distributed Certification of k-Coloring — PODC 2025 Augusto Modanese, Pedro Montealegre, Martín Ríos-Wilson. Brief Announcement: Strong and Hiding Distributed Certification of k-Coloring. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733546. The proofs are in the full version the BA cites, arXiv 2502.13854 v1 (Feb 2025). We formalize the BA's statements, using the v1 definitions and proofs. Numbering: BA Theorems 4.1–4.4 = v1 Theorems 1.1–1.4. We also checked the corrected statements of v3 (Feb 2026, retitled "…of Bipartiteness", co-author B. Jauregui). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ❌ Intent lost. The paper's main result, Theorem 4.2 ("no strong and hiding r-round LCP for 2-colouring on classes containing an r-forgetful graph that is neither an even cycle nor of minimum degree 1, no matter the certificate size, even if not anonymous"), is false. It fails already for r = 1, for anonymous LCPs with O(log n)-bit certificates, and even on a one-graph class, and the authors' corrected v3 version (Theorems 2(1), 3(1), 4) is also false. The upper bounds hold, Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.2 as stated and Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 as existence statements, but the shatter-point decoder is not strongly sound and the watermelon decoder is not even sound. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 4.2 (no strong and hiding LCP for 2-colouring) Theorem 4.2 is false already for r = 1: a counter modulo M > 2N gives a strong, hiding, anonymous LCP with O(log n)-bit certificates for all bipartite graphs, hidden on the 1-forgetful graph θ(5,5,5) (baTheorem42_false). Impact. The main lower bound falls, even on the one-graph class {θ(5,5,5)}, which also refutes the authors' corrected v3 statement (v3Theorem4_false). The same LCP is anonymous, so it refutes v1 Thm 1.5 (order-invariant) too. Details. Each node gets a counter ℓ(v). With M = 5(2N+1) (odd, and larger than twice the number of nodes; nodes know N in the paper's model), a node accepts iff every neighbour's counter is ℓ(v) ± 1 (mod M). Complete: a proper 0/1 colouring is accepted on every bipartite graph. Strongly sound on every graph: along a closed walk through accepting nodes, the integer displacement z satisfies M | z, |z| ≤ L and z ≡ L (mod 2). A walk of length L < 2n < M therefore has even length, and short closed walks suffice for bipartiteness. Hiding, even against identifier-aware extraction algorithms: use θ(5,5,5), i.e. three paths of length 5 between two endpoints. It is bipartite, connected, 1-forgetful under both the BA and v3 definitions, has minimum degree 2, and is not a cycle. Label it t + height (t ∈ ZMod M), with identifiers rotating mod 5 on five nodes. Then node 2's view for t equals node 1's view for t+1: identifiers, ports, labels and degrees all agree. Nodes 1 and 2 are adjacent, so a successful extractor would flip its output at node 1 with every step t ↦ t+1. This is impossible since M is odd. The proof's gap: Lemma 5.3 (v3: Lemma 21) needs the odd closed walk in V(D,n) to have at most √(N/Δʳ) views, and this is never checked. Here every odd cycle of V(D,n) has length ≥ M > 2N. This refutes BA Thm 4.2 for H = all bipartite graphs (baTheorem42_false) and v3's corrected statement for the class {θ(5,5,5)} (v3Theorem4_false). ❌ Theorem 4.2 for anonymous constant-size LCPs (unjustified restriction of the class) Theorem 4.2 fails even for anonymous constant-size LCPs: the paper's own LCP of Lemma 4.1 is complete on all bipartite graphs, strongly sound, and hiding through P₆ ⊔ K₂ (baTheorem42Anon_false). Impact. A second refutation of the main lower bound, caused by a false step of its proof; the authors concede the quantifier issue in v3 §2.2.4 and add G ∩ H = ∅. Details. v1 §5.2 says: "without restriction H only consists of r-forgetful graphs …, since a strong and hiding LCP for H is one for every subclass". This is false, because hiding only needs one hard instance. So the counterexample works for H = all bipartite graphs. ✏️ Slips Definition of r-forgetful (BA, used in Theorem 4.2): it requires every w ∈ Nʳ(u) to move away along the path, which is unsatisfiable for r ≥ 2 (take w = v₁: the distance drops from 1 to 0), so BA Theorem 4.2 is vacuous for r ≥ 2 as written (not_isForgetful_of_two_le). v3 Definition 22 fixes this, and for r = 1 both definitions hold for θ(5,5,5). Lemma 4.1 (δ = 1, part of Thm 4.1), rule "all other neighbours of ⊤ are labelled β ∈ {0,1}": the rule works only if β is the same for all neighbours; if each neighbour may carry its own colour, a 5-cycle with a pendant node is accepted everywhere (literalLCP_not_sound). We prove the lemma with the uniform reading (theorem_4_1). k-col is defined with colours {0,…,k} (k+1 colours). In Lemma 3.2's proof, "proper 2-coloring" should read "k-coloring". Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4.3 (shatter-point decoder is not strongly sound) The paper's decoder accepts a 5-cycle: two type-1 nodes u, u' attached to the same (rejecting) type-0 node can carry different colour vectors (0,0) and (0,1) (shatterLCP_not_stronglySound). Impact. The protocol claim is false, but the theorem holds as an existence statement: graphs with a shatter point include P₆ and P₆ ⊔ K₂, so the counter LCP (hiding against all algorithms) and the constant-size LCP of Lemma 4.1 (anonymous hiding) both work (theorem_4_3). Details. u – w – u' – z' – z – u is an accepted 5-cycle, with w in component 0 and z, z' in component 1. The proof's step "by 2(c), all neighbours of a type-1 node share the same colour" is false. 🛠️ Theorem 4.4 (watermelon decoder is not sound) The paper's decoder accepts every node of a 5-cycle, because rule 2(b) only asks that some entry of a path node records the endpoint's port (watermelonLCP_not_sound). Impact. The protocol claim is false, but the theorem holds as an existence statement, because the counter LCP is hiding on the watermelon θ(5,5,5) (theorem_4_4). Details. A path node never checks the entry facing an endpoint. On a 5-cycle with endpoints v₁, v₂, path node a stores in its v₂-entry the port number that v₁ uses towards a. So v₁ reads the colour of the wrong edge, and every node of the 5-cycle accepts. 🔧 Lemma 4.1 (δ = 1, part of Thm 4.1): soundness argument The soundness argument ("since C is odd, then u ∈ V(C)") proves nothing. Impact. Statement true (degOneLCP_stronglySoundAll, theorem_4_1). Repair. Strong soundness follows from an explicit 2-colouring: a ⊤ node gets 1-β and a ⊥ node gets the β of its ⊤. 🔧 Lemma 4.1 (δ = 1, part of Thm 4.1): Fig. 4 Fig. 4's odd cycle in V(D,4) uses an edge between the views of nodes 3 and 4 that would need a triangle 2-3-4 (fig4_edge_not_compatible). Impact. Statement true (degOneLCP_anonHiding, theorem_4_1). Repair. Hiding uses three labellings of P₆ ⊔ K₂. 🔧 Lemma 4.2 (even cycles), hiding argument The hiding argument mixes C₄ and C₆, whose views differ in N, so the claimed odd cycle is not in any V(D,n) of the paper's own model. Impact. Statement true (lemma_4_2). Repair. A single C₄ with reflection-symmetric ports suffices: two adjacent nodes get identical anonymous views (lemma_4_2). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Network and verifier. One-round LCPs (r = 1) on finite simple port-numbered graphs (ports 0..deg-1, injective), with injective identifiers < N and N = bound n known to every node. bound is arbitrary; all results hold for every choice. The model is deterministic, with no failures. The prover is an adversary that picks arbitrary labels in the soundness properties. Views. A view is N, the node's own identifier, label and degree, and the multiset of neighbour records (port here, port there, identifier, label, degree). This contains the paper's radius-1 view, plus neighbour degrees. The extra degrees only strengthen extraction algorithms, hence strengthen our hiding results. Anonymous algorithms factor through View.anon. Properties. We formalize completeness, soundness, strong (promise) soundness, hiding (some hard instance per algorithm) and anonymous hiding as in v1 §2. Extraction algorithms are arbitrary functions; the paper requires computable ones, which is weaker. Certificate sizes are sets sz n of admissible labels: constant size = a finite label type; the counter LCP uses labels < 5(2N+1). Not covered. General r is not formalized. Thm 4.2 is refuted at r = 1, which suffices since it is stated for every r ≥ 1. Main results in Lean. Dynamic Distributed Subgraph Finding — PODC 2025 Yi-Jun Chang, Lyuting Chen, Yanyu Chen, Gopinath Mishra, Mingyang Yang. Brief Announcement: The Complexity Landscape of Dynamic Distributed Subgraph Finding. PODC 2025. DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733522. Formalized version: arXiv 2411.11544 v3 (full version). Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The two lower bounds hold: Theorem 1.3 (Ω(log log n) for one-round MemDetect(K_s) under edge insertions) and Theorem 1.6 (Ω(log log log n) for one-round Detect(K_s) under node and edge insertions), both on bounded-degree networks, with explicit constants, and so does Theorem 1.4 (O(Δ² log log n) one-round MemList(K₃) under edge insertions), once the periodic updates are also run on the edges of G⁰. The algorithm of Theorem 1.7 (List(K₃) under node and edge insertions) is incorrect, because the rule by which a node infers a triangle is unsound once node insertions are allowed, so Theorem 1.7 and the upper half of Corollary 1.8, the tightness of the Ω(log log log n) bound, are not established. The characterizations of Sections 6–8 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 1.7 (the List(K₃) algorithm under node and edge insertions) The algorithm lists a non-existent triangle: on a network of maximum degree 2 with G⁰ = {v, w}, where round 2 inserts a node x with edges {x, u}, {x, w} and round 3 inserts {u, v}, node v lists {u, v, w} although u and w are not adjacent (Alg17.theorem_1_7_algorithm_unsound). Impact. Theorem 1.7 (existence of some O(Δ log log log n) algorithm) and the upper half of Corollary 1.8 are not established; the lower bounds (Theorems 1.3, 1.6) and Theorem 1.4 are unaffected. Details. In the case t_uv − t_uw ≤ d, the proof lets v list {u, v, w} by reusing the argument for node v in Theorem 1.4. When {u, v} appears, v receives R_edge(u) ∋ j from u. It had received (Signal) from w j rounds earlier. Since only one change happens per round, it concludes that that change was the edge {u, w}. With node insertions, that change can instead be a new node x adjacent to both u and w. In the network above, in round 3, u reports R_edge(u) = {1} and w signalled in round 2, so v lists {u, v, w}. The Lean theorem covers every window d ≥ 1, every implementation of the remaining message parts (bit reports, periodic 1-DBList updates) and every additional output rule. ✏️ Slips The definitions of List(H) and MemList(H) in §1.2 do not say that only real copies may be listed; without that, listing all triples solves List(H), which would contradict Observation 1.1 together with Theorem 1.6. §5.3 shows soundness is meant. The proof of Theorem 1.4 orders the edges as t_vw < t_uw < t_uv, which ignores ties at time 0 (two edges of G⁰), where no Signals exist; such edges are known from G⁰. The last paragraph of the proof of Theorem 1.6 says "node a" for node b. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 1.4 (periodic updates for edges of G⁰) The algorithm never starts periodic updates for edges of G⁰, so with {v, w} ∈ G⁰, {u, w} inserted in round t ≥ 1 and {u, v} more than d rounds later, read literally v never learns {u, w} (no Lean counterexample). Impact. We start the updates in round 1, and Theorem 1.4 then holds (theorem_1_4, alg14_solves). Repair. The paper also argues only that the true triangles are listed. We add explicit listing rules and prove that no node lists a non-triangle. 🔧 Theorem 1.3, proof of Lemma 4.2 (number of classes) A class is a vector of message patterns over all j ∈ [t], so there are 2^{O(Bt²)} classes, not t · 2^{O(Bt)}. Impact. Statement true: this is still n^{o(1)}, so the argument survives (hypothesis h2 of Hard.not_solves_13). 🔧 Theorem 1.3 (choice of b and c) Lemma 4.1 only gives b one friend w.r.t. (a, i), so c = d is possible, and I* may contain b. Impact. Statement true, at the cost of a factor 2 in the count (Hard.select13). Details. If c = d, then d is attached to both cliques in (S2), and a can learn about K^{i*} through d. Repair. We choose b ∉ I* with at least two friends besides itself. 🔧 Theorems 1.3 and 1.6 (Ω(·) proved as "not o(·)") Both lower-bound proofs only use B = o(log log n) (resp. o(log log log n)), so they show "not o(·)" rather than Ω(·). Impact. Statements true: the counting works for B ≤ c · log log n, and we prove the Ω form with c = 1/8 (resp. c = 1/16). 🔧 Theorem 1.6 (possible reporters) The last paragraph of the proof considers only nodes of K^i ∪ {a, b} as possible reporters and forgets the untouched cliques K^j, j ≠ i. Impact. Statement true: those nodes see the same in (S1) and (S4) (theorem_1_6). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Deterministic, synchronous, failure-free; no randomness. Insertion-only dynamic networks on the identifier set V (Fin n in the main theorems), with two change models. EdgeIns: each round inserts at most one edge. NodeEdgeIns: alternatively one new node with arbitrary edges to present nodes. The adversary is any such network. Deletions are not modelled; no checked result uses them. Every node knows G⁰, its identifier and the round number. In each round the change happens first. Then each node sends one message from the alphabet M to each neighbour; B bits means |M| ≤ 2^B. A one-round algorithm must be correct after every round on every network of maximum degree ≤ Δ. Theorem 1.4's algorithm (Theorem14Alg.lean) uses full-history states (FullHist.lean). It uses d = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 2 and T = ⌊d/2⌋. A neighbour list is sent in T blocks of 2Δ bits, using an injective encoding that exists by counting. Each round's message also carries a Signal bit and, to a new neighbour, the two recent records as lists of ages. Not-yet-inserted nodes run with input "absent". They know more than in the paper, so the lower bounds are at least as strong; their outputs are ignored. The lower bounds quantify over all algorithms (arbitrary state spaces). NonVacuity.lean shows that with unbounded messages both problems are solvable in one round. Main results in Lean. Know Your Audience — PODC 2024 Bernadette Charron-Bost, Patrick Lambein-Monette. Brief Announcement: Know Your Audience. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662784. Formalized version: the full version Know your audience: Communication model and computability in anonymous networks, arXiv 2311.17728 v1 (23 pp.); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. Theorem 4.1 says that, with output port awareness, symmetric communications or outdegree awareness, a function is computable in static strongly connected anonymous networks iff it is frequency-based. The direction "frequency-based ⇒ computable" is true, and so are Corollaries 4.3 (size known) and 4.4 (one leader), while "computable ⇒ frequency-based" (and Corollary 4.2) fails only on networks with at most two agents; one condition on vector lengths saves it, and we prove the exact corrected characterisation: "frequency-based on vectors of length ≥ 2" (outdegree and output port awareness), and "symmetric and frequency-based on vectors of length ≥ 3" (symmetric communications). All the paper's examples (average computable, sum not) and its proof idea survive; Section 5 (dynamic networks) was not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 4.1, (ii) ⇒ (i), and Corollary 4.2 (networks with at most two agents) isSingleton(v) = [|v| = 1] is computable in every model, even simple broadcast, and with symmetric communications so is isPair(v) = [|v| = 2], yet neither is frequency-based: isSingleton(a) = 1 ≠ 0 = isSingleton(a, a) and isPair(a, b) = 1 ≠ 0 = isPair(a, b, a, b) (theorem_4_1_ii_imp_i_false, theorem_4_1_false, theorem_4_1_false_symmetric_K2, corollary_4_2_false). Impact. The direction "frequency-based ⇒ computable", Corollaries 4.3 and 4.4, the paper's examples and its proof idea survive, and we prove the exact corrected characterisation. The failures are exactly at the sizes where the network is unique and self-identifying, so every symmetric function is computable there: n = 1 in every model, and n = 2 with symmetric communications, where K₂ is the only 2-agent network and its agents know it after two rounds. In the directed models, where K₂ is not recognisable, the theorem holds at n = 2. Details. The paper's model (§2.1–2.2) puts a self-loop at every agent, and the transition function receives the multiset of received messages. So after round 1 an agent knows its indegree. In a strongly connected network the indegree is 1 iff the agent is alone, from every initial configuration. In a connected bidirectional network, an agent with a single neighbour whose neighbour also has a single neighbour lives in K₂. Agents learn their degree in round 1 and their neighbours' degrees in round 2. Where the proof breaks: the proof of (ii) ⇒ (i) (§4.1) lifts both input vectors along the rings R_n → R_p ← R_m, where p is the lcm of the denominators of the frequencies. A bidirectional ring of size ≤ 2 is a multigraph (R_2 has a double edge and R_1 three loops), not a network of the class (§2.1 networks are simple digraphs ([n], E_t) with self-loops). So for p ≤ 2 (or n, m ≤ 2) Lemma 3.2 does not apply: the proof silently needs sizes ≥ 3. Repair. For outdegree and output port awareness the failure matters only for n = 1. We use directed cycles instead and lift along C_{n'n} → C_n and C_{nn'} → C_{n'} (n, n' ≥ 2), together with Lemma 3.3 at length nn' (frequencyBasedFrom_two_of_computable). For symmetric communications we use bidirectional rings, which needs n, n' ≥ 3 (frequencyBasedFrom_three_of_computable_symmetric). These bounds are optimal, by isSingleton and isPair. The positive algorithm then has to treat n = 1 (and n = 2 for symmetric communications) separately (theorem_4_1_corrected, theorem_4_1_corrected_symmetric, corollary_4_2_corrected*). ✏️ Slips Lemma 3.3: "if f is computed in an anonymous network class then f is multiset-based" holds only on the vector lengths of the networks in the class: computability in C_k says nothing about other lengths. Every use in the paper involves classes with networks of all sizes, so the uses are fine (Computes.perm_eq). Table 1 and §6 (simple broadcast, cited from [20]): the claim that only set-based functions are computable with simple broadcast also fails at n = 1 in this paper's model (isSingleton_computable .broadcast). Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 §4.3, symmetric variant of the algorithm "Up to some permutation of the vertices in B, we may assume that none of the degrees d_{1,2}, …, d_{m−1,m} is zero, since B is strongly connected" assumes a Hamiltonian path in the minimum base, which fails, e.g., for a star with four distinct input values, which is its own minimum base. Impact. The positive result with symmetric communications holds (theorem_4_1_i_imp_ii): our symmetric algorithm does not use this variant, and reads class outdegrees as indegrees in eq. (1). Repair. Propagating eq. (4) along a spanning tree repairs the formula (not formalized). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Static network = simple directed graph on Fin n (n ≥ 1) with a self-loop at every agent and a local output port numbering. Synchronous lock-step rounds with synchronous starts; no failures; deterministic anonymous algorithms. An agent sends send(state, outdegree, port), and its transition gets the multiset of received messages. The models restrict send (CommModel.Allowed): simple broadcast and symmetric communications see only the state, outdegree awareness the state and the outdegree, output port awareness everything. PODC 2024 (brief announcement). DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662786. Formalized version: arXiv 2405.03573 v2, the full version with proofs. Numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The snapshot algorithm, the stable-view theorem and the renaming reduction hold with at least N registers, but Lemmas 4.6–4.7 and Theorem 4.8 are false with fewer, and Section 4 never bounds the number of registers. The proofs of Theorem 4.8 and of snapshot safety (§5.3.2) do not go through, and we prove both with new arguments. Obstruction-free consensus (Section 7) was not checked. With at least N registers everything checked holds: Lemmas 4.5–4.7 as printed. Theorem 4.8: stable views form a DAG with a unique source. The snapshot algorithm of Figure 3 is safe and wait-free. Level N − 1 (footnote 4) already suffices. The renaming reduction of Section 6 is correct. Impact. Snapshot safety itself is true (see Proof gaps); the intended statement covers scans that start after t. This counterexample is not in Lean: our model merges the output step into the last read. Details. Without the printed version, the derivation of safety from Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3 misses two final scans that overlap in time. Repair. Restating the lemma for scans is not enough, so we prove safety by a new chain argument with a stronger durability notion (see Proof gaps). The hypothesis M ≥ N is not merely implied, because the paper itself works with fewer registers than processors in Section 4. Details. In the counterexample the two groups take turns: both members of a group write, one register each, and then both scan. Each processor only ever reads its own group's value. With one register, two processors that alternate write; scan behave the same way (theorem_4_8_needs_registers). This execution also refutes Lemma 4.6 with A = {0}: Ā = {1} is live and covers at most one register, yet never reads from A (lemma_4_6_needs_registers). Exhaustive search finds no such execution with 3 processors and 2 registers. In general, the two groups with minimal views must together have more members than there are registers. Section 2 allows any number M > 0 of registers, and Theorem 4.8 states no bound. Section 4 stresses that its pathology arises "regardless of the number of registers". Its running example (§4.1, reused in §5.1) has 5 processors and 3 registers. The proof of Lemma 4.6 does count N registers ("|R_t^Ā| + |Ā| < N registers"). Section 5 uses N registers. Repair. Lemmas 4.5–4.7 and Theorem 4.8 with N ≤ |R|. The wait-freedom proof only needs a minimal stable view, not Theorem 4.8. Repair. One extra clause in Definition 4.1: wait until every register is rewritten after the views stabilized. Figure 1 has a typo: written ∪ {r} = P should be = R. Figure 3 has the same typo. Definition 3.2 reads "either o[i] ⊆ o[j] or o[i] ⊆ o[j]"; the second disjunct should be o[j] ⊆ o[i]. Typos §5.1, first sentence: "the write-scan loop in Figure 3" should refer to Figure 1. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 4.8 (unique source) The proof claims, by Lemma 4.4, that live processors with a stable view in X (the views reachable from a source S) read only from P_X, but Lemma 4.4 gives the opposite inclusion. Impact. The statement holds with N ≤ |R|; new proof (theorem_4_8, theorem_4_8_unique_source, Exec.false_of_two_closed, Exec.exists_gst). Details. Lemma 4.4 says that processors with a view in X̄ read only from P_X̄. A processor with a view in X may read from a smaller view in X̄. Applying Lemma 4.7 to the closed set P_X̄ yields no contradiction. The GST of Definition 4.1 does not ensure that registers hold the writers' stable views, which Lemma 4.4 needs. Repair. Take two distinct minimal stable views. After a strengthened GST, the processors holding each of them read only from each other. By Lemma 4.5, each group leaves at most its own size of registers to the others. With at least N registers, this pins the partition exactly. The next round-robin write of a group member into the other group's registers then breaks the count. (theorem_4_8, theorem_4_8_unique_source, Exec.false_of_two_closed, Exec.exists_gst) 🛠️ Snapshot safety (§5.3.2, Lemmas 5.5 and 5.8) The derivation of safety from Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3 misses two final scans that overlap in time, and Lemma 5.8 assumes that "durably stored" is preserved over time, which it is not. Impact. Statement true; new proof (snapshot_safety_paper, snapshot_safety). Details. In Lemma 5.8, a write of a value containing W can turn several harmless scanners into threats. Details in differencies.md, item 8. Repair. Call W durable when the registers containing W plus the processors containing W number more than N. Persistence: every scan that starts after a durable time ends with a view containing W. Chain: below a terminated view W there is a chain of nested scans with view W. Each scan in the chain is performed by a new processor with view W, so the chain must reach a scan at whose start W is durable. For two incomparable outputs, the two durable starts would each have to precede the other. This proof needs only level N − 1, so it also proves footnote 4, which the paper states without proof. (snapshot_safety_paper, snapshot_safety, Exec.durable_scan, Exec.chain) Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous read/write shared memory: N processors (P) and |R| multi-writer atomic registers. There are no failures besides stopping, and the schedule is arbitrary (adversarial). The model is deterministic and has no randomness. Processor anonymity: all processors run the same program and differ only in their input. Memory anonymity: each write or read names a physical register, chosen nondeterministically. Writes follow the round-robin written set, and each scan reads every register once, in any order. This over-approximates every wiring permutation, so the positive results hold for all wirings. The concrete counterexample schedules are realizable with suitable wirings. Registers carry a ghost "last writer" field, which the algorithm never reads. Executions are infinite. A terminated processor only takes idle steps. Live means taking infinitely many non-idle steps. Atomicity follows the PlusCal code. The end-of-scan computation and the output step are merged into the last read of the scan. Sections 3 and 6 are formalized on outcomes: participants, groups (= inputs), and outputs. Remark. The "saving grace" argument of Section 6 is correct, but a simpler argument suffices. Two groups with equal-size snapshots appear together in some output sample, so their snapshots are equal and their ranks differ. Main results in Lean. Consecutive Ballots in Paxos — PODC 2020 Eli Goldweber, Nuda Zhang, Manos Kapritsos. Brief Announcement: On the Significance of Consecutive Ballots in Paxos. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405700. Formalized version: arXiv 2006.01885 v1 (full version); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🔧 Easy fix. The main claim holds: a value may be learned once a majority has accepted it in a consecutive span of ballots, and this keeps Paxos safe (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, Lemmas 4.1–4.3), also when combined with Consecutive Proposals (Consecutive Paxos). Definition 6 (CQ Chosen) is written so loosely that the auxiliary Lemmas 4.2′ and 4.3′ are false as stated, the proof of Lemma 4.3′ misses a case and the TLA+ invariant printed in Appendix B is vacuous, but local changes repair all three. The IronFleet/Dafny artifact of §6 was not inspected. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Definition 6 (CQ Chosen), with Lemmas 4.2′ and 4.3′ Both lemmas are false for the literal Definition 6, because the ballot-i accept it requires need not be one of the accepts forming the Consecutive Quorum (lemma_4_3'_literal_false, lemma_4_2'_literal_false). Impact. The proof reads the ballot-i accept as part of the CQ ("the acceptor in Qᵢ that accepted v in ballot i"), and under that reading both lemmas hold (lemma_4_3', lemma_4_2'). Safety is not affected; Lemma 4.3 itself is true, but the paper derives it from the false Lemma 4.3′. Details. Definition 6 says Chosen(i, v) ≡ ∃Qᵢ. CQ(Qᵢ, v) ∧ ∃α ∈ Qᵢ. accept(i, v)_α ∈ sent_α. Counterexample with five acceptors in Classic Paxos: Ballot 3: A, B, C promise; x is proposed and accepted by A. Ballot 5: B, C, D promise, all ⊥; y is proposed and accepted by D. Ballot 9: A reports (3, x), B, C report ⊥; x is proposed and accepted by A, B, C. Then {A, B, C} in ballot 9 is a CQ for x, and A also sent accept(3, x), so "x is chosen in ballot 3". But y was proposed in ballot 5 > 3 (against Lemma 4.3′) and accepted by D in ballot 5 > 3 (against Lemma 4.2′). Safety is not affected: y can never be chosen. Repair. Require the ballot-i accept to be a member's CQ accept (x_α = i; our CQChosen'). Typos In the proof of Lemma 4.1′, "an acceptor that has accepted v in ballot j" should say w. Appendix A writes Chosen(v, i) for the earlier Chosen(i, v) and uses ℤ⁺ for ballots, where Section 3 uses ℕ. Definitions 7–9 are properties of the protocol (Definition 8 is an invariant), not definitions. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Lemma 4.3′ (missing case in the proof) The base case treats i as the largest ballot of the CQ, but when i is a smaller ballot of the CQ the intersecting acceptor may have accepted v in a ballot ≥ j, after promising j, so its promise reports nothing useful. Impact. Statement true (for the intended Definition 6); repaired (propose_eq_of_interval). Details. The base case says the intersecting acceptor accepted v "in ballot i or in some ballot < i". The statement still holds because every ballot in the CQ's span carries v. Repair. Strong induction on the ballot over the whole span [lo, hi] of the CQ: every proposal in a ballot ≥ lo has value v (propose_eq_of_interval). 🔧 Appendix B (ConsecQ, SafeValue), cited by §6.2 The TLA+ check is vacuous as printed: ConsecQ(Q, b, v) ≜ ∀ r ∈ Acceptor : ∧ NotIn(Q, r) ∧ … makes r ∉ Q a top-level conjunct for every acceptor r, so ConsecQ is false for every nonempty Q, AgreedConsecQ never holds, and the invariant SafeValue is true independently of the protocol (tla_agreedConsecQ_false). Impact. This concerns the paper's supporting evidence, not its theorems: safety of Consecutive Paxos holds (theorem_3_2 with cp = true). We judge the typeset text only; the file actually model-checked may differ. Details. NotIn(Q, r) ⟹ … was presumably meant, and the inner ∃ n ∈ msgs : … ⟹ … should presumably be ∀. Even with these changes, ConsecQ does not express Definition 5. Repair. Replace the operator ConsecQ by Definition 5; the invariant then says what cq_propose_eq proves with cp = true. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Single-decree Paxos over asynchronous message passing, in the style of the paper's own TLA+ appendix. The global state holds, for each acceptor, maxBal and its highest accepted proposal. It also holds the set of all messages ever sent. Actions: prepare (1a), promise (1b), propose (2a), accept (2b). Each may fire whenever its guard holds, in any interleaving. A crash is an agent that stops taking steps. Messages can be lost or delayed, because a proposer or learner may use any subset of the sent messages. There is no Byzantine behaviour and no randomness. Ballots are ℕ, with one proposal per ballot. Quorums form an arbitrary intersecting quorum system. The paper's majorities of 2f+1 acceptors are an instance (QuorumSystem.majority); the proofs only use intersection. A flag cp switches the Consecutive Proposals of Definitions 11–12 on (Consecutive Paxos) or off (Classic Paxos). All safety results hold for both. Proposers may use any sent message. That is more than they can actually have received, so the model allows more behaviours and the safety results are stronger. Learning (Definition 3 and its CQ version) is a predicate on the set of messages a learner received. Any two learners, at any two times of an execution, are covered. Main results in Lean. On Using Null Messages in a Byzantine Setting — PODC 2020 Guy Goren, Yoram Moses. Brief Announcement: On Using Null Messages in a Byzantine Setting. PODC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3382734.3405717. Formalized version: the 3-page proceedings brief announcement; numbering follows it. A journal full version exists (Goren, Moses, Optimistically tuning synchronous Byzantine consensus: another win for null messages, Distributed Computing 34(5), 2021, DOI 10.1007/s00446-021-00393-8); it is not open access and was not consulted. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ✅ Correct. Theorem 1.2 (silent validation rounds give knowledge of a global milestone) and Theorem 2.1 (SmallCouncil + any binary BA protocol is binary BA; failure-free runs decide the majority value at time 3 with at most n(t+1.5) bits; at most n(t+1.5) + 2n² bits by correct processes and 4 rounds before the base protocol in general) hold. The brief announcement gives no proofs (Theorem 1.2 is justified "by design", Theorem 2.1 not at all), so the verdict judges the statements only; we reconstructed the proofs. They need 2t < n and the paper's convention that a process receives its own broadcasts ("send to all" includes the sender). Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Typos Theorem 2.1 (2): "at most n(t + 1.5) + 2n² bits are sent by correct processes" bounds the layer before reverting, not the whole run including the base protocol (layer_bits_le). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's synchronous lock-step Byzantine model (Cslib.Byzantine.LockStep) on the complete network of n processes Fin n. Protocols are deterministic functions of input and history; messages are Options, so none is a null message. A static Byzantine set of at most t processes (atMost t) sends arbitrary messages; links are reliable; no signatures. Round r of the model (0-indexed) is the paper's round r+1. The history after r rounds is the local state at time r. SmallCouncil composed with B (smallCouncil t B): messages Bool ⊕ M₂, one-bit layer messages or base-protocol messages. Processes that got a help! run B from round 4 with input est; the others are silent from then on. A process that sends err/help! counts it as received (flag selfRcv := true; false is the broken literal reading). B is an arbitrary protocol with Solves ⊤ B (atMost t) BA (termination, validity, agreement). Theorem 1.2 uses CSLib's interpreted systems (Cslib.Knowledge.System). The points are runs (admissible reliable scenarios) × time, j's local state is (input, history), and K is S5 knowledge. Bits: every layer message is one Bool, so layer bits = layer messages (msgsAt, messages by correct processes to other processes). Main results in Lean. One implicit convention matters and is easy to get wrong: a process receives its own broadcasts. Figure 1 (line 10) has a process without a unanimous recommendation "send err to all", and line 11 has a process that "did not receive any err" decide at time 3. If the sender does not count its own err, the protocol is wrong for every base protocol. Take n = 7, t = 2, Council {0,1,2}. Process 1 is Byzantine and silent, process 6 has input 0 and everyone else input 1. The correct council members recommend MAJ = 1. The null message of 1 tells 6 "recommendation 0", so 6 sees no unanimous recommendation, sets est = 0 and sends err. Nobody else sends err, so 6 decides 0 at time 3. The others got 6's err and run the base protocol with input 1. Declaring 6 Byzantine as well gives the same run with 2 faults, so the base protocol's validity makes them decide 1. Theorem 1.2 has the same issue: if j does not receive its own messages, silence in round m+1 says nothing about φ_j. With the paper's wording ("sends messages to everyone", "send to all"), which includes the sender, both results hold. This is the paper's convention, not an extra assumption: Figure 1 quantifies over all of P including the sender (lines 01–03 for a council member i, lines 06–07 for i = j), and line 08 ("unanimous recommendation from {0,…,t}") only makes sense for a council member if it receives its own recommendation. We prove the results under this convention, or with "φ_j held" as an explicit hypothesis in Theorem 1.2. Formalized version: arXiv 1903.02637 v2 (numbering follows it). Verdict: ✏️ Slip. So the main Theorem 5.2 is verified only in its "⇐" direction (plus conditions (i) and (iii) of "⇒"); its hardest part, the necessity of condition (ii), is not checked. Mistakes in the paper ✏️ Slips §1.2, second paragraph: "X1 + X2 → W (computing w = x1 + x2)" should say w = min(x1, x2). The same sentence has the intended version, and nothing else depends on it. No kinetics, no probabilities: stable computation is the paper's reachability definition (from every configuration reachable from I_x, a stable configuration with output f x is reachable).
