How Fast Reads Affect Multi-Valued Register Simulations — PODC 2019 Soma Chaudhuri, Reginald Frank, Jennifer L. Welch. Brief Announcement: How Fast Reads Affect Multi-Valued Register Simulations. PODC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3293611.3331580. Formalized version: the 3-page brief announcement (author copy from NSF-PAR, retrieved via web.archive; no arXiv or full version), whose proofs are condensed; numbering follows it. The gaps in Section 3 below are of the kind expected from such compression; the Lemma 4.2 gap is not (its one-line justification is false). Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All results hold: Theorem 3.1 (log₂ k reads are needed), Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.5 (a safe/regular simulation whose reads take log₂ k reads needs writes of log₂ k base writes), Lemmas 3.3/3.4, and Theorem 4.1 (no atomic simulation with two readers has reads of log₂ k steps; k > 2). The proof of Lemma 4.2, on which the paper's proof of Theorem 4.1 rests, has a genuine gap: it relies on a claim about decision trees that is false. We found no derivation of the lemma and prove Theorem 4.1 by a new case split. Mistakes in the paper No mistakes in the statements. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 4.2 (same root of T₁ and T₂), used by Theorem 4.1 The proof's key step "a value z whose root-to-leaf path in T₂ does not include r₁ must exist since r₁ is not the root of T₂" is false for decision trees (lemma_4_2_gap). Impact. Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.1 are true; we repair the proof of Theorem 4.1 with a case split (theorem_4_1, setting_false). Details. The proof picks "a value z whose root-to-leaf path in T₂ does not include r₁. Such a value must exist since r₁ is not the root of T₂." This does not follow. In a complete decision tree of depth 2 whose root reads register 1 and whose two children both read register 0, every root-to-leaf path reads register 0, which is not the root (lemma_4_2_gap). The argument after this step is correct; it shows only "if some path of T₂ avoids the root ρ of T₁, contradiction" (lemma_4_2_core). Lemma 4.2 itself is not false: like every step of a proof by contradiction, it is stated under the assumption that the simulation A exists, which Theorem 4.1 refutes, so once Theorem 4.1 is proved it holds trivially (lemma_4_2). This is not a defect of the reductio; the point is that the paper gives no valid derivation of it, and we found none from the facts available at that point. The gap example is about the inference inside the proof (abstract decision trees with the properties of Lemmas 3.3–3.4), not a counterexample to a stated lemma; it cannot be realized by a simulation satisfying the hypotheses, since none exists. Repair. The main argument of Theorem 4.1 (writes W₀(a) W₁(z) W₂(b)) does not need "same root". It only needs that b's path in T₂ reads ρ (with value 0, while R₂ sees ρ = 1). So we split: if some path of T₂ avoids ρ, the Lemma 4.2 argument gives a contradiction (Sec4.caseA); otherwise every path of T₂ reads ρ, and the main argument goes through with ρ read at any depth instead of at the root (Sec4.caseB). (theorem_4_1, setting_false) 🔧 Theorem 4.1, Case 1 (main part of the proof) The first write of 1 to x may lie inside W₁, and then the continuation of Case 1 (R₂ sees r = 1) is not justified. Impact. Statement unaffected; the step is fixed in the formal proof (Sec4.caseB, Case 1a; theorem_4_1). Details. (a) "The first write of 1 to x between the beginning of W₁ and the end of W₂" may lie inside W₁. Then R₁ returns b while only a and z have been written, which already violates regularity. We treat this as a separate case. (b) A smaller point: in Case 2, "R₁ cannot return b, since R₁ read 0 in x" presumes that R₁ reads x. The correct argument: R₁ must return b by regularity, so it follows b's path, which reads x and needs x = 1; but x = 0 at that time. The cases "first write of 1 to x before / after the first write of 0 to r" are exhaustive because one step writes one register. 🔧 Lemma 3.3 (depth of paths) Lemma 3.3's proof bounds the depth of every path of T_i by the step bound, but the bound only constrains paths that occur in executions, and the code may do anything on other branches. Impact. Statement unaffected (lemma_3_3, SeqReads.complete, complete_of_prefixFree). Repair. Count the k paths realized by the executions σ_v: they form a prefix-free family of binary strings of length ≤ log₂ k, hence are exactly all strings of length log₂ k. 🔧 Theorem 3.2 (last step of the proof) Theorem 3.2 counts only reads of the simulated read, so the read may also write, and the last step ("WP writes 1 to each of the log₂ k registers read") forgets that the reader might have written such a register itself. Impact. Statement unaffected, with a stronger form of Lemma 3.4 (theorem_3_2, lemma_3_4, SeqReads.fresh). Repair. The reader cannot have written it: the argument of Lemma 3.4 shows that every read accesses a register for the first time, so it returns the value left by the write. We prove this stronger form of Lemma 3.4. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. CSLib's asynchronous shared-memory model (Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl). Processes are deterministic and there are no crashes. Executions are finite label lists (inv/tau/ret); a tau step is one access to one base object. Wait-freedom is CSLib's WaitFree; only its consequence obstruction-freedom is used. A simulation I : Sim V v₀ ι P L implements a V-valued register with initial value v₀ from atomic binary registers indexed by an arbitrary type ι, with arbitrary initial contents. One writer w; the readers are any processes allowed to read. Safe / regular / atomic (Sim.Safe, Sim.Regular, Sim.Atomic) must hold in every finite execution in which only w writes. Safe: a read overlapping no write returns the latest preceding write's value (or v₀). Regular: every read returns the value of an overlapping or the latest preceding write (or v₀). Atomic: linearizable (CSLib's IsLinearization). Atomic → Regular → Safe is proved. Costs: Sim.accesses lists the base accesses of an execution. ReadReadsLE I r t / ReadStepsLE I r t: every read operation of r performs at most t base reads / steps. SomeWriteWritesGE I w t: some write operation performs at least t base writes. k = |V| = 2^m as in the paper. The hypotheses are only needed for the readers named in the theorem (one reader in Section 3, two in Theorem 4.1) and only for their first reads, so the results are slightly stronger than the paper's. Optimal Record and Replay under Causal Consistency — PODC 2018 Russell L. Jones, Muhammad S. Khan, Nitin H. Vaidya. Brief Announcement: Optimal Record and Replay under Causal Consistency. PODC 2018. DOI 10.1145/3212734.3212789. Formalized version: arXiv 1805.08804 v2 (full version with all proofs); numbering follows it. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. All optimality results hold under strong causal consistency: the offline records for both RnR models are good and least (Theorems 5.3, 5.4, 6.6, 6.7), and the online record for Model 1 is good and least among online schemes (Theorems 5.5, 5.6). Definition 6.4 and the notion of online record need small fixes, both available from the paper's own proofs, and the proofs of two central results, necessity in Theorem 6.7 and sufficiency through Lemma C.1(b), needed new arguments. Mistakes in the paper 🔧 Theorem 5.6 (notion of "online record") "R is an online record of V" is defined for one fixed execution, and in that reading any record of V is online, so Theorem 5.6 would contradict Theorem 5.3. Impact. The intended reading quantifies over recording schemes whose decisions depend only on the recording process's knowledge, uniformly over all executions. In that reading Theorem 5.6 holds (theorem_5_6). Details. The paper also lets process i "check if (o₁, o₂) ∈ SCO(V)". We restrict i's knowledge to the prefix of its own view and, for each observed write of j, the prefix of V_j up to it (SameKnow). That is exactly the paper's bound "process i is aware of (o₁, o₂) ∈ V_j only if it has observed some o³ⱼ with o₁ <_{V_j} o₂ ≤_{V_j} o³ⱼ", it determines every SCO pair between operations i has observed, and it is all the proof of Theorem 5.5 uses. A scheme online for less knowledge is online in our sense, so this is the strongest form of Theorem 5.6. An oracle answering SCO queries about writes i has not observed yet would exceed this bound and would break Theorem 5.6. This remark is argued on paper only, not in Lean. Example: processes 1, 2, 3 write w₁, w₂, w₃; V₁ = w₁w₂w₃, V₂ = w₂w₁w₃, V₃ = w₁w₃w₂. Then (w₁, w₂) is a B₁ edge outside SCO₁ ∪ PO. When 1 observes w₂, the answers (w₁,w₃) ∈ SCO and (w₂,w₃) ∉ SCO reveal w₁ <_{V₃} w₂. The scheme "record V̂_i \ (SCO_i ∪ PO) except the B_i edges the oracle reveals" contains the offline record of Theorem 5.3, so it is good, yet it omits (w₁, w₂). ✏️ Slips Definition 6.4 (and hence Theorem 6.6) omits w₃ ≠ w₄. Read literally, C¹_i(V, o₁, w₂) contains the self-loop (o₁, o₁) whenever o₁ is a write of i, so B_i(V) swallows such edges and Theorem 6.6's record is not good: two processes each write x once, both views order w₁ before w₀, the record is empty, yet swapping both views is a valid replay with other data races (theorem_6_6_literal_false). The intent is evident: the proof of Lemma C.1(a) uses "w³ ≠ w⁴₁, by Definition 6.4", and the definition's wording "two write operations" suggests distinct ones. With w₃ ≠ w₄ added at every level, Theorems 6.6 and 6.7 hold (theorem_6_6, theorem_6_7). Lemma C.1(a), Case 1 of the proof: the record is written Â₁(V) \ (SWO(V) ∪ PO ∪ B₁(V)). The lemma's statement, and Theorem 6.6, have SWO₁(V). With SWO the four cases miss the edges in SWO(V) \ SWO₁(V), and for that record the lemma would indeed fail (lemma_C_1_SWO_record_false). With SWO₁, as stated, the case split is complete. Typos Theorem 6.7, proof, read case: (o³, w⁴) should be (w³, w⁴). Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Theorem 6.7 (construction of the replay) The proof's U₁ = A₁(V) \ {(o₁,o₂)} ∪ {(o₂,o₁)} ∪ C₁(V,o₁,o₂) is not a partial order whenever o₁ is a write of another process and o₂ a write of process 1, because then (o₁,o₂) ∈ C¹₁ (take w₃ = o₁, w₄ = o₂). Impact. Statement true; repaired with a different set of forced constraints (theorem_6_7). Repair. The forced constraints F are computed in the new order of process i: F⁰ uses A_i \ {(o₁,o₂)} instead of A_i, and so do the propagation steps at process i. Then F ⊆ C, so ¬B_i gives acyclicity. Every F-target z satisfies (o₂, z) ∈ F, so (o₂,o₁) closes no cycle. The strong causal pairs of U lie in SWO(V) \ {(o₁,o₂)} ∪ F. The paper's own case "o₂ a read" fits as F ⊆ SWO. 🛠️ Lemma C.1(b) (bad write pairs, Claims C.2 and C.3) The reduction from a violated B_i edge (o, w′) to the "bad write pair" (wᵢ^min, w′) silently changes the m = i clause of Definition 6.5 (which removes a different pair), and the cycle surgery in Claim C.3 builds cycles that may use the removed pair (wᵢ¹, w²). Impact. Statement true; repaired with a new proof (cov_preserved, lemma_C_1_b). Repair. Pick a violated cover of some A_i(V) whose wᵢ^min u is SWO(V)-maximal, preferring one that starts at u. Claim C.2 then holds as in the paper (stepA). For Claim C.3 (stepB), one shows by induction on the level of C (lemmaX) that no cycle of (A_i \ {(u,w)}) ∪ C enters u through a C edge. Hence every A_m(V) segment of the cycle starts at a C-target other than such a u and is preserved in V'. 🔧 Theorem 5.6 (indistinguishable execution) The proof argues that "both orders are valid for future observation" but never builds a strongly causal execution indistinguishable to process i in which the edge is not a B_i edge, which is what is needed to invoke Theorem 5.4. Impact. Statement true (in the uniform reading above); repaired (exists_indistinguishable). Repair. Keep every known prefix. Order all unknown operations by one global strict total order that puts known writes first, extends SCO(V) and PO, and orders w₂ before w₁. This order exists by extend_partialOrder. 🔧 Lemma A.1(b), Case 4 The proof uses the maximality of wᵢ¹ with respect to SCO(V), but derives only (wᵢ¹, o^{ρ,j}) ∈ SCO(V′). Impact. Statement true; (wᵢ¹, o^{ρ,j}) ∈ SCO(V) holds as well, because o^{ρ,j} is a write of process 1 after wᵢ¹ in V₁ (lemma_A_1_b). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Shared memory with read/write operations on variables (Section 2). There is a finite set of operations, each with a process, a kind and a variable. Program order is a strict total order on each process's operations and is fixed across executions. Processes are an arbitrary type. An execution is a writes-to map. A view of process i is a strict total order on Obs i (own operations and all writes) in which every read returns the last write before it (IsViewOf, Explains). Strong causal consistency (Definitions 3.3, 3.4): SCO(V) and V_i ⊇ (SCO(V) ∪ PO|Obs i)⁺. Records and replays are those of RnR Models 1 and 2 (Section 4). A replay is any execution explained by strongly causal views respecting the record. Its read values are unconstrained, and every family of total orders explains some execution (exists_explains). The transitive reduction Â is the cover relation Cov. For finite strict partial orders it is the unique minimal relation generating the order (transGen_cov_eq, cov_le_of_transGen_eq). Online setting (Section 5.2): a record scheme is online if its decision for (o₁, o₂) at i depends only on i's knowledge when it observes o₂ (SameKnow, IsOnline). No failures, no randomness; the adversary chooses the original and the replay views. Main results in Lean. On the Complexity of Reader-Writer Locks — PODC 2016 Danny Hendler. On the Complexity of Reader-Writer Locks. PODC 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933099. Formalized version: the author's copy "ReadersWritersLock-CR" (Extended Abstract, 11 pp., with the proofs of Sections 3 and 5; no arXiv version); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: 🛠️ Hard fix. The lower bound holds: Theorem 5 (n ≤ Wb · 3^Rb, i.e. writer entry O(f(n)) forces reader exit Ω(log(n/f(n)))) and Corollary 6 are proved, but Lemma 1 is false (an expanding step need not be an RMR in the write-back model) and had to be replaced by a new counting lemma. The matching algorithm family A_f is incorrect as written, because of the order of the two counter reads in line 51 and of op for op' in line 47, and with both lines repaired we prove Mutual Exclusion. The liveness and the RMR upper bounds of the repaired A_f, hence the tightness of the tradeoff, were not checked. Mistakes in the paper 🛠️ Lemma 1 (every expanding step is an RMR) False in the write-back CC model with the paper's Definition 1: q writes 1 to v, then p writes 1 to v (a trivial write, so F(v) stays {q}, but p now holds v exclusively), then p reads v — an expanding step without RMR (lemma1_false). Impact. Lemma 1 is used twice in the proof of Theorem 5, which survives: the counting version "every process performs at least as many RMRs as expanding steps in any fragment" is true (lemma1_count) and suffices. Details. Definition 1 lets the familiarity set of v be determined by the last non-trivial step on v, so the trivial write of p does not make F(v) part of p's knowledge, yet it gives p a valid cached copy. The proof of Lemma 1 argues that, since p's copy stayed valid since its last caching step, "there must be a process q ≠ p that writes to v" in between; here the last non-trivial write precedes p's caching step. The same counterexample works in the write-through protocol if a write leaves the writer with a valid copy (lemma1_false_writeThrough). Repair. lemma1_count: charge each expanding step of p without RMR to the earlier RMR of p that created its valid copy. Potential: the number of variables of which p holds a valid copy without knowing their familiarity set; it starts at 0 in every fragment and is increased only by RMRs of p. 🔧 Lemmas 8–9, Theorem 18 (Mutual Exclusion of A_f, line 51) With HelpWCS reading C[i] before W[i] (line 51, if C[i].read() = W[i].read() read left to right), three readers of one group and the writer reach a configuration where the writer and a reader are both in the CS (mutex_violation_literal_order). Impact. The algorithms as written do not satisfy Mutual Exclusion. Reading W[i] first repairs it: Mutual Exclusion then holds for every n, every grouping and unbounded sequence numbers (mutualExclusion_repaired). Details. Writer at line 21 waits for <0,CS> because reader r₂ entered the CS on PREENTRY (so C = 1, W = 0). Reader r starts waiting (C = 2, W = 1) and in HelpWCS reads C = 2; reader r₃ then starts waiting (C = 3, W = 2); r reads W = 2, equal to the C it read, and CASes WSIG[0] to <0,CS>; the writer enters the CS while r₂ is still there. The proof of Lemma 8 treats the two reads as one atomic snapshot ("there is a time t' in which all readers that incremented C[i] … are waiting"). The paper never fixes the order, and nothing in it points to reading W[i] first (the prose, too, says HelpWCS "reads counters C[i] and W[i]"). Repair. Read W[i] first: while the writer is before its CS, W[i] can only grow and every reader counted in W[i] is counted in C[i], so c = w forces every group-i reader in a passage to be waiting when C[i] is read. The invariant (Inv in Alg/Safety.lean) also gives Lemma 11 (lemma11_repaired). ✏️ Slips Line 47 of Algorithm 1 has op instead of op'. With the literal test op = WAIT (the opcode read on entry) a single reader breaks Deadlock Freedom (the writer waits in line 21 forever while the reader is in the remainder section, deadlock_literal_line47) and Mutual Exclusion (mutex_violation_literal_line47). The intent is evident (the branch uses seq' from line 41 and the PREENTRY branch tests op'), and with op' both executions disappear. Deadlock: the reader entered on PREENTRY, the writer then publishes WAIT and waits for <seq,CS>; the exiting reader reads <seq,WAIT> in line 41 but skips HelpWCS because its entry opcode was PREENTRY. Mutual exclusion: a reader that waited on entry reads <1,NOP> on exit and still calls HelpWCS(1); it signals <1,CS> to writer passage 1 before that passage publishes WAIT, then re-enters on PREENTRY, and the writer enters its CS too. Concurrent Entering (§2.1): "any reader that executes at most b steps … enters the CS" should read "after b steps of its entry section". Lemma 3: "steps executed by other processes when they are aware of p" must mean awareness after the step (read literally, a read that makes q aware of p is kept and returns a different value); the proof uses the intended reading. Line 30 of Algorithm 1 writes the group index as ⌊p/f(n)⌋; it should be ⌊p/K⌋, as in the prose. The proof of Lemma 8 writes t' < t where the order is the other way round. Section 4, description of line 14: "one of the readers that read 0 from W[i]" should say C[i]. Typos Lemma 4 writes ⊂ for ⊆. Proof gaps (statements true) 🔧 Theorem 5 (the tradeoff Ω(log (n / f(n)))) The proof relies on the false Lemma 1 and does not show that the readers' poised steps stay expanding after Lemma 2 reorders them, nor that its drain phase leaves all readers poised simultaneously. Impact. Statement true; repaired (theorem5, exact form n ≤ Wb · 3^Rb). Details. (1) Lemma 1 is replaced by lemma1_count, applied to the fragments C₁ ↪ E₂E₃ (writer) and C₁ ↪ E₂ (reader). (2) Whether a step is expanding depends on the steps scheduled before it; it is preserved here because all poised steps are reads or CAS steps, during which familiarity sets only grow (round_expanding). (3) In the phase σ'', a non-expanding write of one reader can change whether another reader's poised step is expanding; the construction (e2_construct) repeats single non-expanding steps until all remaining readers are simultaneously poised on expanding steps. (4) During E₃ each expanding step of the writer adds at most 3^r processes to its awareness set, although the writer itself changes familiarity sets (aw_solo_bound). 🔧 Lemma 2 (one round at most triples awareness) Case 1 of the proof claims that after the writes of σ₂ the value of v differs from the expected value of all CAS steps of σ₃; a write may restore that value. Impact. Statement true: at most one CAS of σ₃ on v succeeds, which keeps the factor 3. We prove it with a greedy schedule (lemma2). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, deterministic crash-free processes: n readers and m writers (Proc n m = Fin n ⊕ Fin m; Theorem 5 is stated for m = 1, theorem5_general for any m). Registers support read, write and CAS; CAS returns the old value, as in the paper. A reader-writer lock is a CSLib implementation (Impl) of lock/unlock (entry/exit section); remainder/entry/CS/exit are CSLib's regions. Executions are arbitrary interleavings (adversarial scheduler); no randomness. Properties (§2.1): Mutual Exclusion; Bounded Exit and Concurrent Entering with bounds that may depend on the configuration (weaker than the paper's constants); Deadlock Freedom in CSLib's form, which the paper's form implies. So our hypotheses are weaker than the paper's. RMRs in the cache-coherent model: any CacheModel (three axioms), with the paper's write-back and write-through protocols as instances (writeBack, writeThrough). WriterEntryRMR/ReaderExitRMR are worst-case bounds over all executions. Awareness and familiarity sets (Definitions 1–2) are computed forward along an execution fragment, starting from AW(p) = {p}, F(v) = ∅ (kstep, Ext.fresh); expanding steps are Definition 3 verbatim. No Broadcast Abstraction for k-Set Agreement — PODC 2024 Sylvain Gay, Achour Mostéfaoui, Matthieu Perrin. Brief Announcement: No Broadcast Abstraction Characterizes k-Set-Agreement in Message-Passing Systems. PODC 2024. DOI 10.1145/3662158.3662818. Formalized version: the extended version (HAL hal-04571653v1, May 2024), which contains the proofs the brief announcement omits; numbering follows it. The OPODIS 2024 version (hal-05521071, "No Symmetric Broadcast Abstraction …") has the same Lemma 9 (its Lemma 15) with the same proof. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. Lemma 9 is false: a content-neutral, compositional broadcast abstraction on top of which k-set agreement is solvable can still admit N-solo executions for every N, and the paper's proof of the main Theorem 1 rests on it. Theorem 1 is true as far as we checked, and we prove it with a repaired adversary, which does not even need content-neutrality, but only for k-SA algorithms that communicate only through the broadcast abstraction. The paper also lets them use point-to-point channels, and its reduction to the channel-free case is unjustified. Mistakes in the paper ⚠️ Proof of Lemma 9 (reduction of A to a channel-free A') "send and receive can be trivially emulated using B" overlooks that SR-Termination also holds for messages of crashed senders, while BC-Global-CS-Termination does not. Impact. The case of a k-SA algorithm A that also uses the point-to-point channels of CAMP_n[B] is not covered. In our Theorem 1 the k-SA algorithm A uses only the broadcast abstraction, so for such A the theorem is not formalized (see differencies.md, item 8). 🛠️ Lemma 9 (a k-SA-solving abstraction has no N-solo execution), and the proof of Theorem 1 Lemma 9 fails for every k: "k-Bounded-Order broadcast restricted to chained messages" is content-neutral and compositional, an algorithm solves k-set agreement on top of it with k + 1 processes, and yet it admits an N-solo execution for every N (lemma9_false). Impact. The paper's proof of Theorem 1 is Lemma 9 plus Lemma 10, so the main result is not established by the paper. Theorem 1 itself is true; we prove it with a different adversary (theorem1_paper, theorem1), with the restriction of the previous item. Our proof shows more: for 1 < k < n no compositional broadcast abstraction is equivalent to k-SA; content-neutrality is not needed. Details. A message is chained if its sender had already delivered one of its own messages when it invoked broadcast for it. The abstraction (chainedBO) requires that among any k + 1 distinct chained messages, two are delivered in the same order by every process. It contains every uniform total-order execution (totalOrder_mem), so it is implementable from consensus. The algorithm (algQ) works as follows. Broadcast a dummy message. Once it has returned and been delivered locally, broadcast the proposal; this message is chained. Decide the value of the first value message delivered. If k + 1 distinct values were decided, the first-delivered value messages of the deciders would be k + 1 chained messages from distinct senders. Two of them would be delivered in the same order by everybody, but each decider delivered its own decided message before the other one (algQ_solves, algQ_wellFormed; admissible executions exist: soloRun_admissible). The N-solo execution: every process invokes its N broadcasts (each returns at once), then delivers its own N messages, then everybody else's. No message is chained, so the ordering property is void (soloExec_mem, soloExec_nSolo). The proof breaks at "αᵢ is indistinguishable from δ, as both executions involve identical B-broadcast and B-delivery steps for pᵢ". Definition 5 constrains only the order of deliveries. Restricting and renaming an N-solo execution cannot change when pᵢ invokes its broadcasts relative to its returns and deliveries, so the local view of pᵢ in δ need not be its view in αᵢ. A further step of the proof is unjustified (it does not matter for the counterexample): δ is finite, while running A' "on δ" needs an admissible continuation in which A' keeps acting, possibly broadcasting after it decided. The paper runs the dummy loop sync-broadcast(synch) on top of B, then renames the synch messages into A's messages. Lemma 9 shows that this does not reproduce A's local views. We keep the paper's scheduler (Algorithm 1), but let the upper layer of each process run a copy of A itself. On top of B, pᵢ's copy invokes A's own messages at the times A wants. Its view is its own invocations, returns and deliveries. Repair. The execution αS (Theorem1.lean, names p_1 … p_{k+1} as in the paper): Each pᵢ, i < k, runs alone until its copy decides. The k-SA objects answer its own proposals. A run alone is admissible (solo_adm), so B produces an execution of S. Restricted to the copy's messages, it is an execution of A on top of S in which pᵢ is the only participant. k-SA-Termination and k-SA-Validity of A then say that the copy decides, and decides pᵢ's own proposal (early_copy, generic fin_copy). p_k runs alone. A proposal to an object already decided by p_1, …, p_{k-1} (a reset) discards the current copy and starts a new one. There are finitely many resets: p_1 decided finitely many objects, and proposals are one-shot. The copy started after the last reset decides p_k's proposal (kk_copy). p_{k+1} runs after p_k's last reset. It first receives the messages p_k sent it before that reset. On objects decided by all of p_1, …, p_k, it adopts p_k's value. Its copy decides its own proposal (z_copy, via the execution gZ). In αS (αS_adm), p_{k+1} receives the other pending messages once its copy has decided. B produces an execution of S. By compositionality, its restriction to the messages of the final copies is an execution of A on top of S (DS_adm) in which p_1, …, p_{k+1} decide k + 1 distinct values (false_of). The paper's footnote 1 (SR-Termination is not proved for γ) is not a gap. Lemma 10 uses γ only as a prefix of an admissible execution (BC-Validity), and Lemma 7 proves SR-Termination in the one case where it needs it. Our counterparts of the γ executions (solo, gZ) are infinite admissible executions. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Broadcast abstractions (Spec.lean). An execution of a broadcast abstraction is a time-indexed sequence of invocations, returns and deliveries, together with its set of correct processes. A broadcast abstraction is a set S of such executions. Each satisfies BC-Validity, BC-No-Duplication, BC-Local-Termination, BC-Global-CS-Termination, unique messages and well-formed invocations. Messages are objects (id, content): algorithms choose contents, identities are fresh. Compositionality (Definition 2), content-neutrality (Definition 3, sender-wise injective renamings) and N-solo executions (Definition 5) follow the paper. Algorithms on top of S (CAMP_n[S]). A is deterministic: its next action (broadcast a content, decide, or wait) is a function of its proposal and local history. An execution is admissible if its broadcast events form an execution in S, A's steps follow A, correct processes take infinitely many steps of A, and faulty processes finitely many steps. A uses only the broadcast abstraction (like the paper's A'; this makes our Theorem 1 weaker than the paper's, whose A may also use channels), never invokes while an invocation is pending, and has at least k + 1 possible proposals. k-SA: validity (a decided value was proposed by a participant), at most k decided values, termination of correct processes. CAMP_n[k-SA] (Camp.lean). Asynchronous processes; any number of crashes (faulty processes take finitely many steps, correct ones infinitely many). Channels are reliable and non-FIFO (SR-Validity, SR-No-Duplication, SR-Termination). There are any number of k-SA objects (validity, agreement, termination, one answer per proposal). B is deterministic and proposes at most once per object; the upper layer is arbitrary but well-formed. B implements S if the broadcast events of every admissible execution form an execution in S. The scheduler is adversarial; there is no randomness. Main results in Lean. Paper Lean File Definitions 2, 3, 5 Compositional, ContentNeutral, BExec.NSolo Spec.lean Lemma 9 (false) lemma9_false (statement Lemma9) Counterexample.lean the counterexample's abstraction and algorithm chainedBO_compositional, chainedBO_contentNeutral, algQ_solves, soloExec_nSolo, totalOrder_mem, soloRun_admissible Counterexample.lean Theorem 1 theorem1_paper (and the stronger theorem1) Theorem1.lean adversarial executions (role of Lemmas 1–8) catRun_adm, solo_adm, Ctx.gZ_adm, Ctx.αS_adm Concat.lean, RunFacts.lean, Theorem1.lean restriction to the final copies (role of Lemma 9) derive_admissible, fin_copy Derive.lean, Adversary.lean Not formalized. The paper's Lemmas 1–8 and 10 for its own sync-broadcast(synch) adversary (we reprove their content for the copy-of-A adversary). Neither is the remark "CAMP_n[∅] with n − k − 1 initial crashes is CAMP_{k+1}[∅]": we work with n processes directly, the extra ones never taking a step. Theorem 1 for algorithms A that also use point-to-point channels is open here: it should still hold, since those messages can be held back until after the decisions and then simulated by the upper layer of p_{k+1}. Trust. No sorry; lemma9_false, theorem1, theorem1_paper use only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Non-vacuity: algQ has admissible executions on top of chainedBO (soloRun_admissible), and chainedBO contains all uniform total-order executions. We do not exhibit an implementation B of some abstraction in our CAMP_n[k-SA] model; no step of the proof of Theorem 1 relies on the hypotheses being vacuous. Everything is paper-local (namespaces Podc.NoBroadcastKSA, Podc.NoBroadcastKSA.Camp).

Distributed Universality — PODC 2014 Michel Raynal, Julien Stainer, Gadi Taubenfeld. Brief Announcement: Distributed Universality: Contention-Awareness; Wait-Freedom; Object Progress, and Other Properties. PODC 2014. DOI 10.1145/2611462.2611503. Formalized version: the full version, IRISA research report PI-2014 (HAL hal-00947657v2, May 2014), with all proofs in the appendices; numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The construction is not contention-aware, contrary to the title, Theorem 2 and property (4) of the abstract: a process that runs alone, after the other processes have completed their operations and stopped, can still be forced to use the k-SC object, because an adopt tag at line N1 does not mean contention, and no repaired construction is proved. Everything else we checked holds: the constructions of Figures 1 and 2 and of Section 4.3 are linearizable (Lemmas 1–4) and non-blocking (Lemmas 5, 6, Corollary 1, Theorem 1); with helping they are wait-free (Theorem 3); at least ℓ objects progress with (k, ℓ)-SC objects (Theorem 4(a)); and (k, ℓ)-SC can be built from a (k, ℓ)-universal construction (Theorem 4(b)). Several proofs needed genuine repairs (Lemma 3, Lemma 6, Theorem 3 and Theorem 4(b)), and properties (3) and (5) of the abstract were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Theorem 2 and abstract property (4) (contention-awareness of Figure 2) With n = 3 processes and k = 1 object, processes 1 and 2 run round 1 concurrently, complete their first operations and stop, and then process 0, running its first operation completely alone, gets adopt at line N1 of round 1 and invokes kSC[1] (theorem_2_not_contention_aware). Impact. The contention-awareness claim of Figure 2, and of the final construction of Section 4.3, is false in the paper's own terms. Non-blocking, linearizability and wait-freedom are unaffected. A weak version holds (fig2_solo_from_init_no_sc): in an execution where a single process takes all the steps from the initial state, no SC object is ever used. Details. Section 4.1 defines a contention-aware construction as one in which "a process … must be able to complete its operation by accessing only read/write registers in the absence of contention". The introduction makes this precise as "no contention during the execution of an operation (i.e., interval contention)". Section 3.4 defines the execution of an operation: it starts when its issuer first proposes it (makes it public) and ends when it is returned. The proof of Theorem 2 (and the text of Section 4.1: "there is at least one object for which p_i has received the tag adopt. This means that there is contention") assumes that an adopt at AC[2r−1] reveals contention. But rounds are numbered per process, and the adopt-commit objects of a round keep the proposals of processes that went through that round earlier. Here is the run: Processes 1 and 2 invoke AC[1][0] (line N1) concurrently with their own operations. Both adopt. They go through kSC[1]. Process 1 completes its operation in round 1, process 2 in round 2. Both stop. Their next operations were fetched by next() but never proposed, so under the paper's definition no operation of theirs is in progress. Process 0 starts its first operation and takes every remaining step alone. At AC[1][0] it sees the stale conflicting proposals, receives adopt, and invokes kSC[1]. Every adopt-commit response in the run satisfies even the strong reading of the no-conflict property. They are exactly the responses of the standard two-phase register implementation cited by the paper, [13, 28] (ACImpl.adopt_on_stale). With the weak reading, which the standard implementation satisfies, even a fully sequential run fails: process 1 completes an operation alone, then process 0 runs alone, adopts process 1's stale value at AC[1][0] and invokes kSC[1] (theorem_2_not_contention_aware_sequential, ACImpl.adopt_after_solo_commit). The theorem records invocation and return times. Every action from process 0's invocation on is by process 0. Every operation of processes 1 and 2 that was ever proposed was returned before that invocation. And kSC[1] was untouched by process 0 at that moment and invoked by it afterwards. The claim survives only under the reading "a single process has taken steps since the initial state" (fig2_solo_from_init_no_sc). That reading contradicts the paper's explicit "interval contention". If instead an operation counted as pending from its next(), every process that ever started would be in contention forever, since its next operation is fetched before the previous one returns. The property would then mean the same weak thing. Repair. No repaired construction is proved. A plausible fix is to let a process skip to rounds that no one has started yet: publish round numbers and start each operation at the largest published round plus one. ✏️ Slips Section 4.3, line 4M of the (k, ℓ)-construction: the text has line 4M propose oper_i[m] instead of Figure 2's ac_op_i[m], and with this version two processes can commit different operations on the same object in the same round (Typo4M.section_4_3_line_4M_unsafe: n = 2, k = 2, ℓ = 1). The intent is evident: Section 4.3 says the algorithm is Figure 2 with only (k, ℓ)-SC substituted, and all our results use Figure 2's line 4M (Mode.Good). The run: process A commits at line N1 on both objects and skips lines 2M–4M. Process B adopts A's value on object 0 at N1, gets object 1 from SC, and at 4M proposes its own operation to the fresh AC[2r][0], where it commits. A and B each return their own operation as the first operation on object 0. Their histories are not prefix-comparable, so the run is not linearizable. Both readings of the adopt-commit specification allow this run, and with Figure 2's line 4M the same schedule is not executable (Typo4M.sched_not_executable_fig2). Lemma 5 is stated "∀ r ≥ 1" but needs some process to complete the adopt-commit part of round r (true in every infinite execution); we state it so. Typos Line 30 of Figure 1 writes GSTATE; the proof of Lemma 2 refers to it as "line 31". Corollary 1 is numbered Corollary 2 in Appendix B. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 3 (valid histories) The definition of "valid" and its "consequence (i)" (R determines VH(R)) silently assume that an operation is never committed in two non-consecutive rounds, which the paper argues only inside the proof of Lemma 3, by a timing case analysis that overlooks some proposers. Impact. Statement true; repaired by an inductive invariant proof (lemma_3, InvB, chain_next). Details. Case (a) of that analysis concludes that p_j commits op_{r1} in round r1 + 1, but it overlooks processes that adopted op_{r1} while already having it in their history: they propose other operations in round r1 + 1. (They wrote GSTATE first, so p_j still learns op_{r1}; this is our invariant PIa.) We replace the paper's "first invalid write" timing argument by state invariants: the ghost sequence G m and the round in which each element was appended; the knowledge invariant (know: after round ρ + 1, a process knows the value of a uniform round ρ); and two proposal/collect invariants (PIa, CI). The proof also needs the adopt-commit validity in the form "the returned value was proposed before the response". This is standard but not written in Section 2.1. 🛠️ Theorem 3 (wait-freedom with lines L1–L5) The proof leaves its last case open ("ℓ_hist_i[m] is a strict prefix of ℓ_hist_h[m] … It perceived it from an indirect increase") and never explains why the helping index stays aligned among the processes. Impact. Statement true; repaired with a different argument (theorem_3, Wst). Details. Fix a correct process p_j whose operation X on x would stay pending forever. Take the first moment the global sequence of x reaches a length L ≡ j (mod n), by the commit of e in round ρ. Until the sequence grows again, every proposal for x of a round > ρ is e or X, and from round ρ + 2 on it is X (Wst.start, Wst.step). Every process with a history of length L helps p_j, adopters of e learn e, and no other operation can be proposed. So the next operation appended is X (Wst.close), a contradiction. 🔧 Lemma 6 (an object progresses forever) The proof counts commits, not operations (a round's commit may repeat an operation committed earlier), and claims that every committed operation becomes visible in GSTATE, which fails if the committer crashes first. Impact. Statement true; repaired (lemma_6, with Exec.G_unbounded and NoRepeat). Details. Repair: an operation committed in round ρ is never proposed from round ρ + 2 on (NoRepeat). So commits in infinitely many rounds give infinitely many distinct operations. Each of them reaches every process that completes round ρ + 1 (the knowledge invariant InvB.know), whether or not the committer survives. 🔧 Section 3.4 and Lemma 4 with lines L1–L5 (start of an operation) Theorem 3's lemmas show that with helping an operation can be linearized before its owner proposes it, so the paper's start of an operation (its first proposal by its issuer) does not contain the linearization point. Impact. Statement true: in Lemma 4, the start of an operation must be its invocation (next()), not its first proposal; we use invocation times (lemma_4_realtime). 🔧 Theorem 4(b) ((k, ℓ)-SC from a (k, ℓ)-UC) The proof instantiates the construction with k registers and returns "the values written in these objects", but with the universal construction used as a black box a read returns the last write, so two processes can return different values for the same entry. Impact. Statement true; repaired with "sticky" first-value objects (Abstract.scFromUC). The paper's register version fails (Abstract.register_counterexample). Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. Asynchronous shared memory, n processes Fin n, k objects Fin k, crash failures: a crashed process stops taking steps, a correct process takes infinitely many (Exec.Correct). The scheduler and all base-object responses are adversarial. One parametrized algorithm (Model.lean, stepFn) covers Figure 1, Figure 2 (ca), lines L1–L5 (help) and (k, ℓ)-SC objects (ℓ). Theorems hold for every mode with Mode.Good (line 4M as in Figure 2). Adopt-commit and (k, ℓ)-SC objects are black boxes with separate invocation and response steps. The adversary picks any response allowed by the specification (acOK, scOK): validity (the value was proposed before the response), agreement, no-conflicting-values (weak reading; strong reading optional). The specifications are always satisfiable (NonVacuity.enabled), and executions where every process is correct exist (NonVacuity.exists_exec). Each step does at most one access to a base object or one register read. A process's writes to its own LAST_OP registers are merged with the adjacent local step. Loops run in increasing object order, and lines 3M/4M handle decided objects first. Line 7's "longest history containing ℓ_hist" is a deterministic fold, which matters only if histories were not prefix-comparable, and they are. Failure Detectors for the IIS Model — PODC 2012 Michel Raynal, Julien Stainer. Brief Announcement: Increasing the Power of the Iterated Immediate Snapshot Model with Failure Detectors. PODC 2012. DOI 10.1145/2332432.2332498. Formalized version: the full version, IRISA research report PI 1991, February 2012 (hal-00670154v1); numbering follows it. Copy of the paper: paper.pdf. Verdict: ⚠️ Weakened. The generic simulation of Figure 3 does not work for Σ, contrary to Section 4.4 and Theorem 4: with two simulators it produces runs whose simulated failure detector is not in Σ*, and no repaired simulation is proved. The simulations for Ω_k (Theorem 2) and ◇P (Theorem 3) hold, and so does the Ω*-based consensus algorithm (Theorem 5), whose agreement proof needed a stronger invariant. The converse simulation (Theorem 1) and the other classes of Section 4.4 were not checked. Mistakes in the paper ❌ Section 4.4 and Theorem 4 (Figure 3 simulates IIS_n[Σ*] in ARW_n[Σ]) With two simulators, a legal Σ history and a fair failure-free schedule, Figure 3 with PROP_{◇P} makes q₁ weakly correct while the simulated quorums contain q₁ forever, even at the strongly correct q₀; so the simulated detector is not in Σ* (Fig3.sigma_simulation_false). Impact. The claim that one predicate covers P, Σ, S, ◇S, S_x, ◇S_x fails for Σ; Theorem 4 ("for the failure detector classes studied in this paper", here t = n − 1) is false for Σ. The Ω_k and ◇P simulations (Theorems 2, 3, Corollary 1) are not affected. Details. p₀ always executes its whole round before p₁ starts. Then p₀ never sees p₁, so SC = {q₀} and q₁ is weakly correct. The paper allows this: Section 4.4 itself notes that with Σ not every correct simulator yields a strongly correct process. In the rounds p₀ owns, its quorum is {p₀}, so it does not wait. In the other rounds (line 4, no wait) its quorum is {p₀, p₁}. That is a legal Σ history: every quorum contains p₀. p₁'s quorum is always {p₀, p₁} and, as owner, it waits for p₀, which has already written. C*.read() returns FD_VAL[i], the last value read, so the simulated Σ* output of q₀ is {q₀, q₁} in every odd round. Σ* requires quorums to eventually contain only strongly correct processes. The proof in Section 4.4 ("can be easily translated") only covers the values read in owned rounds, where the owner waited for its quorum. Repair. Not formalized. Returning only values used in owned rounds would fix the outputs of strongly correct processes, but the literal Σ* also constrains weakly correct processes, whose quorums (here {q₀, q₁} at q₁) need not be strongly correct. Proof gaps (statements true) 🛠️ Lemma 3 / Claim C1 (agreement of the consensus algorithm of Figure 5) The induction for Claim C1 ("all val_ld_seen = true tuples of a round carry the same estimate") ignores that line 13 may adopt the leader's own estimate (first disjunct of line 12) rather than a voted one, and both may be visible at once. Impact. Statement true; repaired (Exec.agreement, theorem5), for every resolution of the choices at lines 12 and 15 and for arbitrary leader outputs. Details. The leader's estimate can change after it was voted for: line 15 lets it adopt a value when its view is mixed, and it may have followed another leader meanwhile. The proof needs to know that the leader named by the voted tuples writes the voted value. The final step of Lemma 3 ("in both cases they adopt v") has the same gap. Repair. A stronger invariant Inv: (C1) the true, undecided tuples of a round share estimate and leader ℓ, and (L) p_ℓ's own tuple (if undecided) carries the same estimate (Exec.inv). It is preserved by a case analysis on containment and immediacy (Exec.inv_succ): a process seeing p_ℓ in a view where all processes name ℓ as leader forces p_ℓ's own view to be of that kind too. Full list of differences (including modelling choices and minor imprecisions): differencies.md. The formalization Model. IIS (Model.lean): an infinite schedule of one-shot immediate snapshot rounds (views satisfy self-inclusion, containment, immediacy), crash failures (non-increasing participation), any number of crashes, asynchrony (all view patterns allowed). Strongly correct processes SC = ⋃ SC_k literally as in Section 2.6 (with "i writes" added to SC₀, which only matters if nobody is correct). Figure 5 (Consensus.lean): the failure-detector output read at line 4 is arbitrary; Ω* (some strongly correct ℓ is eventually output to everybody) is assumed only for termination. The "∃ v" choices at lines 12 and 15 are nondeterministic (Upd allows every witness). Figure 3 (Fig3.lean, Fig3Live.lean): ARW simulators with atomic collect and arw_write_snapshot steps (a sequential run of these objects is a legal run), any fair schedule (correct = infinitely many steps, crash = no more steps), failure-detector histories H i t arbitrary up to the class properties (Ω_k: eventually the same set containing a correct process; ◇P: eventually exactly the correct ones). The simulated IIS schedule is read off the run (simSchedule). Positive results are thus for runs whose base objects behave atomically. Main results in Lean.
